Hauing firſt ſeiz'd his bookes: Or with a logge
Batter his skull, or paunch him with a ſtake,
Or cut his wezand with thy knife. Remember
Firſt to poſſeſſe his Bookes; for without them
Hee's but a Sot, as I am; nor hath not
One Spirit to command: they all do hate him
As rootedly as I. Burne but his Bookes,
He ha's braue Vtenſils (for ſo he calles them)
Which when he ha's a houſe, hee'l decke withall.
And that moſt deeply to conſider, is
The beautie of his daughter: he himſelfe
Cals her a non-pareill: I neuer ſaw a woman
But onely Sycorax my Dam, and ſhe;
But ſhe as farre ſurpaſſeth Sycorax,
As great'ſt do's leaſt.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Is it ſo braue a Laſſe?

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I Lord, ſhe will become thy bed, I warrant,
And bring thee forth braue brood.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Monſter, I will kill this man: his daughter and I will be King and Queene, ſaue our Graces: and Trinculo, and thy ſelfe ſhall be Vice-royes:
Doſt thou like the plot Trinculo?

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.p: Excellent.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: Giue me thy hand, I am ſorry I beate thee:
But while thou liu'ſt keepe a good tongue in thy hea •

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Within this halfe houre will he be aſleepe,
Wilt thou deſtroy him then?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I on mine honour.

sp.speaker: Ariell.
sp.p: This will I tell my Maſter.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Thou mak'ſt me merry: I am full of pleaſure,
Let vs be iocond. Will you troule the Catch
You taught me but whileare?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: At thy requeſt Monſter, I will do reaſon,
Any reaſon: Come on Trinculo, let vs ſing.

lg.l: Flout 'em, and cout 'em: and skowt 'em, and flout 'em,
Thought is free.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.p: That's not the tune.

div.stage: Ariell plaies the tune on a Tabor and Pipe.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: What is this ſame?

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.p: This is the tune of our Catch, plaid by the picture of No-body.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: If thou beeſt a man, ſhew thy ſelfe in thy likenes:
If thou beeſt a diuell, take't as thou liſt.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.p: O forgiue me my ſinnes.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: He that dies payes all debts: I defie thee;
Mercy vpon vs.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.p: Art thou affeard?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: No Monſter, not I.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Be not affeard, the Iſle is full of noyſes,
Sounds, and ſweet aires, that giue delight and hurt not:
Sometimes a thouſand twangling Inſtruments
Will hum about mine eares; and ſometime voices,
That if I then had wak'd after long ſleepe,
Will make me ſleepe againe, and then in dreaming,
The clouds me thought would open, and ſhew riches
Ready to drop vpon me, that when I wak'd
I cri'de to dreame againe.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: This will proue a braue kingdome to me,
Where I ſhall haue my Muſicke for nothing.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.p: When Proſpero is deſtroy'd.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: That ſhall be by and by:
I remember the ſtorie.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: The ſound is going away.
Lets follow it, and after do our worke.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: Leade Monſter,
Wee'l follow: I would I could ſee this Taborer,
He layes it on.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: Wilt come?
Ile follow Stephano.

div.head: Scena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Alonſo, Sebaſtian, Anthonio, Gonzallo, Adrian, Franciſco, &c.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: By'r lakin, I can goe no further, Sir,
My old bones akes: here's a maze trod indeede
Through fourth rights, & Meanders: by your patience,
I needes muſt reſt me.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: Old Lord, I cannot blame thee,
Who, am my ſelfe attach'd with wearineſſe
To th' dulling of my ſpirits: Sit downe, and reſt:
Euen here I will put off my hope, and keepe it
No longer for my Flatterer: he is droun'd
Whom thus we ſtray to finde, and the Sea mocks
Our fruſtrate ſearch on land: well, let him goe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I am right glad, that he's ſo out of hope:
Doe not for one repulſe forgoe the purpoſe
That you reſolu'd t' effect.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: The next aduantage will we take throughly.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let it be to night,
For now they are oppreſs'd with trauaile, they
Will not, nor cannot vſe ſuch vigilance
As when they are freſh.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: I ſay to night: no more.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.p: What harmony is this? my good friends, harke.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.p: Maruellous ſweet Muſicke.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.p: Giue vs kind keepers, heauēs: what were theſe?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: A liuing Drolerie: now I will beleeue
That there are Vnicornes: that in Arabia
There is one Tree, the Phoenix throne, one Phoenix
At this houre reigning there.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Ile beleeue both:
And what do's elſe want credit, come to me
And Ile beſworne 'tis true: Trauellers nere did lye,
Though fooles at home condemne 'em.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: If in Naples
I ſhould report this now, would they beleeue me?
If I ſhould ſay I ſaw ſuch Iſlands;
(For certes, theſe are people of the Iſland)
Who though they are of monſtrous ſhape, yet note
Their manners are more gentle, kinde, then of
Our humaine generation you ſhall finde
Many, nay almoſt any.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Honeſt Lord,
Thou haſt ſaid well: for ſome of you there preſent;
Are worſe then diuels.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: I cannot too much muſe
Such ſhapes, ſuch geſture, and ſuch ſound expreſſing
(Although they want the vſe of tongue) a kinde
Of excellent dumbe diſcourſe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Praiſe in departing.

sp.speaker: Fr.
sp.l: They vaniſh'd ſtrangely.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: No matter, ſince
They haue left their Viands behinde; for wee haue ſtomacks.
Wilt pleaſe you taſte of what is here▪

sp.speaker: Ale.
sp.p: Not I.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Faith Sir, you neede not feare when wee were Boyes
Who would beleeue that there were Mountayneeres,
Dew-lapt, like Buls whoſe throats had hanging at 'em
Wallets of fleſh? or that there were ſuch men
Whoſe heads ſtood in their breſts? which now we finde
Each putter out of fiue for one, will bring vs
Good warrant of.

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: I will ſtand to, and feede,
Although my laſt, no matter, ſince I feele
The beſt is paſt: brother: my Lord, the Duke,
Stand too, and doe as we.

div.stage: Thunder and Lightning. Enter Ariell (like a Harpey) claps his wings vpon the Table, and with a quient deuice the Banquet vaniſhes.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: You are three men of ſinne, whom deſtiny
That hath to inſtrument this lower world,
And what is in't: the neuer ſurfeited Sea,
Hath caus'd to belch vp you; and on this Iſland,
Where man doth not inhabit, you 'mongſt men,
Being moſt vnfit to liue: I haue made you mad;
And euen with ſuch like valour, men hang, and drowne
Their proper ſelues: you fooles, I and my fellowes
Are miniſters of Fate, the Elements
Of whom your ſwords are temper'd, may as well
Wound the loud windes, or with bemockt-at-Stabs
Kill the ſtill cloſing waters, as diminiſh
One dowle that's in my plumbe: My fellow miniſters
Are like-invulnerable: if you could hurt,
Your ſwords are now too maſſie for your ſtrengths,
And will not be vplifted: But remember
(For that's my buſineſſe to you) that you three
From Millaine did ſupplant good Proſpero,
Expos'd vnto the Sea (which hath requit it)
Him, and his innocent childe: for which foule deed,
The Powres, delaying (not forgetting) haue
Incens'd the Seas, and Shores; yea, all the Creatures
Againſt your peace: Thee of thy Sonne, Alonſo
They haue bereft; and doe pronounce by me
Lingring perdition (worſe then any death
Can be at once) ſhall ſtep, by ſtep attend
You, and your wayes, whoſe wraths to guard you from,
Which here, in this moſt deſolate Iſle, elſe fals
Vpon your heads, is nothing but hearts-ſorrow,
And a cleere life enſuing.

div.stage: He vaniſhes in Thunder: then (to ſoft Muſicke.) Enter the ſhapes againe, and daunce (with mockes and mowes) and carrying out the Table.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Brauely the figure of this Harpie, haſt thou
Perform'd (my Ariell) a grace it had deuouring:
Of my Inſtruction, haſt thou nothing bated
In what thou had'ſt to ſay: ſo with good life,
And obſeruation ſtrange, my meaner miniſters
Their ſeuerall kindes haue done: my high charmes work,
And theſe (mine enemies) are all knit vp
In their diſtractions: they now are in my powre;
And in theſe fits, I leaue them, while I viſit
Yong Ferdinand (whom they ſuppoſe is droun'd)
And his, and mine lou'd darling.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: I' th name of ſomething holy, Sir, why ſtand you
In this ſtrange ſtare?

sp.speaker: Al.
sp.l: O, it is monſtrous: monſtrous:
Me thought the billowes ſpoke, and told me of it,
The windes did ſing it to me: and the Thunder
(That deepe and dreadfull Organ-Pipe) pronounc'd
The name of Proſper: it did baſe my Treſpaſſe,
Therefore my Sonne i' th' Ooze is bedded; and
I'le ſeeke him deeper then ere plummet ſounded,
And with him there lye mudded.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: But one feend at a time,
Ile fight their Legions ore.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Ile be thy Second.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: All three of them are deſperate: their great guilt
(Like poyſon giuen to worke a great time after)
Now gins to bite the ſpirits: I doe beſeech you
(That are of ſuppler ioynts) follow them ſwiftly,
And hinder them from what this extaſie
May now prouoke them to.

sp.speaker: Ad.
sp.p: Follow, I pray you.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: If I haue too auſterely puniſh'd you,
Your compenſation makes amends, for I
Haue giuen you here, a third of mine owne life,
Or that for which I liue: who, once againe
I tender to thy hand: All thy vexations
Were but my trials of thy loue, and thou
Haſt ſtrangely ſtood the teſt: here, afore heauen
I ratifie this my rich guift: O Ferdinand,
Doe not ſmile at me, that I boaſt her of,
For thou ſhalt finde ſhe will out-ſtrip all praiſe
And make it halt, behinde her.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: I doe beleeue it
Againſt an Oracle.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Then, as my gueſt, and thine owne acquiſition
Worthily purchas'd, take my daughter: But
If thou do'ſt breake her Virgin-knot, before
All ſanctimonious ceremonies may
With full and holy right, be miniſtred,
No ſweet aſperſion ſhall the heauens let fall
To make this contract grow; but barraine hate,
Sower-ey'd diſdaine, and diſcord ſhall beſtrew
The vnion of your bed, with weedes ſo loathly
That you ſhall hate it both: Therefore take heede,
As Hymens Lamps ſhall light you.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: As I hope
For quiet dayes, faire Iſſue, and long life,
With ſuch loue, as 'tis now the murkieſt den,
The moſt opportune place, the ſtrongſt ſuggeſtion,
Our worſer Genius can, ſhall neuer melt
Mine honor into luſt, to take away
The edge of that dayes celebration,
When I ſhall thinke, or Phoebus Steeds are founderd,
Or Night kept chain'd below.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Fairely ſpoke;
Sit then, and talke with her, ſhe is thine owne;
What Ariell; my induſtrious ſeruāt Ariell.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: What would my potent maſter? here I am.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Thou, and thy meaner fellowes, your laſt ſeruice
Did worthily performe: and I muſt vſe you
In ſuch another tricke: goe bring the rabble
(Ore whom I giue thee powre) here, to this place:
Incite them to quicke motion, for I muſt
Beſtow vpon the eyes of this yong couple
Some vanity of mine Art: it is my promiſe,
And they expect it from me.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: Preſently?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: I: with a twincke.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Before you can ſay come, and goe,
And breathe twice; and cry, ſo, ſo:
Each one tripping on his Toe,
Will be here with mop, and mowe.
Doe you loue me Maſter? no?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Dearely, my delicate Ariell: doe not approach
Till thou do'ſt heare me call.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: Well: I conceiue.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Looke thou be true: doe not giue dalliance
Too much the raigne: the ſtrongeſt oathes, are ſtraw
To th' fire ith' blood: be more abſtenious,
Or elſe good night your vow.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: I warrant you, Sir,
The white cold virgin Snow, vpon my heart
Abates the ardour of my Liuer.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Well.
Now come my Ariell, bring a Corolary,
Rather then want a Spirit; appear, & pertly.
No tongue: all eyes: be ſilent.

sp.speaker: Ir.
sp.l: Ceres, moſt bounteous Lady, thy rich Leas
Of Wheate, Rye, Barley, Fetches, Oates and Peaſe;
Thy Turphie-Mountaines, where liue nibling Sheepe,
And flat Medes thetchd with Stouer, them to keepe:
Thy bankes with pioned, and twilled brims
Which ſpungie Aprill, at thy heſt betrims;
To make cold Nymphes chaſt crownes; & thy broome-groues;
Whoſe ſhadow the diſmiſſed Batchelor loues,
Being laſſe-lorne: thy pole-clipt vineyard,
And thy Sea-marge ſtirrile, and rockey-hard,
Where thou thy ſelfe do'ſt ayre, the Queene o' th Skie,
Whoſe watry Arch, and meſſenger, am I.
Bids thee leaue theſe, & with her ſoueraigne grace,
Here on this graſſe-plot, in this very place
To come, and ſport: here Peacocks flye amaine:
Approach, rich Ceres, her to entertaine.

sp.speaker: Cer.
sp.l: Haile, many-coloured Meſſenger, that nere
Do'ſt diſobey the wife of Iupiter:
Who, with thy ſaffron wings, vpon my flowres
Diffuſeſt hony drops, refreſhing ſhowres,
And with each end of thy blew bowe do'ſt crowne
My boskie acres, and my vnſhrubd downe,
Rich ſcarph to my proud earth: why hath thy Queene
Summond me hither, to this ſhort gras'd Greene?

sp.speaker: Ir.
sp.l: A contract of true Loue, to celebrate,
And ſome donation freely to eſtate
On the bles'd Louers.

sp.speaker: Cer.
sp.l: Tell me heauenly Bowe,
If Venus or her Sonne, as thou do'ſt know,
Doe now attend the Queene? ſince they did plot
The meanes, that duskie Dis, my daughter got,
Her, and her blind-Boyes ſcandald company,
I haue forſworne.

sp.speaker: Ir.
sp.l: Of her ſocietie
Be not afraid: I met her deitie
Cutting the clouds towards Paphos: and her Son
Doue-drawn with her: here thought they to haue done
Some wanton charme, vpon this Man and Maide,
Whoſe vowes are, that no bed-right ſhall be paid
Till Hymens Torch be lighted: but in vaine,
Marſes hot Minion is returnd againe,
Her waſpiſh headed ſonne, has broke his arrowes,
Swears he will ſhoote no more, but play with Sparrows,
And be a Boy right out.

sp.speaker: Cer.
sp.l: Higheſt Queene of State,
Great Iuno comes, I know her by her gate.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.l: How do's my bounteous ſiſter? goe with me
To bleſſe this twaine, that they may proſperous be,
And honourd in their Iſſue.

lg.l: Honor, riches, marriage, bleſſing,
Long continuance, and encreaſing,
Hourely ioyes, be ſtill vpon you,
Iuno ſings her bleſſings on you.
Earths increaſe, foyzon plentie,
Barnes, and Garners, neuer empty.
Vines, with cluſtring bunches growing,
Plants, wtth goodly burthen bowing:
Spring come to you at the fartheſt,
In the very end of Harueſt.
Scarcity and want ſhall ſhun you,
Ceres bleſſing ſo is on you.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: This is a moſt maieſticke viſion, and
Harmonious charmingly: may I be bold
To thinke theſe ſpirits?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Spirits, which by mine Art
I haue from their confines call'd to enact
My preſent fancies.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Let me liue here euer,
So rare a wondred Father, and a wiſe
Makes this place Paradiſe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Sweet now, ſilence:
Iuno and Ceres whiſper ſeriouſly,
There's ſomething elſe to doe: huſh, and be mute
Or elſe our ſpell is mar'd.

div.stage: Iuno and Ceres whiſper, and ſend Iris on employment.

sp.speaker: Iris.
sp.l: You Nimphs cald Nayades of ye windring brooks,
With your ſedg'd crownes, and euer-harmeleſſe lookes,
Leaue your criſpe channels, and on this greene-Land
Anſwere your ſummons▪ Iuno do's command.
Come temperate Nimphes, and helpe to celebrate
A Contract of true Loue: be not too late.
You Sun-burn'd Sicklemen of Auguſt weary,
Come hether from the furrow, and be merry,
Make holly day: your Rye-ſtraw hats put on,
And theſe freſh Nimphes encounter euery one
In Country footing.

div.stage: Enter certaine Reapers (properly habited:) they ioyne with the Nimphes, in a gracefull dance, towards the end whereof, Proſpero ſtarts ſodainly and ſpeakes, after which to a ſtrange hollow and confuſed noyſe, they heauily vaniſh.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I had forgot that foule conſpiracy
Of the beaſt Calliban, and his confederates
Againſt my life: the minute of their plot
Is almoſt come: Well done, auoid: no more.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: This is ſtrange: your fathers in ſome paſſion
That workes him ſtrongly.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Neuer till this day
Saw I him touch'd with anger, ſo diſtemper'd.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: You doe looke (my ſon) in a mou'd ſort,
As if you were diſmaid: be cheerefull Sir,
Our Reuels now are ended: Theſe our actors,
(As I foretold you) were all Spirits, and
Are melted into Ayre, into thin Ayre,
And like the baſeleſſe fabricke of this viſion
The Clowd-capt Towres, the gorgeous Pallaces,
The ſolemne Temples, the great Globe it ſelfe,
Yea, all which it inherit, ſhall diſſolue,
And like this inſubſtantiall Pageant faded
Leaue not a racke behinde: we are ſuch ſtuffe
As dreames are made on; and our little life
Is rounded with a ſleepe: Sir, I am vext,
Beare with my weakeneſſe, my old braine is troubled:
Be not diſturb'd with my infirmitie,
If you be pleas'd, retire into my Cell,
And there repoſe, a turne or two, Ile walke
To ſtill my beating minde.

sp.speaker: Fer. Mir.
sp.l: We wiſh your peace.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Come with a thought; I thank thee Ariell: come.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: Thy thoughts I cleaue to, what's thy pleaſure?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Spirit: We muſt prepare to meet with Caliban.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I my Commander, when I preſented Ceres
I thought to haue told thee of it, but I fear'd
Leaſt I might anger thee.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Say again, where didſt thou leaue theſe varlots?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I told you Sir, they were red-hot with drinking,
So full of valour, that they ſmote the ayre
For breathing in their faces: beate the ground
For kiſſing of their feete; yet alwaies bending
Towards their proiect: then I beate my Tabor,
At which like vnback't colts they prickt their eares,
Aduanc'd their eye-lids, lifted vp their noſes
As they ſmelt muſicke, ſo I charm'd their eares
That Calfe-like, they my lowing follow'd, through
Tooth'd briars, ſharpe firzes, pricking goſſe, & thorns,
Which entred their fraile ſhins: at laſt I left them
I' th' filthy mantled poole beyond your Cell,
There dancing vp to th' chins, that the fowle Lake
Ore-ſtunck their feet.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: This was well done (my bird)
Thy ſhape inuiſible retaine thou ſtill:
The trumpery in my houſe, goe bring it hither
For ſtale to catch theſe theeues.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: I go, I goe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: A Deuill, a borne-Deuill, on whoſe nature
Nurture can neuer ſticke: on whom my paines
Humanely taken, all, all loſt, quite loſt,
And, as with age, his body ouglier growes,
So his minde cankers: I will plague them all,
Euen to roaring: Come, hang on them this line.

div.stage: Enter Ariell, loaden with gliſtering apparell, &c. Enter Caliban, Stephano, and Trinculo, all wet.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.p: Pray you tread ſoftly, that the blinde Mole may not heare a foot fall: we now are neere his Cell.

sp.speaker: St.
sp.l: Monſter, your Fairy, wc you ſay is a harmles Fairy,
Has done little better then plaid the lacke with vs.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: Monſter, I do ſmell all horſe-piſſe, at which
My noſe is in great indignation.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: So is mine. Do you heare Monſter: If I ſhould
Take a diſpleaſure againſt you: Looke you.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.p: Thou wert but a loſt Monſter.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Good my Lord, giue me thy fauour ſtil,
Be patient, for the prize Ile bring thee too
Shall hud winke this miſchance: therefore ſpeake ſoftly,
All's huſht as midnight yet.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.p: I, but to looſe our bottles in the Poole.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: There is not onely diſgrace and diſhonor in that Monſter, but an infinite loſſe.

sp.speaker: Tr.
sp.l: That's more to me then my wetting:
Yet this is your harmleſſe Fairy, Monſter.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: I will fetch off my bottle,
Though I be o're eares for my labour.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: Pre-thee (my King) be quiet. Seeſt thou heere
This is the mouth o' th Cell: no noiſe, and enter:
Do that good miſcheefe, which may make this Iſland
Thine owne for euer, and I thy Caliban
For aye thy foot-licker.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: Giue me thy hand,
I do begin to haue bloody thoughts.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.l: O King Stephano, O Peere: O worthy Stephano,
Looke what a wardrobe heere is for thee.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.p: Let it alone thou foole, it is but traſh.

sp.speaker: Tri.
sp.p: Oh, ho, Monſter: wee know what belongs to a frippery, O King Stephano.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Put off that gowne (Trinculo) by this hand Ile haue that gowne.

sp.speaker: Tri.
sp.p: Thy grace ſhall haue it.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: The dropſie drowne this foole, what doe you meane
To doate thus on ſuch luggage? let's alone
And doe the murther firſt: if he awake,
From toe to crowne hee'l fill our skins with pinches,
Make vs ſtrange ſtuffe.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Be you quiet (Monſter) Miſtris line, is not this my Ierkin? now is the Ierkin vnder the line: now Ierkin you are like to loſe your haire, & proue a bald Ierkin.

sp.speaker: Trin.
sp.p: Doe, doe; we ſteale by lyne and leuell, and't like your grace.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I thank thee for that ieſt; heer's a garment for't: Wit ſhall not goe vn-rewarded while I am King of this Country: Steale by line and leuell, is an excellent paſſe of pate: there's another garment for't.

sp.speaker: Tri.
sp.p: Monſter, come put ſome Lime vpon your fingers, and away with the reſt.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I will haue none on't: we ſhall looſe our time,
And all be turn'd to Barnacles, or to Apes
With foreheads villanous low.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Monſter, lay to your fingers: helpe to beare this away, where my hogſhead of wine is, or Ile turne you out of my kingdome: goe to, carry this.

sp.speaker: Tri.
sp.p: And this.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I, and this.

div.stage: A noyſe of Hunters heard. Enter diuers Spirits in ſhape of Dogs and Hounds, hunting them about: Proſpero and Ariel ſetting them on.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Hey Mountaine, hey.

sp.speaker: Ari.
sp.p: Siluer: there it goes, Siluer.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Fury, Fury: there Tyrant, there: harke, harke.
Goe, charge my Goblins that they grinde their ioynts
With dry Convultions, ſhorten vp their ſinewes
With aged Cramps, & more pinch-ſpotted make them,
Then Pard, or Cat o' Mountaine.

sp.speaker: Ari.
sp.p: Harke, they rore.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Let them be hunted ſoundly: At this houre
Lies at my mercy all mine enemies:
Shortly ſhall all my labours end, and thou
Shalt haue the ayre at freedome: for a little
Follow, and doe me ſeruice.

div.head: Scoena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Proſpero (in his Magicke robes) and Ariel.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Now do's my Proiect gather to a head:
My charmes cracke not: my Spirits obey, and Time
Goes vpright with his carriage: how's the day?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: On the ſixt hower, at which time, my Lord
You ſaid our worke ſhould ceaſe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I did ſay ſo,
When firſt I rais'd the Tempeſt: ſay my Spirit,
How fares the King, and's followers?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Confin'd together
In the ſame faſhion, as you gaue in charge,
Iuſt as you left them; all priſoners Sir
In the Line-groue which weather-fends your Cell,
They cannot boudge till your releaſe: The King,
His Brother, and yours, abide all three diſtracted,
And the remainder mourning ouer them,
Brim full of ſorrow, and diſmay: but chiefly
Him that you term'd Sir, the good old Lord Gonzallo,
His teares runs downe his beard like winters drops
From eaues of reeds: your charm ſo ſtrongly works 'em
That if you now beheld them, your affections
Would become tender.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Doſt thou thinke ſo, Spirit?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: Mine would, Sir, were I humane.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: And mine ſhall.
Haſt thou (which art but aire) a touch, a feeling
Of their afflictions, and ſhall not my ſelfe,
One of their kinde, that relliſh all as ſharpely,
Paſſion as they, be kindlier mou'd then thou art?
Thogh with their high wrongs I am ſtrook to th' quick,
Yet, with my nobler reaſon, gainſt my furie
Doe I take part: the rarer Action is
In vertue, then in vengeance: they, being penitent,
The ſole drift of my purpoſe doth extend
Not a frowne further: Goe, releaſe them Ariell,
My Charmes Ile breake, their ſences Ile reſtore,
And they ſhall be themſelues.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: Ile fetch them, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Ye Elues of hils, brooks, ſtāding lakes & groues,
And ye, that on the ſands with printleſſe foote
Doe chaſe the ebbing-Neptune, and doe flie him
When he comes backe: you demy-Puppets, that
By Moone-ſhine doe the greene ſowre Ringlets make,
Whereof the Ewe not bites: and you, whoſe paſtime
Is to make midnight-Muſhrumps, that reioyce
To heare the ſolemne Curfewe, by whoſe ayde
(Weake Maſters though ye be) I haue bedymn'd
The Noone-tide Sun, call'd forth the mutenous windes,
And twixt the greene Sea, and the azur'd vault
Set roaring warre: To the dread ratling Thunder
Haue I giuen fire, and rifted Ioues ſtowt Oke
With his owne Bolt: The ſtrong baſs'd promontorie
Haue I made ſhake, and by the ſpurs pluckt vp
The Pyne, and Cedar. Graues at my command
Haue wak'd their ſleepers, op'd, and let 'em forth
By my ſo potent Art. But this rough Magicke
I heere abiure: and when I haue requir'd
Some heauenly Muſicke (which euen now I do)
To worke mine end vpon their Sences, that
This Ayrie-charme is for, I'le breake my ſtaffe,
Bury it certaine fadomes in the earth,
And deeper then did euer Plummet ſound
Ile drowne my booke.
sp.stage: Heere enters Ariel before: Then Alonſo with a franticke geſture, attended by Gonzalo. Sebaſtian and Anthonio in like manner attended by Adrian and Franciſco: They all enter the circle which Proſpero had made, and there ſtand charm'd: which Proſpero obſeruing, ſpeakes.
sp.l: A ſolemne Ayre, and the beſt comforter,
To an vnſetled fancie, Cure thy braines
(Now vſeleſſe) boile within thy skull: there ſtand
For you are Spell-ſtopt.
Holy Gonzallo, Honourable man,
Mine eyes ev'n ſociable to the ſhew of thine
Fall fellowly drops: The charme diſſolues apace,
And as the morning ſteales vpon the night
(Melting the darkeneſſe) ſo their riſing ſences
Begin to chace the ignorant fumes that mantle
Their cleerer reaſon. O good Gonzallo
My true preſeruer, and a loyall Sir,
To him thou follow'ſt; I will pay thy graces
Home both in word, and deede: Moſt cruelly
Did thou Alonſo, vſe me, and my daughter:
Thy brother was a furtherer in the Act,
Thou art pinch'd for't now Sebaſtian. Fleſh, and bloud,
You, brother mine, that entertaine ambition,
Expelld remorſe, and nature, whom, with Sebaſtian
(Whoſe inward pinches therefore are moſt ſtrong)
Would heere haue kill'd your King: I do forgiue thee,
Vnnaturall though thou art: Their vnderſtanding
Begins to ſwell, and the approching tide
Will ſhortly fill the reaſonable ſhore
That now ly foule, and muddy: not one of them
That yet lookes on me, or would know me: Ariell,
Fetch me the Hat, and Rapier in my Cell,
I will diſcaſe me, and my ſelfe preſent
As I was ſometime Millaine: quickly Spirit,
Thou ſhalt ere long be free.

div.stage: Ariell ſings, and helps to attire him.

lg.l: Where the Bee ſucks, there ſuck I,
In a Cowſlips bell, I lie,
There I cowch when Owles doe crie,
On the Batts backe I doe flie after Sommer merrily.
Merrily, merrily, ſhall I liue now,
Vnder the bloſſom that hangs on the Bow.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Why that's my dainty Ariell: I ſhall miſſe
Thee, but yet thou ſhalt haue freedome: ſo, ſo, ſo.
To the Kings ſhip, inuiſible as thou art,
There ſhalt thou finde the Marriners aſleepe
Vnder the Hatches: the Maſter and the Boat-ſwaine
Being awake, enforce them to this place;
And preſently, I pre'thee.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: I drinke the aire before me, and returne
Or ere your pulſe twice beate.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: All torment, trouble, wonder, and amazement
Inhabits heere: ſome heauenly power guide vs
Out of this fearefull Country.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Behold Sir King
The wronged Duke of Millaine, Proſpero:
For more aſſurance that a liuing Prince
Do's now ſpeake to thee, I embrace thy body,
And to thee, and thy Company, I bid
A hearty welcome.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: Where thou bee'ſt he or no,
Or ſome inchanted triflle to abuſe me,
(As late I haue beene) I not know: thy Pulſe
Beats as of fleſh, and blood: and ſince I ſaw thee,
Th' affliction of my minde amends, with which
I feare a madneſſe held me▪ this muſt craue
(And if this be at all) a moſt ſtrange ſtory.
Thy Dukedome I reſigne, and doe entreat
Thou pardon me my wrongs: But how ſhold Proſpero
Be liuing and be heere?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Firſt, noble Frend,
Let me embrace thine age, whoſe honor cannot
Be meaſur'd, or confin'd.

sp.speaker: Gonz.
sp.l: Whether this be,
Or be not, I'le not ſweare.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: You doe yet taſte
Some ſubtleties o' th' Iſle, that will not let you
Beleeue things certaine: Wellcome, my friends all,
But you, my brace of Lords, were I ſo minded
I heere could plucke his Highneſſe frowne vpon you
And iuſtifie you Traitors: at this time
I will tell no tales.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: The Diuell ſpeakes in him:

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: No:
For you (moſt wicked Sir) whom to call brother
Would euen infect my mouth, I do forgiue
Thy rankeſt fault; all of them: and require
My Dukedome of thee, which, perforce I know
Thou muſt reſtore.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: If thou beeſt Proſpero
Giue vs particulars of thy preferuation,
How thou haſt met vs heere, whom three howres ſince
Were wrackt vpon this ſhore? where I haue loſt
(How ſharp the point of this remembrance is)
My deere ſonne Ferdinand.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: I am woe for't, Sir.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: Irreparable is the loſſe, and patience
Saies, it is paſt her cure.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I rather thinke
You haue not ſought her helpe, of whoſe ſoft grace
For the like loſſe, I haue her ſoueraigne aid,
And reſt my ſelfe content.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.p: You the like loſſe?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: As great to me, as late, and ſupportable
To make the deere loſſe, haue I meanes much weaker
Then you may call to comfort you; for I
Haue loſt my daughter.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: A daughter?
Oh heauens, that they were liuing both in Nalpes
The King and Queene there, that they were, I wiſh
My ſelfe were mudded in that oo-zie bed
Where my ſonne lies: when did you loſe your daughter?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: In this laſt Tempeſt. I perceiue theſe Lords
At this encounter doe ſo much admire,
That they deuoure their reaſon, and ſcarce thinke
Their eies doe offices of Truth: Their words
Are naturall breath: but howſoeu'r you haue
Beene iuſtled from your ſences, know for certain
That I am Proſpero, and that very Duke
Which was thruſt forth of Millaine, who moſt ſtrangely
Vpon this ſhore (where you were wrackt) was landed
To be the Lord on't: No more yet of this,
For 'tis a Chronicle of day by day,
Not a relation for a break-faſt, nor
Befitting this firſt meeting: Welcome, Sir;
This Cell's my Court: heere haue I few attendants,
And Subiects none abroad: pray you looke in:
My Dukedome ſince you haue giuen me againe,
I will requite you with as good a thing,
At leaſt bring forth a wonder, to content ye
As much, as me my Dukedome.

div.stage: Here Proſpero diſcouers Ferdinand and Miranda, playing at Cheſſei.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.p: Sweet Lord, you play me falſe.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: No my deareſt loue,
I would not for the world.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: Yes, for a ſcore of Kingdomes, you ſhould wrangle,
And I would call it faire play.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: If this proue
A viſion of the Iſland, one deere Sonne
Shall I twice looſe.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: A moſt high miracle.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Though the Seas threaten they are mercifull,
I haue curs'd them without cauſe.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: Now all the bleſſings
Of a glad father, compaſſe thee about:
Ariſe, and ſay how thou cam'ſt heere.

sp.speaker: Mir.
sp.l: O wonder!
How many goodly creatures are there heere?
How beauteous mankinde is? O braue new world
That has ſuch people in't.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: 'Tis new to thee.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: What is this Maid, with whom thou was't at play?
Your eld'ſt acquaintance cannot be three houres:
Is ſhe the goddeſſe that hath ſeuer'd vs,
And brought vs thus together?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: Sir, ſhe is mortall;
But by immortall prouidence, ſhe's mine;
I choſe her when I could not aske my Father
For his aduiſe: nor thought I had one: She
Is daughter to this famous Duke of Millaine,
Of whom, ſo often I haue heard renowne,
But neuer ſaw before: of whom I haue
Receiu'd a ſecond life; and ſecond Father
This Lady makes him to me.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: I am hers.
But O, how odly will it ſound, that I
Muſt aske my childe forgiueneſſe?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: There Sir ſtop,
Let vs not burthen our remembrances, with
A heauineſſe that's gon.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: I haue inly wept,
Or ſhould haue ſpoke ere this: looke downe you gods
And on this couple drop a bleſſed crowne;
For it is you, that haue chalk'd forth the way
Which brought vs hither.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.p: I ſay Amen, Gonzallo.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Was Millaine thruſt from Millaine, that his Iſſue
Should become Kings of Naples? O reioyce
Beyond a common ioy, and ſet it downe
With gold on laſting Pillers: In one voyage
Did Claribell her husband finde at Tunis,
And Ferdinand her brother, found a wife,
Where he himſelfe was loſt: Proſpero, his Dukedome
In a poore Iſle: and all of vs, our ſelues,
When no man was his owne.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: Giue me your hands:
Let griefe and ſorrow ſtill embrace his heart,
That doth not wiſh you ioy.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Be it ſo, Amen.
sp.stage: Enter Ariell, with the Maſter and Boatſwaine amazedly following.
sp.l: O looke Sir, looke Sir, here is more of vs:
I propheſi'd, if a Gallowes were on Land
This fellow could not drowne: Now blaſphemy,
That ſwear'ſt Grace ore-boord, not an oath on ſhore,
Haſt thou no mouth by land?
What is the newes?

sp.speaker: Bot.
sp.l: The beſt newes is, that we haue ſafely found
Our King, and company: The next: our Ship,
Which but three glaſſes ſince, we gaue out ſplit,
Is tyte, and yare, and brauely rig'd, as when
We firſt put out to Sea.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Sir, all this ſeruice
Haue I done ſince I went.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: My trickſey Spirit.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: Theſe are not naturall euens, they ſtrengthen
From ſtrange, to ſtranger: ſay, how came you hither?

sp.speaker: Bot.
sp.l: If I did thinke, Sir, I were well awake,
I'ld ſtriue to tell you: we were dead of ſleepe,
And (how we know not) all clapt vnder hatches,
Where, but euen now, with ſtrange, and ſeuerall noyſes
Of roring, ſhreeking, howling, gingling chaines,
And mo diuerſitie of ſounds, all horrible.
We were awak'd: ſtraight way, at liberty;
Where we, in all our trim, freſhly beheld
Our royall, good, and gallant Ship: our Maſter
Capring to eye her: on a trice, ſo pleaſe you,
Euen in a dreame, were we diuided from them,
And were brought moaping hither.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: Was't well done?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Brauely (my diligence) thou ſhalt be free.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: This is as ſtrange a Maze, as ere men trod,
And there is in this buſineſſe, more then nature
Was euer conduct of: ſome Oracle
Muſt rectifie our knowledge.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Sir, my Leige,
Doe not infeſt your minde, with beating on
The ſtrangeneſſe of this buſineſſe, at pickt leiſure
(Which ſhall be ſhortly ſingle) I'le reſolue you,
(Which to you ſhall ſeeme probable) of euery
Theſe happend accidents: till when, be cheerefull
And thinke of each thing well: Come hither Spirit,
Set Caliban, and his companions free:
Vntye the Spell: How fares my gracious Sir?
There are yet miſſing of your Companie
Some few odde Lads, that you remember not.

div.stage: Enter Ariell, driuing in Caliban, Stephano, and Trinculo in their ſtolne Apparell.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: Euery man ſhift for all the reſt, and let
No man take care for himſelfe; for all is
But fortune: Coragio Bully-Monſter Coraſio.

sp.speaker: Tri.
sp.p: If theſe be true ſpies which I weare in my head, here's a goodly ſight.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: O Setebos, theſe be braue Spirits indeede:
How fine my Maſter is? I am afraid
He will chaſtiſe me.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Ha, ha:
What things are theſe, my Lord Anthonio?
Will money buy em?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Very like: one of them
Is a plaine Fiſh, and no doubt marketable.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Marke but the badges of theſe men, my Lords,
Then ſay if they be true: This miſhapen knaue;
His Mother was a Witch, and one ſo ſtrong
That could controle the Moone; make flowes, and eb • ,
And deale in her command, without her power:
Theſe three haue robd me, and this demy-diuell;
(For he's a baſtard one) had plotted with them
To take my life: two of theſe Fellowes, you
Muſt know, and owne, this Thing of darkeneſſe, I
Acknowledge mine.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.p: I ſhall be pincht to death.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.p: Is not this Stephano, my drunken Butler?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: He is drunke now;
Where had he wine?

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: And Trinculo is reeling ripe: where ſhould they
Finde this grand Liquor that hath gilded 'em?
How cam'ſt thou in this pickle?

sp.speaker: Tri.
sp.l: I haue bin in ſuch a pickle ſince I ſaw you laſt,
That I feare me will neuer out of my bones:
I ſhall not feare fly-blowing.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: Who how now Stephano?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: O touch me not, I am not Stephano, but a Cramp.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: You'ld be King o' the Iſle, Sirha?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I ſhould haue bin a ſore one then.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.p: This is a ſtrange thing as ere I look'd on.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: He is as diſproportion'd in his Manners
As in his ſhape: Goe Sirha, to my Cell,
Take with you your Companions: as you looke
To haue my pardon, trim it handſomely.

sp.speaker: Cal.
sp.l: I that I will: and Ile be wiſe hereafter,
And ſeeke for grace: what a thrice double Aſſe
Was I to take this drunkard for a god?
And worſhip this dull foole?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Goe to, away.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.p: Hence, and beſtow your luggage where you found it.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: Or ſtole it rather.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Sir, I inuite your Highneſſe, and your traine
To my poore Cell: where you ſhall take your reſt
For this one night, which part of it, Ile waſte
With ſuch diſcourſe, as I not doubt, ſhall make it
Goe quicke away▪ The ſtory of my life,
And the particular accidents, gon by
Since I came to this Iſle: And in the morne
I'le bring you to your ſhip, and ſo to Naples,
Where I haue hope to ſee the nuptiall
Of theſe our deere-belou'd, ſolemnized,
And thence retire me to my Millaine, where
Euery third thought ſhall be my graue.

sp.speaker: Alo.
sp.l: I long
To heare the ſtory of your life; which muſt
Take the eare ſtarngely.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I'le deliuer all,
And promiſe you calme Seas, auſpicious gales,
And ſaile, ſo expeditious, that ſhall catch
Your Royall fleete farre off: My Ariel; chicke
That is thy charge: Then to the Elements
Be free, and fare thou well: pleaſe you draw neere.

div.head: EPILOGVE, ſpoken by Proſpero.
div.l: NOw my Charmes are all ore-throwne,
And what ſtrength I haue's mine owne.
Which is moſt faint: now 'tis true
I muſt be heere confinde by you,
Or ſent to Naples, Let me not
Since I haue my Dukedome got,
And pardon'd the deceiuer, dwell
In this bare Iſland, by your Spell,
But releaſe me from my bands
With the helpe of your good hands:
Gentle breath of yours, my Sailes
Muſt fill, or elſe my proiect failes,
Which was to pleaſe: Now I want
Spirits to enforce: Art to inchant,
And my ending is deſpaire,
Vnleſſe I be relieu'd by praier
Which pierces ſo, that it aſſaults
Mercy it ſelfe, and frees all faults.
As you from crimes would pardon'd be,
Let your Indulgence ſet me free.

div.head: The Scene, an vn-inhabited Iſland Names of the Actors.

list.item: Proſpero, the right Duke of Millaine.
Anthonio his brother, the vſurping Duke of Millaine.
Ferdinand, Son to the King of Naples.
Caliban, a ſaluage and deformed ſlaue.

sp.speaker: Valentine.
sp.l: CEaſe to perſwade▪ my louing Protheus;
Home-keeping youth; haue euer homely wits,
Wer't not affection chaines thy tender dayes
To the ſweet glaunces of thy honour'd Loue,
I rather would entreat thy company,
To ſee the wonders of the world abroad,
Then (liuing dully ſluggardiz'd at home)
Weare out thy youth with ſhapeleſſe idleneſſe.
But ſince thou lou'ſt; loue ſtill, and thriue therein,
Euen as I would, when I to loue begin.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Wilt thou be gone? Sweet Valentine ad ew,
Thinke on thy Protheus, when thou (hap'ly) ſeeſt
Some rare note-worthy obiect in thy trauaile.
With me partaker in thy happineſſe,
When thou do'ſt meet good hap; and in thy danger,
(If euer danger doe enuiron thee)
Commend thy grieuance to my holy prayers,
For I will be thy beadeſ-man, Valentine.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: And on a loue-booke pray for my ſucceſſe?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Vpon ſome booke I loue, I'le pray for thee.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: That's on ſome ſhallow Storie of deepe loue,
How yong Leander croſt the Helleſpont.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: That's a deepe Storie, of a deeper loue,
For he was more then ouer-ſhooes in loue.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: 'Tis true; for you are ouer-bootes in loue,
And yet you neuer ſwom the Helleſpont.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Ouer the Bootes? nay giue me not the Boots.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: No, I will not; for it boots thee not.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: To be in loue; where ſcorne is bought with grones:
Coy looks, with hart-ſore ſighes: one fading moments mirth,
With twenty watchfull, weary, tedious nights;
If hap'ly won, perhaps a hapleſſe gaine;
If loſt, why then a grieuous labour won;
How euer: but a folly bought with wit,
Or elſe a wit, by folly vanquiſhed.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: So, by your circumſtance, you call me foole.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: So, by your circumſtance, I feare you'll proue.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: 'Tis Loue you cauill at, I am not Loue.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Loue is your maſter, for he maſters you;
And he that is ſo yoked by a foole,
Me thinkes ſhould not be chronicled for wiſe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Yet Writers ſay; as in the ſweeteſt Bud,
The eating Canker dwels; ſo eating Loue
Inhabits in the fineſt wits of all.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And Writers ſay; as the moſt forward Bud
Is eaten by the Canker ere it blow,
Euen ſo by Loue, the yong, and tender wit
Is turn'd to folly, blaſting in the Bud,
Looſing his verdure, euen in the prime,
And all the faire effects of future hopes.
But wherefore waſte I time to counſaile thee
That art a votary to fond deſire?
Once more adieu: my Father at the Road
Expects my comming, there to ſee me ſhip'd.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: And thither will I bring thee Valentine.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Sweet Protheus, no: Now let vs take our leaue:
To Millaine let me heare from thee by Letters
Of thy ſucceſſe in loue; and what newes elſe
Betideth here in abſence of thy Friend:
And I likewiſe will viſite thee with mine.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: All happineſſe be chance to thee in Millaine.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: As much to you at home: and ſo farewell.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: He after Honour hunts, I after Loue;
He leaues his friends, to dignifie them more;
I loue my ſelfe, my friends, and all for loue:
Thou Iulia▪ thou haſt metamorphis'd me:
Made me neglect my Studies, looſe my time;
Warre with good counſaile; ſet the world at nought;
Made Wit with muſing, weake; hart ſick with thought.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Sir Protheus: 'ſaue you: ſaw you my Maſter?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: But now he parted hence to embarque for Millain.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.l: Twenty to one then, he is ſhip'd already,
And I haue plaid the Sheepe in looſing him.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Indeede a Sheepe doth very often ſtray,
And if the Shepheard be awhile away.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: You conclude that my Maſter is a Shepheard then, and I Sheepe?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: I doe.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Why then my hornes are his hornes, whether I wake or ſleepe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: A ſilly anſwere, and fitting well a Sheepe.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: This proues me ſtill a Sheepe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: True: and thy Maſter a Shepheard.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Nay, that I can deny by a circumſtance.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: It ſhall goe hard but ile proue it by another.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: The Shepheard ſeekes the Sheepe, and not the Sheepe the Shepheard; but I ſeeke my Maſter, and my Maſter ſeekes not me: therefore I am no Sheepe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: The Sheepe for fodder follow the Shepheard, the Shepheard for foode followes not the Sheepe: thou for wages followeſt thy Maſter, thy Maſter for wages followes not thee: therefore thou art a Sheepe.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Such another proofe will make me cry baâ.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: But do'ſt thou heare: gau'ſt thou my Letter to Iulia?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: I Sir: I (a loſt-Mutton) gaue your Letter to her (a lac'd-Mutton) and ſhe (a lac'd-Mutton) gaue mee (a loſt-Mutton) nothing for my labour.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Here's too ſmall a Paſture for ſuch ſtore of Muttons.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: If the ground be ouer-charg'd, you were beſt ſticke her.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Nay, in that you are aſtray: 'twere beſt pound you.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Nay Sir, leſſe then a pound ſhall ſerue me for carrying your Letter.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: You miſtake; I meane the pound, a Pinfold.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.l: From a pound to a pin? fold it ouer and ouer,
'Tis threefold too little for carrying a letter to your louer

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: But what ſaid ſhe?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: I.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Nod-I, why that's noddy.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.l: You miſtooke Sir: I ſay ſhe did nod;
And you aske me if ſhe did nod, and I ſay I.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: And that ſet together is noddy.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Now you haue taken the paines to ſet it together, take it for your paines.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: No, no, you ſhall haue it for bearing the letter.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Well, I perceiue I muſt be faine to beare with you.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Why Sir, how doe you beare with me?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.l: Marry Sir, the letter very orderly,
Hauing nothing but the word noddy for my paines.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Beſhrew me, but you haue a quicke wit.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: And yet it cannot ouer-take your ſlow purſe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Come, come, open the matter in briefe; what ſaid ſhe.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Open your purſe, that the money, and the matter may be both at once deliuered.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Well Sir: here is for your paines: what ſaid ſhe?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Truely Sir, I thinke you'll hardly win her.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Why? could'ſt thou perceiue ſo much from her?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.l: Sir, I could perceiue nothing at all from her;
No, not ſo much as a ducket for deliuering your letter:
And being ſo hard to me, that brought your minde;
I feare ſhe'll proue as hard to you in telling your minde.
Giue her no token but ſtones, for ſhe's as hard as ſteele.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: What ſaid ſhe, nothing?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.l: No, not ſo much as take this for thy pains:
To teſtifie your bounty, I thank you, you haue ceſtern'd me;
In requital whereof, henceforth, carry your letters your ſelfe; And ſo Sir, I'le commend you to my Maſter.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Go, go, be gone, to ſaue your Ship from wrack,
Which cannot periſh hauing thee aboarde,
Being deſtin'd to a drier death on ſhore:
I muſt goe ſend ſome better Meſſenger,
I feare my Iulia would not daigne my lines,
Receiuing them from ſuch a worthleſſe poſt.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: But ſay Lucetta (now we are alone)
Would'ſt thou then counſaile me to fall in loue?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I Madam, ſo you ſtumble not on heedfully.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Of all the faire reſt • of Gentlemen,
That euery day with par'd • encounter me,
In thy opinion which is worthieſt loue?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Pleaſe you repeat their names, ile ſhew my minde,
According to my ſhallow ſimple skill.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: What thinkſt thou of the faire ſir Eglamoure?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: As of a Knight, well-ſpoken, neat, and fine;
But were I you, he neuer ſhould be mine.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: What think'ſt thou of the rich Mercatio?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: Well of his wealth; but of himſelfe, ſo, ſo.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: What think'ſt thou of the gentle Protheus?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: Lord, Lord: to ſee what folly raignes in vs.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: How now? what meanes this paſſion at his name?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Pardon deare Madam, 'tis a paſſing ſhame,
That I (vnworthy body as I am)
Should cenſure thus on louely Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: Why not on Protheus, as of all the reſt?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: Then thus: of many good, I thinke him beſt.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Your reaſon?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: I haue no other but a womans reaſon:
I thinke him ſo, becauſe I thinke him ſo.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: And would'ſt thou haue me caſt my loue on him?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: I: if you thought your loue not caſt away.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Why he, of all the reſt, hath neuer mou'd me.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: Yet he, of all the reſt, I thinke beſt loues ye.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: His little ſpeaking, ſhewes his loue but ſmall.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: Fire that's cloſeſt kept, burnes moſt of all.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: They doe not loue, that doe not ſhew their loue.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: Oh, they loue leaſt, that let men know their loue.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: I would I knew his minde.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: Peruſe this paper Madam.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: To Iulia: ſay, from whom?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: That the Contents will ſhew.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Say, ſay: who gaue it thee?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Sir Valentines page: & ſent I think from Protheus;
He would haue giuen it you, but I being in the way,
Did in your name receiue it: pardon the fault I pray.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Now (by my modeſty) a goodly Broker:
Dare you preſume to harbour wanton lines?
To whiſper, and conſpire againſt my youth?
Now truſt me, 'tis an office of great worth,
And you an officer fit for the place:
There: take the paper: ſee it be return'd,
Or elſe returne no more into my ſight.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: To plead for loue, deſerues more fee, then hate.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Will ye be gon?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: That you may ruminate.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: And yet I would I had ore-look'd the Letter;
It were a ſhame to call her backe againe,
And pray her to a fault, for which I chid her.
What 'foole is ſhe, that knowe • I am a Maid.
And would not force the letter to my view?
Since Maides, in modeſty, ſay no, to that,
Which they would haue the profferer conſtrue, I.
Fie, fie: how way-ward is this fooliſh loue;
That (like a teſtie Babe) will ſcratch the Nurſe,
And preſently, all humbled kiſſe the Rod?
How churliſhly, I chid Lucetta hence,
When willingly, I would haue had her here?
How angerly I taught my brow to frowne,
When inward ioy enforc'd my heart to ſmile?
My pennance is, to call Lucetta backe
And aske remiſſion, for my folly paſt.
What hoe: Lucetta.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: What would your Ladiſhip?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Is't neere dinner time?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: I would it were,
That you might kill your ſtomacke on your meat,
And not vpon your Maid.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.l: What is't that you
Tooke vp ſo gingerly?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: Why didſt thou ſtoope then?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: To take a paper vp, that I let fall.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: And is that paper nothing?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: Nothing concerning me.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Then let it lye, for thoſe that it concernes.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Madam, it will not lye where it concernes,
Vnleſſe it haue a falſe Interpreter.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Some loue of yours, hath writ to you in Rime.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: That I might ſing it (Madam) to a tune:
Giue me a Note, your Ladiſhip can ſet

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: As little by ſuch toyes, as may be poſſible:
Beſt ſing it to the tune of Light O, Loue.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: It is too heauy for ſo light a tune.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: Heauy? belike it hath ſome burden then?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: I: and melodious were it, would you ſing it,

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: And why not you?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: I cannot reach ſo high.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.l: Let's ſee your Song:
How now Minion?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Keepe tune there ſtill; ſo you will ſing it out:
And yet me thinkes I do not like this tune.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: You doe not?

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: No (Madam) tis too ſharpe.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: You (Minion) are too ſaucie.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Nay, now you are too flat;
And marre the concord, with too harſh a deſcant:
There wanteth but a Meane to fill your Song.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: The meane is dround with you vnruly baſe.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: Indeede I bid the baſe for Protheus.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.l: This babble ſhall not henceforth trouble me;
Here is a coile with proteſtation:
Goe, get you gone: and let the papers lye:
You would be fingring them, to anger me.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: She makes it ſtrāge, but ſhe would be beſt pleas'd
To be ſo angred with another Letter.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.l: Nay, would I were ſo angred with the ſame:
Oh hatefull hands, to teare ſuch louing words;
Iniurious Waſpes, to feede on ſuch ſweet hony,
And kill the Bees that yeelde it, with your ſtings;
Ile kiſſe each ſeuerall paper, for amends:
Looke, here is writ, kinde Iulia: vnkinde Iulia,
As in reuenge of thy ingratitude,
I throw thy name againſt the bruzing-ſtones,
Trampling contemptuouſly on thy diſdaine.
And here is writ, Loue wounded Protheus.
Poore wounded name: my boſome, as a bed,
Shall lodge thee till thy wound be throughly heal'd;
And thus I ſearch it with a ſoueraigne kiſſe.
But twice, or thrice, was Protheus written downe:
Be calme (good winde) blow not a word away,
Till I haue found each letter, in the Letter,
Except mine own name: That, ſome whirle-winde beare
Vnto a ragged, fearefull, hanging Rocke,
And throw it thence into the raging Sea.
Loe, here in one line is his name twice writ:
Poore forlorne Protheus, paſſionate Protheus:
To the ſweet Iulia: that ile teare away:
And yet I will not, ſith ſo prettily
He couples it, to his complaining Names;
Thus will I fold them, one vpon another;
Now kiſſe, embrace, contend, doe what you will.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: Madam: dinner is ready: and your father ſtaies.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: Well, let vs goe.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.p: What, ſhall theſe papers lye, like Tel-tales here?

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: If you reſpect them; beſt to take them vp.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: Nay, I was taken vp, for laying them downe.
Yet here they ſhall not lye, for catching cold.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: I ſee you haue a months minde to them.

sp.speaker: Lu.
sp.l: I (Madam) you may ſay what ſights you ſee;
I ſee things too, although you iudge I winke.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: Come, come, wilt pleaſe you goe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Tell me Panthino, what ſad talke was that,
Wherewith my brother held you in the Cloyſter?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: 'Twas of his Nephew Protheus, your Sonne.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why? what of him?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: He wondred that your Lordſhip
Would ſuffer him, to ſpend his youth at home,
While other men, of ſlender reputation
Put forth their Sonnes, to ſeeke preferment out.
Some to the warres, to try their fortune there;
Some, to diſcouer Iſlands farre away:
Some, to the ſtudious Vniuerſities;
For any, or for all theſe exerciſes,
He ſaid, that Protheus, your ſonne, was meet;
And did requeſt me, to importune you
To let him ſpend his time no more at home;
Which would be great impeachment to his age,
In hauing knowne no trauaile in his youth.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Nor need'ſt thou much importune me to that
Whereon, this month I haue bin hamering.
I haue conſider'd well, his loſſe of time,
And how he cannot be a perfect man,
Not being tryed, and tutord in the world:
Experience is by induſtry atchieu'd,
And perfected by the ſwift courſe of time:
Then tell me, whether were I beſt to ſend him?

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: I thinke your Lordſhip is not ignorant
How his companion, youthfull Valentine,
Attends the Emperour in his royall Court.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I know it well.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: 'Twere good, I thinke, your Lordſhip ſent him thither,
There ſhall he practiſe Tilts, and Turnaments;
Heare ſweet diſcourſe, conuerſe with Noble-men,
And be in eye of euery Exerciſe
Worthy his youth, and nobleneſſe of birth.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I like thy counſaile: well haſt thou aduis'd:
And that thou maiſt perceiue how well I like it,
The execution of it ſhall make knowne;
Euen with the ſpeedieſt expedition,
I will diſpatch him to the Emperors Court.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: To morrow, may it pleaſe you, Don Alphonſo,
With other Gentlemen of good eſteeme
Are iournying, to ſalute the Emperor,
And to commend their ſeruice to his will.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Good company: with them ſhall Protheus go:
And in good time: now will we breake with him.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Sweet Loue, ſweet lines, ſweet life,
Here is her hand, the agent of her heart;
Here is her oath for loue, her honors paune;
O that our Fathers would applaud our loues
To ſeale our happineſſe with their conſents.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Oh heauenly Iulia.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: How now? What Letter are you reading there?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: May't pleaſe your Lordſhip, 'tis a word or two
Of commendations ſent from Valentine;
Deliuer'd by a friend, that came from him.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Lend me the Letter: Let me ſee what newes.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: There is no newes (my Lord) but that he writes
How happily he liues, how well-belou'd,
And daily graced by the Emperor;
Wiſhing me with him, partner of his fortune.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: And how ſtand you affected to his wiſh?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: As one relying on your Lordſhips will,
And not depending on his friendly wiſh.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: My will is ſomething ſorted with his wiſh:
Muſe not that I thus ſodainly proceed;
For what I will, I will, and there an end:
I am reſolu'd, that thou ſhalt ſpend ſome time
With Valentinus, in the Emperors Court:
What maintenance he from his friends receiues,
Like exhibition thou ſhalt haue from me,
To morrow be in readineſſe, to goe,
Excuſe it not: for I am peremptory.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: My Lord I cannot be ſo ſoone prouided,
Pleaſe you deliberate a day or two.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Look what thou want'ſt ſhalbe ſent after thee:
No more of ſtay: to morrow thou muſt goe;
Come on Panthino; you ſhall be imployd,
To haſten on his Expedition.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Thus haue I ſhund the fire, for feare of burning,
And drench'd me in the ſea, where I am drown'd.
I fear'd to ſhew my Father Iulias Letter,
Leaſt he ſhould take exceptions to my loue,
And with the vantage of mine owne excuſe
Hath he excepted moſt againſt my loue.
Oh, how this ſpring of loue reſembleth
The vncertaine glory of an Aprill day,
Which now ſhewes all the beauty of the Sun,
And by and by a clowd takes all away.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.l: Sir Protheus, your Fathers call's for you,
He is in haſt, therefore I pray you go.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Why this it is: my heart accords thereto,
And yet a thouſand times it anſwer's no.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Sir, your Gloue.

sp.speaker: Valen.
sp.p: Not mine: my Gloues are on.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Why then this may be yours: for this is but one.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: Ha? Let me ſee: I, giue it me, it's mine:
Sweet Ornament, that deckes a thing diuine,
Ah Siluia, Siluia.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Madam Siluia: Madam Siluia.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: How now Sirha?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Shee is not within hearing Sir.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Why ſir, who had you call her?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Your worſhip ſ • , or elſe I miſtooke.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Well: you'll ſtill be too forward.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: And yet I was laſt chidden for being too ſlow.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Goe to, ſir, tell me: do you know Madam Siluia?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Shee that your worſhip loues?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Why, how know you that I am in loue?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Marry by theſe ſpeciall markes: firſt, you haue learn'd (like Sir Protheus) to wreath your Armes like a Male-content: to relliſh a Loue-ſong, like a Robin-red-breaſt: to walke alone like one that had the peſtilence: to ſigh, like a Schoole-boy that had loſt his A. B. C. to weep like a yong wench that had buried her Grandam: to faſt, like one that takes diet: to watch, like one that feares robbing: to ſpeake puling, like a beggar at Hallow-Maſſe: You were wont, when you laughed, to crow like a cocke; when you walk'd, to walke like one of the Lions: when you faſted, it was preſently after dinner: when you look'd ſadly, it was for want of money: And now you are Metamorphis'd with a Miſtris, that when I looke on you, I can hardly thinke you my Maſter.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Are all theſe things perceiu'd in me?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: They are all perceiu'd without ye.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Without me? they cannot.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Without you? nay, that's certaine: for without you were ſo ſimple, none elſe would: but you are ſo without theſe follies, that theſe follies are within you, and ſhine through you like the water in an Vrinall: that not an eye that ſees you, but is a Phyſician to comment on your Malady.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: But tell me: do'ſt thou know my Lady Siluia?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Shee that you gaze on ſo, as ſhe ſits at ſupper?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Haſt thou obſeru'd that? euen ſhe I meane.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Why ſir, I know her not.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Do'ſt thou know her by my gazing on her, and yet know'ſt her not?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Is ſhe not hard-fauour'd, ſir?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Not ſo faire (boy) as well fauour'd.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Sir, I know that well enough.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: What doſt thou know?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: That ſhee is not ſo faire, as (of you) well-fauourd?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I meane that her beauty is exquiſite,
But her fauour infinite.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: That's becauſe the one is painted, and the other out of all count.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: How painted? and how out of count?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Marry ſir, ſo painted to make her faire, that no man counts of her beauty.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: How eſteem'ſt thou me? I account of her beauty.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: You neuer ſaw her ſince ſhe was deform'd.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: How long hath ſhe beene deform'd?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Euer ſince you lou'd her.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I haue lou'd her euer ſince I ſaw her,
And ſtill I ſee her beautifull.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: If you loue her, you cannot ſee her.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Becauſe Loue is blinde: O that you had mine eyes, or your owne eyes had the lights they were wont to haue, when you chidde at Sir Protheus, for going vngarter'd.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: What ſhould I ſee then?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Your owne preſent folly, and her paſſing deformitie: for hee beeing in loue, could not ſee to garter his hoſe; and you, beeing in loue, cannot ſee to put on your hoſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Belike (boy) then you are in loue, for laſt morning
You could not ſee to wipe my ſhooes.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p:
True ſir: I was in loue with my bed, I thanke you, you ſwing'd me for my loue, which makes mee the
bolder to chide you, for yours.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: In concluſion, I ſtand affected to her.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: I would you were ſet, ſo your affection would ceaſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Laſt night ſhe enioyn'd me,
To write ſome lines to one ſhe loues.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: And haue you?

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: I haue.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Are they not lamely writt?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: No (Boy) but as well as I can do them:
Peace, here ſhe comes.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.l: Oh excellent motion; oh exceeding Puppet:
Now will he interpret to her.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Madam & Miſtres, a thouſand good-morrows.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Oh, 'giue ye-good-ev'n: heer's a million of manners.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Sir Valentine, and ſeruant, to you two thouſand.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: He ſhould giue her intereſt: & ſhe giues it him.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: As you inioynd me; I haue writ your Letter
Vnto the ſecret, nameles friend of yours:
Which I was much vnwilling to proceed in,
But for my duty to your Ladiſhip.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: I thanke you (gentle Seruant) 'tis very Clerkly-done.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Now truſt me (Madam) it came hardly-off:
For being ignorant to whom it goes,
I writ at randome, very doubtfully.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Perchance you think too much of ſo much pains?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: No (Madam) ſo it ſteed you I will write (Pleaſe you command) a thouſand times as much: And yet —

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: A pretty period: well: I gheſſe the ſequell;
And yet I will not name it: and yet I care not.
And yet, take this againe: and yet I thanke you:
Meaning henceforth to trouble you no more.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: And yet you will: and yet, another yet.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: What meanes your Ladiſhip?
Doe you not like it?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Yes, yes: the lines are very queintly writ,
But (ſince vnwillingly) take them againe.
Nay, take them.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Madam, they are for you.

sp.speaker: Silu.
sp.l: I, I: you writ them Sir, at my requeſt,
But I will none of them: they are for you:
I would haue had them writ more mouingly:

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Pleaſe you, Ile write your Ladiſhip another.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: And when it's writ: for my ſake read it ouer,
And if it pleaſe you, ſo: if not: why ſo:

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: If it pleaſe me, (Madam?) what then?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Why if it pleaſe you, take it for your labour;
And ſo good-morrow Seruant.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.l: Oh Ieſt vnſeene: inſcrutible: inuiſible,
As a noſe on a mans face, or a Wethercocke on a ſteeple:
My Maſter ſues to her: and ſhe hath taught her Sutor,
He being her Pupill, to become her Tutor.
Oh excellent deuiſe, was there euer heard a better?
That my maſter being ſcribe,
To himſelfe ſhould write the Letter?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: How now Sir?
What are you reaſoning with your ſelfe?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Nay: I was riming: 'tis you yt haue the reaſon.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: To doe what?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: To be a Spokeſ-man from Madam Siluia.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: To whom?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: To your ſelfe: why, ſhe woes you by a figure.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: What figure?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: By a Letter, I ſhould ſay.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: Why ſhe hath not writ to me?

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.l: What need ſhe,
When ſhee hath made you write to your ſelfe?
Why, doe you not perceiue the ieſt?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: No, beleeue me.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.l: No beleeuing you indeed ſir:
But did you perceiue her earneſt?

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: She gaue me none, except an angry word.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Why ſhe hath giuen you a Letter.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: That's the Letter I writ to her friend.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: And yt letter hath ſhe deliuer'd, & there an end.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I would it were no worſe.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.l: Ile warrant you, 'tis as well:
For often haue you writ to her: and ſhe in modeſty,
Or elſe for want of idle time, could not againe reply,
Or fearing els ſome meſſēger, yt might her mind diſcouer
Her ſelf hath taught her Loue himſelf, to write vnto her louer.
All this I ſpeak in print, for in print I found it.
Why muſe you ſir, 'tis dinner time.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: I haue dyn'd.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: I, but hearken ſir: though the Cameleon Loue can feed on the ayre, I am one that am nouriſh'd by my victuals; and would faine haue meate: oh bee not like your Miſtreſſe, be moued, be moued.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Haue patience, gentle Iulia:

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: I muſt where is no remedy.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: When poſſibly I can, I will returne.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: If you turne not: you will return the ſooner:
Keepe this remembrance for thy Iulia's ſake.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Why then wee'll make exchange;
Here, take you this.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: And ſeale the bargaine with a holy kiſſe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Here is my hand, for my true conſtancie:
And when that howre ore-ſlips me in the day,
Wherein I ſigh not (Iulia) for thy ſake,
The next enſuing howre, ſome foule miſchance
Torment me for my Loues forgetfulneſſe:
My father ſtaies my comming: anſwere not:
The tide is now: nay, not thy tide of teares,
That tide will ſtay me longer then I ſhould,
Iulia, farewell: what, gon without a word?
I, ſo true loue ſhould doe: it cannot ſpeake,
For truth hath better deeds, then words to grace it.

sp.speaker: Panth.
sp.p: Sir Protheus: you are ſtaid for.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Goe: I come, I come:
Alas, this parting ſtrikes poore Louers dumbe.

sp.speaker: Launce.
sp.p:
Nay, 'twill bee this howre ere I haue done weeping: all the kinde of the Launce • , haue this very fault: I haue receiu'd my proportion, like the prodigious
Sonne, and am going with Sir Protheus to the Imperialls Court: I thinke Crab my dog, be the ſowreſt natured dogge that liues: My Mother weeping: my Father wayling: my Siſter crying: our Maid howling: our Catte wringing her hands, and all our houſe in a great perplexitie, yet did not this cruell-hearted Curre ſhedde one teare: he is a ſtone, a very pibble ſtone, and has no more pitty in him then a dogge: a Iew would haue wept to haue ſeene our parting: why my Grandam hauing no eyes, looke you, wept her ſelfe blinde at my parting: nay, Ile ſhew you the manner of it. This ſhooe is my father: no, this left ſhooe is my father; no, no, this left ſhooe is my mother: nay, that cannot bee ſo neyther: yes; it is ſo, it is ſo: it hath the worſer ſole: this ſhooe with the hole in it, is my mother: and this my father: a veng'ance on't, there 'tis: Now ſir, this ſtaffe is my ſiſter: for, looke you, ſhe is as white as a lilly, and as ſmall as a wand: this hat is Nan our maid: I am the dogge: no, the dogge is himſelfe, and I am the dogge: oh, the dogge is me, and I am my ſelfe: I; ſo, ſo: now come I to my Father; Father, your bleſſing: now ſhould not the ſhooe ſpeake a word for weeping: now ſhould I kiſſe my Father; well, hee weepes on: Now come I to my Mother: Oh that ſhe could ſpeake now, like a would-woman: well, I kiſſe her: why there 'tis; heere's my mothers breath vp and downe: Now come I to my ſiſter; marke the moane ſhe makes: now the dogge all this while ſheds not a teare: nor ſpeakes a word: but ſee how I lay the duſt with my teares.

sp.speaker: Panth.
sp.p: Launce, away, away: a Boord: thy Maſter is ſhip'd, and thou art to poſt after with oares; what's the matter? why weep'ſt thou man? away aſſe, you'l looſe the Tide, if you tarry any longer.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.p: It is no matter if the tide were loſt, for it is the vnkindeſt Tide, that euer any man tide.

sp.speaker: Panth.
sp.p: What's the vnkindeſt tide?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Why, he that's tide here, Crab my dog.

sp.speaker: Pant.
sp.p: Tut, man: I meane thou'lt looſe the flood, and in looſing the flood, looſe thy voyage, and in looſing thy voyage, looſe thy Maſter, and in looſing thy Maſter, looſe thy ſeruice, and in looſing thy ſeruice: — why doſt thou ſtop my mouth?

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.p: For feare thou ſhouldſt looſe thy tongue.

sp.speaker: Panth.
sp.p: Where ſhould I looſe my tongue?

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.p: In thy Tale.

sp.speaker: Panth.
sp.p: In thy Taile.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.p: Looſe the Tide, and the voyage, and the Maſter, and the Seruice, and the tide: why man, if the Riuer were drie, I am able to fill it with my teares: if the winde were downe, I could driue the boate with my ſighes.

sp.speaker: Panth.
sp.p: Come: come away man, I was ſent to call thee.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Sir: call me what thou dar'ſt.

sp.speaker: Pant.
sp.p: Wilt thou goe?

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.p: Well, I will goe.

div.head: Scena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Valentine, Siluia, Thurio, Speed, Duke, Protheus.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Seruant.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: Maſter, Sir Thurio frownes on you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I Boy, it's for loue.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: Not of you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Of my Miſtreſſe then.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: 'Twere good you knockt him.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Seruant, you are ſad.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Indeed, Madam, I ſeeme ſo.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: Seeme you that you are not?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Hap'ly I doe.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: So doe Counterfeyts.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: So doe you.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: What ſeeme I that I am not?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Wiſe.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: What inſtance of the contrary?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Your folly.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: And how quoat you my folly?

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: I quoat it in your Ierkin.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: My Ierkin is a doublet.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Well then, Ile double your folly.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: What, angry, Sir Thurio, do you change colour?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Giue him leaue, Madam, he is a kind of Camelion.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: That hath more minde to feed on your bloud, then liue in your ayre.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: You haue ſaid Sir.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: I Sir, and done too for this time.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I know it wel ſir, you alwaies end ere you begin.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: A fine volly of words, gentlemē, & quickly ſhot off

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: 'Tis indeed, Madam, we thank the giuer.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Who is that Seruant?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Your ſelfe (ſweet Lady) for you gaue the fire,
Sir Thurio borrows his wit from your Ladiſhips lookes,
And ſpends what he borrowes kindly in your company

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: Sir, if you ſpend word for word with me, I ſhall make your wit bankrupt.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I know it well ſir: you haue an Exchequer of words,
And I thinke, no other treaſure to giue your followers:
For it appeares by their bare Liueries
That they liue by your bare words.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: No more, gentlemen, no more:
Here comes my father.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Now, daughter Siluia, you are hard beſet.
Sir Valentine, your father is in good health,
What ſay you to a Letter from your friends
Of much good newes?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: My Lord, I will be thankfull,
To any happy meſſenger from thence.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: Know ye Don Antonio, your Countriman?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I, my good Lord, I know the Gentleman
To be of worth, and worthy eſtimation,
And not without deſert ſo well reputed.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: Hath he not a Sonne?

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: I, my good Lord, a Son, that well deſerues
The honor, and regard of ſuch a father.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: You know him well?

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: I knew him as my ſelfe: for from our Infancie
We haue conuerſt, and ſpent our howres together,
And though my ſelfe haue beene an idle Trewant,
Omitting the ſweet benefit of time
To cloath mine age with Angel-like perfection:
Yet hath Sir Protheus (for that's his name)
Made vſe, and faire aduantage of his daies:
His yeares but yong, but his experience old:
His head vn-mellowed, but his Iudgement ripe;
And in a word (for far behinde his worth
Comes all the praiſes that I now beſtow.)
He is compleat in feature, and in minde,
With all good grace, to grace a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Beſhrew me ſir, but if he make this good
He is as worthy for an Empreſſe loue,
As meet to be an Emperors Councellor:
Well, Sir: this Gentleman is come to me
With Commendation from great Potentates,
And heere he meanes to ſpend his time a while,
I thinke 'tis no vn-welcome newes to you.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: Should I haue wiſh'd a thing, it had beene he.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Welcome him then according to his worth:
Siluia, I ſpeake to you, and you Sir Thurio,
For Ʋalentine, I need not cite him to it,
I will ſend him hither to you preſently.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: This is the Gentleman I told your Ladiſhip
Had come along with me, but that his Miſtreſſe
Did hold his eyes, lockt in her Chriſtall lookes.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Be-like that now ſhe hath enfranchis'd them
Vpon ſome other pawne for fealty.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Nay ſure, I thinke ſhe holds them priſoners ſtil.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Nay then he ſhould be blind, and being blind
How could he ſee his way to ſeeke out you?

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: Why Lady, Loue hath twenty paire of eyes.

sp.speaker: Thur.
sp.p: They ſay that Loue hath not an eye at all.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: To ſee ſuch Louers, Thurio, as your ſelfe,
Vpon a homely obiect, Loue can winke.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Haue done, haue done: here comes ye gentleman.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Welcome, deer Protheus: Miſtris, I beſeech you
Confirme his welcome, with ſome ſpeciall fauor.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: His worth is warrant for his welcome hether,
If this be he you oft haue wiſh'd to heare from.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: Miſtris, it is: ſweet Lady, entertaine him
To be my fellow-ſeruant to your Ladiſhip.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Too low a Miſtres for ſo high a ſeruant.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Not ſo, ſweet Lady, but too meane a ſeruant
To haue a looke of ſuch a worthy a Miſtreſſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Leaue off diſcourſe of diſabilitie:
Sweet Lady, entertaine him for your Seruant.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: My dutie will I boaſt of, nothing elſe.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: And dutie neuer yet did want his meed.
Seruant, you are welcome to a worthleſſe Miſtreſſe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Ile die on him that ſaies ſo but your ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: That you are welcome?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: That you are worthleſſe.

sp.speaker: Thur.
sp.p: Madam, my Lord your father wold ſpeak with you.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I wait vpon his pleaſure: Come Sir Thurio,
Goe with me: once more, new Seruant welcome;
Ile leaue you to confer of home affaires,
When you haue done, we looke too heare from you.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Wee'll both attend vpon your Ladiſhip.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Now tell me: how do al from whence you came?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Your frends are wel, & haue thē much cōmended.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: And how doe yours?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: I left them all in health.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: How does your Lady? & how thriues your loue?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: My tales of Loue were wont to weary you,
I know you ioy not in a Loue-diſcourſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I Protheus, but that life is alter'd now,
I haue done pennance for contemning Loue,
Whoſe high emperious thoughts haue puniſh'd me
With bitter faſts, with penitentiall grones,
With nightly teares, and daily hart-ſore ſighes,
For in reuenge of my contempt of loue,
Loue hath chas'd ſleepe from my enthralled eyes,
And made them watchers of mine owne hearts ſorrow.
O gentle Protheus, Loue's a mighty Lord,
And hath ſo humbled me, as I confeſſe
There is no woe to his correction,
Nor to his Seruice, no ſuch ioy on earth:
Now, no diſcourſe, except it be of loue:
Now can I breake my faſt, dine, ſup, and ſleepe,
Vpon the very naked name of Loue.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Enough; I read your fortune in your eye:
Was this the Idoll, that you worſhip ſo?
