sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Euen She; and is ſhe not a heauenly Saint?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: No; But ſhe is an earthly Paragon.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Call her diuine.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: I will not flatter her.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: O flatter me: for Loue delights in praiſes.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: When I was ſick, you gaue me bitter pils,
And I muſt miniſter the like to you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Then ſpeake the truth by her; if not diuine,
Yet let her be a principalitie,
Soueraigne to all the Creatures on the earth,

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Except my Miſtreſſe.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Sweet: except not any,
Except thou wilt except againſt my Loue.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Haue I not reaſon to prefer mine owne?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And I will help thee to prefer her to:
Shee ſhall be dignified with this high honour,
To beare my Ladies traine, left the baſe earth
Should from her veſture chance to ſteale a kiſſe,
And of ſo great a fauor growing proud,
Diſdaine to roote the Sommer-ſwelling flowre,
And make rough winter euerlaſtingly.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Why Ʋalentine, what Bragadiſme is this?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Pardon me (Protheus) all I can is nothing,
To her, whoſe worth, make other worthies nothing;
Shee is alone.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Then let her alone.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Not for the world: why man, ſhe is mine owne,
And I as rich in hauing ſuch a Iewell
As twenty Seas, if all their ſand were pearle,
The water, Nectar, and the Rocks pure gold.
Forgiue me that I doe not dreame on thee,
Becauſe thou ſeeſt me doate vpon my loue:
My fooliſh Riuall that her Father likes
(Onely for his poſſeſſions are ſo huge)
Is gone with her along, and I muſt after,
For Loue (thou know'ſt is full of iealouſie.)

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: But ſhe loues you?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I, and we are betroathd: nay more, our mariage howre,
With all the cunning manner of our flight
Determin'd of: how I muſt climbe her window,
The Ladder made of Cords, and all the means
Plotted, and 'greed on for my happineſſe.
Good Protheus goe with me to my chamber,
In theſe affaires to aid me with thy counſaile.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Goe on before: I ſhall enquire you forth:
I muſt vnto the Road, to diſ-embarque
Some neceſſaries, that I needs muſt vſe,
And then Ile preſently attend you.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Will you make haſte?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I will.
Euen as one heate, another heate expels,
Or as one naile, by ſtrength driues out another.
So the remembrance of my former Loue
Is by a newer obiect quite forgotten,
It is mine, or Valentines praiſe?
Her true perfection, or my falſe tranſgreſſion?
That makes me reaſonleſſe, to reaſon thus?
Shee is faire: and ſo is Iulia that I loue,
(That I did loue, for now my loue is thaw'd,
Which like a waxen Image 'gainſt a fire
Beares no impreſſion of the thing it was.)
Me thinkes my zeale to Valentine is cold,
And that I loue him not as I was wont:
O, but I loue his Lady too-too much,
And that's the reaſon I loue him ſo little.
How ſhall I doate on her with more aduice,
That thus without aduice begin to loue her?
'Tis but her picture I haue yet beheld,
And that hath dazel'd my reaſons light:
But when I looke on her perfections,
There is no reaſon, but I ſhall be blinde.
If I can checke my erring loue, I will,
If not, to compaſſe her Ile vſe my skill.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Launce, by mine honeſty welcome to Padua.

sp.speaker: Laun.
sp.p: Forſweare not thy ſelfe, ſweet youth, for I am not welcome. I reckon this alwaies, that a man is neuer vndon till hee be hang'd, nor neuer welcome to a place, till ſome certaine ſhot be paid, and the Hoſteſſe ſay welcome.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: Come-on you mad-cap: Ile to the Ale-houſe with you preſently; where, for one ſhot of fiue pence, thou ſhalt haue fiue thouſand welcomes: But ſirha, how did thy Maſter part with Madam Iulia?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Marry after they cloas'd in earneſt, they parted very fairely in ieſt.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: But ſhall ſhe marry him?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: How then? ſhall he marry her?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: No, neither.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: What, are they broken?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: No; they are both as whole as a fiſh.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: Why then, how ſtands the matter with them?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Marry thus, when it ſtands well with him, it ſtands well with her.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: What an aſſe art thou, I vnderſtand thee not.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.l: What a blocke art thou, that thou canſt not?
My ſtaffe vnderſtands me?

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: What thou ſaiſt?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: I, and what I do too: looke thee, Ile but leane, and my ſtaffe vnderſtands me.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: It ſtands vnder thee indeed.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Why, ſtand-vnder: and vnder-ſtand is all one.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: But tell me true, wil't be a match?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Aske my dogge, if he ſay I, it will: if hee ſay no, it will: if hee ſhake his taile, and ſay nothing, it will.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: The concluſion is then, that it will.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt neuer get ſuch a ſecret from me, but by a parable.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: 'Tis well that I get it ſo: but Launce, how ſaiſt thou that that my maſter is become a notable Louer?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: I neuer knew him otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: Then how?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: A notable Lubber: as thou reporteſt him to bee.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: Why, thou whorſon Aſſe, thou miſtak'ſt me,

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Why Foole, I meant not thee, I meant thy Maſter.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: I tell thee, my Maſter is become a hot Louer.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Why, I tell thee, I care not, though hee burne himſelfe in Loue. If thou wilt goe with me to the Ale-houſe: if not, thou art an Hebrew, a Iew, and not worth the name of a Chriſtian.

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Becauſe thou haſt not ſo much charity in thee as to goe to the Ale with a Chriſtian: Wilt thou goe?

sp.speaker: Spee.
sp.p: At thy ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: To leaue my Iulia; ſhall I be forſworne?
To loue faire Siluia; ſhall I be forſworne?
To wrong my friend, I ſhall be much forſworne.
And ev'n that Powre which gaue me firſt my oath
Prouokes me to this three-fold periurie.
Loue bad mee ſweare, and Loue bids me for-ſweare;
O ſweet-ſuggeſting Loue, if thou haſt ſin'd,
Teach me (thy tempted ſubiect) to excuſe it.
At firſt I did adore a twinkling Starre,
But now I worſhip a celeſtiall Sunne:
Vn-heedfull vowes may heedfully be broken,
And he wants wit, that wants reſolued will,
To learne his wit, t' exchange the bad for better;
Fie, fie, vnreuerend tongue, to call her bad,
Whoſe ſoueraignty ſo oft thou haſt preferd,
With twenty thouſand ſoule-confirming oathes.
I cannot leaue to loue; and yet I doe:
But there I leaue to loue, where I ſhould loue.
Iulia I looſe, and Valentine I looſe,
If I keepe them, I needs muſt looſe my ſelfe:
If I looſe them, thus finde I by their loſſe,
For Valentine, my ſelfe: for Iulia, Siluia.
I to my ſelfe am deerer then a friend,
For Loue is ſtill moſt precious in it ſelfe,
And Siluia (witneſſe heauen that made her faire)
Shewes Iulia but a ſwarthy Ethiope.
I will forget that Iulia is aliue,
Remembring that my Loue to her is dead.
And Ʋalentine Ile hold an Enemie,
Ayming at Siluia as a ſweeter friend.
I cannot now proue conſtant to my ſelfe,
Without ſome treachery vs'd to Valentine.
This night he meaneth with a Corded-ladder
To climbe celeſtiall Siluia's chamber window,
My ſelfe in counſaile his competitor.
Now preſently Ile giue her father notice
Of their diſguiſing and pretended flight:
Who (all inrag'd) will baniſh Valentine:
For Thurio he intends ſhall wed his daughter,
But Valentine being gon, Ile quickely croſſe
By ſome ſlie tricke, blunt Thurio's dull proceeding.
Loue lend me wings, to make my purpoſe ſwift
As thou haſt lent me wit, to plot this drift.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Counſaile, Lucetta, gentle girle aſſiſt me,
And eu'n in kinde loue, I doe coniure thee,
Who art the Table wherein all my thoughts
Are viſibly Character'd, and engrau'd,
To leſſon me, and tell me ſome good meane
How with my honour I may vndertake
A iourney to my louing Protheus.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Alas, the way is weariſome and long.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: A true-deuoted Pilgrime is not weary
To meaſure Kingdomes with his feeble ſteps,
Much leſſe ſhall ſhe that hath Loues wings to flie,
And when the flight is made to one ſo deere,
Of ſuch diuine perfection as Sir Protheus.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Better forbeare, till Protheus make returne.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Oh, know'ſt yu not, his looks are my ſoules food?
Pitty the dearth that I haue pined in,
By longing for that food ſo long a time.
Didſt thou but know the inly touch of Loue,
Thou wouldſt as ſoone goe kindle fire with ſnow
As ſeeke to quench the fire of Loue with words.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I doe not ſeeke to quench your Loues hot fire,
But qualifie the fires extreame rage,
Leſt it ſhould burne aboue the bounds of reaſon.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: The more thou dam'ſt it vp, the more it burnes:
The Current that with gentle murmure glides
(Thou know'ſt) being ſtop'd, impatiently doth rage:
But when his faire courſe is not hindered,
He makes ſweet muſicke with th' enameld ſtones,
Giuing a gentle kiſſe to euery ſedge
He ouer-taketh in his pilgrimage.
And ſo by many winding nookes he ſtraies
With willing ſport to the wilde Ocean.
Then let me goe, and hinder not my courſe:
Ile be as patient as a gentle ſtreame,
And make a paſtime of each weary ſtep,
Till the laſt ſtep haue brought me to my Loue,
And there Ile reſt, as after much turmoile
A bleſſed ſoule doth in Elizium.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: But in what habit will you goe along?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Not like a woman, for I would preuent
The looſe encounters of laſciuious men:
Gentle Lucetta, fit me with ſuch weedes
As may beſeeme ſome well reputed Page.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Why then your Ladiſhip muſt cut your haire.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: No girle, Ile knit it vp in ſilken ſtrings,
With twentie od-conceited true-loue knots:
To be fantaſtique, may become a youth
Of greater time then I ſhall ſhew to be.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: What faſhion (Madam) ſhall I make your breeches?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: That fits as well, as tell me (good my Lord)
What compaſſe will you weare your Farthingale?
Why eu'n what faſhion thou beſt likes (Lucetta.)

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: You muſt needs haue thē with a cod-peece (Madam)

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Out, out, (Lucetta) that wilbe illfauourd.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: A round hoſe (Madam) now's not worth a pin
Vnleſſe you haue a cod-peece to ſtick pins on.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Lucetta, as thou lou'ſt me let me haue
What thou think'ſt meet, and is moſt mannerly.
But tell me (wench) how will the world repute me
For vndertaking ſo vnſtaid a iourney?
I feare me it will make me ſcandaliz'd.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: If you thinke ſo, then ſtay at home, and go not.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Nay, that I will not.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Then neuer dreame on Infamy, but go:
If Protheus like your iourney, when you come,
No matter who's diſpleas'd, when you are gone:
I feare me he will ſcarce be pleas'd with all.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: That is the leaſt (Lucetta) of my feare:
A thouſand oathes, an Ocean of his teares,
And inſtances of infinite of Loue,
Warrant me welcome to my Protheus.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: All theſe are ſeruants to deceitfull men.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Baſe men, that vſe them to ſo baſe effect;
But truer ſtarres did gouerne Protheus birth,
His words are bonds, his oathes are oracles,
His loue ſincere, his thoughts immaculate,
His teares, pure meſſengers, ſent from his heart,
His heart, as far from fraud, as heauen from earth.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Pray heau'n he proue ſo when you come to him.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Now, as thou lou'ſt me, do him not that wrong,
To beare a hard opinion of his truth:
Onely deſerue my loue, by louing him,
And preſently goe with me to my chamber
To take a note of what I ſtand in need of,
To furniſh me vpon my longing iourney:
All that is mine I leaue at thy diſpoſe,
My goods, my Lands, my reputation,
Onely, in lieu thereof, diſpatch me hence:
Come; anſwere not: but to it preſently,
I am impatient of my tarriance.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Duke, Thurio, Protheus, Valentine, Launce, Speed.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Sir Thurio, giue vs leaue (I pray) a while,
We haue ſome ſecrets to confer about.
Now tell me Protheus, what's your will with me?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: My gracious Lord, that which I wold diſcouer,
The Law of friendſhip bids me to conceale,
But when I call to minde your gracious fauours
Done to me (vndeſeruing as I am)
My dutie pricks me on to vtter that
Which elſe, no worldly good ſhould draw from me:
Know (worthy Prince) Sir Valentine my friend
This night intends to ſteale away your daughter:
My ſelfe am one made priuy to the plot.
I know you haue determin'd to beſtow her
On Thurio, whom your gentle daughter hates,
And ſhould ſhe thus be ſtolne away from you,
It would be much vexation to your age.
Thus (for my duties ſake) I rather choſe
To croſſe my friend in his intended drift,
Then (by concealing it) heap on your head
A pack of ſorrowes, which would preſſe you downe
(Being vnpreuented) to your timeleſſe graue.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Protheus, I thank thee for thine honeſt care,
Which to requite, command me while I liue.
This loue of theirs, my ſelfe haue often ſeene,
Haply when they haue iudg'd me faſt aſleepe,
And oftentimes haue purpos'd to forbid
Sir Ʋalentine her companie, and my Court.
But fearing leſt my iealous ayme might erre,
And ſo (vnworthily) diſgrace the man
(A raſhneſſe that I euer yet haue ſhun'd)
I gaue him gentle lookes, thereby to finde
That which thy ſelfe haſt now diſclos'd to me.
And that thou maiſt perceiue my feare of this,
Knowing that tender youth is ſoone ſuggeſted,
I nightly lodge her in an vpper Towre,
The key whereof, my ſelfe haue euer kept:
And thence ſhe cannot be conuay'd away.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Know (noble Lord) they haue deuis'd a meane
How he her chamber-window will aſcend,
And with a Corded-ladder fetch her downe:
For which, the youthfull Louer now is gone,
And this way comes he with it preſently.
Where (if it pleaſe you) you may intercept him.
But (good my Lord) doe it ſo cunningly
That my diſcouery be not aimed at:
For, loue of you, not hate vnto my friend,
Hath made me publiſher of this pretence.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Vpon mine Honor, he ſhall neuer know
That I had any light from thee of this.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Adiew, my Lord, Sir Valentine is comming.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: Sir Valentine, whether away ſo faſt?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Pleaſe it your Grace, there is a Meſſenger
That ſtayes to beare my Letters to my friends,
And I am going to deliuer them.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: Be they of much import?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: The tenure of them doth but ſignifie
My health, and happy being at your Court.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Nay then no matter: ſtay with me a while,
I am to breake with thee of ſome affaires
That touch me neere: wherein thou muſt be ſecret.
'Tis not vnknown to thee, that I haue ſought
To match my friend Sir Thurio, to my daughter.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I know it well (my Lord) and ſure the Match
Were rich and honourable: beſides, the gentleman
Is full of Vertue, Bounty, Worth, and Qualities
Beſeeming ſuch a Wife, as your faire daughter:
Cannot your Grace win her to fancie him?

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: No, truſt me, She is peeuiſh, ſullen, froward,
Prowd, diſobedient, ſtubborne, lacking duty,
Neither regarding that ſhe is my childe,
Nor fearing me, as if I were her father:
And may I ſay to thee, this pride of hers
(Vpon aduice) hath drawne my loue from her,
And where I thought the remnant of mine age
Should haue beene cheriſh'd by her child-like dutie,
I now am full reſolu'd to take a wife,
And tur • her out, to who will take her in:
Then let her beauty be her wedding dowre:
For me, and my poſſeſſions ſhe eſteemes not.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: What would your Grace haue me to do in this?

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: There is a Lady in Verona heere
Whom I affect: but ſhe is nice, and coy,
And naught eſteemes my aged eloquence.
Now therefore would I haue thee to my Tutor
(For long agone I haue forgot to court,
Beſides the faſhion of the time is chang'd)
How, and which way I may beſtow my ſelfe
To be regarded in her ſun-bright eye.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Win her with gifts, if ſhe reſpect not words,
Dumbe Iewels often in their ſilent kinde
More then quicke words, doe moue a womans minde.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: But ſhe did ſcorne a preſent that I ſent her,

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: A woman ſomtime ſcorns what beſt cōtents her.
Send her another: neuer giue her ore,
For ſcorne at firſt, makes after-loue the more.
If ſhe doe frowne, 'tis not in hate of you,
But rather to beget more loue in you.
If ſhe doe chide, 'tis not to haue you gone,
For why, the fooles are mad, if left alone.
Take no repulſe, what euer ſhe doth ſay,
For, get you gon, ſhe doth not meane away.
Flatter, and praiſe, commend, extoll their graces:
Though nere ſo blacke, ſay they haue Angells faces,
That man that hath a tongue, I ſay is no man,
If with his tongue he cannot win a woman.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: But ſhe I meane, is promis'd by her friends
Vnto a youthfull Gentleman of worth,
And kept ſeuerely from reſort of men,
That no man hath acceſſe by day to her.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Why then I would reſort to her by night.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: I, but the doores be lockt, and keyes kept ſafe,
That no man hath recourſe to her by night.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: What letts but one may enter at her window?

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Her chamber is aloft, far from the ground,
And built ſo ſheluing, that one cannot climbe it
Without apparant hazard of his life.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: Why then a Ladder quaintly made of Cords
To caſt vp, with a paire of anchoring hookes,
Would ſerue to ſcale another Hero's towre,
So bold Leander would aduenture it.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Now as thou art a Gentleman of blood
Aduiſe me, where I may haue ſuch a Ladder.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: When would you vſe it? pray ſir, tell me that.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: This very night; for Loue is like a childe
That longs for euery thing that he can come by.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: By ſeauen a clock, ile get you ſuch a Ladder.

sp.speaker: Duk
sp.l: But harke thee: I will goe to her alone,
How ſhall I beſt conuey the Ladder thither?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: It will be light (my Lord) that you may beare it
Vnder a cloake, that is of any length.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: A cloake as long as thine will ſerue the turne?

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: I my good Lord.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Then let me ſee thy cloake,
Ile get me one of ſuch another length.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Why any cloake will ſerue the turn (my Lord)

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: How ſhall I faſhion me to weare a cloake?
I pray thee let me feele thy cloake vpon me.
What Letter is this ſame? what's here? to Siluia?
And heere an Engine fit for my proceeding,
Ile be ſo bold to breake the ſeale for once.

q.l: My thoughts do harbour with my Siluia nightly,
And ſlaues they are to me, that ſend them flying.
Oh, could their Maſter come, and goe as lightly,
Himſelfe would lodge where (ſenceles) they are lying.
My Herald Thoughts, in thy pure boſome reſt-them,
While I (their King) that thither them importune
Doe curſe the grace, that with ſuch grace hath bleſt them,
Becauſe my ſelfe doe want my ſeruants fortune.
I curſe my ſelfe, for they are ſent by me,
That they ſhould harbour where their Lord ſhould be.

sp.l: What's here? Siluia, this night I will enfranchiſe thee.
'Tis ſo: and heere's the Ladder for the purpoſe.
Why Phaeton (for thou art Merops ſonne)
Wilt thou aſpire to guide the heauenly Car?
And with thy daring folly burne the world?
Wilt thou reach ſtars, becauſe they ſhine on thee?
Goe baſe Intruder, ouer-weening Slaue,
Beſtow thy fawning ſmiles on equall mates,
And thinke my patience, (more then thy deſert)
Is priuiledge for thy departure hence.
Thanke me for this, more then for all the fauors
Which (all too much) I haue beſtowed on thee.
But if thou linger in my Territories
Longer then ſwifteſt expedition
Will giue thee time to leaue our royall Court,
By heauen, my wrath ſhall farre exceed the loue
I euer bore my daughter, or thy ſelfe.
Be gone, I will not heare thy vaine excuſe,
But as thou lou'ſt thy life, make ſpeed from hence.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And why not death, rather then liuing torment?
To die, is to be baniſht from my ſelfe,
And Siluia is my ſelfe: baniſh'd from her
Is ſelfe from ſelfe. A deadly baniſhment:
What light, is light, if Siluia be not ſeene?
What ioy is ioy, if Siluia be not by?
Vnleſſe it be to thinke that ſhe is by
And feed vpon the ſhadow of perfection.
Except I be by Siluia in the night,
There is no muſicke in the Nightingale.
Vnleſſe I looke on Siluia in the day,
There is no day for me to looke vpon.
Shee is my eſſence, and I leaue to be;
If I be not by her faire influence
Foſter'd, illumin'd, cheriſh'd, kept aliue.
I flie not death, to flie his deadly doome,
Tarry I heere, I but attend on death,
But flie I hence, I flie away from life.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Run (boy) run, run, and ſeeke him out.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: So-hough, Soa hough —

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: What ſeeſt thou?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.l: Him we goe to finde,
There's not a haire on's head, but t'is a Valentine.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Valentine?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Who then? his Spirit?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Neither,

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: What then?

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Can nothing ſpeake? Maſter, ſhall I ſtrike?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Who wouldſt thou ſtrike?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Villaine, forbeare.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Why Sir, Ile ſtrike nothing: I pray you.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Sirha, I ſay forbeare: friend Valentine, a word.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: My eares are ſtopt, & cannot hear good newes,
So much of bad already hath poſſeſt them.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Then in dumbe ſilence will I bury mine,
For they are harſh, vn-tuneable, and bad.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Is Siluia dead?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: No, Valentine.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: No Valentine indeed, for ſacred Siluia,
Hath ſhe forſworne me?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: No, Ʋalentine.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: No Valentine, if Siluia haue forſworne me.
What is your newes?

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p: Sir, there is a proclamation, yt you are vaniſhed.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: That thou art baniſh'd: oh that's the newes,
From hence, from Siluia, and from me thy friend.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Oh, I haue fed vpon this woe already,
And now exceſſe of it will make me ſurfet.
Doth Siluia know that I am baniſh'd?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I, I: and ſhe hath offered to the doome
(Which vn-reuerſt ſtands in effectuall force)
A Sea of melting pearle, which ſome call teares;
Thoſe at her fathers churliſh feete ſhe tenderd,
With them vpon her knees, her humble ſelfe,
Wringing her hands, whoſe whitenes ſo became them,
As if but now they waxed pale for woe:
But neither bended knees, pure hands held vp,
Sad ſighes, deepe grones, nor ſiluer-ſhedding teares
Could penetrate her vncompaſſionate Sire;
But Valentine, if he be tane, muſt die.
Beſides, her interceſſion chaf'd him ſo,
When ſhe for thy repeale was ſuppliant,
That to cloſe priſon he commanded her,
With many bitter threats of biding there.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: No more: vnles the next word that thou ſpeak'ſt
Haue ſome malignant power vpon my life:
If ſo: I pray thee breath it in mine eare,
As ending Antheme of my endleſſe dolor.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Ceaſe to lament for that thou canſt not helpe,
And ſtudy helpe for that which thou lament'ſt,
Time is the Nurſe, and breeder of all good;
Here, if thou ſtay, thou canſt not ſee thy loue:
Beſides, thy ſtaying will abridge thy life:
Hope is a louers ſtaffe, walke hence with that
And manage it, againſt deſpairing thoughts:
Thy letters may be here, though thou art hence,
Which, being writ to me, ſhall be deliuer'd
Euen in the milke-white boſome of thy Loue.
The time now ſerues not to expoſtulate,
Come, Ile conuey thee through the City-gate.
And ere I part with thee, confer at large
Of all that may concerne thy Loue-affaires:
As thou lou'ſt Siluia (though not for thy ſelfe)
Regard thy danger, and along with me.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I pray thee Launce, and if thou ſeeſt my Boy
Bid him make haſte, and meet me at the North-gate.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Goe ſirha, finde him out: Come Ʋalentine.

sp.speaker: Val
sp.p: Oh my deere Siluia; hapleſſe Valentine.

sp.speaker: Launce.
sp.p: I am but a foole, looke you, and yet I haue the wit to thinke my Maſter is a kinde of a knaue: but that's all one, if he be but one knaue: He liues not now that knowes me to be in loue, yet I am in loue, but a Teeme of horſe ſhall not plucke that from me: nor who 'tis I loue: and yet 'tis a woman; but what woman, I will not tell my ſelfe: and yet 'tis a Milke-maid: yet 'tis not a maid: for ſhee hath had Goſſips: yet 'tis a maid, for ſhe is her Maſters maid, and ſerues for wages. Shee hath more qualities then a Water-Spaniell, which is much in a bare Chriſtian: Heere is the Cate-log of her Condition. Inprimis. Shee can fetch and carry: why a horſe can doe no more; nay, a horſe cannot fetch, but onely carry, therefore is ſhee better then a Iade. Item. She can milke, looke you, a ſweet vertue in a maid with cleane hands.

sp.speaker: Speed.
sp.p: How now Signior Launce? what newes with your Maſterſhip?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: With my Maſterſhip? why, it is at Sea:

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Well, your old vice ſtill: miſtake the word: what newes then in your paper?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: The black'ſt newes that euer thou heard'ſt.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Why man? how blacke?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Why, as blacke as Inke.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Let me read them?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Fie on thee Iolt-head, thou canſt not read.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Thou lyeſt: I can.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: I will try thee: tell me this: who begot thee?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Marry, the ſon of my Grand-father.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Oh illiterate loyterer▪ it was the ſonne of thy Grand-mother: this proues that thou canſt not read.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Come foole, come: try me in thy paper.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: There: and S. Nicholas be thy ſpeed.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Inprimis ſhe can milke.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: I that ſhe can.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe brewes good Ale.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: And thereof comes the prouerbe: (Bleſſing of your heart, you brew good Ale.)

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe can ſowe.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: That's as much as to ſay (Can ſhe ſo?)

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item ſhe can knit.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: What neede a man care for a ſtock with a wench,
When ſhe can knit him a ſtocke?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe can waſh and ſcoure.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: A ſpeciall vertue: for then ſhee neede not be waſh'd, and ſcowr'd.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe can ſpin.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Then may I ſet the world on wheeles, when ſhe can ſpin for her liuing.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe hath many nameleſſe vertues.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: That's as much as to ſay Baſtard-vertues: that indeede know not their fathers; and therefore haue no names.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Here follow her vices.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Cloſe at the heeles of her vertues.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhee is not to be faſting in reſpect of her breath.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Well: that fault may be mended with a breakfaſt: read on.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe hath a ſweet mouth.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: That makes amends for her ſoure breath.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe doth talke in her ſleepe.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: It's no matter for that; ſo ſhee ſleepe not in her talke.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe is ſlow in words.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Oh villaine, that ſet this downe among her vices;
To be ſlow in words, is a womans onely vertue:
I pray thee out with't, and place it for her chiefe vertue.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe is proud.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Out with that too:
It was Eues legacie, and cannot be t'ane from her.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe hath no teeth.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: I care not for that neither: becauſe I loue cruſts.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe is curſt.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Well: the beſt is, ſhe hath no teeth to bite.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe will often praiſe her liquor.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: If her liquor be good, ſhe ſhall: if ſhe will not,
I will; for good things ſhould be praiſed.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe is too liberall.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Of her tongue ſhe cannot; for that's writ downe ſhe is ſlow of: of her purſe, ſhee ſhall not, for that ile keepe ſhut: Now, of another thing ſhee may, and that cannot I helpe. Well, proceede.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhee hath more haire then wit, and more faults then haires, and more wealth then faults.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Stop there: Ile haue her: ſhe was mine, and not mine, twice or thrice in that laſt Article: rehearſe that once more.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Item, ſhe hath more haire then wit.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: More haire then wit: it may be ile proue it: The couer of the ſalt, hides the ſalt, and therefore it is more then the ſalt; the haire that couers the wit, is more then the wit; for the greater hides the leſſe: What's next?

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: And more faults then haires.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: That's monſtrous: oh that that were out.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: And more wealth then faults.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Why that word makes the faults gracious:
Well, ile haue her: and if it be a match, as nothing is impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: What then?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Why then, will I tell thee, that thy Maſter ſtaies for thee at the North gate.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: For me?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: For thee? I, who art thou? he hath ſtaid for a better man then thee.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: And muſt I goe to him?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Thou muſt run to him; for thou haſt ſtaid ſo long, that going will ſcarce ſerue the turne.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.p: Why didſt not tell me ſooner? 'pox of your loue Letters.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Now will he be ſwing'd for reading my Letter; An vnmannerly ſlaue, that will thruſt himſelfe into ſecrets: Ile after, to reioyce in the boyes correctiō.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Sir Thurio, feare not, but that ſhe will loue you
Now Valentine is baniſh'd from her ſight.

sp.speaker: Th.
sp.l: Since his exile ſhe hath deſpis'd me moſt,
Forſworne my company, and rail'd at me,
That I am deſperate of obtaining her.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: This weake impreſſe of Loue, is as a figure
Trenched in ice, which with an houres heare
Diſſolues to water, and doth looſe his forme.
A little time will melt her frozen thoughts,
And worthleſſe Valentine ſhall be forgot.
How now ſir Protheus, is your countriman
(According to our Proclamation) gon?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Gon, my good Lord.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: My daughter takes his going grieuouſly?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: A little time (my Lord) will kill that griefe.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: So I beleeue: but Thurio thinkes not ſo:
Protheus, the good conceit I hold of thee,
(For thou haſt ſhowne ſome ſigne of good deſert)
Makes me the better to confer with thee.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Longer then I proue loyall to your Grace,
Let me not liue, to looke vpon your Grace.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Thou know'ſt how willingly, I would effect
The match betweene ſir Thurio, and my daughter?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: I doe my Lord.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: And alſo, I thinke, thou art not ignorant
How ſhe oppoſes her againſt my will?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: She did my Lord, when Ʋalentine was here.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I, and peruerſly, ſhe perſeuers ſo:
What might we doe to make the girle forget
The loue of Valentine, and loue ſir Thurio?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: The beſt way is, to ſlander Ʋalentine,
With falſehood, cowardize, and poore diſcent:
Three things, that women highly hold in hate.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: I, but ſhe'll thinke, that it is ſpoke in hate.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I, if his enemy deliuer it.
Therefore it muſt with circumſtance be ſpoken
By one, whom ſhe eſteemeth as his friend.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: Then you muſt vndertake to ſlander him.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: And that (my Lord) I ſhall be loath to doe:
'Tis an ill office for a Gentleman,
Eſpecially againſt his very friend.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Where your good word cannot aduantage him,
Your ſlander neuer can endamage him;
Therefore the office is indifferent,
Being intreated to it by your friend.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: You haue preuail'd (my Lord) if I can doe it
By ought that I can ſpeake in his diſpraiſe,
She ſhall not long continue loue to him:
But ſay this weede her loue from Valentine,
It followes not that ſhe will loue ſir Thurio.

sp.speaker: Th.
sp.l: Therefore, as you vnwinde her loue from him;
Leaſt it ſhould rauell, and be good to none,
You muſt prouide to bottome it on me:
Which muſt be done, by praiſing me as much
As you, in worth diſpraiſe, ſir Ʋalentine.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: And Protheus, we dare truſt you in this kinde,
Becauſe we know (on Valentines report)
You are already loues firme votary,
And cannot ſoone reuolt, and change your minde.
Vpon this warrant, ſhall you haue acceſſe,
Where you, with Siluia, may conferre at large.
For ſhe is lumpiſh, heauy, mellancholly,
And (for your friends ſake) will be glad of you;
Where you may temper her, by your perſwaſion,
To hate yong Ʋalentine, and loue my friend.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: As much as I can doe, I will effect:
But you ſir Thurio, are not ſharpe enough:
You muſt lay Lime, to tangle her deſires
By walefull Sonnets, whoſe compoſed Rimes
Should be full fraught with ſeruiceable vowes.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: I, much is the force of heauen-bred Poeſie.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Say that vpon the altar of her beauty
You ſacrifice your teares, your ſighes, your heart:
Write till your inke be dry▪ and with your teares
Moiſt it againe: and frame ſome feeling line,
That may diſcouer ſuch integrity:
For Orpheus Lute, was ſtrung with Poets ſinewes,
Whoſe golden touch could ſoften ſteele and ſtones;
Make Tygers tame, and huge Leuiathans
Forſake vnſounded deepes, to dance on Sands.
After your dire-lamenting Elegies,
Viſit by night your Ladies chamber-window
With ſome ſweet Conſort; To their Inſtruments
Tune a deploring dumpe: the nights dead ſilence
Will well become ſuch ſweet complaining grieuance:
This, or elſe nothing, will inherit her.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: This diſcipline, ſhowes thou haſt bin in loue.

sp.speaker: Th.
sp.l: And thy aduice, this night, ile put in practiſe:
Therefore, ſweet Protheus, my direction-giuer,
Let vs into the City preſently
To ſort ſome Gentlemen, well skil'd in Muſicke.
I haue a Sonnet, that will ſerue the turne
To giue the on-ſet to thy good aduiſe.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: About it Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: We'll wait vpon your Grace, till after Supper,
And afterward determine our proceedings.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: Euen now about it, I will pardon you.

div.head: Scoena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Valentine, Speed, and certaine Out-lawes.

sp.speaker: 1. Out-l.
sp.p: Fellowes, ſtand faſt: I ſee a paſſenger.

sp.speaker: 2. Out.
sp.p: If there be ten, ſhrinke not, but down with 'em.

sp.speaker: 3. Out.
sp.l: Stand ſir, and throw vs that you haue about 'ye.
If not: we'll make you ſit, and rifle you.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.l: Sir we are vndone; theſe are the Villaines
That all the Trauailers doe feare ſo much.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: My friends.

sp.speaker: 1. Out.
sp.p: That's not ſo, ſir: we are your enemies.

sp.speaker: 2. Out.
sp.p: Peace: we'll heare him.

sp.speaker: 3. Out.
sp.p: I by my beard will we: for he is a proper man.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Then know that I haue little wealth to looſe;
A man I am, croſs'd with aduerſitie:
My riches, are theſe poore habiliments,
Of which, if you ſhould here disfurniſh me,
You take the ſum and ſubſtance that I haue.

sp.speaker: 2. Out.
sp.p: Whether trauell you?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: To Verona.

sp.speaker: 1. Out.
sp.p: Whence came you?

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: From Millaine.

sp.speaker: 3. Out.
sp.p: Haue you long ſoiourn'd there?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Some ſixteene moneths, and longer might haue ſtaid,
If crooked fortune had not thwarted me.

sp.speaker: 1. Out.
sp.p: What, were you baniſh'd thence?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I was.

sp.speaker: 2. Out.
sp.p: For what offence?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: For that which now torments me to rehearſe;
I kil'd a man, whoſe death I much repent,
But yet I ſlew him manfully, in fight,
Without falſe vantage, or baſe treachery.

sp.speaker: 1. Out.
sp.l: Why nere repent it, if it were done ſo;
But were you baniſht for ſo ſmall a fault?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I was, and held me glad of ſuch a doome.

sp.speaker: 2. Out.
sp.p: Haue you the Tongues?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: My youthfull trauaile, therein made me happy,
Or elſe I often had beene often miſerable.

sp.speaker: 3. Out.
sp.l: By the bare ſcalpe of Robin Hoods fat Fryer,
This fellow were a King, for our wilde faction.

sp.speaker: 1. Out.
sp.p: We'll haue him: Sirs, a word.

sp.speaker: Sp.
sp.l: Maſter, be one of them:
It's an honourable kinde of theeuery.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Peace villaine.

sp.speaker: 2. Out.
sp.p: Tell vs this: haue you any thing to take to?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Nothing but my fortune.

sp.speaker: 3. Out.
sp.l: Know then, that ſome of vs are Gentlemen,
Such as the fury of vngouern'd youth
Thruſt from the company of awfull men.
My ſelfe was from Verona baniſhed,
For practiſing to ſteale away a Lady,
And heire and Neece, alide vnto the Duke.

sp.speaker: 2. Out.
sp.l: And I from Mantua, for a Gentleman,
Who, in my moode, I ſtab'd vnto the heart.

sp.speaker: 1. Out.
sp.l: And I, for ſuch like petty crimes as theſe.
But to the purpoſe: for we cite our faults,
That they may hold excus'd our lawleſſe liues;
And partly ſeeing you are beautifide
With goodly ſhape; and by your owne report,
A Linguiſt, and a man of ſuch perfection,
As we doe in our quality much want.

sp.speaker: 2. Out.
sp.l: Indeede becauſe you are a baniſh'd man,
Therefore, aboue the reſt, we parley to you:
Are you content to be our Generall?
To make a vertue of neceſſity,
And liue as we doe in this wilderneſſe?

sp.speaker: 3. Out.
sp.l: What ſaiſt thou? wilt thou be of our conſort?
Say I, and be the captaine of vs all:
We'll doe thee homage, and be rul'd by thee,
Loue thee, as our Commander, and our King.

sp.speaker: 1. Out.
sp.p: But if thou ſcorne our curteſie, thou dyeſt.

sp.speaker: 2. Out.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt not liue, to brag what we haue offer'd.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: I take your offer, and will liue with you,
Prouided that you do no outrages
On ſilly women, or poore paſſengers.

sp.speaker: 3. Out.
sp.l: No, we deteſt ſuch vile baſe practiſes.
Come, goe with vs, we'll bring thee to our Crewes,
And ſhow thee all the Treaſure we haue got;
Which, with our ſelues, all reſt at thy diſpoſe.

div.head: Scoena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Protheus, Thurio, Iulia, Hoſt, Muſitian, Siluia.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Already haue I bin falſe to Valentine,
And now I muſt be as vniuſt to Thurio,
Vnder the colour of commending him,
I haue acceſſe my owne loue to prefer.
But Siluia is too faire, too true, too holy,
To be corrupted with my worthleſſe guifts;
When I proteſt true loyalty to her,
She twits me with my falſehood to my friend;
When to her beauty I commend my vowes,
She bids me thinke how I haue bin forſworne
In breaking faith with Iulia, whom I lou'd;
And notwithſtanding all her ſodaine quips,
The leaſt whereof would quell a louers hope:
Yet (Spaniel-like) the more ſhe ſpurnes my loue,
The more it growes, and fawneth on her ſtill;
But here comes Thurio; now muſt we to her window,
And giue ſome euening Muſique to her eare.

sp.speaker: Th.
sp.p: How now, ſir Protheus, are you crept before vs?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I gentle Thurio, for you know that loue
Will creepe in ſeruice, where it cannot goe.

sp.speaker: Th.
sp.p: I, but I hope, Sir, that you loue not here.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Sir, but I doe: or elſe I would be hence.

sp.speaker: Th.
sp.p: Who, Siluia?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: I, Siluia, for your ſake.

sp.speaker: Th.
sp.l: I thanke you for your owne: Now Gentlemen
Let's tune: and too it luſtily a while.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.l: Now, my yong gueſt; me thinks your' allyeholly;
I pray you why is it?

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: Marry (mine Hoſt) becauſe I cannot be merry.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: Come, we'll haue you merry: ile bring you where you ſhall heare Muſique, and ſee the Gentleman that you ask'd for.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: But ſhall I heare him ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: I that you ſhall.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: That will be Muſique.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: Harke, harke.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: Is he among theſe?

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: I: but peace, let's heare'm.

lg.head: Song.
lg.l: Who is Siluia? what is ſhe?
That all our Swaines commend her?
Holy, faire, and wiſe is ſhe,
The heauen ſuch grace did lend her, that ſhe might admired be.
Is ſhe kinde as ſhe is faire?
For beauty liues with kindneſſe:
Loue doth to her eyes repaire,
To helpe him of his blindneſſe:
And being help'd, inhabits there.
Then to Siluia, let vs ſing,
That Siluia is excelling;
She excels each mortall thing
Vpon the dull earth dwelling.
To her let vs Garlands bring.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.l: How now? are you ſadder then you were before;
How doe you, man? the Muſicke likes you not.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: You miſtake: the Muſitian likes me not.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: Why, my pretty youth?

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: He plaies falſe (father.)

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: How, out of tune on the ſtrings.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.l: Not ſo: but yet
So falſe that he grieues my very heart-ſtrings.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: You haue a quicke eare.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: I, I would I were deafe: it makes me haue a ſlow heart.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: I perceiue you delight not in Muſique.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: Not a whit, when it iars ſo.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: Harke, what fine change is in the Muſique.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: I: that change is the ſpight.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: You would haue them alwaies play but one thing.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.l: I would alwaies haue one play but one thing.
But Hoſt, doth this Sir Protheus, that we talke on,
Often reſort vnto this Gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.l: I tell you what Launce his man told me,
He lou'd her out of all nicke.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: Where is Launce?

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: Gone to ſeeke his dog, which to morrow, by his Maſters command, hee muſt carry for a preſent to his Lady.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: Peace, ſtand aſide, the company parts.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Sir Thurio, feare not you, I will ſo pleade,
That you ſhall ſay, my cunning drift excels.

sp.speaker: Th.
sp.p: Where meete we?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: At Saint Gregories well.

sp.speaker: Th.
sp.p: Farewell.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Madam: good eu'n to your Ladiſhip.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I thanke you for your Muſique (Gentlemen)
Who is that that ſpake?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: One (Lady) if you knew his pure hearts truth,
You would quickly learne to know him by his voice.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Sir Protheus, as I take it.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Sir Protheus (gentle Lady) and your Seruant.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: What's your will?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: That I may compaſſe yours.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: You haue your wiſh: my will is euen this,
That preſently you hie you home to bed:
Thou ſubtile, periur'd, falſe, diſloyall man:
Think'ſt thou I am ſo ſhallow, ſo conceitleſſe,
To be ſeduced by thy flattery,
That has't deceiu'd ſo many with thy vowes▪
Returne, returne and make thy loue amends:
For me (by this pale queene of night I ſweare)
I am ſo farre from granting thy requeſt,
That I deſpiſe thee, for thy wrongfull ſuite;
And by and by intend to chide my ſelfe,
Euen for this time I ſpend in talking to thee.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I grant (ſweet loue) that I did loue a Lady,
But ſhe is dead.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.l: 'Twere falſe, if I ſhould ſpeake it;
For I am ſure ſhe is not buried.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Say that ſhe be: yet Valentine thy friend
Suruiues; to whom (thy ſelfe art witneſſe)
I am betroth'd; and art thou not aſham'd
To wrong him, with thy importunacy?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: I likewiſe heare that Valentine is dead.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: And ſo ſuppoſe am I; for in her graue
Aſſure thy ſelfe, my loue is buried.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Sweet Lady, let me take it from the earth.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Goe to thy Ladies graue and call hers thence,
Or at the leaſt, in hers, ſepulcher thine.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: He heard not that.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Madam: if your heart be ſo obdurate:
Vouchſafe me yet your Picture for my loue,
The Picture that is hanging in your chamber:
To that ile ſpeake, to that ile ſigh and weepe:
For ſince the ſubſtance of your perfect ſelfe
Is elſe deuoted, I am but a ſhadow;
And to your ſhadow, will I make true loue.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: If 'twere a ſubſtance you would ſure deceiue it,
And make it but a ſhadow, as I am.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: I am very loath to be your Idoll Sir;
But, ſince your falſehood ſhall become you well
To worſhip ſhadowes, and adore falſe ſhapes,
Send to me in the morning, and ile ſend it:
And ſo, good reſt.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: As wretches haue ore-night
That wait for execution in the morne.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Hoſt, will you goe?

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: By my hallidome, I was faſt aſleepe.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Pray you, where lies Sir Protheus?

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.l: Marry, at my houſe:
Truſt me, I thinke 'tis almoſt day.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Not ſo: but it hath bin the longeſt night
That ere I watch'd, and the moſt heauieſt.

sp.speaker: Eg.
sp.l: This is the houre that Madam Siluia
Entreated me to call, and know her minde:
Ther's ſome great matter ſhe'ld employ me in.
Madam, Madam.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Who cals?

sp.speaker: Eg.
sp.l: Your ſeruant, and your friend;
One that attends your Ladiſhips command.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Sir Eglamore, a thouſand times good morrow.

sp.speaker: Eg.
sp.l: As many (worthy Lady) to your ſelfe:
According to your Ladiſhips impoſe,
I am thus early come, to know what ſeruice
It is your pleaſure to command me in.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Oh Eglamoure, thou art a Gentleman:
Thinke not I flatter (for I ſweare I doe not)
Valiant, wiſe, remorſe-full, well accompliſh'd.
Thou art not ignorant what deere good will
I beare vnto the baniſh'd Ʋalentine:
Nor how my father would enforce me marry
Vaine Thurio (whom my very ſoule abhor'd.)
Thy ſelfe haſt lou'd, and I haue heard thee ſay
No griefe did euer come ſo neere thy heart,
As when thy Lady, and thy true-loue dide,
Vpon whoſe Graue thou vow'dſt pure chaſtitie:
Sir Eglamoure: I would to Valentine
To Mantua, where I heare, he makes aboad;
And for the waies are dangerous to paſſe,
I doe deſire thy worthy company,
Vpon whoſe faith and honor, I repoſe.
Vrge not my fathers anger (Eglamoure)
But thinke vpon my griefe (a Ladies griefe)
And on the iuſtice of my flying hence,
To keepe me from a moſt vnholy match,
Which heauen and fortune ſtill rewards with plagues.
I doe deſire thee, euen from a heart
As full of ſorrowes, as the Sea of ſands,
To beare me company, and goe with me:
If not, to hide what I haue ſaid to thee,
That I may venture to depart alone.

sp.speaker: Egl.
sp.l: Madam, I pitty much your grieuances,
Which, ſince I know they vertuouſly are plac'd,
I giue conſent to goe along with you,
Wreaking as little what betideth me,
As much, I wiſh all good befortune you.
When will you goe?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: This euening comming.

sp.speaker: Eg.
sp.p: Where ſhall I meete you?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: At Frier Patrickes Cell,
Where I intend holy Confeſſion.

sp.speaker: Eg.
sp.l: I will not faile your Ladiſhip:
Good morrow (gentle Lady.)

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Good morrow, kinde Sir Eglamoure.

sp.speaker: Lau.
sp.p:
When a mans ſeruant ſhall play the Curre with him (looke you) it goes hard: one that I brought vp of a puppy: one that I ſau'd from drowning, when three or foure of his blinde brothers and ſiſters went to it: I haue taught him (euen as one would ſay preciſely, thus I would teach a dog) I was ſent to deliuer him, as a preſent to Miſtris Siluia, from my Maſter; and I came no ſooner into the dyning-chamber, but he ſteps me to her Trencher, and ſteales her Capons-leg: O, 'tis a foule thing, when a Cur cannot keepe himſelfe in all companies: I would haue (as one ſhould ſay) one that takes vpon him to be a dog indeede, to be, as it were, a dog at all things. If I had not had more wit then he, to take a fault vpon me that he did, I thinke verily hee had bin hang'd for't: ſure as I liue he had ſuffer'd for't: you ſhall iudge: Hee thruſts me himſelfe into the company of three or foure gentleman-like-dogs, vnder the Dukes table: hee had not bin there (bleſſe the marke) a piſſing while, but all the chamber ſmelt him: out with the dog (ſaies one) what cur is that (ſaies another) whip him out (ſaies the third) hang him vp (ſaies the Duke.) I hauing bin acquainted with the ſmell before, knew it was Crab; and goes me to the fellow that whips the dogges: friend (quoth I) you meane to whip the dog: I marry doe I (quoth he) you doe him the more wrong (quoth I) 'twas I did the thing you wot of: he makes me no more adoe, but whips me out of the chamber: how many Maſters would doe this for his Seruant? nay, ile be ſworne I haue ſat in the ſtockes, for puddings he hath ſtolne, otherwiſe he had bin executed: I haue ſtood on the Pillorie for Geeſe he hath kil'd, otherwiſe he had ſufferd for't: thou think'ſt not of this now: nay, I remember the tricke you ſeru'd me, when I tooke my leaue of Madam Siluia: did
not I bid thee ſtill marke me, and doe as I doe, when did'ſt thou ſee me heaue vp my leg, and make water againſt a Gentlewomans farthingale? did'ſt thou euer ſee me doe ſuch a tricke?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Sebaſtian is thy name: I like thee well,
And will imploy thee in ſome ſeruice preſently.

sp.speaker: Iu.
sp.p: In what you pleaſe, ile doe what I can.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: I hope thou wilt.
How now you whor-ſon pezant,
Where haue you bin theſe two dayes loytering?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Marry Sir, I carried Miſtris Siluia the dogge you bad me.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: And what ſaies ſhe to my little Iewell?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Marry ſhe ſaies your dog was a cur, and tels you curriſh thanks is good enough for ſuch a preſent.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: But ſhe receiu'd my dog?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: No indeede did ſhe not:
Here haue I brought him backe againe.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: What, didſt thou offer her this from me?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: I Sir, the other Squirrill was ſtolne from me
By the Hangmans boyes in the market place,
And then I offer'd her mine owne, who is a dog
As big as ten of yours, & therefore the guift the greater.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Goe, get thee hence, and finde my dog againe,
Or nere returne againe into my ſight.
Away, I ſay: ſtayeſt thou to vexe me here;
A Slaue, that ſtill an end, turnes me to ſhame:
Sebaſtian, I haue entertained thee,
Partly that I haue neede of ſuch a youth,
That can with ſome diſcretion doe my buſineſſe:
For 'tis no truſting to yond fooliſh Lowt;
But chiefely, for thy face, and thy behauiour,
Which (if my Augury deceiue me not)
Witneſſe good bringing vp, fortune, and truth:
Therefore know thee, for this I entertaine thee.
Go preſently, and take this Ring with thee,
Deliuer it to Madam Siluia;
She lou'd me well, deliuer'd it to me.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: It ſeemes you lou'd not her, not leaue her token:
She is dead belike?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Not ſo: I thinke ſhe liues.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Alas.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Why do'ſt thou cry alas?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: I cannot chooſe but pitty her.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Wherefore ſhould'ſt thou pitty her?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Becauſe, me thinkes that ſhe lou'd you as well
As you doe loue your Lady Siluia:
She dreames on him, that has forgot her loue,
You doate on her, that cares not for your loue.
'Tis pitty Loue, ſhould be ſo contrary:
And thinking on it, makes me cry alas.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Well: giue her that Ring, and therewithall
This Letter: that's her chamber: Tell my Lady,
I claime the promiſe for her heauenly Picture:
Your meſſage done, hye home vnto my chamber,
Where thou ſhalt finde me ſad, and ſolitarie.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: How many women would doe ſuch a meſſage?
Alas poore Protheus, thou haſt entertain'd
A Foxe, to be the Shepheard of thy Lambs;
Alas, poore foole, why doe I pitty him
That with his very heart deſpiſeth me?
Becauſe he loues her, he deſpiſeth me,
Becauſe I loue him, I muſt pitty him.
This Ring I gaue him, when he parted from me,
To binde him to remember my good will:
And now am I (vnhappy Meſſenger)
To plead for that, which I would not obtaine;
To carry that, which I would haue refus'd;
To praiſe his faith, which I would haue diſprais'd.
I am my Maſters true confirmed Loue,
But cannot be true ſeruant to my Maſter,
Vnleſſe I proue falſe traitor to my ſelfe.
Yet will I woe for him but yet ſo coldly,
As (heauen it knowes) I would not haue him ſpeed.
Gentlewoman, good day: I pray you be my meane
To bring me where to ſpeake with Madam Siluia.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: What would you with her, if that I be ſhe?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: If you be ſhe, I doe intreat your patience
To heare me ſpeake the meſſage I am ſent on.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: From whom?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: From my Maſter, Sir Protheus, Madam.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Oh: he ſends you for a Picture?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: I, Madam.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Vrſula, bring my Picture there,
Goe, giue your Maſter this: tell him from me,
One Iulia, that his changing thoughts forget
Would better fit his Chamber, then this Shadow.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Madam, pleaſe you peruſe this Letter;
Pardon me (Madam) I haue vnaduis'd
Deliuer'd you a paper that I ſhould not;
This is the Letter to your Ladiſhip.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: I pray thee let me looke on that againe.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: It may not be: good Madam pardon me.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: There, hold:
I will not looke vpon your Maſters lines:
I know they are ſtuft with proteſtations,
And full of new-found oathes, which he will breake
As eaſily as I doe teare his paper.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Madam, he ſends your Ladiſhip this Ring.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: The more ſhame for him, that he ſends it me;
For I haue heard him ſay a thouſand times,
His Iulia gaue it him, at his departure:
Though his falſe finger haue prophan'd the Ring,
Mine ſhall not doe his Iulia ſo much wrong.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: She thankes you.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: What ſai'ſt thou?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: I thanke you Madam, that you tender her:
Poore Gentlewoman, my Maſter wrongs her much.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Do'ſt thou know her?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Almoſt as well as I doe know my ſelfe.
To thinke vpon her woes, I doe proteſt
That I haue wept a hundred ſeuerall times.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Belike ſhe thinks that Protheus hath forſook her?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: I thinke ſhe doth: and that's her cauſe of ſorrow▪

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Is ſhe not paſſing faire?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: She hath bin fairer (Madam) then ſhe is,
When ſhe did thinke my Maſter lou'd her well;
She, in my iudgement, was as faire as you.
But ſince ſhe did neglect her looking-glaſſe,
And threw her Sun-expelling Maſque away,
The ayre hath ſtaru'd the roſes in her cheekes,
And pinch'd the lilly-tincture of her face,
That now ſhe is become as blacke as I.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: How tall was ſhe?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: About my ſtature: for at Pentecoſt,
When all our Pageants of delight were plaid,
Our youth got me to play the womans part,
And I was trim'd in Madam Iulius gowne,
Which ſerued me as fit, by all mens iudgements,
As if the garment had bin made for me:
Therefore I know ſhe is about my height,
And at that time I made her weepe a good.
For I did play a lamentable part.
(Madam) 'twas Ariadne, paſſioning
For Theſus periury, and vniuſt flight;
Which I ſo liuely acted with my teares:
That my poore Miſtris moued therewithall,
Wept bitterly: and would I might be dead,
If I in thought felt not her very ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: She is beholding to thee (gentle youth)
Alas (poore Lady) deſolate, and left;
I weepe my ſelfe to thinke vpon thy words:
Here youth: there is my purſe; I giue thee this
For thy ſweet Miſtris ſake, becauſe thou lou'ſt her. Farewell.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: And ſhe ſhall thanke you for't, if ere you know her.
A vertuous gentlewoman, milde, and beautifull.
I hope my Maſters ſuit will be but cold,
Since ſhe reſpects my Miſtris loue ſo much.
Alas, how loue can triſle with it ſelfe:
Here is her Picture: let me ſee, I thinke
If I had ſuch a Tyre, this face of mine
Were full as louely, as is this of hers;
And yet the Painter flatter'd her a little,
Vnleſſe I flatter with my ſelfe too much.
Her haire is Aburne, mine is perfect Yellow;
If that be all the difference in his loue,
Ile get me ſuch a coulour'd Perrywig:
Her eyes are grey as glaſſe, and ſo are mine:
I, but her fore-head's low, and mine's as high:
What ſhould it be that he reſpects in her,
But I can make reſpectiue in my ſelfe?
If this fond Loue, were not a blinded god.
Come ſhadow, come, and take this ſhadow vp,
For 'tis thy riuall: O thou ſenceleſſe forme.
Thou ſhalt be worſhip'd, kiſs'd, lou'd, and ador'd;
And were there ſence in his Idolatry,
My ſubſtance ſhould be ſtatue in thy ſtead.
Ile vſe thee kindly, for thy Miſtris ſake
That vs'd me ſo: or elſe by Ioue, I vow,
I ſhould haue ſcratch'd out your vnſeeing eyes,
To make my Maſter out of loue with thee.

sp.speaker: Egl.
sp.l: The Sun begins to guild the weſterne skie,
And now it is about the very houre
That Siluia, at Fryer Patricks Cell ſhould meet me,
She will not faile; for Louers breake not houres,
Vnleſſe it be to come before their time,
So much they ſpur their expedition.
See where ſhe comes: Lady a happy euening.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Amen, Amen: goe on (good Eglamoure)
Out at the Poſterne by the Abbey wall;
I feare I am attended by ſome Spies.

sp.speaker: Egl.
sp.l: Feare not: the Forreſt is not three leagues off,
If we recouer that, we are ſure enough.

sp.speaker: Th.
sp.p: Sir Protheus, what ſaies Siluia to my ſuit?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Oh Sir, I finde her milder then ſhe was,
And yet ſhe takes exceptions at your perſon.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: What? that my leg is too long?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: No, that it is too little.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: Ile weare a Boote, to make it ſomewhat rounder.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: But loue will not be ſpurd to what it loath • .

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: What ſaies ſhe to my face?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: She ſaies it is a faire one.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: Nay then the wanton lyes: my face is blacke.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: But Pearles are faire; and the old ſaying is,
Blacke men are Pearles, in beauteous Ladies eyes.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.l: 'Tis true, ſuch Pearles as put out Ladies eyes,
For I had rather winke, then looke on them.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: How likes ſhe my diſcourſe?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Ill, when you talke of war.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: But well, when I diſcourſe of loue and peace.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: But better indeede, when you hold you peace.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: What ſayes ſhe to my valour?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Oh Sir, ſhe makes no doubt of that.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: She needes not, when ſhe knowes it cowardize.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: What ſaies ſhe to my birth?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: That you are well deriu'd.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: True: from a Gentleman, to a foole.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: Conſiders ſhe my Poſſeſſions?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Oh, I: and pitties them.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: Wherefore?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: That ſuch an Aſſe ſhould owe them.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: That they are out by Leaſe.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Here comes the Duke.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: How now ſir Protheus; how now Thurio?
Which of you ſaw Eglamoure of late?

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: Not I.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Nor I.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: Saw you my daughter?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Neither.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Why then
She's fled vnto that pezant, Valentine;
And Eglamoure is in her Company:
'Tis true: for Frier Laurence met them both
As he, in pennance wander'd through the Forreſt:
Him he knew well: and gueſd that it was ſhe,
But being mask'd, he was not ſure of it.
Beſides ſhe did intend Confeſſion
At Patricks Cell this euen, and there ſhe was not.
Theſe likelihoods confirme her flight from hence;
Therefore I pray you ſtand, not to diſcourſe,
But mount you preſently, and meete with me
Vpon the riſing of the Mountaine foote
That leads toward Mantua, whether they are fled:
Diſpatch (ſweet Gentlemen) and follow me.

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.l: Why this it is, to be a peeuiſh Girle,
That flies her fortune when it followes her:
Ile after; more to be reueng'd on Eglamoure,
Then for the loue of reck-leſſe Siluia.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: And I will follow, more for Siluas loue
Then hate of Eglamoure that goes with her.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: And I will follow, more to croſſe that loue
Then hate for Siluia, that is gone for loue.

sp.speaker: 1. Out.
sp.l: Come, come be patient:
We muſt bring you to our Captaine.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: A thouſand more miſchances then this one
Haue learn'd me how to brooke this patiently.

sp.speaker: 2 Out.
sp.p: Come, bring her away.

sp.speaker: 1 Out.
sp.p: Where is the Gentleman that was with her?

sp.speaker: 3 Out.
sp.l: Being nimble footed, he hath out▪ run vs.
But Moyſes and Valerius follow him:
Goe thou with her to the Weſt end of the wood,
There is our Captaine: Wee'll follow him that's fled,
The Thicket is beſet, he cannot ſcape.

sp.speaker: 1 Out.
sp.l: Come, I muſt bring you to our Captains caue.
Feare not: he beares an honourable minde,
And will not vſe a woman lawleſly.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: O Valentine: this I endure for thee.

div.head: Scoena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Valentine, Protheus, Siluia, Iulia, Duke, Thurio, Out-lawes.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: How vſe doth breed a habit in a man?
This ſhadowy deſart, vnfrequented woods
I better brooke then flouriſhing peopled Townes:
Here can I ſit alone, vn-ſeene of any,
And to the Nightingales complaining Notes
Tune my diſtreſtes, and record my woes.
O thou that doſt inhabit in my breſt,
Leaue not the Manſion ſo long Tenant-leſſe,
Leſt growing ruinous, the building fall,
And leaue no memory of what it was,
Repaire me, with thy preſence, Siluia:
Thou gentle Nimph, cheriſh thy for-lorne ſwaine.
What hallowing, and what ſtir is this to day?
Theſe are my mates, that make their wills their Law,
Haue ſome vnhappy paſſenger in chace;
They loue me well: yet I haue much to doe
To keepe them from vnciuill outrages.
Withdraw thee Valentine: who's this comes heere?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Madam, this ſeruice I haue done for you
(Though you reſpect not aught your ſeruant doth)
To hazard life, and reskew you from him,
That would haue forc'd your honour, and your loue,
Vouchſafe me for my meed, but one faire looke:
(A ſmaller boone then this I cannot beg,
And leſſe then this, I am ſure you cannot giue.)

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: How like a dreame is this? I ſee, and heare:
Loue, lend me patience to forbeare a while.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: O miſerable, vnhappy that I am.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Vnhappy were you (Madam) ere I came:
But by my comming, I haue made you happy.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: By thy approach thou mak'ſt me moſt vnhappy.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: And me, when he approcheth to your preſence

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: Had I beene ceazed by a hungry Lion,
I would haue beene a break-faſt to the Beaſt,
Rather then haue falſe Protheus reskue me:
Oh heauen be iudge how I loue Valentine,
Whoſe life's as tender to me as my ſoule,
And full as much (for more there cannot be)
I doe deteſt falſe periur'd Protheus:
Therefore be gone, ſollicit me no more.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: What dangerous action, ſtood it next to death
Would I not vndergoe, for one calme looke:
Oh 'tis the curſe in Loue, and ſtill approu'd
When women cannot loue, where they're belou'd.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.l: When Protheus cannot loue, where he's belou'd:
Read ouer Iulia's heart, (thy firſt beſt Loue)
For whoſe deare ſake, thou didſt then rend thy faith
Into a thouſand oathes; and all thoſe oathes,
Deſcended into periury, to loue me,
Thou haſt no faith left now, vnleſſe thou'dſt two,
And that's farre worſe then none: better haue none
Then plurall faith, which is too much by one:
Thou Counterfeyt, to thy true friend.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: In Loue,
Who reſpects friend?

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: All men but Protheus.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Nay, if the gentle ſpirit of mouing words
Can no way change you to a milder forme;
Ile wooe you like a Souldier, at armes end,
And loue you 'gainſt the nature of Loue: force ye.

sp.speaker: Sil.
sp.p: Oh heauen.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Ile force thee yeeld to my deſire.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Ruffian: let goe that rude vnciuill touch,
Thou friend of an ill faſhion.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Thou cōmon friend, that's without faith or loue,
For ſuch is a friend now: treacherous man,
Thou haſt beguil'd my hopes; nought but mine eye
Could haue perſwaded me: now I dare not ſay
I haue one friend aliue; thou wouldſt diſproue me:
Who ſhould be truſted, when ones right hand
Is periured to the boſome? Protheus
I am ſorry I muſt neuer truſt thee more,
But count the world a ſtranger for thy ſake:
The priuate wound is deepeſt: oh time, moſt accurſt:
'Mongſt all foes that a friend ſhould be the worſt?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: My ſhame and guilt confounds me:
Forgiue me Valentine: if hearty ſorrow
Be a ſufficient Ranſome for offence,
I tender't heere: I doe as truely ſuffer,
As ere I did commit.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Then I am paid:
And once againe, I doe receiue thee honeſt;
Who by Repentance is not ſatisfied,
Is nor of heauen, nor earth; for theſe are pleas'd:
By Penitence th' Eternalls wrath's appeas'd:
And that my loue may appeare plaine and free,
All that was mine, in Siluia, I giue thee.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Oh me vnhappy.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Looke to the Boy.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Why, Boy?
Why wag: how now? what's the matter? look vp: ſpeak.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: O good ſir, my maſter charg'd me to deliuer a ring to Madam Siluia: wc (out of my neglect) was neuer done.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Where is that ring? boy?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: Heere 'tis▪ this is it.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: How? let me ſee.
Why this is the ring I gaue to Iulia.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Oh, cry you mercy ſir, I haue miſtooke:
This is the ring you ſent to Siluia.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: But how cam'ſt thou by this ring? at my depart
I gaue this vnto Iulia.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: And Iulia her ſelfe did giue it me,
And Iulia her ſelfe hath brought it hither.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: How? Iulia?

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.l: Behold her, that gaue ayme to all thy oathes,
And entertain'd 'em deepely in her heart.
How oft haſt thou with periury cleft the roote?
Oh Protheus, let this habit make thee bluſh.
Be thou aſham'd that I haue tooke vpon me,
Such an immodeſt rayment; if ſhame liue
In a diſguiſe of loue?
It is the leſſer blot modeſty findes,
Women to change their ſhapes, then men their minds.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Then men their minds? tis true: oh heuen, were man
But Conſtant, he were perfect; that one error
Fils him with faults: makes him run through all th' ſins;
Inconſtancy falls-off, ere it begins:
What is in Siluia's face, but I may ſpie
More freſh in Iulia's, with a conſtant eye?

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: Come, come: a hand from either:
Let me be bleſt to make this happy cloſe:
'Twere pitty two ſuch friends ſhould be long foes.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Beare witnes (heauen) I haue my wiſh for euer.

sp.speaker: Iul.
sp.p: And I mine.

sp.speaker: Out-l.
sp.p: A prize: a prize: a prize.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Forbeare, forbeare I ſay: It is my Lord the Duke.
Your Grace is welcome to a man diſgrac'd,
Baniſhed Valentine.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Sir Valentine?

sp.speaker: Thu.
sp.p: Yonder is Siluia: and Siluia's mine.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Thurio giue backe; or elſe embrace thy death:
Come not within the meaſure of my wrath:
Doe not name Siluia thine: if once againe,
Ʋerona ſhall not hold thee: heere ſhe ſtands,
Take but poſſeſſion of her, with a Touch:
I dare thee, but to breath vpon my Loue.

sp.speaker: Thur.
sp.l: Sir Valentine, I care not for her, I:
I hold him but a foole that will endanger
His Body, for a Girle that loues him not:
I claime her not, and therefore ſhe is thine.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: The more degenerate and baſe art thou
To make ſuch meanes for her, as thou haſt done,
And leaue her on ſuch ſlight conditions.
Now, by the honor of my Anceſtry,
I doe applaud thy ſpirit, Valentine,
And thinke thee worthy of an Empreſſe loue:
Know then, I heere forget all former greefes,
Cancell all grudge, repeale thee home againe,
Plead a new ſtate in thy vn-riual'd merit,
To which I thus ſubſcribe: Sir Ʋalentine,
Thou art a Gentleman, and well deriu'd,
Take thou thy Siluia, for thou haſt deſeru'd her.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.l: I thank your Grace, ye gift hath made me happy:
I now beſeech you (for your daughters ſake)
To grant one Boone that I ſhall aske of you.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: I grant it (for thine owne) what ere it be.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Theſe baniſh'd men, that I haue kept withall,
Are men endu'd with worthy qualities:
Forgiue them what they haue committed here,
And let them be recall'd from their Exile:
They are reformed, ciuill, full of good,
And fit for great employment (worthy Lord.)

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Thou haſt preuaild, I pardon them and thee:
Diſpoſe of them, as thou knowſt their deſerts.
Come, let vs goe, we will include all iarres,
With Triumphes, Mirth, and rare ſolemnity.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: And as we walke along, I dare be bold
With our diſcourſe, to make your Grace to ſmile.
What thinke you of this Page (my Lord?)

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: I think the Boy hath grace in him, he bluſhes.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: I warrant you (my Lord) more grace, then Boy.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: What meane you by that ſaying?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Pleaſe you, Ile tell you, as we paſſe along,
That you will wonder what hath fortuned:
Come Protheus, 'tis your pennance, but to heare
The ſtory of your Loues diſcouered.
That done, our day of marriage ſhall be yours,
One Feaſt, one houſe, one mutuall happineſſe.

div.head: The names of all the Actors.

list.item: Thurio: a fooliſh riuall to Valentine.
Eglamoure: Agent for Siluia in her eſcape.
Speed: a clowniſh ſeruant to Valentine.

div.head: Scena prima.
div.stage: Enter Iuſtice Shallow, Slender, Sir Hugh Euans, Maſter Page, Falſtoffe, Bardolph, Nym, Piſtoll, Anne Page, Miſtreſſe Ford, Miſtreſſe Page, Simple.

sp.speaker: Shallow.
sp.p: SIr Hugh, perſwade me not: I will make a Star-Chamber matter of it, if hee were twenty Sir Iohn Falſtoffs, he ſhall not abuſe Robert Shallow Eſquire.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: In the County of Gloceſter, Iuſtice of Peace and Coram.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: I (Coſen Slender) and Cuſt-alorum.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I, and Rato lorum too; and a Gentleman borne (Maſter Parſon) who writes himſelfe Armigero, in any Bill, Warrant, Quittance, or Obligation, Armigero.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: I that I doe, and haue done any time theſe three hundred yeeres.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: All his ſucceſſors (gone before him) hath don't: and all his Anceſtors (that come after him) may: they may giue the dozen white Luces in their Coate.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: It is an olde Coate.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.p: The dozen white Lowſes doe become an old Coat well: it agrees well paſſant: It is a familiar beaſt to man, and ſignifies Loue.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: The Luſe is the freſh-fiſh, the ſalt-fiſh, is an old Coate.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I may quarter (Coz).

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: You may, by marrying.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.p: It is marring indeed, if he quarter it.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Not a whit.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Yes per-lady: if he ha's a quarter of your coat, there is but three Skirts for your ſelfe, in my ſimple coniectures; but that is all one: if Sir Iohn Falſtaffe haue committed diſparagements vnto you, I am of the Church and will be glad to do my beneuolence, to make attonements and compremiſes betweene you.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: The Councell ſhall heare it, it is a Riot.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: It is not meet the Councell heare a Riot: there is no feare of Got in a Riot: The Councell (looke you) ſhall deſire to heare the feare of Got, and not to heare a Riot: take your viza-ments in that.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Ha; o' my life, if I were yong againe, the ſword ſhould end it.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.p: It is petter that friends is the ſword, and end it: and there is alſo another deuice in my praine, which peraduenture prings goot diſcretions with it. There is Anne Page, which is daughter to Maſter Thomas Page, which is pretty virginity.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Miſtris Anne Page? ſhe has browne haire, and ſpeakes ſmall like a woman.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.p: It is that ferry perſon for all the orld, as iuſt as you will deſire, and ſeuen hundred pounds of Moneyes, and Gold, and Siluer, is her Grand-ſire vpon his deaths-bed, (Got deliuer to a ioyfull reſurrections) giue, when ſhe is able to ouertake ſeuenteene yeeres old. It were a goot motion, if we leaue our pribbles and prabbles, and deſire a marriage betweene Maſter Abraham, and Miſtris Anne Page.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Did her Grand-ſire leaue her ſeauen hundred pound?

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: I, and her father is make her a petter penny.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I know the young Gentlewoman, ſhe has good gifts.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Seuen hundred pounds, and poſſibilities, is goot gifts.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Wel, let vs ſee honeſt Mr Page: is Falſtaffe there?

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Shall I tell you a lye? I doe deſpiſe a lyer, as I doe deſpiſe one that is falſe, or as I deſpiſe one that is not true: the Knight Sir Iohn is there, and I beſeech you be ruled by your well-willers: I will peat the doore for Mr. Page. What hoa? Got-pleſſe your houſe heere.

sp.speaker: Mr. Page.
sp.p: Who's there?

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Here is go't's pleſſing and your friend, and Iuſtice Shallow, and heere yong Maſter Slender: that peraduentures ſhall tell you another tale, if matters grow to your likings.
I am glad to ſee your Worſhips well: I thanke you for my Veniſon Maſter Shallow.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Maſter Page, I am glad to ſee you: much good doe it your good heart: I wiſh'd your Veniſon better, it was ill killd: how doth good Miſtreſſe Page? and I thank you alwaies with my heart, la: with my heart.

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: Sir, I thanke you.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Sir, I thanke you: by yea, and no I doe.

sp.speaker: M. Pa.
sp.p: I am glad to ſee you, good Maſter Slender.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: How do's your fallow Greyhound, Sir, I heard ſay he was out-run on Cotſall.

sp.speaker: M. Pa.
sp.p: It could not be iudg'd, Sir.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: You'll not confeſſe: you'll not confeſſe.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: That he will not, 'tis your fault, 'tis your fault: 'tis a good dogge.

sp.speaker: M. Pa.
sp.p: A Cur, Sir.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Sir: hee's a good dog, and a faire dog, can there be more ſaid? he is good, and faire. Is Sir Iohn Falſtaffe heere?

sp.speaker: M. Pa.
sp.p: Sir, hee is within: and I would I could doe a good office betweene you.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: It is ſpoke as a Chriſtians ought to ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: He hath wrong'd me (Maſter Page.)

sp.speaker: M. Pa.
sp.p: Sir, he doth in ſome ſort confeſſe it.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: If it be confeſſed, it is not redreſſed; is not that ſo (M. Page?) he hath wrong'd me, indeed he hath, at a word he hath: beleeue me, Robert Shallow Eſquire, ſaith he is wronged.

sp.speaker: Ma. Pa.
sp.p: Here comes Sir Iohn.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Now, Maſter Shallow, you'll complaine of me to the King?

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Knight, you haue beaten my men, kill'd my deere, and broke open my Lodge.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: But not kiſs'd your Keepers daughter?

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Tut, a pin: this ſhall be anſwer'd.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.l: I will anſwere it ſtrait, I haue done all this:
That is now anſwer'd.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: The Councell ſhall know this.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: 'Twere better for you if it were known in councell: you'll be laugh'd at.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: Pauca verba; (Sir Iohn) good worts.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Good worts? good Cabidge; Slender, I broke your head: what matter haue you againſt me?

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Marry ſir, I haue matter in my head againſt you, and againſt your cony-catching Raſcalls, Bardolf, Nym, and Piſtoll.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: You Banbery Cheeſe.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I, it is no matter.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: How now, Mephoſtophilus?

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I, it is no matter.

sp.speaker: Nym.
sp.p: Slice, I ſay; pauca. pauca: Slice, that's my humor.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Where's Simple my man? can you tell, Coſen?

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: Peace, I pray you: now let vs vnderſtand: there is three Vmpires in this matter, as I vnderſtand; that is, Maſter Page (fidelicet Maſter Page,) & there is my ſelfe, (fidelicet my ſelfe) and the three party is (laſtly, and finally) mine Hoſt of the Gater.

sp.speaker: Ma. Pa.
sp.p: We three to hear it, & end it between them.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Ferry goo't, I will make a priefe of it in my note-booke, and we wil afterwards orke vpon the cauſe, with as great diſcreetly as we can.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: He heares with eares.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: The Teuill and his Tam: what phraſe is this? he heares with eare? why, it is affectations.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Piſtoll, did you picke M. Slenders purſe?

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I, by theſe gloues did hee, or I would I might neuer come in mine owne great chamber againe elſe, of ſeauen groates in mill-ſixpences, and two Edward Shouelboords, that coſt me two ſhilling and two pence a peece of Yead Miller: by theſe gloues.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Is this true, Piſtoll?

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: No, it is falſe, if it is a picke-purſe.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: Ha, thou mountaine Forreyner: Sir Iohn, and Maſter mine, I combat challenge of this Latine Bilboe: word of deniall in thy labras here; word of denial; froth, and ſcum thou lieſt.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: By theſe gloues, then 'twas he.

sp.speaker: Nym.
sp.p: Be auis'd ſir, and paſſe good humours: I will ſay marry trap with you, if you runne the nut-hooks humor on me, that is the very note of it.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: By this hat, then he in the red face had it: for though I cannot remember what I did when you made me drunke, yet I am not altogether an aſſe.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: What ſay you Scarlet, and Iohn?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: Why ſir, (for my part) I ſay the Gentleman had drunke himſelfe out of his fiue ſentences.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: It is his fiue ſences: fie, what the ignorance is.
