sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: And being fap, ſir, was (as they ſay) caſheerd: and ſo concluſions paſt the Car-eires.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I, you ſpake in Latten then to: but 'tis no matter; Ile nere be drunk whilſt I liue againe, but in honeſt, ciuill, godly company for this tricke: if I be drunke, Ile be drunke with thoſe that haue the feare of God, and not with drunken knaues.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: So got-udge me, that is a vertuons minde.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: You heare all theſe matters deni'd, Gentlemen; you heare it.

sp.speaker: Mr. Page.
sp.p: Nay daughter, carry the wine in, wee'll drinke within.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Oh heauen: This is Miſtreſſe Anne Page.

sp.speaker: Mr. Page.
sp.p: How now Miſtris Ford?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Miſtris Ford, by my troth you are very wel met: by your leaue good Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Mr. Page.
sp.p: Wife, bid theſe gentlemen welcome: come, we haue a hot Veniſon paſty to dinner; Come gentlemen, I hope we ſhall drinke downe all vnkindneſſe.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I had rather then forty ſhillings I had my booke of Songs and Sonnets heere: How now Simple, where haue you beene? I muſt wait on my ſelfe, muſt I? you haue not the booke of Riddles about you, haue you?

sp.speaker: Sim.
sp.p: Booke of Riddles? why did you not lend it to Alice Short-cake vpon Alhallowmas laſt, a fortnight afore Michaelmas.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Come Coz, come Coz, we ſtay for you: a word with you Coz: marry this, Coz: there is as 'twere a tender, a kinde of tender, made a farre-off by Sir Hugh here: doe you vnderſtand me?

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I Sir, you ſhall finde me reaſonable; if it be ſo, I ſhall doe that that is reaſon.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Nay, but vnderſtand me.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: So I doe Sir.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Giue eare to his motions; (Mr. Slender) I will deſcription the matter to you, if you be capacity of it.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Nay, I will doe as my Cozen Shallow ſaies: I pray you pardon me, he's a Iuſtice of Peace in his Countrie, ſimple though I ſtand here.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: But that is not the queſtion: the queſtion is concerning your marriage.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: I, there's the point Sir.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: Marry is it: the very point of it, to Mi. An Page.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Why if it be ſo; I will marry her vpon any reaſonable demands.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: But can you affection the 'o-man, let vs command to know that of your mouth, or of your lips: for diuers Philoſophers hold, that the lips is parcell of the mouth: therfore preciſely, cā you carry your good wil to ye maid?

sp.speaker: Sh.
sp.p: Coſen Abraham Slender, can you loue her?

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I hope ſir, I will do as it ſhall become one that would doe reaſon.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: Nay, got's Lords, and his Ladies, you muſt ſpeake poſſitable, if you can carry-her your deſires towards her.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.l: That you muſt:
Will you, (vpon good dowry) marry her?

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I will doe a greater thing then that, vpon your requeſt (Coſen) in any reaſon.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Nay conceiue me, conceiue mee, (ſweet Coz): what I doe is to pleaſure you (Coz:) can you loue the maid?

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I will marry her (Sir) at your requeſt; but if there bee no great loue in the beginning, yet Heauen may decreaſe it vpon better acquaintance, when wee are married, and haue more occaſion to know one another: I hope vpon familiarity will grow more content: but if you ſay mary-her, I will mary-her, that I am freely diſſolued, and diſſolutely.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: It is a fery diſcetion-anſwere; ſaue the fall is in the'ord, diſſolutely: the ort is (according to our meaning) reſolutely: his meaning is good.

sp.speaker: Sh.
sp.p: I: I thinke my Coſen meant well.

sp.speaker: Sl.
sp.p: I, or elſe I would I might be hang'd (la.)

sp.speaker: Sh.
sp.p: Here comes faire Miſtris Anne; would I were yong for your ſake, Miſtris Anne.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: The dinner is on the Table, my Father deſires your worſhips company.

sp.speaker: Sh.
sp.p: I will wait on him, (faire Miſtris Anne.)

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: Od's pleſſed-wil: I wil not be abſēce at the grace.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Wil't pleaſe your worſhip to come in, Sir?

sp.speaker: Sl.
sp.p: No, I thank you forſooth, hartely; I am very well.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: The dinner attends you, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sl.
sp.p: I am not a-hungry, I thanke you, forſooth: goe, Sirha, for all you are my man, goe wait vpon my Coſen Shallow: a Iuſtice of peace ſometime may be beholding to his friend, for a Man; I keepe but three Men, and a Boy yet, till my Mother be dead: but what though, yet I liue like a poore Gentleman borne.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I may not goe in without your worſhip: they will not ſit till you come.

sp.speaker: Sl.
sp.p: I' faith, ile eate nothing: I thanke you as much as though I did.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I pray you Sir walke in.

sp.speaker: Sl.
sp.p: I had rather walke here (I thanke you) I bruiz'd my ſhin th' other day, with playing at Sword and Dagger with a Maſter of Fence (three veneys for a diſh of ſtew'd Prunes) and by my troth, I cannot abide the ſmell of hot meate ſince. Why doe your dogs barke ſo? be there Beares ith' Towne?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I thinke there are, Sir, I heard them talk'd of.

sp.speaker: Sl.
sp.p: I loue the ſport well, but I ſhall as ſoone quarrell at it, as any man in England: you are afraid if you ſee the Beare looſe, are you not?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I indeede Sir.

sp.speaker: Sl.
sp.p: That's meate and drinke to me now: I haue ſeene Sackerſon looſe, twenty times, and haue taken him by the Chaine: but (I warrant you) the women haue ſo cride and ſhrekt at it, that it paſt: But women indeede, cannot abide'em, they are very ill-fauour'd rough things.

sp.speaker: Ma. Pa.
sp.p: Come, gentle M. Slender, come; we ſtay for you.

sp.speaker: Sl.
sp.p: Ile eate nothing, I thanke you Sir.

sp.speaker: Ma. Pa.
sp.p: By cocke and pie, you ſhall not chooſe, Sir: come, come.

sp.speaker: Sl.
sp.p: Nay, pray you lead the way.

sp.speaker: Ma. Pa.
sp.p: Come on, Sir.

sp.speaker: Sl.
sp.p: Miſtris Anne: your ſelfe ſhall goe firſt.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Not I Sir, pray you keepe on.

sp.speaker: Sl.
sp.p: Truely I will not goe firſt: truely-la: I will not doe you that wrong.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I pray you Sir.

sp.speaker: Sl.
sp.p: Ile rather be vnmannerly, then troubleſome: you doe your ſelfe wrong indeede-la.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: Go your waies, and aske of Doctor Caius houſe, which is the way; and there dwels one Miſtris Quickly; which is in the manner of his Nurſe; or his dry-Nurſe; or his Cooke; or his Laundry; his Waſher, and his Ringer.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.p: Well Sir.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: Nay, it is petter yet: giue her this letter; for it is a'oman that altogeathers acquaintāce with Miſtris Anne Page; and the Letter is to deſire, and require her to ſolicite your Maſters deſires, to Miſtris Anne Page: I pray you be gon: I will make an end of my dinner; ther's Pippins and Cheeſe to come.

div.head: Scena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Falſtaffe, Hoſt, Bardolfe, Nym, Piſtoll, Page.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Mine Hoſt of the Garter?

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: What ſaies my Bully Rooke? ſpeake ſchollerly, and wiſely.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Truely mine Hoſt; I muſt turne away ſome of my followers.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: Diſcard, (bully Hercules) caſheere; let them wag; trot, trot.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I ſit at ten pounds a weeke.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: Thou'rt an Emperor (Ceſar, Keiſer and Pheazar) I will entertaine Bardolfe: he ſhall draw; he ſhall tap; ſaid I well (bully Hector?)

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: Doe ſo (good mine Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Ho.
sp.p: I haue ſpoke: let him follow: let me ſee thee froth, and liue: I am at a word: follow.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Bardolfe, follow him: a Tapſter is a good trade: an old Cloake, makes a new Ierkin: a wither'd Seruing-man, a freſh Tapſter: goe, adew.

sp.speaker: Ba.
sp.p: It is a life that I haue deſir'd: I will thriue.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: O baſe hungarian wight: wilt yu the ſpigot wield.

sp.speaker: Ni.
sp.p: He was gotten in drink: is not the humor cōceited?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I am glad I am ſo acquit of this Tinderbox: his Thefts were too open: his filching was like an vnskilfull Singer, he kept not time.

sp.speaker: Ni.
sp.p: The good humor is to ſteale at a minutes reſt.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: Conuay: the wiſe it call: Steale? foh: a fico for the phraſe.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Well ſirs, I am almoſt out at heeles.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: Why then let Kibes enſue.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: There is no remedy: I muſt conicatch, I muſt ſhift.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: Yong Rauens muſt haue foode.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Which of you know Ford of this Towne?

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: I ken the wight: he is of ſubſtance good.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: My honeſt Lads, I will tell you what I am about.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: Two yards, and more.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: No quips now Piſtoll: (Indeede I am in the waſte two yards about: but I am now about no waſte: I am about thrift) briefely: I doe meane to make loue to Fords wife: I ſpie entertainment in her: ſhee diſcourſes: ſhee carues: ſhe giues the leere of inuitation: I can conſtrue the action of her familier ſtile, & the hardeſt voice of her behauior (to be engliſh'd rightly) is, I am Sir Iohn Falſtafs.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: He hath ſtudied her will; and tranſlated her will: out of honeſty, into Engliſh.

sp.speaker: Ni.
sp.p: The Anchor is deepe: will that humor paſſe?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Now, the report goes, ſhe has all the rule of her husbands Purſe: he hath a legend of Angels.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: As many diuels entertaine: and to her Boy ſay I.

sp.speaker: Ni.
sp.p: The humor riſes: it is good: humor me the angels.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I haue writ me here a letter to her: & here another to Pages wife, who euen now gaue mee good eyes too; examind my parts with moſt iudicious illiads: ſometimes the beame of her view, guilded my foote: ſometimes my portly belly.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: Then did the Sun on dung-hill ſhine.

sp.speaker: Ni.
sp.p: I thanke thee for that humour.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: O ſhe did ſo courſe o're my exteriors with ſuch a greedy intention, that the appetite of her eye, did ſeeme to ſcorch me vp like a burning-glaſſe: here's another letter to her: She beares the Purſe too: She is a Region in Guiana: all gold, and bountie: I will be Cheaters to them both, and they ſhall be Exchequers to mee: they ſhall be my Eaſt and Weſt Indies, and I will trade to them both: Goe, beare thou this Letter to Miſtris Page; and thou this to Miſtris Ford: we will thriue (Lads) we will thriue.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.l: Shall I Sir Pandarus of Troy become,
And by my ſide weare Steele? then Lucifer take all.

sp.speaker: Ni.
sp.p: I will run no baſe humor: here take the humor-Letter; I will keepe the hauior of reputation.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.l: Hold Sirha, beare you theſe Letters tightly,
Saile like my Pinnaſſe to theſe golden ſhores.
Rogues, hence, auaunt, vaniſh like haile-ſtones; goe,
Trudge; plod away ith' hoofe: ſeeke ſhelter, packe:
Falſtaffe will learne the honor of the age,
French-thrift, you Rogues, my ſelfe, and skirted Page.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.l: Let Vultures gripe thy guts: for gourd, and
Fullam holds: & high and low beguiles the rich & poore,
Teſter ile haue in pouch when thou ſhalt lacke,
Baſe Phrygian Turke.

sp.speaker: Ni.
sp.l: I haue opperations,
Which be humors of reuenge.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: Wilt thou reuenge?

sp.speaker: Ni.
sp.p: By Welkin, and her Star.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: With wit, or Steele?

sp.speaker: Ni.
sp.l: With both the humors, I:
I will diſcuſſe the humour of this Loue to Ford.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.l: And I to Page ſhall eke vnfold
How Falſtaffe (varlet vile)
His Doue will proue; his gold will hold,
And his ſoft couch defile.

sp.speaker: Ni.
sp.p: My humour ſhall not coole: I will incenſe Ford to deale with poyſon: I will poſſeſſe him with yallowneſſe, for the reuolt of mine is dangerous: that is my true humour.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: Thou art the Mars of Malecontents: I ſecond thee: troope on.

div.head: Scoena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Miſtris Quickly, Simple, Iohn Rugby, Doctor, Caius, Fenton.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: What, Iohn Rugby, I pray thee goe to the Caſement, and ſee if you can ſee my Maſter, Maſter Docter Caius comming: if he doe (I' faith) and finde any body in the houſe; here will be an old abuſing of Gods patience, and the Kings Engliſh.

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.p: Ile goe watch.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Goe, and we'll haue a poſſet for't ſoone at night, (in faith) at the latter end of a Sea-cole-fire: An honeſt, willing, kinde fellow, as euer ſeruant ſhall come in houſe withall: and I warrant you, no tel-tale, nor no breedebate: his worſt fault is, that he is giuen to prayer; hee is ſomething peeuiſh that way: but no body but has his fault: but let that paſſe. Peter Simple, you ſay your name is?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.p: I: for fault of a better.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: And Maſter Slender's your Maſter?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.p: I forſooth.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Do's he not weare a great round Beard, like a Glouers pairing-knife?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.p: No forſooth: he hath but a little wee face; with a little yellow Beard: a Caine colourd Beard.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: A ſoftly-ſprighted man, is he not?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.p: I forſooth: but he is as tall a man of his hands, as any is betweene this and his head: he hath fought with a Warrener.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: How ſay you: oh, I ſhould remember him: do's he not hold vp his head (as it were?) and ſtrut in his gate?

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.p: Yes indeede do's he.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Well, heauen ſend Anne Page, no worſe fortune: Tell Maſter Parſon Euans, I will doe what I can for your Maſter: Anne is a good girle, and I wiſh —

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.p: Out alas: here comes my Maſter.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: We ſhall all be ſhent: Run in here, good young man: goe into this Cloſſet: he will not ſtay long: what Iohn Rugby? Iohn: what Iohn I ſay? goe Iohn, goe enquire for my Maſter, I doubt he be not well, that hee comes not home: (and downe, downe, adowne'a. &c.

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.p: Vat is you ſing? I doe not like des-toyes: pray you goe and vetch me in my Cloſſet, vnboyteene verd; a Box, a greene-a-Box: do intend vat I ſpeake? a greene-a-Box.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: I forſooth ile fetch it you: I am glad hee went not in himſelfe: if he had found the yong man he would haue bin horne-mad.

p.hi: Fe, fe, fe, fe, maifoy, il fait for ehando, Ie man voi a le Court la grand affaires.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Is it this Sir?

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.l: Ony mette le au mon pocket, de-petch quickly:
Vere is dat knaue Rugby?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: What Iohn Rugby, Iohn?

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.p: Here Sir.

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.l: You are Iohn Rugby, aad you are Iacke Rugby:
Come, take-a-your Rapier, and come after my heele to the Court.

sp.speaker: Ru.
sp.p: 'Tis ready Sir, here in the Porch.

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.p: By my trot: I tarry too long: od's-me: que ay ie oublie: dere is ſome Simples in my Cloſſet, dat I vill not for the varld I ſhall leaue behinde.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Ay-me, he'll finde the yong man there, & be mad.

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.l: O Diable, Diable: vat is in my Cloſſet?
Villanie, La-roone: Rugby, my Rapier.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Good Maſter be content.

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.p: Wherefore ſhall I be content-a?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: The yong man is an honeſt man.

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.p: What ſhall de honeſt man do in my Cloſſet: dere is no honeſt man dat ſhall come in my Cloſſet.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: I beſeech you be not ſo flegmaticke: heare the truth of it. He came of an errand to mee, from Parſon Hugh.

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.p: Vell.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.p: I forſooth: to deſire her to —

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Peace, I pray you.

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.p: Peace-a-your tongue: ſpeake-a-your Tale.

sp.speaker: Si.
sp.p: To deſire this honeſt Gentlewoman (your Maid) to ſpeake a good word to Miſtris Anne Page, for my Maſter in the way of Marriage.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: This is all indeede-la: but ile nere put my finger in the fire, and neede not.

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.p: Sir Hugh ſend-a you? Rugby, ballow mee ſome paper: tarry you a littell-a-while.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: I am glad he is ſo quiet if he had bin throughly moued, you ſhould haue heard him ſo loud, and ſo melancholly: but notwithſtanding man, Ile doe yoe your Maſter what good I can: and the very yea, & the no is, ye French Doctor my Maſter, (I may call him my Maſter, looke you, for I keepe his houſe; and I waſh, • ing, brew, bake, ſcowre, dreſſe meat and drinke, make the beds, and doe all my ſelfe.)

sp.speaker: Simp.
sp.p: 'Tis a great charge to come vnder one bodies hand.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Are you a-uis'd o' that? you ſhall finde it a great charge: and to be vp early, and down later but notwithſtanding, (to tell you in your eare, I wold haue no words of it) my Maſter himſelfe is in loue with Miſtris Anne Page: but notwithſtanding that I know Ans mind, that's neither heere nor there.

sp.speaker: Caius.
sp.p: You, lack 'Nape: giue-'a this Letter to Sir Hugh, by gar it is a ſhallenge: I will cut his troat in de Parke, and I will teach a ſouruy lack-a-nape Prieſt to meddle, or make: — you may be gon: it is not good you tarry here: by gar I will cut all his two ſtones: by gar, he ſhall not haue a ſtone to throw at his dogge.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Alas: he ſpeakes but for his friend.

sp.speaker: Caius.
sp.p: It is no matter'a ver dat: do not you tell-a-me dat I ſhall haue Anne Page for my ſelfe? by gar, I vill kill de Iack-Prieſt: and I haue appointed mine Hoſt of de Iarteer to meaſure our weapon: by gar, I wil my ſelfe haue Anne Page.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.l: Sir, the maid loues you, and all ſhall bee well:
We muſt giue folkes leaue to prate: what the good-ier.

sp.speaker: Caius.
sp.p: Rugby, come to the Court with me: by gar, if I haue not Anne Page, I ſhall turne your head out of my dore: follow my heeles, Rugby.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: You ſhall haue An-fooles head of your owne: No, I know Ans mind for that: neuer a woman in Windſor knowes more of Ans minde then I doe, nor can doe more then I doe with her, I thanke heauen.

sp.speaker: Fenton.
sp.p: Who's with in there, hoa?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Who's there, I troa? Come neere the houſe I pray you.

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.p: How now (good woman) how doſt thou?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: The better that it pleaſes your good Worſhip to aske?

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.p: What newes? how do's pretty Miſtris Anne?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: In truth Sir, and ſhee is pretty, and honeſt, and gentle, and one that is your friend, I can tell you that by the way, I praiſe heauen for it.

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.p: Shall I doe any good thinkſt thou? ſhall I not looſe my ſuit?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Troth Sir, all is in his hands aboue: but notwithſtanding (Maſter Fenton) Ile be ſworne on a booke ſhee loues you: haue not your Worſhip a wart aboue your eye?

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.p: Yes marry haue I, what of that?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Wel, thereby hangs a tale: good faith, it is ſuch another Nan; (but (I deteſt) an honeſt maid as euer broke bread: wee had an howres talke of that wart; I ſhall neuer laugh but in that maids company: but (indeed) ſhee is giuen too much to Allicholy and muſing: but for you — well — goe too —

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.p: Well: I ſhall ſee her to day: hold, there's money for thee: Let mee haue thy voice in my behalfe: if thou ſeeſt her before me, commend me. —

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Will I? I faith that wee will: And I will tell your Worſhip more of the Wart, the next time we haue confidence, and of other wooers.

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.p: Well, fare-well, I am in great haſte now.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Fare-well to your Worſhip: truely an honeſt Gentleman: but Anne loues hiim not: for I know Ans minde as well as another do's: out vpon't: what haue I forgot.

div.head: Scoena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Miſtris Page, Miſtris Ford, Maſter Page, Maſter Ford, Piſtoll, Nim, Quickly, Hoſt, Shallow.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: What, haue ſcap'd Loue-letters in the holly-day-time of my beauty, and am I now a ſubiect for them? let me ſee?

p.hi: Aske me no reaſon why I loue you, for though Loue vſe Reaſon for his preciſian, hee admits him not for his Counſailour: you are not yong, no more am I: goe to then, there's ſimpathie: you are merry, ſo am I: ha, ha, then there's more ſimpathie: you loue ſacke, and ſo do I: would you deſire better ſimpathie? Let it ſuffice thee (Miſtris Page) at the leaſt if the Loue of Souldier can ſuffice, that I loue thee: I will not ſay pitty mee, 'tis not a Souldier-like phraſe; but I ſay, loue me:

lg.l: By me, thine owne true Knight, by day or night:
Or any kinde of light, with all his might,
For thee to fight.

sp.l: What a Herod of Iurie is this? O wicked, wicked world:
One that is well-nye worne to peeces with age
To ſhow himſelfe a yong Gallant? What an vnwaied
Behauiour hath this Flemiſh drunkard pickt (with
The Deuills name) out of my conuerſation, that he dares
In this manner aſſay me? why, hee hath not beene thrice
In my Company: what ſhould I ſay to him? I was then
Frugall of my mirth: (heauen forgiue mee:) why Ile
sp.p: Exhibit a Bill in the Parliament for the putting downe of men: how ſhall I be reueng'd on him? for reueng'd I will be? as ſure as his guts are made of puddings.

sp.speaker: Miſ Ford.
sp.p: Miſtris Page, truſt me, I was going to your houſe.

sp.speaker: Miſ Page.
sp.p: And truſt me, I was comming to you: you looke very ill.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.p: Nay, Ile nere beleeee that; I haue to ſhew to the contrary.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: 'Faith but you doe in my minde.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.p: Well: I doe then: yet I ſay, I could ſhew you to the contrary: O Miſtris Page, giue mee ſome counſaile.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: What's the matter, woman?

sp.speaker: Mi. Ford.
sp.p: O woman: if it were not for one trifling reſpect, I could come to ſuch honour.

sp.speaker: Mi. Page.
sp.p: Hang the trifle (woman) take the honour: what is it? diſpence with trifles: what is it?

sp.speaker: Mi. Ford.
sp.p: If I would but goe to hell, for an eternall moment, or ſo: I could be knighted.

sp.speaker: Mi. Page.
sp.p: What thou lieſt? Sir Alice Ford? theſe Knights will hacke, and ſo thou ſhouldſt not alter the article of thy Gentry.

sp.speaker: Mi. Ford.
sp.p:
Wee burne day-light: heere, read, read: perceiue how I might bee knighted, I ſhall thinke the worſe of fat men, as long as I haue an eye to make difference of mens liking: and yet hee would not ſweare:
praiſe womens modeſty: and gaue ſuch orderly and wel-behaued reproofe to al vncomelineſſe, that I would haue ſworne his diſpoſition would haue gone to the truth of his words: but they doe no more adhere and keep place together, then the hundred Pſalms to the tune of Green-ſleeues: What tempeſt (I troa) threw this Whale, (with ſo many Tuns of oyle in his belly) a'ſhoare at Windſor? How ſhall I bee reuenged on him? I thinke the beſt way were, to entertaine him with hope, till the wicked fire of luſt haue melted him in his owne greace: Did you euer heare the like?

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: Letter for letter; but that the name of Page and Ford differs: to thy great comfort in this myſtery of ill opinions, heere's the twyn-brother of thy Letter: but let thine inherit firſt, for I proteſt mine neuer ſhall: I warrant he hath a thouſand of theſe Letters, writ with blancke-ſpace for different names (ſure more): and theſe are of the ſecond edition: hee will print them out of doubt: for he cares not what hee puts into the preſſe, when he would put vs two: I had rather be a Gianteſſe, and lye vnder Mount Pelion: Well; I will find you twentie laſciuious Turtles ere one chaſte man.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.p: Why this is the very ſame: the very hand: the very words: what doth he thinke of vs?

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: Nay I know not: it makes me almoſt readie to wrangle with mine owne honeſty: Ile entertaine my ſelfe like one that I am not acquainted withall: for ſure vnleſſe hee know ſome ſtraine in mee, that I know not my ſelfe, hee would neuer haue boorded me in this furie.

sp.speaker: Mi. Ford.
sp.p: Boording, call you it? Ile bee ſure to keepe him aboue decke.

sp.speaker: Mi. Page.
sp.p: So will I: if hee come vnder my hatches, Ile neuer to Sea againe: Let's bee reueng'd on him: let's appoint him a meeting: giue him a ſhow of comfort in his Suit, and lead him on with a fine baited delay, till hee hath pawn'd his horſes to mine Hoſt of the Garter.

sp.speaker: Mi. Ford.
sp.p: Nay, I wil conſent to act any villany againſt him, that may not ſully the charineſſe of our honeſty: oh that my husband ſaw this Letter: it would giue eternall food to his iealouſie.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: Why look where he comes; and my good man too: hee's as farre from iealouſie, as I am from giuing him cauſe, and that (I hope) is an vnmeaſurable diſtance.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.p: You are the happier woman.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: Let's conſult together againſt this greaſie Knight: Come hither.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Well: I hope, it be not ſo.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.l: Hope is a curtall-dog in ſome affaires:
Sir Iohn affects thy wife.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Why ſir, my wife is not young.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: He wooes both high and low, both rich & poor, both yong and old, one with another (Ford) he loues the Gally-mawfry (Ford) perpend.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Loue my wife?

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.l: With liuer, burning hot: preuent:
Or goe thou like Sir Acteon he, with
Ring-wood at thy heeles: O, odious is the name.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: What name Sir?

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.l: The horne I ſay: Farewell:
Take heed, haue open eye, for theeues doe foot by night.
Take heed, ere ſommer comes, or Cuckoo-birds do ſing.
Away ſir Corporall Nim:
Beleeue it (Page) he ſpeakes ſence.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I will be patient: I will find out this.

sp.speaker: Nim.
sp.p: And this is true: I like not the humor of lying: hee hath wronged mee in ſome humors: I ſhould haue borne the humour'd Letter to her: but I haue a ſword: and it ſhall bite vpon my neceſſitie: he loues your wife; There's the ſhort and the long: My name is Corporall Nim: I ſpeak, and I auouch; 'tis true: my name is Nim: and Falſtaffe loues your wife: adieu, I loue not the humour of bread and cheeſe: adieu.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: The humour of it (quoth'a?) heere's a fellow frights Engliſh out of his wits.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I will ſeeke out Falſtaffe.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: I neuer heard ſuch a drawling-affecting rogue.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: If I doe finde it: well.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: I will not beleeue ſuch a Cataian, though the Prieſt o' th' Towne commended him for a true man.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: 'Twas a good ſenſible fellow: well.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: How now Meg?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Whether goe you (George?) harke you.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.p: How now (ſweet Frank) why art thou melancholy?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: I melancholy? I am not melancholy:
Get you home: goe.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.l: Faith, thou haſt ſome crochets in thy head,
Now: will you goe, Miſtris Page?

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: Haue with you: you'll come to dinner George? Looke who comes yonder: ſhee ſhall bee our Meſſenger to this paltrie Knight.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.p: Truſt me, I thought on her: ſhee'll fit it.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: You are come to ſee my daughter Anne?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: I forſooth: and I pray how do's good Miſtreſſe Anne?

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: Go in with vs and ſee: we haue an houres talke with you.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: How now Maſter Ford?

sp.speaker: For.
sp.p: You heard what this knaue told me, did you not?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Yes, and you heard what the other told me?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Doe you thinke there is truth in them?

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.p: Hang 'em ſlaues: I doe not thinke the Knight would offer it: But theſe that accuſe him in his intent towards our wiues, are a yoake of his diſcarded men: very rogues, now they be out of ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Were they his men?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Marry were they.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: I like it neuer the beter for that,
Do's he lye at the Garter?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: I marry do's he: if hee ſhould intend this voyage toward my wife, I would turne her looſe to him; and what hee gets more of her, then ſharpe words, let it lye on my head.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I doe not miſdoubt my wife: but I would bee loath to turne them together: a man may be too confident: I would haue nothing lye on my head: I cannot be thus ſatiſfied.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Looke where my ranting-Hoſt of the Garter comes: there is eyther liquor in his pate, or mony in his purſe, when hee lookes ſo merrily: How now mine Hoſt?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: How now Bully-Rooke: thou'rt a Gentleman Caueleiro Iuſtice, I ſay.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: I follow, (mine Hoſt) I follow: Good-euen, and twe • ty (good Maſter Page.) Maſter Page, wil you go with vs? we haue ſport in hand.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Tell him Caueleiro-Iuſtice: tell him Bully-Rooke.

sp.speaker: Shall.
sp.p: Sir, there is a fray to be fought, betweene Sir Hugh the Welch Prieſt, and Caius the French Doctor.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Good mine Hoſt o' th' Garter: a word with you.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: What ſaiſt thou, my Bully-Rooke?

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Will you goe with vs to behold it? My merry Hoſt hath had the meaſuring of their weapons; and (I thinke) hath appointed them contrary places: for (beleeue mee) I heare the Parſon is no Ieſter: harke, I will tell you what our ſport ſhall be.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Haſt thou no ſuit againſt my Knight? my gueſt-Caualeire?

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: None, I proteſt: but Ile giue you a pottle of burn'd ſacke, to giue me recourſe to him, and tell him my name is Broome: onely for a • eſt.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: My hand, (Bully:) thou ſhalt haue egreſſe and regreſſe, (ſaid I well?) and thy name ſhall be Broome. It is a merry Knight: will you goe An-heires?

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Haue with you mine Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: I haue heard the French-man hath good skill in his Rapier.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Tut ſir: I could haue told you more: In theſe times you ſtand on diſtance: your Paſſes, Stoccado's, and I know not what: 'tis the heart (Maſter Page) 'tis heere, 'tis heere: I haue ſeene the time, with my long-ſword, I would haue made you fowre tall fellowes skippe like Rattes.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Heere boyes, heere, heere: ſhall we wag?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Haue with you: I had rather heare them ſcold, then fight.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Though Page be a ſecure foole, and ſtands ſo firmely on his wiues frailty; yet, I cannot put-off my opinion ſo eaſily: ſhe was in his company at Pages houſe: and what they made there, I know not. Well, I wil looke further into't, and I haue a diſguiſe, to ſound Falſtaffe; if I finde her honeſt, I looſe not my labor: if ſhe be otherwiſe, 'tis labour well beſtowed.

div.head: Scoena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Falſtaffe, Piſtoll, Robin, Quickly, Bardolffe, Ford.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I will not lend thee a penny.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: Why then the world's mine Oyſter, which I, with ſword will open.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Not a penny: I haue beene content (Sir,) you ſhould lay my countenance to pawne: I haue grated vpon my good friends for three Repreeues for you, and your Coach-fellow Nim; or elſe you had look'd through the grate, like a Geminy of Baboones: I am damn'd in hell, for ſwearing to Gentlemen my friends, you were good Souldiers, and tall-fellowes. And when Miſtreſſe Bright loſt the handle of her Fan, I took't vpon mine honour thou hadſt it not.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: Didſt not thou ſhare? hadſt thou not fifteene pence?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Reaſon, you roague, reaſon: thinkſt thou Ile endanger my ſoule, gratis? at a word, hang no more about mee, I am no gibbet for you: goe, a ſhort knife, and a throng, to your Mannor of Pickt-hatch: goe, you'll not beare a Letter for mee you roague? you ſtand vpon your honor: why, (thou vnconfinable baſeneſſe) it is as much as I can doe to keepe the termes of my hononor preciſe: I, I, I my ſelfe ſometimes, leauing the feare of heauen on the left hand, and hiding mine honor in my neceſſity, am faine to ſhufflle: to hedge, and to lurch, and yet, you Rogue, will en-ſconce your raggs; your Cat-a-Mountaine-lookes, your red-lattice phraſes, and your bold-beating-oathes, vnder the ſhelter of your honor? you will not doe it? you?

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: I doe relent: what would thou more of man?

sp.speaker: Robin.
sp.p: Sir, here's a woman would ſpeake with you.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Let her approach.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Giue your worſhip good morrow.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Good-morrow, good-wife.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Not ſo and't pleaſe your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Good maid then.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.l: Ile be ſworne,
As my mother was the firſt houre I was borne.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I doe beleeue the ſwearer; what with me?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Shall I vouch-ſafe your worſhip a word, or two?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Two thouſand (faire woman) and ile vouchſafe thee the hearing.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: There is one Miſtreſſe Ford, (Sir) I pray come a little neerer this waies: I my ſelfe dwell with M. Doctor Caius:

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Well, on; Miſtreſſe Ford, you ſay.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Your worſhip ſaies very true: I pray your worſhip come a little neerer this waies.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I warrant thee, no-bodie heares: mine owne people, mine owne people.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Are they ſo? heauen-bleſſe them, and make them his Seruants.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Well; Miſtreſſe Ford, what of her?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Why, Sir; ſhee's a good-creature; Lord, Lord, your Worſhip's a wanton: well: heauen forgiue you, and all of vs, I pray—.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Miſtreſſe Ford: come, Miſtreſſe Ford.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Marry this is the ſhort, and the long of it: you haue brought her into ſuch a Canaries, as 'tis wonderfull: the beſt Courtier of them all (when the Court lay at Windſor) could neuer haue brought her to ſuch a Canarie: yet there has beene Knights, and Lords, and Gentlemen, with their Coaches; I warrant you Coach after Coach, letter after letter, gift after gift, ſmelling ſo ſweetly; all Muske, and ſo ruſhling, I warrant you, in ſilke and golde, and in ſuch alligant termes, and in ſuch wine and ſuger of the beſt, and the faireſt, that would haue wonne any womans heart: and I warrant you, they could neuer get an eye-winke of her: I had my ſelfe twentie Angels giuen me this morning, but I defie all Angels (in any ſuch ſort, as they ſay) but in the way of honeſty: and I warrant you, they could neuer get her ſo much as ſippe on a cup with the prowdeſt of them all, and yet there has beene Earles: nay, (which is more) Pentioners, but I warrant you all is one with her.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: But what ſaies ſhee to mee? be briefe my good ſhee-Mercurie.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Marry, ſhe hath receiu'd your Letter: for the which ſhe thankes you a thouſand times; and ſhe giues you to notifie, that her husband will be abſence from his houſe, betweene ten and eleuen.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Ten, and eleuen.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: I, forſooth: and then you may come and ſee the picture (ſhe ſayes) that you wot of: Maſter Ford her huſband will be from home: alas, the ſweet woman leades an ill life with him: hee's a very iealouſie-man; ſhe leads a very frampold life with him, (good hart.)

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.l: Ten, and eleuen.
Woman, commend me to her, I will not faile her.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Why, you ſay well: But I haue another meſſenger to your worſhip: Miſtreſſe Page hath her heartie commendations to you to: and let mee tell you in your eare, ſhee's as fartuous a ciuill modeſt wife, and one (I tell you) that will not miſſe you morning nor euening prayer, as any is in Windſor, who ere bee the other: and ſhee bade me tell your worſhip, that her husband is ſeldome from home, but ſhe hopes there will come a time. I neuer knew a woman ſo doate vpon a man; ſurely I thinke you haue charmes, la: yes in truth.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Not I, I aſſure thee; ſetting the attraction of my good parts aſide, I haue no other charmes.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Bleſſing on your heart for't.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: But I pray thee tell me this: has Fords wife, and Pages wife acquainted each other, how they loue me?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: That were a ieſt indeed: they haue not ſo little grace I hope, that were a tricke indeed: But Miſtris Page would deſire you to ſend her your little Page of al loues: her husband has a maruellous infectiō to the little Page: and truely Maſter Page is an honeſt man: neuer a wife in Windſor leades a better life then ſhe do's: doe what ſhee will, ſay what ſhe will, take all, pay all, goe to bed when ſhe liſt, riſe when ſhe liſt, all is as ſhe will: and truly ſhe deſerues it; for if there be a kinde woman in Windſor, ſhe is one: you muſt ſend her your Page, no remedie.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Why, I will.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Nay▪ but doe ſo then, and looke you, hee may come and goe betweene you both: and in any caſe haue a nay-word, that you may know one anothers minde, and the Boy neuer neede to vnderſtand any thing; for 'tis not good that children ſhould know any wickednes: olde folkes you know, haue diſcretion, as they ſay, and know the world.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Farethee-well, commend mee to them both: there's my purſe, I am yet thy debter: Boy, goe along with this woman, this newes diſtracts me.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.l: This Puncke is one of Cupids Carriers,
Clap on more ſailes, purſue: vp with your fights:
Giue fire: ſhe is my prize, or Ocean whelme them all.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Saiſt thou ſo (old Iacke) go thy waies: Ile make more of thy olde body then I haue done: will they yet looke after thee? wilt thou after the expence of ſo much money, be now a gainer? good Body, I thanke thee: let them ſay 'tis groſſely done, ſo it bee fairely done, no matter.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: Sir Iohn, there's one Maſter Broome below would faine ſpeake with you, and be acquainted with you; and hath ſent your worſhip a mornings draught of Sacke.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Broome is his name?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: I Sir.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Call him in: ſuch Broomes are welcome to mee, that ore' flowes ſuch liquor: ah ha, Miſtreſſe Ford and Miſtreſſe Page, haue I encompaſs'd you? goe to, via.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: 'Bleſſe you ſir.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: And you ſir: would you ſpeake with me?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I make bold, to preſſe, with ſo little preparation vpon you.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: You'r welcome, what's your will? giue vs leaue Drawer.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Sir, I am a Gentleman that haue ſpent much, my name is Broome.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Good Maſter Broome, I deſire more acquaintance of you.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Good Sir Iohn, I ſue for yours: not to charge you, for I muſt let you vnderſtand, I thinke my ſelfe in better plight for a Lender, then you are: the which hath ſomething emboldned me to this vnſeaſon'd intruſion: for they ſay, if money goe before, all waies doe lye open.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Money is a good Souldier (Sir) and will on.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Troth, and I haue a bag of money heere troubles me: if you will helpe to beare it (Sir Iohn) take all, or halfe, for eaſing me of the carriage.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Sir, I know not how I may deſerue to bee your Porter.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I will tell you ſir, if you will giue mee the hearing.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Speake (good Maſter Broome) I ſhall be glad to be your Seruant.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Sir, I heare you are a Scholler: (I will be briefe with you) and you haue been a man long knowne to me, though I had neuer ſo good means as deſire, to make my ſelfe acquainted with you. I ſhall diſcouer a thing to you, wherein I muſt very much lay open mine owne imperfection: but (good Sir Iohn) as you haue one eye vpon my follies, as you heare them vnfolded, turne another into the Regiſter of your owne, that I may paſſe with a reproofe the eaſier, ſith you your ſelfe know how eaſie it is to be ſuch an offender.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Very well Sir, proceed.

sp.speaker: Ford
sp.p: There is a Gentlewoman in this Towne, her husbands name is Ford.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Well Sir.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p:
I haue long lou'd her, and I proteſt to you, beſtowed much on her: followed her with a doating obſeruance: Ingroſs'd opportunities to meete her: fee'd euery ſlight occaſion that could but nigardly giue mee ſight of her: not only bought many preſents to giue her, but haue giuen largely to many, to know what ſhee would haue giuen: briefly, I haue purſu'd her, as Loue hath purſued mee, which hath beene on the wing of all occaſions: but whatſoeuer I haue merited, either in my minde, or in my meanes, meede I am ſure I haue receiued none, vnleſſe Experience be a Iewell, that I haue purchaſed at an infinite rate, and that hath taught mee to ſay this,
" Loue like a ſhadow flies, when ſubſtance Loue purſues,
" Purſuing that that flies, and flying what purſues.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Haue you receiu'd no promiſe of ſatisfaction at her hands?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Neuer.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Haue you importun'd her to ſuch a purpoſe?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Neuer.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Of what qualitie was your loue then?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Like a fair houſe, built on another mans ground, ſo that I haue loſt my edifice, by miſtaking the place, where I erected it.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: To what purpoſe haue you vnfolded this to me?

sp.speaker: For.
sp.p: When I haue told you that, I haue told you all: Some ſay, that though ſhe appeare honeſt to mee, yet in other places ſhee enlargeth her mirth ſo farre, that there is ſhrewd conſtruction made of her. Now (Sir Iohn) here is the heart of my purpoſe: you are a gentleman of excellent breeding, admirable diſcourſe, of great admittance, authenticke in your place and perſon, generally allow'd for your many war-like, court-like, and learned preparations.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: O Sir.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p:
Beleeue it, for you know it: there is money, ſpend it, ſpend it, ſpend more; ſpend all I haue, onely
giue me ſo much of your time in enchange of it, as to lay an amiable ſiege to the honeſty of this Fords wife: vſe your Art of wooing; win her to conſent to you: if any man may, you may as ſoone as any.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Would it apply well to the vehemency of your affection that I ſhould win what you would enioy? Methinkes you preſcribe to your ſelfe very prepoſterouſly.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: O, vnderſtand my drift: ſhe dwells ſo ſecurely on the excellency of her honor, that the folly of my ſoule dares not preſent it ſelfe: ſhee is too bright to be look'd againſt. Now, could I come to her with any detection in my hand; my deſires had inſtance and argument to commend themſelues, I could driue her then from the ward of her purity, her reputation, her marriage-vow, and a thouſand other her defences, which now are too-too ſtrongly embattaild againſt me: what ſay you too't, Sir Iohn?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Maſter Broome, I will firſt make bold with your money: next, giue mee your hand: and laſt, as I am a gentleman, you ſhall, if you will, enioy Fords wife.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: O good Sir.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I ſay you ſhall.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Want no money (Sir Iohn) you ſhall want none.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Want no Miſtreſſe Ford (Maſter Broome) you ſhall want none: I ſhall be with her (I may tell you) by her owne appointment, euen as you came in to me, her aſſiſtant, or goe-betweene, parted from me: I ſay I ſhall be with her betweene ten and eleuen: for at that time the iealious-raſcally-knaue her husband will be forth: come you to me at night, you ſhall know how I ſpeed.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I am bleſt in your acquaintance: do you know Ford Sir?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Hang him (poore Cuckoldly knaue) I know him not: yet I wrong him to call him poore: They ſay the iealous wittolly-knaue hath maſſes of money, for the which his wife ſeemes to me well-fauourd: I will vſe her as the key of the Cuckoldly-rogues Coffer, & ther's my harueſt-home.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I would you knew Ford, ſir, that you might auoid him, if you ſaw him.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Hang him, mechanicall-ſalt-butter rogue; I wil ſtare him out of his wits: I will awe-him with my cudgell: it ſhall hang like a Meteor ore the Cuckolds horns: Maſter Broome, thou ſhalt know, I will predominate ouer the pezant, and thou ſhalt lye with his wife. Come to me ſoone at night: Ford's a knaue, and I will aggrauate his ſtile: thou (Maſter Broome) ſhalt know him for knaue, and Cuckold. Come to me ſoone at night.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: What a damn'd Epicurian-Raſcall is this? my heart is ready to cracke with impatience: who ſaies this is improuident iealouſie? my wife hath ſent to him, the howre is fixt, the match is made: would any man haue thought this? ſee the hell of hauing a falſe woman: my bed ſhall be abus'd, my Coffers ranſack'd, my reputation gnawne at, and I ſhall not onely receiue this villanous wrong, but ſtand vnder the adoption of abhominable termes, and by him that does mee this wrong: Termes, names: Amaimon ſounds well: Lucifer, well: Barbaſon, well: yet they are Diuels additions, the names of fiends: But Cuckold, Wittoll, Cuckold? the Diuell himſelfe hath not ſuch a name. Page is an Aſſe, a ſecure Aſſe; hee will truſt his wife, hee will not be iealous: I will rather truſt a Fleming with my butter, Parſon Hugh the Welſhman with my Cheeſe, an Iriſh-man with my Aqua-vitae-bottle, or a Theefe to walke my ambling gelding, then my wife with her ſelfe. Then ſhe plots, then ſhee ruminates, then ſhee deuiſes: and what they thinke in their hearts they may effect; they will breake their hearts but they will effect. Heauen bee prais'd for my iealouſie: eleuen o' clocke the howre, I will preuent this, detect my wife, bee reueng'd on Falſtaffe, and laugh at Page. I will about it, better three houres too ſoone, then a mynute too late: fie, fie, fie: Cuckold, Cuckold, Cuckold.

div.head: Scena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Caius, Rugby, Page, Shallow, Slender, Hoſt. Caius. Iacke Rugby.

sp.speaker: Rug.
sp.p: Sir.

sp.speaker: Caius.
sp.p: Vat is the clocke, Iack.

sp.speaker: Rug.
sp.p: 'Tis paſt the howre (Sir) that Sir Hugh promis'd to meet.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: By gar, he has ſaue his ſoule, dat he is no-come: hee has pray his Pible well, dat he is no-come: by gar (Iack Rugby) he is dead already, if he be come.

sp.speaker: Rug.
sp.p: Hee is wiſe Sir: hee knew your worſhip would kill him if he came.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: By gar, de herring is no dead, ſo as I vill kill him: take your Rapier, (Iacke) I vill tell you how I vill kill him.

sp.speaker: Rug.
sp.p: Alas ſir, I cannot fence.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: Villanie, take your Rapier.

sp.speaker: Rug.
sp.p: Forbeare: heer's company.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: 'Bleſſe thee, bully-Doctor.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: 'Saue you Mr. Doctor Caius.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Now, good Mr. Doctor.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: 'Giue you good-morrow, ſir.

sp.speaker: Caius.
sp.p: Vat be all you one, two, tree, fowre, come for?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: To ſee thee fight, to ſee thee foigne, to ſee thee trauerſe, to ſee thee heere, to ſee thee there, to ſee thee paſſe thy puncto, thy flock, thy reuerſe, thy diſtance, thy montant: Is he dead, my Ethiopian? Is he dead, my Franciſco? ha Bully? what ſaies my Eſculapius? my Galien? my heart of Elder? ha? is he dead bully-Stale? is he dead?

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: By gar, he is de Coward-Iack-Prieſt of de vorld: he is not ſhow his face.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Thou art a Caſtalion-king-Vrinall: Hector of Greece (my Boy)

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: I pray you beare witneſſe, that me haue ſtay, ſixe or ſeuen, two tree howres for him, and hee is nocome.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: He is the wiſer man (M. Docto) rhe is a curer of ſoules, and you a curer of bodies: if you ſhould fight, you goe againſt the haire of your profeſſions: is it not true, Maſter Page?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Maſter Shallow; you haue your ſelfe beene a great fighter, though now a man of peace.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Body-kins M. Page, though I now be old, and of the peace; if I ſee a ſword out, my finger itches to make one: though wee are Iuſtices, and Doctors, and Church-men (M. Page) wee haue ſome ſalt of our youth in vs, we are the ſons of women (M. Page.)

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: 'Tis true, Mr. Shallow.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: It wil be found ſo, (M. Page:) M. Doctor Caius, I am come to fetch you home: I am ſworn of the peace: you haue ſhow'd your ſelfe a wiſe Phyſician, and Sir Hugh hath ſhowne himſelfe a wiſe and patient Churchman: you muſt goe with me, M. Doctor.

sp.speaker: Hoſt
sp.p: Pardon, Gueſt-Iuſtice; a Mounſeur: Mocke-water.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: Mock-vater? vat is dat?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Mock-water, in our Engliſh tongue, is Valour (Bully.)

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: By gar, then I haue as much Mock-vater as de Engliſhman: ſcuruy-Iack-dog-Prieſt: by gar, mee vill cut his eares.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: He will Clapper-claw thee tightly (Bully.)

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: Clapper-de-claw? vat is dat?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: That is, he will make thee amends.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: By-gar, me doe looke hee ſhall clapper-de-claw me, for by-gar, me vill haue it.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: And I will prouoke him to't, or let him wag.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: Me tanck you for dat.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: And moreouer, (Bully) but firſt, Mr. Ghueſt, and M. Page, & eeke Caualeiro Slender, goe you through the Towne to Frogmore.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Sir Hugh is there, is he?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: He is there, ſee what humor he is in: and I will bring the Doctor about by the Fields: will it doe well?

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: We will doe it.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Adieu, good M. Doctor.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: By-gar, me vill kill de Prieſt, for he ſpeake for a Iack-an-Ape to Anne Page.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Let him die: ſheath thy impatience: throw cold water on thy Choller: goe about the fields with mee through Frogmore, I will bring thee where Miſtris Anne Page is, at a Farm-houſe a Feaſting: and thou ſhalt wooe her: Cride-game, ſaid I well?

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: By-gar, mee dancke you vor dat: by gar I loue you: and I ſhall procure 'a you de good Gueſt: de Earle, de Knight, de Lords, de Gentlemen, my patients.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: For the which, I will be thy aduerſary toward Anne Page: ſaid I well?

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: By-gar, 'tis good: vell ſaid.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Let vs wag then.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: Come at my heeles, Iack Rugby.

div.head: Scoena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Euans, Simple, Page, Shallow, Slender, Hoſt, Caius, Rugby.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.p: I pray you now, good Maſter Slenders ſeruing-man, and friend Simple by your name; which way haue you look'd for Maſter Caius, that calls himſelfe Doctor of Phiſicke.

sp.speaker: Sim.
sp.p: Marry Sir, the pittie-ward, the Parke-ward: euery way: olde Windſor way, and euery way but the Towne-way.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: I moſt fehemently deſire you, you will alſo looke that way.

sp.speaker: Sim.
sp.p: I will ſir.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: 'Pleſſe my ſoule: how full of Chollors I am, and trempling of minde: I ſhall be glad if he haue deceiued me: how melancholies I am? I will knog his Vrinalls about his knaues coſtard, when I haue good oportunities for the orke: 'Pleſſe my ſoule: To ſhallow Ruiers to whoſe falls: melodious Birds ſings Madrigalls: There will we make our Peds of Roſes: and a thouſand fragrant poſies. To ſhallow: 'Mercie on mee, I haue a great diſpoſitions to cry. Melodious birds ſing Madrigalls: — When as I ſat in Pabilon: and a thouſand vagram Poſies. To ſhallow, &c.

sp.speaker: Sim.
sp.p: Yonder he is comming, this way, Sir Hugh.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.l: Hee's welcome: To ſhallow Riuers, to whoſe fals:
Heauen proſper the right: what weapons is he?

sp.speaker: Sim.
sp.p: No weapons, Sir: there comes my Maſter, Mr. Shallow, and another Gentleman; from Frogmore, ouer the ſtile, this way.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Pray you giue mee my gowne, or elſe keepe it in your armes.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: How now Maſter Parſon? good morrow good Sir Hugh: keepe a Gameſter from the dice, and a good Studient from his booke, and it is wonderfull.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Ah ſweet Anne Page.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: 'Saue you, good Sir Hugh.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: 'Pleſſe you from his mercy-ſake, all of you.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.l: What? the Sword, and the Word?
Doe you ſtudy them both, Mr. Parſon?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: And youthfull ſtill, in your doublet and hoſe, this raw-rumaticke day?

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: There is reaſons, and cauſes for it.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: We are come to you, to doe a good office, Mr. Parſon.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Fery-well: what is it?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Yonder is a moſt reuerend Gentleman; who (be-like) hauing receiued wrong by ſome perſon, is at moſt odds with his owne grauity and patience, that euer you ſaw.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: I haue liued foure-ſcore yeeres, and vpward: I neuer heard a man of his place, grauity, and learning, ſo wide of his owne reſpect.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: What is he?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: I thinke you know him: Mr. Doctor Caius the renowned French Phyſician.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Got's-will, and his paſſion of my heart: I had as lief you would tell me of a meſſe of porredge.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: He has no more knowledge in Hibocrates and Galen, and hee is a knaue beſides: a cowardly knaue, as you would deſires to be acquainted withall.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: I warrant you, hee's the man ſhould fight with him.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: O ſweet Anne Page.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: It appeares ſo by his weapons: keepe them aſunder: here comes Doctor Caius.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Nay good Mr. Parſon, keepe in your weapon.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: So doe you, good Mr. Doctor.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Diſarme them, and let them queſtion: let them keepe their limbs whole, and hack our Engliſh.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: I pray you let-a-mee ſpeake a word with your eare; vherefore vill you not meet-a me?

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Pray you vſe your patience in good time.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: By-gar, you are de Coward: de Iack dog: Iohn Ape.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Pray you let vs not be laughing-ſtocks to other mens humors: I deſire you in friendſhip, and I will one way or other make you amends: I will knog your Vrinal about your knaues Cogs-combe.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: Diablo: Iack Rugby: mine Hoſt de Iarteer: haue I not ſtay for him, to kill him? haue I not at deplace I did appoint?

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: As I am a Chriſtians-ſoule, now looke your: this is the place appointed, Ile bee iudgement by mine Hoſt of the Garter.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Peace, I ſay, Gallia and Gaule, French & Welch, Soule-Curer, and Body-Curer.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: I, dat is very good, excellant.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Peace, I ſay: heare mine Hoſt of the Garter, Am I politi • ke? Am I ſubtle? Am I a Machiuell?

Shall I looſe my Doctor? No, hee giues me the Potions and the Motions. Shall I looſe my Parſon? my Prieſt? my Sir Hugh? No, he giues me the Prouerbes, and the No-verbes. Giue me thy hand (Celeſtiall) ſo: Boyes of Art, I haue deceiu'd you both: I haue directed you to wrong places: your hearts are mighty, your skinnes are whole, and let burn'd Sacke be the iſſue: Come, lay their ſwords to pawne: Follow me, Lad of peace, follow, follow, follow.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Truſt me, a mad Hoſt: follow Gentlemen, follow.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: O ſweet Anne Page.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: Ha' do I perceiue dat? Haue you make-a-de-ſot of vs, ha, ha?

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: This is well, he has made vs his vlowting-ſtog: I deſire you that we may be friends: and let vs knog our praines together to be reuenge on this ſame ſcall ſcuruy-cogging-companion the Hoſt of the Garter.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: By gar, with all my heart: he promiſe to bring me where is Anne Page: by gar he deceiue me too.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Well, I will ſmite his noddles: pray you follow.

div.head: Scena Secunda.
div.stage: Miſt. Page, Robin, Ford, Page, Shallow, Slender, Hoſt, Euans, Caius.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Nay keepe your way (little Gallant) you were wont to be a follower, but now you are a Leader: whether had you rather lead mine eyes, or eye your maſters heeles?

sp.speaker: Rob.
sp.p: I had rather (forſooth) go before you like a man, then follow him like a dwarfe.

sp.speaker: M. Pa.
sp.p: O you are a flattering boy, now I ſee you'l be a Courtier.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Well met miſtris Page, whether go you.

sp.speaker: M. Pa.
sp.p: Truly Sir, to ſee your wife, is ſhe at home?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I, and as idle as ſhe may hang together for want of company: I thinke if your husbands were dead, you two would marry.

sp.speaker: M. Pa.
sp.p: Be ſure of that, two other husbands.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Where had you this pretty weather-cocke?

sp.speaker: M. Pa.
sp.p: I cannot tell what (the dickens) his name is my husband had him of, what do you cal your Knights name ſirrah?

sp.speaker: Rob.
sp.p: Sir. Iohn Falſtaffe.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Sir. Iohn Falſtaffe.

sp.speaker: M. Pa.
sp.p: He, he, I can neuer hit on's name; there is ſuch a league betweene my goodman, and he: is your Wife at home indeed?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Indeed ſhe is.

sp.speaker: M. Pa.
sp.p: By your leaue ſir, I am ſicke till I ſee her.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Has Page any braines? Hath he any eies? Hath he any thinking? Sure they ſleepe, he hath no vſe of them: why this boy will carrie a letter twentie mile as eaſie, as a Canon will ſhoot point-blanke twelue ſcore: hee peeces out his wiues inclination; he giues her folly motion and advantage; and now ſhe's going to my wife, & Falſtaffes boy with her: A man may heare this ſhowre ſing in the winde; and Falstaffes boy with her: good plots, they are laide, and our reuolted wiues ſhare damnation together. Well, I will take him, then torture my wife, plucke the borrowed vaile of modeſtie from the ſo-ſeeming Miſt. Page, divulge Page himſelfe for a ſecure and wilfull Acteon, and to theſe violent proceedings all my neighbors ſhall cry aime. The clocke giues me my Qu, and my aſſurance bids me ſearch, there I ſhall finde Falſtaffe: I ſhall be rather praiſd for this, then mock'd, for it is as poſſitiue, as the earth is firme, that Falſtaffe is there: I will go.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Page, &c. Well met Mr Ford.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Truſt me, a good knotte; I haue good cheere at home, and I pray you all go with me.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: I muſt excuſe my ſelfe Mr Ford.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.l: And ſo muſt I Sir,
We haue appointed to dine with Miſtris Anne,
And I would not breake with her for more mony
Then Ile ſpeake of.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: We haue linger'd about a match betweene An Page, and my cozen Slender, and this day wee ſhall haue our anſwer.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I hope I haue your good will Father Page.

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.l: You haue Mr Slender, I ſtand wholly for you,
But my wife (Mr Doctor) is for you altogether.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: I be-gar, and de Maid is loue-a-me: my nurſha-Quickly tell me ſo muſh

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: What ſay you to yong Mr Fenton? He capers, he dances, he has eies of youth: he writes verſes, hee ſpeakes holliday, he ſmels April and May, he wil carry't, he will carry't, 'tis in his buttons, he will carry't.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Not by my conſent I promiſe you. The Gentleman is of no hauing, hee kept companie with the wilde Prince, and Pointz: he is of too high a Region, he knows too much: no, hee ſhall not knit a knot in his fortunes, with the finger of my ſubſtance: if he take her, let him take her ſimply: the wealth I haue waits on my conſent, and my conſent goes not that way.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I beſeech you heartily, ſome of you goe home with me to dinner: beſides your cheere you ſhall haue ſport, I will ſhew you a monſter: Mr Doctor, you ſhal go, ſo ſhall you Mr Page, and you Sir Hugh.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.l: Well, fare you well:
We ſhall haue the freer woing at Mr. Pages.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: Go home Iohn Rugby, I come anon.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Farewell my hearts, I will to my honeſt Knight Falſtaffe, and drinke Canarie with him.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I thinke I ſhall drinke in Pipe-wine firſt with him, Ile make him dance. Will you go, Gentles?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Haue with you, to ſee this Monſter.

div.head: Scena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter M. Ford, M. Page, Seruants, Robin, Falſtaffe, Ford, Page, Caius, Euans.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: What Iohn, what Robert.

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: Quickly, quickly: Is the Buck-basket —

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.p: I warrant. What Robin I ſay.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: Come, come, come.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Heere, ſet it downe.

sp.speaker: M. Pag.
sp.p: Giue your men the charge, we muſt be briefe.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: Marrie▪ as I told you before (Iohn & Robert) be ready here hard-by in the Brew-houſe, & when I ſodainly call you, come forth, and (without any pauſe, or ſtaggering) take this basket on your ſhoulders: yt done, trudge with it in all haſt, and carry it among the Whitſters in Dotchet Mead, and there empty it in the muddie ditch, cloſe by the Thames ſide.

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: You will do it?

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.l: I ha told them ouer and ouer, they lacke no direction
Be gone, and come when you are call'd.

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: Here comes little Robin.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: How now my Eyas-Musket, what newes with you?

sp.speaker: Rob.
sp.p: My M. Sir Iohn is come in at your backe doore (Miſt. Ford, and requeſts your company.

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: You litle Iack-a-lent, haue you bin true to vs

sp.speaker: Rob.
sp.p: I, Ile be ſworne: my Maſter knowes not of your being heere: and hath threatned to put me into euerlaſting liberty, if I tell you of it: for he ſweares he'll turne me away.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Pag.
sp.p: Thou'rt a good boy: this ſecrecy of thine ſhall be a Tailor to thee, and ſhal make thee a new doublet and hoſe. Ile go hide me.

sp.speaker: Mi. Ford.
sp.p: Do ſo: go tell thy Maſter, I am alone: Miſtris Page, remember you your Qu.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Pag.
sp.p: I warrant thee, if I do not act it, hiſſe me.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Go-too then: we'l vſe this vnwholſome humidity, this groſſe-watry Pumpion; we'll teach him to know Turtles from Iayes.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Haue I caught thee, my heauenly Iewell? Why now let me die, for I haue liu'd long enough: This is the period of my ambition: O this bleſſed houre.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: O ſweet Sir Iohn.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Miſtris Ford, I cannot cog, I cannot prate (Miſt. Ford) now ſhall I ſin in my wiſh; I would thy Husband were dead, Ile ſpeake it before the beſt Lord, I would make thee my Lady.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: I your Lady Sir Iohn? Alas, I ſhould bee a pittifull Lady.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Let the Court of France ſhew me ſuch another: I ſee how thine eye would emulate the Diamond: Thou haſt the right arched-beauty of the brow, that becomes the Ship-tyre, the Tyre-valiant, or any Tire of Venetian admittance.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.l: A plaine Kerchiefe, Sir Iohn:
My browes become nothing elſe, nor that well neither.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Thou art a tyrant to ſay ſo: thou wouldſt make an abſolute Courtier, and the firme fixture of thy foote, would giue an excellent motion to thy gate, in a ſemicircled Farthingale. I ſee what thou wert if Fortune thy foe, were not Nature thy friend: Come, thou canſt not hide it.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Beleeue me, ther's no ſuch thing in me.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: What made me loue thee? Let that perſwade thee. Ther's ſomething extraordinary in thee: Come, I cannot cog, and ſay thou art this and that, like a-manie of theſe liſping-hauthorne buds, that come like women in mens apparrell, and ſmell like. Bucklers-berry in ſimple time: I cannot, but I loue thee, none but thee; and thou deſeru'ſt it.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: Do not betray me ſir, I fear you loue M. Page.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Thou mightſt as well ſay, I loue to walke by the Counter-gate, which is as hatefull to me, as the reeke of a Lime-kill.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.l: Well, heauen knowes how I loue you,
And you ſhall one day finde it.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Keepe in that minde, Ile deſerue it.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.l: Nay, I muſt tell you, ſo you doe;
Or elſe I could not be in that minde.

sp.speaker: Rob.
sp.p: Miſtris Ford, Miſtris Ford: heere's Miſtris Page at the doore, ſweating, and blowing, and looking wildely, and would needs ſpeake with you preſently.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: She ſhall not ſee me, I will enſconce mee behinde the Arras.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: Pray you do ſo, ſhe's a very tatling woman. Whats the matter? How now?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.l: O miſtris Ford what haue you done?
You'r ſham'd, y' are ouerthrowne, y' are vndone for euer.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: What's the matter, good miſtris Page?

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: O weladay, miſt. Ford, hauing an honeſt man to your husband, to giue him ſuch cauſe of ſuſpition.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: What cauſe of ſuſpition?

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.l: What cauſe of ſuſpition? Out vpon you:
How am I miſtooke in you?

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: Why (alas) what's the matter?

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: Your husband's comming hether (Woman) with all the Officers in Windſor, to ſearch for a Gentleman, that he ſayes is heere now in the houſe; by your conſent to take an ill aduantage of his abſence: you are vndone.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: 'Tis not ſo, I hope.

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: Pray heauen it be not ſo, that you haue ſuch a man heere: but 'tis moſt certaine your husband's comming, with halfe Windſor at his heeles, to ſerch for ſuch a one, I come before to tell you: If you know your ſelfe cleere, why I am glad of it: but if you haue a friend here, conuey, conuey him out. Be not amaz'd, call all your ſenſes to you, defend your reputation, or bid farwell to your good life for euer.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: What ſhall I do? There is a Gentleman my deere friend: and I feare not mine owne ſhame ſo much, as his perill. I had rather then a thouſand pound he were out of the houſe.

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: For ſhame, neuer ſtand (you had rather, and you had rather:) your husband's heere at hand, bethinke you of ſome conueyance: in the houſe you cannot hide him. Oh, how haue you deceiu'd me? Looke, heere is a basket, if he be of any reaſonable ſtature, he may creepe in heere, and throw fowle linnen vpon him, as if it were going to bucking: Or it is whiting time, ſend him by your two men to Datchet-Meade:

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: He's too big to go in there: what ſhall I do?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.l: Let me ſee't, let me ſee't, O let me ſee't:
Ile in, Ile in: Follow your friends counſell, Ile in.

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: What Sir Iohn Faiſtaſſe? Are theſe your Letters, Knight?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I loue thee, helpe mee away: let me creepe in heere: ile neuer—

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: Helpe to couer your maſter (Boy:) Call your men (Miſt. Ford.) You diſſembling Knight.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: What Iohn, Robert, Iohn; Go, take vp theſe cloathes heere, quickly: Wher's the Cowle-ſtaffe? Look how you drumble? Carry them to the Landreſſe in Datchet mead: quickly, come.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: 'Pray you come nere: if I ſuſpect without cauſe,
Why then make ſport at me, then let me be your ieſt,
I deſerue it: How now? Whether beare you this?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: To the Landreſſe forſooth?

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: Why, what haue you to doe whether they beare it? You were beſt meddle with buck-waſhing.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: Bucke I would I could waſh my ſelfe of ye Buck:
Bucke, bucke, bucke, I bucke: I warrant you Bucke,
And of the ſeaſon too; it ſhall appeare.
sp.p: Gentlemen, I haue dream'd to night, Ile tell you my dreame: heere, heere, heere bee my keyes, aſcend my Chambers, ſearch, ſeeke, finde out: Ile warrant wee'le vnkennell the Fox. Let me ſtop this way firſt: ſo, now vncape.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Good maſter Ford, be contented:
You wrong your ſelfe too much.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: True (maſter Page) vp Gentlemen,
You ſhall ſee ſport anon:
Follow me Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.p: This is fery fantaſticall humors and iealouſies.

sp.speaker: Caius.
sp.l: By gar, 'tis no-the faſhion of France:
It is not iealous in France.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Nay follow him (Gentlemen) ſee the yſſue of his ſearch.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page
sp.p: Is there not a double excellency in this?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.l: I know not which pleaſes me better,
That my husband is deceiued, or Sir Iohn.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: What a taking was hee in, when your husband askt who was in the basket?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: I am halfe affraid he will haue neede of waſhing: ſo throwing him into the water, will doe him a benefit.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Hang him diſhoneſt raſcall: I would all of the ſame ſtraine, were in the ſame diſtreſſe.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: I thinke my husband hath ſome ſpeciall ſuſpition of Falſtaffs being heere: for I neuer ſaw him ſo groſſe in his iealouſie till now.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: I will lay a plot to try that, and wee will yet haue more trickes with Falſtaffe: his diſſolute diſeaſe will ſcarſe obey this medicine.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.p: Shall we ſend that fooliſhion Carion, Miſt. Quickly to him, and excuſe his throwing into the water, and giue him another hope, to betray him to another puniſhment?

sp.speaker: Mist. Page.
sp.p: We will do it: let him be ſent for to morrow eight a clocke to haue amends.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I cannot finde him: may be the knaue bragg'd of that he could not compaſſe.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: Heard you that?

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.p: You vſe me well, M. Ford? Do you?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I, I do ſo.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: Heauen make you better then your thoghts

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Amen.

sp.speaker: Mi. Page.
sp.p: You do your ſelfe mighty wrong (M. Ford)

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I, I: I muſt beare it.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: If there be any pody in the houſe, & in the chambers, and in the coffers, and in the preſſes: heauen forgiue my ſins at the day of iudgement.

sp.speaker: Caius.
sp.p: Be gar, nor I too: there is no-bodies.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Fy, fy, M. Ford, are you not aſham'd? What ſpirit, what diuell ſuggeſts this imagination? I wold not ha your diſtemper in this kind, for ye welth of Windſor caſtle.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: 'Tis my fault (M. Page) I ſuffer for it.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.p: You ſuffer for a pad conſcience: your wife is as honeſt a o' mans, as I will deſires among fiue thouſand, and fiue hundred too.

sp.speaker: Cai
sp.p: By gar, I ſee 'tis an honeſt woman.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Well, I promiſd you a dinner: come, come, walk in the Parke, I pray you pardon me: I wil hereafter make knowne to you why I haue done this. Come wife, come Mi. Page, I pray you pardon me. Pray hartly pardon me.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Let's go in Gentlemen, but (truſt me) we'l mock him: I doe inuite you to morrow morning to my houſe to breakfaſt: after we'll a Birding together, I haue a fine Hawke for the buſh. Shall it be ſo:

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Any thing.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: If there is one, I ſhall make two in the Companie

sp.speaker: Ca.
sp.p: If there be one, or two, I ſhall make-a-theturd.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Pray you go, M. Page.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: I pray you now remembrance to morrow on the lowſie knaue, mine Hoſt.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: Dat is good by gar, withall my heart.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: A lowſie knaue, to haue his gibes, and his mockeries.

div.head: Scoena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Fenton, Anne, Page, Shallow, Slender, Quickly, Page, Miſt. Page.

sp.speaker: Fen:
sp.l: I ſee I cannot get thy Fathers loue,
Therefore no more turne me to him (ſweet Nan.)

sp.speaker: Anne.
sp.p: Alas, how then?

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.l: Why thou muſt be thy ſelfe.
He doth obiect, I am too great of birth,
And that my ſtate being gall'd with my expence,
I ſeeke to heale it onely by his wealth.
Beſides theſe, other barres he layes before me,
My Riots paſt, my wilde Societies,
And tels me 'tis a thing impoſſible
I ſhould loue thee, but as a property.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: May be he tels you true.
No, heauen ſo ſpeed me in my time to come,
Albeit I will confeſſe, thy Fathers wealth
Was the firſt motiue that I woo'd thee (Anne:)
Yet wooing thee, I found thee of more valew
Then ſtampes in Gold, or ſummes in ſealed bagges:
And 'tis the very riches of thy ſelfe,
That now I ayme at.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: Gentle M. Fenton,
Yet ſeeke my Fathers loue, ſtill ſeeke it ſir,
If opportunity and humbleſt ſuite
Cannot attaine it, why then harke you hither.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.l: Breake their talke Miſtris Quickly,
My Kinſman ſhall ſpeake for himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Ile make a ſhaft or a bolt on't, ſlid, tis but venturing.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Be not diſmaid.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.l: No, ſhe ſhall not diſmay me:
I care not for that, but that I am affeard.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Hark ye, M. Slender would ſpeak a word with you

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: I come to him. This is my Fathers choice:
O what a world of vilde ill-fauour'd faults
Lookes handſome in three hundred pounds a yeere?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.l: And how do's good Maſter Fenton?
Pray you a word with you.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.l: Shee's comming; to her Coz:
O boy, thou hadſt a father.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I had a father (M. An) my vncle can tel you good ieſts of him: pray you Vncle tel Miſt. Anne the ieſt how my Father ſtole two Geeſe out of a Pen, good Vnckle.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Miſtris Anne, my Cozen loues you.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I that I do, as well as I loue any woman in Gloceſterſhire.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: He will maintaine you like a Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I that I will, come cut and long-taile, vnder the degree of a Squire.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: He will make you a hundred and fiftie pounds ioynture.

sp.speaker: Anne.
sp.p: Good Maiſter Shallow let him woo for himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: Marrie I thanke you for it: I thanke you for that good comfort: ſhe cals you (Coz) Ile leaue you.

sp.speaker: Anne.
sp.p: Now Maſter Slender.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Now good Miſtris Anne.

sp.speaker: Anne.
sp.p: What is your will?

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: My will? Odd's-hart-lings, that's a prettie ieſt indeede: I ne're made my Will yet (I thanke Heauen:) I am not ſuch a ſickely creature, I giue Heauen praiſe.

sp.speaker: Anne.
sp.p: I meane (M. Slender) what wold you with me?

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Truely, for mine owne part, I would little or nothing with you: your father and my vncle hath made motion,: if it be my lucke, ſo; if not, happy man bee his dole, they can tell you how things go, better then I can: you may aske your father, heere he comes.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Now Mr Slender; Loue him daughter Anne.
Why how now? What does Mr Fenter here?
You wrong me Sir, thus ſtill to haunt my houſe.
I told you Sir, my daughter is diſpoſd of.

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.p: Nay Mr Page, be not impatient.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Good M. Fenton▪ come not to my child.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: She is no match for you.

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.p: Sir, will you heare me?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: No, good M. Fenton.
Come M. Shallow: Come ſonne Slender, in;
Knowing my minde, you wrong me (M. Fenton.)

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Speake to Miſtris Page.

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.l: Good Miſt. Page, for that I loue your daughter
In ſuch a righteous faſhion as I do,
Perforce, againſt all checkes, rebukes, and manners,
I muſt aduance the colours of my loue,
And not retire. Let me haue your good will.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Good mother, do not marry me to yond foole.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: I meane it not, I ſeeke you a better huſband.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: That's my maſter, M. Doctor.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: Alas I had rather be ſet quick i' th earth,
And bowl'd to death with Turnips.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.l: Come, trouble not your ſelfe good M.
Fenton, I will not be your friend, nor enemy:
My daughter will I queſtion how ſhe loues you,
And as I finde her, ſo am I affected:
Till then, farewell Sir, ſhe muſt needs go in,
Her father will be angry.

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.p: Farewell gentle Miſtris: farewell Nan.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: This is my doing now: Nay, ſaide I, will you caſt away your childe on a Foole, and a Phyſitian: Looke on M. Fenton, this is my doing.

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.l: I thanke thee: and I pray thee once to night,
Giue my ſweet Nan this Ring: there's for thy paines.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Now heauen ſend thee good fortune, a kinde heart he hath: a woman would run through fire & water for ſuch a kinde heart. But yet, I would my Maiſter had Miſtris Anne, or I would M. Slender had her: or (in ſooth) I would M. Fenton had her; I will do what I can for them all three, for ſo I haue promiſd, and Ile bee as good as my word, but ſpeciouſly for M. Fenton. Well, I muſt of another errand to Sir Iohn Falstaffe from my two Miſtreſſes: what a beaſt am I to ſlacke it.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Bardolfe I ſay.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: Heere Sir.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Go, fetch me a quart of Sacke, put a toſt in't. Haue I liu'd to be carried in a Basket like a barrow of butchers Offall? and to be throwne in the Thames? Wel, if I be ſeru'd ſuch another tricke, Ile haue my braines 'tane out and butter'd, and giue them to a dogge for a New-yeares gift. The rogues ſlighted me into the riuer with as little remorſe, as they would haue drown'de a blinde bitches Puppies, fifteene i' th litter: and you may know by my ſize, that I haue a kinde of alacrity in ſinking: if the bottome were as deepe as hell, I ſhold down. I had beene drown'd, but that the ſhore was ſheluy and ſhallow: a death that I abhorre: for the water ſwelles a man; and what a thing ſhould I haue beene, when I had beene ſwel'd? I ſhould haue beene a Mountaine of Mummie.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: Here's M. Quickly Sir to ſpeake with you.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Come, let me poure in ſome Sack to the Thames water: for my bellies as cold as if I had ſwallow'd ſnowbals, for pilles to coole the reines. Call her in.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: Come in woman.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.l: By your leaue: I cry you mercy?
Giue your worſhip good morrow.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.l: Take away theſe Challices:
Go, brew me a pottle of Sacke finely.

sp.speaker: Bard.
sp.p: With Egges, Sir?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Simple of it ſelfe: Ile no Pullet-Sperſme in my brewage. How now?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Marry Sir, I come to your worſhip from M. Ford.

sp.speaker: Fal.
