sp.p: Miſt. Ford? I haue had Ford enough: I was thrown into the Ford; I haue my belly full of Ford.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Alas the day, (good-heart) that was not her fault: ſhe do's ſo take on with her men; they miſtooke their erection.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: So did I mine, to build vpon a fooliſh Womans promiſe.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Well, ſhe laments Sir for it, that it would yern your heart to ſee it: her husband goes this morning a birding; ſhe deſires you once more to come to her, betweene eight and nine: I muſt carry her word quickely, ſhe'll make you amends I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Well, I will viſit her, tell her ſo: and bidde her thinke what a man is: Let her conſider his frailety, and then iudge of my merit.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: I will tell her.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Do ſo. Betweene nine and ten ſaiſt thou?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Eight and nine Sir.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Well, be gone: I will not miſſe her.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Peace be with you Sir.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I meruaile I heare not of Mr Broome: he ſent me word to ſtay within: I like his money well. Oh, heere be comes.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Bleſſe you Sir.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.l: Now M. Broome, you come to know
What hath paſt betweene me, and Fords wife.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: That indeed (Sir Iohn) is my buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.l: M. Broome I will not lye to you,
I was at her houſe the houre ſhe appointed me.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: And ſped you Sir?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: very ill-fauouredly M. Broome.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: How ſo ſir, did ſhe change her determination?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: No (M. Broome) but the peaking Curnuto her huſband (M. Broome) dwelling in a continual larum of ielouſie, coms me in the inſtant of our encounter, after we had embraſt, kiſt, proteſted, & (as it were) ſpoke the prologue of our Comedy: and at his heeles, a rabble of his companions, thither prouoked and inſtigated by his diſtemper, and (forſooth) to ſerch his houſe for his wiues Loue.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: What? While you were there?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: While I was there.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.p: And did he ſearch for you, & could not find you?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: You ſhall heare. As good lucke would haue it, comes in one Miſt. Page▪ giues intelligence of Fords approch: and in her inuention, and Fords wiues diſtraction, they conuey'd me into a bucke-basket.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: A Buck-basket?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Yes: a Buck-basket: ram'd mee in with foule Shirts and Smockes, Socks, foule Stockings, greaſie Napkins, that (Maſter Broome) there was the rankeſt compound of villanous ſmell, that euer offended noſtrill.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: And how long lay you there?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Nay, you ſhall heare (Maſter Broome) what I hau • ſufferd, to bring this woman to euill, for your good: Being thus cram'd in the Basket, a couple of Fords knaues, his Hindes, were cald forth by their Miſtris, to carry mee in the name of foule Cloathes to Datchet-lane: they tooke me on their ſhoulders: met the iealous knaue their Maſter in the doore; who ask'd them once or twice what they had in their Baſket? I quak'd for feare leaſt the Lunatique Knaue would haue ſearch'd it: but Fate (ordaining he ſhould be a Cuckold) held his hand: well, on went hee, for a ſearch, and away went I for foule Cloathes: But marke the ſequell (Maſter Broome) I ſuffered the pangs of three ſeuerall deaths: Firſt, an intollerable fright, to be detected with a iealious rotten Bell-weather: Next to be compaſs'd like a good Bilbo in the circumference of a Pecke, hilt to point, heele to head. And then to be ſtopt in like a ſtrong diſtillation with ſtinking Cloathes, that fretted in their owne greaſe: thinke of that, a man of my Kidney; thinke of that, that am as ſubiect to heate as butter; a man of continuall diſſolution, and thaw: it was a miracle to ſcape ſuffocation. And in the height of this Bath (when I was more then halfe ſtew'd in greaſe (like a Dutchdiſh) to be throwne into the Thames, and coold, glowing-hot, in that ſerge like a Horſeſhoo; thinke of that; hiſſing hot: thinke of that (Maſter Broome.)

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: In good ſadneſſe Sir, I am ſorry, that for my ſake you haue ſufferd all this.
My ſuite then is deſperate: You'll vndertake her no more?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Maſter Broome: I will be throwne into Etna, as I haue beene into Thames, ere I will leaue her thus; her Husband is this morning gone a Birding: I haue receiued from her another ambaſſie of meeting: 'twixt eight and nine is the houre (Maſter Broome.)

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: 'Tis paſt eight already Sir.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Is it? I will then addreſſe mee to my appointment: Come to mee at your conuenient leiſure, and you ſhall know how I ſpeede: and the concluſion ſhall be crowned with your enioying her: adiew: you ſhall haue her (Maſter Broome) Maſter Broome, you ſhall cuckold Ford.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Hum: ha? Is this a viſion? Is this a dreame? doe I ſleepe? Maſter Ford awake, awake Maſter Ford: ther's a hole made in your beſt coate (Maſter Ford:) this 'tis to be married; this 'tis to haue Lynnen, and Buck-baskets: Well, I will proclaime my ſelfe what I am: I will now take the Leacher: hee is at my houſe: hee cannot ſcape me: 'tis impoſſible hee ſhould: hee cannot creepe into a halfe-penny purſe, nor into a Pepper-Boxe: But leaſt the Diuell that guides him, ſhould aide him, I will ſearch impoſſible places: though what I am, I cannot auoide; yet to be what I would not, ſhall not make me tame: If I haue hornes, to make one mad, let the prouerbe goe with me, Ile be hornemad.

div.head: Scoena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Miſtris Page, Quickly, William, Euans.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Pag.
sp.p: Is he at M. Fords already think'ſt thou?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Sure he is by this; or will be preſently; but truely he is very couragious mad, about his throwing into the water. Miſtris Ford deſires you to come ſodainely.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Pag.
sp.p: Ile be with her by and by: Ile but bring my yong-man here to Schoole: looke where his Maſter comes; 'tis a playing day I ſee: how now Sir Hugh, no Schoole to day?

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: No: Maſter Slender is let the Boyes leaue to play.

sp.speaker: Qui
sp.p: 'Bleſſing of his heart.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Pag.
sp.p: Sir Hugh, my husband ſaies my ſonne profits nothing in the world at his Booke: I pray you aske him ſome queſtions in his Accidence.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: Come hither William; hold vp your head; come.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Pag.
sp.p: Come-on Sirha; hold vp your head; anſwere your Maſter, be not afraid.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: William, how many Numbers is in Nownes?

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Two.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: Truely, I thought there had bin one Number more, becauſe they ſay od's-Nownes.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: Peace, your tatlings. What is (Faire) William?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Powlcats? there are fairer things then Powlcats, ſure.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: You are a very ſimplicity o' man: I pray you peace. What is (Lapis) William?

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: A Stone.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: And what is a Stone (William?)

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: A Peeble.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: No; it is Lapis: I pray you remember in your praine.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: That is a good William: what is he (William) that do's lend Articles.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Articles are borrowed of the Pronoune; and be thus declined. Singulariter nominatiuo hic haec, hoc.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: Nominatiuo hig, hag, hog: pray you marke: genitiuo huius: Well: what is your Accuſatiue-caſe?

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: I pray you haue your remembrance (childe) Accuſatiuo hing, hang, hog.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Hang-hog, is latten for Bacon, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: Leaue your prables (o' man) What is the Focatiue caſe (William?)

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: Remember William, Focatiue, is caret.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: And that's a good roote.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: O' man, forbeare.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Pag.
sp.p: Peace.

sp.speaker: Eua:
sp.p: What is your Genitiue caſe plurall (William?)

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Genitiue caſe?

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: I.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: 'Vengeance of Ginyes caſe; fie on her; neuer name her (childe) if ſhe be a whore.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: For ſhame o' man.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: You doe ill to teach the childe ſuch words: hee teaches him to hic, and to hac; which they'll doe faſt enough of themſelues, and to call horum; fie vpon you.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.p: O' man, art thou Lunaties? Haſt thou no vnderſtandings for thy Caſes, & the numbers of the Genders? Thou art as fooliſh Chriſtian creatures, as I would deſires.

sp.speaker: Mi. Page.
sp.p: Pre'thee hold thy peace.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: Shew me now (William) ſome declenſions of your Pronounes.

sp.speaker: Will.
sp.p: Forſooth, I haue forgot.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: It is Qui, que, quod; if you forget your Quies, your Ques, and your Quods, you muſt be preeches: Goe your waies and play, go.

sp.speaker: M. Pag.
sp.p: He is a better ſcholler then I thought he was.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: He is a good ſprag-memory: Farewel Mis. Page.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.l: Adieu good Sir Hugh:
Get you home boy, Come we ſtay too long.

div.head: Scena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Falſtoffe, Miſt. Ford, Miſt. Page, Seruants, Ford, Page, Caius, Euans, Shallow.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Mi. Ford, Your ſorrow hath eaten vp my ſufferance; I ſee you are obſequious in your loue, and I profeſſe requitall to a haires bredth, not onely Miſt. Ford, in the ſimple office of loue, but in all the accuſtrement, complement, and ceremony of it: But are you ſure of your husband now?

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.p: Hee's a birding (ſweet Sir Iohn.)

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: What hoa, goſſip Ford: what hoa.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.p: Step into th' chamber, Sir Iohn.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: How now (ſweete heart) whoſe at home beſides your ſelfe?

sp.speaker: Miſ Ford
sp.p: Why none but mine owne people.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: Indeed?

sp.speaker: Miſ. Ford.
sp.p: No certainly: Speake louder.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Pag.
sp.p: Truly, I am ſo glad you haue no body here.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.p: Why woman, your husband is in his olde lines againe: he ſo takes on yonder with my husband, ſo railes againſt all married mankinde; ſo curſes all Eues daughters, of what complexion ſoeuer; and ſo buffettes himſelfe on the for-head: crying peere-out, peere-out, that any madneſſe I euer yet beheld, ſeem'd but tameneſſe, ciuility, and patience to this his diſtemper he is in now: I am glad the fat Knight is not heere.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Why, do's he talke of him?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Of none but him, and ſweares he was caried out the laſt time hee ſearch'd for him, in a Basket: Proteſts to my husband he is now heere, & hath drawne him and the reſt of their company from their ſport, to make another experiment of his ſuſpition: But I am glad the Knight is not heere; now he ſhall ſee his owne foolerie.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: How neere is he Miſtris Page?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Pag.
sp.p: Hard by, at ſtreet end; he wil be here anon.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: I am vndone, the Knight is heere.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Why then you are vtterly ſham'd, & hee's but a dead man. What a woman are you? Away with him, away with him▪ Better ſhame, then murther.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Which way ſhould he go? How ſhould I beſtow him? Shall I put him into the basket againe?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.l: No, Ile come no more i' th Basket:
May I not go out ere he come?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Alas: three of Mr. Fords brothers watch the doore with Piſtols, that none ſhall iſſue out: otherwiſe you might ſlip away ere hee came: But what make you heere?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: What ſhall I do? Ile creepe vp into the chimney.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: There they alwaies vſe to diſcharge their Birding-peeces: creepe into the Kill-hole.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Where is it?

sp.speaker: Mist. Ford.
sp.p: He will ſeeke there on my word: Neyther Preſſe, Coffer, Cheſt, Trunke, Well, Vault, but he hath an abſtract for the remembrance of ſuch places, and goes to them by his Note: There is no hiding you in the houſe.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Ile go out then.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: If you goe out in your owne ſemblance, you die Sir Iohn, vnleſſe you go out diſguis'd.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: How might we diſguiſe him?

sp.speaker: Mist. Page.
sp.p: Alas the day I know not, there is no womans gowne bigge enough for him: otherwiſe he might put on a hat, a muffler, and a kerchiefe, and ſo eſcape.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Good hearts, deuiſe ſomething: any extremitie, rather then a miſchiefe.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: My Maids Aunt the fat woman of Brainford, has a gowne aboue.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: On my word it will ſerue him: ſhee's as big as he is: and there's her thrum'd hat, and her muffler too: run vp Sir Iohn.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Go, go, ſweet Sir Iohn: Miſtriis Page and I will looke ſome linnen for your head.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Quicke, quicke, wee'le come dreſſe you ſtraight: put on the gowne the while.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: I would my husband would meete him in this ſhape: he cannot abide the old woman of Brainford; he ſweares ſhe's a witch, forbad her my houſe, and hath threatned to beate her.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Heauen guide him to thy husbands cudgell: and the diuell guide his cudgell afterwards.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: But is my husband comming?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: I in good ſadneſſe is he, and talkes of the basket too, howſoeuer he hath had intelligence.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Wee'l try that: for Ile appoint my men to carry the basket againe, to meete him at the doore with it, as they did laſt time.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Nay, but hee'l be heere preſently: let's go dreſſe him like the witch of Brainford.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Ile firſt direct direct my men, what they ſhall doe with the basket: Goe vp, Ile bring linnen for him ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.l: Hang him diſhoneſt Varlet,
We cannot miſuſe enough:
We'll leaue a proofe by that which we will doo,
Wiues may be merry, and yet honeſt too:
We do not acte that often, ieſt, and laugh,
'Tis old, but true, Still Swine eats all the draugh.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Go Sirs, take the basket againe on your ſhoulders: your Maſter is hard at doore: if hee bid you ſet it downe, obey him: quickly, diſpatch.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: Come, come, take it vp.

sp.speaker: 2 Ser.
sp.p: Pray heauen it be not full of Knight againe.

sp.speaker: 1 Ser.
sp.p: I hope not, I had liefe as beare ſo much lead.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p:
I, but if it proue true (Mr. Page) haue you any way then to vnfoole me againe. Set downe the basket villaine: ſome body call my wife: Youth in a basket: Oh you Panderly Raſcals, there's a knot: a gin, a packe, a conſpiracie againſt me: Now ſhall the diuel be ſham'd. What wife I ſay: Come, come forth: behold what honeſt
cloathes you ſend forth to bleaching.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Why, this paſſes M. Ford: you are not to goe looſe any longer, you muſt be pinnion'd.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.p: Why, this is Lunaticks: this is madde, as a mad dogge.

sp.speaker: Shall.
sp.p: Indeed M. Ford, thi is not well indeed.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: So ſay I too Sir, come hither Miſtris Ford, Miſtris Ford, the honeſt woman, the modeſt wife, the vertuous creature, that hath the iealious foole to her husband: I ſuſpect without cauſe (Miſtris) do I?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Heauen be my witneſſe you doe, if you ſuſpect me in any diſhoneſty.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Well ſaid Brazon-face, hold it out: Come forth ſirrah.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: This paſſes.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Are you not aſham'd, let the cloths alone.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I ſhall finde you anon.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: 'Tis vnreaſonable; will you take vp your wiues cloathes? Come, away.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Empty the basket I ſay.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: Why man, why?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Maſter Page, as I am a man, there was one conuay'd out of my houſe yeſterday in this basket: why may not he be there againe, in my houſe I am ſure he is: my Intelligence is true, my iealouſie is reaſonable, pluck me out all the linnen.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: If you find a man there, he ſhall dye a Fleas death.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Heer's no man.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: By my fidelity this is not well Mr. Ford: This wrongs you.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.p: Mr Ford, you muſt pray, and not follow the imaginations of your owne heart: this is iealouſies.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Well, hee's not heere I ſeeke for.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: No, nor no where elſe but in your braine.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Helpe to ſearch my houſe this one time: if I find not what I ſeeke, ſhew no colour for my extremity: Let me for euer be your Table-ſport: Let them ſay of me, as iealous as Ford, that ſearch'd a hollow Wall-nut for his wiues Lemman. Satisfie me once more, once more ſerch with me.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: What hoa (Miſtris Page,) come you and the old woman downe: my husband will come into the Chamber.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Old woman? what old womans that?

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: Why it is my maids Aunt of Brainford.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: A witch, a Queane, an olde couzening queane: Haue I not forbid her my houſe. She comes of errands do's ſhe? We are ſimple men, wee doe not know what's brought to paſſe vnder the profeſſion of Fortune-telling. She workes by Charmes, by Spels, by th' Figure, & ſuch dawbry as this is, beyond our Element: wee know nothing. Come downe you Witch, you Hagge you, come downe I ſay.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Nay, good ſweet husband, good Gentlemen, let him ſtrike the old woman.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Come mother Prat, Come giue me your hand.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Ile Prat-her: Out of my doore, you Witch, you Ragge, you Baggage, you Poulcat, you Runnion, out, out: Ile coniure you, Ile fortune-tell you.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Are you not aſham'd? I thinke you haue kill'd the poore woman.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Nay he will do it, 'tis a goodly credite for you.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Hang her witch.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: By yea, and no, I thinke the o' man is a witch indeede: I like not when a o' man has a great peard; I ſpie a great peard vnder his muffler.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Will you follow Gentlemen, I beſeech you follow: ſee but the iſſue of my iealouſie: If I cry out thus vpon no traile, neuer truſt me when I open againe.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Let's obey his humour a little further:
Come Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Truſt me he beate him moſt pittifully.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Nay by th' Maſſe that he did not: he beate him moſt vnpittifully, me thought.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Ile haue the cudgell hallow'd, and hung ore the Altar, it hath done meritorious ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: What thinke you? May we with the warrant of woman hood, and the witneſſe of a good conſcience, purſue him with any further reuenge?

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: The ſpirit of wantonneſſe is ſure ſcar'd out of him, if the diuell haue him not in fee-ſimple, with fine and recouery, he will neuer (I thinke) in the way of waſte, attempt vs againe.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Shall we tell our husbands how wee haue ſeru'd him?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Yes, by all meanes: if it be but to ſcrape the figures out of your husbands braines: if they can find in their hearts, the poore vnuertuous fat Knight ſhall be any further afflicted, wee two will ſtill bee the miniſters.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Ile warrant, they'l haue him publiquely ſham'd, and me thinkes there would be no period to the ieſt, ſhould he not be publikely ſham'd.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.l: Come, to the Forge with it, then ſhape it:
I would not haue things coole.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: Sir, the Germane deſires to haue three of your horſes: the Duke himſelfe will be to morrow at Court, and they are going to meet him.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: What Duke ſhould that be comes ſo ſecretly? I heare not of him in the Court: let mee ſpeake with the Gentlemen, they ſpeake Engliſh?

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: I Sir? Ile call him to you.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: They ſhall haue my horſes, but Ile make them pay: Ile ſauce them, they haue had my houſes a week at commaund: I haue turn'd away my other gueſts, they muſt come off, Ile ſawce them, come.

div.head: Scena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Page, Ford, Miſtris Page, Miſtris Ford, and Euans.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: 'Tis one of the beſt diſcretions of a o' man as euer I did looke vpon.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: And did he ſend you both theſe Letters at an inſtant?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: VVithin a quarter of an houre.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: Pardon me (wife) henceforth do what yu wilt:
I rather will ſuſpect the Sunne with gold,
Then thee with wantonnes: Now doth thy honor ſtand
(In him that was of late an Heretike)
As firme as faith.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: 'Tis well, 'tis well, no more:
Be not as extreme in ſubmiſſion, as in offence,
But let our plot go forward: Let our wiues
Yet once againe (to make vs publike ſport)
Appoint a meeting with this old fat-fellow,
Where we may take him, and diſgrace him for it.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: There is no better way then that they ſpoke of.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: How? to ſend him word they'll meete him in the Parke at midnight? Fie, fie, he'll neuer come.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: You ſay he has bin throwne in the Riuers: and has bin greeuouſly peaten, as an old o' man: me-thinkes there ſhould be terrors in him, that he ſhould not come: Me-thinkes his fleſh is puniſh'd, hee ſhall haue no deſires.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: So thinke I too.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.l: Deuiſe but how you'l vſe him whē he comes,
And let vs two deuiſe to bring him thether.

sp.speaker: Miſ Page.
sp.l: There is an old tale goes, that Herne the
Hunter (ſometime a keeper heere in Windſor Forreſt)
Doth all the winter time, at ſtill midnight
Walke round about an Oake, with great rag'd-hornes,
And there he blaſts the tree, and takes the cattle,
And make milch-kine yeeld blood, and ſhakes a chaine
In a moſt hideous and dreadfull manner.
You haue heard of ſuch a Spirit, and well you know
The ſuperſtitious idle-headed-Eld
Receiu'd, and did deliuer to our age
This tale of Herne the Hunter, for a truth.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Why yet there want not many that do feare
In deepe of night to walke by this Hernes Oake:
But what of this?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.l: Marry this is our deuiſe,
That Falstaffe at that Oake ſhall meete with vs.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Well, let it not be doubted but he'll come,
And in this ſhape, when you haue brought him thether,
What ſhall be done with him? What is your plot?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Pa.
sp.l: That likewiſe haue we thoght vpon: & thus:
Nan Page (my daughter) and my little ſonne,
And three or foure more of their growth, wee'l dreſſe
Like Vrchins, Ouphes, and Fairies, greene and white,
With rounds of waxen Tapers on their heads,
And rattles in their hands; vpon a ſodaine,
As Falſtaffe, ſhe, and I, are newly met,
Let them from forth a ſaw-pit ruſh at once
With ſome diffuſed ſong: Vpon their ſight
We two, in great amazedneſſe will flye:
Then let them all encircle him about,
And Fairy-like to pinch the vncleane Knight;
And aske him why that houre of Fairy Reuell,
In their ſo ſacred pathes, he dares to tread
In ſhape prophane.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: And till he tell the truth,
Let the ſuppoſed Fairies pinch him, ſound,
And burne him with their Tapers.

sp.speaker: Miſt Page.
sp.l: The truth being knowne,
We'll all preſent our ſelues; diſ-horne the ſpirit,
And mocke him home to Windſor.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: The children muſt
Be practis'd well to this, or they'll neu'r doo't.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: I will teach the children their behauiours: and I will be like a Iacke-an-Apes alſo, to burne the Knight with my Taber.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: That will be excellent,
Ile go buy them vizards.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: My Nan ſhall be the Queene of all the Fairies, finely attired in a robe of white.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: That ſilke will I go buy, and in that time
Shall M. Slender ſteale my Nan away,
And marry her at Eaton: go, ſend to Falſtaffe ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: Nay, Ile to him againe in name of Broome,
Hee'l tell me all his purpoſe: ſure hee'l come.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.l: Feare not you that: Go get vs properties
And tricking for our Fayries.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.l: Let vs about it,
It is admirable pleaſures, and ferry honeſt knaueries.

sp.speaker: Miſ. Page.
sp.l: Go Miſt. Ford,
Send quickly to Sir Iohn, to know his minde:
Ile to the Doctor, he hath my good will,
And none but he to marry with Nan Page:
That Slender (though well landed) is an Ideot:
And he, my husband beſt of all affects:
The Doctor is well monied, and his friends
Potent at Court: he, none but he ſhall haue her,
Though twenty thouſand worthier come to craue her.

div.head: Scena Quinta.
div.stage: Enter Hoſt, Simple, Falſtaffe, Bardolfe, Euans, Caius, Quickly.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: What wouldſt thou haue? (Boore) what? (thick skin) ſpeake, breathe, diſcuſſe: breefe, ſhort, quicke, ſnap.

sp.speaker: Simp.
sp.p: Marry Sir, I come to ſpeake with Sir Iohn Falſtaffe from M. Slender.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: There's his Chamber, his Houſe, his Caſtle, his ſtanding-bed and truckle-bed: 'tis painted about with the ſtory of the Prodigall, freſh and new: go, knock and call: hee'l ſpeake like an Anthropophaginian vnto thee: Knocke I ſay.

sp.speaker: Simp.
sp.p: There's an olde woman, a fat woman gone vp into his chamber: Ile be ſo bold as ſtay Sir till ſhe come downe: I come to ſpeake with her indeed.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Ha? A fat woman? The Knight may be robb'd: Ile call, Bully-Knight, Bully Sir Iohn: ſpeake from thy Lungs Military: Art thou there? It is thine Hoſt, thine Epheſian cals.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: How now, mine Hoſt?

sp.speaker: Host.
sp.p: Here's a Bohemian-Tartar taries the comming downe of thy fat-woman: Let her deſcend (Bully) let her deſcend: my Chambers are honourable: Fie, priuacy? Fie.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: There was (mine Hoſt) an old-fat-woman euen now with me, but ſhe's gone.

sp.speaker: Simp.
sp.p: Pray you Sir, was't not the Wiſe-woman of Brainford?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I marry was it (Muſſel-ſhell) what would you with her?

sp.speaker: Simp.
sp.p: My Maſter (Sir) my maſter Slender, ſent to her ſeeing her go thorough the ſtreets, to know (Sir) whether one Nim (Sir) that beguil'd him of a chaine, had the chaine, or no.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I ſpake with the old woman about it.

sp.speaker: Sim.
sp.p: And what ſayes ſhe, I pray Sir?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Marry ſhee ſayes, that the very ſame man that beguil'd Maſter Slender of his Chaine, cozon'd him of it.

sp.speaker: Simp.
sp.p:
I would I could haue ſpoken with the Woman
her ſelfe, I had other things to haue ſpoken with her too, from him.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: What are they? let vs know.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: I: come: quicke.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I may not conceale them (Sir.)

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Conceale them, or thou di'ſt.

sp.speaker: Sim.
sp.p: Why ſir, they were nothing but about Miſtris Anne Page, to know if it were my Maſters fortune to haue her, or no.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: 'Tis, 'tis his fortune.

sp.speaker: Sim.
sp.p: What Sir?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: To haue her, or no: goe; ſay the woman told me ſo.

sp.speaker: Sim.
sp.p: May I be bold to ſay ſo Sir?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I Sir: like who more bold.

sp.speaker: Sim.
sp.p: I thanke your worſhip: I ſhall make my Maſter glad with theſe tydings.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Thou are clearkly: thou art clearkly (Sir Iohn) was there a wiſe woman with thee?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I that there was (mine Hoſt) one that hath taught me more wit, then euer I learn'd before in my life: and I paid nothing for it neither, but was paid for my learning.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: Out alas (Sir) cozonage: meere cozonage.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Where be my horſes? ſpeake well of them varletto.

sp.speaker: Bar.
sp.p: Run away with the cozoners: for ſo ſoone as I came beyond Eaton, they threw me off, from behinde one of them, in a ſlough of myre; and ſet ſpurres, and away; like three Germane-diuels; three Doctor Fauſtaffes.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: They are gone but to meete the Duke (villaine) doe not ſay they be fled: Germanes are honeſt men.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Where is mine Hoſt?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: What is the matter Sir?

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: Haue a care of your entertainments: there is a friend of mine come to Towne, tels mee there is three Cozen-Iermans, that has cozend all the Hoſts of Readins, of Maidenhead; of Cole-brooke, of horſes and money: I tell you for good will (looke you) you are wiſe, and full of gibes, and vlouting-ſtocks: and 'tis not conuenient you ſhould be cozoned. Fare you well.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: Ver' is mine Hoſt de Iarteere?

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Here (Maſter Doctor) in perplexitie, and doubtfull delemma.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: I cannot tell vat is dat: but it is tell-a-me, dat you make grand preparation for a Duke de Iamanie: by my trot: der is no Duke that the Court is know, to come: I tell you for good will: adieu.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Huy and cry, (villaine) goe: aſſiſt me Knight, I am vndone: fly, run: huy, and cry (villaine) I am vndone.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p:
I would all the world might be cozond, for I haue beene cozond and beaten too: if it ſhould come to the eare of the Court, how I haue beene transformed; and how my transformation hath beene waſhd, and cudgeld, they would melt mee out of my fat drop by drop, and liquor Fiſhermens-boots with me: I warrant they would whip me with their fine wits, till I were as creſt-falne as a dride-peare: I neuer proſper'd, ſince I forſwore my ſelfe at Primer •
: well, if my winde were but long enough; I would repent: Now? Whence come you?

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: From the two parties forſooth.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: The Diuell take one partie, and his Dam the other: and ſo they ſhall be both beſtowed; I haue ſuffer'd more for their ſakes; more then the villanous inconſtancy of mans diſpoſition is able to beare.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.p: And haue not they ſuffer'd? Yes, I warrant; ſpeciouſly one of them; Miſtris Ford (good heart) is beaten blacke and blew, that you cannot ſee a white ſpot about her.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: What tell'ſt thou mee of blacke, and blew? I was beaten my ſelfe into all the colours of the Rainebow: and I was like to be apprehended for the Witch of Braineford, but that my admirable dexteritie of wit, my counterfeiting the action of an old woman deliuer'd me, the knaue Conſtable had ſet me ith' Stocks, ith' common Stocks, for a Witch.

sp.speaker: Qu▪
sp.p: Sir: let me ſpeake with you in your Chamber, you ſhall heare how things goe, and (I warrant) to your content: here is a Letter will ſay ſomewhat: (good-hearts) what a-doe here is to bring you together? Sure, one of you do's not ſerue heauen well, that you are ſo croſſ'd.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Come vp into my Chamber.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Maſter Fenton, talke not to mee, my minde is heauy: I will giue ouer all.

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.l: Yet heare me ſpeake: aſſiſt me in my purpoſe,
And (as I am a gentleman) ile giue thee
A hundred pound in gold, more then your loſſe.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: I will heare you (Maſter Fenton) and I will (at the leaſt) keepe your counſell.

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.l: From time to time, I haue acquainted you
With the deare loue I beare to faire Anne Page,
Who, mutually, hath anſwer'd my affection,
(So farre forth, as her ſelfe might be her chooſer)
Euen to my wiſh; I haue a letter from her
Of ſuch contents, as you will wonder at;
The mirth whereof, ſo larded with my matter,
That neither (ſingly) can be manifeſted
Without the ſhew of both: fat Falſtaffe
Hath a great Scene; the image of the ieſt
Ile ſhow you here at large (harke good mine Hoſt:)
To night at Hernes-Oke, iuſt 'twixt twelue and one,
Muſt my ſweet Nan preſent the Faerie-Queene:
The purpoſe why, is here: in which diſguiſe
VVhile other Ieſts are ſomething ranke on foote,
Her father hath commanded her to ſlip
Away with Slender, and with him, at Eaton
Immediately to Marry: She hath conſented: Now Sir,
Her Mother, (euen ſtrong againſt that match
And firme for Doctor Caius) hath appointed
That he ſhall likewiſe ſhuffle her away,
While other ſports are tasking of their mindes,
And at the Deanry, where a Prieſt attends
Strait marry her: to this her Mothers plot
She ſeemingly obedient) likewiſe hath
Made promiſe to the Doctor: Now, thus it reſts,
Her Father meanes ſhe ſhall be all in white;
And in that habit, when Slender ſees his time
To take her by the hand, and bid her goe,
She ſhall goe with him: her Mother hath intended
(The better to deuote her to the Doctor;
For they muſt all be mask'd, and vizarded)
That quaint in greene, ſhe ſhall be looſe en-roab'd,
With Ribonds-pendant, flaring 'bout her head;
And when the Doctor ſpies his vantage ripe,
To pinch her by the hand, and on that token,
The maid hath giuen conſent to go with him.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.p: Which meanes ſhe to deceiue? Father, or Mother.

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.l: Both (my good Hoſt) to go along with me:
And heere it reſts, that you'l procure the Vicar
To ſtay for me at Church, 'twixt twelue, and one,
And in the lawfull name of marrying,
To giue our hearts vnited ceremony.

sp.speaker: Hoſt.
sp.l: Well, husband your deuice; Ile to the Vicar,
Bring you the Maid, you ſhall not lacke a Prieſt.

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.l: So ſhall I euermore be bound to thee;
Beſides, Ile make a preſent recompence.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Pre'thee no more pratling: go, Ile hold, this is the third time: I hope good lucke lies in odde numbers: Away, go, they ſay there is Diuinity in odde Numbers, either in natiuity, chance, or death: away.

sp.speaker: Qai.
sp.p: Ile prouide you a chaine, and Ile do what I can to get you a paire of hornes.

sp.speaker: Fall.
sp.p: Away I ſay, time weares, hold vp your head & mince. How now M. Broome? Maſter Broome, the matter will be knowne to night, or neuer. Bee you in the Parke about midnight, at Hernes-Oake, and you ſhall ſee wonders.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Went you not to her yeſterday (Sir) as you told me you had appointed?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I went to her (Maſter Broome) as you ſee, like a poore-old-man, but I came from her (Maſter Broome) like a poore-old-woman; that ſame knaue (Ford hir huſband) hath the ſineſt mad diuell of • ealouſie in him (Maſter Broome) that euer gouern'd Frenſie. I will tell you, he beate me greeuouſly, in the ſhape of a woman: (for in the ſhape of Man (Maſter Broome) I feare not Goliah with a Weauers beame, becauſe I know alſo, life is a Shuttle) I am in haſt, go along with mee, Ile tell you all (Maſter Broome:) ſince I pluckt Geeſe, plaide Trew • nt, and whipt Top, I knew not what 'twas to be beaten, till lately. Follow mee, Ile tell you ſtrange things of this knaue Ford, on whom to night I will be reuenged, and I will deliuer his wife into your hand. Follow, ſtraunge things in hand (M. Broome) follow.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Come, come: wee'll couch i' th Caſtle-ditch, till we ſee the light of our Fairies. Remember ſon Slender, my

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I forſooth, I haue ſpoke with her, & we haue a nay-word, how to know one another. I come to her in white, and cry Mum; ſhe cries Budget, and by that we know one another.

sp.speaker: Shal.
sp.p: That's good too: But what needes either your Mum, or her Budget? The white will decipher her well enough. It hath ſtrooke ten a'clocke.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: The night is darke, Light and Spirits will become it wel: Heauen proſper our ſport. No man means euill but the deuill, and we ſhal know him by his hornes. Lets away: follow me.

div.head: Scena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Miſt. Page, Miſt. Ford, Caius.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Mr Doctor, my daughter is in green, when you ſee your time, take her by the hand, away with her to the Deauerie, and diſpatch it quickly: go before into the Parke: we two muſt go together.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: I know vat I haue to do, adieu.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Fare you well (Sir.) my husband will not reioyce ſo much at the abuſe of Falſtaffe, as he will chafe at the Doctors marrying my daughter: But 'tis no matter; better a little chiding, then a great deale of heartbreake.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Where is Nan now? and her troop of Fairies? and the Welch-deuill Herne?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: They are all couch'd in a pit hard by Hernes Oake, with obſcur'd Lights; which at the very inſtant of Falſtaffes and our meeting, they will at once diſplay to the night.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: That cannot chooſe but amaze him.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: If he be not amaz'd he will be mock'd: If he be amaz'd, he will euery way be mock'd.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: Wee'll betray him finely.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.l: Againſt ſuch Lewdſters, and their lechery,
Thoſe that betray them, do no treachery.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Ford.
sp.p: The houre drawes-on: to the Oake, to the Oake.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.p: Trib, trib Fairies: Come, and remember your parts: be pold (I pray you) follow me into the pit, and when I giue the watch-'ords, do as I pid you: Come, come, trib, trib.

div.head: Scena Quinta.
div.stage: Enter Falſtaffe, Miſtris Page, Mistris Ford, Euans, Anne Page, Fairies, Page, Ford, Quickly, Slender, Fenton, Caius, Pistoll.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p:
The Windſor-bell hath ſtroke twelue: the Minute drawes-on: Now the hot-bloodied-Gods aſſiſt me: Remember lou • , thou was't a Bull for thy Europa, Loue ſet on thy hornes. O powerfull Loue, that in ſome reſpects makes a Beaſt a Man: in ſom other, a Man a beaſt. You were alſo (Iupiter) a Swan, for the loue of Leda: O
omnipotent Loue, how nere the God drew to the complexion of a Gooſe: a fault done firſt in the forme of a beaſt, (O Ioue, a beaſtly fault:) and then another fault, in the ſemblance of a Fowle, thinke on't (Ioue) a fowle-fault. When Gods haue hot backes, what ſhall poore men do? For me, I am heere a Windſor Stagge, and the fatteſt (I thinke) i' th Forreſt. Send me a coole rut-time (Ioue) or who can blame me to piſſe my Tallow? Who comes heere? my Doe?

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.l: Sir Iohn? Art thou there (my Deere?)
My male-Deere?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: My Doe, with the blacke Scut? Let the skie raine Potatoes: let it thunder, to the tune of Greeneſleeues, haile-kiſſing Comfits, and ſnow Eringoes: Let there come a tempeſt of prouocation, I will ſhelter mee heere.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: Miſtris Page is come with me (ſweet hart.)

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Diuide me like a brib'd-Bucke, each a Haunch: I will keepe my ſides to my ſelfe, my ſhoulders for the fellow of this walke; and my hornes I bequeath your husbands. Am I a Woodman, ha? Speake I like Herne the Hunter? Why, now is Cupid a child of conſcience, he makes reſtitution. As I am a true ſpirit, welcome.

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: Alas, what noiſe?

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: Heauen forgiue our ſinnes.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: What ſhould this be?

sp.speaker: M. Ford. M. Page.
sp.p: Away, away.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.l: I thinke the diuell wil not haue me damn'd,
Leaſt the oyle that's in me ſhould ſet hell on fire;
He would neuer elſe croſſe me thus.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.l: Fairies blacke, gray, greene, and white,
You Moone-ſhine reuellers, and ſhades of night.
You Orphan heires of fixed deſtiny,
Attend your office, and your quality.
Crier Hob-goblyn, make the Fairy Oyes.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.l: Elues, liſt your names: Silence you aiery toyes.
Cricket, to Windſor-chimnies ſhalt thou leape;
Where fires thou find'ſt vnrak'd, and hearths vnſwept,
There pinch the Maids as blew as Bill-berry,
Our radiant Queene, hates Sluts, and Sluttery.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.l: They are Fairies, he that ſpeaks to them ſhall die,
Ile winke, and couch: No man their workes muſt eie.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.l: Wher's Bede? Go you, and where you find a maid
That ere ſhe ſleepe has thrice her prayers ſaid,
Raiſe vp the Organs of her fantaſie,
Sleepe ſhe as ſound as careleſſe infancie,
But thoſe as ſleepe, and thinke not on their ſins,
Pinch them armes, legs, backes, ſhoulders, ſides, & ſhins.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: About, about:
Search Windſor Caſtle (Elues) within, and out.
Strew good • k • (Ouphes) on euery ſacred roome,
That it may ſtand till the perpetuall doome,
In ſtate as wholſome, as in ſtate 'tis ſit,
Worthy the Owner, and the Owner it.
The ſeuerall Chai • of Order, tooke you ſ • owre
With iuyce of Balme; and euery precious flowre,
Each faire Inſtalment, Coate, and ſeu'rall Creſt,
With loyall Blazon, euermore be bleſt.
And Nightly-meadow-Fairies, looke you ſing
Like to the Garters-Compaſſe, in a ring,
Th' expreſſure that it beares: Greene let it be,
Mote fertile-freſh then all the Field to ſee:
And, Hony Soit Qui Mal-y-Pence, write
In Emrold-tuffes, Flowres purple, blew, and white,
Like Saphire-pearle, and rich embroiderie,
Buckled below faire Knight-hoods bending knee;
Fairies vſe Flowres for their characterie.
Away, diſperſe: But till 'tis one a clocke,
Our Dance of Cuſtome, round about the Oke
Of Herne the Hunter, let vs not forget.

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.l: Pray you lock hand in hand: your ſelues in order ſet:
And twenty glow-wormes ſhall our Lanthornes bee
To guide our Meaſure round about the Tree.
But ſtay, I ſmell a man of middle earth.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.l: Heauens defend me from that Welſh Fairy,
Leaſt he transforme me to a peece of Cheeſe.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: Vilde worme, thou waſt ore-look'd euen in thy birth.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: With Triall-fire touch me his finger end:
If he be chaſte, the flame will backe deſcend
And turne him to no paine: but if he ſtart,
It is the fleſh of a corrupted hart.

sp.speaker: Piſt.
sp.p: A triall, come.

sp.speaker: Eua.
sp.p: Come: will this wood take fire?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Oh, oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Qui.
sp.l: Corrupt, corrupt, and tainted in deſire.
About him (Fairies) ſing a ſcornfull rime,
And as you trip, ſtill pinch him to your time.

lg.head: The Song.
lg.l: Fie on ſinnefull phantaſie▪ Fie on Luſt, and Luxurie:
Luſt is but a bloudy fire, kindled with vnchaste deſire,
Fed in heart whoſe flames aſpire,
As thoughts do blow them higher and higher.
Pinch him (Fairies) mutually: Pinch him for his villanie.
Pinch him, and burne him, and turne him about,
Till Candles, & Star-light, & Moone-ſhine be out.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Nay do not flye, I thinke we haue watcht you now: VVill none but Herne the Hunter ſerue your turne?

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.l: I pray you come, hold vp the ieſt no higher.
Now (good Sir Iohn) how like you Windſor wiues?
See you theſe husband? Do not theſe faire yoakes
Become the Forreſt better then the Towne?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: Now Sir, whoſe a Cuckold now?
Mr Broome, Falstaffes a Knaue, a Cuckoldly knaue,
Heere are his hornes Maſter Broome:
sp.p: And Maſter Broome, he hath enioyed nothing of Fords, but his Buck-basket, his cudgell, and twenty pounds of money, which muſt be paid to Mr Broome, his horſes are arreſted for it, Mr Broome.

sp.speaker: M. Ford.
sp.p: Sir Iohn, we haue had ill lucke: wee could neuer meete: I will neuer take you for my Loue againe, but I will alwayes count you my Deere.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I do begin to perceiue that I am made an Aſſe.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I, and an Oxe too: both the proofes are extant.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: And theſe are not Fairies▪ I was three or foure times in the thought they were not Fairies, and yet the guiltineſſe of my minde, the ſodaine ſurprize of my powers, droue the groſſeneſſe of the foppery into a receiu'd beleefe, in deſpight of the teeth of all rime and reaſon, that they were Fairies. See now how wit may be made a Iacke-a-Lent, when 'tis vpon ill imployment.

sp.speaker: Euant.
sp.p: Sir Iohn Falstaffe, ſerue Got, and leaue your deſires, and Fairies will not pinſe you.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: VVell ſaid Fairy Hugh.

sp.speaker: Euans.
sp.p: And leaue you your iealouzies too, I pray you.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: I will neuer miſtruſt my wife againe, till thou art able to woo her in good Engliſh.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Haue I laid my braine in the Sun, and dri'de it, that it wants matter to preuent ſo groſſe ore-reaching as this? Am I ridden with a Welch Goate too? Shal I haue a Coxcombe of Frize? Tis time I were choak'd with a peece of toaſted Cheeſe.

sp.speaker: Eu.
sp.p: Seeſe is not good to giue putter; your belly is al putter.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Seeſe, and Putter? Haue I liu'd to ſtand at the taunt of one that makes Fritters of Engliſh? This is enough to be the decay of luſt and late-walking through the Realme.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Why Sir Iohn, do you thinke though wee would haue thruſt vertue out of our hearts by the head and ſhoulders, and haue giuen our ſelues without ſcruple to hell, that euer the deuill could haue made you our delight?

sp.speaker: Ford
sp.p: What, a hodge-pudding? A bag of flax?

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: A puft man?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Old, cold, wither'd, and of intollerable entrailes?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: And one that is as ſlanderous as Sathan?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: And as poore as Iob?

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: And as wicked as his wife?

sp.speaker: Euan.
sp.p: And giuen to Fornications, and to Tauernes, and Sacke, and Wine, and Metheglins, and to drinkings and ſwearings, and ſtarings? Pribles and prables?

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: Well, I am your Theame: you haue the ſtart of me. I am deiected: I am not able to anſwer the Welch Flannell, Ignorance it ſelfe is a plummet ore me, vſe me as you will.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: Marry Sir, wee'l bring you to Windſor to one Mr Broome, that you haue cozon'd of money, to whom you ſhould haue bin a Pander: ouer and aboue that you haue ſuffer'd, I thinke, to repay that money will be a biting affliction.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Yet be cheerefull Knight▪ thou ſhalt eat a poſſet to night at my houſe, wher I will deſire thee to laugh at my wife, that now laughes at thee: Tell her Mr Slender hath married her daughter.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.p: Doctors doubt that;
If Anne Page be my daughter, ſhe is (by this) Doctour Caius wife.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Whoa hoe, hoe, Father Page.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Sonne? How now? How now Sonne,
Haue you diſpatch'd?

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: Diſpatch'd? Ile make the beſt in Glofterſhire know on't: would I were hang'd la, elſe.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Of what ſonne?

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I came yonder at Eaton to marry Miſtris Anne Page, and ſhe's a great lubberly boy. If it had not bene i' th Church, I would haue ſwing'd him, or hee ſhould haue ſwing'd me. If I did not thinke it had beene Anne Page, would I might neuer ſtirre, and 'tis a Poſt-maſters Boy.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Vpon my life then, you tooke the wrong.

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: What neede you tell me that? I think ſo, when I tooke a Boy for a Girle: If I had bene married to him, (for all he was in womans apparrell) I would not haue had him.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Why this is your owne folly,
Did not I tell you how you ſhould know my daughter,
By her garments?

sp.speaker: Slen.
sp.p: I went to her in greene, and cried Mum, and ſhe cride budget, as Anne and I had appointed, and yet it was not Anne, but a Poſt-maſters boy.

sp.speaker: Mist. Page.
sp.p: Good George be not angry, I knew of your purpoſe: turn'd my daughter into white, and indeede ſhe is now with the Doctor at the Deanrie, and there married.

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: Ver is Miſtris Page: by gar I am cozoned, I ha married oon Garſoon, a boy; oon peſant, by gar. A boy, it is not An Page, by gar, I am cozened.

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: VVhy? did you take her in white?

sp.speaker: Cai.
sp.p: I bee gar, and 'tis a boy: be gar, Ile raiſe all Windſor.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.p: This is ſtrange: Who hath got the right Anne?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: My heart miſgiues me, here comes Mr Fenton.
How now Mr Fenton?

sp.speaker: Anne.
sp.p: Pardon good father, good my mother pardon

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Now Miſtris:
How chance you went not with Mr Slender?

sp.speaker: M. Page.
sp.p: Why went you not with Mr Doctor, maid?

sp.speaker: Fen.
sp.l: You do amaze her: heare the truth of it,
You would haue married her moſt ſhamefully,
Where there was no proportion held in loue:
The truth is, ſhe and I (long ſince contracted)
Are now ſo ſure that nothing can diſſolue vs:
Th' offence is holy, that ſhe hath committed,
And this deceit looſes the name of craft,
Of diſobedience, or vnduteous title,
Since therein ſhe doth euitate and ſhun
A thouſand irreligious curſed houres
Which forced marriage would haue brought vpon her.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: Stand not amaz'd, here is no remedie:
In Loue, the heauens themſelues do guide the ſtate,
Money buyes Lands, and wiues are ſold by fate.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: I am glad, though you haue tane a ſpecial ſtand to ſtrike at me, that your Arrow hath glanc'd.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Well, what remedy? Fenton, heauen giue thee ioy, what cannot be eſchew'd, muſt be embrac'd.

sp.speaker: Fal.
sp.p: When night-dogges run, all ſorts of Deere are chac'd.

sp.speaker: Miſt. Page.
sp.l: Well, I will muſe no further: Mr Fenton,
Heauen giue you many, many merry dayes:
Good husband, let vs euery one go home,
And laugh this ſport ore by a Countrie fire,
Sir Iohn and all.

sp.speaker: Ford.
sp.l: Let it be ſo (Sir Iohn:)
To Maſter Broome, you yet ſhall hold your word,
For he, to night, ſhall lye with Miſtris Ford▪

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Of Gouernment, the properties to vnfold,
Would ſeeme in me t' affect ſpeech & diſcourſe,
Since I am put to know, that your owne Science
Exceedes (in that) the liſts of all aduice
My ſtrength can giue you: Then no more remaines
But that, to your ſufficiency, as your worth is able,
And let them worke: The nature of our People,
Our Cities Inſtitutions, and the Termes
For Common Iuſtice, y' are as pregnant in
As Art, and practiſe, hath inriched any
That we remember: There is our Commiſſion,
From which, we would not haue you warpe; call hither,
I ſay, bid come before vs Angelo:
What figure of vs thinke you, he will beare.
For you muſt know, we haue with ſpeciall ſoule
Elected him our abſence to ſupply;
Lent him our terror, dreſt him with our loue,
And giuen his Deputation all the Organs
Of our owne powre: What thinke you of it?

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.l: If any in Vienna be of worth
To vndergoe ſuch ample grace, and honour,
It is Lord Angelo.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: Looke where he comes.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Alwayes obedient to your Graces will▪
I come to know your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Angelo:
There is a kinde of Character in thy life,
That to th' obſeruer, doth thy hiſtory
Fully vnfold: Thy ſelfe, and thy belongings
Are not thine owne ſo proper, as to waſte
Thy ſelfe vpon thy vertues; they on thee:
Heauen doth with vs, as we, with Torches doe,
Not light them for themſelues: For if our vertues
Did not goe forth of vs, 'twere all alike
As if we had them not: Spirits are not finely touch'd,
But to fine iſſues: nor nature neuer lends
The ſmalleſt ſcruple of her excellence,
But like a thrifty goddeſſe, ſhe determines
Her ſelfe the glory of a creditour,
Both thanks, and vſe; but I do bend my ſpeech
To one that can my part in him aduertiſe;
Hold therefore Angelo:
In our remoue, be thou at full, our ſelfe:
Mortallitie and Mercie in Vienna
Liue in thy tongue, and heart: Old Eſcalus
Though firſt in queſtion, is thy ſecondary.
Take thy Commiſſion.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Now good my Lord
Let there be ſome more teſt, made of my mettle,
Before ſo noble, and ſo great a figure
Be ſtamp't vpon it.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: No more euaſion:
We haue with a leauen'd, and prepared choice
Proceeded to you; therefore take your honors:
Our haſte from hence is of ſo quicke condition,
That it prefers it ſelfe, and leaues vnqueſtion'd
Matters of needfull value: We ſhall write to you
As time, and our concernings ſhall importune,
How it goes with vs, and doe looke to know
What doth befall you here. So fare you well:
To th' hopefull execution doe I leaue you,
Of your Commiſſions.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Yet giue leaue (my Lord▪)
That we may bring you ſomething on the way.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: My haſte may not admit it,
Nor neede you (on mine honor) haue to doe
With any ſcruple: your ſcope is as mine owne,
So to inforce, or qualifie the Lawes
As to your ſoule ſeemes good: Giue me your hand,
Ile priuily away: I loue the people,
But doe not like to ſtage me to their eyes:
Though it doe well, I doe not relliſh well
Their lowd applauſe, and Aues vehement:
Nor doe I thinke the man of ſafe diſcretion
That do's affect it. Once more fare you well.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: The heauens giue ſafety to your purpoſes.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Lead forth, and bring you backe in happineſſe.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: I thanke you, fare you well.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.l: I ſhal deſire you, Sir, to giue me leaue
To haue free ſpeech with you; and it concernes me
To looke into the bottome of my place:
A powre I haue, but of what ſtrength and nature,
I am not yet inſtructed.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo with me: Let vs with-draw together,
And we may ſoone our ſatisfaction haue
Touching that point.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Ile wait vpon your honor.

div.head: Scena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Lucio, and two other Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: If the Duke, with the other Dukes, come not to compoſition with the King of Hungary, why then all the Dukes fall vpon the King.

sp.speaker: 1. Gent.
sp.p: Heauen grant vs its peace, but not the King of Hungaries.

sp.speaker: 2. Gent.
sp.p: Amen.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Thou conclud'ſt like the Sanctimonious Pirat, that went to ſea with the ten Commandements, but ſcrap'd one out of the Table.

sp.speaker: 2. Gent.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt not Steale?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I, that he raz'd.

sp.speaker: 1. Gent.
sp.p: Why? 'twas a commandement, to command the Captaine and all the reſt from their functions: they put forth to ſteale: There's not a Souldier of vs all, that in the thankſ-giuing before meate, do ralliſh the petition well, that praies for peace.

sp.speaker: 2. Gent.
sp.p: I neuer heard any Souldier diſlike it.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I beleeue thee: for I thinke thou neuer was't where Grace was ſaid.

sp.speaker: 2. Gent.
sp.p: No? a dozen times at leaſt.

sp.speaker: 1. Gent.
sp.p: What? In meeter?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: In any proportion. or in any language.

sp.speaker: 1. Gent.
sp.p: I thinke, or in any Religion.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I, why not? Grace, is Grace, deſpight of all controuerſie: as for example; Thou thy ſelfe art a wicked villaine, deſpight of all Grace.

sp.speaker: 1. Gent.
sp.p: Well: there went but a paire of ſheeres betweene vs.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I grant: as there may betweene the Liſts, and the Veluet. Thou art the Liſt.

sp.speaker: 1. Gent.
sp.p: And thou the Veluet; thou art good veluet; thou'rt a three pild-peece I warrant thee: I had as liefe be a Lyſt of an Engliſh Kerſey, as be pil'd, as thou art pil'd, for a French Veluet. Do I ſpeake feelingly now?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I thinke thou do'ſt: and indeed with moſt painfull feeling of thy ſpeech: I will, out of thine owne confeſſion, learne to begin thy health; but, whilſt I liue forget to drinke after thee.

sp.speaker: 1. Gen.
sp.p: I think I haue done my ſelfe wrong, haue I not?

sp.speaker: 2. Gent.
sp.p: Yes, that thou haſt; whether thou art tainted, or free.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Behold, behold, where Madam Mitigation comes. I haue purchaſ'd as many diſeaſes vnder her Roofe, As come to

sp.speaker: 2. Gent.
sp.p: To what, I pray?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Iudge.

sp.speaker: 2. Gent.
sp.p: To three thouſand Dollours a yeare.

sp.speaker: 1. Gent.
sp.p: I, and more.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: A French crowne more.

sp.speaker: 1. Gent.
sp.p: Thou art alwayes figuring diſeaſes in me; but thou art full of error, I am ſound.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Nay, not (as one would ſay) healthy: but ſo ſound, as things that are hollow; thy bones are hollow; Impiety has made a feaſt of thee.

sp.speaker: 1. Gent.
sp.p: How now, which of your hips has the moſt profound Ciatica?

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.p: Well, well: there's one yonder arreſted, and carried to priſon, was worth fiue thouſand of you all.

sp.speaker: 2. Gent.
sp.p: Who's that I pray'thee?

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.p: Marry Sir, that's Claudio, Signior Claudio.

sp.speaker: 1. Gent.
sp.p: Claudio to priſon? 'tis not ſo.

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.p: Nay, but I know 'tis ſo: I ſaw him arreſted: ſaw him carried away: and which is more, within theſe three daies his head to be chop'd off.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: But, after all this fooling, I would not haue it ſo: Art thou ſure of this?

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.p: I am too ſure of it: and it is for getting Madam Iulietta with childe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Beleeue me this may be: he promis'd to meete me two howres ſince, and he was euer preciſe in promiſe keeping.

sp.speaker: 2. Gent.
sp.p: Beſides you know, it drawes ſomthing neere to the ſpeech we had to ſuch a purpoſe.

sp.speaker: 1. Gent.
sp.p: But moſt of all agreeing with the proclamatiō.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Away: let's goe learne the truth of it.

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.p: Thus, what with the war; what with the ſweat, what with the gallowes, and what with pouerty, I am Cuſtom-ſhrunke. How now? what's the newes with you.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Yonder man is carried to priſon.

sp.speaker: Baw.
sp.p: Well: what has he done?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: A Woman.

sp.speaker: Baw.
sp.p: But what's his offence?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Groping for Trowts, in a peculiar Riuer.

sp.speaker: Baw.
sp.p: What? is there a maid with child by him?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: No: but there's a woman with maid by him you haue not heard of the proclamation, haue you?

sp.speaker: Baw.
sp.p: What proclamation, man?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: All howſes in the Suburbs of Vienna muſt bee pluck'd downe.

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.p: And what ſhall become of thoſe in the Citie?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: They ſhall ſtand for ſeed: they had gon down to, but that a wiſe Burger put in for them.

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.p: But ſhall all our houſes of reſort in the Suburbs be puld downe?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: To the ground, Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.p: Why heere's a change indeed in the Commonwealth: what ſhall become of me?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Come: feare not you: good Counſellors lacke no Clients: though you change your place, you neede not change your Trade: Ile bee your Tapſter ſtill; courage, there will bee pitty taken on you; you that haue worne your eyes almoſt out in the ſeruice, you will bee conſidered.

sp.speaker: Bawd.
sp.p: What's to doe heere, Thomas Tapſter? let's withdraw?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Here comes Signior Claudio, led by the Prouoſt to priſon: and there's Madam Iuliet.

div.head: Scena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Prouoſt, Claudio, Iuliet, Officers, Lucio, & 2. Gent.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Fellow, why do'ſt thou ſhow me thus to th' world? Beare me to priſon, where I am committed.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: I do it not in euill diſpoſition, But from Lord Angelo by ſpeciall charge.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Thus can the demy-god (Authority)
Make vs pay downe, for our offence, by waight
The words of heauen▪ on whom it will, it will,
On whom it will not (ſoe) yet ſtill 'tis iuſt.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Why how now Claudio▪ whence comes this reſtraint.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: From too much liberty, (my Lucio) Liberty
As ſurfet is the father of much faſt,
So euery Scope by the immoderate vſe
Turnes to reſtraint: Our Natures doe purſue
Like Rats that rauyn downe their proper Bane,
A thirſty euill, and when we drinke, we die.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: If I could ſpeake ſo wiſely vnder an arreſt, I would ſend for certaine of my Creditors: and yet, to ſay the truth, I had as lief haue the foppery of freedome, as the mortality of impriſonment: what's thy offence, Claudio?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: What (but to ſpeake of) would offend againe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: What, is't murder?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Lecherie?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Call it ſo.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Away, Sir, you muſt goe.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: One word, good friend:
Lucio, a word with you.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: A hundred:
If they'll doe you any good: Is Lechery ſo look'd after?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Thus ſtands it with me: vpon a true contract
I got poſſeſſion of Iulietas bed,
You know the Lady, ſhe is faſt my wife,
Saue that we doe the denunciation lacke
Of outward Order. This we came not to,
Onely for propogation of a Dowre
Remaining in the Coffer of her friends,
From whom we thought it meet to hide our Loue
Till Time had made them for vs. But it chances
The ſtealth of our moſt mutuall entertainment
With Character too groſſe, is writ on Iuliet.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: With childe, perhaps?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: Vnhappely, euen ſo.
And the new Deputie, now for the Duke,
Whether it be the fault and glimpſe of newnes,
Or whether that the body publique, be
A horſe whereon the Gouernor doth ride,
Who newly in the Seate, that it may know
He can command; lets it ſtrait feele the ſpur:
Whether the Tirranny be in his place,
Or in his Eminence that fills it vp
I ſtagger in: But this new Gouernor
Awakes me all the inrolled penalties
Which haue (like vn-ſcowr'd Armor) hung by th' wall
So long, that ninteene Zodiacks haue gone round,
And none of them beene worne; and for a name
Now puts the drowſie and neglected Act
Freſhly on me: 'tis ſurely for a name.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I warrant it is: And thy head ſtands ſo tickle on thy ſhoulders, that a milke-maid, if ſhe be in loue, may ſigh it off: Send after the Duke, and appeale to him.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: I haue done ſo, but hee's not to be found.
I pre'thee (Lucio) doe me this kinde ſeruice:
This day, my ſiſter ſhould the Cloyſter enter,
And there receiue her approbation.
Acquaint her with the danger of my ſtate,
Implore her, in my voice, that ſhe make friends
To the ſtrict deputie: bid her ſelfe aſſay him,
I haue great hope in that: for in her youth
There is a prone and ſpeechleſſe dialect,
Such as moue men: beſide, ſhe hath proſperous Art
When ſhe will play with reaſon, and diſcourſe,
And well ſhe can perſwade.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I pray ſhee may; aſwell for the encouragement of the like, which elſe would ſtand vnder greeuous impoſition: as for the enioying of thy life, who I would be ſorry ſhould bee thus fooliſhly loſt, at a game of ticke-tacke: Ile to her.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: I thanke you good friend Lucio.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Within two houres.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Come Officer, away.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: No: holy Father, throw away that thought,
Beleeue not that the dribling dart of Loue
Can pierce a compleat boſome: why, I deſire thee
To giue me ſecret harbour, hath a purpoſe
More graue, and wrinkled, then the aimes, and ends
Of burning youth.

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.p: May your Grace ſpeake of it?

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: My holy Sir, none better knowes then you
How I haue euer lou'd the life remoued
And held in idle price, to haunt aſſemblies
Where youth, and coſt, witleſſe brauery keepes.
I haue deliuerd to Lord Angelo
(A man of ſtricture and firme abſtinence)
My abſolute power, and place here in Ʋienna,
And he ſuppoſes me trauaild to Poland,
(For ſo I haue ſtrewd it in the common eare)
And ſo it is receiu'd: Now (pious Sir)
You will demand of me, why I do this.

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.p: Gladly, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: We haue ſtrict Statutes, and moſt biting Laws,
(The needfull bits and curbes to headſtrong weedes,)
Which for this foureteene yeares, we haue let ſlip,
Euen like an ore-growne Lyon in a Caue
That goes not out to prey: Now, as fond Fathers,
Hauing bound vp the threatning twigs of birch,
Onely to ſticke it in their childrens ſight,
For terror, not to vſe: in time the rod
More mock'd, then fear'd: ſo our Decrees,
Dead to infliction, to themſelues are dead,
And libertie, plucks Iuſtice by the noſe;
The Baby beates the Nurſe, and quite a thwart
Goes all decorum.

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.l: It reſted in your Grace
To vnlooſe this tyde-vp Iuſtice, when you pleaſ'd:
And it in you more dreadfull would haue ſeem'd
Then in Lord Angelo.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: I doe feare: too dreadfull:
Sith 'twas my fault, to giue the people ſcope,
'T would be my tirrany to ſtrike and gall them,
For what I bid them doe: For, we bid this be done
When euill deedes haue their permiſſiue paſſe,
And not the puniſhment: therefore indeede (my father)
I haue on Angelo impos'd the office,
Who may in th' ambuſh of my name, ſtrike home,
And yet, my nature neuer in the fight
To do in ſlander: And to behold his ſway
I will, as 'twere a brother of your Order,
Viſit both Prince, and People: Therefore I pre'thee
Supply me with the habit, and inſtruct me
How I may formally in perſon beare
Like a true Frier: Moe reaſons for this action
At our more leyſure, ſhall I render you;
Onely, this one: Lord Angelo is preciſe,
Stands at a guard with Enuie: ſcarce confeſſes
That his blood flowes: or that his appetite
Is more to bread then ſtone: hence ſhall we ſee
If power change purpoſe: what our Seemers be.

div.head: Scena Quinta.
div.stage: Enter Iſabell and Franciſca a Nun.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: And haue you Nuns no farther priuiledges?

sp.speaker: Nun.
sp.p: Are not theſe large enough?

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.l: Yes truely; I ſpeake not as deſiring more,
But rather wiſhing a more ſtrict reſtraint
Vpon the Siſterſtood, the Votariſts of Saint Clare.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Hoa? peace be in this place.

sp.speaker: Iſa:
sp.p: Who's that which cals?

sp.speaker: Nun.
sp.l: It is a mans voice: gentle Iſabella
Turne you the key, and know his buſineſſe of him;
You may; I may not: you are yet vnſworne:
When you haue vowd, you muſt not ſpeake with men,
But in the preſence of the Prioreſſe;
Then if you ſpeake, you muſt not ſhow your face;
Or if you ſhow your face, you muſt not ſpeake:
He cals againe: I pray you anſwere him.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Peace and proſperitie: who is't that cals?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Haile Virgin, (if you be) as thoſe cheeke-Roſes
Proclaime you are no leſſe: can you ſo ſteed me,
As bring me to the fight of Iſabella,
A Nouice of this place, and the faire Siſter
To her vnhappie brother Claudio?

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.l: Why her vnhappy Brother? Let me aske,
The rather for I now muſt make you know
I am that Iſabella, and his Siſter.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Gentle & faire: your Brother kindly greets you;
Not to be weary with you; he's in priſon.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Woe me; for what?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: For that, which if my ſelfe might be his Iudge,
He ſhould receiue his puniſhment, in thankes:
He hath got his friend with childe.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Sir, make me not your ſtorie.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: 'Tis true; I would not, though 'tis my familiar ſin,
With Maids to ſeeme the Lap wing, and to ieſt
Tongue, far from heart: play with all Virgins ſo:
I hold you as a thing en-skied, and ſainted,
By your renouncement, an imortall ſpirit
And to be talk'd with in ſincerity,
As with a Saint.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: You doe blaſpheme the good, in mocking me.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Doe not beleeue it: fewnes, and truth; tis thus,
Your brother, and his louer haue embrac'd;
As thoſe that feed, grow full: as bloſſoming Time
That from the ſeednes, the bare fallow brings
To teeming foyſon: euen ſo her plenteous wombe
Expreſſeth his full Tilth, and husbandry.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Some one with childe by him? my coſen Iuliet?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Is ſhe your coſen?

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Adoptedly, as ſchoole-maids change their names By vaine, though apt affection.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: She it is.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Oh, let him marry her.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: This is the point.
The Duke is very ſtrangely gone from hence;
Bore many gentlemen (my ſelfe being one)
In hand, and hope of action: but we doe learne,
By thoſe that know the very Nerues of State,
His giuing-out, were of an infinite diſtance
From his true meant deſigne: vpon his place,
(And with full line of his authority)
Gouernes Lord Angelo; A man, whoſe blood
Is very ſnow-broth: one, who neuer feeles
The wanton ſtings, and motions of the ſence;
But doth rebate, and blunt his naturall edge
With profits of the minde: Studie, and faſt
He (to giue feare to vſe, and libertie,
Which haue, for long, run-by the hideous law,
As Myce, by Lyons) hath pickt out an act,
Vnder whoſe heauy ſence, your brothers life
Fals into forfeit: he arreſts him on it,
And followes cloſe the rigor of the Statute
To make him an example: all hope is gone,
Vnleſſe you haue the grace, by your faire praier
To ſoften Angelo: And that's my pith of buſineſſe
'Twixt you, and your poore brother.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.l: Doth he ſo,
Seeke his life?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Has cenſur'd him already,
And as I heare, the Prouoſt hath a warrant
For's execution.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Alas: what poore Abilitie's in me, to doe him good.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Aſſay the powre you haue.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: My power? alas, I doubt.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Our doubts are traitors
And makes vs looſe the good we oft might win,
By fearing to attempt: Goe to Lord Angelo
And let him learne to know, when Maidens ſue
Men giue like gods: but when they weepe and kneele,
All their petitions, are as freely theirs
As they themſelues would owe them.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Ile ſee what I can doe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: But ſpeedily.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.l: I will about it ſtrait;
No longer ſtaying, but to giue the Mother
Notice of my affaire: I humbly thanke you:
Commend me to my brother: ſoone at night
Ile ſend him certaine word of my ſucceſſe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I take my leaue of you.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: Good ſir, adieu.

div.head: Scoena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Angelo, Eſcalus, and ſeruants, Iuſtice.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: We muſt not make a ſcar-crow of the Law,
Setting it vp to feare the Birds of prey,
And let it keepe one ſhape, till cuſtome make it
Their pearch, and not their terror.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.l: I, but yet
Let vs be keene, and rather cut a little
Then fall, and bruiſe to death: alas, this gentleman
Whom I would ſaue, had a moſt noble father,
Let but your honour know
(Whom I beleeue to be moſt ſtrait in vertue)
That in the working of your owne affections,
Had time coheard with Place, or place with wiſhing,
Or that the reſolute acting of our blood
Could haue attained th' effect of your owne purpoſe,
Whether you had not ſometime in your life
Er'd in this point, which now you cenſure him,
And puld the Law vpon you.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: 'Tis one thing to be tempted (Eſcalus)
Another thing to fall: I not deny
The Iury paſſing on the Priſoners life
May in the ſworne-twelue haue a thiefe, or two
Guiltier then him they try; what's open made to Iuſtice,
That Iuſtice ceizes; What knowes the Lawes
That theeues do paſſe on theeues? 'Tis very pregnant,
The Iewell that we finde, we ſtoope, and take't,
Becauſe we ſee it; but what we doe not ſee,
We tread vpon, and neuer thinke of it.
You may not ſo extenuate his offence,
For I haue had ſuch faults; but rather tell me
When I, that cenſure him, do ſo offend,
Let mine owne Iudgement patterne out my death,
And nothing come in partiall. Sir, he muſt dye.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Be it as your wiſedome will.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Where is the Prouoſt?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: Here if it like your honour.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: See that Claudio
Be executed by nine to morrow morning,
Bring him his Confeſſor, let him be prepar'd,
For that's the vtmoſt of his pilgrimage.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.l: Well: heauen forgiue him; and forgiue vs all:

l.hi: Some riſe by ſinne, and ſome by vertue fall:

sp.l: Some run from brakes of Ice, and anſwere none,
And ſome condemned for a fault alone.

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: Come, bring them away: if theſe be good people in a Common-weale, that doe nothing but vſe their abuſes in common houſes, I know no law: bring them away.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: How now Sir, what's your name? And what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: If it pleaſe your honour, I am the poore Dukes Conſtable, and my name is Elbow; I doe leane vpon Iuſtice Sir, and doe bring in here before your good honor, two notorious Benefactors.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Benefactors? Well: What Benefactors are they? Are they not Malefactors?

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: If it pleaſe your honour, I know not well what they are: But preciſe villaines they are, that I am ſure of and void of all prophanation in the world, that good Chriſtians ought to haue.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: This comes off well: here's a wiſe Officer.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Goe to: What quality are they of? Elbow is your name?
Why do'ſt thou not ſpeake Elbow?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: He cannot Sir: he's out at Elbow.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: What are you Sir?

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: He Sir: a Tapſter Sir: parcell Baud: one that ſerues a bad woman: whoſe houſe Sir was (as they ſay) pluckt downe in the Suborbs: and now ſhee profeſſes a hot-houſe; which, I thinke is a very ill houſe too.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: How know you that?

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: My wife Sir? whom I deteſt before heauen, and your honour.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: How? thy wife?

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: I Sir: whom I thanke heauen is an honeſt woman.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Do'ſt thou deteſt her therefore?

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: I ſay ſir, I will deteſt my ſelfe alſo, as well as ſhe, that this houſe, if it be not a Bauds houſe, it is pitty of her life, for it is a naughty houſe.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: How do'ſt thou know that, Conſtable?

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: Marry ſir, by my wife, who, if ſhe had bin a woman Cardinally giuen, might haue bin accus'd in fornication, adultery, and all vncleanlineſſe there.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: By the womans meanes?

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: I ſir, by Miſtris Ouer-dons meanes: but as ſhe ſpit in his face, ſo ſhe defide him.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Sir, if it pleaſe your honor, this is not ſo.

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: Proue it before theſe varlets here, thou honorable man, proue it.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Doe you heare how he miſplaces?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Sir, ſhe came in great with childe: and longing (ſauing your honors reuerence) for ſtewd prewyns; ſir, we had but two in the houſe, which at that very diſtant time ſtood, as it were in a fruit diſh (a diſh of ſome three pence; your honours haue ſeene ſuch diſhes) they are not China-diſhes, but very good diſhes.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Go too: go too: no matter for the diſh ſir.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: No indeede ſir not of a pin; you are therein in the right: but, to the point: As I ſay, this Miſtris Elbow, being (as I ſay) with childe, and being great bellied, and longing (as I ſaid) for prewyns: and hauing but two in the diſh (as I ſaid) Maſter Froth here, this very man, hauing eaten the reſt (as I ſaid) & (as I ſay) paying for them very honeſtly: for, as you know Maſter Froth, I could not giue you three pence againe.

sp.speaker: Fro.
sp.p: No indeede.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Very well: you being then (if you be remembred) cracking the ſtones of the foreſaid prewyns.

sp.speaker: Fro.
sp.p: I, ſo I did indeede.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Why, very well: I telling you then (if you be remembred) that ſuch a one, and ſuch a one, were paſt cure of the thing you wot of, vnleſſe they kept very good diet, as I told you.

sp.speaker: Fro.
sp.p: All this is true.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Why very well then.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Come: you are a tedious foole: to the purpoſe: what was done to Elbowes wife, that hee hath cauſe to complaine of? Come me to what was done to her.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Sir, your honor cannot come to that yet.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: No ſir, nor I meane it not.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Sir, but you ſhall come to it, by your honours leaue: And I beſeech you, looke into Maſter Froth here ſir, a man of foure-ſcore pound a yeare; whoſe father died at Hallowmas: Was't not at Hallowmas Maſter Froth?

sp.speaker: Fro.
sp.p: Allhallond-Eue.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Why very well: I hope here be truthes: he Sir, ſitting (as I ſay) in a lower chaire, Sir, 'twas in the bunch of Grapes, where indeede you haue a delight to ſit, haue you not?

sp.speaker: Fro.
sp.p: I haue ſo, becauſe it is an open roome, and good for winter.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Why very well then: I hope here be truthes.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: This will laſt out a night in Ruſsia
When nights are longeſt there: Ile take my leaue,
And leaue you to the hearing of the cauſe;
Hoping youle finde good cauſe to whip them all.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: I thinke no leſſe: good morrow to your Lordſhip. Now Sir, come on: What was done to Elbowes wife, once more?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Once Sir? there was nothing done to her once.

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: I beſeech you Sir, aske him what this man did to my wife.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I beſeech your honor, aske me.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Well ſir, what did this Gentleman to her?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I beſeech you ſir, looke in this Gentlemans face: good Maſter Froth looke vpon his honor; 'tis for a good purpoſe: doth your honor marke his face?

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: I ſir, very well.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Nay, I beſeech you marke it well.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Well, I doe ſo.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Doth your honor ſee any harme in his face?

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Why no.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Ile be ſuppoſd vpon a booke, his face is the worſt thing about him: good then: if his face be the worſt thing about him, how could Maſter Froth doe the Conſtables wife any harme? I would know that of your honour.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: He's in the right (Conſtable) what ſay you to it?

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: Firſt, and it like you, the houſe is a reſpected houſe; next, this is a reſpected fellow; and his Miſtris is a reſpected woman.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: By this hand Sir, his wife is a more reſpected perſon then any of vs all.

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: Varlet, thou lyeſt; thou lyeſt wicked varlet: the time is yet to come that ſhee was euer reſpected with man, woman, or childe.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Sir, ſhe was reſpected with him, before he married with her.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Which is the wiſer here; Iuſtice or Iniquitie? Is this true?

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: O thou caytiffe: O thou varlet: O thou wicked Hanniball; I reſpected with her, before I was married to her? If euer I was reſpected with her, or ſhe with me, let not your worſhip thinke mee the poore Dukes Officer: proue this, thou wicked Hanniball, or ile haue mine action of battry on thee.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: If he tooke you a box' oth' eare, you might haue your action of ſlander too.

sp.speaker: Elb.
sp.p: Marry I thanke your good worſhip for it: what is't your Worſhips pleaſure I ſhall doe with this wicked Caitiffe?

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Truly Officer, becauſe he hath ſome offences in him, that thou wouldſt diſcouer, if thou couldſt, let him continue in his courſes, till thou knowſt what they are.

sp.speaker: Elb.
