Forerunning more requitall.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: You make my bonds ſtill greater.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Oh your deſert ſpeaks loud, & I ſhould wrong it
To locke it in the wards of couert boſome
When it deſerues with characters of braſſe
A forted reſidence 'gainſt the tooth of time,
And razure of obliuion: Giue we your hand
And let the Subiect ſee, to make them know
That outward curteſies would faine proclaime
Fauours that keepe within: Come Eſcalus,
You muſt walke by vs, on our other hand:
And good ſupporters are you.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: Now is your time
Speake loud, and kneele before him.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Iuſtice, O royall Duke, vaile your regard
Vpon a wrong'd (I would faine haue ſaid a Maid)
Oh worthy Prince, diſhonor not your eye
By throwing it on any other obiect,
Till you haue heard me, in my true complaint,
And giuen me Iuſtice, Iuſtice, Iuſtice, Iuſtice.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Relate your wrongs;
In what, by whom? be briefe:
Here is Lord Angelo ſhall giue you Iuſtice,
Reueale your ſelfe to him.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Oh worthy Duke,
You bid me ſeeke redemption of the diuell,
Heare me your ſelfe: for that which I muſt ſpeake
Muſt either puniſh me, not being beleeu'd,
Or wring redreſſe from you:
Heare me: oh heare me, heere.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: My Lord, her wits I feare me are not firme:
She hath bin a ſuitor to me, for her Brother
Cut off by courſe of Iuſtice.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: By courſe of Iuſtice.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: And ſhe will ſpeake moſt bitterly, and ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Moſt ſtrange: but yet moſt truely wil I ſpeake,
That Angelo's forſworne, is it not ſtrange?
That Angelo's a murtherer, is't not ſtrange?
That Angelo is an adulterous thiefe,
An hypocrite, a virgin violator,
Is it not ſtrange? and ſtrange?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Nay it is ten times ſtrange?

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.l: It is not truer he is Angelo,
Then this is all as true, as it is ſtrange;
Nay, it is ten times true, for truth is truth
To th' end of reckning.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Away with her: poore ſoule
She ſpeakes this, in th' infirmity of ſence.

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.l: Oh Prince, I coniure thee, as thou beleeu'ſt
There is another comfort, then this world,
That thou neglect me not, with that opinion
That I am touch'd with madneſſe: make not impoſſible
That which but ſeemes vnlike, 'tis not impoſſible
But one, the wickedſt caitiffe on the ground
May ſeeme as ſhie, as graue, as iuſt, as abſolute:
As Angelo, euen ſo may Angelo
In all his dreſſings, caracts, titles, formes,
Be an arch-villaine: Beleeue it, royall Prince
If he be leſſe, he's nothing, but he's more,
Had I more name for badneſſe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: By mine honeſty
If ſhe be mad, as I beleeue no other,
Her madneſſe hath the oddeſt frame of ſenſe,
Such a dependancy of thing, on thing,
As ere I heard in madneſſe.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Oh gracious Duke
Harpe not on that; nor do not baniſh reaſon
For inequality, but let your reaſon ſerue
To make the truth appeare, where it ſeemes hid,
And hide the falſe ſeemes true.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Many that are not mad
Haue ſure more lacke of reaſon:
What would you ſay?

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I am the Siſter of one Claudio,
Condemnd vpon the Act of Fornication
To looſe his head, condemn'd by Angelo,
I, (in probation of a Siſterhood)
Was ſent to by my Brother; one Lucio
As then the Meſſenger.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: That's I, and't like your Grace:
I came to her from Claudio, and deſir'd her,
To try her gracious fortune with Lord Angelo,
For her poore Brothers pardon.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: That's he indeede.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: You were not bid to ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: No, my good Lord,
Nor wiſh'd to hold my peace.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: I wiſh you now then,
Pray you take note of it: and when you haue
A buſineſſe for your ſelfe: pray heauen you then
Be perfect.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I warrant your honor.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: The warrant's for your ſelfe: take heede to't.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: This Gentleman told ſomewhat of my Tale.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: It may be right, but you are i' the wrong
To ſpeake before your time: proceed,

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: I went
To this pernicious Caitiffe Deputie.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: That's ſomewhat madly ſpoken.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Pardon it,
The phraſe is to the matter.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Mended againe: the matter: proceed.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: In briefe, to ſet the needleſſe proceſſe by:
How I perſwaded, how I praid, and kneel'd,
How he refeld me, and how I replide
(For this was of much length) the vild concluſion
I now begin with griefe, and ſhame to vtter.
He would not, but by gift of my chaſte body
To his concupiſcible intemperate luſt
Releaſe my brother; and after much debatement,
My ſiſterly remorſe, confutes mine honour,
And I did yeeld to him: But the next morne betimes,
His purpoſe ſurfetting, he ſends a warrant
For my poore brothers head.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: This is moſt likely.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: Oh that it were as like as it is true.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: By heauen (fond wretch) yu knowſt not what thou ſpeak'ſt,
Or elſe thou art ſuborn'd againſt his honor
In hatefull practiſe: firſt his Integritie
Stands without blemiſh: next it imports no reaſon,
That with ſuch vehemency he ſhould purſue
Faults proper to himſelfe: if he had ſo offended
He would haue waigh'd thy brother by himſelfe,
And not haue cut him off: ſome one hath ſet you on:
Confeſſe the truth, and ſay by whoſe aduice
Thou cam'ſt heere to complaine.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: And is this all?
Then oh you bleſſed Miniſters aboue
Keepe me in patience, and with ripened time
Vnfold the euill, which is heere wrapt vp
In countenance: heauen ſhield your Grace from woe,
As I thus wrong'd, hence vnbeleeued goe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I know you'ld faine be gone: An Officer:
To priſon with her: Shall we thus permit
A blaſting and a ſcandalous breath to fall,
On him ſo neere vs? This needs muſt be a practiſe;
Who knew of your intent and comming hither?

sp.speaker: Iſa.
sp.p: One that I would were heere, Frier Lodowick.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: A ghoſtly Father, belike:
Who knowes that Lodowicke?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My Lord, I know him, 'tis a medling Fryer,
I doe not like the man: had he been Lay my Lord,
For certaine words he ſpake againſt your Grace
In your retirment, I had ſwing'd him ſoundly.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Words againſt mee? this 'a good Fryer belike
And to ſet on this wretched woman here
Againſt our Subſtitute: Let this Fryer be found.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: But yeſternight my Lord, ſhe and that Fryer
I ſaw them at the priſon: a ſawcy Fryar,
A very ſcuruy fellow.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: Bleſſed be your Royall Grace:
I haue ſtood by my Lord, and I haue heard
Your royall eare abus'd: firſt hath this woman
Moſt wrongfully accus'd your Subſtitute,
Who is as free from touch, or ſoyle with her
As ſhe from one vngot.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: We did beleeue no leſſe.
Know you that Frier Lodowick that ſhe ſpeakes of?

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: I know him for a man diuine and holy,
Not ſcuruy, nor a temporary medler
As he's reported by this Gentleman:
And on my truſt, a man that neuer yet
Did (as he vouches) miſ-report your Grace.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: My Lord, moſt villanouſly, beleeue it.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: Well: he in time may come to cleere himſelfe;
But at this inſtant he is ſicke, my Lord:
Of a ſtrange Feauor; vpon his meere requeſt
Being come to knowledge, that there was complaint
Intended 'gainſt Lord Angelo, came I hether
To ſpeake as from his mouth, what he doth know
Is true, and falſe: And what he with his oath
And all probation will make vp full cleare
When ſoeuer he's conuented: Firſt for this woman,
To iuſtifie this worthy Noble man
So vulgarly and perſonally accus'd,
Her ſhall you heare diſproued to her eyes,
Till ſhe her ſelfe confeſſe it.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Good Frier, let's heare it:
Doe you not ſmile at this, Lord Angelo?
Oh heauen, the vanity of wretched fooles.
Giue vs ſome ſeates, Come coſen Angelo,
In this I'll be impartiall: be you Iudge
Of your owne Cauſe: Is this the Witnes Frier?
Firſt, let her ſhew your face, and after, ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Pardon my Lord, I will not ſhew my face
Vntill my husband bid me.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: What, are you married?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: No my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Are you a Maid?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: No my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: A Widow then?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Neither, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: Why you are nothing then: neither Maid, Widow, nor Wife?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: My Lord, ſhe may be a Puncke: for many of them, are neither Maid, Widow, nor Wife.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: Silence that fellow: I would he had ſome cauſe to prattle for himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Well my Lord.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: My Lord, I doe confeſſe I nere was married,
And I confeſſe beſides, I am no Maid,
I haue known my husband, yet my husband
Knowes not, that euer he knew me.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: He was drunk then, my Lord, it can be no better.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: For the benefit of ſilence, would thou wert ſo to.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Well, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: This is no witneſſe for Lord Angelo.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Now I come to't, my Lord.
Shee that accuſes him of Fornication,
In ſelfe-ſame manner, doth accuſe my husband,
And charges him, my Lord, with ſuch a time,
When I'le depoſe I had him mine Armes
With all th' effect of Loue.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Charges ſhe moe then me?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Not that I know.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: No? you ſay your husband.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Why iuſt, my Lord, and that is Angelo,
Who thinkes he knowes, that he nere knew my body,
But knows, he thinkes, that he knowes Iſabels.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: This is a ſtrange abuſe: Let's ſee thy face.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: My husband bids me, now I will vnmaske.
This is that face, thou cruell Angelo
Which once thou ſworſt, was worth the looking on:
This is the hand, which with a vowd contract
Was faſt belockt in thine: This is the body
That tooke away the match from Iſabell,
And did ſupply thee at thy garden-houſe
In her Imagin'd perſon.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Know you this woman?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Carnallie ſhe ſaies.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: Sirha, no more.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Enoug my Lord.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: My Lord, I muſt confeſſe, I know this woman,
And fiue yeres ſince there was ſome ſpeech of marriage
Betwixt my ſelfe, and her: which was broke off,
Partly for that her promis'd proportions
Came ſhort of Compoſition: But in chiefe
For that her reputation was diſ-valued
In leuitie: Since which time of fiue yeres
I neuer ſpake with her, ſaw her, nor heard from her
Vpon my faith, and honor.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Noble Prince,
As there comes light from heauen, and words frō breath,
As there is ſence in truth, and truth in vertue,
I am affianced this mans wife, as ſtrongly
As words could make vp vowes: And my good Lord,
But Tueſday night laſt gon, in's garden houſe,
He knew me as a wife. As this is true,
Let me in ſafety raiſe me from my knees,
Or elſe for euer be confixed here
A Marble Monument.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I did but ſmile till now,
Now, good my Lord, giue me the ſcope of Iuſtice,
My patience here is touch'd: I doe perceiue
Theſe poore informall women, are no more
But inſtruments of ſome more mightier member
That ſets them on. Let me haue way, my Lord
To finde this practiſe out.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I, with my heart,
And puniſh them to your height of pleaſure.
Thou fooliſh Frier, and thou pernicious woman
Compact with her that's gone: thinkſt thou, thy oathes,
Though they would ſwear downe each particular Saint,
Were teſtimonies againſt his worth, and credit
That's ſeald in approbation? you, Lord Eſcalus
Sit with my Cozen, lend him your kinde paines
To finde out this abuſe, whence 'tis deriu'd.
There is another Frier that ſet them on,
Let him be ſent for.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.l: Would he were here, my Lord, for he indeed
Hath ſet the women on to this Complaint;
Your Prouoſt knowes the place where he abides,
And he may fetch him.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Goe, doe it inſtantly:
And you, my noble and well-warranted Coſen
Whom it concernes to heare this matter forth,
Doe with your iniuries as ſeemes you beſt
In any chaſtiſement; I for a while
Will leaue you; but ſtir not you till you haue
Well determin'd vpon theſe Slanderers.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: My Lord, wee'll doe it throughly: Signior Lucio, did not you ſay you knew that Frier Lodowick to be a diſhoneſt perſon?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Cucullus non facit Monachum, honeſt in nothing but in his Clothes, and one that hath ſpoke moſt villanous ſpeeches of the Duke.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: We ſhall intreat you to abide heere till he come, and inforce them againſt him: we ſhall finde this Frier a notable fellow.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: As any in Vienna, on my word.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Call that ſame Iſabell here once againe, I would ſpeake with her: pray you, my Lord, giue mee leaue to queſtion, you ſhall ſee how Ile handle her.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Not better then he, by her owne report.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Say you?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p:
Marry ſir, I thinke, if you handled her priuately
She would ſooner confeſſe, perchance publikely ſhe'll be aſham'd.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: I will goe darkely to worke with her.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: That's the way: for women are light at midnight.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.l: Come on Miſtris, here's a Gentlewoman,
Denies all that you haue ſaid.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: My Lord, here comes the raſcall I ſpoke of,
Here, with the Prouoſt.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: In very good time: ſpeake not you to him, till we call vpon you.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Mum.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Come Sir, did you ſet theſe women on to ſlander Lord Angelo? they haue confeſ'd you did.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: 'Tis falſe.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: How? Know you where you are?

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Reſpect to your great place; and let the diuell
Be ſometime honour'd, for his burning throne.
Where is the Duke? 'tis he ſhould heare me ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.l: The Duke's in vs: and we will heare you ſpeake,
Looke you ſpeake iuſtly.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Boldly, at leaſt. But oh poore ſoules,
Come you to ſeeke the Lamb here of the Fox;
Good night to your redreſſe: Is the Duke gone?
Then is your cauſe gone too: The Duke's vniuſt,
Thus to retort your manifeſt Appeale,
And put your triall in the villaines mouth,
Which here you come to accuſe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: This is the raſcall: this is he I ſpoke of.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.l: Why thou vnreuerend, and vnhallowed Fryer:
Is't not enough thou haſt ſuborn'd theſe women,
To accuſe this worthy man? but in foule mouth,
And in the witneſſe of his proper eare,
To call him villaine; and then to glance from him,
To th' Duke himſelfe, to taxe him with Iniuſtice?
Take him hence; to th' racke with him: we'll towze you
Ioynt by ioynt, but we will know his purpoſe:
What? vniuſt?

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Be not ſo hot: the Duke dare
No more ſtretch this finger of mine, then he
Dare racke his owne: his Subiect am I not,
Nor here Prouinciall: My buſineſſe in this State
Made me a looker on here in Vienna,
Where I haue ſeene corruption boyle and bubble,
Till it ore-run the Stew: Lawes, for all faults,
But faults ſo countenanc'd, that the ſtrong Statutes
Stand like the forfeites in a Barbers ſhop,
As much in mocke, as marke.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.l: Slander to th' State:
Away with him to priſon.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: What can you vouch againſt him Signior Lucio?
Is this the man that you did tell vs of?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: 'Tis he, my Lord: come hither goodman bald-pate, doe you know me?

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: I remember you Sir, by the ſound of your voice,
I met you at the Priſon, in the abſence of the Duke.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Oh, did you ſo? and do you remember what you ſaid of the Duke.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: Moſt notedly Sir.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Do you ſo Sir: And was the Duke a fleſh-monger, a foole, and a coward, as you then reported him to be?

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: You muſt (Sir) change perſons with me, ere you make that my report: you indeede ſpoke ſo of him, and much more, much worſe.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Oh thou damnable fellow: did not I plucke thee by the noſe, for thy ſpeeches?

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: I proteſt, I loue the Duke, as I loue my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Harke how the villaine would cloſe now, after his treaſonable abuſes.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.p: Such a fellow is not to be talk'd withall: Away with him to priſon: Where is the Prouoſt? away with him to priſon: lay bolts enough vpon him: let him ſpeak no more: away with thoſe Giglets too▪ and with the other confederate companion.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: Stay Sir, ſtay a while.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: What, reſiſts he? helpe him Lucio.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Come ſir, come ſir, come ſir: foh ſir, why you bald-pated lying raſcall: you muſt be hooded muſt you? ſhow your knaues viſage with a poxe to you: ſhow your ſheepe-biting face, and be hang'd an houre: will't not off?

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Thou art the firſt knaue, that ere mad'ſt a Duke.
Firſt Prouoſt, let me bayle theſe gentle three:
Sneake not away Sir, for the Fryer, and you,
Muſt haue a word anon: lay hold on him.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: This may proue worſe then hanging.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: What you haue ſpoke, I pardon: ſit you downe,
We'll borrow place of him; Sir, by your leaue:
Ha'ſt thou or word, or wit, or impudence,
That yet can doe thee office? If thou ha'ſt
Rely vpon it, till my tale be heard,
And hold no longer out.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Oh, my dread Lord,
I ſhould be guiltier then my guiltineſſe,
To thinke I can be vndiſcerneable,
When I perceiue your grace, like powre diuine,
Hath look'd vpon my paſſes. Then good Prince,
No longer Seſſion hold vpon my ſhame,
But let my Triall, be mine owne Confeſſion:
Immediate ſentence then, and ſequent death,
Is all the grace I beg.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Come hither Mariana,
Say: was't thou ere contracted to this woman?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: I was my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Goe take her hence, and marry her inſtantly.
Doe you the office (Fryer) which conſummate,
Returne him here againe: goe with him Prouoſt.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.l: My Lord, I am more amaz'd at his diſhonor,
Then at the ſtrangeneſſe of it.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Come hither Iſabell,
Your Frier is now your Prince: As I was then
Aduertyſing, and holy to your buſineſſe,
(Not changing heart with habit) I am ſtill,
Atturnied at your ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Oh giue me pardon
That I, your vaſſaile, haue imploid, and pain'd
Your vnknowne Soueraigntie.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: You are pardon'd Iſabell:
And now, deere Maide, be you as free to vs.
Your Brothers death I know ſits at your heart:
And you may maruaile, why I obſcur'd my ſelfe,
Labouring to ſaue his life: and would not rather
Make raſh remonſtrance of my hidden powre,
Then let him ſo be loſt: oh moſt kinde Maid,
It was the ſwift celeritie of his death,
Which I did thinke, with ſlower foot came on,
That brain'd my purpoſe: but peace be with him,
That life is better life paſt fearing death,
Then that which liues to feare: make it your comfort,
So happy is your Brother.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.p: I doe my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: For this new-maried man, approaching here,
Whoſe ſalt imagination yet hath wrong'd
Your well defended honor: you muſt pardon
For Mariana's ſake: But as he adiudg'd your Brother,
Being criminall, in double violation
Of ſacred Chaſtitie, and of promiſe-breach,
Thereon dependant for your Brothers life,
The very mercy of the Law cries out
Moſt audible, euen from his proper tongue.
An Angelo for Claudio, death for death:
Haſte ſtill paies haſte, and leaſure, anſwers leaſure;
Like doth quit like, and Meaſure ſtill for Meaſure:
Then Angelo, thy fault's thus manifeſted;
Which though thou would'ſt deny, denies thee vantage.
We doe condemne thee to the very Blocke
Where Claudio ſtoop'd to death; and with like haſte.
Away with him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Oh my moſt gracious Lord,
I hope you will not mocke me with a husband?

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: It is your husband mock't you with a husband,
Conſenting to the ſafe-guard of your honor,
I thought your marriage fit: elſe Imputation,
For that he knew you▪ might reproach your life,
And choake your good to come: For his Poſſeſſions,
Although by confutation they are ours;
We doe en-ſtate, and widow you with all,
To buy you a better husband.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Oh my deere Lord,
I craue no other, nor no better man.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Neuer craue him, we are definitiue.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Gentle my Liege.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: You doe but looſe your labour.
Away with him to death: Now Sir, to you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Oh my good Lord, ſweet Iſabell, take my part,
Lend me your knees, and all my life to come,
I'll lend you all my life to doe you ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Againſt all ſence you doe importune her,
Should ſhe kneele downe, in mercie of this fact,
Her Brothers ghoſt, his paued bed would breake,
And take her hence in horror.

sp.speaker: Mar.

l.hi: Iſabell:

sp.l: Sweet Iſabel, doe yet but kneele by me,
Hold vp your hands, ſay nothing: I'll ſpeake all.
They ſay beſt men are moulded out of faults,
And for the moſt, become much more the better
For being a little bad: So may my husband.
Oh Iſabel: will you not lend a knee?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: He dies for Claudio's death.

sp.speaker: Iſab.
sp.l: Moſt bounteous Sir.
Looke if it pleaſe you, on this man condemn'd,
As if my Brother liu'd: I partly thinke,
A due ſinceritie gouerned his deedes,
Till he did looke on me: Since it is ſo,
Let him not die: my Brother had but Iuſtice,
In that he did the thing for which he dide.
For Angelo, his Act did not ore-take his bad intent,
And muſt be buried but as an intent
That periſh'd by the way: thoughts are no ſubiects
Intents, but meerely thoughts.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Meerely my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Your ſuite's vnprofitable: ſtand vp I ſay:
I haue bethought me of another fault.
Prouoſt, how came it Claudio was beheaded
At an vnuſuall howre?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: It was commanded ſo.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Had you a ſpeciall warrant for the deed?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: No my good Lord: it was by priuate meſſage.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: For which I doe diſcharge you of your office,
Giue vp your keyes.

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: Pardon me, noble Lord,
I thought it was a fault, but knew it not,
Yet did repent me after more aduice,
For teſtimony whereof, one in the priſon
That ſhould by priuate order elſe haue dide,
I haue reſeru'd aliue.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.p: What's he?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: His name is Barnardine.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I would thou hadſt done ſo by Claudio:
Goe fetch him hither, let me looke vpon him.

sp.speaker: Eſc.
sp.l: I am ſorry, one ſo learned, and ſo wiſe
As you, Lord Angelo, haue ſtil appear'd,
Should ſlip ſo groſſelie, both in the heat of bloud
And lacke of temper'd iudgement afterward.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I am ſorrie, that ſuch ſorrow I procure,
And ſo deepe ſticks it in my penitent heart,
That I craue death more willingly then mercy,
'Tis my deſeruing, and I doe entreat it.

div.stage: Enter Barnardine and Prouoſt, Claudio, Iulietta.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Which is that Barnardine?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.p: This my Lord.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: There was a Friar told me of this man.
Sirha, thou art ſaid to haue a ſtubborne ſoule
That apprehends no further then this world,
And ſquar'ſt thy life according: Thou'rt condemn'd,
But for thoſe earthly faults, I quit them all,
And pray thee take this mercie to prouide
For better times to come: Frier aduiſe him,
I leaue him to your hand. What muffeld fellow's that?

sp.speaker: Pro.
sp.l: This is another priſoner that I ſau'd,
Who ſhould haue di'd when Claudio loſt his head,
As like almoſt to Claudio, as himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: If he be like your brother, for his ſake
Is he pardon'd, and for your louelie ſake
Giue me your hand, and ſay you will be mine,
He is my brother too: But fitter time for that:
By this Lord Angelo perceiues he's ſafe,
Methinkes I ſee a quickning in his eye:
Well Angelo, your euill quits you well.
Looke that you loue your wife: her worth, worth yours
I finde an apt remiſſion in my ſelfe:
And yet heere's one in place I cannot pardon,
You ſirha, that knew me for a foole, a Coward,
One all of Luxurie, an aſſe, a mad man:
Wherein haue I ſo deſeru'd of you
That you extoll me thus?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Faith my Lord, I ſpoke it but according to the trick: if you will hang me for it you may: but I had rather it would pleaſe you, I might be whipt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Whipt firſt, ſir, and hang'd after.
Proclaime it Prouoſt round about the Citie;
If any woman wrong'd by this lewd fellow
(As I haue heard him ſweare himſelfe there's one whom he begot with childe) let her appeare,
And he ſhall marry her: the nuptiall finiſh'd,
Let him be whipt and hang'd.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I beſeech your Highneſſe doe not marry me to a Whore: your Highneſſe ſaid euen now I made you a Duke, good my Lord do not recompence me, in making me a Cuckold.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Vpon mine honor thou ſhalt marrie her,
Thy ſlanders I forgiue, and therewithall
Remit thy other forfeits: take him to priſon,
And ſee our pleaſure herein executed.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Marrying a punke my Lord, is preſſing to death,
Whipping and hanging.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Slandering a Prince deſerues it.
She Claudio that you wrong'd, looke you reſtore.
Ioy to you Mariana, loue her Angelo:
I haue confes'd her, and I know her vertue.
Thanks good friend, Eſcalus, for thy much goodneſſe,
There's more behinde that is more gratulate.
Thanks Prouoſt for thy care, and ſecrecie,
We ſhall imploy thee in a worthier place.
Forgiue him Angelo, that brought you home
The head of Ragozine for Claudio's,
Th' offence pardons it ſelfe. Deere Iſabell,
I haue a motion much imports your good,
Whereto if you'll a willing eare incline;
What's mine is yours, and what is yours is mine.
So bring vs to our Pallace, where wee'll ſhow
What's yet behinde, that meete you all ſhould know.

div.head: The Scene Vienna. The names of all the Actors.
Scena prima.
div.stage: Enter the Duke of Epheſus, with the Merchant of Siracuſa, Iaylor, and other attendants.

sp.speaker: Marchant.
sp.l: PRoceed Solinus to procure my fall,
And by the doome of death end woes and all.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Merchant of Siracuſa, plead no more.
I am not partiall to infringe our Lawes;
The enmity and diſcord which of late
Sprung from the rancorous outrage of your Duke,
To Merchants our well-dealing Countrimen,
Who wanting gilders to redeeme their liues,
Haue ſeal'd his rigorous ſtatutes with their blouds,
Excludes all pitty from our threatning lookes:
For ſince the mortall and inteſtine iarres
Twixt thy ſeditious Countrimen and vs,
It hath in ſolemne Synodes beene decreed,
Both by the Siracuſians and our ſelues,
To admit no trafficke to our aduerſe townes:
Nay more, if any borne at Epheſus
Be ſeene at any Siracuſian Marts and Fayres:
Againe, if any Siracuſian borne
Come to the Bay of Epheſus, he dies:
His goods confiſcate to the Dukes diſpoſe,
Vnleſſe a thouſand markes be leuied
To quit the penalty, and to ranſome him:
Thy ſubſtance, valued at the higheſt rate,
Cannot amount vnto a hundred Markes,
Therefore by Law thou art condemn'd to die.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Yet this my comfort, when your words are done,
My woes end likewiſe with the euening Sonne.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Well Siracuſian; ſay in briefe the cauſe
Why thou departedſt from thy natiue home?
And for what cauſe thou cam'ſt to Epheſus.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: A heauier taske could not haue beene impos'd,
Then I to ſpeake my griefes vnſpeakeable:
Yet that the world may witneſſe that my end
Was wrought by nature, not by vile offence,
Ile vtter what my ſorrow giues me leaue.
In Syracuſa was I borne, and wedde
Vnto a woman, happy but for me,
And by me; had not our hap beene bad:
With her I liu'd in ioy, our wealth increaſt
By proſperous voyages I often made
To Epidamium, till my factors death,
And he great care of goods at randone left,
Drew me from kinde embracements of my ſpouſe;
From whom my abſence was not ſixe moneths olde,
Before her ſelfe (almoſt at fainting vnder
The pleaſing puniſhment that women beare)
Had made prouiſion for her following me,
And ſoone, and ſafe, arriued where I was:
There had ſhe not beene long, but ſhe became
A ioyfull mother of two goodly ſonnes:
And, which was ſtrange, the one ſo like the other,
As could not be diſtinguiſh'd but by names.
That very howre, and in the ſelfe-ſame Inne,
A meane woman was deliuered
Of ſuch a burthen Male, twins both alike:
Thoſe, for their parents were exceeding poore,
I bought, and brought vp to attend my ſonnes.
My wife, not meanely prowd of two ſuch boyes,
Made daily motions for our home returne:
Vnwilling I agreed, alas, too ſoone wee came aboord.
A league from Epidamium had we ſaild
Before the alwaies winde-obeying deepe
Gaue any Tragicke Inſtance of our harme:
But longer did we not retaine much hope;
For what obſcured light the heauens did grant,
Did but conuay vnto our fearefull mindes
A doubtfull warrant of immediate death,
Which though my ſelfe would gladly haue imbrac'd,
Yet the inceſſant weepings of my wife,
Weeping before for what ſhe ſaw muſt come,
And pitteous playnings of the prettie babes
That mourn'd for faſhion, ignorant what to feare,
Forſt me to ſeeke delayes for them and me,
And this it was: (for other meanes was none)
The Sailors ſought for ſafety by our boate,
And left the ſhip then ſinking ripe to vs.
My wife, more carefull for the latter borne,
Had faſtned him vnto a ſmall ſpare Maſt,
Such as ſea-faring men prouide for ſtormes:
To him one of the other twins was bound,
Whil'ſt I had beene like heedfull of the other.
The children thus diſpos'd, my wife and I,
Fixing our eyes on whom our care was fixt,
Faſtned our ſelues at eyther end the maſt,
And floating ſtraight, obedient to the ſtreame,
Was carried towards Corinth, as we thought.
At length the ſonne gazing vpon the earth,
Diſperſt thoſe vapours that offended vs,
And by the benefit of his wiſhed light
The ſeas waxt calme, and we diſcouered
Two ſhippes from farre, making amaine to vs:
Of Corinth that, of Epidarus this,
But ere they came, oh let me ſay no more,
Gather the ſequell by that went before.

sp.speaker: Duk.
sp.l: Nay forward old man, doe not breake off ſo,
For we may pitty, though not pardon thee.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Oh had the gods done ſo, I had not now
Worthily tearm'd them mercileſſe to vs:
For ere the ſhips could meet by twice fiue leagues,
We were encountred by a mighty rocke,
Which being violently borne vp,
Our helpefull ſhip was ſplitted in the midſt;
So that in this vniuſt diuorce of vs,
Fortune had left to both of vs alike,
What to delight in, what to ſorrow for,
Her part, poore ſoule, ſeeming as burdened
With leſſer waight, but not with leſſer woe,
Was carried with more ſpeed before the winde,
And in our ſight they three were taken vp
By Fiſhermen of Corinth, as we thought.
At length another ſhip had ſeiz'd on vs,
And knowing whom it was their hap to ſaue,
Gaue healthfull welcome to their ſhip-wrackt gueſts,
And would haue reft the Fiſhers of their prey,
Had not their backe beene very ſlow of ſaile;
And therefore homeward did they bend their courſe.
Thus haue you heard me ſeuer'd from my bliſſe,
That by miſfortunes was my life prolong'd,
To tell ſad ſtories of my owne miſhaps.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: And for the ſake of them thou ſorroweſt for,
Doe me the fauour to dilate at full,
What haue befalne of them and they till now.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: My yongeſt boy, and yet my eldeſt care,
At eighteene yeeres became inquiſitiue
After his brother; and importun'd me
That his attendant, ſo his caſe was like,
Reft of his brother, but retain'd his name,
Might beare him company in the queſt of him:
Whom whil'ſt I laboured of a loue to ſee,
I hazarded the loſſe of whom I lou'd.
Fiue Sommers haue I ſpent in fartheſt Greece,
Roming cleane through the bounds of Aſia,
And coaſting homeward, came to Epheſus:
Hopeleſſe to finde, yet loth to leaue vnſought
Or that, or any place that harbours men:
But heere muſt end the ſtory of my life,
And happy were I in my timelie death,
Could all my trauells warrant me they liue.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Hapleſſe Egeon whom the fates haue markt
To beare the extremitie of dire miſhap:
Now truſt me, were it not againſt our Lawes,
Againſt my Crowne, my oath, my dignity,
Which Princes would they may not diſanull,
My ſoule ſhould ſue as aduocate for thee:
But though thou art adiudged to the death,
And paſſed ſentence may not be recal'd
But to our honours great diſparagement:
Yet will I fauour thee in what I can;
Therefore Marchant, Ile limit thee this day
To ſeeke thy helpe by beneficiall helpe,
Try all the friends thou haſt in Epheſus,
Beg thou, or borrow, to make vp the ſumme,
And liue: if no, then thou art doom'd to die:
Iaylor, take him to thy cuſtodie.

sp.speaker: Iaylor.
sp.p: I will my Lord.

sp.speaker: Merch.
sp.l: Hopeleſſe and helpeleſſe doth Egean wend,
But to procraſtinate his liueleſſe end.

div.stage: Enter Antipholis Erotes, a Marchant, and Dromio.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Therefore giue out you are of Epidamium,
Leſt that your goods too ſoone be confiſcate:
This very day a Syracuſian Marchant
Is apprehended for a riuall here,
And not being able to buy out his life,
According to the ſtatute of the towne,
Dies ere the wearie ſunne ſet in the Weſt:
There is your monie that I had to keepe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Goe beare it to the Centaure, where we hoſt,
And ſtay there Dromio, till I come to thee;
Within this houre it will be dinner time,
Till that Ile view the manners of the towne,
Peruſe the traders, gaze vpon the buildings,
And then returne and ſleepe within mine Inne,
For with long trauaile I am ſtiffe and wearie.
Get thee away.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.l: Many a man would take you at your word,
And goe indeede, hauing ſo good a meane.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: A truſtie villaine ſir, that very oft,
When I am dull with care and melancholly,
Lightens my humour with his merry ieſts:
What will you walke with me about the towne,
And then goe to my Inne and dine with me?

sp.speaker: E. Mar.
sp.l: I am inuited ſir to certaine Marchants,
Of whom I hope to make much benefit:
I craue your pardon, ſoone at fiue a clocke,
Pleaſe you, Ile meete with you vpon the Mart,
And afterward conſort you till bed time:
My preſent buſineſſe cals me from you now.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Farewell till then: I will goe looſe my ſelfe,
And wander vp and downe to view the Citie.

sp.speaker: E. Mar.
sp.p: Sir, I commend you to your owne content.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: He that commends me to mine owne content,
Commends me to the thing I cannot get:
I to the world am like a drop of water,
That in the Ocean ſeekes another drop,
Who falling there to finde his fellow forth,
(Vnſeene, inquiſitiue) confounds himſelfe.
So I, to finde a Mother and a Brother,
In queſt of them (vnhappie a) looſe my ſelfe.
Here comes the almanacke of my true date:
What now? How chance thou art return'd ſo ſoone.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: Return'd ſo ſoone, rather approacht too late:
The Capon burnes, the Pig fals from the ſpit;
The clocke hath ſtrucken twelue vpon the bell:
My Miſtris made it one vpon my cheeke:
She is ſo hot becauſe the meate is colde:
The meate is colde, becauſe you come not home:
You come not home, becauſe you haue no ſtomacke:
You haue no ſtomacke, hauing broke your faſt:
But we that know what 'tis to faſt and pray,
Are penitent for your default to day.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Stop in your winde ſir, tell me this I pray?
Where haue you left the mony that I gaue you.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: Oh ſixe pence that I had a wenſday laſt,
To pay the Sadler for my Miſtris crupper:
The Sadler had it Sir, I kept it not.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I am not in a ſportiue humor now:
Tell me, and dally not, where is the monie?
We being ſtrangers here, how dar'ſt thou truſt
So great a charge from thine owne cuſtodie.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: I pray you ieſt ſir as you ſit at dinner:
I from my Miſtris come to you in poſt:
If I returne I ſhall be poſt indeede.
For ſhe will ſcoure your fault vpon my pate:
Me thinkes your maw, like mine, ſhould be your • ooke,
And ſtrike you home without a meſſenger.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Come Dromio, come, theſe • eſts are out of ſeaſon,
Reſerue them till a merrier houre then this:
Where is the gold I gaue in charge to thee?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: To me ſir? why you gaue no gold to me?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Come on ſir knaue, haue done your fooliſhnes,
And tell me how thou ha • t diſpos'd thy charge▪

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: My charge was but to fetch you f • ō the Mart
Home to your houſe, the Phoenix ſir, to dinner;
My Miſtris and her ſiſter ſtaies for you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Now as I am a Chriſtian anſwer me,
In what ſafe place you haue beſtow'd my monie;
Or I ſhall breake that merrie ſconce of yours
That ſtands on tricks, when I am vndiſpos'd:
Where is the thouſand Markes thou hadſt of me?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: I haue ſome markes of yours vpon my pate:
Some of my Miſtris markes vpon my ſhoulders:
But not a thouſand markes betweene you both.
If I ſhould pay your worſhip thoſe againe,
Perchance you will not beare them patiently.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Thy Miſtris markes? what Miſtris ſlaue haſt thou?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: Your worſhips wife, my Miſtris at the Phoenix;
She that doth faſt till you come home to dinner:
And praies that you will hie you home to dinner.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What wilt thou flout me thus vnto my face
Being forbid? There take you that ſir knaue.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: What meane you ſir, for God ſake hold your hands:
Nay, and you will not ſir, Ile take my heeles.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Vpon my life by ſome deuiſe or other,
The villaine is ore-wrought of all my monie.
They ſay this towne is full of coſenage:
As nimble Iuglers that deceiue the eie:
Darke working Sorcerers that change the minde:
Soule-killing Witches, that deforme the bodie:
Diſguiſed Cheaters, prating Mountebankes;
And manie ſuch like-liberties of ſinne:
If it proue ſo, I will be gone the ſooner:
Ile to the Centaur to goe ſeeke this ſlaue,
I greatly feare my monie is not ſafe.

div.head: Actus Secundus.
div.stage: Enter Adriana, wife to Antipholis Sereptus, with Luciana her Siſter.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Neither my husband nor the ſlaue return'd,
That in ſuch haſte I ſent to ſeeke his Maſter?
Sure Luciana it is two a clocke.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Perhaps ſome Merchant hath inuited him,
And from the Mart he's ſomewhere gone to dinner:
Good Siſter let vs dine, and neuer fret;
A man is Maſter of his libertie:
Time is their Maſter, and when they ſee time,
They'll goe or come; if ſo, be patient Siſter.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Why ſhould their libertie then ours be more?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Becauſe their buſineſſe ſtill lies out adore.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Looke when I ſerue him ſo, he takes it thus.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Oh, know he is the bridle of your will.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: There's none but aſſes will be bridled ſo.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why, headſtrong liberty is laſht wi • h woe:
There's nothing ſituate vnder • ens eye,
But hath his bound in earth, in • ea, in skie.
The beaſts, the fiſhes, and the winged fowles
Are their males ſubiects, and at • he • r controules:
Man more diuine, the Maſter of all theſe,
Lord of the wide world, and wilde watry ſeas,
Indued with intellectual ſence and ſoules,
Of more preheminence then fiſh and fowles,
Are maſters to their females, and their Lords:
Then let your will attend on their accords.

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.p: This ſeruitude makes you to keepe vnwed.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.p: Not this, but troubles of the marriage bed.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: But were you wedded, you wold bear ſome ſway

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Ere I learned loue; Ile practiſe to obey.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: How if your husband ſtart ſome other where?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Till he come home againe, I would for beare.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Patience vnmou'd, no maruel though ſhe pauſe,
They can be meeke, that haue no other cauſe:
A wretched ſoule bruis'd with aduerſitie,
We bid be quiet when we heare it crie.
But were we burdned with like waight of paine,
As much, or more, we ſhould our ſelues complaine:
So thou that haſt no vnkinde mate to greeue thee,
With vrging helpeleſſe patience would releeue me;
But if thou liue to ſee like right bereft • ,
This foole-beg'd patience in thee will be left.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Well, I will marry one day but to trie:
Heere comes your man, now is your husband nie.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Say, is your tardie maſter now at hand?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: Nay, hee's at too hands with mee, and that my two eares can witneſſe.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Say, didſt thou ſpeake with him? knowſt thou his minde?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: I, I, he told his minde vpon mine eare,
Beſhrew his hand, I ſcarce could vnderſtand it.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Spake hee ſo doubtfully, thou couldſt not feele his meaning.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: Nay, hee ſtrooke ſo plainly, I could too well feele his blowes; and withall ſo doubtfully, that I could ſcarce vnderſtand them.

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.l: But ſay, I prethee, is he comming home?
It ſeemes he hath great care to pleaſe his wife.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: Why Miſtreſſe, ſure my Maſter is horne mad.

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.p: Horne mad, thou villaine?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: I meane not Cuckold mad,
But ſure he is ſtarke mad:
When I deſir'd him to come home to dinner,
He ask'd me for a hundred markes in gold:
'Tis dinner time▪ quoth I: my gold, quoth he:
Your meat doth burne, quoth I: my gold quoth he:
Will you come, quoth I: my gold, quoth he;
Where is the thouſand markes I gaue thee villaine?
The Pigge quoth I, is burn'd: my gold, quoth he:
My miſtreſſe, ſir, quoth I: hang vp thy Miſtreſſe:
I know not thy miſtreſſe, out on thy miſtreſſe.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.p: Quoth who?

sp.speaker: E. Dr.
sp.p: Quoth my Maſter, I know quoth he, no houſe, no wife, no miſtreſſe: ſo that my arrant due vnto my tongue, I thanke him, I bare home vpon my ſhoulders: for in concluſion, he did beat me there.

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.p: Go back againe, thou ſlaue, & fetch him home.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.l: Goe backe againe, and be new beaten home▪
For Gods ſake ſend ſome other meſſenger.

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.p: Backe ſlaue, or I will breake thy pate a-croſſe.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.l: And he will bleſſe yt croſſe with other beating▪
Betweene you, I ſhall haue a holy head.

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.p: Hence prating peſant, fetch thy Maſter home.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.l: Am I ſo round with you, as you with me,
That like a foot-ball you doe ſpurne me thus:
You ſpurne me hence, and he will ſpurne me hither,
If I laſt in this ſeruice, you muſt caſe me in leather.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.p: Fie how impatience lowreth in your face.

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.l: His company muſt do his minions grace,
Whil'ſt I at home ſtarue for a merrie looke:
Hath homelie age th' alluring beauty tooke
From my poore checke? then he hath waſted it.
Are my diſcourſes dull? Barren my wit,
If voluble and ſharpe diſcourſe be mar'd,
Vnkindneſſe blunts it more then marble hard.
Doe their gay veſtments his affections baite?
That's not my fault, hee's maſter of my ſtate.
What ruines are in me that can be found,
By him not ruin'd? Then is he the ground
Of my defeatures. My decayed faire,
A ſunnie looke of his, would ſoone repaire.
But, too vnruly Deere, he breakes the pale,
And feedes from home; poore I am but his ſtale.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.p: Selfe-harming Iealouſie; fie beat it hence.

sp.speaker: Ad.
sp.l: Vnfeeling fools can with ſuch wrongs diſpence:
I know his eye doth homage other-where,
Or elſe, what lets it but he would be here?
Siſter, you know he promis'd me a chaine,
Would that alone, a loue he would detaine,
So he would keepe faire quarter with his bed:
I ſee the Iewell beſt enamaled
Will looſe his beautie: yet the gold bides ſtill
That others touch, and often touching will,
Where gold and no man that hath a name,
By falſhood and corruption doth it ſhame:
Since that my beautie cannot pleaſe his eie,
Ile weepe (what's left away) and weeping die.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.p: How manie fond fooles ſerue mad Ielouſie?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The gold I gaue to Dromio is laid vp
Safe at the Centaur, and the heedfull ſlaue
Is wandred forth in care to ſeeke me out
By computation and mine hoſts report.
I could not ſpeake with Dromio, ſince at firſt
I ſent him from the Mart? ſee here he comes.
How now ſir, is your merrie humor alter'd?
As you loue ſtroakes, ſo ieſt with me againe:
You know no Centaur? you receiu'd no gold?
Your Miſtreſſe ſent to haue me home to dinner?
My houſe was at the Phoenix? Waſt thou mad,
That thus ſo madlie thou did didſt anſwere me?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: What anſwer ſir? when ſpake I ſuch a word?

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.p: Euen now, euen here, not halfe an howre ſince.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.l: I did not ſee you ſince you ſent me hence
Home to the Centaur with the gold you gaue me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Villaine, thou didſt denie the golds receit,
And toldſt me of a Miſtreſſe, and a dinner,
For which I hope thou feltſt I was diſpleas'd.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.l: I am glad to ſee you in this merrie vaine,
What meanes this ieſt, I pray you Maſter tell me?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Yea, doſt thou ieere & flowt me in the teeth?
Thinkſt yu I ieſt? hold, take thou that, & that. Beats Dro.

sp.speaker: S. Dr.
sp.l: Hold ſir, for Gods ſake, now your ieſt is earneſt,
Vpon what bargaine do you giue it me?

sp.speaker: Antiph.
sp.l: Becauſe that I familiarlie ſometimes
Doe vſe you for my foole, and chat with you,
Your ſawcineſſe will ieſt vpon my loue,
And make a Common of my ſerious howres,
When the ſunne ſhines, let fooliſh gnats make ſport,
But creepe in crannies, when he hides his beames:
If you will ieſt with me, know my aſpect,
And faſhion your demeanor to my lookes,
Or I will beat this method in your ſconce.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Sconce call you it? ſo you would leaue battering, I had rather haue it a head, and you vſe theſe blows long, I muſt get a ſconce for my head, and Inſconce it to, or elſe I ſhall ſeek my wit in my ſhoulders, but I pray ſir, why am I beaten?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Doſt thou not know?

sp.speaker: S. Dro,
sp.p: Nothing ſir, but that I am beaten.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Shall I tell you why?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: I ſir, and wherefore; for they ſay, euery why hath a wherefore.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why firſt for flowting me, and then wherefore, for vrging it the ſecond time to me.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Was there euer anie man thus beaten out of ſeaſon, when in the why and the wherefore, is neither rime nor reaſon. Well ſir, I thanke you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Thanke me ſir, for what?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Marry ſir, for this ſomething that you gaue me for nothing.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Ile make you amends next, to giue you nothing for ſomething. But ſay ſir, is it dinner time?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: No ſir, I thinke the meat wants that I haue.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: In good time ſir: what's that?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Baſting.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Well ſir, then 'twill be drie.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: If it be ſir, I pray you eat none of it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Your reaſon?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Leſt it make you chollericke, and purchaſe me another drie baſting.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Well ſir, learne to ieſt in good time, there's a time for all things.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: I durſt haue denied that before you vvere ſo chollericke.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: By what rule ſir?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Marry ſir, by a rule as plaine as the plaine bald pate of Father time himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Let's heare it.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: There's no time for a man to recouer his haire that growes bald by nature.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: May he not doe it by fine and recouerie?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Yes, to pay a fine for a perewig, and recouer the loſt haire of another man.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why, is Time ſuch a niggard of haire, being (as it is) ſo plentifull an excrement?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Becauſe it is a bleſſing that hee beſtowes on beaſts, and what he hath ſcanted them in haire, hee hath giuen them in wit.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why, but theres manie a man hath more haire then wit.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Not a man of thoſe but he hath the wit to loſe his haire.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why thou didſt conclude hairy men plain dealers without wit.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: The plainer dealer, the ſooner loſt; yet he looſeth it in a kinde of iollitie.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: For what reaſon.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: For two, and ſound ones to.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Nay not ſound I pray you.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Sure ones then.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Nay, not ſure in a thing falſing.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Certaine ones then.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Name them.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: The one to ſaue the money that he ſpends in trying: the other, that at dinner they ſhould not drop in his porrage.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: You would all this time haue prou'd, here is no time for all things.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Marry and did ſir: namely, in no time to recouer haire loſt by Nature.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: But your reaſon was not ſubſtantiall, why there is no time to recouer.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Thus I mend it: Time himſelfe is bald, and therefore to the worlds end, will haue bald followers.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I knew 'twould be a bald concluſion: but ſoft, who wafts vs yonder.

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.l: I, I. Antipholus, looke ſtrange and frowne,
Some other Miſtreſſe hath thy ſweet aſpects:
I am not Adriana, nor thy wife.
The time was once, when thou vn-vrg'd wouldſt vow,
That neuer words were muſicke to thine eare,
That neuer obiect pleaſing in thine eye,
That neuer touch well welcome to thy hand,
That neuer meat ſweet-fauour'd in thy taſte,
Vnleſſe I ſpake, or look'd, or touch'd, or caru'd to thee.
How comes it now, my Husband, oh how comes it,
That thou art then eſtranged from thy ſelfe?
Thy ſelfe I call it, being ſtrange to me:
That vndiuidable Incorporate
Am better then thy deere ſelfes better part.
Ah doe not teare away thy ſelfe from me;
For know my loue: as eaſie maiſt thou fall
A drop of water in the breaking gulfe,
And take vnmingled thence that drop againe
Without addition or diminiſhing,
As take from me thy ſelfe, and not me too.
How deerely would it touch thee to the quicke,
Shouldſt thou but heare I were licencious?
And that this body conſecrate to thee,
By Ruffian Luſt ſhould be contaminate?
Wouldſt thou not ſpit at me, and ſpurne at me,
And hurle the name of husband in my face,
And teare the ſtain'd skin of my Harlot brow,
And from my falſe hand cut the wedding ring,
And breake it with a deepe-diuorcing vow?
I know thou canſt, and therefore ſee thou doe it.
I am poſſeſt with an adulterate blot,
My bloud is mingled with the crime of luſt:
For if we two be one, and thou play falſe,
I doe digeſt the poiſon of thy fleſh,
Being ſtrumpeted by thy contagion▪
Keepe then faire league and truce with thy true bed,
I liue diſtain'd, thou vndiſhonoured.

sp.speaker: Antip.
sp.l: Plead you to me faire dame? I know you not:
In Epheſus I am but two houres old,
As ſtrange vnto your towne, as to your talke,
Who euery word by all my wit being ſcan'd,
Wants wit in all, one word to vnderſtand.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.l: Fie brother, how the world is chang'd with you:
When were you wont to vſe my ſiſter thus?
She ſent for you by Dromio home to dinner.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: By Dromio?

sp.speaker: Drom.
sp.p: By me.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: By thee, and this thou didſt returne from him.
That he did buffet thee, and in his blowes,
Denied my houſe for his, me for his wife.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Did you conuerſe ſir with this gentlewoman:
What is the courſe and drift of your compact?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: I ſir? I neuer ſaw her till this time.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Villaine thou lieſt, for euen her verie words,
Didſt thou deliuer to me on the Mart.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: I neuer ſpake with her in all my life.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: How can ſhe thus then call vs by our names?
Vnleſſe it be by inſpiration.

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.l: How ill agrees it with your grauitie,
To counterfeit thus groſely with your ſlaue,
Abetting him to thwart me in my moode;
Be it my wrong, you are from me exempt,
But wrong not that wrong with a more contempt.
Come I will faſten on this ſleeue of thine:
Thou art an Elme my husband, I a Vine:
Whoſe weakneſſe married to thy ſtranger ſtate,
Makes me with thy ſtrength to communicate:
If ought poſſeſſe thee from me, it is droſſe,
Vſurping Iuie, Brier, or idle Moſſe,
Who all for want of pruning, with intruſion,
Infect thy ſap, and liue on thy confuſion.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: To mee ſhee ſpeakes, ſhee moues mee for her theame;
What, was I married to her in my dreame?
Or ſleepe I now, and thinke I heare all this?
What error driues our eies and eares amiſſe?
Vntill I know this ſure vncertaintie,
Ile entertaine the free'd fallacie.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Dromio, goe bid the ſeruants ſpred for dinner.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.l: Oh for my beads, I croſſe me for a ſinner.
This is the Fairie land, oh ſpight of ſpights,
We talke with Goblins, Owles and Sprights;
If we obay them not, this will inſue:
They'll ſucke our breath, or pinch vs blacke and blew.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Why prat'ſt thou to thy ſelfe, and anſwer'ſt not?
Dromio, thou Dromio, thou ſnaile, thou ſlug, thou ſot.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: I am transformed Maſter, am I not?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I thinke thou art in minde, and ſo am I.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Nay Maſter, both in minde, and in my ſhape.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Thou haſt thine owne forme.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: No, I am an Ape.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: If thou art chang'd to ought, 'tis to an Aſſe.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.l: 'Tis true ſhe rides me, and I long for graſſe.
'Tis ſo, I am an Aſſe, elſe it could neuer be,
But I ſhould know her as well as ſhe knowes me.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Come, come, no longer will I be a foole,
To put the finger in the eie and weepe;
Whil'ſt man and Maſter laughes my woes to ſcorne:
Come ſir to dinner, Dromio keepe the gate:
Husband Ile dine aboue with you to day,
And ſhriue you of a thouſand idle prankes:
Sirra, if any aske you for your Maſter,
Say he dines forth, and let no creature enter:
Come ſiſter, Dromio play the Porter well.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Am I in earth, in heauen, or in hell?
Sleeping or waking, mad or well aduiſde:
Knowne vnto theſe, and to my ſelfe diſguiſde:
Ile ſay as they ſay, and perſeuer ſo:
And in this miſt at all aduentures go.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Maſter, ſhall I be Porter at the gate?

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: I, and let none enter, leaſt I breake your pate.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Come, come, Antipholus, we dine to late.

div.head: Scena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Antipholus of Epheſus, his man Dromio, Angelo the Goldſmith, and Balthaſer the Merchant.

sp.speaker: E. Anti.
sp.l: Good ſignior Angelo you muſt excuſe vs all,
My wife is ſhrewiſh when I keepe not howres;
Say that I lingerd with you at your ſhop
To ſee the making of her Carkanet,
And that to morrow you will bring it home.
But here's a villaine that would face me downe
He met me on the Mart, and that I beat him,
And charg'd him with a thouſand markes in gold,
And that I did denie my wife and houſe;
Thou drunkard thou, what didſt thou meane by this?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: Say what you wil ſir, but I know what I know,
That you beat me at the Mart I haue your hand to ſhow;
If ye skin were parchment, & ye blows you gaue were ink,
Your owne hand-writing would tell you what I thinke.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.p: I thinke thou art an aſſe.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: Marry ſo it doth appeare
By the wrongs I ſuffer, and the blowes I beare,
I ſhould kicke being kickt, and being at that paſſe,
You would keepe from my heeles, and beware of an aſſe.

sp.speaker: E. An.
sp.l: Y' are ſad ſignior Balthazar, pray God our cheer
May anſwer my good will, and your good welcom here.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.p: I hold your dainties cheap ſir, & your welcom deer.

sp.speaker: E. An.
sp.l: Oh ſignior Balthazar, either at fleſh or fiſh,
A table full of welcome, makes ſcarce one dainty diſh.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.p: Good meat ſir is comon that euery churle affords.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: And welcome more common, for thats nothing but words.

sp.speaker: Bal.
sp.p: Small cheere and great welcome, makes a merrie feaſt.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.l: I, to a niggardly Hoſt, and more ſparing gueſt:
But though my cates be meane, take them in good part,
Better cheere may you haue, but not with better hart.
But ſoft, my doore is lockt; goe bid them let vs in.

p.hi: Maud, Briget, Marian, Ciſley, Gillian, Ginn.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.l: Mome, Malthorſe, Capon, Coxcombe, Idiot, Patch,
Either get thee from the dore, or ſit downe at the hatch:
Doſt thou coniure for wenches, that yu calſt for ſuch ſtore,
When one is one too many, goe get thee from the dore.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: What patch is made our Porter? my Maſter ſtayes in the ſtreet.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Let him walke from whence he came, leſt hee catch cold on's feet.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.p: Who talks within there? hoa, open the dore.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Right ſir, Ile tell you when, and you'll tell me wherefore.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Wherefore? for my dinner: I haue not din'd to day.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Nor to day here you muſt not come againe when you may.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: What art thou that keep'ſt mee out from the howſe I owe?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: The Porter for this time Sir, and my name is Dromio.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: O villaine, thou haſt ſtolne both mine office and my name,
The one nere got me credit, the other mickle blame:
If thou hadſt beene Dromio to day in my place,
Thou wouldſt haue chang'd thy face for a name, or thy name for an aſſe.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: What a coile is there Dromio? who are thoſe at the gate?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: Let my Maſter in Luce.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Faith no, hee comes too late, and ſo tell your Maſter.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: O Lord I muſt laugh, haue at you with a Prouerbe,
Shall I ſet in my ſtaffe.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Haue at you with another, that's when? can you tell?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: If thy name be called Luce, Luce thou haſt anſwer'd him well.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Doe you heare you minion, you'll let vs in I hope?

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: I thought to haue askt you.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: And you ſaid no.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: So come helpe, well ſtrooke, there was blow for blow.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Thou baggage let me in.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Can you tell for whoſe ſake?

sp.speaker: E. Drom.
sp.p: Maſter, knocke the doore hard.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: Let him knocke till it ake.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: You'll crie for this minion, if I beat the doore downe.

sp.speaker: Luce.
sp.p: What needs all that, and a paire of ſtocks in the towne?

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Who is that at the doore yt keeps all this noiſe?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: By my troth your towne is troubled with vnruly boies.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Are you there Wife? you might haue come before.

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.p: Your wife ſir knaue? go get you from the dore.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: If you went in paine Maſter, this knaue wold goe ſore.

sp.speaker: Angelo.
sp.p: Heere is neither cheere ſir, nor welcome, we would faine haue either.

sp.speaker: Baliz.
sp.p: In debating which was beſt, wee ſhall part with neither.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: They ſtand at the doore, Maſter, bid them welcome hither.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: There is ſomething in the winde, that we cannot get in.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: You would ſay ſo Maſter, if your garments were thin.
Your cake here is warme within: you ſtand here in the cold.
It would make a man mad as a Bucke to be ſo bought and ſold.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Go fetch me ſomething, Ile break ope the gate.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Breake any breaking here, and Ile breake your knaues pate.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: A man may breake a word with your ſir, and words are but winde;
I and breake it in your face, ſo he break it not behinde.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: It ſeemes thou want'ſt breaking, out vpon thee hinde.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: Here's too much out vpon thee, I pray thee let me in.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: I, when fowles haue no feathers, and fiſh haue no ſin.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Well, Ile breake in: go borrow me a crow.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: A crow without feather, Maſter meane you ſo;
For a fiſh without a finne, ther's a fowle without afether,
If a crow help vs in ſirra, wee'll plucke a crow together.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Go, get thee gon, fetch me an iron Crow.

sp.speaker: Balth.
sp.l: Haue patience ſir, oh let it not be ſo,
Heerein you warre againſt your reputation,
And draw within the compaſſe of ſuſpect
Th' vnuiolated honor of your wife.
Once this your long experience of your wiſedome,
Her ſober vertue, yeares, and modeſtie,
Plead on your part ſome cauſe to you vnknowne;
And doubt not ſir, but ſhe will well excuſe
Why at this time the dores are made againſt you.
Be rul'd by me, depart in patience,
And let vs to the Tyger all to dinner,
And about euening come your ſelfe alone,
To know the reaſon of this ſtrange reſtraint:
If by ſtrong hand you offer to breake in
Now in the ſtirring paſſage of the day,
A vulgar comment will be made of it;
And that ſuppoſed by the common rowt
Againſt your yet vngalled eſtimation,
That may with foule intruſion enter in,
And dwell vpon your graue when you are dead;
For ſlander liues vpon ſucceſſion;
For euer hows'd, where it gets poſſeſſion.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.l: You haue preuail'd, I will depart in quiet,
And in deſpight of mirth meane to be merrie:
I know a wench of excellent diſcourſe,
Prettie and wittie; wilde, and yet too gentle;
There will we dine: this woman that I meane
My wife (but I proteſt without deſert)
Hath oftentimes vpbraided me withall:
To her will we to dinner, get you home
And fetch the chaine, by this I know 'tis made,
Bring it I pray you to the Porpentine,
For there's the houſe: That chaine will I beſtow
(Be it for nothing but to ſpight my wife)
Vpon mine hoſteſſe there, good ſir make hafte▪
Since mine owne doores refuſe to entertaine me,
Ile knocke elſe-where, to ſee if they'll diſdaine me.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Ile meet you at that place ſome houre hence.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Do ſo, this ieſt ſhall coſt me ſome expence.

div.stage: Enter Iuliana, with Antipholus of Siracuſia.

sp.speaker: Iulia.
sp.l: And may it be that you haue quite forgot
A husbands office? ſhall Antipholus
Euen in the ſpring of Loue, thy Loue-ſprings rot?
Shall loue in buildings grow ſo ruinate?
If you did wed my ſiſter for her wealth,
Then for her wealths-ſake vſe her with more kindneſſe:
Or if you like elſe-where doe it by ſtealth,
Muffle your falſe loue with ſome ſhew of blindneſſe:
Let not my ſiſter read it in your eye:
Be not thy tongue thy owne ſhames Orator:
Looke ſweet, ſpeake faire, become diſloyaltie:
Apparell vice like vertues harbenger:
Beare a faire preſence, though your heart be tainted,
Teach ſinne the carriage of a holy Saint,
Be ſecret falſe: what need ſhe be acquainted?
What ſimple thiefe brags of his owne attaine?
'Tis double wrong to truant with your bed,
And let her read it in thy lookes at boord:
Shame hath a baſtard fame, well managed,
Ill deeds is doubled with an euill word:
Alas poore women, make vs not beleeue
(Being compact of credit) that you loue vs,
Though others haue the arme, ſhew vs the ſleeue:
We in your motion turne, and you may moue vs.
Then gentle brother get you in againe;
Comfort my ſiſter, cheere her, call her wiſe;
'Tis holy ſport to be a little vaine,
When the ſweet breath of flatterie conquers ſtrife.

sp.speaker: S. Anti.
sp.l: Sweete Miſtris, what your name is elſe I know not;
Nor by what wonder you do hit of mine:
Leſſe in your knowledge, and your grace you ſhow not,
Then our earths wonder, more then earth diuine.
Teach me deere creature how to thinke and ſpeake:
Lay open to my earthie groſſe conceit:
Smothred in errors, feeble, ſhallow, weake,
The foulded meaning of your words deceit:
Againſt my ſoules pure truth, why labour you,
To make it wander in an vnknowne field?
Are you a god? would you create me new?
Transforme me then, and to your powre Ile yeeld.
But if that I am I, then well I know,
Your weeping ſiſter is no wife of mine,
Nor to her bed no homage doe I owe:
Farre more, farre more, to you doe I decline:
Oh traine me not ſweet Mermaide with thy note,
To drowne me in thy ſiſter floud of teares:
Sing Siren for thy ſelfe, and I will dote:
Spread ore the ſiluer waues thy golden haires;
And as a bud Ile take thee, and there lie:
And in that glorious ſuppoſition thinke,
He gaines by death, that hath ſuch meanes to die:
Let Loue, being light, be drowned if ſhe ſinke.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: What are you mad, that you doe reaſon ſo?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Not mad, but mated, how I doe not know.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: It is a fault that ſpringeth from your eie.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: For gazing on your beames faire ſun being by.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Gaze when you ſhould, and that will cleere your ſight.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: As good to winke ſweet loue, as looke on night.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Why call you me loue? Call my ſiſter ſo.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Thy ſiſters ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: That's my ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: No: it is thy ſelfe, mine owne ſelfes better part:
Mine eies cleere eie, my deere hearts deerer heart;
My foode, my fortune, and my ſweet hopes aime;
My ſole earths heauen, and my heauens claime.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: All this my ſiſter is, or elſe ſhould be.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Call thy ſelfe ſiſter ſweet, for I am thee:
Thee will I loue, and with thee lead my life;
Thou haſt no husband yet, nor I no wife:
Giue me thy hand.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Oh ſoft ſir, hold you ſtill:
Ile fetch my ſiſter to get her good will.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why how now Dromio, where run'ſt thou ſo faſt?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Doe you know me ſir? Am I Dromio? Am I your man? Am I my ſelfe?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Thou art Dromio, thou art my man, thou art thy ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: I am an aſſe, I am a womans man, and beſides my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: What womans man? and how beſides thy ſelfe?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.l: Marrie ſir, beſides my ſelfe, I am due to a woman:
One that claimes me, one that haunts me, one that will haue me.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: What claime laies ſhe to thee?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Marry ſir, ſuch claime as you would lay to your horſe, and ſhe would haue me as a beaſt, not that I beeing a beaſt ſhe would haue me, but that ſhe being a verie beaſtly creature layes claime to me.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: What is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: A very reuerent body: I ſuch a one, as a man may not ſpeake of, without he ſay ſir reuerence, I haue but leane lucke in the match, and yet is ſhe a wondrous fat marriage.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: How doſt thou meane a fat marriage?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Marry ſir, ſhe's the Kitchin wench, & al greaſe, and I know not what vſe to put her too, but to make a Lampe of her, and run from her by her owne light. I warrant, her ragges and the Tallow in them, will burne a Poland Winter: If ſhe liues till doomeſday, ſhe'l burne a weeke longer then the whole World.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: What complexion is ſhe of?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Swart like my ſhoo, but her face nothing like ſo cleane kept: for why? ſhe ſweats a man may goe ouer-ſhooes in the grime of it.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: That's a fault that water will mend.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: No ſir, 'tis in graine, Noahs ſtood could not do it.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: What's her name?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Nell Sir: but her name is three quarters, that's an Ell and three quarters, will not meaſure her from hip to hip.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Then ſhe beares ſome bredth?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: No longer from head to foot, then from hippe to hippe: ſhe is ſphericall, like a globe: I could find out Countries in her.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: In what part of her body ſtands Ireland?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Marry ſir in her buttockes, I found it out by the bogges.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Where Scotland?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: I found it by the barrenneſſe, hard in the palme of the hand.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Where France?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: In her forhead, arm'd and reuerted, making warre againſt her heire.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Where England?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: I look'd for the chalkle Cliffes, but I could find no whiteneſſe in them. But I gueſſe, it ſtood in her chin by the ſalt theume that ranne betweene France, and it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Where Spaine?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Faith I ſaw it not: but I felt it hot in her breth.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Where America, the Indies?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Oh ſir, vpon her noſe, all ore embelliſhed with Rubies, Carbuncles, Saphires, declining their rich Aſpect to the hot breath of Spaine, who ſent whole Armadoes of Carrects to be ballaſt at her noſe.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Where ſtood Belgia, the Netherlands?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Oh ſir, I did not looke ſo low. To conclude, this drudge or Diuiner layd claime to mee, call'd mee Dromio, ſwore I was aſſur'd to her, told me what priuie markes I had about mee, as the marke of my ſhoulder, the Mole in my necke, the great Wart on my left arme, that I amaz'd ranne from her as a witch. And I thinke, if my breſt had not beene made of faith, and my heart of ſteele, ſhe had transform'd me to a Curtull dog, & made me turne i' th wheele.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.l: Go hie thee preſently poſt to the rode,
And if the winde blow any way from ſhore,
I will not harbour in this Towne to night.
If any Barke put forth, come to the Mart,
Where I will walke till thou returne to me:
If euerie one knowes vs, and we know none,
'Tis time I thinke to trudge, packe, and be gone.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.l: As from a Beare a man would run for life,
So flie I from her that would be my wife.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.l: There's none but Witches do inhabite heere,
And therefore 'tis hie time that I were hence:
She that doth call me husband, euen my ſoule
Doth for a wife abhorre. But her faire ſiſter
Poſſeſt with ſuch a gentle ſoueraigne grace,
Of ſuch inchanting preſence and diſcourſe,
Hath almoſt made me Traitor to my ſelfe:
But leaſt my ſelfe be guilty to ſelfe wrong,
Ile ſtop mine eares againſt the Mermaids ſong.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: Mr Antipholus.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: I that's my name.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: I know it well ſir, loe here's the chaine,
I thought to haue tane you at the Porpentine,
The chaine vnfiniſh'd made me ſtay thus long.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: What is your will that I ſhal do with this?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: What pleaſe your ſelfe ſir: I haue made it for you.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Made it for me ſir, I beſpoke it not.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Not once, nor twice, but twentie times you haue:
Go home with it, and pleaſe your Wife withall,
And ſoone at ſupper time Ile viſit you,
And then receiue my money for the chaine.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.l: I pray you ſir receiue the money now,
For feare you ne're ſee chaine, nor mony more.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.p: You are a merry man ſir, fare you well.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What I ſhould thinke of this, I cannot tell:
But this I thinke, there's no man is ſo vaine,
That would refuſe ſo faire an offer'd Chaine.
I ſee a man heere needs not liue by ſhifts,
When in the ſtreets he meetes ſuch Golden gifts:
Ile to the Mart, and there for Dromio ſtay,
If any ſhip put out, then ſtraight away.

div.head: Scoena Prima.
div.stage: Enter a Merchant, Goldſmith, and an Officer.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: You know ſince Pentecoſt the ſum is due,
And ſince I haue not much importun'd you,
Nor now I had not, but that I am bound
To Perſia, and want Gilders for my voyage:
Therefore make preſent ſatisfaction,
Or Ile attach you by this Officer.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: Euen iuſt the ſum that I do owe to you,
Is growing to me by Antipholus,
And in the inſtant that I met with you,
He had of me a Chaine, at fiue a clocke
I ſhall receiue the money for the ſame:
Pleaſeth you walke with me downe to his houſe,
I will diſcharge my bond, and thanke you too.

div.stage: Enter Antipholus Epheſ. Dromio from the Courtizans.

sp.speaker: Offi.
sp.p: That labour may you ſaue: See where he comes.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: While I go to the Goldſmiths houſe, go thou
And buy a ropes end, that will I beſtow
Among my wife, and their confederates,
For locking me out of my doores by day:
But ſoft I ſee the Goldſmith; get thee gone,
Buy thou a rope, and bring it home to me.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: I buy a thouſand pound a yeare, I buy a rope.

sp.speaker: Eph. Am.
sp.l: A man is well holpe vp that truſts to you,
I promiſed your preſence, and the Chaine,
But neither Chaine nor Goldſmith came to me:
Belike you thought our loue would laſt too long
If it were chain'd together: and therefore came not.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: Sauing your merrie humor: here's the note
How much your Chaine weighs to the vtmoſt charect,
The fineneſſe of the Gold, and chargefull faſhion,
Which doth amount to three odde Duckets more
Then I ſtand debted to this Gentleman,
I pray you ſee him preſently diſcharg'd,
For he is bound to Sea, and ſtayes but for it.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.l: I am not furniſh'd with the preſent monie:
Beſides I haue ſome buſineſſe in the towne,
Good Signior take the ſtranger to my houſe,
And with you take the Chaine, and bid my wife
Disburſe the ſumme, on the receit thereof,
Perchance I will be there as ſoone as you.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.p: Then you will bring the Chaine to her your ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: No beare it with you, leaſt I come not time enough.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.p: Well ſir, I will? Haue you the Chaine about you?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And if I haue not ſir, I hope you haue:
Or elſe you may returne without your money.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: Nay come I pray you ſir, giue me the Chaine:
Both winde and tide ſtayes for this Gentleman,
And I too blame haue held him heere too long.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.l: Good Lord, you vſe this dalliance to excuſe
Your breach of promiſe to the Porpentine,
I ſhould haue chid you for not bringing it,
But like a ſhrew you firſt begin to brawle.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: The houre ſteales on, I pray you ſir diſpatch.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.p: You heare how he importunes me, the Chaine.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why giue it to my wife, and fetch your mony.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: Come, come, you know I gaue it you euen now.
Either ſend the Chaine, or ſend me by ſome token.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Fie, now you run this humor out of breath,
Come where's the Chaine, I pray you let me ſee it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: My buſineſſe cannot brooke this dalliance,
Good ſir ſay, whe'r you'l anſwer me, or no:
If not, Ile leaue him to the Officer.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I anſwer you? What ſhould I anſwer you.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.p: The monie that you owe me for the Chaine.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I owe you none, till I receiue the Chaine.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.p: You know I gaue it you halfe an houre ſince.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: You gaue me none, you wrong mee much to ſay ſo.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: You wrong me more ſir in denying it.
Conſider how it ſtands vpon my credit.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Well Officer, arreſt him army ſuite.

sp.speaker: Offi.
sp.p: I do, and charge you in the Dukes name to obey me.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: This touches me in reputation.
Either conſent to pay this ſum for me,
Or I attach you by this Officer.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Conſent to pay thee that I never had:
Arreſt me fooliſh fellow if thou dar'ſt.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: Heere is thy fee, arreſt him Officer.
I would not ſpare my brother in this caſe,
If he ſhould ſcorne me ſo apparantly.

sp.p: I do arreſt you ſir, you heare the ſuite.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I do obey thee, till I giue thee baile.
But ſirrah, you ſhall buy this ſport as deere,
As all the mettall in your ſhop will anſwer.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: Sir, ſir, I ſhall haue Law in Epheſus,
To your notorious ſhame, I doubt it not.

div.stage: Enter Dromio Sira. from the Bay.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.l: Maſter, there's a Barke of Epidamium,
That ſtaies but till her Owner comes aboord,
And then ſir ſhe beares away. Our fraughtage ſir,
I haue conuei'd aboord, and I haue bought
The Oyle, the Balſamum, and Aqua-vitae.
The ſhip is in her trim, the merrie winde
Blowes faire from land: they ſtay for nought at all,
But for their Owner, Maſter, and your ſelfe.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: How now? a Madman? Why thou peeuiſh ſheep
What ſhip of Epidamium ſtaies for me.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: A ſhip you ſent me too, to hier waftage.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Thou drunken ſlaue, I ſent thee for a rope,
And told thee to what purpoſe, and what end.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.l: You ſent me for a ropes end as ſoone,
You ſent me to the Bay ſir, for a Barke.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I will debate this matter at more leiſure
And teach your eares to liſt me with more heede:
To Adriana Villaine hie thee ſtraight:
Giue her this key, and tell her in the Deske
That's couer'd o're with Turkiſh Tapiſtrie,
There is a purſe of Duckets, let her ſend it:
Tell her, I am arreſted in the ſtreete,
And that ſhall baile me: hie thee ſlaue, be gone,
On Officer to priſon, till it come.

sp.speaker: S. Dromio.
sp.l: To Adriana, that is where we din'd,
Where Dowſabell did claime me for her husband,
She is too bigge I hope for me to compaſſe,
Thither I muſt, although againſt my will:
For ſeruants muſt their Maſters mindes fulfill.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Ah Luciana, did he tempt thee ſo?
Might'ſt thou perceiue auſteerely in his eie,
That he did plead in earneſt, yea or no:
Look'd he or red or pale, or ſad or merrily?
What obſeruation mad'ſt thou in this caſe?
Oh, his hearts Meteors tilting in his face.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Firſt he deni'de you had in him no right.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: He meant he did me none: the more my ſpight

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Then ſwore he that he was a ſtranger heere.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: And true he ſwore, though yet forſworne hee were.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Then pleaded I for you.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: And what ſaid he?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: That loue I begg'd for you, he begg'd of me.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: With what perſwaſion did he tempt thy loue?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: With words, that in an honeſt ſuit might moue.
Firſt, he did praiſe my beautie, then my ſpeech.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Did'ſt ſpeake him faire?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Haue patience I beſeech.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: I cannot, nor I will not hold me ſtill,
My tongue, though not my heart, ſhall have his will.
He is deformed, crooked, old, and ſere,
Ill-fac'd, worſe bodied, ſhapeleſſe euery where:
