Vicious, vngentle, fooliſh, blunt, vnkinde,
Stigmaticall in making worſe in minde.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Who would be iealous then of ſuch a one?
No euill loſt is wail'd, when it is gone.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Ah but I thinke him better then I ſay:
And yet would herein others eies were worſe:
Farre from her neſt the Lapwing cries away:
My heart praies for him, though my tongue doe curſe.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Here goe: the deske, the purſe, ſweet now make haſte.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: How haſt thou loſt thy breath?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: By running faſt.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Where is thy Maſter Dromio? Is he well?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.l: No, he's in Tartar limbo, worſe then hell:
A diuell in an euerlaſting garment hath him;
On whoſe hard heart is button'd vp with ſteele:
A Feind, a Fairie, pittileſſe and ruffe:
A Wolfe, nay worſe, a fellow all in buffe▪
A back friend, a ſhoulder-clapper, one that countermāds
The paſſages of allies, creekes, and narrow lands:
A hound that runs Counter, and yet draws drifoot well,
One that before the Iudgmēt carries poore ſoules to hel.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Why man, what is the matter?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: I doe not know the matter, hee is reſted on the caſe.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: What is he arreſted? tell me at whoſe ſuite?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: I know not at whoſe ſuite he is areſted well; but is in a ſuite of buffe which reſted him, that can I tell, will you ſend him Miſtris redemption, the monie in his deske.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Go fetch it Siſter: this I wonder at.
Thus he vnknowne to me ſhould be in debt:
Tell me, was he areſted on a band?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.l: Not on a band, but on a ſtronger thing:
A chaine, a chaine, doe you not here it ring.

sp.speaker: Adria.
sp.p: What, the chaine?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.l: No, no, the bell, 'tis time that I were gone:
It was two ere I left him, and now the clocke ſtrikes one.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: The houres come backe, that did I neuer here.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Oh yes, if any houre meete a Serieant, a turnes backe for verie feare.

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.p: As if time were in debt: how fondly do'ſt thou reaſon?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.l: Time is a verie bankerout, and owes more then he's worth to ſeaſon.
Nay, he's a theefe too: haue you not heard men ſay,
That time comes ſtealing on by night and day?
If I be in debt and theft, and a Serieant in the way,
Hath he not reaſon to turne backe an houre in a day?

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Go Dromio, there's the monie, beare it ſtraight,
And bring thy Maſter home imediately.
Come ſiſter, I am preſt downe with conceit:
Conceit, my comfort and my iniurie.

div.l: There's not a man I meete but doth ſalute me
As if I were their well acquainted friend,
And euerie one doth call me by my name:
Some tender monie to me, ſome inuite me;
Some other giue me thankes for kindneſſes;
Some offer me Commodities to buy.
Euen now a' tailor cal'd me in his ſhop,
And ſhow'd me Silkes that he had bought for me,
And therewithall tooke meaſure of my body.
Sure theſe are but imaginarie wiles,
And lapland Sorcerers inhabite here.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Maſter, here's the gold you ſent me for: what haue you got the picture of old Adam new apparel'd?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: What gold is this? What Adam do'ſt thou meane?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Not that Adam that kept the Paradiſe: but that Adam that keepes the priſon; hee that goes in the calues-skin, that was kil'd for the Prodigall: hee that came behinde you ſir, like an euill angel, and bid you forſake your libertie.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I vnderſtand thee not.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: No? why 'tis a plaine caſe: he that went like a Baſe-Viole in a caſe of leather; the man ſir, that when gentlemen are tired giues them a ſob, and reſts them: he ſir, that takes pittie on decaied men, and giues them ſuites of durance: he that ſets vp his reſt to doe more exploits with his Mace, then a Moris Pike.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: What thou mean'ſt an officer?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: I ſir, the Serieant of the Band: he that brings any man to anſwer it that breakes his Band: one that thinkes a man alwaies going to bed, and ſaies, God giue you good reſt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Well ſir, there reſt in your foolerie:
Is there any ſhips puts forth to night? may we be gone?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Why ſir, I brought you word an houre ſince, that the Barke Expedition put forth to night, and then were you hindred by the Serieant to tarry for the Hoy Delay: Here are the angels that you ſent for to deliuer you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The fellow is diſtract, and ſo am I,
And here we wander in illuſions:
Some bleſſed power deliuer vs from hence.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Well met, well met, Maſter Antipholous:
I ſee ſir you haue found the Gold-ſmith now:
Is that the chaine you promis'd me to day.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Sathan auoide, I charge thee tempt me not.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Maſter, is this Miſtris Sathan?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: It is the diuell.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Nay, ſhe is worſe, ſhe is the diuels dam: And here ſhe comes in the habit of a light wench, and thereof comes, that the wenches ſay God dam me, That's as much to ſay, God make me a light wench: It is written▪ they appeare to men like angels of light, light is an effect of fire, and fire will burne: ergo, light wenches will burne, come not neere her.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Your man and you are maruailous merrie ſir.
Will you goe with me, wee'll mend our dinner here?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Maſter, if do expect ſpoon-meate, or beſpeake a long ſpoone.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why Dromio?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Marrie he muſt haue a long ſpoone that muſt eate with the diuell.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Auoid then fiend, what tel'ſt thou me of ſupping?
Thou art, as you are all a ſorcereſſe:
I coniure thee to leaue me, and be gon.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Giue me the ring of mine you had at dinner,
Or for my Diamond the Chaine you promis'd,
And Ile be gone ſir, and not trouble you.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p:
Some diuels aske but the parings of ones naile,
a ruſh, a haire, a drop of blood, a pin, a nut, a cherrieſtone: but ſhe more couetous, wold haue a chaine: Maſter be wiſe, and if you giue it her, the diuell will ſhake her Chaine, and fright vs with it.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: I pray you ſir my Ring, or elſe the Chaine,
I hope you do not meane to cheate me ſo?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Auant thou witch: Come Dromio let vs go.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Flie pride ſaies the Pea-cocke, Miſtris that you know.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Now out of doubt Antipholus is mad,
Elſe would he neuer ſo demeane himſelfe,
A Ring he hath of mine worth fortie Duckets,
And for the ſame he promis'd me a Chaine,
Both one and other he denies me now:
The reaſon that I gather he is mad,
Beſides this preſent inſtance of his rage,
Is a mad tale he told to day at dinner,
Of his owne doores being ſhut againſt his entrance.
Belike his wife acquainted with his fits,
On purpoſe ſhut the doores againſt his way:
My way is now to hie home to his houſe,
And tell his wife, that being Lunaticke,
He ruſh'd into my houſe, and tooke perforce
My Ring away. This courſe I fitteſt chooſe,
For fortie Duckets is too much to looſe.

div.stage: Enter Antipholus Epheſ. with a Iailor.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: Feare me not man, I will not breake away,
Ile giue thee ere I leaue thee ſo much money
To warrant thee as I am reſted for.
My wife is in a wayward moode to day,
And will not lightly truſt the Meſſenger,
That I ſhould be attach'd in Epheſus,
I tell you 'twill ſound harſhly in her eares.
sp.stage: Enter Dromio Eph. with a ropes end.
sp.l: Heere comes my Man, I thinke he brings the monie.
How now ſir? Haue you that I ſent you for?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: Here's that I warrant you will pay them all.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: But where's the Money?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: Why ſir, I gaue the Monie for the Rope.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Fiue hundred Duckets villaine for a rope?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: Ile ſerue you ſir fiue hundred at the rate.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: To what end did I bid thee hie thee home?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: To a ropes end ſir, and to that end am I return'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: And to that end ſir, I will welcome you.

sp.speaker: Offi.
sp.p: Good ſir be patient.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: Nay 'tis for me to be patient, I am in aduerſitie.

sp.speaker: Offi.
sp.p: Good now hold thy tongue.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: Nay, rather perſwade him to hold his hands.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Thou whoreſon ſenſeleſſe Villaine.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: I would I were ſenſeleſſe ſir, that I might not feele your blowes.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Thou art ſenſible in nothing but blowes, and ſo is an Aſſe.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: I am an Aſſe indeede, you may prooue it by my long eares. I haue ſerued him from the houre of my Natiuitie to this inſtant, and haue nothing at his hands for my ſeruice but blowes. When I am cold, he heates me with beating: when I am warme, he cooles me with beating: I am wak'd with it when I ſleepe, rais'd with it when I ſit, driuen out of doores with it when I goe from home, welcom'd home with it when I returne, nay I beare it on my ſhoulders, as a begger woont her brat: and I thinke when he hath lam'd me, I ſhall begge with it from doore to doore.

div.stage: Enter Adriana, Luciana, Courtizan, and a Schoolemaſter, call'd Pinch.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Come goe along, my wife is comming yonder.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: Miſtris reſpice finem, reſpect your end, or rather the propheſie like the Parrat, beware the ropes end.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Wilt thou ſtill talke?

sp.speaker: Curt.
sp.p: How ſay you now? Is not your husband mad?

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.l: His inciuility confirmes no leſſe:
Good Doctor Pinch, you are a Coniurer,
Eſtabliſh him in his true ſence againe,
And I will pleaſe you what you will demand.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Alas how fiery, and how ſharpe he lookes.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Marke, how he trembles in his extaſie.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: Giue me your hand, and let mee feele your pulſe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: There is my hand, and let it feele your eare.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.l: I charge thee Sathan, hous'd within this man,
To yeeld poſſeſſion to my holie praiers,
And to thy ſtate of darkneſſe hie thee ſtraight,
I coniure thee by all the Saints in heauen.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Peace doting wizard, peace; I am not mad.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Oh that thou wer't not, poore diſtreſſed ſoule.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.l: You Minion you, are theſe your Cuſtomers?
Did this Companion with the ſaffron face
Reuell and feaſt it at my houſe to day,
Whil'ſt vpon me the guiltie doores were ſhut,
And I denied to enter in my houſe.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: O husband, God doth know you din'd at home
Where would you had remain'd vntill this time,
Free from theſe ſlanders, and this open ſhame.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Din'd at home? Thou Villaine, what ſayeſt thou?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Sir ſooth to ſay, you did not dine at home.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Were not my doores lockt vp, and I ſhut out?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Perdie, your doores were lockt, and you ſhut out.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: And did not ſhe her ſelfe reuile me there?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Sans Fable, ſhe her ſelfe reuil'd you there.

sp.speaker: Anti.
sp.p: Did not her Kitchen maide raile, taunt, and ſcorne me?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Certis ſhe did, the kitchin veſtall ſcorn'd you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: And did not I in rage depart from thence?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.l: In veritie you did, my bones beares witneſſe,
That ſince haue felt the vigor of his rage.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Is't good to ſooth him in theſe crontraries?

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.l: It is no ſhame, the fellow finds his vaine,
And yeelding to him, humors well his frenſie.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Thou haſt ſubborn'd the Goldſmith to arreſt mee.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Alas, I ſent you Monie to redeeme you,
By Dromio heere, who came in haſt for it.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.l: Monie by me? Heart and good will you might,
But ſurely Maſter not a ragge of Monie.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Wentſt not thou to her for a purſe of Duckets.

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.p: He came to me, and I deliuer'd it.

sp.speaker: Luci.
sp.p: And I am witneſſe with her that ſhe did:

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.l: God and the Rope-maker beare me witneſſe,
That I was ſent for nothing but a rope.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.l: Miſtris, both Man and Maſter is poſſeſt,
I know it by their pale and deadly lookes,
They muſt be bound and laide in ſome darke roome.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Say wherefore didſt thou locke me forth to day,
And why doſt thou denie the bagge of gold?

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: I did not gentle husband locke thee forth.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.l: And gentle Mr I receiu'd no gold:
But I confeſſe ſir, that we were lock'd out.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Diſſembling Villain, thou ſpeak'ſt falſe in both

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Diſſembling harlot, thou art falſe in all,
And art confederate with a damned packe,
To make a loathſome abiect ſcorne of me:
But with theſe nailes, Ile plucke out theſe falſe eyes,
That would behold in me this ſhamefull ſport.

div.stage: Enter three or foure, and offer to binde him: Hee ſtriues.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Oh binde him, binde him, let him not come neere me.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: More company, the fiend is ſtrong within him

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Aye me poore man, how pale and wan he looks.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: What will you murther me, thou Iailor thou?
I am thy priſoner, wilt thou ſuffer them to make a reſcue?

sp.speaker: Offi.
sp.p: Maſters let him go: he is my priſoner, and you ſhall not haue him.

sp.speaker: Pinch.
sp.p: Go binde this man, for he is franticke too.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: What wilt thou do, thou peeuiſh Officer?
Haſt thou delight to ſee a wretched man
Do outrage and diſpleaſure to himſelfe?

sp.speaker: Offi.
sp.l: He is my priſoner, if I let him go,
The debt he owes will be requir'd of me.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: I will diſcharge thee ere I go from thee,
Beare me forthwith vnto his Creditor,
And knowing how the debt growes I will pay it.
Good Maſter Doctor ſee him ſafe conuey'd
Home to my houſe, oh moſt vnhappy day.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Oh moſt vnhappie ſtrumpet.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Maſter, I am heere entred in bond for you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Out on thee Villaine, wherefore doſt thou mad mee?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Will you be bound for nothing, be mad good Maſter, cry the diuell.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: God helpe poore ſoules, how idlely doe they talke.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Go beare him hence, ſiſter go you with me:
Say now, whoſe ſuite is he arreſted at?

div.stage: Exeunt. Manet Offic. Adri. Luci. Courtizan

sp.speaker: Off.
sp.p: One Angelo a Goldſmith, do you know him?

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: I know the man: what is the ſumme he owes?

sp.speaker: Off.
sp.p: Two hundred Duckets.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Say, how growes it due.

sp.speaker: Off.
sp.p: Due for a Chaine your husband had of him.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: He did beſpeake a Chain for me, but had it not.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: When as your husband all in rage to day.
Came to my houſe, and tooke away my Ring,
The Ring I ſaw vpon his finger now,
Straight after did I meete him with a Chaine.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: It may be ſo, but I did neuer ſee it.
Come Iailor, bring me where the Goldſmith is,
I long to know the truth heereof at large.

div.stage: Enter Antipholus Siracuſia with his Rapier drawne, and Dromio Sirac.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: God for thy mercy, they are looſe againe.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: And come with naked ſwords,
Let's call more helpe to haue them bound againe.

sp.speaker: Off.
sp.p: Away, they'l kill vs.

div.stage: Exeunt omnes, as faſt as may be, frighted.

sp.speaker: S. Ant.
sp.p: I ſee theſe Witches are affraid of ſwords.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: She that would be your wife, now ran from you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Come to the Centaur, fetch our ſtuffe from thence:
I long that we were ſafe and ſound aboord.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: Faith ſtay heere this night, they will ſurely do vs no harme: you ſaw they ſpeake vs faire, giue vs gold: me thinkes they are ſuch a gentle Nation, that but for the Mountaine of mad fleſh that claimes mariage of me, I could finde in my heart to ſtay heere ſtill, and turne Witch.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I will not ſtay to night for all the Towne,
Therefore away, to get our ſtuffe aboord.

div.head: Scoena Prima.
div.stage: Enter the Merchant and the Goldſmith.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: I am ſorry Sir that I haue hindred you,
But I proteſt he had the Chaine of me,
Though moſt diſhoneſtly he doth denie it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: How is the man eſteem'd heere in the Citie?

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: Of very reuerent reputation ſir,
Of credit infinite, highly belou'd,
Second to none that liues heere in the Citie:
His word might beare my wealth at any t • me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Speake ſoftly, yonder as I thinke he walkes.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: 'Tis ſo: and that ſelfe chaine about his necke,
Which he forſwore moſt monſtrouſly to haue.
Good ſir draw neere to me, Ile ſpeake to him:
Signior Antipholus, I wonder much
That you would put me to this ſhame and trouble,
And not without ſome ſcandall to your ſelfe,
With circumſtance and oaths, ſo to denie
This Chaine, which now you weare ſo openly.
Beſide the charge, the ſhame, impriſonment,
You haue done wrong to this my honeſt friend,
Who but for ſtaying on our Controuerſie,
Had hoiſted ſaile, and put to ſea to day:
This Chaine you had of me, can you deny it?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I thinke I had, I neuer did deny it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes that you did ſir, and forſwore it too.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Who heard me to denie it or forſweare it?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Theſe eares of mine thou knowſt did hear thee:
Fie on thee wretch, 'tis pitty that thou liu'ſt
To walke where any honeſt men reſort.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Thou art a Villaine to impeach me thus,
Ile proue mine honor, and mine honeſtie
Againſt thee preſently, if thou dar'ſt ſtand:

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I dare and do defie thee for a villaine.

div.stage: They draw. Enter Adriana, Luciana, Courtezan, & others.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Hold, hurt him not for God ſake, he is mad,
Some get within him, take his ſword away:
Binde Dromio too, and beare them to my houſe.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.l: Runne maſter run, for Gods ſake take a houſe,
This is ſome Priorie, in, or we are ſpoyl'd.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.p: Be quiet people, wherefore throng you hither?

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: To fetch my poore diſtracted husband hence,
Let vs come in, that we may binde him faſt,
And beare him home for his recouerie.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.p: I knew he vvas not in his perfect wits.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I am ſorry now that I did draw on him.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.p: How long hath this poſſeſſion held the man.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: This weeke he hath beene heauie, ſower ſad,
And much different from the man he was:
But till this afternoone his paſſion
Ne're brake into extremity of rage.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Hath he not loſt much wealth by wrack of ſea,
Buried ſome deere friend, hath not elſe his eye
Stray'd his affection in vnlawfull loue,
A ſinne preuailing much in youthfull men,
Who giue their eies the liberty of gazing.
Which of theſe ſorrowes is he ſubiect too?

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: To none of theſe, except it be the laſt,
Namely, ſome loue that drew him oft from home.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.p: You ſhould for that haue reprehended him.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Why ſo I did.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.p: I but not rough enough.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: As roughly as my modeſtie would let me.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.p: Haply in priuate.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: And in aſſemblies too.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.p: I, but not enough.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: It was the copie of our Conference.
In bed he ſlept not for my vrging it,
At boord he fed not for my vrging it:
Alone, it was the ſubiect of my Theame:
In company I often glanced it:
Still did I tell him, it was vilde and bad.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: And thereof came it, that the man was mad.
The venome clamors of a iealous woman,
Poiſons more deadly then a mad dogges tooth.
It ſeemes his ſleepes were hindred by thy railing,
And thereof comes it that his head is light.
Thou ſaiſt his meate was ſawc'd with thy vpbraidings,
Vnquiet meales make ill digeſtions,
Thereof the raging fire of feauer bred,
And what's a Feauer, but a fit of madneſſe?
Thou ſayeſt his ſports were hindred by thy bralles.
Sweet recreation barr'd, what doth enſue
But moodie and dull melancholly,
Kinſman to grim and comfortleſſe diſpaire,
And at her heeles a huge infectious troope
Of pale diſtemperatures, and foes to life?
In food, in ſport, and life-preſeruing reſt
To be diſturb'd, would mad or man, or beaſt:
The conſequence is then, thy iealous fits
Hath ſcar'd thy husband from the vſe of wits.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: She neuer reprehended him but mildely,
When he demean'd himſelfe, rough, rude, and wildly,
Why beare you theſe rebukes, and anſwer not?

sp.speaker: Adri.
sp.l: She did betray me to my owne reproofe,
Good people enter, and lay hold on him.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.p: No, not a creature enters in my houſe.

sp.speaker: Ad.
sp.p: Then let your ſeruants bring my husband forth

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Neither: he tooke this place for ſanctuary,
And it ſhall priuiledge him from your hands,
Till I haue brought him to his wits againe,
Or looſe my labour in aſſaying it.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: I will attend my husband, be his nurſe,
Diet his ſickneſſe, for it is my Office,
And will haue no atturney but my ſelfe,
And therefore let me haue him home with me.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.l: Be patient, for I will not let him ſtirre,
Till I haue vs'd the approoued meanes I haue,
With wholſome ſirrups, drugges, and holy prayers
To make of him a formall man againe:
It is a branch and parcell of mine oath,
A charitable dutie of my order,
Therefore depart, and leaue him heere with me.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: I will not hence, and leaue my husband heere:
And ill it doth beſeeme your holineſſe
To ſeparate the husband and the wife.

sp.speaker: Ab.
sp.p: Be quiet and depart, thou ſhalt not haue him.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Complaine vnto the Duke of this indignity.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Come go, I will fall proſtrate at his feete,
And neuer riſe vntill my teares and prayers
Haue won his grace to come in perſon hither,
And take perforce my husband from the Abbeſſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: By this I thinke the Diall points at fiue:
Anon I' me ſure the Duke himſelfe in perſon
Comes this way to the melancholly vale;
The place of depth, and ſorrie execution,
Behinde the ditches of the Abbey heere.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.p: Vpon what cauſe?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: To ſee a reuerent Siracuſian Merchant,
Who put vnluckily into this Bay
Againſt the Lawes and Statutes of this Towne,
Beheaded publikely for his offence.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.p: See where they come, we wil behold his death.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Kneele to the Duke before he paſſe the Abbey.

div.stage: Enter the Duke of Epheſus, and the Merchant of Siracuſe bare head, with the Headſman, & other Officers.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Yet once againe proclaime it publikely,
If any friend will pay the ſumme for him,
He ſhall not die, ſo much we tender him.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Iuſtice moſt ſacred Duke againſt the Abbeſſe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: She is a vertuous and a reuerend Lady,
It cannot be that ſhe hath done thee wrong.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: May it pleaſe your Grace, Antipholus my husbād,
Who I made Lord of me, and all I had,
At your important Letters this ill day,
A moſt outragious fit of madneſſe tooke him:
That deſp'rately he hurried through the ſtreete,
With him his bondman, all as mad as he,
Doing diſpleaſure to the Citizens,
By ruſhing in their houſes: bearing thence
Rings, Iewels, any thing his rage did like.
Once did I get him bound, and ſent him home,
Whil'ſt to take order for the wrongs I went,
That heere and there his furie had committed,
Anon I wot not, by what ſtrong eſcape
He broke from thoſe that had the guard of him,
And with his mad attendant and himſelfe,
Each one with irefull paſſion, with drawne ſwords
Met vs againe, and madly bent on vs
Chac'd vs away: till raiſing of more aide
We came againe to binde them: then they fled
Into this Abbey, whether we purſu'd them,
And heere the Abbeſſe ſhuts the gates on vs,
And will not ſuffer vs to fetch him out,
Nor ſend him forth, that we may beare him hence.
Therefore moſt gracious Duke with thy command,
Let him be brought forth, and borne hence for helpe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Long ſince thy husband ſeru'd me in my wars
And I to thee ingag'd a Princes word,
When thou didſt make him Maſter of thy bed,
To do him all the grace and good I could.
Go ſome of you, knocke at the Abbey gate,
And bid the Lady Abbeſſe come to me:
I will determine this before I ſtirre.
Oh Miſtris, Miſtris, ſhift and ſaue your ſelfe,
My Maſter and his man are both broke looſe,
Beaten the Maids a-row, and bound the Doctor,
Whoſe beard they haue ſindg'd off with brands of fire,
And euer as it blaz'd, they threw on him
Great pailes of puddled myre to quench the haire;
My Mr preaches patience to him, and the while
His man with Cizers nickes him like a foole:
And ſure (vnleſſe you ſend ſome preſent helpe)
Betweene them they will kill the Coniurer.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Peace foole, thy Maſter and his man are here,
And that is falſe thou doſt report to vs.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: Miſtris, vpon my life I tel you true,
I haue not breath'd almoſt ſince I did ſee it.
He cries for you, and vowes if he can take you,
To ſcorch your face, and to disfigure you:
Harke, harke, I heare him Miſtris: flie, be gone.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Come ſtand by me, feare nothing: guard with Halberds.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: Ay me, it is my husband: witneſſe you,
That he is borne about inuiſible,
Euen now we hous'd him in the Abbey heere.
And now he's there, paſt thought of humane reaſon.

div.stage: Enter Antipholus, and E. Dromio of Epheſus.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.l: Iuſtice moſt gracious Duke, oh grant me iuſtice,
Euen for the ſeruice that long ſince I did thee,
When I be • rid thee in the warres, and tooke
Deepe ſcarres to ſaue thy life; euen for the blood
That then I loſt for thee, now grant me iuſtice.

sp.speaker: Mar. Fat.
sp.p: Vnleſſe the feare of death doth make me dore, I ſee my ſonne Antipholus and Dromio.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.l: Iuſtice (ſweet Prince) againſt yt Woman there:
She whom thou gau'ſt to me to be my wife;
That hath abuſed and diſhonored me,
Euen in the ſtrength and height of iniurie:
Beyond imagination is the wrong
That ſhe this day hath ſhameleſſe throwne on me.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Diſcouer how, and thou ſhalt finde me iuſt.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.l: This day (great Duke) ſhe ſhut the doores vpon me,
While ſhe with Harlots feaſted in my houſe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: A greeuous fault: ſay woman, didſt thou ſo?

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: No my good Lord. My ſelfe, he, and my ſiſter,
To day did dine together: ſo befall my ſoule,
As this is falſe he burthens me withall.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Nere may I looke on day, nor ſleepe on night,
But ſhe tels to your Highneſſe ſimple truth.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: O periur'd woman! They are both forſworne,
In this the Madman iuſtly chargeth them.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.l: My Liege, I am aduiſed what I ſay,
Neither diſturbed with the effect of Wine,
Nor headie-raſh prouoak'd with raging ire,
Albeit my wrongs might make one wiſer mad.
This woman lock'd me out this day from dinner;
That Goldſmith there, were he not pack'd with her,
Could witneſſe it: for he was with me then,
Who parted with me to go fetch a Chaine,
Promiſing to bring it to the Porpentine,
Where Balthaſar and I did dine together.
Our dinner done, and he not comming thither,
I went to ſeeke him. In the ſtreet I met him,
And in his companie that Gentleman.
There did this periur'd Goldſmith ſweare me downe,
That I this day of him receiu'd the Chaine,
Which God he knowes, I ſaw not. For the which,
He did arreſt me with an Officer.
I did obey, and ſent my Peſant home
For certaine Duckets: he with none return'd.
Then fairely I beſpoke the Officer
To go in perſon with me to my houſe.
By 'th 'way, we met my wife, her ſiſter, and a rabble more
Of vilde Confederates: Along with them
They brought one Pinch, a hungry leane-fac'd Villaine;
A meere Anatomie, a Mountebanke,
A thred-bare Iugler, and a Fortune-teller,
A needy-hollow-ey'd-ſharpe-looking-wretch;
A liuing dead man. This pernicious ſlaue,
Forſooth tooke on him as a Coniurer:
And gazing in mine eyes, feeling my pulſe,
And with no-face (as 'twere) out-facing me,
Cries out, I was poſſeſt. Then altogether
They fell vpon me, bound me, bore me thence,
And in a darke and dankiſh vault at home
There left me and my man, both bound together,
Till gnawing with my teeth my bonds in ſunder,
I gain'd my freedome; and immediately
Ran hether to your Grace, whom I beſeech
To giue me ample ſatisfaction
For theſe deepe ſhames, and great indignities.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: My Lord, in truth, thus far I witnes with him:
That he din'd not at home, but was lock'd out.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: But had he ſuch a Chaine of thee, or no?

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.l: He had my Lord, and when he ran in heere,
Theſe people ſaw the Chaine about his necke.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Beſides, I will be ſworne theſe eares of mine,
Heard you confeſſe you had the Chaine of him,
After you firſt forſwore it on the Mart,
And thereupon I drew my ſword on you:
And then you fled into this Abbey heere,
From whence I thinke you are come by Miracle.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.l: I neuer came within theſe Abbey wals,
Nor euer didſt thou draw thy ſword on me:
I neuer ſaw the Chaine, ſo helpe me heauen:
And this is falſe you burthen me withall.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why what an intricate impeach is this?
I thinke you all haue drunke of Circes cup:
If heere you hous'd him, heere he would haue bin.
If he were mad, he would not pleade ſo coldly:
You ſay he din'd at home, the Goldſmith heere
Denies that ſaying▪ Sirra, what ſay you?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: Sir he din'de with her there, at the Porpentine.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: He did, and from my finger ſnacht that Ring.

sp.speaker: E. Anti.
sp.p: Tis true (my Liege) this Ring I had of her.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Saw'ſt thou him enter at the Abbey heere?

sp.speaker: Curt.
sp.p: As ſure (my Liege) as I do ſee your Grace.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why this is ſtraunge: Go call the Abbeſſe hither.
I thinke you are all mated, or ſtarke mad.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Moſt mighty Duke, vouchſafe me ſpeak a word:
Haply I ſee a friend will ſaue my life,
And pay the ſum that may deliuer me.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Speake freely Siracuſian what thou wilt.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Is not your name ſir call'd Antipholus?
And is not that your bondman Dromio?

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: Within this houre I was his bondman ſir,
But he I thanke him gnaw'd in two my cords,
Now am I Dromio, and his man, vnbound.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.p: I am ſure you both of you remember me.

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.l: Our ſelues we do remember ſir by you:
For lately we were bound as you are now.
You are not Pinches patient, are you ſir?

sp.speaker: Father.
sp.p: Why looke you ſtrange on me? you know me well.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.p: I neuer ſaw you in my life till now.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: Oh! griefe hath chang'd me ſince you ſaw me laſt,
And carefull houres with times deformed hand,
Haue written ſtrange defeatures in my face:
But tell me yet, doſt thou not know my voice?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Neither.

sp.speaker: Fat.
sp.p: Dromio, nor thou?

sp.speaker: Dro.
sp.p: No truſt me ſir, nor I.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: I am ſure thou doſt?

sp.speaker: E. Dromio.
sp.p: I ſir, but I am ſure I do not, and whatſoeuer a man denies, you are now bound to beleeue him.

sp.speaker: Fath.
sp.l: Not know my voice, oh times e • tremity
Haſt thou ſo crack'd and ſplitted my poore tongue
In ſeuen ſhort yeares, that heere my onely ſonne
Knowes not my feeble key of vntun'd cares?
Though now this grained face of mine be hid
In ſap-conſuming Winters drizled ſnow,
And all the Conduits of my blood froze vp:
Yet hath my night of life ſome memorie:
My waſting lampes ſome fading glimmer left;
My dull deafe eares a little vſe to heare:
All theſe old witneſſes, I cannot erre.
Tell me, thou art my ſonne Antipholus.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I neuer ſaw my Father in my life.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: But ſeuen yeares ſince, in Siracuſa boy
Thou know'ſt we parted, but perhaps my ſonne,
Thou ſham'ſt to acknowledge me in miſerie.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The Duke, and all that know me in the City,
Can witneſſe with me that it is not ſo.
I ne're ſaw Siracuſa in my life.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: I tell thee Siracuſian, twentie yeares
Haue I bin Patron to Antipholus,
During which time, he ne're ſaw Siracuſa:
I ſee thy age and dangers make thee dote.

div.stage: Enter the Abbeſſe with Antipholus Siracuſa, and Dromio Sir.

sp.speaker: Abbeſſe.
sp.p: Moſt mightie Duke, behold a man much wrong'd.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: I ſee two husbands, or mine eyes deceiue me.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: One of theſe men is genius to the other:
And ſo of theſe, which is the naturall man,
And which the ſpirit? Who deciphers them?

sp.speaker: S. Dromio.
sp.p: I Sir am Dromio, command him away.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: I Sir am Dromio, pray let me ſtay.

sp.speaker: S. Ant.
sp.p: Egeon art thou not? or elſe his ghoſt.

sp.speaker: S. Drom.
sp.p: Oh my olde Maſter, who hath bound him heere?

sp.speaker: Abb.
sp.l: Who euer bound him, I will loſe his bonds,
And gaine a husband by his libertie:
Speake olde Egeon, if thou bee'ſt the man
That hadſt a wife once call'd Aemilia,
That bore thee at a burthen two faire ſonnes?
Oh if thou bee'ſt the ſame Egeon, ſpeake:
And ſpeake vnto the ſame Aemilia.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Why heere begins his Morning ſtorie right:
Theſe two Antipholus, theſe two ſo like,
And theſe two Dromio's, one in ſemblance:
Beſides her vrging of her wracke at ſea,
Theſe are the parents to theſe children,
Which accidentally are met together.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.l: If I dreame not, thou art Aemilia,
If thou art ſhe, tell me, where is that ſonne
That floated with thee on the fatall rafte.

sp.speaker: Abb.
sp.l: By men of Epidamium, he, and I,
And the twin Dromio, all were taken vp;
But by and by, rude Fiſhermen of Corinth
By force tooke Dromio, and my ſonne from them,
And me they left with thoſe of Epidamium.
What then became of them, I cannot tell:
I, to this fortune that you ſee mee in.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Antipholus thou cam'ſt from Corinth firſt.

sp.speaker: S. Ant.
sp.p: No ſir, not I, I came from Siracuſe.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Stay, ſtand apart, I know not which is which.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.p: I came from Corinth my moſt gracious Lord

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: And I with him.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.l: Brought to this Town by that moſt famous Warriour,
Duke Menaphon, your moſt renowned Vnckle.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: Which of you two did dine with me to day?

sp.speaker: S. Ant.
sp.p: I, gentle Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.p: And are not you my husband?

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.p: No, I ſay nay to that.

sp.speaker: S. Ant.
sp.l: And ſo do I, yet did ſhe call me ſo:
And this faire Gentlewoman her ſiſter heere
Did call me brother. What I told you then,
I hope I ſhall haue leiſure to make good,
If this be not a dreame I ſee and heare.

sp.speaker: Goldſmith.
sp.p: That is the Chaine ſir, which you had of mee.

sp.speaker: S. Ant.
sp.p: I thinke it be ſir, I denie it not.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.p: And you ſir for this Chaine arreſted me.

sp.speaker: Gold.
sp.p: I thinke I did ſir, I deny it not.

sp.speaker: Adr.
sp.l: I ſent you monie ſir to be your baile
By Dromio, but I thinke he brought it not.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: No, none by me.

sp.speaker: S. Ant.
sp.l: This purſe of Duckets I receiu'd from you,
And Dromio my man did bring them me:
I ſee we ſtill did meete each others man,
And I was tane for him, and he for me,
And thereupon theſe errors are aroſe.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.p: Theſe Duckets pawne I for my father heere.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: It ſhall not neede, thy father hath his life.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Sir I muſt haue that Diamond from you.

sp.speaker: E. Ant.
sp.p: There take it, and much thanks for my good cheere.

sp.speaker: Abb.
sp.l: Renowned Duke, vouchſafe to take the paines
To go with vs into the Abbey heere,
And heare at large diſcourſed all our fortunes,
And all that are aſſembled in this place:
That by this ſimpathized one daies error
Haue ſuffer'd wrong. Goe, keepe vs companie,
And we ſhall make full ſatisfaction.
Thirtie three yeares haue I but gone in trauaile
Of you my ſonnes, and till this preſent houre
My heauie burthen are deliuered:
The Duke my husband, and my children both,
And you the Kalenders of their Natiuity,
Go to a Goſſips feaſt, and go with mee,
After ſo long greefe ſuch Natiuitie.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: With all my heart, Ile Goſſip at this feaſt.

div.stage: Exeunt omnes. Manet the two Dromio's and two Brothers.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Maſt▪ ſhall I fetch your ſtuffe from ſhipbord?

sp.speaker: E. An.
sp.p: Dromio, what ſtuffe of mine haſt thou imbarkt

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Your goods that lay at hoſt ſir in the Centaur.

sp.speaker: S. Ant.
sp.l: He ſpeakes to me, I am your maſter Dromio.
Come go with vs, wee'l looke to that anon,
Embrace thy brother there, reioyce with him.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.l: There is a fat friend at your maſters houſe,
That kitchin'd me for you to day at dinner:
She now ſhall be my ſiſter, not my wife.

sp.speaker: E.D.
sp.l: Me thinks you are my glaſſe, & not my brother:
I ſee by you, I am a ſweet-fac'd youth,
Will you walke in to ſee their goſſipping?

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Not I ſir, you are my elder.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.p: That's a queſtion, how ſhall we trie it.

sp.speaker: S. Dro.
sp.p: Wee'l draw Cuts for the Signior, till then, lead thou firſt.

sp.speaker: E. Dro.
sp.l: Nay then thus:
We came into the world like brother and brother:
And now let's go hand in hand, not one before another.

div.head: Scena prima.
div.stage: Enter Leonato Gouernour of Meſſina, Innogen his wife, Hero his daughter, and Beatrice his Neece, with a meſſenger.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: I Learne in this Letter, that Don Peter of Arragon, comes this night to Meſſina.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: He is very neere by this: he was not three Leagues off when I left him.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: How many Gentlemen haue you loſt in this action?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: But few of any ſort, and none of name.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: A victorie is twice it ſelfe, when the atchieuer brings home full numbers: I finde heere, that Don Peter hath beſtowed much honor on a yong Florentine, called Claudio.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: Much deſeru'd on his part, and equally remembred by Don Pedro, he hath borne himſelfe beyond the promiſe of his age, doing in the figure of a Lambe, the feats of a Lion, he hath indeede better bettred expectation, then you muſt expect of me to tell you how.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: He hath an Vnckle heere in Meſſina, wil be very much glad of it.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: I haue alreadie deliuered him letters, and there appeares much ioy in him, euen ſo much, that ioy could not ſhew it ſelfe modeſt enough, without a badg of bitterneſſe.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: Did he breake out into teares?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: In great meaſure.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: A kinde ouerflow of kindneſſe, there are no faces truer, then thoſe that are ſo waſh'd, how much better is it to weepe at ioy, then to ioy at weeping?

sp.speaker: Bea.
sp.p:
I pray you, is Signior Mountant •
return'd from the warres, or no?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: I know none of that name, Lady, there was none ſuch in the armie of any ſort.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: What is he that you aske for Neece?

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: My couſin meanes Signior Benedick of Padua

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: O he's return'd, and as pleaſant as euer he was.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: He ſet vp his bils here in Meſſina, & challeng'd Cupid at the Flight: and my Vnckles foole reading the Challenge, ſubſcrib'd for Cupid, and challeng'd him at the Burbolt. I pray you, how many hath hee kil'd and eaten in theſe warres? But how many hath he kil'd? for indeed, I promis'd to eate all of his killing.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: 'Faith Neece, you taxe Signior Benedicke too much, but hee'l be meet with you, I doubt it not.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: He hath done good ſeruice Lady in theſe wars.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: You had muſty victuall, and he hath holpe to ease it: he's a very valiant Trencher-man, hee hath an excellent ſtomacke.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: And a good ſouldier too Lady.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: And a good ſouldier to a Lady. But what is he to a Lord?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: A Lord to a Lord, a man to a man, ſtuft with all honourable vertues.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: It is ſo indeed, he is no leſſe then a ſtuft man: but for the ſtuffing well, we are all mortall.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: You muſt not (ſir) miſtake my Neece, there is a kind of merry war betwixt Signior Benedick, & her: they neuer meet, but there's a skirmiſh of wit between them.

sp.speaker: Bea.
sp.p: Alas, he gets nothing by that. In our laſt conflict, foure of his fiue wits went halting off, and now is the whole man gouern'd with one: ſo that if hee haue wit enough to keepe himſelfe warme, let him beare it for a difference betweene himſelfe and his horſe: For it is all the wealth that he hath left, to be knowne a reaſonable creature. Who is his companion now? He hath euery month a new ſworne brother.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: I'st poſſible?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Very eaſily poſſible: he weares his faith but as the faſhion of his hat, it euer changes with ye next block.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: I ſee (Lady) the Gentleman is not in your bookes.

sp.speaker: Bea.
sp.p: No, and he were, I would burne my ſtudy. But I pray you, who is his companion? Is there no young ſquarer now, that will make a voyage with him to the diuell?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: He is moſt in the company of the right noble Claudio.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: O Lord, he will hang vpon him like a diſeaſe: he is ſooner caught then the peſtilence, and the taker runs preſently mad. God helpe the noble Claudio, if hee haue caught the Benedict, it will coſt him a thouſand pound ere he be cur'd.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: I will hold friends with you Lady.

sp.speaker: Bea.
sp.p: Do good friend.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: You'l ne're run mad Neece.

sp.speaker: Bea.
sp.p: No, not till a hot Ianuary.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: Don Pedro is approach'd.

div.stage: Enter don Pedro, Claudio, Benedicke, Balthaſar, and Iohn the baſtard.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Good Signior Leonato, you are come to meet your trouble: the faſhion of the world is to auoid coſt, and you encounter it.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Neuer came trouble to my houſe in the likenes of your Grace: for trouble being gone, comfort ſhould remaine: but when you depart from me, ſorrow abides, and happineſſe takes his leaue.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: You embrace your charge too willingly: I thinke this is your daughter.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: Her mother hath many times told me ſo.

sp.speaker: Bened.
sp.p: Were you in doubt that you askt her?

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: Signior Benedicke, no, for then were you a childe.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: You haue it full Benedicke, we may gheſſe by this, what you are, being a man, truely the Lady fathers her ſelfe: be happie Lady, for you are like an honorable father.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: If Signior Leonato be her father, ſhe would not haue his head on her ſhoulders for al Meſſina, as like him as ſhe is.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: I wonder that you will ſtill be talking, ſignior Benedicke▪ no body markes you.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: What my deere Ladie Diſdaine! are you yet liuing?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Is it poſſible Diſdaine ſhould die, while ſhee hath ſuch meete foode to feede it, as Signior Benedicke? Curteſie it ſelfe muſt conuert to Diſdaine, if you come in her preſence.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Then is curteſie a turne-coate, but it is certaine I am loued of all Ladies, onely you excepted: and I would I could finde in my heart that I had not a hard heart, for truely I loue none.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: A deere happineſſe to women, they would elſe haue beene troubled with a pernitious Su • er, I thanke God and my cold blood, I am of your humour for that, I had rather heare my Dog barke at a Crow, than a man ſweare he loues me.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: God keepe your Ladiſhip ſtill in that minde, ſo ſome Gentleman or other ſhall ſcape a predeſtinate ſcratcht face.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Scratching could not make it worſe, and 'twere ſuch a face as yours were.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Well, you are a rare Parrat teacher.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: A bird of my tongue, is better than a beaſt of your.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: I would my horſe had the ſpeed of your tongue, and ſo good a continuer, but keepe your way a Gods name, I haue done.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: You alwaies end with a Iades tricke, I know you of old.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: This is the ſumme of all: Leonato, ſignior Claudio, and ſignior Benedicke; my deere friend Leonato, hath inuited you all, I tell him we ſhall ſtay here, at the leaſt a moneth, and he heartily praies ſome occaſion may detaine vs longer: I dare ſweare hee is no hypocrite, but praies from his heart.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: If you ſweare, my Lord, you ſhall not be forſworne, let mee bid you welcome, my Lord, being reconciled to the Prince your brother: I owe you all duetie.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: I thanke you, I am not of many words, but I thanke you.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Pleaſe it your grace leade on?

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Your hand Leonato, we will goe together.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Benedicke, didſt thou note the daughter of ſignior Leonato?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: I noted her not, but I lookt on her.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Is ſhe not a modeſt yong Ladie?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Doe you queſtion me as an honeſt man ſhould doe, for my ſimple true iudgement? or would you haue me ſpeake after my cuſtome, as being a profeſſed tyrant to their ſexe?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: No, I pray thee ſpeake in ſober iudgement.

sp.speaker: Bene:
sp.p: Why yfaith me thinks ſhee's too low for a hie praiſe, too browne for a faire praiſe, and too little for a great praiſe, onely this commendation I can affoord her, that were ſhee other then ſhe is, ſhe were vnhandſome, and being no other, but as ſhe is, I doe not like her.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Thou think'ſt I am in ſport, I pray thee tell me truely how thou lik'ſt her.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Would you buie her, that you enquier after her?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Can the world buie ſuch a iewell?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Yea, and a caſe to put it into, but ſpeake you this with a ſad brow? Or doe you play the flowting iacke, to tell vs Cupid is a good Hare-finder, and Vulcan a rare Carpenter: Come, in what key ſhall a man take you to goe in the ſong?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: In mine eie, ſhe is the ſweeteſt Ladie that euer I lookt on.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: I can ſee yet without ſpectacles, and I ſee no ſuch matter: there's her coſin, and ſhe were not poſſeſt with a furie, exceedes her as much in beautie, as the firſt of Maie doth the laſt of December: but I hope you haue no intent to turne husband, haue you?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: I would ſcarce truſt my ſelfe, though I had ſworne the contrarie, if Hero would be my wife.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Iſt come to this? in faith hath not the world one man but he will weare his cap with ſuſpition? ſhall I neuer ſee a batcheller of three ſcore againe? goe to yfaith, and thou wilt needes thruſt thy necke into a yoke, weare the print of it, and ſigh away ſundaies: looke, don Pedro is returned to ſeeke you.

div.stage: Enter don Pedro, Iohn the baſtard.

sp.speaker: Pedr.
sp.p: What ſecret hath held you here, that you followed not to Leonatoes?

sp.speaker: Bened.
sp.p: I would your Grace would conſtraine mee to tell.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: I charge thee on thy allegeance.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: You heare, Count Claudio, I can be ſecret as a dumbe man, I would haue you thinke ſo (but on my allegiance, marke you this, on my allegiance) hee is in loue, With who? now that is your Graces part: marke how ſhort his anſwere is, with Hero, Leonatoes ſhort daughter.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: If this were ſo, ſo were it vttred.

sp.speaker: Bened.
sp.p: Like the old tale, my Lord, it is not ſo, nor 'twas not ſo: but indeede, God forbid it ſhould be ſo.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: If my paſſion change not ſhortly, God forbid it ſhould be otherwiſe.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Amen, if you loue her, for the Ladie is verie well worthie.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: You ſpeake this to fetch me in, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Pedr.
sp.p: By my troth I ſpeake my thought.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: And in faith, my Lord, I ſpoke mine.

sp.speaker: Bened.
sp.p: And by my two faiths and troths, my Lord, I ſpeake mine.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: That I loue her, I feele.

sp.speaker: Pedr.
sp.p: That ſhe is worthie, I know.

sp.speaker: Bened.
sp.p: That I neither feele how ſhee ſhould be loued, nor know how ſhee ſhould be worthie, is the opinion that fire cannot melt out of me, I will die in it at the ſtake.

sp.speaker: Pedr.
sp.p: Thou waſt euer an obſtinate heretique in the deſpight of Beautie.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: And neuer could maintaine his part, but in the force of his will.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: That a woman conceiued me, I thanke her: that ſhe brought mee vp, I likewiſe giue her moſt humble thankes: but that I will haue a • echare winded in my forehead, or hang my bugle in an inuiſible baldricke, all women ſhall pardon me: becauſe I will not do them the wrong to miſtruſt any, I will doe my ſelfe the right to truſt none: and the fine is, (for the which I may goe the finer) I will liue a Batchellor.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: I ſhall ſee thee ere I die, looke pale with loue.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: With anger, with ſickneſſe, or with hunger, my Lord, not with loue: proue that euer I looſe more blood with loue, then I will get againe with drinking, picke out mine eyes with a Ballet-makers penne, and hang me vp at the doore of a brothel-houſe for the ſigne of blinde Cupid.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Well, if euer thou dooſt fall from this faith, thou wilt proue a notable argument.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: If I do, hang me in a bottle like a Cat, & ſhoot at me, and he that hit's me, let him be clapt on the ſhoulder, and cal'd Adam.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Well, as time ſhall trie: In time the ſauage Bull doth beare the yoake.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: The ſauage bull may, but if euer the ſenſible Benedicke beare it, plucke off the bulles hornes, and ſet them in my forehead, and let me be vildely painted, and in ſuch great Letters as they write, heere is good horſe to hire: let them ſignifie vnder my ſigne, here you may ſee Benedicke the married man.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: If this ſhould euer happen, thou wouldſt bee horne mad.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Nay, if Cupid haue not ſpent all his Quiuer in Venice, thou wilt quake for this ſhortly.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: I looke for an earthquake too then.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Well, you will temporize with the houres, in the meane time, good Signior Benedicke, repaire to Leonatoes, commend me to him, and tell him I will not faile him at ſupper, for indeede he hath made great preparation.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: I haue almoſt matter enough in me for ſuch an Embaſſage, and ſo I commit you.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: To the tuition of God. From my houſe, if I had it.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: The ſixt of Iuly. Your louing friend, Benedick.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Nay mocke not, mocke not; the body of your diſcourſe is ſometime guarded with fragments, and the guardes are but ſlightly baſted on neither, ere you flout old ends any further, examine your conſcience, and ſo I leaue you.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: My Liege, your Highneſſe now may doe mee good.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.l: My loue is thine to teach, teach it but how,
And thou ſhalt ſee how apt it is to learne
Any hard Leſſon that may do thee good.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Hath Leonato any ſonne my Lord?

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.l: No childe but Hero, ſhe's his onely heire.
Doſt thou affect her Claudio?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: O my Lord,
When you went onward on this ended action,
I look'd vpon her with a ſouldiers eie,
That lik'd, but had a rougher taske in hand,
Than to driue liking to the name of loue:
But now I am return'd, and that warre-thoughts
Haue left their places vacant: in their roomes,
Come thronging ſoft and delicate deſires,
All prompting mee how faire yong Hero is,
Saying I lik'd her ere I went to warres.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.l: Thou wilt be like a louer preſently,
And tire the hearer with a booke of words:
If thou doſt loue faire Hero, cheriſh it,
And I will breake with her: waſt not to this end,
That thou beganſt to twiſt ſo fine a ſtory?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: How ſweetly doe you miniſter to loue,
That know loues griefe by his complexion!
But leſt my liking might too ſodaine ſeeme,
I would haue ſalu'd it with a longer treatiſe.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: What need ye bridge much broder then the flood?
The faireſt graunt is the neceſſitie:
Looke what will ſerue, is fit: 'tis once, thou loueſt,
And I will fit thee with the remedie,
I know we ſhall haue reuelling to night,
I will aſſume thy part in ſome diſguiſe,
And tell faire Hero I am Claudio,
And in her boſome Ile vnclaſpe my heart,
And take her hearing priſoner with the force
And ſtrong incounter of my amorous tale:
Then after, to her father will I breake,
And the concluſion is, ſhee ſhall be thine,
In practiſe let vs put it preſently.

div.stage: Enter Leonato and an old man, brother to Leonato.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: How now brother, where is my coſen your ſon: hath he prouided this muſicke?

sp.speaker: Old.
sp.p: He is very buſie about it, but brother, I can tell you newes that you yet dreamt not of.

sp.speaker: Lo.
sp.p: Are they good?

sp.speaker: Old.
sp.p: As the euents ſtamps them, but they haue • good couer: they▪ ſhew well outward, the Prince and Count Claudio walking in a thick pleached alley in my orchard, were thus ouer-heard by a man of mine: the Prince diſcouered to Claudio that hee loued my niece your daughter, and meant to acknowledge it this night in a dance, and if hee found her accordant, hee meant to take the preſent time by the top, and inſtantly breake with you of it.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: Hath the fellow any wit that told you this?

sp.speaker: Old.
sp.p: A good ſharpe fellow, I will ſend for him, and queſtion him your ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: No, no; wee will hold it as a dreame, till it appeare it ſelfe: but I will acquaint my daughter withall, that ſhe may be the better prepared for an anſwer, if peraduenture this bee true: goe you and tell her of it: cooſins, you know what you haue to doe, O I crie you mercie friend, goe you with mee and I will vſe your skill, good coſin haue a care this buſie time.

div.stage: Enter Sir Iohn the Baſtard, and Conrade his companion.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: What the good yeere my Lord, why are you thus out of meaſure ſad?

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.p: There is no meaſure in the occaſion that breeds, therefore the ſadneſſe is without limit.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: You ſhould heare reaſon.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: And when I haue heard it, what bleſſing bringeth it?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: If not a preſent remedy, yet a patient ſufferance.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.p: I wonder that thou (being as thou ſaiſt thou art, borne vnder Saturne) goeſt about to apply a morall medicine, to a mortifying miſchiefe: I cannot hide what I am: I muſt bee ſad when I haue cauſe, and ſmile at no mans ieſts, eat when I haue ſtomacke, and wait for no mans leiſure: ſleepe when I am drowſie, and tend on no mans buſineſſe, laugh when I am merry, and claw no man in his humor.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p:
Yea, but you muſt not make the ful ſhow of this, till you may doe it without controllment, you haue of
late ſtood out againſt your brother, and hee hath tane you newly into his grace, where it is impoſſible you ſhould take root, but by the faire weather that you make your ſelfe, it is needful that you frame the ſeaſon for your owne harueſt.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: I had rather be a canker in a hedge, then a roſe in his grace, and it better fits my bloud to be diſdain'd of all, then to faſhion a carriage to rob loue from any: in this (though I cannot be ſaid to be a flattering honeſt man) it muſt not be denied but I am a plaine dealing villaine, I am truſted with a muſſell, and enfranchiſde with a clog, therefore I haue decreed, not to ſing in my cage: if I had my mouth, I would bite: if I had my liberty, I would do my liking: in the meane time, let me be that I am, and ſeeke not to alter me.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: Can you make no vſe of your diſcontent?

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.l: I will make all vſe of it, for I vſe it onely.
Who comes here? what newes Borachio?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: I came yonder from a great ſupper, the Prince your brother is royally entertained by Leonato, and I can giue you intelligence of an intended marriage.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: Will it ſerue for any Modell to build miſchiefe on? What is hee for a foole that betrothes himſelfe to vnquietneſſe?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Mary it is your brothers right hand.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: Who, the moſt exquiſite Claudio?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Euen he.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: A proper ſquier, and who, and who, which way lookes he?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Mary on Hero, the daughter and Heire of Leonato.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: A very forward March-chicke, how came you to this?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Being entertain'd for a perfumer, as I was ſmoaking a muſty roome, comes me the Prince and Claudio, hand in hand in ſad conference: I whipt behind the Arras, and there heard it agreed vpon, that the Prince ſhould wooe Hero for himſelfe, and hauing obtain'd her, giue her to Count Claudio.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: Come, come, let vs thither, this may proue food to my diſpleaſure, that young ſtart-vp hath all the glorie of my ouerthrow: if I can croſſe him any way, I bleſſe my ſelfe euery way, you are both ſure, and will aſſiſt mee?

sp.speaker: Conr.
sp.p: To the death my Lord.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: Let vs to the great ſupper, their cheere is the greater that I am ſubdued, would the Cooke were of my minde: ſhall we goe proue whats to be done?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Wee'll wait vpon your Lordſhip.

div.head: Actus Secundus.
div.stage: Enter Leonato, his brother, his wife, Hero his daughter, and Beatrice his neece, and a kinſman.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: Was not Count Iohn here at ſupper?

sp.speaker: Brother.
sp.p: I ſaw him not.

sp.speaker: Beatrice.
sp.p: How tartly that Gentleman lookes, I neuer can ſee him, but I am heart-burn'd an howre after.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: He is of a very melancholy diſpoſition.

sp.speaker: Beatrice.
sp.p: Hee were an excellent man that were made iuſt in the mid-way betweene him and Benedicke, the one is too like an image and ſaies nothing, and the other too like my Ladies eldeſt ſonne, euermore tatling.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Then halfe ſignior Benedicks tongue in Count Iohns mouth, and halfe Count Iohns melancholy in Signior Benedicks face.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: With a good legge, and a good foot vnckle, and money enough in his purſe, ſuch a man would winne any woman in the world, if he could get her good will.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: By my troth Neece, thou wilt neuer get thee a husband, if thou be ſo ſhrewd of thy tongue.

sp.speaker: Brother.
sp.p: Infaith ſhee's too curſt.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Too curſt is more then curſt, I ſhall leſſen Gods ſending that way: for it is ſaid, God ſends a curſt Cow ſhort hornes, but to a Cow too curſt he ſends none.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: So, by being too curſt, God will ſend you no hornes.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Iuſt, if he ſend me no husband, for the which bleſſing, I am at him vpon my knees euery morning and euening: Lord, I could not endure a husband with a beard on his face, I had rather lie in the woollen.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: You may light vpon a husband that hath no beard.

sp.speaker: Batrice.
sp.p: What ſhould I doe with him? dreſſe him in my apparell, and make him my waiting gentlewoman? he that hath a beard, is more then a youth: and he that hath no beard, is leſſe then a man: and hee that is more then a youth, is not for mee: and he that is leſſe then a man, I am not for him: therefore I will euen take ſixepence in earneſt of the Berrord, and leade his Apes into hell.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Well then, goe you into hell.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: No, but to the gate, and there will the Deuill meete mee like an old Cuckold with hornes on his head, and ſay, get you to heauen Beatrice, get you to heauen, heere's no place for you maids, ſo deliuer I vp my Apes, and away to S. Peter: for the heauens, hee ſhewes mee where the Batchellers ſit, and there liue wee as merry as the day is long.

sp.speaker: Brother.
sp.p: Well neece, I truſt you will be rul'd by your father.

sp.speaker: Beatrice.
sp.p: Yes faith, it is my coſens dutie to make curtſie, and ſay, as it pleaſe you: but yet for all that coſin, let him be a handſome fellow, or elſe make an other curſie, and ſay, father, as it pleaſe me.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: Well neece, I hope to ſee you one day ſitted with a husband.

sp.speaker: Beatrice.
sp.p: Not till God make men of ſome other mettall then earth, would it not grieue a woman to be ouer-maſtred with a peece of valiant duſt? to make account of her life to a clod of waiward marle? no vnckle, ile none: Adams ſonnes are my brethren, and truly I hold it a ſinne to match in my kinred.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Daughter, remember what I told you, if the Prince doe ſolicit you in that kinde, you know your anſwere.

sp.speaker: Beatrice.
sp.p: The fault will be in the muſicke coſin, if you be not woed in good time: if the Prince bee too important, tell him there is meaſure in euery thing, & ſo dance out the anſwere, for heare me Hero, wooing, wedding, & repenting, is as a Scotch ijgge, a meaſure, and a cinque-pace: the firſt ſuite is hot and haſty like a Scotch ijgge (and full as fantaſticall) the wedding manerly modeſt, (as a meaſure) full of ſtate & aunchentry, and then comes repentance, and with his bad legs falls into the cinque-pace faſter and faſter, till he ſinkes into his graue.

sp.speaker: Leonata.
sp.p: Coſin you apprehend paſſing ſhrewdly.

sp.speaker: Beatrice.
sp.p: I haue a good eye vnckle, I can ſee a Church by daylight.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: The reuellers are entring brother, make good roome.

div.stage: Enter Prince, Pedro, Claudio, and Benedicke, and Balthaſar, or dumbe Iohn, Maskers with a drum.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Lady, will you walke about with your friend?

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: So you walke ſoftly, and looke ſweetly, and ſay nothing, I am yours for the walke, and eſpecially when I walke away.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: With me in your company.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: I may ſay ſo when I pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: And when pleaſe you to ſay ſo?

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: When I like your fauour, for God defend the Lute ſhould be like the caſe.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: My viſor is Philemons roofe, within the houſe is Loue.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: Why then your viſor ſhould be thatcht.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Speake low if you ſpeake Loue.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Well, I would you did like me.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: So would not I for your owne ſake, for I haue manie ill qualities.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Which is one?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I ſay my prayers alowd.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: I loue you the better, the hearers may cry Amen.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: God match me with a good dauncer.

sp.speaker: Balt.
sp.p: Amen.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: And God keepe him out of my ſight when the daunce is done: anſwer Clarke.

sp.speaker: Balt.
sp.p: No more words the Clarke is anſwered.

sp.speaker: Vrſula.
sp.p: I know you well enough, you are Signior Anthonio.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: At a word, I am not.

sp.speaker: Vrſula.
sp.p: I know you by the wagling of your head.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: To tell you true, I counterfet him.

sp.speaker: Vrſu.
sp.p: You could neuer doe him ſo ill well, vnleſſe you were the very man: here's his dry hand vp & down, you are he, you are he.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: At a word I am not.

sp.speaker: Ʋrſula.
sp.p: Come, come, doe you thinke I doe not know you by your excellent wit? can vertue hide it ſelfe? goe to, mumme, you are he, graces will appeare, and there's an end.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Will you not tell me who told you ſo?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: No, you ſhall pardon me.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Nor will you not tell me who you are?

sp.speaker: Bened.
sp.p: Not now.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: That I was diſdainfull, and that I had my good wit out of the hundred merry tales: well, this was Signior Benedicke that ſaid ſo.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: What's he?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: I am ſure you know him well enough.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Not I, beleeue me.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Did he neuer make you laugh?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: I pray you what is he?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Why he is the Princes ieaſter, a very dull foole, onely his gift is, in deuiſing impoſsible ſlanders, none but Libertines delight in him, and the commendation is not in his witte, but in his villanie, for hee both pleaſeth men and angers them, and then they laugh at him, and beat him: I am ſure he is in the Fleet, I would he had boorded me.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: When I know the Gentleman, Ile tell him what you ſay.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Do, do, hee'l but breake a compariſon or two on me, which peraduenture (not markt, or not laugh'd at) ſtrikes him into melancholly, and then there's a Partridge wing ſaued, for the foole will eate no ſupper that night. We muſt follow the Leaders.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: In euery good thing.

sp.speaker: Bea.
sp.p: Nay, if they leade to any ill, I will leaue them at the next turning.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: Sure my brother is amorous on Hero, and hath withdrawne her father to breake with him about it: the Ladies follow her, and but one viſor remaines.

sp.speaker: Borachio.
sp.p: And that is Claudio, I know him by his bearing.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: Are not you ſignior Benedicke?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: You know me well, I am hee.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: Signior, you are verie neere my Brother in his loue, he is enamor'd on Hero, I pray you diſſwade him from her, ſhe is no equall for his birth: you may do the part of an honeſt man in it.

sp.speaker: Claudio.
sp.p: How know you he loues her?

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: I heard him ſweare his affection,

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: So did I too, and he ſwore he would marrie her to night.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: Come, let vs to the banquet.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Thus anſwere I in name of Benedicke,
But heare theſe ill newes with the eares of Claudio:
'Tis certaine ſo, the Prince woes for himſelfe:
Friendſhip is conſtant in all other things,
Saue in the Office and affaires of loue:
Therefore all hearts in loue vſe their owne tongues.
Let euerie eye negotiate for it ſelfe,
And truſt no Agent: for beautie is a witch,
Againſt whoſe charmes, faith melteth into blood:
This is an accident of hourely proofe,
Which I miſtruſted not. Farewell therefore Hero.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Count Claudio.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Yea, the ſame.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Come, will you go with me?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Whither?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Euen to the next Willow, about your own buſineſſe, Count. What faſhion will you weare the Garland off? About your necke, like an Vſurers chaine? Or vnder your arme, like a Lieutenants ſcarfe? You muſt weare it one way, for the Prince hath got your Hero.

sp.speaker: Clau:
sp.p: I wiſh him ioy of her.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Why that's ſpoken like an honeſt Drouier, ſo they ſel Bullockes: but did you thinke the Prince wold haue ſerued you thus?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: I pray you leaue me.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Ho now you ſtrike like the blindman, 'twas the boy that ſtole your meate, and you'l beat the poſt.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: If it will not be, Ile leaue you.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Alas poore hurt fowle, now will he creepe into ſedges: But that my Ladie Beatrice ſhould know me, & not know me: the Princes foole! Hah? It may be I goe vnder that title, becauſe I am merrie: yea but ſo I am apt to do my ſelfe wrong: I am not ſo reputed, it is the baſe (though bitter) diſpoſition of Beatrice, that putt's the world into her perſon, and ſo giues me out: well, Ile be reuenged as I may.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Now Signior, where's the Count, did you ſee him?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Troth my Lord, I haue played the part of Lady Fame, I found him heere as melancholy as a Lodge in a Warren, I told him, and I thinke, told him true, that your grace had got the will of this young Lady, and I offered him my company to a willow tree, either to make him a garland, as being forſaken, or to binde him a rod, as being worthy to be whipt.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: To be whipt, what's his fault?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: The ſlat tranſgreſſion of a Schoole-boy, who being ouer-ioyed with finding a birds neſt, ſhewes it his companion, and he ſteales it.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Wilt thou make a truſt, a tranſgreſſion? the tranſgreſſion is in the ſtealer.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Yet it had not beene amiſſe the rod had beene made, and the garland too, for the garland he might haue worne himſelfe, and the rod hee might haue beſtowed on you, who (as I take it) haue ſtolne his birds neſt.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: I will but teach them to ſing, and reſtore them to the owner.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: If their ſinging anſwer your ſaying▪ by my faith you ſay honeſtly.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: The Lady Beatrice hath a quarrell to you, the Gentleman that daunſt with her, told her ſhee is much wrong'd by you.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: O ſhe miſuſde me paſt the indurance of a block: an oake but with one greene leafe on it, would haue anſwered her: my very viſor began to aſſume life, and ſcold with her: ſhee told mee, not thinking I had beene my ſelfe, that I was the Princes Ieſter, and that I was duller then a great thaw, hu • ling ieſt vpon ieſt, with ſuch impoſſible conueiance vpon me, that I ſtood like a man at a marke, with a whole army ſhooting at me: ſhee ſpeakes poynyards, and euery word ſtabbes: if her breath were as terrible as terminations, there were no liuing neere her, ſhe would infect to the north ſtarre: I would not marry her, though ſhe were indowed with all that Adam had left him before he tranſgreſt, ſhe would haue made Hercules haue turnd ſpit, yea, and haue cleft his club to make the fire too: come, talke not of her, you ſhall finde her the infernall Ate in good apparell. I would to God ſome ſcholler would coniure her, for certainely while ſhe is heere, a man may liue as quiet in hell, as in a ſanctuary, and people ſinne vpon purpoſe, becauſe they would goe thither, ſo indeed all diſquiet, horror, and perturbation followes her.

div.stage: Enter Claudio and Beatrice, Leonato, Hero.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Looke heere ſhe comes.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Will your Grace command mee any ſeruice to the worlds end? I will goe on the ſlighteſt arrand now to the Antypodes that you can deuiſe to ſend me on: I will fetch you a tooth-picker now from the furtheſt inch of Aſia: bring you the length of Preſter Iohns foot: fetch you a hayre off the great Chams beard: doe you any embaſſage to the Pigmies, rather then hould three words conference, with this Harpy: you haue no employment for me?

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: None, but to deſire your good company.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: O God ſir, heeres a diſh I loue not, I cannot indure this Lady tongue.

sp.speaker: Pedr.
sp.p: Come Lady, come, you haue loſt the heart of Signior Benedicke.

sp.speaker: Beatr.
sp.p: Indeed my Lord, hee lent it me a while, and I gaue him vſe for it, a double heart for a ſingle one, marry once before he wonne it of mee, with falſe dice, therefore your Grace may well ſay I haue loſt it.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: You haue put him downe Lady, you haue put him downe.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: So I would not he ſhould do me, my Lord, leſt I ſhould prooue the mother of fooles: I haue brought Count Claudio, whom you ſent me to ſeeke.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Why how now Count, wherfore are you ſad?

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: Not ſad my Lord.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: How then? ſicke?

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: Neither, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: The Count is neither ſad, nor ſicke, nor merry, nor well: but ciuill Count, ciuill as an Orange, and ſomething of a iealous complexion.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Ifaith Lady, I thinke your blazon to be true, though Ile be ſworne, if hee be ſo, his conceit is falſe: heere Claudio, I haue wooed in thy name, and faire Hero is won, I haue broke with her father, and his good will obtained, name the day of marriage, and God giue thee ioy.

sp.speaker: Leona.
sp.p: Count, take of me my daughter, and with her my fortunes: his grace hath made the match, & all grace ſay, Amen to it.

sp.speaker: Beatr.
sp.p: Speake Count, tis your Qu.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: Silence is the perfecteſt Herault of ioy, I were but little happy if I could ſay, how much? Lady, as you are mine, I am yours, I giue away my ſelfe for you, and doat vpon the exchange.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Speake coſin, or (if you cannot) ſtop his mouth with a kiſſe, and let not him ſpeake neither.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Infaith Lady you haue a merry heart.

sp.speaker: Beatr.
sp.p: Yea my Lord I thanke it, poore foole it keepes on the windy ſide of Care, my cooſin tells him in his eare that he is in my heart.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: And ſo ſhe doth cooſin.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Good Lord for alliance: thus goes euery one to the world but I, and I am ſun-burn'd, I may ſit in a corner and cry, heigh ho for a husband.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Lady Beatrice, I will get you one.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: I would rather haue one of your fathers getting: hath your Grace ne're a brother like you? your father got excellent husbands, if a maid could come by them.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: Will you haue me? Lady.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: No, my Lord, vnleſſe I might haue another for working-daies, your Grace is too coſtly to weare euerie day: but I beſeech your Grace pardon mee, I was borne to ſpeake all mirth, and no matter.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: Your ſilence moſt offends me, and to be merry, beſt becomes you, for out of queſtion, you were born in a merry howre.

sp.speaker: Beatr.
sp.p: No ſure my Lord, my Mother cried, but then there was a ſtarre daunſt, and vnder that was I borne: coſins God giue you ioy.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: Neece, will you looke to thoſe rhings I told you of?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: I cry you mercy Vncle, by your Graces pardon.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: By my troth a pleaſant ſpirited Lady.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: There's little of the melancholy element in her my Lord, ſhe is neuer ſad, but when ſhe ſleepes, and not euer ſad then: for I haue heard my daughter ſay, ſhe hath often dreamt of vnhappineſſe, and wakt her ſelfe with laughing.

sp.speaker: Pedro.
sp.p: Shee cannot indure to heare tell of a husband.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: O, by no meanes, ſhe mocks all her wooers out of ſuite.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: She were an excellent wife for Benedick.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p:
O Lord, my Lord, if they were but a weeke
married, they would talke themſelues madde.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: Counte Claudio, when meane you to goe to Church?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: To morrow my Lord, Time goes on crutches, till Loue haue all his rites.

sp.speaker: Leonata.
sp.p: Not till monday, my deare ſonne, which is hence a iuſt ſeuen night, and a time too briefe too, to haue all things anſwer minde.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: Come, you ſhake the head at ſo long a breathing, but I warrant thee Claudio, the time ſhall not goe dully by vs, I will in the interim, vndertake one of Hercules labors, which is, to bring Signior Benedicke and the Lady Beatrice into a mountaine of affection, th' one with th' other, I would faine haue it a match, and I doubt not but to faſhion it, if you three will but miniſter ſuch aſſiſtance as I ſhall giue you direction.

sp.speaker: Leonata.
sp.p: My Lord, I am for you, though it coſt mee ten nights watchings.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: And I my Lord.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: And you to gentle Hero?

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: I will doe any modeſt office, my Lord, to helpe my coſin to a good husband.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: And Benedick is not the vnhopefulleſt husband that I know: thus farre can I praiſe him, hee is of a noble ſtraine, of approued valour, and confirm'd honeſty, I will teach you how to humour your coſin, that ſhee ſhall fall in loue with Benedicke, and I, with your two helpes, will ſo practiſe on Benedicke, that in deſpight of his quicke wit, and his queaſie ſtomacke, hee ſhall fall in loue with Beatrice: if wee can doe this, Cupid is no longer an Archer, his glory ſhall be ours, for wee are the onely loue-gods, goe in with me, and I will tell you my drift.

sp.speaker: Ioh.
sp.p: It is ſo, the Count Claudio ſhal marry the daughter of Leonato.

sp.speaker: Bora.
sp.p: Yea my Lord, but I can croſſe it.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: Any barre, any croſſe, any impediment, will be medicinable to me, I am ſicke in diſpleaſure to him, and whatſoeuer comes athwart his affection, ranges euenly with mine, how canſt thou croſſe this marriage?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Not honeſtly my Lord, but ſo couertly, that no diſhoneſty ſhall appeare in me.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: Shew me breefely how.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: I thinke I told your Lordſhip a yeere ſince, how much I am in the fauour of Margaret, the waiting gentlewoman to Hero.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: I remember.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: I can at any vnſeaſonable inſtant of the night, appoint her to look out at her Ladies chamber window.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: What life is in that, to be the death of this marriage?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: The poyſon of that lies in you to temper, goe you to the Prince your brother, ſpare not to tell him, that hee hath wronged his Honor in marrying the renowned Claudio, whoſe eſtimation do you mightily hold vp, to a contaminated ſtale, ſuch a one as Hero.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: What proofe ſhall I make of that?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Proofe enough, to miſuſe the Prince, to vexe Claudio, to vndoe Hero, and kill Leonato, looke you for any other iſſue?

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: Onely to deſpight them, I will endeauour any thing.

sp.speaker: Bor.
