sp.p: Goe then, finde me a meete howre, to draw on Pedro and the Count Claudio alone, tell them that you know that Hero loues me, intend a kinde of zeale both to the Prince and Claudio (as in a loue of your brothers honor who hath made this match) and his friends reputation, who is thus like to be coſen'd with the ſemblance of a maid, that you haue diſcouer'd thus: they will ſcarcely beleeue this without triall: offer them inſtances which ſhall beare no leſſe likelihood, than to ſee mee at her chamber window, heare me call Margaret, Hero; heare Margaret terme me Claudio, and bring them to ſee this the very night before the intended wedding, for in the meane time, I will ſo faſhion the matter, that Hero ſhall be abſent, and there ſhall appeare ſuch ſeeming truths of Heroes diſloyaltie, that iealouſie ſhall be cal'd aſſurance, and all the preparation ouerthrowne.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: Grow this to what aduerſe iſſue it can, I will put it in practiſe: be cunning in the working this, and thy fee is a thouſand ducates.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Be thou conſtant in the accuſation, and my cunning ſhall not ſhame me.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.p: I will preſentlie goe learne their day of marriage.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Signior.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: In my chamber window lies a booke, bring it hither to me in the orchard.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I am heere already ſir.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: I know that, but I would haue thee hence, and heere againe. I doe much wonder, that one man ſeeing how much another man is a foole, when he dedicates his behauiours to loue, will after hee hath laught at ſuch ſhallow follies in others, become the argument of his owne ſcorne, by falling in loue, & ſuch a man is Claudio, I haue known when there was no muſicke with him but the drum and the fife, and now had hee rather heare the taber and the pipe: I haue knowne when he would haue walkt ten mile afoot, to ſee a good armor, and now will he lie ten nights awake caruing the faſhion of a new dublet: he was wont to ſpeake plaine, & to the purpoſe (like an honeſt man & a ſouldier) and now is he turn'd orthography, his words are a very fantaſticall banquet, iuſt ſo many ſtrange diſhes: may I be ſo conuerted, & ſee with theſe eyes? I cannot tell, I thinke not: I will not bee ſworne, but loue may transforme me to an oyſter, but Ile take my oath on it, till he haue made an oyſter of me, he ſhall neuer make me ſuch a foole: one woman is faire, yet I am well: another is wiſe, yet I am well: another vertuous, yet I am well: but till all graces be in one woman▪ one woman ſhall not come in my grace: rich ſhee ſhall be, that's certaine: wiſe, or Ile none: vertuous, or Ile neuer cheapen her: faire, or Ile neuer looke on her: milde, or come not neere me: Noble, or not for an Angell: of good diſcourſe: an excellent Muſitian, and her haire ſhal be of what colour it pleaſe God, hah! the Prince and Monſieur Loue, I will hide me in the Arbor.

div.stage: Enter Prince, Leonato, Claudio, and Iacke Wilſon.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Come, ſhall we heare this muſicke?

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: Yea my good Lord: how ſtill the euening is,
As huſht on purpoſe to grace harmonie.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: See you where Benedicke hath hid himſelfe?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: O very well my Lord: the muſicke ended,
Wee'll fit the kid-foxe with a penny worth.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: Come Balthaſar, wee'll heare that ſong again.

sp.speaker: Balth.
sp.l: O good my Lord, taxe not ſo bad a voyce,
To ſlander muſicke any more then once.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: It is the witneſſe ſtill of excellency,
To ſlander Muſicke any more then once.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.l: It is the witneſſe ſtill of excellencie,
To put a ſtrange face on his owne perfection,
I pray thee ſing, and let me woe no more.

sp.speaker: Balth.
sp.l: Becauſe you talke of wooing, I will ſing,
Since many a wooer doth commence his ſuit,
To her he thinkes not worthy, yet he wooes,
Yet will he ſweare he loues.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.l: Nay pray thee come,
Or if thou wilt hold longer argument,
Doe it in notes.

sp.speaker: Balth.
sp.l: Note this before my notes,
Theres not a note of mine that's worth the noting.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.l: Why theſe are very crotchets that he ſpeaks,
Note notes forſooth, and nothing.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Now diuine aire, now is his ſoule rauiſht, is it not ſtrange that ſheepes guts ſhould hale ſoules out of mens bodies? well, a horne for my money when all's done.

lg.l: Sigh no more Ladies, ſigh no more,
Men were deceiuers euer,
One foote in Sea and one on ſhore,
To one thing conſtant neuer,
Then ſigh not ſo, but let them goe,
And be you blithe and bonnis,
Conuerting all your ſounds of woe,
Into hey nony nony.
Sing no more ditties, ſing no moe,
Of dumps ſo dull and heauy,
The fraud of men were euer ſo,
Since ſummer firſt was leauy,
Then ſigh not ſo, &c.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: By my troth a good ſong.

sp.speaker: Balth.
sp.p: And an ill ſinger, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: Ha, no, no faith, thou ſingſt well enough for a ſhift.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: And he had been a dog that ſhould haue howld thus, they would haue hang'd him, and I pray God his bad voyce bode no miſchiefe, I had as liefe haue heard the night-rauen, come what plague could haue come after it.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: Yea marry, doſt thou heare Balthaſar? I pray thee get vs ſome excellent muſick: for to morrow night we would haue it at the Lady Heroes chamber window.

sp.speaker: Balth.
sp.p: The beſt I can, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: Do ſo, farewell. Come hither Leonato, what was it you told me of to day, that your Niece Beatrice was in loue with ſignior Benedicke?

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: O I, ſtalke on, ſtalke on, the foule ſits. I did neuer thinke that Lady would haue loued any man.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: No nor I neither, but moſt wonderful, that ſhe ſhould ſo dote on Signior Benedicke, whom ſhee hath in all outward behauiours ſeemed euer to abhorre.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Is't poſſible? ſits the winde in that corner?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: By my troth my Lord, I cannot tell what to thinke of it, but that ſhe loues him with an inraged affection, it is paſt the infinite of thought.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: May be ſhe doth but counterfeit.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: Faith like enough.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: O God! counterfeit? there was neuer counterfeit of paſſion, came ſo neere the life of paſſion as ſhe diſcouers it.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: Why what effects of paſſion ſhewes ſhe?

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: Baite the hooke well, this fiſh will bite.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: What effects my Lord? ſhee will ſit you, you heard my daughter tell you how.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: She did indeed.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: How, how I pray you? you amaze me, I would haue thought her ſpirit had beene inuincible againſt all aſſaults of affection.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: I would haue ſworne it had, my Lord, eſpecially againſt Benedicke.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: I ſhould thinke this a gull, but that the white-bearded fellow ſpeakes it: knauery cannot ſure hide himſelfe in ſuch reuerence.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: He hath tane th' infection, hold it vp.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: Hath ſhee made her affection known to Benedicke?

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: No, and ſweares ſhe neuer will, that's her torment.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: 'Tis true indeed, ſo your daughter ſaies: ſhall I, ſaies ſhe, that haue ſo oft encountred him with ſcorne, write to him that I loue him?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: This ſaies ſhee now when ſhee is beginning to write to him, for ſhee'll be vp twenty times a night, and there will ſhe ſit in her ſmocke, till ſhe haue writ a ſheet of paper: my daughter tells vs all.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Now you talke of a ſheet of paper, I remember a pretty ieſt your daughter told vs of.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: O when ſhe had writ it, & was reading it ouer, ſhe found Benedicke and Beatrice betweene the ſheete.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: That.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: O ſhe tore the letter into a thouſand halfpence, raild at her ſelf, that ſhe ſhould be ſo immodeſt to write, to one that ſhee knew would flout her: I meaſure him, ſaies ſhe, by my owne ſpirit, for I ſhould flout him if hee writ to mee, yea though I loue him, I ſhould.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Then downe vpon her knees ſhe falls, weepes, ſobs, beates her heart, teares her hayre, praies, curſes, O ſweet Benedicke, God giue me patience.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: She doth indeed, my daughter ſaies ſo, and the extaſie hath ſo much ouerborne her, that my daughter is ſomtime afeard ſhe will doe a deſperate out-rage to her ſelfe, it is very true.

sp.speaker: Princ.
sp.p: It were good that Benedicke knew of it by ſome other, if ſhe will not diſcouer it.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: To what end? he would but make a ſport of it, and torment the poore Lady worſe.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: And he ſhould, it were an almes to hang him, ſhee's an excellent ſweet Lady, and (out of all ſuſpition,) ſhe is vertuous.

sp.speaker: Claudio.
sp.p: And ſhe is exceeding wiſe.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: In euery thing, but in louing Benedicke.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: O my Lord, wiſedome and bloud combating in ſo tender a body, we haue ten proofes to one, that bloud hath the victory, I am ſorry for her, as I haue iuſt cauſe, being her Vncle, and her Guardian.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: I would ſhee had beſtowed this dotage on mee, I would haue daft all other reſpects, and made her halfe my ſelfe: I pray you tell Benedicke of it, and heare what he will ſay.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Were it good thinke you?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Hero thinkes ſurely ſhe wil die, for ſhe ſaies ſhe will die, if hee loue her not, and ſhee will die ere ſhee make her loue knowne, and ſhe will die if hee wooe her, rather than ſhee will bate one breath of her accuſtomed croſſeneſſe.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p:
She doth well, if ſhe ſhould make tender of her
loue, 'tis very poſſible hee'l ſcorne it, for the man (as you know all) hath a contemptible ſpirit.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: He is a very proper man.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: He hath indeed a good outward happines.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: 'Fore God, and in my minde very wiſe.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: He doth indeed ſhew ſome ſparkes that are like wit.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: And I take him to be valiant.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: As Hector, I aſſure you, and in the managing of quarrels you may ſee hee is wiſe, for either hee auoydes them with great diſcretion, or vndertakes them with a Chriſtian-like feare.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: If hee doe feare God, a muſt neceſſarilie keepe peace, if hee breake the peace, hee ought to enter into a quarrell with feare and trembling.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: And ſo will he doe, for the man doth fear God, howſoeuer it ſeemes not in him, by ſome large ieaſts hee will make: well, I am ſorry for your niece, ſhall we goe ſee Benedicke, and tell him of her loue,

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: Neuer tell him, my Lord, let her weare it out with good counſell.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Nay that's impoſſible, ſhe may weare her heart out firſt.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Well, we will heare further of it by your daughter, let it coole the while, I loue Benedicke well, and I could wiſh he would modeſtly examine himſelfe, to ſee how much he is vnworthy to haue ſo good a Lady.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: My Lord, will you walke? dinner is ready.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: If he do not doat on her vpon this, I wil neuer truſt my expectation.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Let there be the ſame Net ſpread for her, and that muſt your daughter and her gentlewoman carry: the ſport will be, when they hold one an opinion of anothers dotage, and no ſuch matter, that's the Scene that I would ſee, which will be meerely a dumbe ſhew: let vs ſend her to call him into dinner.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: This can be no tricke, the conference was ſadly borne, they haue the truth of this from Hero, they ſeeme to pittie the Lady: it ſeemes her affections haue the full bent: loue me? why it muſt be requited: I heare how I am cenſur'd, they ſay I will beare my ſelfe proudly, if I perceiue the loue come from her: they ſay too, that ſhe will rather die than giue any ſigne of affection: I did neuer thinke to marry, I muſt not ſeeme proud, happy are they that heare their detractions, and can put them to mending: they ſay the Lady is faire, 'tis a truth, I can beare them witneſſe: and vertuous, tis ſo, I cannot reprooue it, and wiſe, but for louing me, by my troth it is no addition to her witte, nor no great argument of her folly; for I wil be horribly in loue with her, I may chance haue ſome odde quirkes and remnants of witte broken on mee, becauſe I haue rail'd ſo long againſt marriage: but doth not the appetite alter? a man loues the meat in his youth, that he cannot indure in his age. Shall quips and ſentences, and theſe paper bullets of the braine awe a man from the careere of his humour? No, the world muſt be peopled. When I ſaid I would die a batcheler, I did not think I ſhould liue till I were maried, here comes Beatrice: by this day, ſhee's a faire Lady, I doe ſpie ſome markes of loue in her.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Againſt my wil I am ſent to bid you come in to dinner.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Faire Beatrice, I thanke you for your paines.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: I tooke no more paines for thoſe thankes, then you take paines to thanke me, if it had been painefull, I would not haue come.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: You take pleaſure then in the meſſage.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Yea iuſt ſo much as you may take vpon a kniues point, and choake a daw withall: you haue no ſtomacke ſignior, fare you well.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Ha, againſt my will I am ſent to bid you come into dinner: there's a double meaning in that: I tooke no more paines for thoſe thankes then you tooke paines to thanke me, that's as much as to ſay, any paines that I take for you is as eaſie as thankes: if I do not take pitty of her I am a villaine, if I doe not loue her I am a Iew, I will goe get her picture.

div.head: Actus Tertius.
div.stage: Enter Hero and two Gentlemen, Margaret, and Vrſula.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: Good Margaret runne thee to the parlour,
There ſhalt thou finde my Coſin Beatrice,
Propoſing with the Prince and Claudio,
Whiſper her eare, and tell her I and Vrſula,
Walke in the Orchard, and our whole diſcourſe
Is all of her, ſay that thou ouer-heardſt vs,
And bid her ſteale into the pleached bower,
Where hony-ſuckles ripened by the ſunne,
Forbid the ſunne to enter: like fauourites,
Made proud by Princes, that aduance their pride,
Againſt that power that bred it, there will ſhe hide her,
To liſten our purpoſe, this is thy office,
Beare thee well in it, and leaue vs alone.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Ile make her come I warrant you preſently.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: Now Vrſula, when Beatrice doth come,
As we do trace this alley vp and downe,
Our talke muſt onely be of Benedicke,
When I doe name him, let it be thy part,
To praiſe him more then euer man did merit,
My talke to thee muſt be how Benedicke
Is ſicke in loue with Beatrice: of this matter,
Is little Cupids craſty arrow made,
That onely wounds by heare-ſay: now begin,
For looke where Beatrice like a Lapwing runs
Cloſe by the ground, to heare our conference.

sp.speaker: Vrſ.
sp.l: The pleaſant'ſt angling is to ſee the fiſh
Cut with her golden ores the ſiluer ſtreame,
And greedily deuoure the treacherous baite:
So angle we for Beatrice, who euen now,
Is couched in the wood-bine couerture,
Feare you not my part of the Dialogue.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: Then go we neare her that her eare looſe nothing,
Of the falſe ſweete baite that we lay for it:
No truely Vrſula, ſhe is too diſdainfull,
I know her ſpirits are as coy and wilde,
As Haggerds of the rocke.

sp.speaker: Ʋrſula.
sp.l: But are you ſure,
That Benedicke loues Beatrice ſo intirely?

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.p: So ſaies the Prince, and my new trothed Lord.

sp.speaker: Vrſ.
sp.p: And did they bid you tell her of it, Madam?

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: They did intreate me to acquaint her of it,
But I perſwaded them, if they lou'd Benedicke,
To wiſh him wraſtle with affection,
And neuer to let Beatrice know of it.

sp.speaker: Vrſula.
sp.l: Why did you ſo, doth not the Gentleman
Deſerue as full as fortunate a bed,
As euer Beatrice ſhall couch vpon?

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: O God of loue! I know he doth deſerue,
As much as may be yeelded to a man:
But Nature neuer fram'd a womans heart,
Of prowder ſtuffe then that of Beatrice:
Diſdaine and Scorne ride ſparkling in her eyes,
Miſ-prizing what they looke on, and her wit
Values it ſelfe ſo highly, that to her
All matter elſe ſeemes weake: ſhe cannot loue,
Nor take no ſhape nor proiect of affection,
Shee is ſo ſelfe indeared.

sp.speaker: Vrſula.
sp.l: Sure I thinke ſo,
And therefore certainely it were not good
She knew his loue, left ſhe make ſport at it.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: Why you ſpeake truth, I neuer yet ſaw man,
How wiſe, how noble, yong, how rarely featur'd.
But ſhe would ſpell him backward: if faire fac'd,
She would ſweare the gentleman ſhould be her ſiſter:
If blacke, why Nature drawing of an anticke,
Made a foule blot: if tall, a launce ill headed:
If low, an agot very vildlie cut:
If ſpeaking, why a vane blowne with all windes:
If ſilent, why a blocke moued with none.
So turnes ſhe euery man the wrong ſide out,
And neuer giues to Truth and Vertue, that
Which ſimpleneſſe and merit purchaſeth.

sp.speaker: Vrſu.
sp.p: Sure, ſure, ſuch carping is not commendable.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: No, not to be ſo odde, and from all faſhions,
As Beatrice is, cannot be commendable,
But who dare tell her ſo? if I ſhould ſpeake,
She would mocke me into ayre, O ſhe would laugh me
Out of my ſelfe, preſſe me to death with wit,
Therefore let Benedicke like couered fire,
Conſume away in ſighes, waſte inwardly:
It were a better death, to die with mockes,
Which is as bad as die with tickling.

sp.speaker: Ʋrſu.
sp.p: Yet tell her of it, heare what ſhee will ſay.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: No, rather I will goe to Benedicke,
And counſaile him to fight againſt his paſſion,
And truly Ile deuiſe ſome honeſt ſlanders,
To ſtaine my coſin with, one doth not know,
How much an ill word may impoiſon liking.

sp.speaker: Ʋrſu.
sp.l: O doe not doe your coſin ſuch a wrong,
She cannot be ſo much without true iudgement,
Hauing ſo ſwift and excellent a wit
As ſhe is priſde to haue, as to refuſe
So rare a Gentleman as ſignior Benedicke.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: He is the onely man of Italy,
Alwaies excepted, my deare Claudio.

sp.speaker: Vrſu.
sp.l: I pray you be not angry with me, Madame,
Speaking my fancy: Signior Benedicke,
For ſhape, for bearing argument and valour,
Goes formoſt in report through Italy.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: Indeed he hath an excellent good name.

sp.speaker: Ʋrſu.
sp.l: His excellence did earne it ere he had it:
When are you married Madame?

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: Why euerie day to morrow, come goe in,
Ile ſhew thee ſome attires, and haue thy counſell,
Which is the beſt to furniſh me to morrow.

sp.speaker: Vrſu.
sp.l: Shee's tane I warrant you,
We haue caught her Madame?

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: If it proue ſo, then louing goes by haps,
Some Cupid kills with arrowes, ſome with traps.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.l: What fire is in mine eares? can this be true?
Stand I condemn'd for pride and ſcorne ſo much?
Contempt, farewell, and maiden pride, adew,
No glory liues behinde the backe of ſuch.
And Benedicke, loue on, I will requite thee,
Taming my wilde heart to thy louing hand:
If thou doſt loue, my kindeneſſe ſhall incite thee
To binde our loues vp in a holy band.
For others ſay thou doſt deſerue, and I
Beleeue it better then reportingly.

div.stage: Enter Prince, Claudio, Benedicke, and Leonato.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: I doe but ſtay till your marriage be conſummate, and then go I toward Arragon.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Ile bring you thither my Lord, if you'l vouchſafe me.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Nay, that would be as great a ſoyle in the new gloſſe of your marriage, as to ſhew a childe his new coat and forbid him to weare it, I will onely bee bold with Benedicke for his companie, for from the crowne of his head, to the ſole of his foot, he is all mirth, he hath twice or thrice cut Cupids bow-ſtring, and the little hang-man dare not ſhoot at him, he hath a heart as ſound as a bell, and his tongue is the clapper, for what his heart thinkes, his tongue ſpeakes.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Gallants, I am not as I haue bin.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: So ſay I, methinkes you are ſadder.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: I hope he be in loue.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Hang him truant, there's no true drop of bloud in him to be truly toucht with loue, if he be ſad, he wants money.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: I haue the tooth-ach.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Draw it.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Hang it.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: You muſt hang it firſt, and draw it afterwards.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: What? ſigh for the tooth-ach.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Where is but a humour or a worme.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Well, euery one cannot maſter a griefe, but hee that has it.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Yet ſay I, he is in loue.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: There is no appearance of fancie in him, vnleſſe it be a fancy that he hath to ſtrange diſguiſes, as to bee a Dutchman to day, a Frenchman to morrow: vnleſſe hee haue a fancy to this foolery, as it appeares hee hath, hee is no foole for fancy, as you would haue it to appeare he is.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: If he be not in loue vvith ſome vvoman, there is no beleeuing old ſignes, a bruſhes his hat a mornings, What ſhould that bode?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Hath any man ſeene him at the Barbers?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: No, but the Barbers man hath beene ſeen with him, and the olde ornament of his cheeke hath alreadie ſtuft tennis balls.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Indeed he lookes yonger than hee did, by the loſſe of a beard.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Nay a rubs himſelfe vvith Ciuit, can you ſmell him out by that?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: That's as much as to ſay, the ſweet youth's in loue.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: The greateſt note of it is his melancholy.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: And vvhen vvas he vvont to vvaſh his face?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Yea, or to paint himſelfe? for the which I heare vvhat they ſay of him.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Nay, but his ieſting ſpirit, vvhich is now crept into a lute-ſtring, and now gouern'd by ſtops.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Indeed that tels a heauy tale for him: conclude, he is in loue.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Nay, but I know who loues him.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: That would I know too, I warrant one that knowes him not.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Yes, and his ill conditions, and in deſpight of all, dies for him.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Shee ſhall be buried with her face vpwards.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Yet is this no charme for the tooth-ake, old ſignior, walke aſide with mee, I haue ſtudied eight or nine wiſe words to ſpeake to you, which theſe hobby-horſes muſt not heare.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: For my life to breake with him about Beatrice.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: 'Tis euen ſo, Hero and Margaret haue by this played their parts with Beatrice, and then the two Beares will not bite one another when they meete.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: My Lord and brother, God ſaue you.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Good den brother.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: If your leiſure ſeru'd, I would ſpeake with you.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.p: In priuate?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: If it pleaſe you, yet Count Claudio may heare, for what I would ſpeake of, concernes him.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Baſta.
sp.p: Meanes your Lordſhip to be married to morrow?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: You know he does.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: I know not that when he knowes what I know.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: If there be any impediment, I pray you diſcouer it.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: You may thinke I loue you not, let that appeare hereafter, and ayme better at me by that I now will manifeſt, for my brother (I thinke, he holds you well, and in deareneſſe of heart) hath holpe to effect your enſuing marriage: ſurely ſute ill ſpent, and labour ill beſtowed.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Why, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Baſtard.
sp.p: I came hither to tell you, and circumſtances ſhortned, (for ſhe hath beene too long a talking of) the Lady is diſloyall.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Who Hero?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Euen ſhee, Leonatoes Hero, your Hero, euery mans Hero.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Diſloyall?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: The word is too good to paint out her wickedneſſe, I could ſay ſhe were worſe, thinke you of a worſe title, and I will fit her to it: wonder not till further warrant: goe but with mee to night, you ſhal ſee her chamber window entred, euen the night before her wedding day, if you loue her, then to morrow wed her: But it would better fit your honour to change your minde.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: May this be ſo?

sp.speaker: Princ.
sp.p: I will not thinke it.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: If you dare not truſt that you ſee, confeſſe not that you know: if you will follow mee, I will ſhew you enough, and when you haue ſeene more, & heard more, proceed accordingly.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: If I ſee any thing to night, why I ſhould not marry her to morrow in the congregation, where I ſhold wedde, there will I ſhame her.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: And as I wooed for thee to obtaine her, I will ioyne with thee to diſgrace her.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: I will diſparage her no farther, till you are my witneſſes, beare it coldly but till night, and let the iſſue ſhew it ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: O day vntowardly turned!

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: O miſchiefe ſtrangelie thwarting!

sp.speaker: Baſtard.
sp.p: O plague right well preuented! ſo will you ſay, when you haue ſeene the ſequele.

div.stage: Enter Dogbery and his compartner with the watch.

sp.speaker: Dog.
sp.p: Are you good men and true?

sp.speaker: Verg.
sp.p: Yea, or elſe it were pitty but they ſhould ſuffer ſaluation body and ſoule.

sp.speaker: Dogb.
sp.p: Nay, that were a puniſhment too good for them, if they ſhould haue any allegiance in them, being choſen for the Princes watch.

sp.speaker: Verges.
sp.p: Well, giue them their charge, neighbour Dogbery.

sp.speaker: Dog.
sp.p: Firſt, who thinke you the moſt deſartleſſe man to be Conſtable?

sp.speaker: Watch. 1.
sp.p: Hugh Ote-cake ſir, or George Sea-coale, for they can write and reade.

sp.speaker: Dogb.
sp.p: Come hither neighbour Sea-coale, God hath bleſt you with a good name: to be a wel-fauoured man, is the gift of Fortune, but to write and reade, comes by Nature.

sp.speaker: Watch 2.
sp.p: Both which Maſter Conſtable

sp.speaker: Dogb.
sp.p: You haue: I knew it would be your anſwere: well, for your fauour ſir, why giue God thankes, & make no boaſt of it, and for your writing and reading, let that appeare when there is no need of ſuch vanity, you are thought heere to be the moſt ſenſleſſe and fit man for the Conſtable of the watch: therefore beare you the lanthorne: this is your charge: You ſhall comprehend all vagrom men, you are to bid any man ſtand in the Princes name.

sp.speaker: Watch 2.
sp.p: How if a will not ſtand?

sp.speaker: Dogb.
sp.p: Why then take no note of him, but let him go, and preſently call the reſt of the Watch together, and thanke God you are ridde of a knaue.

sp.speaker: Ʋerges.
sp.p: If he will not ſtand when he is bidden, hee is none of the Princes ſubiects.

sp.speaker: Dogb.
sp.p: True, and they are to meddle with none but the Princes ſubiects: you ſhall alſo make no noiſe in the ſtreetes: for, for the Watch to babble and talke, is moſt tollerable, and not to be indured.

sp.speaker: Watch.
sp.p: We will rather ſleepe than talke, wee know what belongs to a Watch.

sp.speaker: Dog.
sp.p: Why you ſpeake like an ancient and moſt quiet watchman, for I cannot ſee how ſleeping ſhould offend: only haue a care that your bills be not ſtolne: well, you are to call at all the Alehouſes, and bid them that are drunke get them to bed.

sp.speaker: Watch.
sp.p: How if they will not?

sp.speaker: Dogb.
sp.p: Why then let them alone till they are ſober, if they make you not then the better anſwere, you may ſay, they are not the men you tooke them for.

sp.speaker: Watch.
sp.p: Well ſir.

sp.speaker: Dogb.
sp.p: If you meet a theefe, you may ſuſpect him, by vertue of your office, to be no true man▪ and for ſuch kinde of men, the leſſe you meddle or make with them, why the more is for your honeſty.

sp.speaker: Watch.
sp.p: If wee know him to be a thiefe, ſhall wee not lay hands on him.

sp.speaker: Dogb.
sp.p: Truly by your office you may, but I think they that touch pitch will be defil'd: the moſt peaceable way for you, if you doe take a theefe, is, to let him ſhew himſelfe what he is, and ſteale out of your company.

sp.speaker: Ver.
sp.p: You haue bin alwaies cal'd a merciful mā partner.

sp.speaker: Dog.
sp.p: Truely I would not hang a dog by my will, much more a man who hath anie honeſtie in him.

sp.speaker: Verges.
sp.p: If you heare a child crie in the night you muſt call to the nurſe, and bid her ſtill it.

sp.speaker: Watch.
sp.p: How if the nurſe be aſleepe and will not heare vs?

sp.speaker: Dog.
sp.p: Why then depart in peace, and let the childe wake her with crying, for the ewe that will not heare her Lambe when it baes, will neuer anſwere a calfe when he bleates.

sp.speaker: Verges.
sp.p: 'Tis verie true.

sp.speaker: Dog.
sp.p: This is the end of the charge: you conſtable are to preſent the Princes owne perſon, if you meete the Prince in the night, you may ſtaie him.

sp.speaker: Verges.
sp.p: Nay birladie that I thinke a cannot.

sp.speaker: Dog.
sp.p: Fiue ſhillings to one on't with anie man that knowes the Statues, he may ſtaie him, marrie not without the prince be willing, for indeed the watch ought to offend no man, and it is an offence to ſtay a man againſt his will.

sp.speaker: Ʋerges.
sp.p: Birladie I thinke it be ſo.

sp.speaker: Dog.
sp.p: Ha, ah ha, well maſters good night, and there be anie matter of weight chances, call vp me, keepe your fellowes counſailes, and your owne, and good night, come neighbour.

sp.speaker: Watch.
sp.p: Well maſters, we heare our charge, let vs go ſit here vpon the Church bench till two, and then all to bed.

sp.speaker: Dog.
sp.p: One word more, honeſt neighbors. I pray you watch about ſignior Leonatoes doore, for the wedding being there to morrow, there is a great coyle to night, adiew, be vigitant I beſeech you.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: What, Conrade?

sp.speaker: Watch.
sp.p: Peace, ſtir not.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Conrade I ſay.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: Here man, I am at thy elbow.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Mas and my elbow itcht, I thought there would a ſcabbe follow.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: I will owe thee an anſwere▪ for that, and now forward with thy tale.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Stand thee cloſe then vnder this penthouſe, for it driſſels raine, and I will, like a true drunkard, vtter all to thee.

sp.speaker: Watch.
sp.p: Some treaſon maſters, yet ſtand cloſe.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Therefore know, I haue earned of Don Iohn a thouſand Ducates.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: Is it poſſible that anie villanie ſhould be ſo deare?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Thou ſhould'ſt rather aske if it were poſſible anie villanie ſhould be ſo rich? for when rich villains haue neede of poore ones, poore ones may make what price they will.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: I wonder at it.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: That ſhewes thou art vnconfirm'd, thou knoweſt that the faſhion of a doublet, or a hat, or a cloake, is nothing to a man.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: Yes, it is apparell.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: I meane the faſhion.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: Yes the faſhion is the faſhion.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Tuſh, I may as well ſay the foole's the foole, but ſeeſt thou not what a deformed theefe this faſhion is?

sp.speaker: Watch.
sp.p: I know that deformed, a has bin a vile theefe, this vii. yeares, a goes vp and downe like a gentle man: I remember his name.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Did'ſt thou not heare ſome bodie?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: No, 'twas the vaine on the houſe.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Seeſt thou not (I ſay) what a deformed thiefe this faſhion is, how giddily a turnes about all the Hot-blouds, betweene foureteene & fiue & thirtie, ſometimes faſhioning them like Pharaoes ſouldiours in the rechie painting, ſometime like god Bels prieſts in the old Church window, ſometime like the ſhauen Hercules in the ſmircht worm eaten tapeſtrie, where his cod-peece ſeemes as maſſie as his club.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: All this I ſee, and ſee that the faſhion weares out more apparrell then the man; but art not thou thy ſelfe giddie with the faſhion too that thou haſt ſhifted out of thy tale into telling me of the faſhion?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Not ſo neither, but know that I haue to night wooed Margaret the Lady Heroes gentle-woman, by the name of Hero, ſhe leanes me out at her miſtris chamber-vvindow, bids me a thouſand times good night: I tell this tale vildly. I ſhould firſt tell thee how the Prince Claudio and my Maſter planted, and placed, and poſſeſſed by my Maſter Don Iohn, ſaw a far off in the Orchard this amiable incounter.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: And thought thy Margaret was Hero?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Two of them did, the Prince and Claudio, but the diuell my Maſter knew ſhe was Margaret and partly by his oathes, which firſt poſſeſt them, partly by the darke night which did deceiue them, but chiefely, by my villanie, which did confirme any ſlander that Don Iohn had made, away vvent Claudio enraged, ſwore hee vvould meete her as he was apointed next morning at the Temple, and there, before the whole congregation ſhame her with vvhat he ſaw o're night, and ſend her home againe vvithout a husband.

sp.speaker: Watch. 1.
sp.p: We charge you in the Princes name ſtand.

sp.speaker: Watch. 2.
sp.p: Call vp the right maſter Conſtable, vve haue here recouered the moſt dangerous peece of lechery, that euer vvas knowne in the Common-wealth.

sp.speaker: Watch. 1.
sp.p: And one Deformed is one of them, I know him, a vveares a locke.

sp.speaker: Conr.
sp.p: Maſt • maſters.

sp.speaker: Watch. 2.
sp.p: Youre be made bring deformed forth I warrant you,

sp.speaker: Conr.
sp.p: Maſters, neuer ſpeake, vve charge you, let vs obey you to goe vvith vs.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: We are like to proue a goodly commoditie, being taken vp of theſe mens bils.

sp.speaker: Conr.
sp.p: A commoditie in queſtion I warrant you, come vveele obey you.

div.stage: Enter Hero, and Margaret, and Ʋrſula.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: Good Vrſula wake my coſin Beatrice, and deſire her to riſe.

sp.speaker: Ʋrſu.
sp.p: I will Lady.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.p: And bid her come hither.

sp.speaker: Vrſ.
sp.p: Well.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Troth I thinke your other rebato were better.

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.p: No pray thee good Meg, Ile vveare this.

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: By my troth's not ſo good, and I vvarrant your coſin vvill ſay ſo.

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.p: My coſin's a foole, and thou art another, ile vveare none but this.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I like the new tire vvithin excellently, if the haire vvere a thought browner: and your gown's a moſt rare faſhion yfaith, I ſaw the Dutcheſſe of Millaines gowne that they praiſe ſo.

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.p: O that exceedes they ſay.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: By my troth's but a night-gowne in reſpect of yours, cloth a gold and cuts and lac'd with ſiluer, ſet with pearles, downe ſleeues, ſide ſleeues, and skirts, round vnderborn with a blewiſh tinſel, but for a fine queint gracefull and excellent faſhion, yours is worth ten on't.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: God giue mee ioy to weare it, for my heart is exceeding heauy.

sp.speaker: Marga.
sp.p: 'Twill be heauier ſoone, by the waight of a man.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: Fie vpon thee, art not aſham'd?

sp.speaker: Marg.
sp.p: Of what Lady? of ſpeaking honourably? is not marriage honourable in a beggar? is not your Lord honourable without marriage? I thinke you would haue me ſay, ſauing your reuerence a husband: and bad thinking doe not wreſt true ſpeaking, Ile offend no body, is there any harme in the heauier for a husband? none I thinke, and it be the right husband, and the right wife, otherwiſe 'tis light and not heauy, aske my Lady Beatrice elſe, here ſhe comes.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: Good morrow Coze.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Good morrow ſweet Hero.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: Why how now? do you ſpeake in the ſick tune?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: I am out of all other tune, me thinkes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Claps into Light a loue, (that goes without a burden,) do you ſing it and Ile dance it.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Ye Light aloue with your heeles, then if your husband haue ſtables enough, you'll looke he ſhall lacke no barnes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: O illegitimate conſtruction! I ſcorne that with my heeles.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: 'Tis almoſt fiue a clocke coſin, 'tis time you were ready, by my troth I am exceeding ill, hey ho.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: For a hauke, a horſe, or a husband?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: For the letter that begins them all, H.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Well, and you be not turn'd Turke, there's no more ſayling by the ſtarre.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: What meanes the foole trow?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Nothing I, but God ſend euery one rheir harts deſire.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: Theſe gloues the Count ſent mee, they are an excellent perfume.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: I am ſtuft coſin, I cannot ſmell.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: A maid and ſtuft! there's goodly catching of colde.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: O God helpe me, God help me, how long haue you profeſt apprehenſion?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Euer ſince you left it, doth not my wit become me rarely?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: It is not ſeene enough, you ſhould weare it in your cap, by my troth I am ſicke.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Get you ſome of this diſtill'd carduus benedictus and lay it to your heart, it is the onely thing for a qualm.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: There thou prickſt her with a thiſſell.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Benedictus, why benedictus? you haue ſome morall in this benedictus.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Morall? no by my troth, I haue no morall meaning, I meant plaine holy thiſſell, you may thinke perchance that I thinke you are in loue, nay birlady I am not ſuch a foole to thinke what I liſt, nor I liſt not to thinke what I can, nor indeed I cannot thinke, if I would thinke my hart out of thinking, that you are in loue, or that you will be in loue, or that you can be in loue: yet Benedicke was ſuch another, and now is he become a man, he ſwore hee would neuer marry, and yet now in deſpight of his heart he eates his meat without grudging, and how you may be conuerted I know not, but me thinkes you looke with your eies as other women doe.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: What pace is this that thy tongue keepes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Not a falſe gallop.

sp.speaker: Vrſula.
sp.p: Madam, withdraw, the Prince, the Count, ſignior Benedicke, Don Iohn, and all the gallants of the towne are come to fetch you to Church.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: Helpe to dreſſe mee good coze, good Meg, good Vrſula.

div.stage: Enter Leonato, and the Conſtable, and the Headborough.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: What would you with mee, honeſt neighbour?

sp.speaker: Conſt. Dog.
sp.p: Mary ſir I would haue ſome confidence with you, that decernes you nearely.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Briefe I pray you, for you ſee it is a buſie time with me.

sp.speaker: Conſt. Dog.
sp.p: Mary this it is ſir.

sp.speaker: Headb.
sp.p: Yes in truth it is ſir.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: What is it my good friends?

sp.speaker: Con. Do.
sp.p: Goodman Verges ſir ſpeakes a little of the matter, an old man ſir, and his wits are not ſo blunt, as God helpe I would deſire they were, but infaith honeſt as the skin betweene his browes.

sp.speaker: Head.
sp.p: Yes I thank God, I am as honeſt as any man liuing, that is an old man, and no honeſter then I.

sp.speaker: Con. Dog.
sp.p: Compariſons are odorous, palabras, neighbour Verges.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Neighbours, you are tedious.

sp.speaker: Con. Dog.
sp.p: It pleaſes your worſhip to ſay ſo, but we are the poore Dukes officers, but truely for mine owne part, if I were as tedious as a King I could finde in my heart to beſtow it all of your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: All thy tediouſneſſe on me, ah?

sp.speaker: Conſt. Dog.
sp.p: Yea, and 'twere a thouſand times more than 'tis, for I heare as good exclamation on your Worſhip as of any man in the Citie, and though I bee but a poore man, I am glad to heare it.

sp.speaker: Head.
sp.p: And ſo am I.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: I would faine know what you haue to ſay.

sp.speaker: Head.
sp.p: Marry ſir our watch to night, excepting your worſhips preſence, haue tane a couple of as arrant knaues as any in Meſſina.

sp.speaker: Con. Dog.
sp.p: A good old man ſir, hee will be talking as they ſay, when the age is in the wit is out, God helpe vs, it is a world to ſee: well ſaid yfaith neighbour Verges, well, God's a good man, and two men ride of a horſe, one muſt ride behinde, an honeſt ſoule yfaith ſir, by my troth he is, as euer broke bread, but God is to bee worſhipt, all men are not alike, alas good neighbour.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Indeed neighbour he comes too ſhort of you.

sp.speaker: Con. Do.
sp.p: Gifts that God giues.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: I muſt leaue you.

sp.speaker: Con. Dog.
sp.p: One word ſir, our watch ſir haue indeede comprehended two aſpitious perſons, & we would haue them this morning examined before your worſhip.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Take their examination your ſelfe, and bring it me, I am now in great haſte, as may appeare vnto you.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: It ſhall be ſuffigance.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Drinke ſome wine ere you goe: fare you well.

sp.speaker: Meſſenger.
sp.p: My Lord, they ſtay for you to giue your daughter to her husband.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Ile wait vpon them, I am ready.

sp.speaker: Dogb.
sp.p: Goe good partner, goe get you to Francis Sea-coale, bid him bring his pen and inkehorne to the Gaole: we are now to examine thoſe men.

sp.speaker: Verges.
sp.p: And we muſt doe it wiſely.

sp.speaker: Dogb.
sp.p:
Wee will ſpare for no witte I warrant you:
heere's that ſhall driue ſome of them to a non-come, only get the learned writer to ſet downe our excommunication, and meet me at the Iaile.

div.head: Actus Quartus.
div.stage: Enter Prince, Bastard, Leonato, Frier, Claudio, Benedicke, Hero, and Beatrice.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: Come Frier Francis, be briefe, onely to the plaine forme of marriage, and you ſhal recount their particular duties afterwards.

sp.speaker: Fran.
sp.p: You come hither, my Lord, to marry this Lady.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: To be married to her: Frier, you come to marrie her.

sp.speaker: Frier.
sp.p: Lady, you come hither to be married to this Count.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: I doe.

sp.speaker: Frier.
sp.p: If either of you know any inward impediment why you ſhould not be conioyned, I charge you on your ſoules to vtter it.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: Know you anie, Hero?

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: None my Lord.

sp.speaker: Frier.
sp.p: Know you anie, Count?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: I dare make his anſwer, None.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: O what men dare do! what men may do! what men daily do!

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: How now! interiections? why then, ſome be of laughing, as ha, ha, he.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Stand thee by Frier, father, by your leaue,
Will you with free and vnconſtrained ſoule
Giue me this maid your daughter?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: As freely ſonne as God did giue her me.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: And what haue I to giue you back, whoſe worth
May counterpoiſe this rich and precious gift?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Nothing, vnleſſe you render her againe.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Sweet Prince, you learn me noble thankfulnes:
There Leonato, take her backe againe,
Giue not this rotten Orenge to your friend,
Shee's but the ſigne and ſemblance of her honour:
Behold how like a maid ſhe bluſhes heere!
O what authoritie and ſhew of truth
Can cunning ſinne couer it ſelfe withall!
Comes not that bloud, as modeſt euidence,
To witneſſe ſimple Vertue? would you not ſweare
All you that ſee her, that ſhe were a maide,
By theſe exterior ſhewes? But ſhe is none:
She knowes the heat of a luxurious bed:
Her bluſh is guiltineſſe, not modeſtie.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: What doe you meane, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Not to be married,
Not to knit my ſoule to an approued wanton.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Deere my Lord, if you in your owne proofe,
Haue vanquiſht the reſiſtance of her youth,
And made defeat of her virginitie.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: I know what you would ſay: if I haue knowne her,
You will ſay, ſhe did imbrace me as a husband,
And ſo extenuate the forehand ſinne: No Leonato,
I neuer tempted her with word too large,
But as a brother to his ſiſter, ſhewed
Baſhfull ſinceritie and comely loue.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: And ſeem'd I euer otherwiſe to you?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Out on thee ſeeming, I will write againſt it,
You ſeeme to me as Diane in her Orbe,
As chaſte as is the budde ere it be blowne:
But you are more intemperate in your blood,
Than Venus, or thoſe pampred animalls,
That rage in ſauage ſenſualitie.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: Is my Lord well, that he doth ſpeake ſo wide?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Sweete Prince, why ſpeake not you?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: What ſhould I ſpeake?
I ſtand diſhonour'd that haue gone about,
To linke my deare friend to a common ſtale.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Are theſe things ſpoken, or doe I but dreame?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Sir, they are ſpoken, and theſe things are true.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: This lookes not like a nuptiall.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: True, O God!

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Leonato, ſtand I here?
Is this the Prince? is this the Princes brother?
Is this face Heroes? are our eies our owne?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: All this is ſo, but what of this my Lord?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Let me but moue one queſtion to your daughter,
And by that fatherly and kindly power,
That you haue in her, bid her anſwer truly.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: I charge thee doe, as thou art my childe.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: O God defend me how am I beſet,
What kinde of catechizing call you this?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: To make you anſwer truly to your name.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: Is it not Hero? who can blot that name
With any iuſt reproach?

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: Marry that can Hero,
Hero it ſelfe can blot out Heroes vertue.
What man was he, talkt with you yeſternight,
Out at your window betwixt twelue and one?
Now if you are a maid, anſwer to this.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.p: I talkt with no man at that howre my Lord.

sp.speaker: Prince.
sp.l: Why then you are no maiden. Leonato,
I am ſorry you muſt heare: vpon mine honor,
My ſelfe, my brother, and this grieued Count
Did ſee her, heare her, at that howre laſt night,
Talke with a ruffian at her chamber window,
Who hath indeed moſt like a liberall villaine,
Confeſt the vile encounters they haue had
A thouſand times in ſecret.

sp.speaker: Iohn.
sp.l: Fie, fie, they are not to be named my Lord,
Not to be ſpoken of,
There is not chaſtitie enough in language,
Without offence to vtter them: thus pretty Lady
I am ſorry for thy much miſgouernment.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: O Hero! what a Hero hadſt thou beene
If halfe thy outward graces had beene placed
About thy thoughts and counſailes of thy heart?
But fare thee well, moſt foule, moſt faire, farewell
Thou pure impiety, and impious puritie,
For thee Ile locke vp all the gates of Loue,
And on my eie-lids ſhall Coniecture hang,
To turne all beauty into thoughts of harme,
And neuer ſhall it more be gracious.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Hath no mans dagger here a point for me?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Why how now coſin, wherfore ſink you down?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.l: Come, let vs go: theſe things come thus to light,
Smother her ſpirits vp.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: How doth the Lady?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.l: Dead I thinke, helpe vncle,
Hero, why Hero, Vncle, Signor Benedicke, Frier.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.l: O Fate! take not away thy heauy hand,
Death is the faireſt couer for her ſhame
That may be wiſht for.

sp.speaker: Beatr.
sp.p: How now coſin Hero?

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.p: Haue comfort Ladie.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Doſt thou looke vp?

sp.speaker: Frier.
sp.p: Yea, wherefore ſhould ſhe not?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Wherfore? Why doth not euery earthly thing
Cry ſhame vpon her? Could ſhe heere denie
The ſtorie that is printed in her blood?
Do not liue Hero, do not ope thine eyes:
For did I thinke thou wouldſt not quickly die,
Thought I thy ſpirits were ſtronger then thy ſhames,
My ſelfe would on the reward of reproaches
Strike at thy life. Grieu'd I, I had but one?
Chid I, for that at frugal Natures frame?
O one too much by thee: why had I one?
Why euer was't thou louelie in my eies?
Why had I not with charitable hand
Tooke vp a beggars iſſue at my gates,
Who ſmeered thus, and mir'd with infamie,
I might haue ſaid, no part of it is mine:
This ſhame deriues it ſelfe from vnknowne loines,
But mine, and mine I lou'd, and mine I prais'd,
And mine that I was proud on mine ſo much,
That I my ſelfe, was to my ſelfe not mine:
Valewing of her, why ſhe, O ſhe is falne
Into a pit of Inke, that the wide ſea
Hath drops too few to waſh her cleane againe,
And ſalt too little, which may ſeaſon giue
To her foule tainted fleſh.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Sir, ſir, be patient: for my part, I am ſo attired in wonder, I know not what to ſay.

sp.speaker: Bea.
sp.p: O on my ſoule my coſin is belied.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Ladie, were you her bedfellow laſt night?

sp.speaker: Bea.
sp.l: No truly: not although vntill laſt night,
I haue this tweluemonth bin her bedfellow.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Confirm'd, confirm'd, O that is ſtronger made
Which was before barr'd vp with ribs of iron.
Would the Princes lie, and Claudio lie,
Who lou'd her ſo, that ſpeaking of her foulneſſe,
Waſh'd it with teares? Hence from her, let her die.

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.p: Heare me a little, for I haue onely bene ſilent ſo long, and giuen way vnto this courſe of fortune, by noting of the Ladie, I haue markt.
sp.l: A thouſand bluſhing apparitions,
To ſtart into her face, a thouſand innocent ſhames,
In Angel whiteneſſe beare away thoſe bluſhes,
And in her eie there hath appear'd a fire
To burne the errors that theſe Princes hold
Againſt her maiden truth. Call me a foole,
Truſt not my reading, nor my obſeruations,
Which with experimental ſeale doth warrant
The tenure of my booke: truſt not my age,
My reuerence, calling, nor diuinitie,
If this ſweet Ladie lye not guiltleſſe heere,
Vnder ſome biting error.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Friar, it cannot be:
Thou ſeeſt that all the Grace that ſhe hath left,
Is, that ſhe wil not adde to her damnation,
A ſinne of periury, ſhe not denies it:
Why ſeek'ſt thou then to couer with excuſe,
That which appeares in proper nakedneſſe?

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.p: Ladie, what man is he you are accus'd of?

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: They know that do accuſe me, I know none:
If I know more of any man aliue
Then that which maiden modeſtie doth warrant,
Let all my ſinnes lacke mercy. O my Father,
Proue you that any man with me conuerſt,
At houres vnmeete, or that I yeſternight
Maintain'd the change of words with any creature,
Refuſe me, hate me, torture me to death.

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.p: There is ſome ſtrange miſpriſion in the Princes.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.l: Two of them haue the verie bent of honor,
And if their wiſedomes be miſled in this:
The practiſe of it liues in Iohn the baſtard,
Whoſe ſpirits toile in frame of villanies.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: I know not: if they ſpeake but truth of her,
Theſe hands ſhall teare her: If they wrong her honour,
The proudeſt of them ſhall wel heare of it.
Time hath not yet ſo dried this bloud of mine,
Nor age ſo eate vp my inuention,
Nor Fortune made ſuch hauocke of my meanes,
Nor my bad life reſt me ſo much of friends,
But they ſhall finde, awak'd in ſuch a kinde,
Both ſtrength of limbe, and policie of minde,
Ability in meanes, and choiſe of friends,
To quit me of them throughly.

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.l: Pauſe awhile:
And let my counſell ſway you in this caſe,
Your daughter heere the Princeſſe (left for dead)
Let her awhile be ſecretly kept in,
And publiſh it, that ſhe is dead indeed:
Maintaine a mourning oſtentation,
And on your Families old monument,
Hang mournfull Epitaphes, and do all rites,
That appertaine vnto a buriall.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: What ſhall become of this? What wil this do?

sp.speaker: Fri.
sp.l: Marry this wel carried, ſhall on her behalfe,
Change ſlander to remorſe, that is ſome good,
But not for that dreame I on this ſtrange courſe,
But on this trauaile looke for greater birth:
She dying, as it muſt be ſo maintain'd,
Vpon the inſtant that ſhe was accus'd,
Shal be lamented, pittied, and excus'd
Of euery hearer: for it ſo fals out,
That what we haue, we prize not to the worth,
Whiles we enioy it; but being lack'd and loſt,
Why then we racke the value, then we finde
The vertue that poſſeſsion would not ſhew vs
Whiles it was ours, ſo will it fare with Claudio:
When he ſhal heare ſhe dyed vpon his words,
Th' Idea of her life ſhal ſweetly creepe
Into his ſtudy of imagination.
And euery louely Organ of her life,
Shall come apparel'd in more precious habite:
More mouing delicate, and ful of life,
Into the eye and proſpect of his ſoule
Then when ſhe liu'd indeed: then ſhal he mourne,
If euer Loue had intereſt in his Liuer,
And wiſh he had not ſo accuſed her:
No, though he thought his accuſation true:
Let this be ſo, and doubt not but ſucceſſe
Wil faſhion the euent in better ſhape,
Then I can lay it downe in likelihood.
But if all ayme but this be leuelld falſe,
The ſuppoſition of the Ladies death,
Will quench the wonder of her infamie.
And if it ſort not well, you may conceale her,
As beſt befits her wounded reputation,
In ſome recluſiue and religious life,
Out of all eyes, tongues, mindes and iniuries.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.l: Signior Leonato, let the Frier aduiſe you,
And though you know my inwardneſſe and loue
Is very much vnto the Prince and Claudio.
Yet, by mine honor, I will deale in this▪
As ſecretly and iuſtlie, as your ſoule
Should with your bodie.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Being that I flow in greefe,
The ſmalleſt twine may lead me.

sp.speaker: Frier.
sp.l: 'Tis well conſented, preſently away,
For to ſtrange ſores, ſtrangely they ſtraine the cure,
Come Lady, die to liue, this wedding day
Perhaps is but prolong'd, haue patience & endure.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Lady Beatrice, haue you wept all this while?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Yea, and I will weepe a while longer.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: I will not deſire that.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: You haue no reaſon, I doe it freely.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Surelie I do beleeue your fair coſin is wrong'd.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Ah, how much might the man deſerue of mee that would right her!

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Is there any way to ſhew ſuch friendſhip?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: A verie euen way, but no ſuch friend.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: May a man doe it?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: It is a mans office, but not yours.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: I doe loue nothing in the world ſo well as you, is not that ſtrange?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: As ſtrange as the thing I know not, it were as poſſible for me to ſay, I loued nothing ſo well as you, but beleeue me not, and yet I lie not, I confeſſe nothing, nor I deny nothing, I am ſorry for my couſin.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: By my ſword Beatrice thou lou'ſt me.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Doe not ſweare by it and eat it.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: I will ſweare by it that you loue mee, and I will make him eat it that ſayes I loue not you.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Will you not eat your word?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: With no ſawce that can be deuiſed to it, I proteſt I loue thee.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Why then God forgiue me.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: What offence ſweet Beatrice?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: You haue ſtayed me in a happy howre; I was about to proteſt I loued you.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: And doe it with all thy heart.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: I loue you with ſo much of my heart, that none is left to proteſt.

sp.speaker: Bened.
sp.p: Come, bid me doe any thing for thee.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Kill Claudio.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Ha, not for the wide world.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: You kill me to denie, farewell.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Tarrie ſweet Beatrice.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: I am gone, though I am heere, there is no loue in you, nay I pray you let me goe.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Infaith I will goe.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Wee'll be friends firſt.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: You dare eaſier be friends with mee, than fight with mine enemy.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Is Claudio thine enemie?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Is a not approued in the height a villaine, that hath ſlandered, ſcorned, diſhonoured my kinſwoman? O that I were a man! what, beare her in hand vntill they come to take hands, and then with publike accuſation vncouered ſlander, vnmittigated rancour? O God that I were a man! I would eat his heart in the market-place.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Heare me Beatrice.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Talke with a man out at a window, a proper ſaying.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Nay but Beatrice.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Sweet Hero, ſhe is wrong'd, ſhee is ſlandered, ſhe is vndone.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Beat?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Princes and Counties! ſurelie a Princely teſtimonie, a goodly Count, Comfect, a ſweet Gallant ſurelie, O that I were a man for his ſake! or that I had any friend would be a man for my ſake! But manhood is melted into curſies, valour into complement, and men are onelie turned into tongue, and trim ones too: he is now as valiant as Hercules, that only tells a lie, and ſweares it: I cannot be a man with wiſhing, therfore I will die a woman with grieuing.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Tarry good Beatrice, by this hand I loue thee.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Vſe it for my loue ſome other way then ſwearing by it.

sp.speaker: Bened.
sp.p: Thinke you in your ſoule the Count Claudio hath wrong'd Hero?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Yea, as ſure as I haue a thought, or a ſoule.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Enough, I am engagde, I will challenge him, I will kiſſe your hand, and ſo leaue you: by this hand Claudio ſhall render me a deere account: as you heare of me, ſo thinke of me: goe comfort your cooſin, I muſt ſay ſhe is dead, and ſo farewell.

div.stage: Enter the Conſtables, Borachio, and the Towne Clerke in gownes.

sp.speaker: Keeper.
sp.p: Is our whole diſſembly appeard?

sp.speaker: Cowley.
sp.p: O a ſtoole and a cuſhion for the Sexton.

sp.speaker: Sexton.
sp.p: Which be the malefactors?

sp.speaker: Andrew.
sp.p: Marry that am I, and my partner.

sp.speaker: Cowley.
sp.p: Nay that's certaine, wee haue the exhibition to examine.

sp.speaker: Sexton.
sp.p: But which are the offenders that are to be examined, let them come before maſter Conſtable.

sp.speaker: Kemp.
sp.p: Yea marry, let them come before mee, what is your name, friend?

sp.speaker: Kem.
sp.p: Pray write downe Borachio. Yours ſirra.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: I am a Gentleman ſir, and my name is Conrade.

sp.speaker: Kee.
sp.p:
Write downe Maſter gentleman Conrade •
: maiſters, doe you ſerue God: maiſters, it is proued alreadie that you are little better than falſe knaues, and it will goe neere to be thought ſo ſhortly, how anſwer you for your ſelues?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: Marry ſir, we ſay we are none.

sp.speaker: Kemp.
sp.p: A maruellous witty fellow I aſſure you, but I will goe about with him: come you hither ſirra, a word in your eare ſir, I ſay to you, it is thought you are falſe knaues.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Sir, I ſay to you, we are none.

sp.speaker: Kemp.
sp.p: Well, ſtand aſide, 'fore God they are both in a tale: haue you writ downe that they are none?

sp.speaker: Sext.
sp.p: Maſter Conſtable, you goe not the way to examine, you muſt call forth the watch that are their accuſers.

sp.speaker: Kemp.
sp.p: Yea marry, that's the efteſt way, let the watch come forth: maſters, I charge you in the Princes name, accuſe theſe men.

sp.speaker: Watch 1.
sp.p: This man ſaid ſir, that Don Iohn the Princes brother was a villaine.

sp.speaker: Kemp.
sp.p: Write down, Prince Iohn a villaine: why this is flat periurie, to call a Princes brother villaine.

sp.speaker: Bora.
sp.p: Maſter Conſtable.

sp.speaker: Kemp.
sp.p: Pray thee fellow peace, I do not like thy looke I promiſe thee.

sp.speaker: Sexton.
sp.p: What heard you him ſay elſe?

sp.speaker: Watch 2.
sp.p: Mary that he had receiued a thouſand Dukates of Don Iohn, for accuſing the Lady Hero wrongfully.

sp.speaker: Kemp.
sp.p: Flat Burglarie as euer was committed.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: Yea by th' maſſe that it is.

sp.speaker: Sexton.
sp.p: What elſe fellow?

sp.speaker: Watch 1.
sp.p: And that Count Claudio did meane vpon his words, to diſgrace Hero before the whole aſſembly, and not marry her.

sp.speaker: Kemp.
sp.p: O villaine! thou wilt be condemn'd into euerlaſting redemption for this.

sp.speaker: Sexton.
sp.p: What elſe?

sp.speaker: Watch.
sp.p: This is all.

sp.speaker: Sexton.
sp.p: And this is more maſters then you can deny, Prince Iohn is this morning ſecretly ſtolne away: Hero was in this manner accus'd, in this very manner refus'd, and vpon the griefe of this ſodainely died: Maſter Conſtable, let theſe men be bound, and brought to Leonato, I will goe before, and ſhew him their examination.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: Come, let them be opinion'd.

sp.speaker: Sex.
sp.p: Let them be in the hands of Coxcombe.

sp.speaker: Kem.
sp.p: Gods my life, where's the Sexton? let him write downe the Princes Officer Coxcombe: come, binde them thou naughty varlet.

sp.speaker: Couley.
sp.p: Away, you are an aſſe, you are an aſſe.

sp.speaker: Kemp.
sp.p: Doſt thou not ſuſpect my place? doſt thou not ſuſpect my yeeres? O that hee were heere to write mee downe an aſſe! but maſters, remember that I am an aſſe: though it be not written down, yet forget not yt I am an aſſe: No thou villaine, yu art full of piety as ſhall be prou'd vpon thee by good witneſſe, I am a wiſe fellow, and which is more, an officer, and which is more, a houſhoulder, and which is more, as pretty a peece of fleſh as any in Meſſina, and one that knowes the Law, goe to, & a rich fellow enough, goe to, and a fellow that hath had loſſes, and one that hath two gownes, and euery thing handſome about him: bring him away: O that I had been writ downe an aſſe!

div.head: Actus Quintus.

sp.speaker: Brother.
sp.l: If you goe on thus, you will kill your ſelfe,
And 'tis not wiſedome thus to ſecond griefe,
Againſt your ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I pray thee ceaſe thy counſaile,
Which falls into mine eares as profitleſſe,
As water in a ſiue: giue not me counſaile,
Nor let no comfort delight mine eare,
But ſuch a one whoſe wrongs doth ſute with mine.
Bring me a father that ſo lou'd his childe,
Whoſe ioy of her is ouer-whelmed like mine,
And bid him ſpeake of patience,
Meaſure his woe the length and bredth of mine,
And let it anſwere euery ſtraine for ſtraine,
As thus for thus, and ſuch a griefe for ſuch,
In euery lineament, branch, ſhape, and forme:
If ſuch a one will ſmile and ſtroke his beard,
And ſorrow, wagge, crie hem, when he ſhould grone,
Patch griefe with prouerbs, make misfortune drunke,
With candle-waſters: bring him yet to me,
And I of him will gather patience:
But there is no ſuch man for brother, men
Can counſaile, and ſpeake comfort to that griefe,
Which they themſelues not feele, but to ſting it,
Their counſaile turnes to paſſion, which before,
Would giue preceptiall medicine to rage,
Fetter ſtrong madneſſe in a ſilken thred,
Charme ache with ayre, and agony with words,
No, no, 'tis all mens office, to ſpeake patience
To thoſe that wring vnder the load of ſorrow:
But no mans vertue nor ſufficiencie
To be ſo morall, when he ſhall endure
The like himſelfe: therefore giue me no counſaile,
My griefs cry lowder then aduertiſement.

sp.speaker: Broth.
sp.p: Therein do men from children nothing differ.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.l: I pray thee peace, I will be fleſh and bloud,
For there was neuer yet Philoſopher,
That could endure the tooth-ake patiently,
How euer they haue writ the ſtile of gods,
And made a puſh at chance and ſufferance.

sp.speaker: Brother.
sp.l: Yet bend not all the harme vpon your ſelfe,
Make thoſe that doe offend you, ſuffer too.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: There thou ſpeak'ſt reaſon, nay I will doe ſo,
My ſoule doth tell me, Hero is belied,
And that ſhall Claudio know, ſo ſhall the Prince,
And all of them that thus diſhonour her.

sp.speaker: Brot.
sp.p: Here comes the Prince and Claudio haſtily.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Good den, good den.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Good day to both of you.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Heare you my Lords?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: We haue ſome haſte Leonato.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Some haſte my Lord! wel, fareyouwel my Lord,
Are you ſo haſty now? well, all is one.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Nay, do not quarrell with vs, good old man.

sp.speaker: Brot.
sp.l: If he could rite himſelfe with quarrelling,
Some of vs would lie low.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: Who wrongs him?

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Marry yu doſt wrong me, thou diſſembler, thou:
Nay, neuer lay thy hand vpon thy ſword,
I feare thee not.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: Marry beſhrew my hand,
If it ſhould giue your age ſuch cauſe of feare,
Infaith my hand meant nothing to my ſword.

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.l: Tuſh, tuſh, man, neuer fleere and ieſt at me,
I ſpeake not like a do • ard, nor a foole,
As vnder priuiledge of age to bragge,
What I haue done being yong, or what would doe,
Were I not old, know Claudio to thy head,
Thou haſt ſo wrong'd my innocent childe and me,
That I am forc'd to lay my reuerence by,
And with grey haires and bruiſe of many daies,
Doe challenge thee to triall of a man,
I ſay thou haſt belied mine innocent childe.
Thy ſlander hath gone through and through her heart,
And ſhe lies buried with her anceſtors:
O in a tombe where neuer ſcandall ſlept,
Saue this of hers, fram'd by thy villanie.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: My villany?

sp.speaker: Leonato.
sp.p: Thine Claudio, thine I ſay.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: You ſay not right old man.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: My Lord, my Lord,
Ile proue it on his body if he dare,
Deſpight his nice fence, and his actiue practiſe,
His Maie of youth, and bloome of luſtihood.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: Away, I will not haue to do with you.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Canſt thou ſo daffe me? thou haſt kild my child,
If thou kilſt me, boy, thou ſhalt kill a man.

sp.speaker: Bro.
sp.l: He ſhall kill two of vs, and men indeed,
But that's no matter, let him kill one firſt:
Win me and weare me, let him anſwere me,
Come follow me boy, come ſir boy, come follow me
Sir boy, ile whip you from your foyning fence,
Nay, as I am a gentleman, I will.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Brother.

sp.speaker: Brot.
sp.l: Content your ſelf, God knows I lou'd my neece,
And ſhe is dead, ſlander'd to death by villaines,
That dare as well anſwer a man indeede,
As I dare take a ſerpent by the tongue.
Boyes, apes, braggarts, Iackes, milke-ſops.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Brother Anthony.

sp.speaker: Brot.
sp.l: Hold you content, what man? I know them, yea
And what they weigh, euen to the vtmoſt ſcruple,
Scambling, out-facing, faſhion-monging boyes,
That lye, and cog, and flout, depraue, and ſlander,
Goe antiquely, and ſhow outward hidiouſneſſe,
And ſpeake of halfe a dozen dang'rous words,
How they might hurt their enemies, if they durſt.
And this is all.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: But brother Anthonie.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Come, 'tis no matter,
Do not you meddle, let me deale in this.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.l: Gentlemen both, we will not wake your patience
My heart is ſorry for your daughters death:
But on my honour ſhe was charg'd with nothing
But what was true, and very full of proofe.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: My Lord, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: I will not heare you.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: No come brother, away, I will be heard.

sp.speaker: Bro.
sp.p: And ſhall, or ſome of vs will ſmart for it.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: See, ſee, here comes the man we went to ſeeke.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Now ſignior, what newes?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Good day my Lord.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Welcome ſignior, you are almoſt come to part almoſt a fray.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Wee had likt to haue had our two noſes ſnapt off with two old men without teeth.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Leonato and his brother, what think'ſt thou? had wee fought, I doubt we ſhould haue beene too yong for them.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: In a falſe quarrell there is no true valour, I came to ſeeke you both.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: We haue beene vp and downe to ſeeke thee, for we are high proofe melancholly, and would faine haue it beaten away, wilt thou vſe thy wit?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: It is in my ſcabberd, ſhall I draw it?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Doeſt thou weare thy wit by thy ſide?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Neuer any did ſo, though verie many haue been beſide their wit, I will bid thee drawe, as we do the minſtrels, draw to pleaſure vs.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: As I am an honeſt man he lookes pale, art thou ſicke, or angrie?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: What, courage man: what though care kil'd a cat, thou haſt mettle enough in thee to kill care.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Sir, I ſhall meete your wit in the careere, and you charge it againſt me, I pray you chuſe another ſubiect.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Nay then giue him another ſtaffe, this laſt was broke croſſe.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: By this light, he changes more and more, I thinke he be angrie indeede.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: If he be, he knowes how to turne his girdle.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Shall I ſpeake a word in your eare?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: God bleſſe me from a challenge.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: You are a villaine, I ieſt not, I will make it good how you dare, with what you dare, and when you dare: do me right, or I will proteſt your cowardiſe: you haue kill'd a ſweete Ladie, and her death ſhall fall heauie on you, let me heare from you.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Well, I will meete you, ſo I may haue good cheare.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: What, a feaſt, a feaſt?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: I faith I thanke him, he hath bid me to a calues head and a Capon, the which if I doe not carue moſt curiouſly, ſay my knife's naught, ſhall I not finde a woodcocke too?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Sir, your wit ambles well, it goes eaſily.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Ile tell thee how Beatrice prais'd thy wit the other day: I ſaid thou hadſt a fine wit: true ſaies ſhe, a fine little one: no ſaid I, a great wit: right ſaies ſhee, a great groſſe one: nay ſaid I, a good wit: iuſt ſaid ſhe, it hurts no body: nay ſaid I, the gentleman is wiſe: certain ſaid ſhe, a wiſe gentleman: nay ſaid I, he hath the tongues: that I beleeue ſaid ſhee, for hee ſwore a thing to me on munday night, which he forſwore on tueſday morning: there's a double tongue, there's two tongues: thus did ſhee an howre together tranſ-ſhape thy particular vertues, yet at laſt ſhe concluded with a ſigh, thou waſt the propreſt man in Italie.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: For the which ſhe wept heartily, and ſaid ſhee car'd not.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Yea that ſhe did, but yet for all that, and if ſhee did not hate him deadlie, ſhee would loue him dearely, the old mans daughter told vs all.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: All, all, and moreouer, God ſaw him vvhen he was hid in the garden.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: But when ſhall we ſet the ſauage Bulls hornes on the ſenſible Benedicks head?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Yea and text vnder-neath, heere dwells Benedicke the married man.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Fare you well, Boy, you know my minde, I will leaue you now to your goſſep-like humor, you breake ieſts as braggards do their blades, which God be thanked hurt not: my Lord, for your manie courteſies I thank you, I muſt diſcontinue your companie, your brother the Baſtard is fled from Meſſina: you haue among you, kill'd a ſweet and innocent Ladie: for my Lord Lackebeard there, he and I ſhall meete, and till then peace be with him.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: He is in earneſt.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: In moſt profound earneſt, and Ile warrant you, for the loue of Beatrice.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: And hath challeng'd thee.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Moſt ſincerely.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: What a prettie thing man is, when he goes in his doublet and hoſe, and leaues off his wit.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: He is then a Giant to an Ape, but then is an Ape a Doctor to ſuch a man.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: But ſoft you, let me be, plucke vp my heart, and be ſad, did he not ſay my brother was fled?

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: Come you ſir, if iuſtice cannot tame you, ſhee ſhall nere weigh more reaſons in her ballance, nay, and you be a curſing hypocrite once, you muſt be lookt to.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: How now, two of my brothers men bound? Borachio one.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Harken after their offence my Lord▪

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Officers, what offence haue theſe men done?

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: Marrie ſir, they haue committed falſe report, moreouer they haue ſpoken vntruths, ſecondarily they are ſlanders, ſixt and laſtly, they haue belyed a Ladie, thirdly, they haue verified vniuſt things, and to conclude they are lying knaues.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Firſt I aske thee what they haue done, thirdlie I aske thee vvhat's their offence, ſixt and laſtlie why they are committed, and to conclude, what you lay to their charge.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Rightlie reaſoned, and in his owne diuiſion, and by my troth there's one meaning vvell ſuted.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Who haue you offended maſters, that you are thus bound to your anſwer? this learned Conſtable is too cunning to be vnderſtood, vvhat's your offence?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Sweete Prince, let me go no farther to mine anſwere: do you heare me, and let this Count kill mee: I haue deceiued euen your verie eies: vvhat your wiſedomes could not diſcouer, theſe ſhallow fooles haue brought to light, vvho in the night ouerheard me confeſſing to this man, how Don Iohn your brother incenſed me to ſlander the Ladie Hero, how you were brought into the Orchard, and ſaw me court Margaret in Heroes garments, how you diſgrac'd her vvhen you ſhould marrie her: my villanie they haue vpon record, vvhich I had rather ſeale vvith my death, then repeate ouer to my ſhame: the Ladie is dead vpon mine and my maſters falſe accuſation: and briefelie, I deſire nothing but the reward of a villaine.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Runs not this ſpeech like yron through your bloud?

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: I haue drunke poiſon whiles he vtter'd it.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: But did my Brother ſet thee on to this?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Yea, and paid me richly for the practiſe of it.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: He is compos'd and fram'd of treacherie,
And fled he is vpon this villanie.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Sweet Hero, now thy image doth appeare
In the rare ſemblance that I lou'd it firſt.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: Come, bring away the plaintiffes, by this time our Sexton hath reformed Signior Leonato of the matter: and maſters, do not forget to ſpecifie when time & place ſhall ſerue, that I am an Aſſe.

sp.speaker: Con. 2.
sp.p: Here, here comes maſter Signior Leonato, and the Sexton too.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: Which is the villaine? let me ſee his eies,
That when I note another man like him,
I may auoide him: vvhich of theſe is he?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: If you vvould know your wronger, looke on me.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Art thou thou the ſlaue that with thy breath haſt kild mine innocent childe?

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.p: Yea, euen I alone.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: No, not ſo villaine, thou belieft thy ſelfe,
Here ſtand a paire of honourable men,
A third is fled that had a hand in it:
I thanke you Princes for my daughters death,
Record it with your high and worthie deedes,
'Twas brauely done, if you bethinke you of it.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: I know not how to pray your patience,
Yet I muſt ſpeake, chooſe your reuenge your ſelfe,
Impoſe me to what penance your inuention
Can lay vpon my ſinne, yee ſinn'd I not,
But in miſtaking.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: By my ſoule nor I,
And yet to ſatisfie this good old man,
I vvould bend vnder anie heauie vvaight,
That heele enioyne me to.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: I cannot bid you bid my daughter liue,
That vvere impoſſible, but I praie you both,
Poſſeſſe the people in Meſſina here,
How innocent ſhe died, and if your loue
Can labour aught in ſad inuention,
Hang her an epitaph vpon her toomb,
And ſing it to her bones, ſing it to night:
To morrow morning come you to my houſe,
And ſince you could not be my ſonne in law,
Be yet my Nephew: my brother hath a daughter,
Almoſt the copie of my childe that's dead,
And ſhe alone is heire to both of vs,
Giue her the right you ſhould haue giu'n her coſin,
And ſo dies my reuenge.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: O noble ſir!
Your ouer kindneſſe doth wring teares from me,
I do embrace your offer, and diſpoſe
For henceforth of poore Claudio.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: To morrow then I will expect your comming,
To night I take my leaue, this naughtie man
Shall face to face be brought to Margaret,
Who I beleeue was packt in all this wrong,
Hired to it by your brother.

sp.speaker: Bor.
sp.l: No by my ſoule ſhe was not,
Nor knew not what ſhe did when ſhe ſpoke to me,
But alwaies hath bin iuſt and vertuous,
In anie thing that I do know by her.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: Moreouer ſir, which indeede is not vnder white and black, this plaintiffe here, the offendour did call mee aſſe, I beſeech you let it be remembred in his puniſhment, and alſo the vvatch heard them talke of one Deformed, they ſay he weares a key in his eare and a lock hanging by it, and borrowes monie in Gods name, the which he hath vs'd ſo long, and neuer paied, that now men grow hard-harted and will lend nothing for Gods ſake: praie you examine him vpon that point.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: I thanke thee for thy care and honeſt paines.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: Your vvorſhip ſpeakes like a moſt thankefull and reuerend youth, and I praiſe God for you.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: There's for thy paines.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: God ſaue the foundation.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Goe, I diſcharge thee of thy priſoner, and I thanke thee.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: I leaue an arrant knaue vvith your vvorſhip, which I beſeech your worſhip to correct your ſelfe, for the example of others: God keepe your vvorſhip, I wiſh your worſhip vvell, God reſtore you to health, I humblie giue you leaue to depart, and if a merrie meeting may be wiſht, God prohibite it: come neighbour.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Vntill to morrow morning, Lords, farewell.

sp.speaker: Brot.
sp.p: Farewell my Lords, vve looke for you to morrow.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: We will not faile.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: To night ile mourne with Hero:

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Bring you theſe fellowes on, weel talke vvith Margaret, how her acquaintance grew vvith this lewd fellow.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Praie thee ſweete Miſtris Margaret, deſerue vvell at my hands, by helping mee to the ſpeech of Beatrice.

sp.speaker: Mar.
