sp.p: Will you then write me a Sonnet in praiſe of my beautie?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: In ſo high a ſtile Margaret, that no man liuing ſhall come ouer it, for in moſt comely truth thou deſerueſt it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: To haue no man come ouer me, why, ſhall I alwaies keepe below ſtaires?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Thy wit is as quicke as the grey-hounds mouth, it catches.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: And yours, as blunt as the Fencers foiles, which hit, but hurt not.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: A moſt manly wit Margaret, it will not hurt a woman: and ſo I pray thee call Beatrice, I giue thee the bucklers.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Giue vs the ſwords, wee haue bucklers of our owne.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: If you vſe them Margaret, you muſt put in the pikes with a vice, and they are dangerous weapons for Maides.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Well, I will call Beatrice to you, who I thinke hath legges.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: And therefore will come. The God of loue that ſits aboue, and knowes me, and knowes me, how pittifull I deſerue. I meane in ſinging, but in louing, Leander the good ſwimmer, Tro • lous the firſt imploier of pandars, and a whole booke full of theſe quondam carpet-mongers, whoſe name yet runne ſmoothly in the euen rode of a blanke verſe, why they were neuer ſo truely turned ouer and ouer as my poore ſelfe in loue: marrie I cannot ſhew it rime, I haue tried, I can finde out no rime to Ladie but babie, an innocent rime: for ſcorne, horne, a hard time: for ſchoole foole, a babling time: verie ominous endings, no, I was not borne vnder a riming Plannet, for I cannot wooe in feſtiuall tearmes: Enter Beatrice. ſweete Beatrice would'ſt thou come when I cal'd thee?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Yea Signior, and depart when you bid me.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: O ſtay but till then.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Then, is ſpoken: fare you well now, and yet ere I goe, let me goe with that I came, which is, with knowing what hath paſt betweene you and Claudio.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Onely foule words, and thereupon I will kiſſe thee.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Foule words is but foule wind, and foule wind is but foule breath, and foule breath is noiſome, therefore I will depart vnkiſt.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Thou haſt frighted the word out of his right ſence, ſo forcible is thy wit, but I muſt tell thee plainely, Claudio vndergoes my challenge, and either I muſt ſhortly heare from him, or I will ſubſcribe him a coward, and I pray thee now tell me, for which of my bad parts didſt thou firſt fall in loue with me?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: For them all together, which maintain'd ſo politique a ſtate of euill, that they will not admit any good part to intermingle with them: but for which of my good parts did you firſt ſuffer loue for me?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Suffer loue! a good epithite, I do ſuffer loue indeede, for I loue thee againſt my will.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: In ſpight of your heart I think, alas poore heart, if you ſpight it for my ſake, I will ſpight it for yours, for I will neuer loue that which my friend hates.

sp.speaker: Bened.
sp.p: Thou and I are too wiſe to wooe peaceablie.

sp.speaker: Bea.
sp.p: It appeares not in this confeſſion, there's not one wiſe man among twentie that will praiſe himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: An old, an old inſtance Beatrice, that liu'd in the time of good neighbours, if a man doe not erect in this age his owne tombe ere he dies, hee ſhall liue no longer in monuments, then the Bels ring, & the Widdow weepes.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: And how long is that thinke you?

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Queſtion, why an hower in clamour and a quarter in rhewme, therfore is it moſt expedient for the wife, if Don worme (his conſcience) finde no impediment to the contrarie, to be the trumpet of his owne vertues, as I am to my ſelfe ſo much for praiſing my ſelfe, who I my ſelfe will beare witneſſe is praiſe worthie, and now tell me, how doth your coſin?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Verie ill.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: And how doe you?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Verie ill too.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Serue God, loue me, and mend, there will I leaue you too, for here comes one in haſte.

sp.speaker: Vrſ.
sp.p: Madam, you muſt come to your Vncle, yonders old coile at home, it is prooued my Ladie Hero hath bin falſelie accuſde, the Prince and Claudio mightilie abuſde, and Don Iohn is the author of all, who is fled and gone: will you come preſentlie?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Will you go heare this newes Signior?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: I will hue in thy heart, die in thy lap, and be buried in thy eies: and moreouer, I will goe with thee to thy Vncles.

div.stage: Enter Claudio, Prince, and three or foure with Tapers.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Is this the monument of Leonato?

sp.speaker: Lord.
sp.p: It is my Lord.

l.hi: Done to death by ſlanderous tongues,

sp.l: Was the Hero that here lies:

l.hi: Death in guerdon of her wrongs,

sp.l: Giues her fame which neuer dies:

l.hi: So the life that dyed with ſhame,
Liues in death with glorious fame.
Hang thou there vpon the tombe,
Praiſing her when I am dombe.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Now muſick ſound & ſing your ſolemn hymne

lg.head: Song.
lg.l: Pardon goddeſſe of the night,
Thoſe that ſlew thy virgin knight,
For the which with ſongs of woe,
Round about her tombe they goe:
Midnight aſſiſt our mone, helpe vs to ſigh and grone
Heauily, heauily.
Graues yawne and yeelde your dead,
Till death be vttered,
Heauenly, heauenly.

sp.speaker: Lo.
sp.p: Now vnto thy bones good night, yeerely will I do this right.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Good morrow maſters, put your Torches out,
The wolues haue preied, and looke, the gentle day
Before the wheeles of Phoebus, round about
Dapples the drowſie Eaſt with ſpots of grey:
Thanks to you all, and leaue vs, fare you well.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Good morrow maſters, each his ſeuerall way.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Come let vs hence, and put on other weedes,
And then to Leonatoes we will goe.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: And Hymen now with luckier iſſue ſpeeds,
Then this for whom we rendred vp this woe.

div.stage: Enter Leonato, Bene. Marg. Vrſula, old man, Frier, Hero.

sp.speaker: Frier.
sp.p: Did I not tell you ſhe was innocent?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: So are the Prince and Claudio who accus'd her,
Vpon the errour that you heard debated:
But Margaret was in ſome fault for this,
Although againſt her will as it appeares,
In the true courſe of all the queſtion.

sp.speaker: Old.
sp.p: Well, I am glad that all things ſort ſo well.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.l: And ſo am I, being elſe by faith enforc'd
To call young Claudio to a reckoning for it.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Well daughter, and you gentlewomen all,
Withdraw into a chamber by your ſelues,
And when I ſend for you, come hither mask'd:
The Prince and Claudio promis'd by this howre
To viſit me, you know your office Brother,
You muſt be father to your brothers daughter,
And giue her to young Claudio.

sp.speaker: Old.
sp.p: Which I will doe with confirm'd countenance.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Frier, I muſt intreat your paines, I thinke.

sp.speaker: Frier.
sp.p: To doe what Signior?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.l: To binde me, or vndoe me, one of them:
Signior Leonato, truth it is good Signior,
Your neece regards me with an eye of fauour.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: That eye my daughter lent her, 'tis moſt true.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: And I doe with an eye of loue require her.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: The ſight whereof I thinke you had from me,
From Claudio, and the Prince, but what's your will?

sp.speaker: Bened.
sp.l: Your anſwer ſir is Enigmaticall,
But for my will, my will is, your good will
May ſtand with ours, this day to be conioyn'd,
In the ſtate of honourable marriage,
In which (good Frier) I ſhall deſire your helpe.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: My heart is with your liking.

sp.speaker: Frier.
sp.p: And my helpe.

div.stage: Enter Prince and Claudio, with attendants.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Good morrow to this faire aſſembly.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.l: Good morrow Prince, good morrow Claudio:
We heere attend you, are you yet determin'd,
To day to marry with my brothers daughter?

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.p: Ile hold my minde were ſhe an Ethiope.

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: Call her forth brother, heres the Frier ready.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Good morrow Benedike, why what's the matter?
That you haue ſuch a Februarie face,
So full of froſt, of ſtorme, and clowdineſſe.

sp.speaker: Claud.
sp.l: I thinke he thinkes vpon the ſauage bull:
Tuſh, feare not man, wee'll tip thy hornes with gold,
And all Europa ſhall reioyce at thee,
As once Europa did at luſty Ioue,
When he would play the noble beaſt in loue.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.l: Bull Ioue ſir, had an amiable low,
And ſome ſuch ſtrange bull leapt your fathers Cow,
A got a Calfe in that ſame noble ſeat,
Much like to you, for you haue iuſt his b • eat.

div.stage: Enter brother, Hero, Beatrice, Margaret, Vrſula.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.l: For this I owe you: here comes other recknings.
Which is the Lady I muſt ſeize vpon?

sp.speaker: Leo.
sp.p: This ſame is ſhe, and I • oe giue you her.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: Why thou ſhe's mine, ſweet let me ſee your face.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.l: No that you ſhal not, till you take her hand,
Before this Frier, and ſweare to marry her.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: Giue me your hand before this holy Frier,
I am your husband if you like of me.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: And when I liu'd I was your other wife,
And when you lou'd, you were my other husband.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Another Hero?

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: Nothing certaine • .
One Hero died, but I doe liue,
And ſurely as I liue, I am a maid.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: The former Hero, Hero that is dead.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Shee died my Lord, but whiles her ſlander liu'd.

sp.speaker: Frier.
sp.l: All this amazement can I qualifie,
When after that the holy rites are ended,
Ile tell you largely of faire Heroes death:
Meane time let wonder ſeeme familiar,
And to the chappell let vs preſently.

sp.speaker: Ben.
sp.p: Soft and faire Frier, which is Beatrice?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: I anſwer to that name, what is your will?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Doe not you loue me?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Why no, no more then reaſon.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Why then your Vncle, and the Prince, & Claudio, haue beene deceiued, they ſwore you did.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: Doe not you loue mee?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Troth no, no more then reaſon.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.l: Why then my Coſin Margaret and Ʋrſula
Are much deceiu'd, for they did ſweare you did.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: They ſwore you were almoſt ſicke for me.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: They ſwore you were wel-nye dead for me.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Tis no matter, then you doe not loue me?

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: No truly, but in friendly recompence.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Come Coſin, I am ſure you loue the gentlemā.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.l: And Ile be ſworne vpon't, that he loues her,
For heres a paper written in his hand,
A halting ſonnet of his owne pure braine,
Faſhioned to Beatrice.

sp.speaker: Hero.
sp.l: And heeres another,
Writ in my coſins hand, ſtolne from her pocket,
Containing her affection vnto Benedicke.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: A miracle, here's our owne hands againſt our hearts: come I will haue thee, but by this light I take thee for pittie.

sp.speaker: Beat.
sp.p: I would not denie you, but by this good day, I yeeld vpon great perſwaſion, & partly to ſaue your life, for I was told, you were in a conſumption.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Peace I will ſtop your mouth.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: How doſt thou Benedicke the married man?

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Ile tell thee what Prince: a Colledge of witte-crackers cannot flout mee out of my humour, doſt thou think I care for a Satyre or an Epigram? no, if a man will be beaten with braines, a ſhall weare nothing handſome about him: in briefe, ſince I do purpoſe to marry, I will thinke nothing to any purpoſe that the world can ſay againſt it, and therefore neuer flout at me, for I haue ſaid againſt it: for man is a giddy thing, and this is my concluſion: for thy part Claudio, I did thinke to haue beaten thee, but in that thou art like to be my kinſman, liue vnbruis'd, and loue my couſin.

sp.speaker: Cla.
sp.p: I had well hop'd yu wouldſt haue denied Beatrice, yt I might haue cudgel'd thee out of thy ſingle life, to make thee a double dealer, which out of queſtiō thou wilt be, if my Couſin do not looke exceeding narrowly to thee.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Come, come, we are friends, let's haue a dance ere we are married, that we may lighten our own hearts, and our wiues heeles.

sp.speaker: Leon.
sp.p: Wee'll haue dancing afterward.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Firſt, of my vvord, therfore play muſick. Prince, thou art ſad, get, thee a vvife, get thee a vvife, there is no ſtaff more reuerend then one tipt with horn.

sp.speaker: Meſſen.
sp.l: My Lord, your brother Iohn is tane in flight,
And brought with armed men backe to Meſſina.

sp.speaker: Bene.
sp.p: Thinke not on him till to morrow, ile deuiſe thee braue puniſhments for him: ſtrike vp Pipers.

div.head: Actus primus.
div.stage: Enter Ferdinand King of Nauarre, Berowne, Longauill, and Dumane.

sp.speaker: Ferdinand.
sp.l: LEt Fame, that all hunt after in their liues,
Liue regiſtred vpon our brazen Tombes,
And then grace vs in the diſgrace of death:
when ſpight of cormorant deuouring Time,
Th' endeuour of this preſent breath may buy:
That honour which ſhall bate his ſythes keene edge,
And make vs heyres of all eternitie:
Therefore braue Conquerours, for ſo you are,
That warre againſt your owne affections,
And the huge Armie of the worlds deſires.
Our late edict ſhall ſtrongly ſtand in force,
Nauar ſhall be the wonder of the world.
Our Court ſhall be a little Achademe,
Still and contemplatiue in liuing Art.
You three, Berowne, Dumaine, and Longauill,
Haue ſworne for three yeeres terme, to liue with me:
My fellow Schollers, and to keepe thoſe ſtatutes
That are recorded in this ſcedule heere.
Your oathes are paſt, and now ſubſcribe your names:
That his owne hand may ſtrike his honour downe,
That violates the ſmalleſt branch heerein:
If you are arm'd to doe, as ſworne to do,
Subſcribe to your deepe oathes, and keepe it to.

sp.speaker: Longauill.
sp.l: I am reſolu'd, 'tis but a three yeeres faſt:
The minde ſhall banquet, though the body pine,
Fat paunches haue leane pates: and dainty bits,
Make rich the ribs, but bankerout the wits.

sp.speaker: Dumane.
sp.l: My louing Lord, Dumane is mortified,
The groſſer manner of theſe worlds delights,
He throwes vpon the groſſe worlds baſer ſlaues:
To loue, to wealth, to pompe, I pine and die,
With all theſe liuing in Philoſophie.

sp.speaker: Berowne.
sp.l: I can but ſay their proteſtation ouer,
So much, deare Liege, I haue already ſworne,
That is, to liue and ſtudy heere three yeeres.
But there are other ſtrict obſeruances:
As not to ſee a woman in that terme,
Which I hope well is not enrolled there.
And one day in a weeke to touch no foode:
And but one meale on euery day beſide:
The which I hope is not enrolled there.
And then to ſleepe but three houres in the night,
And not be ſeene to winke of all the day.
When I was wont to thinke no harme all night,
And make a darke night too of halfe the day:
Which I hope well is not enrolled there.
O, theſe are barren taskes, too hard to keepe,
Not to ſee Ladies, ſtudy, faſt, not ſleepe.

sp.speaker: Ferd.
sp.p: Your oath is paſt, to paſſe away from theſe.

sp.speaker: Berow.
sp.l: Let me ſay no my Liedge, and if you pleaſe,
I onely ſwore to ſtudy with your grace,
And ſtay heere in your Court for three yeeres ſpace.

sp.speaker: Longa.
sp.p: You ſwore to that Berowne, and to the reſt.

sp.speaker: Berow.
sp.l: By yea and nay ſir, than I ſwore in ieſt.
What is the end of ſtudy, let me know?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.p: Why that to know which elſe wee ſhould not know.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Things hid & bard (you meane) frō cōmon ſenſe.

sp.speaker: Ferd.
sp.p: I, that is ſtudies god-like recompence.

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.l: Come on then, I will ſweare to ſtudie ſo,
To know the thing I am forbid to know:
As thus, to ſtudy where I well may dine,
When I to faſt expreſſely am forbid.
Or ſtudie where to meet ſome Miſtreſſe fine,
When Miſtreſſes from common ſenſe are hid.
Or hauing ſworne too hard a keeping oath,
Studie to breake it, and not breake my troth.
If ſtudies gaine be thus, and this be ſo,
Studie knowes that which yet it doth not know,
Sweare me to this, and I will nere ſay no.

sp.speaker: Ferd.
sp.l: Theſe be the ſtops that hinder ſtudie quite,
And traine our intellects to vaine delight.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Why? all delights are vaine, and that moſt vaine
Which with paine purchas'd, doth inherit paine,
As painefully to poare vpon a Booke,
To ſeeke the light of truth, while truth the while
Doth falſely blinde the eye-ſight of his looke:
Light ſeeeking light, doth light of light beguile:
So ere you finde where light in darkeneſſe lies,
Your light growes darke by loſing of your eyes.
Studie me how to pleaſe the eye indeede,
By fixing it vpon a fairer eye,
Who dazling ſo, that eye ſhall be his heed,
And giue him light that it was blinded by.
Studie is like the heauens glorious Sunne,
That will not be deepe ſearch'd with ſawcy lookes:
Small haue continuall plodders euer wonne,
Saue baſe authoritie from others Bookes.
Theſe earthly Godfathers of heauens lights,
That giue a name to euery fixed Starre,
Haue no more profit of their ſhining nights,
Then thoſe that walke and wot not what they are.
Too much to know, is to know nought but fame▪
And euery Godfather can giue a name.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.p: How well hee's read, to reaſon againſt reading.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Proceeded well, to ſtop all good proceeding.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: Hee weedes the corne, and ſtill lets grow the weeding.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: The Spring is neare when greene geeſſe are a breeding.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: How followes that?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Fit in his place and time.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: In reaſon nothing.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Something then in rime.

sp.speaker: Ferd.
sp.l: Berowne is like an enuious ſneaping Froſt,
That bites the firſt borne infants of the Spring.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Wel, ſay I am, why ſhould proud Summer boaſt,
Before the Birds haue any cauſe to ſing?
Why ſhould I ioy in any abortiue birth?
At Chriſtmas I no more deſire a Roſe,
Then wiſh a Snow in Mayes new fangled ſhowes:
But like of each thing that in ſeaſon growes.
So you to ſtudie now it is too late,
That were to clymbe ore the houſe to vnlocke the gate.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.p: Well, fit you out: go home Berowne: adue.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: No my good Lord, I haue ſworn to ſtay with you.
And though I haue for barbariſme ſpoke more,
Then for that Angell knowledge you can ſay,
Yet confident Ile keepe what I haue ſworne,
And bide the pennance of each three yeares day.
Giue me the paper, let me reade the ſame,
And to the ſtricteſt decrees Ile write my name.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.p: How well this yeelding reſcues thee from ſhame.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Item. That no woman ſhall come within a mile of my Court.
Hath this bin proclaimed?

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: Foure dayes agoe.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Let's ſee the penaltie.
On paine of looſing her tongue.
Who deuis'd this penaltie?

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: Marry that did I.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Sweete Lord, and why?

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: To fright them hence with that dread penaltie, A dangerous law againſt gentilitie. Item, If any man be ſeene to talke with a woman within the tearme of three yeares, hee ſhall indure ſuch publique ſhame as the reſt of the Court ſhall poſſibly deuiſe.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: This Article my Liedge your ſelfe muſt breake,
For well you know here comes is Embaſſie
The French Kings daughter, with your ſelfe to ſpeake:
A Maide of grace and compleate maieſtie,
About ſurrender vp of Aquitaine:
To her decrepit, ſicke, and bed-rid Father.
Therefore this Article is made in vaine,
Or vainly comes th' admired Princeſſe hither.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: What ſay you Lords?
Why, this was quite forgot.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: So Studie euermore is ouerſhot,
While it doth ſtudy to haue what it would,
It doth forget to doe the thing it ſhould:
And when it hath the thing it hunteth moſt,
'Tis won as townes with fire, ſo won, ſo loſt.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: We muſt of force diſpence with this Decree,
She muſt lye here on meere neceſſitie.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Neceſſity will make vs all forſworne
Three thouſand times within this three yeeres ſpace:
For euery man with his affects is borne,
Not by might maſtred, but by ſpeciall grace.
If I breake faith, this word ſhall breake for me,
I am forſworne on meere neceſſitie.
So to the Lawes at large I write my name,
And he that breakes them in the leaſt degree,
Stands in attainder of eternall ſhame.
Suggeſtions are to others as to me:
But I beleeue although I ſeeme ſo loth,
I am the laſt that will laſt keepe his oth.
But is there no quicke recreation granted?

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.l: I that there is, our Court you know is hanted
With a refined trauailer of Spaine,
A man in all the worlds new faſhion planted,
That hath a mint of phraſes in his braine:
One, who the muſicke of his owne vaine tongue,
Doth rauiſh like inchanting harmonie:
A man of complements whom right and wrong
Haue choſe as vmpire of their mutinie.
This childe of fancie that Armado hight,
For interim to our ſtudies ſhall relate,
In high-borne words the worth of many a Knight:
From tawnie Spaine loſt in the worlds debate.
How you delight my Lords, I know not I,
But I proteſt I loue to heare him lie,
And I will vſe him for my Minſtrelſie.

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.l: Armado is a moſt illuſtrious wight,
A man of fire, new words, faſhions owne Knight.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: Coſtard the ſwaine and he, ſhall be our ſport,
And ſo to ſtudie, three yeeres is but ſhort.

div.stage: Enter a Conſtable with Coſtard with a Letter.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: Which is the Dukes owne perſon.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: This fellow, What would'ſt?

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: I my ſelfe reprehend his owne perſon, for I am his graces Tharborough: But I would ſee his own perſon in fleſh and blood.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: This is he.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.l: Signeor Arme, Arme commends you:
Ther's villanie abroad, this letter will tell you more.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Sir the Contempts thereof are as touching mee.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.p: A letter from the magnificent Armado.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: How low ſoeuer the matter, I hope in God for high words.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: A high hope for a low heauen, God grant vs patience.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: To heare, or forbeare hearing.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: To heare meekely ſir, and to laugh moderately, or to forbeare both.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Well ſir, be it as the ſtile ſhall giue vs cauſe to clime in the merrineſſe.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: The matter is to me ſir, as concerning Iaquenetta.
The manner of it is, I was taken with the manner.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: In what manner?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: In manner and forme following ſir all thoſe three. I was ſeene with her in the Mannor houſe, ſitting with her vpon the Forme, and taken following her into the Parke: which put to gether, is in manner and forme following. Now ſir for the manner; It is the manner of a man to ſpeake to a woman, for the forme in ſome forme.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: For the following ſir.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: As it ſhall follow in my correction, and God defend the right.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.p: Will you heare this Letter with attention?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: As we would heare an Oracle.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Such is the ſimplicitie of man to harken after the fleſh.

sp.speaker: Ferdinand.
sp.p: GReat Deputie, the Welk • ns Vicegerent, and ſole dominator of Nauar, my ſoules earths God, and bodies foſtring patrone:

sp.speaker: Coſt.
sp.p: Not a vvord of Coſtard yet.

sp.speaker: Coſt.
sp.p: It may be ſo: but if he ſay it is ſo, he is in telling true: but ſo.

sp.speaker: Ferd.
sp.p: Peace,

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Be to me, and euery man that dares not fight.

sp.speaker: Ferd.
sp.p: No words,

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Of other mens ſecrets I beſeech you.

sp.speaker: Ferd.
sp.p: So it is beſieged with ſable coloured melancholie, I did commend the blacke oppreſſing humour to the moſt wholeſome Phyſicke of thy health-giuing ayre: And as I am a Gentleman, betooke my ſelfe to walke: the time When? about the ſixt houre, When beaſts moſt graſe, birds beſt pecke, and men ſit downe to that nouriſhment which is called ſupper: So much for the time When. Now for the ground Which? which I meane I walkt vpon, it is ycliped, Thy Parke. Then for the place Where? where I meane I did encounter that obſcene and moſt prepoſterous euent that draweth from my ſnow-white pen the ebon coloured Inke, which heere thou vieweſt, beholdeſt, ſuruayeſt, or ſeeſt. But to the place Where? It standeth North North-eaſt and by Eaſt from the Weſt corner of thy curious knotted garden; There did I ſee that low ſpirited Swaine, that baſe Minow of thy myrth, (Clown. Mee?) that vnletered ſmall knowing ſoule, (Clow Me?) that ſhallow vaſſall (Clow. Still mee?) which as I remember, hight Coſtard, (Clow. O me) ſorted and conſorted contrary to thy eſtabliſhed proclaymed Edict and Continet, Cannon: Which with, ô with, but with this I paſſion to ſay wherewith:

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: With a Wench.

sp.speaker: Ferd.
sp.p: With a childe of our Grandmother E • e, a female; or for thy more ſweet vnderſtanding a woman: him, I (as my euer eſteemed dutie prickes me on) haue ſent to thee, to receiue the meed of puniſhment by thy ſweet Graces Officer Anthony Dull, a man of good repute, carriage, bearing, & estimation.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: Me, an't ſhall pleaſe you? I am Anthony Dull.

sp.speaker: Ferd.
sp.p: For Iaquenetta (ſo is the weaker veſſell called) which I apprehended with the aforeſaid Swaine, I keeper her as a veſſell of thy Lawes furie, and ſhall at the leaſt of thy ſweet notice, bring her to triall. Thine in all complements of deuoted and heart-burning heat of dutie.
Don Adriana de Armado.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: This is not ſo well as I looked for, but the beſt that euer I heard.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.p: I the beſt, for the worſt. But ſirra, What ſay you to this?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Sir I confeſſe the Wench.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.p: Did you heare the Proclamation?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I doe confeſſe much of the hearing it, but little of the marking of it.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.p: It was proclaimed a yeeres impriſonment to bee taken with a Wench.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I was taken with none ſir, I was taken vvith a Damoſell.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.p: Well, it was proclaimed Damoſell.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: This was no Damoſell neyther ſir, ſhee was a Virgin.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.p: It is ſo varried to, for it was proclaimed Virgin.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: If it were, I denie her Virginitie: I was taken with a Maide.

sp.speaker: Fer.
sp.p: This Maid will not ſerue your turne ſir.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: This Maide will ſerue my turne ſir.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Sir I will pronounce your ſentence: You ſhall faſt a Weeke with Branne and water.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I had rather pray a Moneth with Mutton and Porridge.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: And Don Armado ſhall be your keeper.
My Lord Berowne, ſee him deliuer'd ore,
And goe we Lords to put in practice that,
Which each to other hath ſo ſtrongly ſworne.

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.l: Ile lay my head to any good mans hat,
Theſe oathes and lawes will proue an idle ſcorne.
Sirra, come on.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I ſuffer for the truth ſir: for true it is, I was taken with Iaquenetta, and Iaquenetta is a true girle, and therefore welcome the ſowre cup of proſperitie, affliction may one day ſmile againe, and vntill then ſit downe ſorrow.

div.stage: Enter Armado and Moth his Page.

sp.speaker: Arma.
sp.p: Boy, What ſigne is it when a man of great ſpirit growes melancholy?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: A great ſigne ſir, that he will looke ſad.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Why? ſadneſſe is one and the ſelfe-ſame thing deare impe.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: No no, O Lord ſir no.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: How canſt thou part ſadneſſe and melancholy my tender Iuuenall?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: By a familiar demonſtration of the working, my tough ſigneur.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Why tough ſigneur? Why tough ſigneur?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Why tender Iuuenall? Why tender Iuuenall?

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I ſpoke it tender Iuuenall, as a congruent apathaton, appertaining to thy young daies, which we may nominate tender.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: And I tough ſigneur, as an appertinent title to your olde time, which we may name tough.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Pretty and apt.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: How meane you ſir, I pretty, and my ſaying apt? or I apt, and my ſaying prettie?

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Thou pretty becauſe little.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Little pretty, becauſe little: wherefore apt?

sp.speaker: Brag
sp.p: And therefore apt, becauſe quicke.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Speake you this in my praiſe Maſter?

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: In thy condigne praiſe.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I will praiſe an Eele with the ſame praiſe.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: What? that an Eele is ingenuous.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: That an Eele is quicke.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I doe ſay thou art quicke in anſweres. Thou heat'ſt my bloud.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I am anſwer'd ſir.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I loue not to be croſt.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: He ſpeakes the meere contrary, croſſes loue not him.

sp.speaker: Br.
sp.p: I haue promis'd to ſtudy iij. yeres with the Duke.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: You may doe it in an houre ſir.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: How many is one thrice told?

sp.speaker: Bra.
sp.p: I am ill at reckning, it fits the ſpirit of a Tapſter.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: You are a gentleman and a gameſter fir.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I confeſſe both, they are both the varniſh of a compleat man.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Then I am ſure you know how much the groſſe ſumme of deuſ-ace amounts to.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: It doth amount to one more then two.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Which the baſe vulgar call three.

sp.speaker: Br.
sp.p: True.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Why ſir is this ſuch a peece of ſtudy? Now here's three ſtudied, ere you'll thrice wink, & how eaſie it is to put yeres to the word three, and ſtudy three yeeres in two words, the dancing horſe will tell you.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: A moſt fine Figure.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: To proue you a Cypher.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I will heereupon confeſſe I am in loue: and as it is baſe for a Souldier to loue; ſo am I in loue with a baſe wench. If drawing my ſword againſt the humour of affection, would deliuer mee from the reprobate thought of it, I would take Deſire priſo • , and ranſome him to any French Courtier for a n • deuis'd curtſie. I thinke ſcorne to ſigh, me thinkes I ſhould out-ſweare Cupid. Comfort me Boy, What great men haue beene in loue?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Hercules Maſter.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Moſt ſweete Hercules: more authority deare Boy, name more; and ſweet my childe let them be men of good repute and carriage.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sampſon Maſter, he was a man of good carriage, great carriage: for hee carried the Towne-gates on his backe like a Porter: and he was in loue.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: O well-knit Sampſon, ſtrong ioynted Sampſon; I doe excell thee in my rapier, as much as thou didſt mee in carrying gates. I am in loue too. Who was Sampſons loue my deare Moth?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: A Woman, Maſter.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Of what complexion?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Of all the foure, or the three, or the two, or one of the foure.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Tell me preciſely of what complexion?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Of the ſea-water Greene ſir.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Is that one of the foure complexions?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: As I haue read ſir, and the beſt of them too.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Greene indeed is the colour of Louers: but to haue a Loue of that colour, methinkes Sampſon had ſmall reaſon for it. He ſurely affected her for her wit.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: It was ſo ſir, for ſhe had a greene wit.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: My Loue is moſt immaculate white and red.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Moſt immaculate thoughts Maſter, are mask'd vnder ſuch colours.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Define, define, well educated infant.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: My fathers witte, and my mothers tongue aſſiſt mee.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Sweet inuocation of a childe, moſt pretty and patheticall.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: If ſhee be made of white and red,
Her faults will nere be knowne:
For bluſh-in cheekes by faults are bred,
And feares by pale white ſhowne:
Then if ſhe feare, or be to blame,
By this you ſhall not know,
For ſtill her cheekes poſſeſſe the ſame,
Which natiue ſhe doth owe:
A dangerous rime maſter againſt the reaſon of white and redde.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Is there not a ballet Boy, of the King and the Begger?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: The world was very guilty of ſuch a Ballet ſome three ages ſince, but I thinke now 'tis not to be found: or if it were, it would neither ſerue for the writing, nor the tune.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I will haue that ſubiect newly writ ore, that I may example my digreſſion by ſome mighty preſident. Boy, I doe loue that Countrey girle that I tooke in the Parke with the rationall hinde Coſtard: ſhe deſerues well.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: To bee whip'd: and yet a better loue then my Maſter.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Sing Boy, my ſpirit grows heauy in ioue.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: And that's great maruell, louing a light wench.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I ſay ſing.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Forbeare till this company be paſt.

sp.speaker: Conſt.
sp.p: Sir, the Dukes pleaſure, is that you keepe Coſtard ſafe, and you muſt let him take no delight, nor no penance, but hee muſt faſt three daies a weeke: for this Damſell, I muſt keepe her at the Parke, ſhee is alowd for the Day-woman. Fare you well.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I do betray my ſelfe with bluſhing: Maide.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.p: Man.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I wil viſit thee at the Lodge.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.p: That's here by.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I know where it is ſituate.

sp.speaker: Mai.
sp.p: Lord how wiſe you are!

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I will tell thee wonders.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: With what face?

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I loue thee.

sp.speaker: Mai.
sp.p: So I heard you ſay.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: And ſo farewell.

sp.speaker: Mai.
sp.p: Faire weather after you.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Come Iaquenetta, away.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Villaine, thou ſhalt faſt for thy offences ere thou be pardoned.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Well ſir, I hope when I doe it, I ſhall doe it on a full ſtomacke.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt be heauily puniſhed.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I am more bound to you then your fellowes, for they are but lightly rewarded.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Take away this villaine, ſhut him vp.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Come you tranſgreſſing ſlaue, away.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Let mee not bee pent vp ſir, I will faſt being looſe.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: No ſir, that were faſt and looſe: thou ſhalt to priſon.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Well, if euer I do ſee the merry dayes of deſolation that I haue ſeene, ſome ſhall ſee.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: What ſhall ſome ſee?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Nay nothing, Maſter Moth, but what they looke vpon. It is not for priſoners to be ſilent in then words, and therefore I will ſay nothing: I thanke God, I haue as little patience as another man, and therefore I can be quiet.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I doe affect the very ground (which is baſe) where her ſhooe (which is baſer) guided by her foote (which is baſeſt) doth tread. I ſhall be forſworn (which ia a great argument of falſhood) if I loue. And how can that be true loue, which is falſly attempted? Loue is a familiar, Loue is a Diuell. There is no euill Angell but Loue, yet Sampſon was ſo tempted, and he had an excellent ſtrength: Yet was Salomon ſo ſeduced, and hee had a very good witte. Cupids But ſhaft is too hard for Hercules Clubbe, and therefore too much ods for a Spaniards Rapier: The firſt and ſecond cauſe will not ſerue my turne: the Paſſado hee reſpects not, the Duello he regards not; his diſgrace is to be called Boy, but his glorie is to ſubdue men. Adue Valour, ruſt Rapier, bee ſtill Drum, for your manager is in loue; yea hee loueth. Aſſiſt me ſome extemporall god of Rime, for I am ſure I ſhall turne Sonnet. Deuiſe Wit, write Pen, for I am for whole volumes in folio.

div.head: Actus Secunda.
div.stage: Enter the Princeſſe of France, with three attending Ladies, and three Lords.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Now Madam ſummon vp your deareſt ſpirits,
Conſider who the King your father ſends:
To whom he ſends, and what's his Embaſſie.
Your ſelfe, held precious in the worlds eſteeme,
To parlee with the ſole inheritour
Of all perfections that a man may owe,
Matchleſſe Nauarre, the plea of no leſſe weight
Then Aquitaine, a Dowrie for a Queene.
Be now as prodigall of all deare grace,
As Nature was in making Graces deare,
When ſhe did ſtarue the generall world beſide,
And prodigally gaue them all to you.

sp.speaker: Queen.
sp.l: Good L. Boyet, my beauty though but mean,
Needs not the painted flouriſh of your praiſe:
Beauty is bought by iudgement of the eye,
Not vttred by baſe ſale of chapmens tongues:
I am leſſe proud to heare you tell my worth,
Then you much wiling to be counted wiſe,
In ſpending your wit in the praiſe of mine.
But now to taske the tasker, good Boyet,

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: You are not ignorant all-telling fame
Doth noyſe abroad Nauar hath made a vow,
Till painefull ſtudie ſhall out-weare three yeares,
No woman may approach his ſilent Court:
Therefore to's ſeemeth it a needfull courſe,
Before we enter his forbidden gates,
To know his pleaſure, and in that behalfe
Bold of your worthineſſe, we ſingle you,
As our beſt mouing faire ſoliciter:
Tell him, the daughter of the King of France,
On ſerious buſineſſe crauing quicke diſpatch,
Importunes perſonall conference with his grace.
Haſte, ſignifie ſo much while we attend,
Like humble viſag'd ſuters his high will.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Proud of imployment, willingly I goe.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: All pride is willing pride, and yours is ſo:
Who are the Votaries my louing Lords, that are vow-fellowes with this vertuous Duke?

sp.speaker: Lor.
sp.p: Longauill is one.

sp.speaker: Princ.
sp.p: Know you the man?

sp.speaker: 1 Lady.
sp.l: I know him Madame at a marriage feaſt,
Betweene L. Perigort and the beautious heire
Of Iaques Fauconbridge ſolemnized.
In Normandie ſaw I this Longauill,
A man of ſoueraigne parts he is eſteem'd:
Well fitted in Arts, glorious in Armes:
Nothing becomes him ill that he would well.
The onely ſoyle of his faire vertues gloſſe,
If vertues gloſſe will ſtaine with any ſoile,
Is a ſharp wit match'd with too blunt a Will:
Whoſe edge hath power to cut whoſe will ſtill wills,
It ſhould none ſpare that come within his power.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Some merry mocking Lord belike, iſt ſo?

sp.speaker: Lad. 1.
sp.p: They ſay ſo moſt, that moſt his humors know.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Such ſhort liu'd wits do wither as they grow.
Who are the reſt?

sp.speaker: 2. Lad.
sp.l: The yong Dumaine, a well accompliſht youth,
Of all that Vertue loue, for Vertue loued.
Moſt power to doe moſt harme, leaſt knowing ill:
For he hath wit to make an ill ſhape good,
And ſhape to win grace though ſhe had no wit.
I ſaw him at the Duke Alanſoes once,
And much too little of that good I ſaw,
Is my report to his great worthineſſe.

sp.speaker: Roſſa.
sp.l: Another of theſe Students at that time,
Was there with him, as I haue heard a truth.
Berowne they call him, but a merrier man,
Within the limit of becomming mirth,
I neuer ſpent an houres talke withall.
His eye begets occaſion for his wit,
For euery obiect that the one doth catch,
The other turnes to a mirth-mouing ieſt.
Which his faire tongue (conceits expoſitor)
Deliuers in ſuch apt and gracious words,
That aged eares play treuant at his tales,
And yonger hearings are quite rauiſhed.
So ſweet and voluble is his diſcourſe.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: God bleſſe my Ladies, are they all in loue?
That euery one her owne hath garniſhed,
With ſuch bedecking ornaments of praiſe.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Heere comes Boyet.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Now, what admittance Lord?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Nauar had notice of your faire approach,
And he and his competitors in oath,
Were all addreſt to meete you gentle Lady
Before I came: Marrie thus much I haue learnt,
He rather meanes to lodge you in the field,
Like one that comes heere to beſiege his Court,
Then ſeeke a diſpenſation for his oath:
To let you enter his vnpeopled houſe.
sp.stage: Enter Nauar, Longauill, Dumaine, and Berowne.
sp.l: Heere comes Nauar.

sp.speaker: Nau.
sp.p: Faire Princeſſe, welcom to the Court of Nauar.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Faire I giue you backe againe, and welcome I haue not yet: the roofe of this Court is too high to bee yours, and welcome to the wide fields, too baſe to be mine.

sp.speaker: Nau.
sp.p: You ſhall be welcome Madam to my Court.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: I wil be welcome then, Conduct me thither.

sp.speaker: Nau.
sp.p: Heare me deare Lady, I haue ſworne an oath.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Our Lady helpe my Lord, he'll be forſworne.

sp.speaker: Nau.
sp.p: Not for the world faire Madam, by my will.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Why, will ſhall breake it will, and nothing els.

sp.speaker: Nau.
sp.p: Your Ladiſhip is ignorant what it is.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Were my Lord ſo, his ignorance were wiſe,
Where now his knowledge muſt proue ignorance.
I heare your grace hath ſworne out Houſeekeeping:
'Tis deadly ſinne to keepe that oath my Lord,
And ſinne to breake it:
But pardon me, I am too ſodaine bold,
To teach a Teacher ill beſeemeth me.
Vouchſafe to read the purpoſe of my comming,
And ſodainly reſolue me in my ſuite.

sp.speaker: Nau.
sp.p: Madam, I will, if ſodainly I may.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: You will the ſooner that I were away,
For you'll proue periur'd if you make me ſtay.

sp.speaker: Berow.
sp.p: Did not I dance with you in Brabant once?

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Did not I dance with you in Brabant once?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I know you did.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: How needleſſe was it then to ask the queſtion?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: You muſt not be ſo quicke.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: 'Tis long of you yt ſpur me with ſuch queſtions.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Your wit's too hot, it ſpeeds too faſt, 'twill tire.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Not till it leaue the Rider in the mire.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: What time a day?

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: The howre that fooles ſhould aske.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Now faire befall your maske.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Faire fall the face it couers.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: And ſend you many louers.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Amen, ſo you be none.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Nay then will I be gone.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Madame, your father heere doth intimate,
The paiment of a hundred thouſand Crownes,
Being but th' one halfe, of an intire ſumme,
Disburſed by my father in his warres.
But ſay that he, or we, as neither haue
Receiu'd that ſumme; yet there remaines vnpaid
A hundred thouſand more: in ſurety of the which,
One part of Aquitaine is bound to vs,
Although not valued to the moneys worth.
If then the King your father will reſtore
But that one halfe which is vnſatisfied,
We will giue vp our right in Aquitaine,
And hold faire friendſhip with his Maieſtie:
But that it ſeemes he little purpoſeth,
For here he doth demand to haue repaie,
An hundred thouſand Crownes, and not demands
One paiment of a hundred thouſand Crownes,
To haue his title liue in Aquitaine.
Which we much rather had depart withall,
And haue the money by our father lent,
Then Aquitane, ſo guelded as it is.
Deare Princeſſe, were not his requeſts ſo farre
From reaſons yeelding, your faire ſelfe ſhould make
A yeelding 'gainſt ſome reaſon in my breſt,
And goe well ſatisfied to France againe.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: You doe the King my Father too much wrong,
And wrong the reputation of your name,
In ſo vnſeeming to confeſſe receyt
Of that which hath ſo faithfully beene paid.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: I doe proteſt I neuer heard of it,
And if you proue it, Ile repay it backe,
Or yeeld vp Aquitaine.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: We arreſt your word:
Boyet, you can produce acquittances
For ſuch a ſumme, from ſpeciall Officers,
Of Charles his Father.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Satisfie me ſo.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: So pleaſe your Grace, the packet is not come
Where that and other ſpecialties are bound,
To morrow you ſhall haue a ſight of them.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: It ſhall ſuffice me; at which enterview,
All liberall reaſon would I yeeld vnto:
Meane time, receiue ſuch welcome at my hand,
As Honour, without breach of Honour may
Make tender of, to thy true worthineſſe.
You may not come faire Princeſſe in my gates,
But heere without you ſhall be ſo receiu'd,
As you ſhall deeme your ſelfe lodg'd in my heart,
Though ſo deni'd farther harbour in my houſe:
Your owne good thoughts excuſe me, and farewell,
To morrow we ſhall viſit you againe.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Sweet health & faire deſires conſort your grace.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Thy own wiſh wiſh I thee, in euery place.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Lady, I will commend you to my owne heart.

sp.speaker: La. Ro.
sp.l: Pray you doe my commendations,
I would be glad to ſee it.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I would you heard it grone.

sp.speaker: La. Ro.
sp.p: Is the ſoule ſicke?.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Sicke at the heart.

sp.speaker: La. Ro.
sp.p: Alacke, let it bloud.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Would that doe it good?

sp.speaker: La. Ro.
sp.p: My Phiſicke ſaies I.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Will you prick't with your eye.

sp.speaker: La. Ro.
sp.p: No poynt, with my knife.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Now God ſaue thy life.

sp.speaker: La. Ro.
sp.p: And yours from long liuing.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I cannot ſtay thankſ-giuing.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Sir, I pray you a word: What Lady is that ſame?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: The heire of Alanſon, Roſalin her name.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: A gallant Lady, Mounſier fare you well.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: I beſeech you a word: what is ſhe in the white?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: A woman ſomtimes, if you ſaw her in the light.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Perchance light in the light: I deſire her name.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Shee hath but one for her ſelfe,
To deſire that were a ſhame.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Pray you ſir, whoſe daughter?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Her Mothers, I haue heard.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Gods bleſſing a your beard.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Good ſir be not offended,
Shee is an heyre of Faulconbridge.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Nay, my choller is ended:
Shee is a moſt ſweet Lady.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Not vnlike ſir, that may be.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: What's her name in the cap.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Katherine by good hap.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Is ſhe wedded, or no.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: To her will ſir, or ſo.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: You are welcome ſir, adiew.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Fare well to me ſir, and welcome to you.

sp.speaker: La. Ma.
sp.l: That laſt is Beroune, the mery mad-cap Lord.
Not a word with him, but a ieſt.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: And euery ieſt but a word.

sp.speaker: Pri.
sp.p: It was well done of you to take him at his word.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I was as willing to grapple, as he was to boord.

sp.speaker: La. Ma.
sp.l: Two hot Sheepes marie:
And wherefore not Ships?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: No Sheepe (ſweet Lamb) vnleſſe we feed on your lips.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: You Sheep & I paſture: ſhall that finiſh the ieſt?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: So you grant paſture for me.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Not ſo gentle beaſt.
My lips are no Common, though ſeuerall they be.

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.p: Belonging to whom?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: To my fortunes and me.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Good wits wil be iangling, but gentles agree.
This ciuill warre of wits were much better vſed
On Nauar and his bookemen, for heere 'tis abus'd.

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: If my obſeruation (which very ſeldome lies
By the hearts ſtill rhetoricke, diſcloſed with eyes)
Deceiue me not now, Nauar is infected.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: With what?

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.p: With that which we Louers intitle affected.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Your reaſon.

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.l: Why all his behauiours doe make their retire,
To the court of his eye, peeping thorough deſire.
His hart like an Agot with your print impreſſed,
Proud with his forme, in his eie pride expreſſed.
His tongue all impatient to ſpeake and not ſee,
Did ſtumble with haſte in his eie-ſight to be,
All ſences to that ſence did make their repaire,
To feele onely looking on faireſt of faire:
Me thought all his ſences were lockt in his eye,
As Iewels in Chriſtall for ſome Prince to buy.
Who tendring their own worth from whence they were glaſt,
Did point out to buy them along as you paſt.
His faces owne margent did coate ſuch amazes,
That all eyes ſaw his eies inchanted with gazes.
Ile giue you Aquitaine, and all that is his,
And you giue him for my ſake, but one louing Kiſſe.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Come to our Pauillion, Boyet is diſpoſde.

sp.speaker: Bro.
sp.l: But to ſpeak that in words, which his eie hath diſclos'd.
I onelie haue made a mouth of his eie,
By adding a tongue, which I know will not lie.

sp.speaker: Lad. Ro.
sp.p: Thou art an old Loue-monger, and ſpeakeſt skilfully.

sp.speaker: Lad. Ma.
sp.p: He is Cupids Grandfather, and learnes news of him.

sp.speaker: Lad. 2.
sp.p: Then was Venus like her mother, for her father is but grim.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Do you heare my mad wenches?

sp.speaker: La. 1.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: What then, do you ſee?

sp.speaker: Lad. 2.
sp.p: I, our way to be gone.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: You are too hard for me.

sp.speaker: Bra.
sp.p: Warble childe, make paſſionate my ſenſe of hearing.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Concolinel.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Sweete Ayer, go tenderneſſe of yeares: take this Key, giue enlargement to the ſwaine, bring him feſtinatly hither: I muſt imploy him in a letter to my Loue.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Will you win your loue with a French braule?

sp.speaker: Bra.
sp.p: How meaneſt thou, brauling in French?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: No my compleat maſter, but to Iigge off a tune at the tongues end, canarie to it with the feete, humour it with turning vp your eie: ſigh a note and ſing a note, ſometime through the throate: if you ſwallowed loue with ſinging, loue ſometime through: noſe as if you ſnuft vp loue by ſmelling loue with your hat penthouſe-like ore the ſhop of your eies, with your armes croſt on your thinbellie doublet, like a Rabbet on a ſpit, or your hands in your pocket, like a man after the old painting, and keepe not too long in one tune, but a ſnip and away: theſe are complements, theſe are humours, theſe betraie nice wenches that would be betraied without theſe, and make them men of note: do you note men that moſt are affected to theſe?

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: How haſt thou purchaſed this experience?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: By my penne of obſeruation.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: But O, but O.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: The Hobbie-horſe is forgot.

sp.speaker: Bra.
sp.p: Cal'ſt thou my loue Hobbi-horſe.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: No Maſter, the Hobbie-horſe is but a Colt, and and your Loue perhaps, a Hacknie:
But haue you forgot your Loue?

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Almoſt I had.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Negligent ſtudent, learne her by heart.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: By heart, and in heart Boy.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: And out of heart Maſter: all thoſe three I will proue.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: What wilt thou proue?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: A man, if I liue (and this) by, in, and without, vpon the inſtant: by heart you loue her, becauſe your heart cannot come by her: in heart you loue her, becauſe your heart is in loue with her: and out of heart you loue her, being out of heart that you cannot enioy her.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I am all theſe three.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: And three times as much more, and yet nothing at all.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Fetch hither the Swaine, he muſt carrie mee a letter.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: A meſſage well ſimpathis'd, a Horſe to be embaſſadour for an Aſſe.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Ha, ha, What ſaieſt thou?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Marrie ſir, you muſt ſend the Aſſe vpon the Horſe for he is verie ſlow gated: but I goe.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: The way is but ſhort, away.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: As ſwift as Lead ſir.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Thy meaning prettie ingenious, is not Lead a mettall heauie, dull, and ſlow?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Minnime honeſt Maſter, or rather Maſter no.

sp.speaker: Brad.
sp.p: I ſay Lead is ſlow.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: You are too ſwift ſir to ſay ſo.
Is that Lead ſlow which is fir'd from a Gunne?

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.l: Sweete ſmoke of Rhetorike,
He reputes me a Cannon, and the Bullet that's he:
I ſhoote thee at the Swaine.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Thump then, and I flee.

sp.speaker: Bra.
sp.l: A moſt acute iuuenall, voluble and free of grace,
By thy fauour ſweet Welkin, I muſt ſigh in thy face.
Moſt rude melancholie, Valour giues thee place.
My Herald is return'd.

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.p: A wonder Maſter, here's a Coſtard broken in a ſhin.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: Some enigma, ſome riddle, come, thy Lenuoy begin.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: No egma, no riddle, no lenuoy, no ſalue, in thee male ſir. Or ſir, Plantan, a plaine Plantan: no lenuoy, no lenuoy, no Salue ſir, but a Plantan.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: By vertue thou inforceſt laughter, thy ſillie thought, my ſpleene, the heauing of my lunges prouokes me to rediculous ſmyling: O pardon me my ſtars, doth the inconſiderate take ſalue for lenuoy, and the word lenuoy for a ſalue?

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.p: Doe the wiſe thinke them other, is not lenuoy a ſalue?

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: No Page, it is an epilogue or diſcourſe to make plaine,
Some obſcure precedence that hath to fore bin faine.
Now will I begin your morrall, and do you follow with my lenuoy.
The Foxe, the Ape, and the Humble-Bee,
Were ſtill at oddes, being but three.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Vntill the Gooſe came out of doore,
Staying the oddes by adding foure.

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.p: A good Lenuoy, ending in the Gooſe: would you deſire more?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: The Boy hath ſold him a bargaine, a Gooſe, that's flat
Sir, your penny-worth is good, and your Gooſe be fat▪
To ſell a bargaine well is as cunning as faſt and looſe:
Let me ſee a fat Lenuoy, I that's a fat Gooſe.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.l: Come hither, come hither:
How did this argument begin?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: By ſaying that a Coſtard was broken in a ſhin.
Then cal'd you for the Lenuoy.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: True, and I for a Plantan:
Thus came your argument in:
Then the Boyes fat Lenuoy, the Gooſe that you bought,
And he ended the market.

sp.speaker: Ar.
sp.p: But tell me: How was there a Coſtard broken in a ſhin?

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.p: I will tell you ſencibly.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.l: Thou haſt no feeling of it Moth,
I will ſpeake that Lenuoy.
I Coſtard running out, that was ſafely within,
Fell ouer the threſhold, and broke my ſhin.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: We will talke no more of this matter.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Till there be more matter in the ſhin.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Sirra Coſtard, I will infranchiſe thee.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: O, marrie me to one Francis, I ſmell ſome Lenuoy, ſome Gooſe in this.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: By my ſweete ſoule, I meane, ſetting thee at libertie. Enfreedoming thy perſon: thou wert emured, reſtrained, captiuated, bound.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: True, true, and now you will be my purgation, and let me looſe.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I giue thee thy libertie, ſet thee from durance, and in lieu thereof, impoſe on thee nothing but this: Beare this ſignificant to the countrey Maide Iaquenetta: there is remuneration, for the beſt ward of mine honours is rewarding my dependants. Moth, follow.

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.l: Like the ſequell I.
Signeur Coſtard adew.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: My ſweete ounce of mans fleſh, my in-conie Iew: Now will I looke to his remuneration. Remuneration, O, that's the Latine word for three-farthings: Three-farthings remuneration, What's the price of this yncle? i.d. no, Ile giue you a remuneration: Why? It carries it remuneration: Why? It is a fairer name then a French-Crowne. I will neuer buy and ſell out of this word.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: O my good knaue Coſtard, exceedingly well met.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Pray you ſir, How much Carnation Ribbon may a man buy for a remuneration?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: What is a remuneration?

sp.speaker: Coſt.
sp.p: Marrie ſir, halfe pennie farthing.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: O, Why then three farthings worth of Silke.

sp.speaker: Coſt.
sp.p: I thanke your worſhip, God be wy you.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: O ſtay ſlaue, I muſt employ thee:
As thou wilt win my fauour, good my knaue,
Doe one thing for me that I ſhall intreate.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: When would you haue it done ſir?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: O this after-noone.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Well, I will doe it ſir: Fare you well.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: O thou knoweſt not what it is.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I ſhall know ſir, when I haue done it.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Why villaine thou muſt know firſt.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I wil come to your worſhip to morrow morning.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: It muſt be done this after-noone,
Harke ſlaue, it is but this:
The Princeſſe comes to hunt here in the Parke,
And in her traine there is a gentle Ladie:
When tongues ſpeak ſweetly, then they name her name,
And Roſaline they call her, aske for her:
And to her white hand ſee thou do commend
This ſeal'd vp counſaile. Ther's thy guerdon: goe.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Gardon, O ſweete gardon, better then remuneration, a leuenpence-farthing better: moſt ſweete gardon. I will doe it ſir in print: gardon, remuneration.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: O, and I forſooth in loue,
I that haue beene loues whip?
A verie Beadle to a humerous ſigh: A Criticke,
Nay, a night-watch Conſtable.
A domineering pedant ore the Boy,
Then whom no mortall ſo magnificent.
This wimpled, whyning, purblinde waiward Boy,
This ſignior Iunios gyant drawfe, don Cupid,
Regent of Loue-rimes, Lord of folded armes,
Th' annointed ſoueraigne of ſighes and groanes:
Liedge of all loyterers and male contents:
Dread Prince of Placcats, King of Codpeeces.
Sole Emperator and great generall
Of trotting Parrators (O my little heart.)
And I to be a Corporall of his field,
And weare his colours like a Tumblers hoope.
What? I loue, I ſue, I ſeeke a wife,
A woman that is like a Germane Cloake,
Still a repairing: euer out of frame,
And neuer going a right, being a Watch:
But being watcht, that it may ſtill goe right.
Nay, to be periurde, which is worſt of all:
And among three, to loue the worſt of all,
A whitly wanton, with a veluet brow.
With two pitch bals ſtucke in her face for eyes.
I, and by heauen, one that will doe the deede,
Though Argus were her Eunuch and her garde.
And I to ſigh for her, to watch for her,
To pray for her, go to: it is a plague
That Cupid will impoſe for my neglect,
Of his almighty dreadfull little might.
Well, I will loue, write, ſigh, pray, ſhue, grone,
Some men muſt loue my Lady, and ſome lone.

div.head: Actus Quartus.
div.stage: Enter the Princeſſe, a Forreſter, her Ladies, and her Lords.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Was that the King that ſpurd his horſe ſo hard,
Againſt the ſteepe vpriſing of the hill?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I know not, but I thinke it was not he.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Who ere a was, a ſhew'd a mounting minde:
Well Lords, to day we ſhall haue our diſpatch,
On Saterday we will returne to France.
Then Forreſter my friend, Where is the Buſh
That we muſt ſtand and play the murtherer in?

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l: Hereby vpon the edge of yonder Coppice,
A Stand where you may make the faireſt ſhoote.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: I thanke my beautie, I am faire that ſhoote,
And thereupon thou ſpeak'ſt the faireſt ſhoote.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.p: Pardon me Madam, for I meant not ſo.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: What, what? Firſt praiſe me, & then again ſay no.
O ſhort liu'd pride. Not faire? alacke for woe.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.p: Yes Madam faire.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Nay, neuer paint me now,
Where faire is not, praiſe cannot mend the brow.
Here (good my glaſſe) take this for telling true:
Faire paiment for foule words, is more then due.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.p: Nothing but faire is that which you inherit.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: See, ſee, my beautie will be ſau'd by merit.
O hereſie in faire, fit for theſe dayes,
A giuing hand, though foule, ſhall haue faire praiſe.
But come, the Bow: Now Mercie goes to kill,
And ſhooting well, is then accounted ill:
Thus will I ſaue my credit in the ſhoote,
Not wounding, pittie would not let me do't:
If wounding, then it was to ſhew my skill,
That more for praiſe, then purpoſe meant to kill.
And out of queſtion, ſo it is ſometimes:
Glory growes guiltie of deteſted crimes,
When for Fames ſake, for praiſe an outward part,
We bend to that, the working of the hart.
As I for praiſe alone now ſeeke to ſpill
The poore Deeres blood, that my heart meanes no ill.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Do not curſt wiues hold that ſelfe-ſoueraigntie
Onely for praiſe ſake, when they ſtriue to be
Lords ore their Lords?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Onely for praiſe and praiſe we may afford,
To any Lady that ſubdewes a Lord.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Here comes a member of the common-wealth.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: God dig-you-den all, pray you which is the head Lady?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Thou ſhalt know her fellow, by the reſt that haue no heads.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Which is the greateſt Lady, the higheſt?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: The thickeſt, and the talleſt.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: The thickeſt, & the talleſt: it is ſo, truth is truth.
And your waſte Miſtris, were as ſlender as my wit,
One a theſe Maides girdles for your waſte ſhould be fit.
Are not you the chiefe womā? You are the thickeſt here?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: What's your will ſir? What's your will?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: I haue a Letter from Monſier Berowne,
To one Lady Roſaline.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: O thy letter, thy letter: He's a good friend of mine.
Stand a ſide good bearer.
Boyet, you can carue,
Breake vp this Capon.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: I am bound to ſerue.
This Letter is miſtooke: it importeth none here:
It is writ to Iaquenetta.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: We will reade it, I ſweare.
Breake the necke of the Waxe, and euery one giue eare.

body.p: BY heauen, that thou art faire, is moſt infallible: true that thou art beauteous, truth it ſelfe that thou art louely: more fairer then faire, beautifull then beautious, truer then truth it ſelfe: haue comiſeration on thy heroicall Vaſſall. The magnanimous and moſt illuſtrate King Cophetua ſet eie vpon the pernicious and indubitate Begger Zenelophon: and he it was that might rightly ſay, Veni, vidi, vici: Which to annothanize in the vulgar, O baſe and obſcure vulgar; videliſet, He came, See, and ouercame: hee came one; ſee, two; couercame three: Who came? the King. Why did he come? to ſee. Why did he ſee? to ouercome. To whom came he? to the Begger. What ſaw he? the Begger. Who ouercame he? the Begger. The concluſion is victorie: On whoſe ſide? the King: the captiue is inricht: On whoſe ſide? the Beggers. The cataſtrophe is a Nuptiall: on whoſe ſide? the Kings: no, on both in one, or one in both. I am the King (for ſo ſtands the compariſon) thou the Begger, for ſo witneſſeth thy lowlineſſe. Shall I command thy loue? I may. Shall I enforce thy loue? I could. Shall I entreate thy loue? I will. What, ſhalt thou exchange for ragges, roabes: for tittles titles, for thy ſelfe mee. Thus expecting thy reply, I prophane my lips on thy foote, my eyes on thy picture, and my heart on thy euerie part.

closer.signed: Thine in the deareſt deſigne of induſtrie, Don Adriana de Armatho.

sp.l: Thus doſt thou heare the Nemean Lion roare,
Gainſt thee thou Lambe, that ſtandeſt as his pray:
Submiſſiue fall his princely feete before,
And he from forrage will incline to play.
But if thou ſtriue (poore ſoule) what art thou then?
Foode for his rage, repaſture for his den.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: What plume of feathers is hee that indited this Letter? What veine? What Wethercocke? Did you euer heare better?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I am much deceiued, but I remember the ſtile.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Elſe your memorie is bad, going ore it erewhile.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: This Armando is a Spaniard that keeps here in court
A Phantaſime, a Monarcho, and one that makes ſport
To the Prince and his Booke-mates.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Thou fellow, a word.
Who gaue thee this Letter?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I told you, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: To whom ſhould'ſt thou giue it?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: From my Lord to my Lady.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: From which Lord, to which Lady?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: From my Lord Berowne, a good maſter of mine,
To a Lady of France, that he call'd Roſaline.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Thou haſt miſtaken his letter. Come Lords away.
Here ſweete, put vp this, 'twill be thine another day.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Who is the ſhooter? Who is the ſhooter?

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Shall I teach you to know.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I my continent of beautie.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Why ſhe that beares the Bow. Finely put off.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: My Lady goes to kill hornes, but if thou marrie,
Hang me by the necke, if hornes that yeare miſcarrie.
Finely put on.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Well then, I am the ſhooter.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: And who is your Deare?

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: If we chooſe by the hornes, your ſelfe come not neare. Finely put on indeede.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.p: You ſtill wrangle with her Boyet, and ſhee ſtrikes at the brow.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: But ſhe her ſelfe is hit lower:
Haue I hit her now.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Shall I come vpon thee with an old ſaying, that was a man when King Pippin of France was a little boy, as touching the hit it.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p: So I may anſwere thee with one as old that was a woman when Queene Guinouer of Brittaine was a little wench, as touching the hit it.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: Thou canſt not hit it, hit it, hit it,
Thou canſt not hit it my good man.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: I cannot, cannot, cannot:
And I cannot, another can.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: By my troth moſt pleaſant, how both did fit it.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: A marke marueilous well ſhot, for they both did hit.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: A mark, O marke but that marke: a marke ſaies my Lady.
Let the mark haue a pricke in't, to meat at, if it may be.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Wide a' th bow hand. yfaith your hand is out.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Indeede a' muſt ſhoote nearer, or heele ne're hit the clout.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: And if my hand be out, then belike your hand is in.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Then will ſhee get the vpſhoot by cleauing the is in.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Come, come, you talke greaſely, your lips grow foule,

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: She's too hard for you at pricks, ſir challenge her to boule.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I feare too much rubbing: good night my good Oule.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: By my ſoule a Swaine, a moſt ſimple Clowne.
Lord, Lord, how the Ladies and I haue put him downe.
O my troth moſt ſweete ieſts, moſt inconie vulgar wit,
When it comes ſo ſmoothly off, ſo obſcenely, as it were, ſo fit.
Armathor ath to the ſide, O a moſt dainty man.
To ſee him walke before a Lady, and to beare her Fan.
To ſee him kiſſe his hand, and how moſt ſweetly a will ſweare:
And his Page at other ſide, that handfull of wit,
Ah heauens, it is moſt patheticall nit.
Sowla, ſowla.

div.stage: Enter Dull, Holofernes, the Pedant and Nathaniel.

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.p: Very reuerent ſport truely, and done in the teſtimony of a good conſcience.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: The Deare was (as you know) ſanguis in blood, ripe as a Pomwater, who now hangeth like a Iewell in the eare of Celo the ſkie; the welken the heauen, and anon falleth like a Crab on the face of Terra, the ſoyle, the land, the earth.

sp.speaker: Curat. Nath.
sp.p: Truely M. Holofernes, the epythithes are ſweetly varied like a ſcholler at the leaſt: but ſir I aſſure ye, it was a Bucke of the firſt head.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Sir Nathaniel, haud credo.

sp.speaker: Dul.
sp.p: 'Twas not a haud credo, 'twas a Pricket.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Moſt barbarous intimation: yet a kinde of inſinuation, as it were in via, in way of explication facere: as it were replication, or rather oſtentare, to ſhow as it were his inclination after his vndreſſed, vnpoliſhed, vneducated, vnpruned, vntrained, or rather vnlettered, or rathereſt vnconfirmed faſhion, to inſert againe my haud credo for a Deare.

sp.speaker: Dul.
sp.p: I ſaid the Deare was not a haud credo, 'twas a Pricket.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Twice ſod ſimplicitie, his coctus, O thou monſter Ignorance, how deformed dooſt thou looke.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.l: Sir hee hath neuer fed of the dainties that are bred in a booke.
He hath not eate paper as it were:
He hath not drunke inke.
sp.p: His intellect is not repleniſhed, hee is onely an animall, onely ſenſible in the duller parts: and ſuch barren plants are ſet before vs, that we thankfull ſhould be: which we taſte and feeling, are for thoſe parts that doe fructifie in vs more then he.
sp.l: For as it would ill become me to be vaine, indiſcreet, or a foole;
So were there a patch ſet on Learning, to ſee him in a Schoole.
But omne bene ſay I, being of an old Fathers minde,
Many can brooke the weather, that loue not the winde.

sp.speaker: Dul.
sp.p: You two are book-men: Can you tell by your wit, What was a month old at Cains birth, that's not fiue weekes old as yet?

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Dictiſima goodman Dull, dictiſima goodman Dull.

sp.speaker: Dul.
sp.p: What is dictima?

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: A title to Phebe, to Luna, to the Moone.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: The Moone was a month old when Adam was no more.
And wrought not to fiue-weekes when he came to fiueſcore.
Th' alluſion holds in the Exchange.

sp.speaker: Dul.
sp.p: 'Tis true indeede, the Colluſion holds in the Exchange.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: God comfort thy capacity, I ſay th' alluſion holds in the Exchange.

sp.speaker: Dul.
sp.p: And I ſay the poluſion holds in the Exchange: for the Moone is neuer but a month old: and I ſay beſide that, 'twas a Pricket that the Princeſſe kill'd.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Sir Nathaniel, will you heare an extemporall Epytaph on the death of the Deare, and to humour the ignorant call'd the Deare, the Princeſſe kill'd a Pricket.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Perge, good M. Holofernes, perge, ſo it ſhall pleaſe you to abrogate ſcurilitie.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: I will ſomething affect the letter, for it argues facilitie.

l.hi: The prayfull Princeſſe pearſt and prickt a prettie pleaſing Pricket,
Some ſay a Sore, but not a ſore, till now made ſore with ſhooting.
The Dogges did yell, put ell to Sore, then Sorell iumps from thicket:
Or Pricket-ſore, or elſe Sorell, the people fall a hooting.

sp.l: If Sore be ſore, then ell to Sore, makes fiftie ſores O ſorell:

l.hi: Of one ſore I an hundred make by adding but one more L.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: A rare talent.

sp.speaker: Dul.
sp.p: If a talent be a claw, looke how he clawes him with a talent.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: This is a gift that I haue ſimple: ſimple, a fooliſh extrauagant ſpirit, full of formes, figures, ſhapes, obiects, Ideas, apprehenſions, motions, reuolutions. Theſe are begot in the ventricle of memorie, nouriſht in the wombe of primater, and deliuered vpon the mellowing of occaſion: but the gift is good in thoſe in whom it is acute, and I am thankfull for it.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Sir, I praiſe the Lord for you, and ſo may my pariſhioners, for their Sonnes are well tutor'd by you, and their Daughters profit very greatly vnder you: you are a good member of the common-wealth.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p:
Mehercle, If their Sonnes be ingennous, they
ſhall want no inſtruction: If their Daughters be capable, I will put it to them. But Vir ſapis qui pauca loquitur, a ſoule Feminine ſaluteth vs.

sp.speaker: Iaqu.
sp.p: God giue you good morrow M. Perſon.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Maſter Perſon, quaſi Perſon? And if one ſhould be perſt, Which is the one?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Marry M. Schoolemaſter, hee that is likeſt to a hogſhead.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Of perſing a Hogshead, a good luſter of conceit in a curph of Earth, Fire enough for a Flint, Pearle enough for a Swine: 'tis prettie, it is well.

sp.speaker: Iaqu.
sp.p: Good Maſter Parſon be ſo good as reade mee this Letter, it was giuen mee by Coſtard, and ſent mee from Don Armatho: I beſeech you reade it.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Facile procor gellida, quando pecas omnia ſub vmbraruminat, and ſo forth. Ah good old Mantuan, I may ſpeake of thee as the traueiler doth of Venice, vemchie, vencha, que non te vnde, que non te perreche. Old Mantuam, old Mantuan. Who vnderſtandeth thee not, vt re ſol la mi fa: Vnder pardon ſir, What are the contents? or rather as Horrace ſayes in his, What my ſoule verſes.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: I ſir, and very learned.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.l: Let me heare a ſtaffe, a ſtanze, a verſe, Lege domine.
If Loue make me forſworne, how ſhall I ſweare to loue?
Ah neuer faith could hold, if not to beautie vowed.
Though to my ſelfe forſworn, to thee Ile faithfull proue.
Thoſe thoughts to mee were Okes, to thee like Oſiers bowed.
Studie his byas leaues, and makes his booke thine eyes.
Where all thoſe pleaſures liue, that Art would comprehend.
If knowledge be the marke, to know thee ſhall ſuffice.
Well learned is that tongue, that well can thee cōmend.
All ignorant that ſoule, that ſees thee without wonder.
Which is to me ſome praiſe, that I thy parts admire;
Thy eye Ioues lightning beares, thy voyce his dreadfull thunder.
Which not to anger bent, is muſique, and ſweet fire.
Celeſtiall as thou art, Oh pardon loue this wrong,
That ſings heauens praiſe, with ſuch an earthly tongue.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: You finde not the apoſtraphas, and ſo miſſe the accent. Let me ſuperuiſe the cangenet.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Here are onely numbers ratified, but for the elegancy, facility, & golden cadence of poeſie caret: Ouiddius Naſo was the man. And why in deed Naſo, but for ſmelling out the odoriferous flowers of fancy? the ierkes of inuention imitarie is nothing: So doth the Hound his maſter, the Ape his keeper, the tyred Horſe his rider: But Damoſella virgin, Was this directed to you?

sp.speaker: Iaq.
sp.p: I ſir from one mounſier Berowne, one of the ſtrange Queenes Lords.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: I will ouerglance the ſuperſcript.
sp.q: To the ſnow-white hand of the moſt beautious Lady Roſaline.
sp.p: I will looke againe on the intellect of the Letter, for the nomination of the partie written to the perſon written vnto.
sp.q: Your Ladiſhips in all deſired imployment, Berowne.

sp.speaker: Per.
sp.p: Sir Holofernes, this Berowne is one of the Votaries with the King, and here he hath framed a Letter to a ſequent of the ſtranger Queenes: which accidentally, or by the way of progreſſion, hath miſcarried. Trip and goe my ſweete, deliuer this Paper into the hand of the King, it may concerne much: ſtay not thy complement, I forgiue thy duetie, adue.

sp.speaker: Maid.
sp.l: Good Coſtard go with me:
Sir God ſaue your life.

sp.speaker: Coſt.
sp.p: Haue with thee my girle.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Sir you haue done this in the feare of God very religiouſly: and as a certaine Father ſaith

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Sir tell not me of the Father, I do feare colourable colours. But to returne to the Verſes, Did they pleaſe you ſir Nathaniel?

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Marueilous well for the pen.

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: I do dine to day at the fathers of a certaine Pupill of mine, where if (being repaſt) it ſhall pleaſe you to gratifie the table with a Grace, I will on my priuiledge I haue with the parents of the foreſaid Childe or Pupill, vndertake your bien vonuto, where I will proue thoſe Verſes to be very vnlearned, neither ſauouring of Poetrie, Wit, nor Inuention. I beſeech your Societie.

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.p: And thanke you to: for ſocietie (ſaith the text) is the happineſſe of life.

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.l: And certes the text moſt infallibly concludes it.
Sir I do inuite you too, you ſhall not ſay me nay: pauca verba.
Away, the gentles are at their game, and we will to our recreation.

div.stage: Enter Berowne with a Paper in his hand, alone.

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.l: The King he is hunting the Deare,
I am courſing my ſelfe.
sp.p: They haue pitcht a Toyle, I am toyling in a pytch, pitch that defiles; defile, a foule word: Well, ſet thee downe ſorrow; for ſo they ſay the foole ſaid, and ſo ſay I, and I the foole: Well proued wit. By the Lord this Loue is as mad as Aiax, it kils ſheepe, it kils mee, I a ſheepe: Well proued againe a my ſide. I will not loue; if I do hang me: yfaith I will not. O but her eye: by this light, but for her eye, I would not loue her; yes, for her two eyes. Well, I doe nothing in the world but lye, and lye in my throate. By heauen I doe loue, and it hath taught mee to Rime, and to be mallicholie: and here is part of my Rime, and heere my mallicholie. Well, ſhe hath one a' my Sonnets already, the Clowne bore it, the Foole ſent it, and the Lady hath it: ſweet Clowne, ſweeter Foole, ſweeteſt Lady. By the world, I would not care a pin, if the other three were in. Here comes one with a paper, God giue him grace to grone.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Ay mee!

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Shot by heauen: proceede ſweet Cupid, thou haſt thumpt him with thy Birdbolt vnder the left pap: in faith ſecrets.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: So ſweete a kiſſe the golden Sunne giues not,
To thoſe freſh morning drops vpon the Roſe,
As thy eye beames, when their freſh rayſe haue ſmot.
The night of dew that on my cheekes downe flowes.
Nor ſhines the ſiluer Moone one halfe ſo bright,
Through the tranſparent boſome of the deepe,
As doth thy face through teares of mine giue light:
Thou ſhin'ſt in euery teare that I doe weepe,
No drop, but as a Coach doth carry thee:
So rideſt thou triumphing in my woe.
Do but behold the teares that ſwell in me,
And they thy glory through my griefe will ſhow:
But doe not loue thy ſelfe, then thou wilt keepe
My teares for glaſſes, and ſtill make me weepe.
O Queene of Queenes, how farre doſt thou excell,
No thought can thinke, nor tongue of mortall tell.
How ſhall ſhe know my griefes? Ile drop the paper.
Sweet leaues ſhade folly. Who is he comes heere?
What Longauill, and reading: liſten eare.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Now in thy likeneſſe, one more foole appeare.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Ay me, I am forſworne.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Why he comes in like a periure, wearing papers.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: In loue I hope, ſweet fellowſhip in ſhame.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: One drunkard loues another of the name.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: Am I the firſt yt haue been periur'd ſo?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: I could put thee in comfort, not by two that I know,
Thou makeſt the triumphery, the corner cap of ſocietie,
