The ſhape of Loues Tiburne, that hangs vp ſimplicitie.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: I feare theſe ſtubborn lines lack power to moue.
O ſweet Maria, Empreſſe of my Loue,
Theſe numbers will I teare, and write in proſe.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: O Rimes are gards on wanton Cupids hoſe,
Disfigure not his Shop.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: This ſame ſhall goe.

l.hi: Did not the heauenly Rhetoricke of thine eye,
'Gainſt whom the world cannot hold argument,
Perſwade my heart to this falſe periurie?
Vowes for thee broke deſerue not puniſhment.
A woman I forſwore, but I will proue,
Thou being a Goddeſſe, I forſwore not thee.
My Vow was earthly, thou a heauenly Loue.
Thy grace being gain'd, cures all diſgrace in me.
Vowes are but breath; and breath a vapour is.
Then thou faire Sun, which on my earth doeſt ſhine,
Exhalest this vapor-vow, in thee it is:
If broken then, it is no fault of mine:
If by me broke, What foole is not ſo wiſe,
To looſe an oath, to win a Paradiſe?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: This is the liuer veine, which makes fleſh a deity.
A greene Gooſe, a Coddeſſe, pure pure Idolatry.
God amend vs, God amend, we are much out o' th' way.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: By whom ſhall I ſend this (company?) Stay.

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.l: All hid, all hid, an old infant play,
Like a demie God, here ſit I in the skie,
And wretched fooles ſecrets heedfully ore-eye.
More Sacks to the myll. O heauens I haue my wiſh,
Dumaine transform'd, foure Woodcocks in a diſh.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: O moſt diuine Kate.

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.p: O moſt prophane coxcombe.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: By heauen the wonder of a mortall eye.

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.p: By earth ſhe is not, corporall, there you lye.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Her Amber haires for foule hath amber coted.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: An Amber coloured Rauen was well noted.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: As vpright as the Cedar.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Stoope I ſay her ſhoulder is with-child.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: As faire as day.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I as ſome daies, but then no ſunne muſt ſhine.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: O that I had my wiſh?

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: And I had mine.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: And mine too good Lord.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Amen, ſo I had mine: Is not that a good word?

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: I would forget her, but a Feuer ſhe
Raignes in my bloud, and will remembred be.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: A Feuer in your bloud, why then inciſion
Would let her out in Sawcers, ſweet miſpriſion.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Once more Ile read the Ode that I haue writ.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Once more Ile marke how Loue can varry Wit.

q.l: On a day, alack the day:
Loue, whoſe Month is euery May,
Spied a bloſſome paſſing faire,
Playing in the wanton ayre:
Through the Veluet, leaues the winde,
All vnſeene, can paſſage finde.
That the Louer ſicke to death,
Wiſh himſelfe the heauens breath.
Ayre (quoth he) thy cheekes may blowe,
Ayre, would I might triumph ſo.
But alacke my hand is ſworne,
Nere to plucke thee from thy throne:
Vow alacke for youth vnmeete,
Youth ſo apt to plucke a ſweet.
Doe not call it ſinne in me,
That I am forſworne for thee.
Thou for whom loue would ſweare,
Iuno but an Aethiop were,
And denie himſelfe for Ioue.
Turning mortall for thy Loue.

sp.l: This will I ſend, and ſomething elſe more plaine.
That ſhall expreſſe my true-loues faſting paine.
O would the King, Berowne and Longauill,
Were Louers too, ill to example ill,
Would from my forehead wipe a periur'd note:
For none offend, where all alike doe dote.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.l: Dumaine, thy Loue is farre from charitie,
That in Loues griefe deſir'ſt ſocietie:
You may looke pale, but I ſhould bluſh I know,
To be ore-heard, and taken napping ſo.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Come ſir, you bluſh: as his, your caſe is ſuch,
You chide at him, offending twice as much.
You doe not loue Maria? Longauile,
Did neuer Sonnet for her ſake compile;
Nor neuer lay his wreathed armes athwart
His louing boſome, to keepe downe his heart.
I haue beene cloſely ſhrowded in this buſh,
And markt you both, and for you both did bluſh.
I heard your guilty Rimes, obſeru'd your faſhion:
Saw ſighes reeke from you, noted well your paſſion.
Aye me, ſayes one! O Ioue, the other cries!
On her haires were Gold, Chriſtall the others eyes.
You would for Paradiſe breake Faith and troth,
And Ioue for your Loue would infringe an oath.
What will Berowne ſay when that he ſhall heare
Faith infringed, which ſuch zeale did ſweare.
How will he ſcorne? how will he ſpend his wit?
How will he triumph, leape, and laugh at it?
For all the wealth that euer I did ſee,
I would not haue him know ſo much by me.

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.l: Now ſtep I forth to whip hypocriſie.
Ah good my Liedge, I pray thee pardon me.
Good heart, What grace haſt thou thus to reproue
Theſe wormes for louing, that art moſt in loue?
Your eyes doe make no couches in your teares.
There is no certaine Princeſſe that appeares.
You'll not be periur'd, 'tis a hatefull thing:
Tuſh, none but Minſtrels like of Sonnetting.
But are you not aſham'd? nay, are you not
All three of you, to be thus much ore'ſhot?
You found his Moth, the King your Moth did ſee:
But I a Beame doe finde in each of three.
O what a Scene of fool'ry haue I ſeene.
Of ſighes, of grones, of ſorrow, and of teene:
O me, with what ſtrict patience haue I ſat,
To ſee a King transformed to a Gnat?
To ſee great Hercules whipping a Gigge,
And profound Salomon tuning a Iygge?
And Neſtor play at puſh-pin with the boyes,
And Critticke Tymon laugh at idle toyes.
Where lies thy griefe? O tell me good Dumaine;
And gentle Longauill, where lies thy paine?
And where my Liedges? all about the breſt:
A Candle hoa!

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Too bitter is thy ieſt.
Are wee betrayed thus to thy ouer-view?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Not you by me, but I betrayed to you.
I that am honeſt, I that hold it ſinne
To breake the vow I am ingaged in.
I am betrayed by keeping company
With men, like men of inconſtancie.
When ſhall you ſee me write a thing in rime?
Or grone for Ioane? or ſpend a minutes time,
sp.p: In pruning mee, when ſhall you heare that I will praiſe a hand, a foot, a face, an eye: a gate, a ſtate, a brow, a breſt, a waſte, a legge, a limme.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Soft, Whither a-way ſo faſt?
A true man, or a theefe, that gallops ſo.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I poſt from Loue, good Louer let me go.

sp.speaker: Iaqu.
sp.p: God bleſſe the King.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: What Preſent haſt thou there?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Some certaine treaſon.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: What makes treaſon heere?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Nay it makes nothing ſir.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: If it marre nothing neither,
The treaſon and you goe in peace away together.

sp.speaker: Iaqu.
sp.l: I beſeech your Grace let this Letter be read,
Our perſon miſ-doubts it: it was treaſon he ſaid.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Berowne, read it ouer.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Where hadſt thou it?

sp.speaker: Iaqu.
sp.p: Of Coſtard.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Where hadſt thou it?

sp.speaker: Coſt.
sp.p: Of Dun Adramadio, Dun Adramadio.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: How now, what is in you? why doſt thou tear it?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: A toy my Liedge, a toy: your grace needes not feare it.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: It did moue him to paſſion, and therefore let's heare it.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: It is Berowns writing, and heere is his name.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Ah you whoreſon loggerhead, you were borne to doe me ſhame.
Guilty my Lord, guilty: I confeſſe, I confeſſe.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: That you three fooles, lackt mee foole, to make vp the meſſe.
He, he, and you: and you my Liedge, and I,
Are picke-purſes in Loue, and we deſerue to die.
O diſmiſſe this audience, and I ſhall tell you more.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Now the number is euen.

sp.speaker: Berow.
sp.p: True true, we are fowre: will theſe Turtles be gone?

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Hence ſirs, away.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Walk aſide the true folke, & let the traytors ſtay.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Sweet Lords, ſweet Louers, O let vs imbrace,
As true we are as fleſh and bloud can be,
The Sea will ebbe and flow, heauen will ſhew his face:
Young bloud doth not obey an old decree.
We cannot croſſe the cauſe why we are borne:
Therefore of all hands muſt we be forſworne.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: What, did theſe rent lines ſhew ſome loue of thine?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Did they, quoth you? Who ſees the heauenly Roſaline,
That (like a rude and ſauage man of Inde.)
At the firſt opening of the gorgeous Eaſt,
Bowes not his vaſſall head, and ſtrooken blinde,
Kiſſes the baſe ground with obedient breaſt?
What peremptory Eagle-ſighted eye
Dares looke vpon the heauen of her brow,
That is not blinded by her maieſtie?

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: What zeale, what furie, hath inſpir'd thee now?
My Loue (her Miſtres) is a gracious Moone,
Shee (an attending Starre) ſcarce ſeene a light.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: My eyes are then no eyes, nor I Berowne.
O, but for my Loue, day would turne to night,
Of all complexions the cul'd ſoueraignty,
Doe meet as at a faire in her faire cheeke,
Where ſeuerall Worthies make one dignity,
Where nothing wants, that want it ſelfe doth ſeeke.
Lend me the flouriſh of all gentle tongues,
Fie painted Rethoricke, O ſhe needs it not,
To things of ſale, a ſellers praiſe belongs:
She paſſes prayſe, then prayſe too ſhort doth blot.
A withered Hermite, fiueſcore winters worne,
Might ſhake off fiftie, looking in her eye:
Beauty doth varniſh Age, as if new borne,
And giues the Crutch the Cradles infancie.
O 'tis the Sunne that maketh all things ſhine.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: By heauen, thy Loue is blacke as Ebonie.

sp.speaker: Berow.
sp.l: Is Ebonie like her? O word diuine?
A wife of ſuch wood were felicitie.
O who can giue an oth? Where is a booke?
That I may ſweare Beauty doth beauty lacke,
If that ſhe learne not of her eye to looke:
No face is faire that is not full ſo blacke.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: O paradoxe, Blacke is the badge of hell,
The hue of dungeons, and the Schoole of night:
And beauties creſt becomes the heauens well.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Diuels ſooneſt tempt reſembling ſpirits of light.
O if in blacke my Ladies browes be deckt,
It mournes, that painting vſurping haire
Should rauiſh doters with a falſe aſpect:
And therfore is ſhe borne to make blacke, faire.
Her fauour turnes the faſhion of the dayes,
For natiue bloud is counted painting now:
And therefore red that would auoyd diſpraiſe,
Paints it ſelfe blacke, to imitate her brow.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: To look like her are Chimny-ſweepers blacke.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: And ſince her time, are Colliers counted bright.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: And Aethiops of their ſweet complexion crake.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Dark needs no Candles now, for dark is light.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Your miſtreſſes dare neuer come in raine,
For feare their colours ſhould be waſht away.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: 'Twere good yours did: for ſir to tell you plaine,
Ile finde a fairer face not waſht to day.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Ile proue her faire, or talke till dooms-day here.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: No Diuell will fright thee then ſo much as ſhee.

sp.speaker: Duma.
sp.p: I neuer knew man hold vile ſtuffe ſo deere.

sp.speaker: Lou.
sp.p: Looke, heer's thy loue, my foot and her face ſee.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: O if the ſtreets were paued with thine eyes,
Her feet were much too dainty for ſuch tread.

sp.speaker: Duma.
sp.l: O vile, then as ſhe goes what vpward lyes?
The ſtreet ſhould ſee as ſhe walk'd ouer head.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: But what of this, are we not all in loue?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: O nothing ſo ſure, and thereby all forſworne.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Then leaue this chat, & good Berown now proue
Our louing lawfull, and our fayth not torne.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: I marie there, ſome flattery for this euill.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: O ſome authority how to proceed,
Some tricks, ſome quillets, how to cheat the diuell.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Some ſalue for periurie.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: O 'tis more then neede.
Haue at you then affections men at armes,
Conſider what you firſt did ſweare vnto:
To faſt, to ſtudy, and to ſee no woman:
Flat treaſon againſt the Kingly ſtate of youth.
Say, Can you faſt? your ſtomacks are too young:
And abſtinence ingenders maladies.
And where that you haue vow'd to ſtudie (Lords)
In that each of you haue forſworne his Booke
Can you ſtill dreame and pore, and thereon looke.
For when would you my Lord, or you, or you,
Haue found the ground of ſtudies excellence,
Without the beauty of a womans face;
From womens eyes this doctrine I deriue,
They are the Ground, the Bookes, the Achadems,
From whence doth ſpring the true Promethean fire.
Why, vniuerſall plodding poyſons vp
The nimble ſpirits in the arteries,
As motion and long during action tyres
The ſinnowy vigour of the trauailer.
Now for not looking on a womans face,
You haue in that forſworne the vſe of eyes:
And ſtudie too, the cauſer of your vow.
For where is any Author in the world,
Teaches ſuch beauty as a womans eye:
Learning is but an adiunct to our ſelfe,
And where we are, our Learning likewiſe is.
Then when our ſelues we ſee in Ladies eyes,
With our ſelues.
Doe we not likewiſe ſee our learning there?
O we haue made a Vow to ſtudie, Lords,
And in that vow we haue forſworne our Bookes:
For when would you (my Leege) or you, or you?
In leaden contemplation haue found out
Such fiery Numbers as the prompting eyes,
Of beauties tutors haue inrich'd you with:
Other ſlow Arts intirely keepe the braine:
And therefore finding barraine practizers,
Scarce ſhew a harueſt of their heauy toyle.
But Loue firſt learned in a Ladies eyes,
Liues not alone emured in the braine:
But with the motion of all elements,
Courſes as ſwift as thought in euery power,
And giues to euery power a double power,
Aboue their functions and their offices.
It addes a precious ſeeing to the eye:
A Louers eyes will gaze an Eagle blinde.
A Louers eare will heare the loweſt ſound.
When the ſuſpicious head of theft is ſtopt.
Loues feeling is more ſoft and ſenſible,
Then are the tender hornes of Cockled Snayles.
Loues tongue proues dainty, Bachus groſſe in taſte,
For Valour, is not Loue a Hercules?
Still climing trees in the Heſporides.
Subtill as Sphinx, as ſweet and muſicall,
As bright Apollo's Lute, ſtrung with his haire.
And when Loue ſpeakes, the voyce of all the Gods,
Make heauen drowſie with the harmonie.
Neuer durſt Poet touch a pen to write,
Vntill his Inke were tempred with Loues ſighes:
O then his lines would rauiſh ſauage eares,
And plant in Tyrants milde humilitie.
From womens eyes this doctrine I deriue.
They ſparcle ſtill the right promethean fire,
They are the Bookes, the Arts, the Achademes,
That ſhew, containe, and nouriſh all the world.
Elſe none at all in ought proues excellent.
Then fooles you were theſe women to forſweare:
Or keeping what is ſworne, you will proue fooles,
For Wiſedomes ſake, a word that all men loue:
Or for Loues ſake, a word that loues all men.
Or for Mens ſake, the author of theſe Women:
Or Womens ſake, by whom we men are Men.
Let's once looſe our oathes to finde our ſelues,
Or elſe we looſe our ſelues, to keepe our oathes▪
It is religion to be thus forſworne.
For Charity it ſelfe fulfills the Law:
And who can ſeuer loue from Charity.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Saint Cupid then, and Souldiers to the field.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Aduance your ſtandards, & vpon them Lords.
Pell, mell, downe with them: but be firſt aduis'd,
In conflict that you get the Sunne of them.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Now to plaine dealing, Lay theſe glozes by,
Shall we reſolue to woe theſe girles of France?

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: And winne them too, therefore let vs deuiſe,
Some entertainment for them in their Tents.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Firſt from the Park let vs conduct them thither,
Then homeward euery man attach the hand
Of his faire Miſtreſſe, in the afternoone
We will with ſome ſtrange paſtime ſolace them:
Such as the ſhortneſſe of the time can ſhape,
For Reuels, Dances, Maskes, and merry houres,
Fore-runne faire Loue, ſtrewing her way with flowres.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Away, away, no time ſhall be omitted,
That will be time, and may by vs be fitted.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Alone, alone ſowed Cockell, reap'd no Corne,
And Iuſtice alwaies whirles in equall meaſure:
Light Wenches may proue plagues to men forſworne,
If ſo, our Copper buyes no better treaſure.

div.head: Actus Quartus.
div.stage: Enter the Pedant, Curate and Dull.

sp.speaker: Curat.
sp.p: I praiſe God for you ſir, your reaſons at dinner haue beene ſharpe & ſententious: pleaſant without ſcurrillity, witty without affection, audacious without impudency, learned without opinion, and ſtrange without hereſie: I did conuerſe this quondam day with a companion of the Kings, who is intituled, nominated, or called, Don Adriano de Armatho.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Noui hominum tanquam te, His humour is lofty, his diſcourſe peremptorie: his tongue filed, his eye ambitious, his gate maieſticall, and his generall behauiour vaine, ridiculous, and thraſonicall. He is too picked, too ſpruce, too affected, too odde, as it were, too peregrinat, as I may call it.

sp.speaker: Curat.
sp.p: A moſt ſingular and choiſe Epithat,

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: He draweth out the thred of his verboſitie, finer then the ſtaple of his argument. I abhor ſuch phanaticall phantaſims, ſuch inſociable and poynt deuiſe companions, ſuch rackers of ortagriphie, as to ſpeake dout fine, when he ſhould ſay doubt; det, when he ſhold pronounce debt; de • t, not det: he clepeth a Calf, Caufe: halfe, haufe: neighbour vocatur nebour; neigh abreuiated ne: this is abhominable, which he would call abhominable: it inſinuateth me of infamie: ne inteligis domine, to make franti • ke, lunaticke?

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: Bome boon for boon preſcian, a little ſcratcht, 'twil ſerue.

sp.speaker: Curat.
sp.p: Vides ne quis venit?

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Chirra.

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p:
Quar •
Chirra, not Sirra?

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Men of peace well incountred.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Moſt millitarie ſir ſalutation▪

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: They haue beene at a great feaſt of Languages, and ſtolne the ſcraps.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: O they haue liu'd long on the almes-basket of words. I maruell thy M. hath not eaten thee for a word, for thou art not ſo long by the head as honorificabilitudinitatibus: Thou art eaſier ſwallowed then a flap dragon.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Peace, the peale begins.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Mounſier, are you not lettred?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Yes, yes, he • eaches boyes the Horne-booke:
What is Abſpeld backward with the horn on his head?

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: Ba, puericia with a horne added.

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.p: Ba moſt ſeely Sheepe, with a horne: you heare his learning.

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: Quis quis, thou Conſonant?

sp.speaker: Pag
sp.p: The laſt of the fiue Vowels if You repeat them, or the fift if I.

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: I will repeat them: a e I.

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.p: The She • pe, the other two concludes it o u.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Now by the ſalt waue of the mediteranium, a ſweet tutch, a quicke vene we of wit, ſnip ſnap, quick & home, it reioyceth my intellect, true wit.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Offered by a childe to an olde man: which is wit-old.

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: What is the figure? What is the figure?

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Hornes.

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: Thou diſputes like an Infant: goe whip thy Gigge.

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.p: Lend me your Horne to make one, and I will whip about your Infamie vnum cita a gigge of a Cuckolds horne.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: And I had but one penny in the world, thou ſhouldſt haue it to buy Ginger bread: Hold, there is the very Remuneration I had of thy Maiſter, thou halfpenny purſe of wit, thou Pidgeon-egge of diſcretion. O & the heauens were ſo pleaſed, that thou wert but my Baſtard; What a ioyfull father wouldſt thou make mee? Goe to, thou haſt it ad dungil, at the fingers ends, as they ſay.

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: Oh I ſmell falſe Latine, dunghel for vnguem.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Artſ-man preambulat, we will bee ſingled from the barbarous. Do you not educate youth at the Charghouſe on the top of the Mountaine?

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: Or Mons the hill.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: At your ſweet pleaſure, for the Mountaine.

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: I doe ſans queſtion.

sp.speaker: Bra.
sp.p: Sir, it is the Kings moſt ſweet pleaſure and affection, to congratulate the Princeſſe at her Pauilion, in the poſteriors of this day, which the rude multitude call the after-noone.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: The poſterior of the day, moſt generous ſir, is liable, congruent, and meaſurable for the after-noone: the word is well culd, choſe, ſweet, and apt I doe aſſure you ſir, I doe aſſure.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Sir, the King is a noble Gentleman, and my familiar, I doe aſſure ye very good friend: for what is inward betweene vs, let it paſſe. I doe beſeech thee remember thy curteſie. I beſeech thee apparell thy head: and among other importunate & moſt ſerious deſignes, and of great import indeed too: but let that paſſe, for I muſt tell thee it will pleaſe his Grace (by the world) ſometime to leane vpon my poore ſhoulder, and with his royall finger thus dallie with my excrement, with my muſtachio: but ſweet heart let that paſſe. By the world I recount no fable, ſome certaine ſpeciall honours it pleaſeth his greatneſſe to impart to Armado a Souldier, a man of trauell, that hath ſeene the world: but let that paſſe; the very all of all is: but ſweet heart, I do implore ſecrecie, that the King would haue mee preſent the Princeſſe (ſweet chucke) with ſome delightfull oſtentation, or ſhow, or pageant, or anticke, or fire-worke: Now, vnderſtanding that the Curate and your ſweet ſelf are good at ſuch eruptions, and ſodaine breaking out of myrth • . i • were) I haue acquainted you withall, to the end to craue your aſſiſtance.

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: Sir, you ſhall preſent before her the Nine Worthies. Sir Holofernes, as concerning ſome entertainment of time, ſome ſhow in the poſterior of this day, to bee rendred by our aſſiſtants the Kings command: and this moſt gallant, illuſtrate and learned Gentleman, before the Princeſſe: I ſay none ſo ſit as to preſent the Nine Worthies.

sp.speaker: Curat.
sp.p: Where will you finde men worthy enough to preſent them?

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: Ioſua, your ſelfe: my ſelfe, and this gallant gentleman Iudas Machabeus; this Swaine (becauſe of his great limme or • oynt) ſhall paſſe Pompey the great, the Page Hercules.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Pardon ſir, error: He is not quantitie enough for that Worthies thumb, hee is not ſo big as the end of his Club.

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: Shall I haue audience? he ſhall preſent Hercules in minoritie: his enter and exit ſhall bee ſtrangling a Snake; and I will haue an Apologie for that purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.p: An excellent deuice: ſo if any of the audience hiſſe, you may cry, Well done Hercules, now thou cruſheſt the Snake; that is the way to make an offence gracious, though few haue the grace to doe it.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: For the reſt of the Worthies?

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: I will play three my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.p: Thrice worthy Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Shall I tell you a thing?

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: We attend.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: We will haue, if this fadge not, an Antique. I beſeech you follow.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Via good-man Dull, thou haſt ſpoken no word all this while.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.p: Nor vnderſtood none neither ſir.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Alone, we will employ thee.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.p:
Ile make one in a dance, or ſo: or I will play
on the taber to the Worthies, & let them dance the hey.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Moſt Dull, honeſt Dull, to our ſport away.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Sweet hearts we ſhall be rich ere we depart,
If fairings come thus plentifully in.
A Lady wal'd about with Diamonds: Look you, what I haue from the louing King.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Madam, came nothing elſe along with that?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Nothing but this yes as much loue in Rime,
As would be cram'd vp in a ſheet of paper
Writ on both ſides the leaſe, margent and all,
That he was faine to ſeale on Cupids name.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: That was the way to make his god-head wax:
For he hath beene fiue thouſand yeeres a Boy.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.p: I, and a ſhrewd vnhappy gallowes too.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: You'll nere be friends with him, a kild your ſiſter.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.p: He made her melancholy, ſad, and heauy, and ſo ſhe died: had ſhe beene Light like you, of ſuch a merrie nimble ſtirring ſpirit, ſhe might a bin a Grandam ere ſhe died. And ſo may you: For a light heart liues long.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: What's your darke meaning mouſe, of this light word?

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: A light condition in a beauty darke.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: We need more light to finde your meaning out.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.l: You'll marre the light by taking it in ſnuffe:
Therefore Ile darkely end the argument.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: Look what you doe, you doe it ſtil i' th darke.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: So do not you, for you are a light Wench.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: Indeed I waigh not you, and therefore light.

sp.speaker: Ka.
sp.p: You waigh me not, O that's you care not for me.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: Great reaſon: for paſt care, is ſtill paſt cure.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Well bandied both, a ſet of Wit well played.
But Roſaline, you haue a Fauour too?
Who ſent it? and what is it?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: I would you knew.
And if my face were but as faire as yours.
My Fauour were as great, be witneſſe this.
Nay, I haue Verſes too, I thanke Berowne,
The numbers true, and were the numbring too,
I were the faireſt goddeſſe on the ground.
I am compar'd to twenty thouſand fairs.
O he hath drawne my picture in his letter.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Any thing like?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: Much in the letters, nothing in the praiſe.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Beauteous as Incke: a good concluſion.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: Faire as a text B. in a Coppie booke.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Ware penſals. How? Let me not die your debtor,
My red Dominicall, my golden letter.
O that your face were full of Ocs.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: A Pox of that ieſt, and I beſhrew all Shrowes:
But Katherine, what was ſent to you
From faire Dumaine?

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: Madame, this Gloue.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Did he not ſend you twaine?

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.l: Yes Madame: and moreouer,
Some thouſand Verſes of a faithfull Louer.
A huge tranſlation of hypocriſie,
Vildly compiled, profound ſimplicitie.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: This, and theſe Pearls, to me ſent Longauile.
The Letter is too long by halfe a mile.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: I thinke no leſſe: Doſt thou wiſh in heart
The Chaine were longer, and the Letter ſhort.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I, or I would theſe hands might neuer part.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.p: We are wiſe girles to mocke our Louers ſo.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: They are worſe fooles to purchaſe mocking ſo.
That ſame Berowne ile torture ere I goe.
O that I knew he were but in by th' weeke,
How I would make him fawne, and begge, and ſeeke,
And wait the ſeaſon, and obſerue the times,
And ſpend his prodigall wits in booteles rimes.
And ſhape his ſeruice wholly to my deuice,
And make him proud to make me proud that ieſts.
So pertaunt like would I o' reſway his ſtate,
That he ſhold be my foole, and I his fate.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: None are ſo ſurely caught▪ when they are catcht,
As Wit turn'd foole, follie in Wiſedome hatch'd:
Hath wiſedoms warrant, and the helpe of Schoole,
And Wits owne grace to grace a learned Foole?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: The bloud of youth burns not with ſuch exceſſe,
As grauities reuolt to wantons be.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Follie in Fooles beares not ſo ſtrong a note,
As fool'ry in the Wiſe, when Wit doth dote:
Since all the power thereof it doth apply,
To proue by Wit, worth in ſimplicitie.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Heere comes Boyet, and mirth in his face.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: O I am ſtab'd with laughter, Wher's her Grace?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Thy newes Boyet?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Prepare Madame, prepare.
Arme Wenches arme, incounters mounted are,
Againſt your Peace, Loue doth approach, diſguis'd:
Armed in arguments, you'll be ſurpriz'd.
Muſter your Wits, ſtand in your owne defence,
Or hide your heads like Cowards, and flie hence.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Saint Dennis to S. Cupid: What are they,
That charge their breath againſt vs? Say ſcout ſay.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Vnder the coole ſhade of a Siccamore,
I thought to cloſe mine eyes ſome halfe an houre:
When lo to interrupt my purpos'd reſt,
Toward that ſhade I might behold addreſt,
The King and his companions: warely
I ſtole into a neighbour thicket by,
And ouer-heard, what you ſhall ouer-heare:
That by and by diſguis'd they will be heere.
Their Herald is a pretty knauiſh Page:
That well by heart hath con'd his embaſſage,
Action and accent did they teach him there.
Thus muſt thou ſpeake, and thus thy body beare.
And euer and anon they made a doubt,
Preſence maieſticall would put him out:
For quoth the King, an Angell ſhalt thou ſee:
Yet feare not thou, but ſpeake audaciouſly.
The Boy reply'd, An Angell is not euill:
I ſhould haue fear'd her, had ſhe beene a deuill▪
With that all laugh'd, and clap'd him on the ſhoulder,
Making the bold wagg by their praiſes bolder.
One rub'd his elboe thus, and fleer'd, and ſwore,
A better ſpeech was neuer ſpoke before.
Another with his finger and his thumb,
Cry'd via, we will doo't, come what will come.
The third he caper'd and cried, All goes well.
The fourth turn'd on the toe, and downe he fell:
With that they all did tumble on the ground,
With ſuch a zelous laughter ſo profound,
That in this ſpleene ridiculous appeares,
To checke their folly paſſions ſolemne teares.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.p: But what, but what, come they to viſit vs?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: They do, they do; and are apparel'd thus,
Like Muſcouites, or Ruſſians, as I geſſe.
Their purpoſe is to parlee, to court, and dance,
And euery one his Loue-feat will aduance,
Vnto his ſeuerall Miſtreſſe: which they'll know
By fauours ſeuerall, which they did beſtow.

sp.speaker: Queen.
sp.l: And will they ſo? the Gallants ſhall be taskt:
For Ladies; we will euery one be maskt,
And not a man of them ſhall haue the grace
Deſpight of ſute, to ſee a Ladies face.
Hold Roſaline, this Fauour thou ſhalt weare,
And then the King will court thee for his Deare:
Hold, take thou this my ſweet, and giue me thine,
So ſhall Berowne take me for Roſaline.
And change your Fauours too, ſo ſhall your Loues
Woo contrary, deceiu'd by theſe remoues.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Come on then, weare the fauours moſt in ſight.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.p: But in this changing, What is your intent?

sp.speaker: Queen.
sp.l: The effect of my intent is to croſſe theirs:
They doe it but in mocking merriment,
And mocke for mocke is onely my intent.
Their ſeuerall counſels they vnboſome ſhall,
To Loues miſtooke, and ſo be mockt withall.
Vpon the next occaſion that we meete,
With Viſages diſplayd to talke and greete.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: But ſhall we dance, if they deſire vs too't?

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: No, to the death we will not moue a foot,
Nor to their pen'd ſpeech render we no grace:
But while 'tis ſpoke, each turne away his face.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Why that contempt will kill the keepers heart,
And quite diuorce his memory from his part.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.l: Therefore I doe it, and I make no doubt,
The reſt will ere come in, if he be out.
Theres no ſuch ſport, as ſport by ſport orethrowne:
To make theirs ours, and ours none but our owne.
So ſhall we ſtay mocking entended game,
And they well mockt, depart away with ſhame.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: The Trompet ſounds, be maskt, the maskers come.

div.stage: Enter Black moores with muſicke, the Boy with a ſpeech, and the reſt of the Lords diſguiſed.

p.hi: All haile, the richeſt Beauties on the earth.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Beauties no richer then rich Taffata.

sp.speaker: Pag.

p.hi: A holy parcell of the faireſt dames that euer turn'd their backes to mortall viewes.

sp.stage: The Ladies turne their backes to him.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Their eyes villaine, their eyes.

l.hi: That euer turn'd their eyes to mortall viewes.
Out

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: True, out indeed.

l.hi: Out of your fauours heauenly ſpirits vouchſafe
Not to beholde.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Once to behold, rogue.

l.hi: Once to behold with your Sunne beamed eyes,
With your Sunne beamed eyes.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: They will not anſwer to that Epythite,
You were beſt call it Daughter beamed eyes.

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.p: They do not marke me, and that brings me out.

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.p: Is this your perfectneſſe? be gon you rogue.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: What would theſe ſtrangers?
Know their mindes Boyet.
If they doe ſpeake our language, 'tis our will
That ſome plaine man recount their purpoſes.
Know what they would?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p: What would you with the Princes?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Nothing but peace, and gentle viſitation.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: What would they, ſay they?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Nothing but peace, and gentle viſitation.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Why that they haue, and bid them ſo be gon.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: She ſaies you haue it, and you may be gon.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Say to her we haue meaſur'd many miles,
To tread a Meaſure with you on the graſſe.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: They ſay that they haue meaſur'd many a mile,
To tread a Meaſure with you on this graſſe.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: It is not ſo. Aske them how many inches
Is in one mile? If they haue meaſur'd manie,
The meaſure then of one is eaſlie told:

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: If to come hither, you haue meaſur'd miles,
And many miles: the Princeſſe bids you tell,
How many inches doth fill vp one mile?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Tell her we meaſure them by weary ſteps.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: She heares her ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: How manie wearie ſteps,
Of many wearie miles you haue ore-gone,
Are numbred in the trauell of one mile?

sp.speaker: Bero.
sp.l: We number nothing that we ſpend for you,
Our dutie is ſo rich, ſo infinite,
That we may doe it ſtill without accompt.
Vouchſafe to ſhew the ſunſhine of your face,
That we (like ſauages) may worſhip it.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: My face is but a Moone, and clouded too.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Bleſſed are clouds, to doe as ſuch clouds do.
Vouchſafe bright Moone, and theſe thy ſtars to ſhine,
(Thoſe clouds remooued) vpon our waterie eyne.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: O vaine peticioner, beg a greater matter,
Thou now requeſts but Mooneſhine in the water.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Then in our meaſure, vouchſafe but one change.
Thou bidſt me begge, this begging is not ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: Play muſicke then: nay you muſt doe it ſoone.
Not yet no dance: thus change I like the Moone.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Will you not dance? How come you thus eſtranged?

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: You tooke the Moone at full, but now ſhee's changed?

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Yet ſtill ſhe is the Moone, and I the Man.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: The muſick playes, vouchſafe ſome motion to it: Our eares vouchſafe it.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: But your legges ſhould doe it.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Since you are ſtrangers, & come here by chance,
Wee'll not be nice, take hands, we will not dance.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Why take you hands then?

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: Onelie to part friends.
Curtſie ſweet hearts, and ſo the Meaſure ends.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: More meaſure of this meaſure, be not nice.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: We can afford no more at ſuch a price.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Priſe your ſelues: What buyes your companie?

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Your abſence onelie.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: That can neuer be.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: Then cannot we be bought: and ſo adue,
Twice to your Viſore, and halfe once to you.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: If you denie to dance, let's hold more chat.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: In priuate then.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: I am beſt pleas'd with that.

sp.speaker: Be.
sp.p: White handed Miſtris, one ſweet word with thee.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Hony, and Milke, and Suger: there is three.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Nay then two treyes, an if you grow ſo nice
Methegline, Wort, and Malmſey; well runne dice:
There's halfe a dozen ſweets.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Seuenth ſweet adue, ſince you can cogg,
Ile play no more with you.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: One word in ſecret.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Let it not be ſweet.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Thou greeu'ſt my gall.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Gall, bitter.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Therefore meete.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: Will you vouchſafe with me to change a word?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Name it.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Faire Ladie.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Say you ſo? Faire Lord:
Take you that for your faire Lady.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Pleaſe it you,
As much in priuate, and Ile bid adieu.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: What, was your vizard made without a tong?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: I know the reaſon Ladie why you aske.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: O for your reaſon, quickly ſir, I long.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: You haue a double tongue within your mask.
And would affoord my ſpeechleſſe vizard halfe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Veale quoth the Dutch-man: is not Veale a Calfe?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: A Calfe faire Ladie?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: No, a faire Lord Calfe.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Let's part the word.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No, Ile not be your halfe:
Take all and weane it, it may proue an Oxe.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Looke how you but your ſelfe in thoſe ſharpe mockes.
Will you giue hornes chaſt Ladie? Do not ſo.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Then die a Calfe before your horns do grow.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: One word in priuate with you ere I die.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Bleat ſoftly then, the Butcher heares you cry.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: The tongues of mocking wenches are as keen
As is the Razors edge, inuiſible:
Cutting a ſmaller haire then may be ſeene,
Aboue the ſenſe of ſence ſo ſenſible:
Seemeth their conference, their conceits haue wings,
Fleeter then arrows, bullets wind, thoght, ſwifter things

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Not one word more my maides, breake off, breake off.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: By heauen, all drie beaten with pure ſcoffe.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Farewell madde Wenches, you haue ſimple wits.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Twentie adieus my frozen Muſcouits.
Are theſe the breed of wits ſo wondred at?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p: Tapers they are, with your ſweete breathes puft out.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Wel-liking wits they haue, groſſe, groſſe, fat, fat.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: O pouertie in wit, Kingly poore flout.
Will they not (thinke you) hang themſelues to night?
Or euer but in vizards ſhew their faces:
This pert Berowne was out of count'nance quite.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: They were all in lamentable caſes.
The King was vveeping ripe for a good word.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Berowne did ſweare himſelfe out of all ſuite.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Dumaine was at my ſeruice, and his ſword:
No point (quoth I:) my ſeruant ſtraight vvas mute.

sp.speaker: Ka.
sp.l: Lord Longauill ſaid I came ore his hart:
And trow you vvhat he call'd me?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Qualme perhaps.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: Yes in good faith.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Go ſickneſſe as thou art.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Well, better wits haue worne plain ſtatute caps,
But vvil you heare; the King is my loue ſworne.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: And quicke Berowne hath plighted faith to me.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: And Longauill was for my ſeruice borne.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Dumaine is mine as ſure as barke on tree.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Madam, and prettie miſtreſſes giue care,
Immediately they will againe be heere
In their owne ſhapes: for it can neuer be,
They will digeſt this harſh indignitie.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Will they returne?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: They will they will, God knowes,
And leape for ioy, though they are lame with blowes:
Therefore change Fauours, and when they repaire,
Blow like ſweet Roſes, in this ſummer aire.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: How blovv? how blovv? Speake to bee vnderſtood.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Faire Ladies maskt, are Roſes in their bud:
Diſmaskt, their damaske ſweet commixture ſhowne,
Are Angels vailing clouds, or Roſes blowne.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Auant perplexitie: What ſhall vve do,
If they returne in their owne ſhapes to wo?

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: Good Madam, if by me you'l be aduis'd,
Let's mocke them ſtill as well knowne as diſguis'd:
Let vs complaine to them vvhat fooles were heare,
Diſguis'd like Muſcouites in ſhapeleſſe geare:
And wonder what they were, and to what end
Their ſhallow ſhowes, and Prologue vildely pen'd:
And their rough carriage ſo ridiculous,
Should be preſented at our Tent to vs.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p: Ladies, withdraw: the gallants are at hand.

sp.speaker: Quee.
sp.p: Whip to our Tents, as Roes runnes ore Land.

div.stage: Enter the King and the reſt.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Faire ſir, God ſaue you. Wher's the Princeſſe?

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Gone to her Tent.
Pleaſe it your Maieſtie command me any ſeruice to her?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: That ſhe vouchſafe me audience for one word.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: I will, and ſo will ſhe, I know my Lord.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: This fellow pickes vp wit as Pigeons peaſe,
And vtters it againe, when Ioue doth pleaſe.
He is Wits Pedler, and retailes his Wares,
At Wakes, and Waſſels, Meetings, M • kets, Faires.
And we that ſell by groſſe, the Lord doth know,
Haue not the grace to grace it with ſuch ſhow.
This Gallant pins the Wenches on his ſleeue.
Had he bin Adam, he had tempted Eue.
He can carue too, and liſpe: Why this is he,
That kiſt away his hand in courteſie.
This is the Ape of Forme, Monſieur the nice,
That when he plaies at Tables, chides the Dice
In honorable tearmes: Nay he can ſing
A meane moſt meanly, and in Vſhering
Mend him who can: the Ladies call him ſweete.
The ſtaires as he treads on them kiſſe his feete.
This is the flower that ſmiles on euerie one,
To ſhew his teeth as white as Whales bone.
And conſciences that wil not die in debt,
Pay him the dutie of honie-tongued Boyet.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: A bliſter on his ſweet tongue with my hart,
That put Armathoes Page out of his part.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: See where it comes. Behauiour what wer't thou,
Till this madman ſhew'd thee? And what art thou now?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: All haile ſweet Madame, and faire time of day.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Faire in all Haile is foule, as I conceiue.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Conſtrue my ſpeeches better, if you may.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Then wiſh me better, I wil giue you leaue.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: We came to viſit you, and purpoſe now
To leade you to our Court, vouchſafe it then.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: This field ſhal hold me, and ſo hold your vow:
Nor God, nor I, delights in periur'd men.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Rebuke me not for that which you prouoke:
The vertue of your eie muſt breake my oth.

sp.speaker: Q.
sp.l: You nickname vertue: vice you ſhould haue ſpoke:
For vertues office neuer breakes men troth.
Now by my maiden honor, yet as pure
As the vnſallied Lilly, I proteſt,
A world of torments though I ſhould endure,
I would not yeeld to be your houſes gueſt:
So much I hate a breaking cauſe to be
Of heauenly oaths, vow'd with integritie.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: O you haue liu'd in deſolation heere,
Vnſeene, vnuiſited, much to our ſhame.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Not ſo my Lord, it is not ſo I ſweare,
We haue had paſtimes heere, and pleaſant game,
A meſſe of Ruſſians left vs but of late.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: How Madam? Ruſsians?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: I in truth, my Lord.
Trim gallants, full of Courtſhip and of ſtate.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: Madam ſpeake true. It is not ſo my Lord:
My Ladie (to the manner of the daies)
In curteſie giues vndeſeruing praiſe.
We foure indeed confronted were with foure
In Ruſsia habit: Heere they ſtayed an houre,
And talk'd apace: and in that houre (my Lord)
They did not bleſſe vs with one happy word.
I dare not call them fooles; but this I thinke,
When they are thirſtie, fooles would faine haue drinke.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: This ieſt is drie to me. Gentle ſweete,
Your wits makes wiſe things fooliſh when we greete
With eies beſt ſeeing, heauens fierie eie:
By light we looſe light; your capacitie
Is of that nature, that to your huge ſtoore,
Wiſe things ſeeme fooliſh, and rich things but poore.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: This proues you wiſe and rich: for in my eie

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I am a foole, and full of pouertie.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: But that you take what doth to you belong,
It were a fault to ſnatch words from my tongue.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: O, I am yours and all that I poſſeſſe.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: All the foole mine.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I cannot giue you leſſe.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: Which of the Vizards what it that you wore?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Where? when? What Vizard?
Why demand you this?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: There, then, that vizard, that ſuperfluous caſe,
That hid the worſe, and ſhew'd the better face.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: We are diſcried,
They'l mocke vs now downeright.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: Let vs confeſſe, and turne it to a ieſt.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.p: Amaz'd my Lord? Why lookes your Highnes ſadde?

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.l: Helpe hold his browes, hee'l ſound: why looke you pale?
Sea-ſicke I thinke comming from Muſcouie.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Thus poure the ſtars down plagues for periury.
Can any face of braſſe hold longer out?
Heere ſtand I Ladie dart thy skill at me,
Bruiſe me with ſcorne, confound me with a flout.
Thruſt thy ſharpe wit quite through my ignorance.
Cut me to peeces with thy keene conceit:
And I will wiſh thee neuer more to dance,
Nor neuer more in Ruſsian habit waite.
O! neuer will I truſt to ſpeeches pen'd,
Nor to the motion of a Schoole-boies tongue
Nor neuer come in vizard to my friend,
Nor woo in rime like a blind-harpers ſongue,
Taffata phraſes, ſilken tearmes preciſe,
Three-pil'd Hyperboles, ſpruce affection;
Figures pedanticall, theſe ſummer flies,
Haue blowne me full of maggot oſtentation.
I do forſweare them, and I heere proteſt,
By this white Gloue (how white the hand God knows)
Henceforth my woing minde ſhall be expreſt
In ruſſet yeas, and honeſt kerſie noes.
And to begin Wench, ſo God helpe me law,
My loue to thee is ſound, ſans cracke or flaw.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: Sans, ſans, I pray you.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Yet I haue a tricke
Of the old rage: beare with me, I am ſicke.
Ile leaue it by degrees: ſoft, let vs ſee,
Write Lord haue mercie on vs, on thoſe three,
They are infected, in their hearts it lies:
They haue the plague, and caught it of your eyes:
Theſe Lords are viſited, you are not free:
For the Lords tokens on you do I ſee.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: No, they are free that gaue theſe tokens to vs.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Our ſtates are forfeit, ſeeke not to vndo vs.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: It is not ſo; for how can this be true,
That you ſtand forfeit, being thoſe that ſue.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Peace, for I will not haue to do with you.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: Nor ſhall not, if I do as I intend.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Speake for your ſelues, my wit is at an end.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Teach vs ſweete Madame, for our rude tranſgreſsion, ſome faire excuſe.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: The faireſt is confeſsion.
Were you not heere but euen now, diſguis'd?

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Madam, I was.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: And were you well aduis'd?

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: I was faire Madam.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: When you then were heere,
What did you whiſper in your Ladies eare?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: That more then all the world I did reſpect her

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: When ſhee ſhall challenge this, you will reiect her.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Vpon mine Honor no.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Peace, peace, forbeare: your oath once broke, you force not to forſweare.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Deſpiſe me when I breake this oath of mine.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: I will, and therefore keepe it. Roſaline,
What did the Ruſsian whiſper in your eare?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Madam, he ſwore that he did hold me deare
As precious eye-ſight, and did value me
Aboue this World: adding thereto moreouer,
That he vvould Wed me, or elſe die my Louer.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: God giue thee ioy of him: the Noble Lord Moſt honorably doth vphold his word.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What meane you Madame?
By my life, my troth,
I neuer ſwore this Ladie ſuch an oth.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: By heauen you did; and to confirme it plaine, you gaue me this: But take it ſir againe.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: My faith and this, the Princeſſe I did giue,
I knew her by this Iewell on her ſleeue.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Pardon me ſir, this Iewell did ſhe weare,
And Lord Berowne (I thanke him) is my deare.
What? Will you haue me, or your Pearle againe?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Neither of either, I remit both twaine.
I ſee the tricke on't: Heere was a conſent,
Knowing aforehand of our merriment,
To daſh it like a Chriſtmas Comedie.
Some carry-tale, ſome pleaſe-man, ſome ſlight Zanie,
Some mumble-newes, ſome trencher-knight, ſom Dick
That ſmiles his cheeke in yeares, and knowes the trick
To make my Lady laugh, when ſhe's diſpos'd;
Told our intents before: which once diſclos'd,
The Ladies did change Fauours, and then we
Following the ſignes, woo'd but the ſigne of ſhe.
Now to our periurie, to adde more terror,
We are againe forſworne in will and error.
Much vpon this tis: and might not you
Foreſtall our ſport, to make vs thus vntrue?
Do not you know my Ladies foot by 'th ſquier?
And laugh vpon the apple of her eie?
And ſtand betweene her backe ſir, and the fire,
Holding a trencher, ieſting merrilie?
You put our Page out: go, you are alowd.
Die when you will, a ſmocke ſhall be your ſhrowd.
You leere vpon me, do you? There's an eie
Wounds like a Leaden ſword.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Full merrily hath this braue manager, this carreere bene run.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Loe, he is tilting ſtraight. Peace, I haue don.
Welcome pure wit, thou part'ſt a faire fray.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: O Lord ſir, they would kno,
Whether the three worthies ſhall come in, or no.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: What, are there but three?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: No ſir, but it is var • fine,
For euerie one purſents three.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: And three times thrice is nine.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Not ſo ſir, vnder correction ſir, I hope it is not ſo. You cannot beg vs ſir, I can aſſure you ſir, we know what we know: I hope ſir three times thrice ſir.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Is not nine.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Vnder correction ſir, wee know where-vntill it doth amount.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: By Ioue, I alwaies tooke three threes for nine.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: O Lord ſir, it were pittie you ſhould get your liuing by reckning ſir.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: How much is it?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O Lord ſir, the parties themſelues, the actors ſir will ſhew where-vntill it doth amount: for mine owne part, I am (as they ſay, but to perfect one man in one poore man) Pompion the great ſir.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Art thou one of the Worthies?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: It pleaſed them to thinke me worthie of Pompey the great: for mine owne part, I know not the degree of the Worthie, but I am to ſtand for him.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Go, bid them prepare.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: We will turne it finely off ſir, we wil take ſome care.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Berowne, they will ſhame vs:
Let them not approach.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: We are ſhame-proofe my Lord: and 'tis ſome policie, to haue one ſhew worſe then the Kings and his companie.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: I ſay they ſhall not come.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Nay my good Lord, let me ore-rule you now;
That ſport beſt pleaſes, that doth leaſt know how.
Where Zeale ſtriues to content, and the contents
Dies in the Zeale of that which it preſents:
Their forme confounded, makes moſt forme in mirth,
When great things labouring periſh in their birth.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: A right deſcription of our ſport my Lord.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Annointed, I implore ſo much expence of thy royall ſweet breath, as will vtter a brace of words.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Doth this man ſerue God?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Why aske you?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: He ſpeak's not like a man of God's making.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: That's all one my faire ſweet honie Monarch: For I proteſt, the Schoolmaſter is exceeding fantaſticall: Too too vain, too too vaine. But we wil put it (as they ſay) to Fortuna delaguar, I wiſh you the peace of minde moſt royall cupplement.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Here is like to be a good preſence of Worthies; He preſents Hector of Troy, the Swaine Pompey ye great, the Pariſh Curate Alexander, Armadoes Page Hercules, the Pedant Iudas Machabeus: And if theſe foure Worthies in their firſt ſhew thriue, theſe foure will change habites, and preſent the other fiue.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: There is fiue in the firſt ſhew.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: You are deceiued, tis not ſo.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: The Pedant, the Braggart, the Hedge-Prieſt, the Foole, and the Boy,
Abate throw at Novum, and the whole world againe,
Cannot pricke out fiue ſuch, take each one in's vaine.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: The ſhip is vnder ſaile, and here ſhe coms amain.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: You lie, you are not he.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: With Libbards head on knee.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Well ſaid old mocker,
I muſt needs be friends with thee.

p.hi: I Pompey am, Pompey ſurnam'd the big.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: The great.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: It is great ſir: Pompey ſurnam'd the great:

l.hi: That oft in field, with Targe and Shield, did make my foe to ſweat:
And trauailing along this coaſt, I heere am come by chance,
And lay my Armes before the legs of this ſweet Laſſe of France.

sp.l: If your Ladiſhip would ſay thankes Pompey, I had done.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Great thankes great Pompey.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Tis not ſo much worth: but I hope I was perfect. I made a little fault in great.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: My hat to a halfe-penie, Pompey prooues the beſt Worthie.

l.hi: When in the world I liu'd, I was the worldes Commander:
By Eaſt, Weſt, North, & South, I ſpred my conquering might
My Scutcheon plaine declares that I am Aliſander.

sp.speaker: Boiet.
sp.l: Your noſe ſaies no, you are not:
For it ſtands too right.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Your noſe ſmels no, in this moſt tender ſmelling Knight.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: The Conqueror is diſmaid:
Proceede good Alexander.

p.hi: When in the world I liued, I was the worldes Commander.

sp.speaker: Boiet.
sp.p: Moſt true, 'tis right: you were ſo Aliſander.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Pompey the great.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: your ſeruant and Coſtard.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Take away the Conqueror, take away Aliſander

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p:
O ſir, you haue ouerthrowne Aliſander the conqueror: you will be ſcrap'd out of the painted cloth for
this: your Lion that holds his Pollax ſitting on a cloſe ſtoole, will be giuen to Aiax. He will be the ninth worthie. A Conqueror, and affraid to ſpeake? Runne away for ſhame Aliſander. There an't ſhall pleaſe you: a fooliſh milde man, an honeſt man, looke you, & ſoon daſht. He is a maruellous good neighbour inſooth, and a verie good Bowler: but for Aliſander, alas you ſee, how 'tis a little ore-parted. But there are Worthies a comming, will ſpeake their minde in ſome other ſort.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Stand aſide good Pompey.

div.stage: Enter Pedant for Iudas, and the Boy for Hercules.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Great Hercules is preſented by this Impe,
Whoſe Club kil'd Cerberus that three-headed Canus,
And when he was a babe, a childe, a ſhrimpe,
Thus did he ſtrangle Serpents in his Manus:
Quoniam, he ſeemeth in minoritie,
Ergo, I come with this Apologie.
Keepe ſome ſtate in thy exit, and vaniſh.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Iudas I am.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: A Iudas?

l.hi: Not Iſcariot ſir.
Iudas I am, ycliped Machabeus.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Iudas Machabeus clipt, is plaine Iudas.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: A kiſsing traitor. How art thou prou'd Iudas?

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: The more ſhame for you Iudas.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: What meane you ſir?

sp.speaker: Boi.
sp.p: To make Iudas hang himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Begin ſir, you are my elder.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Well follow'd, Iudas was hang'd on an Elder.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: I will not be put out of countenance.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Becauſe thou haſt no face.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: What is this?

sp.speaker: Boi.
sp.p: A Citterne head.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: The head of a bodkin.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: A deaths face in a ring.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: The face of an old Roman coine, ſcarce ſeene.

sp.speaker: Boi.
sp.p: The pummell of Caeſars Faulchion.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: The caru'd-bone face on a Flaske.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: S. Georges halfe cheeke in a brooch.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: I, and in a brooch of Lead.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: I, and worne in the cap of a Tooth-drawer.
And now forward, for we haue put thee in countenance

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: You haue put me out of countenance.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Falſe, we haue giuen thee faces.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: But you haue out-fac'd them all.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: And thou wer't a Lion, we would do ſo.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.l: Therefore as he is, an Aſſe, let him go:
And ſo adieu ſweet Iude. Nay, why doſt thou ſtay?

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: For the latter end of his name.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: For the Aſſe to the Iude: giue it him. Iud-as away.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: This is not generous, not gentle, not humble.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: A light for monſieur Iudas, it growes darke, he may ſtumble.

sp.speaker: Que.
sp.p: Alas poore Machabeus, how hath hee beene baited.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Hide thy head Achilles, heere comes Hector in Armes.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Though my mockes come home by me, I will now be merrie.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Hector was but a Troyan in reſpect of this.

sp.speaker: Boi.
sp.p: But is this Hector?

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: I thinke Hector was not ſo • leane timber'd.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: His legge is too big for Hector.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: More Calfe certaine.

sp.speaker: Boi.
sp.p: No, he is beſt indued in the ſmall.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: This cannot be Hector.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: He's a God or a Painter, for he makes faces.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: The Armipotent Mars, of Launces the almighty, gaue Hector a gift.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: A gilt Nutmegge.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: A Lemmon.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: Stucke with Cloues.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: No clouen.

sp.speaker: Brag.

l.hi: The Armipotent Mars of Launces the almighty,

sp.l: Gaue Hector a gift, the heire of Illion;

l.hi: A man ſo breathed, that certaine he would fight: yea
From morne till night, out of his Pauillion.

sp.l: I am that Flower.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: That Mint.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: That Cullambine.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Sweet Lord Longauill reine thy tongue.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: I muſt rather giue it the reine: for it runnes againſt Hector.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: I, and Hector's a Grey-hound.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.l: The ſweet War-man is dead and rotten,
Sweet chuckes, beat not the bones of the buried:
But I will forward with my deuice;
Sweet Royaltie beſtow on me the ſence of hearing.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Speake braue Hector, we are much delighted.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I do adore thy ſweet Graces ſlipper.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: Loues her by the foot.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: He may not by the yard.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Fellow Hector, ſhe is gone; ſhe is two moneths on her way.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: What meaneſt thou?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Faith vnleſſe you play the honeſt Troyan, the poore Wench is caſt away: ſhe's quick, the child brags in her belly alreadie: tis yours.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Doſt thou infamonize me among Potentates? Thou ſhalt die.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Then ſhall Hector be whipt for Iaquenetta that is quicke by him, and hang'd for Pompey, that is dead by him.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Moſt rare Pompey.

sp.speaker: Boi.
sp.p: Renowned Pompey.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Greater then great, great, great, great Pompey: Pompey the huge.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Hector trembles.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Pompey is moued, more Atees more Atees ſtirre them, or ſtirre them on.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Hector will challenge him.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I, if a' haue no more mans blood in's belly, then will ſup a Flea.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: By the North-pole I do challenge thee.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I wil not fight with a pole like a Northern man; Ile flaſh, Ile do it by the ſword: I pray you let mee borrow my Armes againe.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Roome for the incenſed Worthies.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Ile do it in my ſhirt.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Moſt reſolute Pompey.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.l: Maſter, let me take you a button hole lower:

Do you not ſee Pompey is vncaſing for the combat: what
meane you? you will loſe your reputation.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Gentlemen and Souldiers pardon me, I will not combat in my ſhirt.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: You may not denie it, Pompey hath made the challenge.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Sweet bloods, I both may, and will.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: What reaſon haue you for't?

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.l: The naked truth of it is, I haue no ſhirt,
I go woolward for penance.

sp.speaker: Boy.
sp.p: True, and it was inioyned him in Rome for want of Linnen: ſince when, Ile be ſworne he wore none, but a diſhclout of Iaquenettas, and that hee weares next his heart for a fauour.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: God ſaue you Madame.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Welcome Marcade, but that thou interrupteſt our merriment.

sp.speaker: Marc.
sp.p: I am ſorrie Madam, for the newes I bring is heauie in my tongue. The King your father

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Dead for my life.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Euen ſo: My tale is told.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Worthies away, the Scene begins to cloud.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: For mine owne part, I breath free breath: I haue ſeene the day of wrong, through the little hole of diſcretion, and I will right my ſelfe like a Souldier.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: How fare's your Maieſtie?

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Boyet prepare, I will away to night.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Madame not ſo, I do beſeech you ſtay.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: Prepare I ſay. I thanke you gracious Lords
For all your faire endeuours and entreats:
Out of a new ſad-ſoule, that you vouchſafe,
In your rich wiſedome to excuſe, or hide,
The liberall oppoſition of our ſpirits,
If ouer-boldly we haue borne our ſelues,
In the conuerſe of breath (your gentleneſſe
Was guiltie of it.) Farewell worthie Lord:
A heauie heart beares not a humble tongue.
Excuſe me ſo, comming ſo ſhort of thankes,
For my great ſuite, ſo eaſily obtain'd.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: The extreme parts of time, extremelie formes
All cauſes to the purpoſe of his ſpeed:
And often at his verie looſe-decides
That, which long proceſſe could not arbitrate.
And though the mourning brow of progenie
Forbid the ſmiling curteſie of Loue:
The holy ſuite which faine it would conuince,
Yet ſince loues argument was firſt on foote,
Let not the cloud of ſorrow iuſtle it
From what it purpos'd: ſince to waile friends loſt,
Is not by much ſo wholſome profitable,
As to reioyce at friends but newly found,

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: I vnderſtand you not, my greefes are double.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Honeſt plain words, beſt pierce the ears of griefe
And by theſe badges vnderſtand the King,
For your faire ſakes haue we neglected time,
Plaid foule play with our oaths: your beautie Ladies
Hath much deformed vs, faſhioning our humors
Euen to the oppoſed end of our intents.
And what in vs hath ſeem'd ridiculous:
As Loue is full of vnbefitting ſtraines,
All wanton as a childe, skipping and vaine.
Form'd by the eie, and therefore like the eie.
Full of ſtraying ſhapes, of habits, and of formes
Varying in ſubiects as the eie doth roule,
To euerie varied obiect in his glance:
Which partie-coated preſence of looſe loue
Put on by vs, if in your heauenly eies,
Haue misbecom'd our oathes and grauities.
Thoſe heauenlie eies that looke into theſe faults,
Suggeſted vs to make: therefore Ladies
Our loue being yours, the error that Loue makes
Is likewiſe yours. We to our ſelues proue falſe,
By being once falſe, for euer to be true
To thoſe that make vs both, faire Ladies you.
And euen that falſhood in it ſelfe a ſinne,
Thus purifies it ſelfe, and turnes to grace.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: We haue receiu'd your Letters, full of Loue:
Your Fauours, the Ambaſſadors of Loue.
And in our maiden counſaile rated them,
At courtſhip, pleaſantieſt, and curteſie,
As bumbaſt and as lining to the time:
But more deuout then theſe are our reſpects
Haue we not bene, and therefore met your loues
In their owne faſhion, like a merriment.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: Our letters Madam, ſhew'd much more then ieſt.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: So did our lookes.

sp.speaker: Roſa.
sp.p: We did not coat them ſo.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Now at the lateſt minute of the houre,
Grant vs your loues.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: A time me thinkes too ſhort,
To make a world-without-end bargaine in;
No, no my Lord, your Grace is periur'd much,
Full of deare guiltineſſe, and therefore this:
If for my Loue (as there is no ſuch cauſe)
You will do ought, this ſhall you do for me.
Your oth I will not truſt: but go with ſpeed
To ſome forlorne and naked Hermitage,
Remote from all the pleaſures of the world:
There ſtay, vntill the twelue Celeſtiall Signes
Haue brought about their annuall reckoning.
If this auſtere inſociable life,
Change not your offer made in heate of blood:
If froſts, and faſts, hard lodging, and thin weeds
Nip not the gaudie bloſſomes of your Loue,
But that it beare this triall, and laſt loue:
Then at the expiration of the yeare,
Come challenge me, challenge me by theſe deſerts,
And by this Virgin palme, now kiſſing thine,
I will be thine: and till that inſtant ſhut
My wofull ſelfe vp in a mourning houſe,
Raining the teares of lamentation,
For the remembrance of my Fathers death.
If this thou do denie, let our hands part,
Neither intitled in the others hart.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: If this, or more then this, I would denie,
To flatter vp theſe powers of mine with reſt,
The ſodaine hand of death cloſe vp mine eie.
Hence euer then, my heart is in thy breſt.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: And what to me my Loue? and what to me?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: You muſt be purged too, your ſins are rack'd.
You are attaint with faults and periurie:
Therefore if you my fauor meane to get,
A tweluemonth ſhall you ſpend, and neuer reſt,
But ſeeke the wearie beds of people ſicke.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: But what to me my loue? but what to me?

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.l: A wife? a beard, faire health, and honeſtie,
With three-fold loue, I wiſh you all theſe three.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: O ſhall I ſay, I thanke you gentle wife?

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.l: Not ſo my Lord, a tweluemonth and a day,
Ile marke no words that ſmoothfac'd wooers ſay.
Come when the King doth to my Ladie come:
Then if I haue much loue, Ile giue you ſome.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Ile ſerue thee true and faithfully till then.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.p: Yet ſweare not, leaſt ye be forſworne agen▪

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: What ſaies Maria?

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.l: At the tweluemonths end,
Ile change my blacke Gowne, for a faithfull friend.

sp.speaker: Lon.
sp.p: Ile ſtay with patience: but the time is long.

sp.speaker: Mari.
sp.p: The liker you, few taller are ſo yong.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Studies my Ladie? Miſtreſſe, looke on me,
Behold the window of my heart, mine eie:
What humble ſuite attends thy anſwer there,
Impoſe ſome ſeruice on me for my loue.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Oft haue I heard of you my Lord Berowne,
Before I ſaw you: and the worlds large tongue
Proclaimes you for a man repleate with mockes,
Full of compariſons, and wounding floutes:
Which you on all eſtates will execute,
That lie within the mercie of your wit.
To weed this Wormewood from your fruitfull braine,
And therewithall to win me, if you pleaſe,
Without the which I am not to be won:
You ſhall this tweluemonth terme from day to day,
Viſite the ſpeechleſſe ſicke, and ſtill conuerſe
With groaning wretches: and your taske ſhall be,
With all the fierce endeuour of your wit,
To enforce the pained impotent to ſmile.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: To moue wilde laughter in the throate of death?
It cannot be, it is impoſſible.
Mirth cannot moue a ſoule in agonie.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Why that's the way to choke a gibing ſpirit,
Whoſe influence is begot of that looſe grace,
Which ſhallow laughing hearers giue to fooles:
A ieſts proſperitie, lies in the eare
Of him that heares it, neuer in the tongue
Of him that makes it: then, if ſickly eares,
Deaft with the clamors of their owne deare grones,
Will heare your idle ſcornes; continue then,
And I will haue you, and that fault withall.
But if they will not, throw away that ſpirit,
And I ſhal finde you emptie of that fault,
Right ioyfull of your reformation.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: A tweluemonth? Well: befall what will befall,
Ile ieſt a tweluemonth in an Hoſpitall.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: I ſweet my Lord, and ſo I take my leaue.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: No Madam, we will bring you on your way.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Our woing doth not end like an old Play:
Iacke hath not Gill: theſe Ladies courteſie
Might wel haue made our ſport a Comedie.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Come ſir, it wants a tweluemonth and a day,
And then 'twil end.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: That's too long for a play.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Sweet Maieſty vouchſafe me.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Was not that Hector?

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: The worthie Knight of Troy.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: I wil kiſſe thy royal finger, and take leaue. I am a Votarie, I haue vow'd to Iaquenetta to holde the Plough for her ſweet loue three yeares. But moſt eſteemed greatneſſe, wil you heare the Dialogue that the two Learned men haue compiled, in praiſe of the Owle and the Cuckow? It ſhould haue followed in the end of our ſhew.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Call them forth quickely, we will do ſo.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.p: Holla, Approach.

div.l: This ſide is Hiems, Winter.
This Ver, the Spring: the one maintained by the Owle,
Th' other by the Cuckow.
Ver, begin.

lg.l: When Daſies pied, and Violets blew,
And Cuckow-buds of yellow hew:
And Ladie-ſmockes all ſiluer white,
Do paint the Medowes with delight.
The Cuckow then on euerie tree,
Mockes married men, for thus ſings he,
Cuckow.
Cuckow, Cuckow: O word of feare,
Vnpleaſing to a married eare.
When Shepheards pipe on Oaten ſtrawes,
And merrie Larkes are Ploughmens clockes:
When Turtles tread, and Rookes and Dawes,
And Maidens bleach their ſummer ſmockes:
The Cuckow then on euerie tree
Mockes married men; for thus ſings he,
Cuckow.
Cuckow, Cuckow: O word of feare,
Vnpleaſing to a married eare.
When Iſicles hang by the wall,
And Dicke the Sphepheard blowes his naile;
And Tom beares Logges into the hall,
And Milke comes frozen home in paile:
When blood is nipt, and waies be fowle,
Then nightly ſings the ſtaring Owle
Tu-whit to-who.
A merrie note,
While greaſie Ione doth keele the pot.
When all aloud the winde doth blow,
And coſſing drownes the Parſons ſaw:
And birds ſit brooding in the ſnow,
And Marrians noſe lookes red and raw:
When roaſted Crabs hiſſe in the bowle,
Then nightly ſings the ſtaring Owle,
Tu-whit to who:
A merrie note,
While greaſie Ione doth keele the pot.

sp.speaker: Brag.
sp.l: The Words of Mercurie,
Are harſh after the ſongs of Apollo:
You that way; we this way.

div.head: Actus primus.

sp.speaker: Theſeus.
sp.l: NOw faire Hippolita, our nuptiall houre
Drawes on apace: foure happy daies bring in
Another Moon: but oh, me thinkes, how ſlow
This old Moon wanes; She lingers my deſires
Like to a Step-dame, or a Dowager,
Long withering out a yong mans reuennew.

sp.speaker: Hip.
sp.l: Foure daies wil quickly ſteep thēſelues in nights
Foure nights wil quickly dreame away the time:
And then the Moone, like to a ſiluer bow,
Now bent in heauen, ſhal behold the night
Of our ſolemnities.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Go Philoſtrate,
Stirre vp the Athenian youth to merriments,
Awake the pert and nimble ſpirit of mirth,
Turne melancholy forth to Funerals:
The pale companion is not for our pompe,
Hippolita, I woo'd thee with my ſword,
And wonne thy loue, doing thee iniuries:
But I will wed thee in another key,
With pompe, with triumph, and with reuelling.

div.stage: Enter Egeus and his daughter Hermia, Lyſander, and Demetrius.

sp.speaker: Ege.
sp.p: Happy be Theſeus, our renowned Duke.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.p: Thanks good Egeus: what's the news with thee?

sp.speaker: Ege.
sp.l: Full of vexation, come I, with complaint
Againſt my childe, my daughter Hermia.
My Noble Lord,
This man hath my conſent to marrie her.
And my gracious Duke,
This man hath bewitch'd the boſome of my childe:
Thou, thou Lyſander, thou haſt giuen her rimes,
And interchang'd loue-tokens with my childe:
Thou haſt by Moone-light at her window ſung,
With faining voice, verſes of faining loue,
And ſtolne the impreſſion of her fantaſie,
With bracelets of thy haire, rings, gawdes, conceits,
Knackes, trifles, Noſe-gaies, ſweet meats (meſſengers
Of ſtrong preuailment in vnhardned youth)
With cunning haſt thou filch'd my daughters heart,
Turn'd her obedience (which is due to me)
To ſtubborne harſhneſſe. And my gracious Duke,
Be it ſo ſhe will not heere before your Grace,
Conſent to marrie with Demetrius,
I beg the ancient priuiledge of Athens;
As ſhe is mine, I may diſpoſe of her;
Which ſhall be either to this Gentleman,
Or to her death, according to our Law,
Immediately prouided in that caſe.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: What ſay you Hermia? be aduis'd faire Maide,
To you your Father ſhould be as a God;
One that compos'd your beauties; yea and one
To whom you are but as a forme in waxe
By him imprinted: and within his power,
To leaue the figure, or disfigure it:
Demetrius is a worthy Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.p: So is Lyſander.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: In himſelfe he is.
But in this kinde, wanting your fathers voyce.
The other muſt be held the worthier.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.p: I would my father look'd but with my eyes.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.p: Rather your eies muſt with his iudgment looke.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: I do entreat your Grace to pardon me.
I know not by what power I am made bold,
Nor how it may concerne my modeſtie
In ſuch a preſence heere to pleade my thoughts:
But I beſeech your Grace, that I may know
The worſt that may befall me in this caſe,
If I refuſe to wed Demetrius.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Either to dye the death, or to abiure
For euer the ſociety of men.
Therefore faire Hermia queſtion your deſires,
Know of your youth, examine well your blood,
Whether (if you yeeld not to your fathers choice)
You can endure the liuerie of a Nunne,
For aye to be in ſhady Cloiſter mew'd,
To liue a barren ſiſter all your life,
Chanting faint hymnes to the cold fruitleſſe Moone,
Thrice bleſſed they that maſter ſo their blood,
To vndergo ſuch maiden pilgrimage,
But earthlier happie is the Roſe diſtil'd,
Then that which withering on the virgin thorne,
Growes, liues, and dies, in ſingle bleſſedneſſe.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: So will I grow, ſo liue, ſo die my Lord,
Ere I will yeeld my virgin Patent vp
Vnto his Lordſhip, whoſe vnwiſhed yoake,
My ſoule conſents not to giue ſoueraignty.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: Take time to pauſe, and by the next new Moon
The ſealing day betwixt my loue and me,
For euerlaſting bond of fellowſhip:
Vpon that day either prepare to dye,
For diſobedience to your fathers will,
Or elſe to wed Demetrius as hee would,
Or on Dianaes Altar to proteſt
For aie, auſterity, and ſingle life.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.l: Relent ſweet Hermia, and Lyſander, yeelde
Thy crazed title to my certaine right.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: You haue her fathers loue, Demetrius:
Let me haue Hermiaes: do you marry him.

sp.speaker: Egeus.
sp.l: Scornfull Lyſander, true, he hath my Loue;
And what is mine, my loue ſhall render him.
And ſhe is mine, and all my right of her,
I do eſtate vnto Demetrius.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: I am my Lord, as well deriu'd as he,
As well poſſeſt: my loue is more then his:
My fortunes euery way as fairely ranck'd
(If not with vantage) as Demetrius:
And (which is more then all theſe boaſts can be)
I am belou'd of beauteous Hermia.
Why ſhould not I then proſecute my right?
Demetrius, Ile auouch it to his head,
Made loue to Nedars daughter, Helena,
And won her ſoule: and ſhe (ſweet Ladie) dotes,
Deuoutly dotes, dotes in Idolatry,
Vpon this ſpotted and inconſtant man.

sp.speaker: The.
sp.l: I muſt confeſſe, that I haue heard ſo much,
And with Demetrius thought to haue ſpoke thereof:
But being ouer-full of ſelfe-affaires,
My minde did loſe it. But Demetrius come,
And come Egeus, you ſhall go with me,
I haue ſome priuate ſchooling for you both.
For you faire Hermia, looke you arme your ſelfe,
To fit your fancies to your Fathers will;
Or elſe the Law of Athens yeelds you vp
(Which by no meanes we may extenuate)
To death, or to a vow of ſingle life.
Come my Hippolita▪ what cheare my loue?
Demetrius and Egeus go along:
I muſt imploy you in ſome buſineſſe
Againſt our nuptiall, and conferre with you
Of ſomething, neerely that concernes your ſelues.

sp.speaker: Ege.
sp.p: With dutie and deſire we follow you.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: How now my loue? Why is your cheek ſo pale?
How chance the Roſes there do fade ſo faſt?

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: Belike for want of raine, which I could well
Beteeme them, from the tempeſt of mine eyes.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: For ought that euer I could reade,
Could euer heare by tale or hiſtorie,
The courſe of true loue neuer did run ſmooth,
But either it was different in blood.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.p: O croſſe! too high to be enthral'd to loue.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.p: Or elſe miſgraffed, in reſpect of yeares.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.p: O ſpight! too old to be ingag'd to yong.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.p: Or elſe it ſtood vpon the choiſe of merit.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.p: O hell! to chooſe loue by anothers eie.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: Or if there were a ſimpathie in choiſe,
Warre, death, or ſickneſſe, did lay ſiege to it;
Making it momentarie, as a ſound:
Swift as a ſhadow, ſhort as any dreame,
Briefe as the lightning in the collied night,
That (in a ſpleene) vnfolds both heauen and earth;
And ere a man hath power to ſay, behold,
The iawes of darkneſſe do deuoure it vp:
So quicke bright things come to confuſion.

sp.speaker: Her.
sp.l: If then true Louers haue beene euer croſt,
It ſtands as an edict in deſtinie:
Then let vs teach our triall patience,
Becauſe it is a cuſtomarie croſſe,
As due to loue, as thoughts, and dreames, and ſighes,
Wiſhes and teares; poore Fancies followers.

sp.speaker: Lyſ.
sp.l: A good perſwaſion; therefore heare me Hermia,
I haue a Widdow Aunt, a dowager,
Of great reuennew, and ſhe hath • o childe,
From Athens is her houſe remou • ſeuen leagues,
And ſhe reſpects me, as her onely ſonne:
There gentle Hermia, may I marrie thee,
And to that place, the ſharpe Athenian Law
Cannot purſue vs. If thou lou'ſt me, then
Steale forth thy fathers houſe to morrow night:
And in the wood, a league without the towne,
