She's apt to learne, and thankefull for good turnes:
Signior Petruchio, will you go with vs,
Or ſhall I ſend my daughter Kate to you.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I pray you do. Ile attend her heere,
And woo her with ſome ſpirit when ſhe comes,
Say that ſhe raile, why then Ile tell her plaine,
She ſings as ſweetly as a Nightinghale:
Say that ſhe frowne, Ile ſay ſhe lookes as cleere
As morning Roſes newly waſht with dew:
Say ſhe be mute, and will not ſpeake a word,
Then Ile commend her volubility,
And ſay ſhe vtcereth piercing eloquence:
If ſhe do bid me packe, Ile giue her thankes,
As though ſhe bid me ſtay by her a weeke:
If ſhe denie to wed, Ile craue the day
When I ſhall aske the banes, and when be married.
But heere ſhe comes, and now Petruchio ſpeake.
Good morrow Kate, for thats your name I heare.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Well haue you heard, but ſomething hard of hearing:
They call me Katerine, that do talke of me.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: You lye infaith, for you are call'd plaine Kate,
And bony Kate, and ſometimes Kate the curſt:
But Kate, the prettieſt Kate in Chriſtendome,
Kate of Kate-hall, my ſuper-daintie Kate,
For dainties are all Kates, and therefore Kate
Take this of me, Kate of my conſolation,
Hearing thy mildneſſe prais'd in euery Towne,
Thy vertues ſpoke of, and thy beautie ſounded,
Yet not ſo deepely as to thee belongs,
My ſelfe am moou'd to woo thee for my wife.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Mou'd, in good time, let him that mou'd you hether
Remoue you hence: I knew you at the firſt
You were a mouable.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Why, what's a mouable?

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: A ioyn'd ſtoole.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Thou haſt hit it: come ſit on me.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Aſſes are made to beare, and ſo are you.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Women are made to beare, and ſo are you.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: No ſuch Iade as you, if me you meane.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Alas good Kate, I will not burthen thee,
For knowing thee to be but yong and light.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Too light for ſuch a ſwaine as you to catch,
And yet as heauie as my waight ſhould be.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Shold be, ſhould: buzze.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Well tane, and like a buzzard.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Oh ſlow-wing'd Turtle, ſhal a buzard take thee?

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: I for a Turtle, as he takes a buzard.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Come, come you Waſpe, y' faith you are too angrie.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: If I be waſpiſh, beſt beware my ſting.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: My remedy is then to plucke it out.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: I, if the foole could finde it where it lies.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Who knowes not where a Waſpe does, weare his ſting? In his taile.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: In his tongue?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Whoſe tongue.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Yours if you talke of tales, and ſo farewell.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: What with my tongue in your taile.
Nay, come againe, good Kate, I am a Gentleman,

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: That Ile trie.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: I ſweare Ile cuffe you, if you ſtrike againe.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: So may you looſe your armes,
If you ſtrike me, you are no Gentleman,
And if no Gentleman, why then no armes.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: A Herald Kate? Oh put me in thy bookes.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: What is your Creſt, a Coxcombe?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: A combleſſe Cocke, ſo Kate will be my Hen.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: No Cocke of mine, you crow too like a crauen

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Nay come Kate, come: you muſt not looke ſo ſowre.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: It is my faſhion when I ſee a Crab.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Why heere's no crab, and therefore looke not ſowre.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: There is, there is.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Then ſhew it me.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Had I a glaſſe, I would.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: What, you meane my face.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Well aym'd of ſuch a yong one.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Now by S. George I am too yong for you.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Yet you are wither'd.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: 'Tis with cares.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: I care not.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Nay heare you Kate. Inſooth you ſcape not ſo.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: I chafe you if I tarrie. Let me go.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: No, not a whit, I finde you paſſing gentle:
'Twas told me you were rough, and coy, and ſullen,
And now I finde report a very liar:
For thou art pleaſant, g • meſome, paſſing courteous,
But ſlow in ſpeech: yet ſweet as ſpring-time flowers.
Thou canſt not frowne, thou canſt not looke a ſconce,
Nor bite the lip, as angry wenches will,
Nor haſt thou pleaſure to be croſſe in talke:
But thou with mildneſſe entertain'ſt thy wooers,
With gentle conference, ſoft, and affable.
Why does the world report that Kate doth limpe?
Oh ſland'rous world: Kate like the hazle twig
Is ſtraight, and ſlender, and as browne in hue
As hazle nuts, and ſweeter then the kernels:
Oh let me ſee thee walke: thou doſt not halt.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Go foole, and whom thou keep'ſt command.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Did euer Dian ſo become a Groue
As Kate this chamber with her princely gate:
O be thou Dian, and let her be Kate,
And then let Kate be chaſte, and Dian ſportfull.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Where did you ſtudy all this goodly ſpeech?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: It is extempore, from my mother wit.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: A witty mother, witleſſe elſe her ſonne.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Am I not wiſe?

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: Yes, keepe you warme.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Marry ſo I meane ſweet Katherine in thy bed:
And therefore ſetting all this chat aſide,
Thus in plaine termes: your father hath conſented
That you ſhall be my wife; your dowry greed on,
And will you, • ill you, I will marry you.
Now Kate, I am a husband for your turne,
For by this light, whereby I ſee thy beauty,
Thy beauty that doth make me like thee well,
Thou muſt be married to no man but me,
For I am he am borne to tame you Kate,
And bring you from a wilde Kate to a Kate
Conformable as other houſhold Kates:
Heere comes your father, neuer make deniall▪
I muſt, and will haue Katherine to my wife.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Now Signior Petruchio, how ſpeed you with my daughter?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: How but well ſir? how but well?
It were impoſſible I ſhould ſpeed amiſſe.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Why how now daughter Katherine, in your dumps?

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.l: Call you me daughter? now I promiſe you
You haue ſhewd a tender fatherly regard,
To wiſh me wed to one halfe Lunaticke,
A mad-cap ruffian, and a ſwearing lacke,
That thinkes with oathes to face the matter out.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Father, 'tis thus, your ſelfe and all the world
That talk'd of her, haue talk'd amiſſe of her:
If ſhe be curſt, it is for pollicie,
For ſhee's not froward, but modeſt as the Doue,
Shee is not hot, but temperate as the morne,
For patience ſhee will proue a ſecond Griſſell,
And Romane Lucrece for her chaſtitie:
And to conclude, we haue greed ſo well together,
That vpon ſonday is the wedding day.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Ile ſee thee hang'd on ſonday firſt.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Hark Petruchio, ſhe ſaies ſhee'll ſee thee hang'd firſt.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Is this your ſpeeding? nay thē godnight our part.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Be patient gentlemen, I chooſe her for my ſelfe,
If ſhe and I be pleas'd, what's that to you?
'Tis bargain'd twixt vs twaine being alone,
That ſhe ſhall ſtill be curſt in company.
I tell you 'tis incredible to beleeue
How much ſhe loues me: oh the kindeſt Kate,
Shee hung about my necke, and kiſſe on kiſſe
Shee vi'd ſo faſt, proteſting oath on oath,
That in a twinke ſhe won me to her loue.
Oh you are nouices, 'tis a world to ſee
How tame when men and women are alone.
A meacocke wretch can make the curſteſt ſhrew:
Giue me thy hand Kate, I will vnto Venice
To buy apparell 'gainſt the wedding day;
Prouide the feaſt father, and bid the gueſts,
I will be ſure my Katherine ſhall be fine.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: I know not what to ſay, but giue me your hāds,
God ſend you ioy, Petruchio, 'tis a match.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Tra. Amen ſay we, we will be witneſſes.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Father, and wife, and gentlemen adieu,
I will to Venice, ſonday comes apace,
We will haue rings, and things, and fine array,
And kiſſe me Kate, we will be married a ſonday.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Was euer match clapt vp ſo ſodainly?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Faith Gentlemen now I play a marchants part,
And venture madly on a deſperate Mart.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Twas a commodity lay fretting by you,
'Twill bring you gaine, or periſh on the ſeas.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: The gaine I ſeeke, is quiet me the match.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.l: No doubt but he hath got a quiet catch:
But now Baptiſta, to your yonger daughter,
Now is the day we long haue looked for,
I am your neighbour, and was ſuter firſt.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: And I am one that loue Bianca more
Then words can witneſſe, or your thoughts can gueſſe.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Yongling thou canſt not loue ſo deare as I.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Gray-beard thy loue doth freeze.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.l: But thine doth frie,
Skipper ſtand backe, 'tis age that nouriſheth.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: But youth in Ladies eyes that floriſheth.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Content you gentlemen, I wil cōpound this ſtrife
'Tis deeds muſt win the prize, and he of both
That can aſſure my daughter greateſt dower,
Shall haue my Biancas loue.
Say ſignior Gremio, what can you aſſure her?

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.l: Firſt, as you know, my houſe within the City
Is richly furniſhed with plate and gold,
Baſons and ewers to laue her dainty hands:
My hangings all of tirian tapeſtry:
In Iuory cofers I haue ſtuft my crownes:
In Cypros cheſts my arras counterpoints,
Coſtly apparell, tents, and Canopies,
Fine Linnen, Turky cuſhions boſt with pearle,
Vallens of Venice gold, in needle worke:
Pewter and braſſe, and all things that belongs
To houſe or houſe-keeping: then at my farme
I haue a hundred milch-kine to the pale,
Sixe-ſcore fat Oxen ſtanding in my ſtalls,
And all things anſwerable to this portion.
My ſelfe am ſtrooke in yeeres I muſt confeſſe,
And if I die to morrow this is hers,
If whil'ſt I liue ſhe will be onely mine.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: That only came well in: ſir, liſt to me,
I am my fathers heyre and onely ſonne,
If I may haue your daughter to my wife,
Ile leaue her houſes three or foure as good
Within rich Piſa walls, as any one
Old Signior Gremio has in Padua,
Beſides, two thouſand Duckets by the yeere
Of fruitfull land, all which ſhall be her ioynter.
What, haue I pincht you Signior Gremio?

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.l: Two thouſand Duckets by the yeere of land,
My Land amounts not to ſo much in all:
That ſhe ſhall haue, beſides an Argoſie
That now is lying in Marcellus roade:
What, haue I choakt you with an Argoſie?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Gremio, 'tis knowne my father hath no leſſe
Then three great Argoſies, beſides two Galliaſſes
And twelue tite Gallies, theſe I will aſſure her,
And twice as much what ere thou offreſt next.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.l: Nay, I haue offred all, I haue no more,
And ſhe can haue no more then all I haue,
If you like me, ſhe ſhall haue me and mine.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Why then the maid is mine from all the world
By your firme promiſe, Gremio is out-vied.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: I muſt confeſſe your offer is the beſt,
And let your father make her the aſſurance,
Shee is your owne, elſe you muſt pardon me:
If you ſhould die before him, where's her dower?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: That's but a cauill: he is olde, I young.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: And may not yong men die as well as old?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Well gentlemen, I am thus reſolu'd,
On ſonday next, you know
My daughter Katherine is to be married:
Now on the ſonday following, ſhall Bianca
Be Bride to you, if you make this aſſurance:
If not, to Signior Gremio:
And ſo I take my leaue, and thanke you both.

sp.speaker: Cre.
sp.l: Adieu good neighbour: now I feare thee not:
Sirra, yong gameſter, your father were a foole
To giue thee all, and in his wayning age
Set foot vnder thy table: tut, a toy,
An olde Italian foxe is not ſo kinde my boy.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: A vengeance on your crafty withered hide,
Yet I haue fac'd it with a card of ten:
'Tis in my head to doe my maſter good:
I ſee no reaſon but ſuppos'd Lucentio
Muſt get a father, call'd ſuppos'd Ʋincentio,
And that's a wonder: fathers commonly
Doe get their children: but in this caſe of woing,
A childe ſhall get a ſire, if I faile not of my cunning.

div.head: Actus Tertia.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Fidler forbeare you grow too forward Sir,
Haue you ſo ſoone forgot the entertainment
Her ſiſter Katherine welcom'd you withall.

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.l: But wrangling pedant, this is
The patroneſſe of heauenly harmony:
Then giue me leaue to haue prerogatiue,
And when in Muſicke we haue ſpent an houre,
Your Lecture ſhall haue leiſure for as much.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Prepoſterous Aſſe that neuer read ſo farre,
To know the cauſe why muſicke was ordain'd:
Was it not to refreſh the minde of man
After his ſtudies, or his vſuall paine?
Then giue me leaue to read Philoſophy,
And while I pauſe, ſerue in your harmony.

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.p: Sirra, I will not beare theſe braues of thine.

sp.speaker: Bianc.
sp.l: Why gentlemen, you doe me double wrong,
To ſtriue for that which reſteth in my choice:
I am no breeching ſcholler in the ſchooles,
Ile not be tied to howres, nor pointed times,
But learne my Leſſons as I pleaſe my ſelfe,
And to cut off all ſtrife: heere ſit we downe,
Take you your inſtrument, play you the whiles,
His Lecture will be done ere you haue tun'd.

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.p: You'll leaue his Lecture when I am in tune?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: That will be neuer, tune your inſtrument.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Where left we laſt?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Heere Madam: Hic Ibat Simois, hic eſt ſigeria tellus, hic ſteterat Priamiregia Celſa ſenis.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Conſter them.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Hic Ibat, as I told you before. Simois, I am Lucentio, hic eſt, ſonne vnto Vincentio of Piſa, Sigeriatellus, diſguiſed thus to get your loue, hic ſteterat, and that Lucentio that comes a wooing, priami, is my man Tranio, regia, bearing my port, celſa ſenis that we might beguile the old Pantalowne.

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.p: Madam, my Inſtrument's in tune.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Let's heare, oh fie, the treble iarres.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Spit in the hole man, and tune againe.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Now let mee ſee if I can conſter it. Hic ibat ſimois, I know you not, hic eſt ſigeria tellus, I truſt you not, hic ſtaterat priami, take heede he heare vs not, regia preſume not, Celſa ſenis, deſpaire not.

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.p: Madam, tis now in tune.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: All but the baſe.

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.p: The baſe is right, 'tis the baſe knaue that iars.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: How fiery and forward our Pedant is,
Now for my life the knaue doth court my loue,
Pedaſcule, Ile watch you better yet:
In time I may beleeue, yet I miſtruſt.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Miſtruſt it not, for ſure Aeacides
Was Atax cald ſo from his grandfather.

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.l: I muſt beleeue my maſter, elſe I promiſe you,
I ſhould be arguing ſtill vpon that doubt,
But let it reſt, now Litio to you:
Good maſter take it not vnkindly pray
That I haue beene thus pleaſant with you both.

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.l: You may go walk, and giue me leaue a while,
My Leſſons make no muſicke in three parts.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Are you ſo formall ſir, well I muſt waite
And watch withall, for but I be deceiu'd,
Our fine Muſitian groweth amorous.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: Madam, before you touch the inſtrument,
To learne the order of my fingering,
I muſt begin with rudiments of Art,
To teach you gamoth in a briefer ſort,
More pleaſant, pithy, and effectuall,
Then hath beene taught by any of my trade,
And there it is in writing fairely drawne.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Why, I am paſt my gamouth long agoe.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Yet read the gamouth of Hortentio.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Gamouth I am, the ground of all accord:
Are, to plead Hortenſio's paſſion:
Beeme, Bianca take him for thy Lord
Cfavt, that loues with all affection:
D ſolre, one Cliffe, two notes haue I,
Elami, ſhow pitty or I die.
Call you this gamouth? tut I like it not,
Old faſhions pleaſe me beſt, I am not ſo nice
To charge true rules for old inuentions.

sp.speaker: Nicke.
sp.l: Miſtreſſe, your father prayes you leaue your books,
And helpe to dreſſe your ſiſters chamber vp,
You know to morrow is the wedding day.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Farewell ſweet maſters both, I muſt be gone.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Faith Miſtreſſe then I haue no cauſe to ſtay.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: But I haue cauſe to pry into this pedant,
Methinkes he lookes as though he were in loue:
Yet if thy thoughts Bianca be ſo humble
To caſt thy wandring eyes on euery ſtale:
Seize thee that Liſt, if once I finde thee ranging,
Hortenſio will be quit with thee by changing.

div.stage: Enter Baptiſta, Gremio, Tranio, Katherine, Bianca, and others, attendants.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Signior Lucentio, this is the pointed day
That Katherine and Petruchio ſhould be married,
And yet we heare not of our ſonne in Law:
What will be ſaid, what mockery will it be?
To want the Bride-groome when the Prieſt attends
To ſpeake the ceremoniall rites of marriage?
What ſaies Lucentio to this ſhame of ours?

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: No ſhame but mine, I muſt forſooth be forſt
To giue my hand oppos'd againſt my heart
Vnto a mad-braine rudes by, full of ſpleene,
Who woo'd in haſte, and meanes to wed at leyſure:
I told you I, he was a franticke foole,
Hiding his bitter ieſts in blunt behauiour,
And to be noted for a merry man;
Hee'll wooe a thouſand, point the day of marriage,
Make friends, inuite, and proclaime the banes,
Yet neuer meanes to wed where he hath woo'd:
Now muſt the world point at poore Katherine,
And ſay, loe, there is man Petruchio's wife
If it would pleaſe him come and marry her.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Patience good Katherine and Baptiſta too,
Vpon my life Petruchio meanes but well,
What euer fortune ſtayes him from his word,
Though he be blunt, I know him paſſing wiſe,
Though he be merry, yet withall he's honeſt.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Would Katherine had neuer ſeen him though.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Goe girle, I cannot blame thee now to weepe,
For ſuch an iniurie would vexe a very ſaint,
Much more a ſhrew of impatient humour.

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: Maſter, maſter, newes, and ſuch newes as you neuer heard of,

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Is it new and olde too? how may that be?

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: Why, is it not newes to heard of Petruchio's comming?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Is he come?

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: Why no ſir.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: What then?

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: He is comming.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: When will he be heere?

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: When he ſtands where I am, and ſees you there.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: But ſay, what to thine olde newes?

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: Why Petruchio is comming, in a new hat and an old ierkin, a paire of olde breeches thrice turn'd; a paire of bootes that haue beene candle-caſes, one buckled, another lac'd: an olde ruſty ſword tane out of the Towne Armory, with a broken hilt, and chapeleſſe: with two broken points: his horſe hip'd with an olde mothy ſaddle, and ſtirrops of no kindred: beſides poſſeſt with the glanders, and like to moſe in the chine, troubled with the Lampaſſe, infected with the faſhions, full of Windegalls, ſped with Spauins, raied with the Yellowes, paſt cure of the Fiues, ſtarke ſpoyl'd with the Staggers, begnawne with the Bots, Waid in the backe, and ſhoulder-ſhotten, neere leg'd before, and with a halfe-chekt Bitte, & a headſtall of ſheepes leather, which being reſtrain'd to keepe him from ſtumbling, hath been often burſt, and now repaired with knots: one girth ſixe times peec'd, and a womans Crupper of velure, which hath two letters for her name, fairely ſet down in ſtuds, and heere and there peec'd with packthred.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Who comes with him?

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: Oh ſir, his Lackey, for all the world Capariſon'd like the horſe: with a linnen ſtock on one leg, and a kerſey boot-hoſe on the other, gartred with a red and blew lift; an old hat, & the humor of forty fancies prickt in't for a feather: a monſter, a very monſter in apparell, & not like a Chriſtian foot-boy, or a gentlemans Lacky.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: 'Tis ſome od humor pricks him to this faſhion,
Yet oftentimes he goes but meane apparel'd.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: I am glad he's come, howſoere he comes.

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: Why ſir, he comes not.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Didſt thou not ſay hee comes?

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: Who, that Petruchio came?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: I, that Petruchio came.

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: No ſir, I ſay his horſe comes with him on his backe.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Why that's all one.

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: Nay by S. Iamy, I hold you a penny, a horſe and a man is more then one, and yet not many.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Come, where be theſe gallants? who's at home?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: You are welcome ſir.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: And yet I come not well.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: And yet you halt not.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Not ſo well apparell'd as I wiſh you were.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Were it better I ſhould ruſh in thus:
But where is Kate? where is my louely Bride?
How does my father? gentles methinkes you frowne,
And wherefore gaze this goodly company,
As if they ſaw ſome wondrous monument,
Some Commet, or vnuſuall prodigie?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Why ſir, you know this is your wedding day▪
Firſt were we ſad, fearing you would not come,
Now ſadder that you come ſo vnprouided:
Fie, doff this habit, ſhame to your eſtate,
An eye-ſore to our ſolemne feſtiuall.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: And tell vs what occaſion of import
Hath all ſo long detain'd you from your wife,
And ſent you hither ſo vnlike your ſelfe?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Tedious it were to tell, and harſh to heare,
Sufficeth I am come to keepe my word.
Though in ſome part inforced to digreſſe,
Which at more leyſure I will ſo excuſe,
As you ſhall well be ſatisfied with all▪
But where is Kate? I ſtay too long from her,
The morning weares, 'tis time we were at Church.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: See not your Bride in theſe vnreuerent robes,
Goe to my chamber, put on clothes of mine.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Not I, beleeue me, thus Ile viſit her.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: But thus I truſt you will not marry her.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Good ſooth euen thus: therefore ha done with words,
To me ſhe's married, not vnto my cloathes:
Could I repaire what ſhe will weare in me,
As I can change theſe poore accoutrements,
'Twere well for Kate, and better for my ſelfe.
But what a foole am I to chat with you,
When I ſhould bid good morrow to my Bride?
And ſeale the title with a louely kiſſe.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: He hath ſome meaning in his mad attire,
We will perſwade him be it poſſible,
To put on better ere he goe to Church.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Ile after him, and ſee the euent of this.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: But ſir, Loue concerneth vs to adde
Her fathers liking, which to bring to paſſe
As before imparted to your worſhip,
I am to get a man what ere he be,
It skills not much, weele fit him to our turne,
And he ſhall be Vincentio of Piſa,
And make aſſurance heere in Padua
Of greater ſummes then I haue promiſed,
So ſhall you quietly enioy your hope,
And marry ſweet Bianca with conſent.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Were it not that my fellow ſchoolemaſter
Doth watch Bianca's ſteps ſo narrowly:
'Twere good me-thinkes to ſteale our marriage,
Which once perform'd, let all the world ſay no,
Ile keepe mine owne deſpite of all the world.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: That by degrees we meane to looke into,
And watch our vantage in this buſineſſe,
Wee'll ouer-reach the grey-beard Gremio,
The narrow prying father Minola,
The quaint Muſician, amorous Litio,
All for my Maſters ſake Lucentio.
Signior Gremio, came you from the Church?

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: As willingly as ere I came from ſchoole.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: And is the Bride & Bridegroom coming home?

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.l: A bridegroome ſay you? 'tis a groome indeed,
A grumlling groome, and that the girle ſhall finde.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Curſter then ſhe, why 'tis impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Why hee's a deuill, a deuill, a very fiend.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Why ſhe's a deuill, a deuill, the deuils damme.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.l: Tut, ſhe's a Lambe, a Doue, a foole to him:
Ile tell you ſir Lucentio; when the Prieſt
Should aske if Katherine ſhould be his wife,
I, by goggs woones quoth he, and ſwore ſo loud,
That all amaz'd the Prieſt let fall the booke,
And as he ſtoop'd againe to take it vp,
This mad-brain'd bridegroome tooke him ſuch a cuffe,
That downe ſell Prieſt and booke, and booke and Prieſt,
Now take them vp quoth he, if any liſt.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: What ſaid the wench when he roſe againe?

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Trembled and ſhooke: for why, he ſtamp'd and ſwore, as if the Vicar meant to cozen him: but after many ceremonies done, hee calls for wine, a health quoth he, as if he had beene aboord carowſing to his Mates after a ſtorme, quaft off the Muſcadell, and threw the ſops all in the Sextons face: hauing no other reaſon, but that his beard grew thinne and hungerly, and ſeem'd to aske him ſops as hee was drinking: This done, hee tooke the Bride about the necke, and kiſt her lips with ſuch a clamorous ſmacke, that at the parting all the Church did eccho: and I ſeeing this, came thence for very ſhame, and after mee I know the rout is comming, ſuch a mad marryage neuer was before: harke, harke, I heare the minſtrels play.

div.stage: Enter Petruchio, Kate, Bianca, Hortenſio, Baptiſta.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Gentlemen & friends, I thank you for your pains,
I know you thinke to dine with me to day,
And haue prepar'd great ſtore of wedding cheere,
But ſo it is, my haſte doth call me hence,
And therefore heere I meane to take my leaue.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Is't poſſible you will away to night?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I muſt away to day before night come,
Make it no wonder: if you knew my buſineſſe,
You would intreat me rather goe then ſtay:
And honeſt company, I thanke you all,
That haue beheld me giue away my ſelfe
To this moſt patient, ſweet, and vertuous wife,
Dine with my father, drinke a health to me,
For I muſt hence, and farewell to you all.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Let vs intreat you ſtay till after dinner.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: It may not be.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: Let me intreat you.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: It cannot be.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: Let me intreat you.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: I am content.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: Are you content to ſtay?

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I am content you ſhall entreat me ſtay,
But yet not ſtay, entreat me how you can.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: Now if you loue me ſtay.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Grumio, my horſe.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: I ſir, they be ready, the Oates haue eaten the horſes.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Nay then,
Doe what thou canſt, I will not goe to day,
No, nor to morrow, not till I pleaſe my ſelfe,
The dore is open ſir, there lies your way,
You may be iogging whiles your bootes are greene:
For me, Ile not be gone till I pleaſe my ſelfe,
'Tis like you'll proue a iolly ſurly groome,
That take it on you at the firſt ſo roundly.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: O Kate content thee, prethee be not angry.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.l: I will be angry, what haſt thou to doe?
Father, be quiet, he ſhall ſtay my leiſure.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: I marry ſir, now it begins to worke.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.l: Gentlemen, forward to the bridall dinner,
I ſee a woman may be made a foole
If ſhe had not a ſpirit to reſiſt.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: They ſhall goe forward Kate at thy command,
Obey the Bride you that attend on her.
Goe to the feaſt, reuell and domineere,
Carowſe full meaſure to her maiden-head,
Be madde and merry, or goe hang your ſelues:
But for my bonny Kate, ſhe muſt with me:
Nay, looke not big, nor ſtampe, nor ſtare, nor fret,
I will be maſter of what is mine owne,
Shee is my goods, my chattels, ſhe is my houſe,
My houſhold-ſtuffe, my field, my barne,
My horſe, my oxe, my aſſe, my any thing,
And heere ſhe ſtands, touch her who euer dare,
Ile bring mine action on the proudeſt he
That ſtops my way in Padua: Grumio
Draw forth thy weapon, we are beſet with theeues,
Reſcue thy Miſtreſſe if thou be a man:
Feare not ſweet wench, they ſhall not touch thee Kate,
Ile buckler thee againſt a Million.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Nay, let them goe, a couple of quiet ones.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Went they not quickly, I ſhould die with laughing.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Of all mad matches neuer was the like.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Miſtreſſe, what is your opinion of your ſiſter?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: That being mad her ſelfe, ſhe's madly mated.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: I warrant him Petruchio is Kated.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Neighbours and friends, though Bride & Bridegroom wants
For to ſupply the places at the table,
You know there wants no iunkets at the feaſt:
Lucentio, you ſhall ſupply the Bridegroomes place,
And let Bianca take her ſiſters roome.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Shall ſweet Bianca practiſe how to bride it?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: She ſhall Lucentio: come gentlemen lets goe.

sp.speaker: Gru.:
sp.p: Fie, fie on all tired Iades, on all mad Maſters, & all foule waies: was euer man ſo beaten? was euer man ſo raide? was euer man ſo weary? I am ſent before to make a fire, and they are comming after to warme them: now were not I a little pot, & ſoone hot; my very lippes might freeze to my teeth, my tongue to the roofe of my mouth, my heart in my belly, ere I ſhould come by a fire to thaw me, but I with blowing the fire ſhall warme my ſelfe: for conſidering the weather, a taller man then I will take cold: Holla, hoa Curtis.

sp.speaker: Curt.
sp.p: Who is that calls ſo coldly?

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p:
A piece of Ice: if thou doubt it, thou maiſt ſlide from my ſhoulder to my heele, with no
greater a run but my head and my necke. A fire good Curtis.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Is my maſter and his wife comming Grumio?

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Oh I Curtis I, and therefore fire, fire, caſt on no water.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Is ſhe ſo hot a ſhrew as ſhe's reported.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: She was good Curtis before this froſt: but thou know'ſt winter tames man, woman, and beaſt: for it hath tam'd my old maſter, and my new miſtris, and my ſelfe fellow Curtis.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Away you three inch foole, I am no beaſt.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Am I but three inches? Why thy horne is a foot and ſo long am I at the leaſt. But wilt thou make a fire, or ſhall I complaine on thee to our miſtris, whoſe hand (ſhe being now at hand) thou ſhalt ſoone feele, to thy cold comfort, for being ſlow in thy hot office.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: I prethee good Grumio, tell me, how goes the world?

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: A cold world Curtis in euery office but thine, & therefore fire: do thy duty, and haue thy dutie, for my Maſter and miſtris are almoſt frozen to death.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: There's fire readie, and therefore good Grumio the newes.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Why Iacke boy, ho boy, and as much newes as wilt thou.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Come, you are ſo full of conicatching.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Why therefore fire, for I haue caught extreme cold. Where's the Cooke, is ſupper ready, the houſe trim'd, ruſhes ſtrew'd, cobwebs ſwept, the ſeruingmen in their new fuſtian, the white ſtockings, and euery officer his wedding garment on? Be the Iackes faire within, the Gils fai • without, the Carpets laide, and euerie thing in order?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: All readie: and therefore I pray thee newes.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Firſt know my horſe is tired, my maſter & miſtris falne out.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Out of their ſaddles into the durt, and thereby hangs a tale.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Let's ha't good Grumio.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Lend thine eare.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Heere.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: There.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: This 'tis to feele a tale, not to heare a tale.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: And therefore 'tis cal'd a ſenſible tale: and this Cuffe was but to knocke at your eare, and beſeech liſtning: now I begin, Inprimis wee came downe a fowle hill, my Maſter riding behinde my Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Both of one horſe?

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: What's that to thee?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Why a horſe.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Tell thou the tale: but hadſt thou not croſt me, thou ſhouldſt haue heard how her horſe fel, and ſhe vnder her horſe: thou ſhouldſt haue heard in how miery a place, how ſhe was bemoil'd, how hee left her with the horſe vpon her, how he beat me becauſe her horſe ſtumbled, how ſhe waded through the durt to plucke him off me: how he ſwore, how ſhe prai'd, that neuer prai'd before: how I cried, how the horſes ranne away, how her bridle was burſt: how I loſt my crupper, with manie things of worthy memorie, which now ſhall die in obliuion, and thou returne vnexperienc'd to thy graue.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: By this reckning he is more ſhrew than ſhe.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: I, and that thou and the proudeſt of you all ſhall finde when he comes home. But what talke I of this? Call forth Nathaniel, Ioſeph, Nicholas, Phillip, Walter, Sugerſop and the reſt: let their heads bee ſlickely comb'd, their blew coats bruſh'd, and their garters of an indifferent knit, let them curtſie with their left legges, and not preſume to touch a haire of my Maſters horſe-taile, till they kiſſe their hands. Are they all readie?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: They are.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Call them forth.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Do you heare ho? you muſt meete my maiſter to countenance my miſtris.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Why ſhe hath a face of her owne.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Who knowes not that?

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Thou it ſeemes, that cals for company to countenance her.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: I call them forth to credit her.

div.stage: Enter foure or fiue ſeruing men.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Why ſhe comes to borrow nothing of them.

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.p: Welcome home Grumio.

sp.speaker: Phil.
sp.p: How now Grumio.

sp.speaker: Ioſ.
sp.p: What Grumio.

sp.speaker: Nick.
sp.p: Fellow Grumio.

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.p: How now old lad.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Welcome you: how now you: what you: fellow you: and thus much for greeting. Now my ſpruce companions, is all readie, and all things neate?

sp.speaker: Nat.
sp.p: All things is readie, how neere is our maſter?

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: E'ne at hand, alighted by this: and therefore be not—Cockes paſſion, ſilence, I heare my maſter.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Where be theſe knaues? What no man at doore
To hold my ſtirrop, nor to take my horſe?
Where is Nathaniel, Gregory, Phillip.

sp.speaker: All ſer.
sp.p: Heere, heere ſir, heere ſir.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Heere ſir, heere ſir, heere ſir, heere ſir.
You logger-headed and vnpolliſht groomes:
What? no attendance? no regard? no dutie?
Where is the fooliſh knaue I ſent before?

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Heere ſir, as fooliſh as I was before.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: You pezant, ſwain, you horſon malt-horſe drudg
Did I not bid thee meete me in the Parke,
And bring along theſe raſcal knaues with thee?

sp.speaker: Grumio.
sp.l: Nathaniels coate ſir was not fully made,
And Gabrels pumpes were all vnpinkt i' th heele:
There was no Linke to colour Peters hat,
And Walters dagger was not come from ſheathing:
There were none fine, but Adam, Rafe, and Gregory,
The reſt were ragged, old, and beggerly,
Yet as they are, heere are they come to meete you.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Go raſcals, go, and fetch my ſupper in.
Where is the life that late I led?
Where are thoſe? Sit downe Kate,
And welcome. Soud, ſoud, ſoud, ſoud.
Why when I ſay? Nay good ſweete Kate be merrie.
Off with my boots, you rogues: you villaines, when?

l.hi: It was the Friar of Orders gray,
As he forth walked on his way.

sp.l: Out you rogue, you plucke my foote awrie,
Take that, and mend the plucking of the other.
Be merrie Kate: Some water heere: what hoa.
Where's my Spaniel Troilus? Sirra, get you hence,
And bid my cozen Ferdinand come hither:
One Kate that you muſt kiſſe, and be acquainted with.
Where are my Slippers? Shall I haue ſome water?
Come Kate and waſh, & welcome heartily:
you horſon villaine, will you let it fall?

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Patience I pray you, 'twas a fault vnwilling.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: A horſon beetle-headed flap-ear'd knaue:
Come Kate ſit downe, I know you haue a ſtomacke,
Will you giue thankes, ſweete Kate, or elſe ſhall I?
What's this, Mutton?

sp.speaker: 1. Ser.
sp.p: I.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Who brought it?

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.p: I.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: 'Tis burnt, and ſo is all the meate:
What dogges are theſe? Where is the raſcall Cooke?
How durſt you villaines bring it from the dreſſer
And ſerue it thus to me that loue it not?
There, take it to you, trenchers, cups, and all:
You heedleſſe iolt-heads, and vnmanner'd ſlaues.
What, do you grumble? Ile be with you ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: I pray you husband be not ſo diſquiet,
The meate was well, if you were ſo contented.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: I tell thee Kate, 'twas burnt and dried away,
And I expreſſely am forbid to touch it:
For it engenders choller, planteth anger,
And better 'twere that both of vs did faſt,
Since of our ſelues, our ſelues are chollericke,
Then feede it with ſuch ouer-roſted fleſh:
Be patient, to morrow't ſhalbe mended,
And for this night we'l faſt for companie.
Come I wil bring thee to thy Bridall chamber.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Peter didſt euer ſee the like.

sp.speaker: Peter.
sp.p: He kils her in her owne humor.

sp.speaker: Grumio.
sp.p: Where is he?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: In her chamber, making a ſermon of continencie to her, and railes, and ſweares, and rates, that ſhee (poore ſoule) knowes not which way to ſtand, to looke, to ſpeake, and ſits as one new riſen from a dreame. Away, away, for he is comming hither.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Thus haue I politickely begun my reigne,
And 'tis my hope to end ſucceſſefully:
My Faulcon now is ſharpe, and paſſing emptie,
And til ſhe ſtoope, ſhe muſt not be full gorg'd,
For then ſhe neuer lookes vpon her lure.
Another way I haue to man my Haggard,
To make her come, and know her Keepers call:
That is, to watch her, as we watch theſe Kites,
That baite, and beare, and will not be obedient:
She eate no meate to day, nor none ſhall eate.
Laſt night ſhe ſlept not, nor to night ſhe ſhall not:
As with the meate, ſome vndeſerued fault
Ile finde about the making of the bed,
And heere Ile fling the pillow, there the boulſter,
This way the Couerlet, another way the ſheets:
I, and amid this hurlie I intend,
That all is done in reuerend care of her,
And in concluſion, ſhe ſhal watch all night,
And if ſhe chance to nod, Ile raile and brawle,
And with the clamor keepe her ſtil awake:
This is a way to kil a Wife with kindneſſe,
And thus Ile curbe her mad and headſtrong humor:
He that knowes better how to tame a ſhrew,
Now let him ſpeake, 'tis charity to ſhew.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Is't poſsible friend Liſio, that miſtris Bianca
Doth fancie any other but Lucentio,
I tel you ſir, ſhe beares me faire in hand.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Sir, to ſatisfie you in what I haue ſaid,
Stand by, and marke the manner of his teaching.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Now Miſtris, profit you in what you reade?

sp.speaker: Bian▪
sp.p: What Maſter reade you firſt, reſolue me that?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: I reade, that I profeſſe the Art to loue.

sp.speaker: Bian
sp.p: And may you proue ſir Maſter of your Art.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: While you ſweet deere ptoue Miſtreſſe of my heart.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Quicke proceeders marry, now tel me I pray, you that durſt ſweare that your miſtris Bianca Lou'd me in the World ſo wel as Lucentio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Oh deſpightful Loue, vnconſtant womankind,
I tel thee Liſio this is wonderfull.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: Miſtake no more, I am not Liſio,
Nor a Muſitian as I ſeeme to bee,
But one that ſcorne to liue in this diſguiſe,
For ſuch a one as leaues a Gentleman,
And makes a God of ſuch a Cullion;
Know ſir, that I am cal'd Hortenſio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Signior Hortenſio, I haue often heard
Of your entire affection to Bianca,
And ſince mine eyes are witneſſe of her lightneſſe,
I wil with you, if you be ſo contented,
Forſweare Bianca, and her loue for euer.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: See how they kiſſe and court: Signior Lucentio,
Heere is my hand, and heere I firmly vow
Neuer to woo her more, but do forſweare her
As one vnworthie all the former fauours
That I haue fondly flatter'd them withall.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: And heere I take the like vnfained oath,
Neuer to marrie with her, though ſhe would intreate,
Fie on her, ſee how beaſtly ſhe doth court him.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: Would all the world but he had quite forſworn
For me, that I may ſurely keepe mine oath.
I wil be married to a wealthy Widdow,
Ere three dayes paſſe, which hath as long lou'd me,
As I haue lou'd this proud diſdainful Haggard,
And ſo farewel ſignior Lucentio,
Kindneſſe in women, not their beauteous lookes
Shal win my loue, and ſo I take my leaue,
In reſolution, as I ſwore before.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Miſtris Bianca, bleſſe you with ſuch grace,
As longeth to a Louers bleſſed caſe:
Nay, I haue tane you napping gentle Loue,
And haue forſworne you with Hortenſio.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Tranio you ieſt, but haue you both forſworne mee?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Miſtris we haue.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Then we are rid of Liſio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I' faith hee'l haue a luſtie Widdow now,
That ſhalbe woo'd, and wedded in a day.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: God giue him ioy.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: I, and hee'l tame her.

sp.speaker: Bianca.
sp.p: He ſayes ſo Tranio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Faith he is gone vnto the taming ſchoole.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: The taming ſchoole: what is there ſuch a place?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I miſtris, and Petruchio is the maſter,
That teacheth trickes eleuen and twentie long,
To tame a ſhrew, and charme her chattering tongue.

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.l: Oh Maſter, maſter I haue watcht ſo long,
That I am dogge-wearie, but at laſt I ſpied
An ancient Angel comming downe the hill,
Wil ſerue the turne.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: What is he Biondello?

sp.speaker: Bio.
sp.l: Maſter, a Marcantant, or a pedant,
I know not what, but formall in apparrell,
In gate and countenance ſurely like a Father.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: And what of him Tranio?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: If he be credulous, and truſt my tale,
Ile make him glad to ſeeme Vincentio,
And giue aſſurance to Baptiſta Minola.
As if he were the right Ʋincentio.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Take me your loue, and then let me alone.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: God ſaue you ſir.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: And you ſir, you are welcome,
Trauaile you farre on, or are you at the fartheſt?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Sir at the fartheſt for a weeke or two,
But then vp farther, and as farre as Rome,
And ſo to Tripolie, if God lend me life.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: What Countreyman I pray?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Of Mantua.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Of Mantua Sir, marrie God forbid,
And come to Padua careleſſe of your life.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: My life ſir? how I pray? for that goes hard.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: 'Tis death for any one in Mantua
To come to Padua, know you not the cauſe?
Your ſhips are ſtaid at Venice, and the Duke
For priuate quarrel 'twixt your Duke and him,
Hath publiſh'd and proclaim'd it openly:
'Tis meruaile, but that you are but newly come,
you might haue heard it elſe proclaim'd about.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Alas ſir, it is worſe for me then ſo,
For I haue bils for monie by exchange
From Florence, and muſt heere deliuer them.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Wel ſir, to do you courteſie,
This wil I do, and this I wil aduiſe you.
Firſt tell me, haue you euer beene at Piſa?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I ſir, in Piſa haue I often bin,
Piſa renowned for graue Citizens.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Among them know you one Vincentio?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I know him not, but I haue heard of him:
A Merchant of incomparable wealth.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: He is my father ſir, and ſooth to ſay,
In count'nance ſomewhat doth reſemble you.

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: As much as an apple doth an oyſter, & all one.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: To ſaue your life in this extremitie,
This fauor wil I do you for his ſake,
And thinke it not the worſt of all your fortunes,
That you are like to Sir Vincentio.
His name and credite ſhal you vndertake,
And in my houſe you ſhal be friendly lodg'd,
Looke that you take vpon you as you ſhould,
you vnderſtand me ſir: ſo ſhal you ſtay
Til you haue done your buſineſſe in the Citie:
If this be court'ſie ſir, accept of it.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Oh ſir I do, and wil repute you euer
The patron of my life and libertie.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Then go with me, to make the matter good,
This by the way I let you vnderſtand,
My father is heere look'd for euerie day,
To paſſe aſſurance of a dowre in marriage
'Twixt me, and one Baptiſtas daughter heere:
In all theſe circumſtances Ile inſtruct you,
Go with me to cloath you as becomes you.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: No, no forſooth I dare not for my life.

sp.speaker: Ka.
sp.l: The more my wrong, the more his ſpite appears,
What, did he marrie me to famiſh me?
Beggers that come vnto my fathers doore,
Vpon intreatie haue a preſent almes,
If not, elſewhere they meete with charitie:
But I, who neuer knew how to intreat,
Nor neuer needed that I ſhould intreate,
Am ſtaru'd for meate▪ giddie for lacke of ſleepe:
With oathes kept waking, and with brawling fed,
And that which ſpights me more then all theſe wants,
He does it vnder name of perfect loue:
As who ſhould ſay▪ if I ſhould ſleepe or eate▪
'Twere deadly ſickneſſe, or elſe preſent death.
I prethee go, and get me ſome repaſt,
I care not what, ſo it be holſome ſoode.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: What ſay you to a Neats foote?

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: 'Tis paſsing good, I prethee let me haue it.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.l: I feare it is too chollericke a meate.
How ſay you to a fat Tripe finely broyl'd?

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: I like it well, good Grumio fetch it me.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.l: I cannot tell, I feare 'tis chollericke.
What ſay you to a peece of Beefe and Muſtard?

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: A diſh that I do loue to feede vpon.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: I, but the Muſtard is too hot a little.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Why then the Beefe, and let the Muſtard reſt.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.l: Nay then I wil not, you ſhal haue the Muſtard
Or elſe you get no beefe of Grumio.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Then both or one, or any thing thou wilt.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Why then the Muſtard without the beefe.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Go get thee gone, thou falſe deluding ſlaue,
That feed'ſt me with the verie name of meate.
Sorrow on thee, and all the packe of you
That triumph thus vpon my miſery:
Go get thee gone, I ſay.

div.stage: Enter Petruchio, and Hortenſio with meate.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: How fares my Kate, what ſweeting all a-mort?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Miſtris, what cheere?

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Faith as cold as can be.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Plucke vp thy ſpirits, looke cheerfully vpon me.
Heere Loue, thou ſeeſt how diligent I am,
To dreſſe thy meate my ſelfe, and bring it thee.
I am ſure ſweet Kate, this kindneſſe merites thankes.
What, not a word? Nay then, thou lou'ſt it not:
And all my paines is ſorted to no proofe.
Heere take away this diſh.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: I pray you let it ſtand.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: The pooreſt ſeruice is repaide with thankes,
And ſo ſhall mine before you touch the meate.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: I thanke you ſir.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: Signior Petruchio, fie you are too blame:
Come Miſtris Kate, Ile beare you companie.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Eate it vp all Hortenſio, if thou loueſt mee:
Much good do it vnto thy gentle heart:
Kate eate apace; and now my honie Loue,
Will we returne vnto thy Fathers houſe,
And reuell it as brauely as the beſt,
With ſilken coats and caps, and golden Rings,
With Ruffes and Cuffes, and Fardingales, and things:
With Scarfes, and Fannes, & double change of brau'ry,
With Amber Bracelets, Beades, and all this knau'ry.
What haſt thou din'd? The Tailor ſtaies thy leaſure,
To decke thy bodie with his ruffling treaſure.
Come Tailor, let vs ſee theſe ornaments.
Lay forth the gowne. What newes with you ſir?

sp.speaker: Fel.
sp.p: Heere is the cap your Worſhip did beſpeake.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Why this was moulded on a porrenger,
A Veluet diſh: Fie, fie, 'tis lewd and filthy,
Why 'tis a cockle or a walnut-ſhell,
A knacke, a toy, a tricke, a babies cap:
Away with it, come let me haue a bigger.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Ile haue no bigger, this doth fit the time,
And Gentlewomen weare ſuch caps as theſe.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: When you are gentle, you ſhall haue one too,
And not till then.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: That will not be in haſt.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Why ſir I truſt I may haue leaue to ſpeake,
And ſpeake I will. I am no childe, no babe,
Your betters haue indur'd me ſay my minde,
And If you cannot, beſt you ſtop your eares.
My tongue will tell the anger of my heart,
Or els my heart concealing it wil breake,
And rather then it ſhall, I will be free,
Euen to the vttermoſt as I pleaſe in words.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Why thou ſaiſt true, it is paltrie cap,
A cuſtard coffen, a bauble, a ſilken pie,
I loue thee well in that thou lik'ſt it not.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Loue me, or loue me not, I like the cap,
And it I will haue, or I will haue none.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Thy gowne, why I: come Tailor let vs ſee't.
Oh mercie God, what masking ſtuffe is heere?
Whats this? a ſleeue? 'tis like demi cannon,
What, vp and downe caru'd like an apple Tart?
Heers ſnip, and nip, and cut, and ſliſh and ſlaſh,
Like to a Cenſor in a barbers ſhoppe:
Why what a deuils name Tailor cal'ſt thou this?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: I ſee ſhees like to haue neither cap nor gowne.

sp.speaker: Tai.
sp.l: You bid me make it orderlie and well,
According to the faſhion, and the time.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Marrie and did: but if you be remembred,
I did not bid you marre it to the time▪
Go hop me ouer euery kennell home,
For you ſhall hop without my cuſtome ſir:
Ile none of it; hence, make your beſt of it.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: I neuer ſaw a better faſhion'd gowne,
More queint, more pleaſing, nor more commendable:
Belike you meane to make a puppet of me.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Why true, he meanes to make a puppet of thee.

sp.speaker: Tail.
sp.p: She ſaies your Worſhip meanes to make a puppet of her.

sp.speaker: Pet
sp.l: Oh monſtrous arrogance:
Thou lyeſt, thou thred, thou thimble,
Thou yard three quarters, halfe yard, quarter, naile,
Thou Flea, thou Nit, thou winter cricket thou:
Brau'd in mine owne houſe with a skeine of thred:
Away thou Ragge, thou quantitie, thou remnant,
Or I ſhall ſo be-mete thee with thy yard,
As thou ſhalt thinke on prating whil'ſt thou liu'ſt:
I tell thee I, that thou haſt marr'd her gowne.

sp.speaker: Tail.
sp.l: Your worſhip is deceiu'd, the gowne is made
Iuſt as my maſter had direction:
Grumio gaue order how it ſhould be done.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: I gaue him no order, I gaue him the ſtuffe.

sp.speaker: Tail.
sp.p: But how did you deſire it ſhould be made?

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Marrie ſir with needle and thred.

sp.speaker: Tail.
sp.p: But did you not requeſt to haue it cut?

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Thou haſt fac'd many things.

sp.speaker: Tail.
sp.p: I haue.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Face not mee: thou haſt brau'd manie men, braue not me; I will neither bee fac'd nor brau'd. I ſay vnto thee, I bid thy Maſter cut out the gowne, but I did not bid him cut it to peeces. Ergo thou lieſt.

sp.speaker: Tail.
sp.p: Why heere is the note of the faſhion to teſtify.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Reade it.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: The note lies in's throate if he ſay I ſaid ſo.

sp.speaker: Tail.
sp.p: Inprimis, a looſe bodied gowne.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Maſter, if euer I ſaid looſe-bodied gowne, ſow me in the skirts of it, and beate me to death with a bottome of browne thred: I ſaid a gowne.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Proceede.

sp.speaker: Tai.
sp.p: With a ſmall compaſt cape.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: I confeſſe the cape.

sp.speaker: Tai.
sp.p: With a trunke ſleeue.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: I confeſſe two ſleeues.

sp.speaker: Tai.
sp.p: The ſleeues curiouſly cut.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: I there's the villanie.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Error i' th bill ſir, error i' th bill? I commanded the ſleeues ſhould be cut out, and ſow'd vp againe, and that Ile proue vpon thee, though thy little finger be armed in a thimble.

sp.speaker: Tail.
sp.p: This is true that I ſay, and I had thee in place where thou ſhouldſt know it.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: I am for thee ſtraight: take thou the bill, giue me thy meat-yard, and ſpare not me.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: God-a-mercie Grumio, then hee ſhall haue no oddes.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Well ſir in breefe the gowne is not for me.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: You are i' th right ſir, 'tis for my miſtris.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Go take it vp vnto thy maſters vſe.

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.p: Villaine, not for thy life: Take vp my Miſtreſſe gowne for thy maſters vſe.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Why ſir, what's your conceit in that?

sp.speaker: Gru.
sp.l: Oh ſir, the conceit is deeper then you think for:
Take vp my Miſtris gowne to his maſters vſe.
Oh fie, fie, fie.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Hortenſio, ſay thou wilt ſee the Tailor paide:
Go take it hence, be gone, and ſay no more.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: Tailor, Ile pay thee for thy gowne to morrow,
Take no vnkindneſſe of his haſtie words:
Away I ſay, commend me to thy maſter.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Well, come my Kate, we will vnto your fathers,
Euen in theſe honeſt meane habiliments:
Our purſes ſhall be proud, our garments poore:
For 'tis the minde that makes the bodie rich.
And as the Sunne breakes through the darkeſt clouds,
So honor peereth in the meaneſt habit.
What is the Iay more precious then the Larke?
Becauſe his feathers are more beautifull.
Or is the Adder better then the Eele▪
Becauſe his painted skin contents the eye.
Oh no good Kate: neither art thou the worſe
For this poore furniture, and meane array.
If thou accountedſt it ſhame, lay it on me,
And therefore frolicke, we will hence forthwith,
To feaſt and ſport vs at thy fathers houſe,
Go call my men, and let vs ſtraight to him,
And bring our horſes vnto Long-lane end,
There wil we mount, and thither walke on foote,
Let's ſee, I thinke 'tis now ſome ſeuen a clocke,
And well we may come there by dinner time.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: I dare aſſure you ſir, 'tis almoſt two,
And 'twill be ſupper time ere you come there.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: It ſhall be ſeuen ere I go to horſe:
Looke what I ſpeake, or do, or thinke to doe,
You are ſtill croſſing it, ſirs let't alone,
I will not goe to day, and ere I doe,
It ſhall be what a clock I ſay it is.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Why ſo this gallant will command the ſunne.

div.stage: Enter Tranio, and the Pedant dreſt like Vincentio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Sirs, this is the houſe, pleaſe it you that I call.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I what elſe, and but I be deceiued,
Signior Baptiſta may remember me
Neere twentie yeares a goe in Genoa.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Where we were lodgers, at the Pegaſus,
Tis well, and hold your owne in any caſe
With ſuch auſteritie as longeth to a father.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: I warrant you: but ſir here comes your boy,
Twere good he were ſchool'd.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Feare you not him: ſirra Biondello,
Now doe your dutie throughlie I aduiſe you:
Imagine 'twere the right Vincentio.

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: Tut, feare not me.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: But haſt thou done thy errand to Baptiſta.

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.l: I told him that your father was at Venice,
And that you look't for him this day in Padua.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Th' art a tall fellow, hold thee that to drinke,
Here comes Baptiſta: ſet your countenance ſir.

div.stage: Enter Baptiſta and Lucentio: Pedant booted and bare headed.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Signior Baptiſta you are happilie met:
Sir, this is the gentleman I told you of,
I pray you ſtand good father to me now,
Giue me Bianca for my patrimony.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.l: Soft ſon: ſir by your leaue, hauing com to Padua
To gather in ſome debts, my ſon Lucentio
Made me acquainted with a waighty cauſe
Of loue betweene your daughter and himſelfe:
And for the good report I heare of you,
And for the loue he beareth to your daughter,
And ſhe to him: to ſtay him not too long,
I am content in a good fathers care
To haue him matcht, and if you pleaſe to like
No worſe then I, vpon ſome agreement
Me ſhall you finde readie and willing
With one conſent to haue her ſo beſtowed:
For curious I cannot be with you
Signior Baptiſta, of whom I heare ſo well.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Sir, pardon me in what I haue to ſay,
Your plainneſſe and your ſhortneſſe pleaſe me well:
Right true it is your ſonne Lucentio here
Doth loue my daughter, and ſhe loueth him,
Or both diſſemble deepely their affections:
And therefore if you ſay no more then this,
That like a Father you will deale with him,
And paſſe my daughter a ſufficient dower,
The match is made, and all is done,
Your ſonne ſhall haue my daughter with conſent.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: I thanke you ſir, where then doe you know beſt
We be affied and ſuch aſſurance tane,
As ſhall with either parts agreement ſtand.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Not in my houſe Lucentio, for you know
Pitchers haue eares, and I haue manie ſeruants,
Beſides old Gremio is harkning ſtill,
And happilie we might be interrupted.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: Then at my lodging, and it like you,
There doth my father lie: and there this night
Weele paſſe the buſineſſe priuately and well:
Send for your daughter by your ſeruant here,
My Boy ſhall fetch the Scriuener preſentlie,
The worſt is this that at ſo ſlender warning,
You are like to haue a thin and ſlender pittance.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: It likes me well:
Cambio hie you home, and bid Bianca make her readie ſtraight:
And if you will tell what hath hapned,
Lucentios Father is arriued in Padua,
And how ſhe's like to be Lucentios wife.

sp.speaker: Biond.
sp.p: I praie the gods ſhe may withall my heart.

sp.speaker: Tran.
sp.l: Dallie not with the gods, but get thee gone.
Signior Baptiſta, ſhall I leade the way,
Welcome, one meſſe is like to be your cheere,
Come ſir, we will better it in Piſa.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: I follow you.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: What ſaiſt thou Biondello.

sp.speaker: Biond.
sp.p: You ſaw my Maſter winke and laugh vpon you?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Biondello, what of that?

sp.speaker: Biond.
sp.p: Faith nothing: but has left mee here behinde to expound the meaning or morrall of his ſignes and tokens.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I pray thee moralize them.

sp.speaker: Biond.
sp.p: Then thus: Baptiſta is ſafe talking with the deceiuing Father of a deceitfull ſonne.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: And what of him?

sp.speaker: Biond.
sp.p: His daughter is to be brought by you to the ſupper.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: And then.

sp.speaker: Bio.
sp.p: The old Prieſt at Saint Lukes Church is at your command at all houres.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: And what of all this.

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: I cannot tell, expect they are buſied about a counterfeit aſſurance: take you aſſurance of her, Cum preuilegio ad Impremendum ſolem, to th' Church take the Prieſt, Clarke, and ſome ſufficient honeſt witneſſes:
sp.l: If this be not that you looke for, I haue no more to ſay,
But bid Bianca farewell for euer and a day.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Hear'ſt thou Biondello.

sp.speaker: Biond.
sp.p: I cannot tarry: I knew a wench maried in an afternoone as ſhee went to the Garden for Parſeley to ſtuffe a Rabit, and ſo may you ſir: and ſo adew ſir, my Maſter hath appointed me to goe to Saint Lukes to bid the Prieſt be readie to come againſt you come with your appendix.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I may and will, if ſhe be ſo contented:
She will be pleas'd, then wherefore ſhould I doubt:
Hap what hap may, Ile roundly goe about her:
It ſhall goe hard if Cambio goe without her.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Come on a Gods name, once more toward our fathers:
Good Lord how bright and goodly ſhines the Moone.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: The Moone, the Sunne: it is not Moonelight now.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: I ſay it is the Moone that ſhines ſo bright.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: I know it is the Sunne that ſhines ſo bright.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Now by my mothers ſonne, and that's my ſelfe,
It ſhall be moone, or ſtarre, or what I liſt,
Or ere I iourney to your Fathers houſe:
Goe on, and fetch our horſes backe againe,
Euermore croſt and croſt, nothing but croſt.

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.p: Say as he ſaies, or we ſhall neuer goe.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Forward I pray, ſince we haue come ſo farre,
And be it moone, or ſunne, or what you pleaſe:
And if you pleaſe to call it a ruſh Candle,
Henceforth I vowe it ſhall be ſo for me.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: I ſay it is the Moone.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: I know it is the Moone.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Nay then you lye: it is the bleſſed Sunne.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Then God be bleſt, it in the bleſſed ſun,
But ſunne it is not, when you ſay it is not▪
And the Moone changes euen as your minde:
What you will haue it nam'd, euen that it is,
And ſo it ſhall be ſo for Katherine.

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.p: Petruchio, goe thy waies, the field is won.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Well, forward, forward, thus the bowle ſhould run,
And not vnluckily againſt the Bias:
But ſoft, Company is comming here▪
Good morrow gentle Miſtris, where away:
Tell me ſweete Kate, and tell me truely too,
Haſt thou beheld a freſher Gentlewoman:
Such warre of white and red within her cheekes:
What ſtars do ſpangle heauen with ſuch beautie,
As thoſe two eyes become that heauenly face?
Faire louely Maide, once more good day to thee:
Sweete Kate embrace her for her beauties ſake.

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.p: A will make the man mad to make the woman of him.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Yong budding Virgin, faire, and freſh, & ſweet,
Whether away, or whether is thy aboade?
Happy the Parents of ſo faire a childe;
Happier the man whom fauourable ſtars
A lots thee for his louely bedfellow.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Why how now Kate, I hope thou art not mad,
This is a man old, wrinckled, faded, withered,
And not a Maiden, as thou ſaiſt he is.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Pardon old father my miſtaking eies,
That haue bin ſo bedazled with the ſunne,
That euery thing I looke on ſeemeth greene:
Now I perceiue thou art a reuerent Father:
Pardon I pray thee for my mad miſtaking.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Do good old grandſire, & withall make known
Which way thou trauelleſt, if along with vs,
We ſhall be ioyfull of thy companie.

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.l: Faire Sir, and you my merry Miſtris,
That with your ſtrange encounter much amaſde me:
My name is call'd Vincentio, my dwelling Piſa,
And bound I am to Padua, there to viſite
A ſonne of mine, which long I haue not ſeene.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: What is his name?

sp.speaker: Vinc.
sp.p: Lucentio gentle ſir.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Happily met, the happier for thy ſonne:
And now by Law, as well as reuerent age,
I may intitle thee my louing Father,
The ſiſter to my wife, this Gentlewoman,
Thy Sonne by this hath married: wonder not,
Nor be not grieued, ſhe is of good eſteeme,
Her dowrie wealthie, and of worthie birth;
Beſide, ſo qualified, as may beſeeme
The Spouſe of any noble Gentleman:
Let me imbrace with old Vincentio,
And wander we to ſee thy honeſt ſonne,
Who will of thy arriuall be full ioyous.

sp.speaker: Vinc.
sp.l: But is this true, or is it elſe your pleaſure,
Like pleaſant trauailors to breake a left
Vpon the companie you ouertake?

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.p: I doe aſſure thee father ſo it is.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Come goe along and ſee the truth hereof,
For our firſt merriment hath made thee iealous.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: Well Petruchio, this has put me in heart;
Haue to my Widdow, and if ſhe froward,
Then haſt thou taught Hortentio to be vntoward.

div.stage: Enter Biondello, Lucentio and Bianea, Gremio is out before.

sp.speaker: Biond.
sp.p: Softly and ſwiftly ſir, for the Prieſt is ready.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I flie Biondello; but they may chance to neede thee at home, therefore leaue vs.

sp.speaker: Biond.
sp.p: Nay faith, Ile ſee the Church a your backe, and then come backe to my miſtris as ſoone as I can.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: I maruaile Cambio comes not all this while.

div.stage: Enter Petruchio, Kate, Ʋincentio, Grumio with Attendants.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Sir heres the doore, this is Lucentios houſe,
My Fathers beares more toward the Market-place,
Thither muſt I, and here I leaue you ſir.

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.l: You ſhall not chooſe but drinke before you go,
I thinke I ſhall command your welcome here;
And by all likelihood ſome cheere is toward.

sp.speaker: Grem.
sp.p: They're buſie within, you were beſt knocke lowder.

div.stage: Pedant lookes out of the window.

sp.speaker: Ped
sp.p: What's he that knockes as he would beat downe the gate?

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.p: Is Signior Lucentio within ſir?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: He's within ſir, but not to be ſpoken withall.

sp.speaker: Vinc.
sp.p: What if a man bring him a hundred pound or two to make merrie withall.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Keepe your hundred pounds to your ſelfe, hee ſhall neede none ſo long as I liue.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Nay, I told you your ſonne was well beloued in Padua: doe you heare ſir, to leaue friuolous circumſtances, I pray you tell ſignior Lucentio that his Father is come from Piſa, and is here at the doore to ſpeake with him.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Thou lieſt his Father is come from Padua, and here looking out at the window.

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.p: Art thou his father?

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: I ſir, ſo his mother ſaies, if I may beleeue her.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Why how now gentleman: why this is flat knauerie to take vpon you another mans name.

sp.speaker: Peda.
sp.p: Lay hands on the villaine, I beleeue a meanes to coſen ſome bodie in this Citie vnder my countenance.

sp.speaker: Bio.
sp.p: I haue ſeene them in the Church together, God ſend'em good ſhipping: but who is here? mine old Maſter Ʋincentio: now wee are vndone and brough to nothing.

sp.speaker: Ʋin.
sp.p: Come hither crackhempe.

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: I hope I may chooſe Sir.

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.p: Come hither you rogue, what haue you forgot mee?

sp.speaker: Biond.
sp.p: Forgot you, no ſir: I could not forget you, for I neuer ſaw you before in all my life.

sp.speaker: Ʋinc.
sp.p: What, you notorious villaine, didſt thou neuer ſee thy Miſtris father, Vincentio?

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: What my old worſhipfull old maſter? yes marie ſir ſee where he lookes out of the window.

sp.speaker: Ʋin.
sp.p: Iſt ſo indeede.

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: Helpe, helpe, helpe, here's a mad man will murder me.

sp.speaker: Pedan.
sp.p: Helpe, ſonne, helpe ſignior Baptiſta.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Pree the Kate let's ſtand aſide and ſee the end of this controuerſie.

div.stage: Enter Pedant with ſeruants, Baptiſta, Tranio.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Sir, what are you that offer to beate my ſeruant?

sp.speaker: Vinc.
sp.p: What am I ſir: nay what are you ſir: oh immortall Goddes: oh fine villaine, a ſilken doubtlet, a veluet hoſe, a ſcarlet cloake, and a copataine hat: oh I am vndone, I am vndone: while I plaie the good husband at home, my ſonne and my ſeruant ſpend all at the vniuerſitie.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: How now, what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Bapt.
sp.p: What is the man lunaticke?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Sir, you ſeeme a ſober ancient Gentleman by your habit: but your words ſhew you a mad man: why ſir, what cernes it you, if I weare Pearle and gold: I thank my good Father, I am able to maintaine it.

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.p: Thy father: oh villaine, he is a Saile-maker in Bergamo.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: You miſtake ſir, you miſtake ſir, praie what do you thinke is his name?

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.p: His name, as if I knew not his name: I haue brought him vp euer ſince he was three yeeres old, and his name is Tronio.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Awaie, awaie mad aſſe, his name is Lucentio, and he is mine onelie ſonne and heire to the Lands of me ſignior Vincentio.

sp.speaker: Ven.
sp.p: Lucentio: oh he hath murdred his Maſter; laie hold on him I charge you in the Dukes name: oh my ſonne, my ſonne: tell me thou villaine, where is my ſon Lucentio?

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.p: Call forth an officer: Carrie this mad knaue to the Iaile: father Baptiſta, I charge you ſee that hee be forth comming.

sp.speaker: Vinc.
sp.p: Carrie me to the Iaile?

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Staie officer, he ſhall not go to priſon.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Talke not ſignior Gremio: I ſaie he ſhall goe to priſon.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Take heede ſignior Baptiſta, leaſt you be conicatcht in this buſineſſe: I dare ſweare this is the right Vincentio.

sp.speaker: Ped.
sp.p: Sweare if thou dar'ſt.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Naie, I dare not ſweare it.

sp.speaker: Tran.
sp.p: Then thou wert beſt ſaie that I am not Lucentio.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Yes, I know thee to be ſignior Lucentio.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Awaie with the dotard, to the Iaile with him.

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.p: Thus ſtrangers may be haild and abuſd: oh monſtrous villaine.

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.p: Oh we are ſpoil'd, and yonder he is, denie him, forſweare him, or elſe we are all vndone.

div.stage: Exit Biondello, Tranio and Pedant as faſt as may be.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Pardon ſweete father.

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.p: Liues my ſweete ſonne?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Pardon deere father.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: How haſt thou offended, where is Lucentio?

sp.speaker: Luc:
sp.l: Here's Lucentio, right ſonne to the right Ʋincentio,
That haue by marriage made thy daughter mine,
While counterfeit ſuppoſes bleer'd thine eine.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Here's packing with a witneſſe to deceiue vs all.

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.l: Where is that damned villaine Tranio,
That fac'd and braued me in this matter ſo?

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Why, tell me is not this my Cambio?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Cambio is chang'd into Lucentio.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Loue wrought theſe miracles. Biancas loue
Made me exchange my ſtate with Tranio,
While he did beare my countenance in the towne,
And happilie I haue arriued at the laſt
Vnto the wiſhed hauen of my bliſſe:
What Tranio did, my ſelfe enforſt him to;
Then pardon him ſweete Father for my ſake.

sp.speaker: Ʋin.
sp.p: Ile ſlit the villaines noſe that would haue ſent me to the Iaile.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: But doe you heare ſir, haue you married my daughter without asking my good will?

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.p: Feare not Baptiſta, we will content you, goe to: but I will in to be reueng'd for this villanie.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: And I to ſound the depth of this knauerie.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Looke not pale Bianca, thy father will not frown.

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.l: My cake is doug • h but Ile in among the reſt,
Out of hope of all, but my ſhare of the feaſt.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Husband let's follow, to ſee the end of this adoe.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Firſt kiſſe me Kate, and we will.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: What in the midſt of the ſtreete?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: What art thou aſham'd of me?

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Mo ſir, God forbid, but aſham'd to kiſſe.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Why then let's home againe: Come Sirra let's awaie.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: Nay, I will giue thee a kiſſe, now praie thee Loue ſtaie.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Is not this well? come my ſweete Kate.
Better once then neuer, for neuer to late.

div.head: Actus Quintus.
div.stage: Enter Baptiſta, Vincentio, Gremio, the Pedant, Lucentio, and Bianca. Tranio, Biondello Grumio, and Widdow: The Seruingmen with Tranio bringing in a Banquet.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: At laſt, though long, our iarring notes agree,
And time it is when raging warre is come,
To ſmile at ſcapes and perils ouerblowne:
My faire Bianca bid my father welcome,
While I with ſelfeſame kindneſſe welcome thine:
Brother Petruchio, ſiſter Katerina,
And thou Hortentio with thy louing Widdow:
Feaſt with the beſt, and welcome to my houſe,
My Banket is to cloſe our ſtomakes vp
After our great good cheere: praie you ſit downe,
For now we ſit to chat as well as eate.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Nothing but ſit and ſit, and eate and eate.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Padua affords this kindneſſe, ſonne Petruchio.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Padua affords nothing but what is kinde.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: For both our ſakes I would that word were true.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Now for my life Hortentio feares his Widow.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Then neuer truſt me if I be affeard.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: You are verie ſencible, and yet you miſſe my ſence:
I meane Hortentio is afeard of you.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: He that is giddie thinks the world turns round.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Roundlie replied.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: Miſtris, how meane you that?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Thus I conceiue by him.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Conceiues by me, how likes Hortentio that?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: My Widdow ſaies, thus ſhe conceiues her tale.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Verie well mended: kiſſe him for that good Widdow.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.l: He that is giddie thinkes the world turnes round,
I praie you tell me what you meant by that.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: Your housband being troubled with a ſhrew,
Meaſures my husbands ſorrow by his woe:
And now you know my meaning.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: A verie meane meaning.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Right, I meane you.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: And I am meane indeede, reſpecting you.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: To her Kate.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: To her Widdow.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: A hundred marks, my Kate does put her down.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: That's my office

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Spoke like an Officer: ha to the lad.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: How likes Cremio theſe quicke witted folkes?

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.p: Beleeue me ſir, they But together well.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Head, and but an haſtie witted bodie,
Would ſay your Head and But were head and horne.

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.p: I Miſtris Bride, hath that awakened you?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: I, but not frighted me, therefore Ile ſleepe againe.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Nay that you ſhall not ſince you haue begun:
Haue at you for a better ieſt or too.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Am I your Bird, I meane to ſhift my buſh,
And then purſue me as you draw your Bow.
You are welcome all.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: She hath preuented me, here ſignior Tranio,
This bird you aim'd at, though you hit her not,
Therefore a health to all that ſhot and miſt.

sp.speaker: Tri.
sp.l: Oh ſir, Lucentio ſlipt me like his Gray-hound,
Which runs himſelfe, and catches for his Maſter.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: A good ſwift ſimile, but ſomething curriſh.

sp.speaker: Tra.
sp.l: 'Tis well ſir that you hunted for your ſelfe:
'Tis thought your Deere does hold you at a baie.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Oh, oh Petruchio, Tranio hits you now.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I thanke thee for that gird good Tranio.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Confeſſe, confeſſe, hath he not hit you here?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: A has a little gald me I confeſſe:
And as the Ieſt did glaunce awaie from me,
'Tis ten to one it maim'd you too out right.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Now in good ſadneſſe ſonne Petruchio,
I thinke thou haſt the verieſt ſhrew of all.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Well, I ſay no: and therefore ſir aſſurance,
Let's each one ſend vnto his wife,
And he whoſe wife is moſt obedient,
To come at firſt when he doth ſend for her,
Shall win the wager which we will propoſe.

sp.speaker: Hort.
sp.p: Content, what's the wager?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Twentie crownes.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Twentie crownes,
Ile venture ſo much of my Hawke or Hound,
But twentie times ſo much vpon my Wife.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: A hundred then.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Content.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: A match, 'tis done.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Who ſhall begin?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: That will I.
Goe Biondello, bid your Miſtris come to me.

sp.speaker: Bio.
sp.p: Igoe.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Sonne, Ile be your halfe, Bianca comes.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Ile haue no halues: Ile beare it all my ſelfe.
How now, what newes?

sp.speaker: Bio.
sp.l: Sir, my Miſtris ſends you word
That ſhe is buſie, and ſhe cannot come.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: How? ſhe's buſie, and ſhe cannot come: is that an anſwere?

sp.speaker: Gre.
sp.l: I, and a kinde one too:
Praie God ſir your wife ſend you not a worſe.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: I hope better.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Sirra Biondello, goe and intreate my wife to come to me forthwith.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Oh ho, intreate her, nay then ſhee muſt needes come.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: I am affraid ſir, doe what you can
sp.l: Yours will not be entreated: Now, where's my wife?

sp.speaker: Bion.
sp.l: She ſaies you haue ſome goodly Ieſt in hand,
She will not come: ſhe bids you come to her.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Worſe and worſe, ſhe will not come:
Oh vilde, intollerable, not to be indur'd:
Sirra Grumio, goe to your Miſtris.
Say I command her come to me.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: I know her anſwere.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: She will not.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: The fouler fortune mine, and there an end.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.p: Now by my hollidam here comes Katerina.

sp.speaker: Kat.
sp.p: What is your will ſir, that you ſend for me?

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.p: Where is your ſiſter, and Hortenſios wife?

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.p: They ſit conferring by the Parler fire.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Goe fetch them hither, if they denie to come,
Swinge me them ſoundly forth vnto their husbands.
Away I ſay, and bring them hither ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Here is a wonder, if you talke of a wonder.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: And ſo it is: I wonder what it boads.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Marrie peace it boads, and loue, and quiet life,
An awfull rule, and right ſupremicie:
And to be ſhort, what not, that's ſweete and happie.

sp.speaker: Bap.
sp.l: Now faire befall thee good Petruchio;
The wager thou haſt won, and I will adde
Vnto their loſſes twentie thouſand crownes,
Another dowrie to another daughter,
For ſhe is chang'd as ſhe had neuer bin.

sp.speaker: Petr.
sp.l: Nay, I will win my wager better yet,
And ſhow more ſigne of her obedience,
Her new built vertue and obedience.
See where ſhe comes, and brings your froward Wiues
As priſoners to her womanlie perſwaſion:
Katerine, that Cap of yours becomes you not,
Off with that bable, throw it vnderfoote.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: Lord let me neuer haue a cauſe to ſigh,
Till I be brought to ſuch a ſillie paſſe.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Fie what a fooliſh dutie call you this?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: I would your dutie were as fooliſh too:
The wiſdome of your dutie faire Bianca,
Hath coſt me fiue hundred crownes ſince ſupper time.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: The more foole you for laying on my dutie.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Katherine I charge thee tell theſe head-ſtrong women, what dutie they doe owe their Lords and huſbands.

sp.speaker: Wid.
