sp.p: Come, come, your mocking: we will haue no telling.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Come on I ſay, and firſt begin with her.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: She ſhall not.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: I ſay ſhe ſhall, and firſt begin with her.

sp.speaker: Kate.
sp.l: Fie, fie, vnknit that thretaning vnkinde brow,
And dart not ſcornefull glances from thoſe eies,
To wound thy Lord, thy King, thy Gouernour.
It blots thy beautie, as froſts doe bite the Meads,
Confounds thy fame, as whirlewinds ſhake faire budds,
And in no ſence is meete or amiable.
A woman mou'd, is like a fountaine troubled,
Muddie, ill ſeeming, thicke, hereft of beautie,
And while it is ſo, none ſo dry or thirſtie
Will daigne to ſip, or touch one drop of it.
Thy husband is thy Lord, thy life, thy keeper,
Thy head, thy ſoueraigne: One that cares for thee,
And for thy maintenance. Commits his body
To painfull labour, both by ſea and land:
To watch the night in ſtormes, the day in cold,
Whil'ſt thou ly'ſt warme at home, ſecure and ſafe,
And craues no other tribute at thy hands,
But loue, faire lookes, and true obedience;
Too little payment for ſo great a debt.
Such dutie as the ſubiect owes the Prince,
Euen ſuch a woman oweth to her husband:
And when ſhe is froward, peeuiſh, ſullen, ſowre,
And not obedient to his honeſt will,
What is ſhe but a foule contending Rebell,
And graceleſſe Traitor to her louing Lord?
I am aſham'd that women are ſo ſimple,
To offer warre, where they ſhould kneele for peace:
Or ſeeke for rule, ſupremacie, and ſway,
When they are bound to ſerue, loue, and obay.
Why are our bodies ſoft, and weake, and ſmooth,
Vnapt to toyle and trouble in the world,
But that our ſoft conditions, and our harts,
Should well agree with our externall parts?
Come, come, you froward and vnable wormes,
My minde hath bin as bigge as one of yours,
My heart as great, my reaſon haplie more,
To bandie word for word, and frowne for frowne;
But now I ſee our Launces are but ſtrawes:
Our ſtrength as weake, our weakeneſſe paſt compare,
That ſeeming to be moſt, which we indeed leaſt are.
Then vale your ſtomackes, for it is no boote,
And place your hands below your husbands foote:
In token of which dutie, if he pleaſe,
My hand is readie, may it do him eaſe.

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.p: Why there's a wench: Come on, and kiſſe mee Kate.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Well go thy waies olde Lad for thou ſhalt ha't.

sp.speaker: Vin.
sp.p: Tis a good hearing, when children are toward.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: But a harſh hearing, when women are froward,

sp.speaker: Pet.
sp.l: Come Kate, weee'le to bed,
We three are married, but you two are ſped.
'Twas I wonne the wager, though you hit the white,
And being a winner, God giue you good night.

sp.speaker: Horten.
sp.p: Now goe thy wayes, thou haſt tam'd a curſt Shrow.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Tis a wonder, by your leaue, ſhe wil be tam'd ſo.

div.head: Scoena Prima.
div.stage: Enter yong Bertram Count of Roſſillion, his Mother, and Helena, Lord Lafew, all in blacke.

sp.speaker: Mother.
sp.p: IN deliuering my ſonne from me, I burie a ſecond husband.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: And I in going Madam, weep ore my fathers death anew; but I muſt attend his maieſties command, to whom I am now in Ward, euermore in ſubiection.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: You ſhall find of the King a husband Madame, you ſir a father. He that ſo generally is at all times good, muſt of neceſſitie hold his vertue to you, whoſe worthineſſe would ſtirre it vp where it wanted rather then lack it where there is ſuch abundance.

sp.speaker: Mo.
sp.p: What hope is there of his Maieſties amendment?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: He hath abandon'd his Phiſitions Madam, vnder whoſe practiſes he hath perſecuted time with hope, and finds no other aduantage in the proceſſe, but onely the looſing of hope by time.

sp.speaker: Mo.
sp.p: This yong Gentlewoman had a father, O that had, how ſad a paſſage tis, whoſe skill was almoſt as great as his honeſtie, had it ſtretch'd ſo far, would haue made nature immortall, and death ſhould haue play for lacke of worke. Would for the Kings ſake hee were liuing, I thinke it would be the death of the Kings diſeaſe.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: How call'd you the man you ſpeake of Madam?

sp.speaker: Mo.
sp.p: He was famous ſir in his profeſſion, and it was his great right to be ſo: Gerard de Narbon.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: He was excellent indeed Madam, the King very latelie ſpoke of him admiringly, and mourningly: hee was skilfull enough to haue liu'd ſtil, if knowledge could be ſet vp againſt mortallitie.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: What is it (my good Lord) the King languiſhes of?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: A Fiſtula my Lord.

sp.speaker: Roſ
sp.p: I heard not of it before.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I would it were not notorious. Was this Gentlewoman the Daughter of Gerard de Narbon?

sp.speaker: Mo.
sp.p: His ſole childe my Lord, and bequeathed to my ouer looking. I haue thoſe hopes of her good, that her education promiſes her diſpoſitions ſhee inherits, which makes faire gifts fairer: for where an vncleane mind carries vertuous qualities, there commendations go with pitty, they are vertues and traitors too: in her they are the better for their ſimpleneſſe; ſhe deriues her honeſtie, and atcheeues her goodneſſe.

sp.speaker: Lafew.
sp.p: Your commendations Madam get from her teares.

sp.speaker: Mo.
sp.p: 'Tis the beſt brine a Maiden can ſeaſon her praiſe in. The remembrance of her father neuer approches her heart, but the tirrany of her ſorrowes takes all liuelihood from her cheeke. No more of this Helena, go too, no more leaſt it be rather thought you affect a ſorrow, then to haue—

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.p: I doe affect a ſorrow indeed, but I haue it too.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Moderate lamentation is the right of the dead, exceſſiue greefe the enemie to the liuing.

sp.speaker: Mo.
sp.p: If the liuing be enemie to the greefe, the exceſſe makes it ſoone mortall.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: Maddam I deſire your holie wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: How vnderſtand we that?

sp.speaker: Mo.
sp.l: Be thou bleſt Bertrame, and ſucceed thy father
In manners as in ſhape: thy blood and vertue
Contend for Empire in thee, and thy goodneſſe
Share with thy birth-right. Loue all, truſt a few,
Doe wrong to none: be able for thine enemie
Rather in power then vſe: and keepe thy friend
Vnder thy owne lifes key. Be checkt for ſilence,
But neuer tax'd for ſpeech. What heauen more wil,
That thee may furniſh, and my prayers plucke downe,
Fall on thy head. Farwell my Lord,
'Tis an vnſeaſon'd Courtier, good my Lord
Aduiſe him.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.l: He cannot want the beſt
That ſhall attend his loue.

sp.speaker: Mo.
sp.p: Heauen bleſſe him: Farwell Bertram.

sp.speaker: Ro.
sp.p: The beſt wiſhes that can be forg'd in your thoghts be ſeruants to you: be comfortable to my mother, your Miſtris, and make much of her.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Farewell prettie Lady, you muſt hold the credit of your father.

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.l: O were that all, I thinke not on my father,
And theſe great teares grace his remembrance more
Then thoſe I ſhed for him. What was he like?
I haue forgott him. My imagination
Carries no fauour in't but Bertrams.
I am vndone, there is no liuing, none,
If Bertram be away. 'Twere all one,
That I ſhould loue a bright particuler ſtarre,
And think to wed it, he is ſo aboue me
In his bright radience and colaterall light,
Muſt I be comforted, not in his ſphere;
Th' ambition in my loue thus plagues it ſelfe:
The hind that would be mated by the Lion
Muſt die for loue. 'Twas prettie, though a plague
To ſee him euerie houre to ſit and draw
His arched browes, his hawking eie, his curles
In our hearts table: heart too capeable
Of euerie line and tricke of his ſweet fauour.
But now he's gone, and my idolatrous fancie
Muſt ſanctifie his Reliques. Who comes heere?
One that goes with him: I loue him for his ſake,
And yet I know him a notorious Liar,
Thinke him a great way foole, ſolie a coward,
Yet theſe fixt euils ſit ſo fit in him,
That they take place, when Vertues ſteely bones
Lookes bleake i' th cold wind: withall, full ofte we ſee
Cold wiſedome waighting on ſuperfluous follie.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Saue you faire Queene.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: And you Monarch.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: And no.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Are you meditating on virginitie?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: If you haue ſome ſtaine of ſouldier in you: Let mee aske you a queſtion. Man is enemie to virginitie, how may we barracado it againſt him?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Keepe him out.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: But he aſſailes, and our virginitie though valiant, in the defence yet is weak: vnfold to vs ſome warlike reſiſtance.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: There is none: Man ſetting downe before you, will vndermine you, and blow you vp.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Bleſſe our poore Virginity from vnderminers and blowers vp. Is there no Military policy how Virgins might blow vp men?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Virginity beeing blowne downe, Man will quicklier be blowne vp: marry in blowing him downe againe, with the breach your ſelues made, you loſe your Citty. It is not politicke, in the Common-wealth of Nature, to preſerue virginity. Loſſe of Virginitie, is rationall encreaſe, and there was neuer Virgin goe, till virginitie was firſt loſt. That you were made of, is mettall to make Virgins. Virginitie, by beeing once loſt, may be ten times found: by being euer kept, it is euer loſt: 'tis too cold a companion: Away with't.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I will ſtand for't a little, though therefore I die a Virgin.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: There's little can bee ſaide in't, 'tis againſt the rule of Nature. To ſpeake on the part of virginitie, is to accuſe your Mothers; which is moſt infallible diſobedience. He that hangs himſelfe is a Virgin: Virginitie murthers it ſelfe, and ſhould be buried in highwayes out of all ſanctified limit, as a deſperate Offendreſſe againſt Nature. Virginitie breedes mites, much like a Cheeſe, conſumes it ſelfe to the very payring, and ſo dies with feeding his owne ſtomacke. Beſides, Virginitie is peeuiſh, proud, ydle, made of ſelfe-loue, which is the moſt inhibited ſinne in the Cannon. Keepe it not, you cannot chooſe but looſe by't. Out with't: within ten yeare it will make it ſelfe two, which is a goodly increaſe, and the principall it ſelfe not much the worſe. Away with't.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: How might one do ſir, to looſe it to her owne liking?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Let mee ſee. Marry ill, to like him that ne're it likes. 'Tis a commodity wil loſe the gloſſe with lying: The longer kept, the leſſe worth: Off with't while 'tis vendible. Anſwer the time of requeſt, Virginitie like an olde Courtier, weares her cap out of faſhion, richly ſuted, but vnſuteable, iuſt like the brooch & the toothpick, which were not now: your Date is better in your Pye and your Porredge, then in your cheeke: and your virginity, your old virginity, is like one of our French wither'd peares, it lookes ill, it eates drily, marry 'tis a wither'd peare: it was formerly better, marry yet 'tis a wither'd peare: Will you any thing with it?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Not my virginity yet:
There ſhall your Maſter haue a thouſand loues,
A Mother, and a Miſtreſſe, and a friend,
A Phenix, Captaine, and an enemy▪
A guide, a Goddeſſe, and a Soueraigne,
A Counſellor, a Traitoreſſe, and a Deare:
His humble ambition, proud humility:
His iarring, concord: and his diſcord, dulcet:
His faith, his ſweet diſaſter: with a world
Of pretty fond adoptious chriſtendomes
That blinking Cupid goſſips. Now ſhall he:
I know not what he ſhall, God ſend him well,
The Courts a learning place, and he is one.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: What one ifaith?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: That I wiſh well, 'tis pitty.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: What's pitty?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: That wiſhing well had not a body in't,
Which might be felt, that we the poorer borne,
Whoſe baſer ſtarres do ſhut vs vp in wiſhes,
Might vvith effects of them follow our friends,
And ſhew what vve alone muſt thinke, which neuer
Returnes vs thankes.

sp.speaker: Pag.
sp.l: Monſieur Parrolles,
My Lord cals for you.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Little Hellen farewell, if I can remember thee, I will thinke of thee at Court.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Monſieur Parolles, you were borne vnder a charitable ſtarre.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Vnder Mars I.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I eſpecially thinke, vnder Mars.

sp.speaker: Par
sp.p: Why vnder Mars?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: The warres hath ſo kept you vnder, that you muſt needes be borne vnder Mars.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: When he was predominant.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: When he was retrograde I thinke rather.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why thinke you ſo?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: You go ſo much backward when you fight.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: That's for aduantage.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: So is running away,
When feare propoſes the ſafetie:
sp.p: But the compoſition that your valour and feare makes in you, is a vertue of a good wing, and I like the weare well.

sp.speaker: Paroll.
sp.p:
I am ſo full of buſineſſes, I cannot anſwere thee acutely: I will returne perfect Courtier, in the which my inſtruction ſhall ſerue to naturalize thee, ſo thou wilt be capeable of a Courtiers councell, and vnderſtand what aduice ſhall thruſt vppon thee, elſe thou dieſt in thine vnthankfulnes, and thine ignorance makes thee away, farewell: When thou haſt leyſure, ſay thy praiers: when thou haſt none, remember thy Friends:
Get thee a good husband, and vſe him as he vſes thee: So farewell.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Our remedies oft in our ſelues do lye,
Which we aſcribe to heauen: the fated skye
Giues vs free ſcope, onely doth backward pull
Our ſlow deſignes, when we our ſelues are dull.
What power is it, which mounts my loue ſo hye,
That makes me ſee, and cannot feede mine eye?
The mightieſt ſpace in fortune, Nature brings
To ioyne like, likes; and kiſſe like natiue things.
Impoſſible be ſtrange attempts to thoſe
That weigh their paines in ſence, and do ſuppoſe
What hath beene, cannot be. Who euer ſtroue
To ſhew her merit, that did miſſe her loue?
(The Kings diſeaſe) my proiect may deceiue me,
But my intents are fixt, and will not leaue me.

div.stage: Enter the King of France with Letters, and diuers Attendants.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: The Florentines and Senoys are by th' eares,
Haue fought with equall fortune, and continue
A brauing warre.

sp.speaker: 1. Lo. G.
sp.p: So tis reported ſir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Nay tis moſt credible, we heere receiue it,
A certaintie vouch'd from our Coſin Auſtria,
With caution, that the Florentine will moue vs
For ſpeedie ayde: wherein our deereſt friend
Preiudicates the buſineſſe, and would ſeeme
To haue vs make deniall.

sp.speaker: 1. Lo. G.
sp.l: His loue and wiſedome
Approu'd ſo to your Maieſty, may pleade
For ampleſt credence.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: He hath arm'd our anſwer,
And Florence is deni'de before he comes:
Yet for our Gentlemen that meane to ſee
The Tuſcan ſeruice, freely haue they leaue
To ſtand on either part.

sp.speaker: 2. Lo. E.
sp.l: It well may ſerue
A nurſſerie to our Gentrie, who are ſicke
For breathing, and exploit.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: What's he comes heere.

sp.speaker: 1. Lor. G.
sp.l: It is the Count Roſignoll my good Lord,
Yong Bertram.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Youth, thou bear'ſt thy Fathers face,
Franke Nature rather curious then in haſt
Hath well compos'd thee: Thy Fathers morall parts
Maiſt thou inherit too: Welcome to Paris.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: My thankes and dutie are your Maieſties.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: I would I had that corporall ſoundneſſe now,
As when thy father, and my ſelfe, in friendſhip
Firſt tride out ſouldierſhip: he did looke farre
Into the ſeruice of the time, and was
Diſcipled of the braueſt. He laſted long,
But on vs both did haggiſh Age ſteale on,
And wore vs out of act: It much repaires me
To talke of your good father; in his youth
He had the wit, which I can well obſerue
To day in our yong Lords: but they may ieſt
Till their owne ſcorne returne to them vnnoted
Ere they can hide their leuitie in honour:
So like a Courtier, contempt nor bitterneſſe
Were in his pride, or ſharpneſſe; if they were,
His equall had awak'd them, and his honour
Clocke to it ſelfe, knew the true minute when
Exception bid him ſpeake: and at this time
His tongue obey d his hand. Who were below him,
He vs'd as creatures of another place,
And bow'd his eminent top to their low rankes,
Making them proud of his humilitie,
In their poore praiſe he humbled: Such a man
Might be a copie to theſe yonger times;
Which followed well, would demonſtrate them now
But goers backward.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: His good remembrance ſir
Lies richer in your thoughts, then on his tombe:
So in approofe liues not his Epitaph,
As in your royall ſpeech.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Would I were with him he would alwaies ſay,
(Me thinkes I heare him now) his plauſiue words
He ſcatter'd not in eares, but grafted them
To grow there and to beare: Let me not liue,
This his good melancholly oft began
On the Cataſtrophe and heele of paſtime
When it was out: Let me not liue (quoth hee)
After my flame lackes oyle, to be the ſnuffe
Of yonger ſpirits, whoſe apprehenſiue ſenſes
All but new things diſdaine; whoſe iudgements are
Meere fathers of their garments: whoſe conſtancies
Expire before their faſhions: this he wiſh'd.
I after him, do after him wiſh too:
Since I nor wax nor honie can bring home,
I quickly were diſſolued from my hiue
To giue ſome Labourers roome.

sp.speaker: L. 2. E.
sp.l: You'r loued Sir,
They that leaſt lend it you, ſhall lacke you firſt.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: I fill a place I know't: how long iſt Count
Since the Phyſitian at your fathers died?
He was much fam'd.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Some ſix moneths ſince my Lord.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: If he were liuing, I would try him yet.
Lend me an arme: the reſt haue worne me out
With ſeuerall applications: Nature and ſickneſſe
Debate it at their leiſure. Welcome Count,
My ſonne's no deerer.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Thanke your Maieſty.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.p: I will now heare, what ſay you of this gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Maddam the care I haue had to euen your content, I wiſh might be found in the Kalender of my paſt endeuours, for then we wound our Modeſtie, and make foule the clearneſſe of our deſeruings, whenof our ſelues we publiſh them.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.p: What doe's this knaue heere? Get you gone ſirra: the complaints I haue heard of you I do not all beleeue, 'tis my ſlowneſſe that I doe not: For I know you lacke not folly to commit them, & haue abilitie enough to make ſuch knaueries yours.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: 'Tis not vnknown to you Madam, I am a poore fellow.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.p: Well ſir.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: No maddam,

'Tis not ſo well that I am poore, though manie
of the rich are damn'd, but if I may haue your Ladiſhips good will to goe to the world, Isbell the woman and w will doe as we may.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.p: Wilt thou needes be a begger?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I doe beg your good will in this caſe.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: In what caſe?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: In Isbels caſe and mine owne: ſeruice is no heritage, and I thinke I ſhall neuer haue the bleſſing of God, till I haue iſſue a my bodie: for they ſay barnes are bleſſings.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Tell me thy reaſon why thou wilt marrie?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: My poore bodie Madam requires it, I am driuen onby the fleſh, and hee muſt needes goe that the diuell driues.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Is this all your worſhips reaſon?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Faith Madam I haue other holie reaſons, ſuch as they are.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: May the world know them?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I haue beene Madam a wicked creature, as you and all fleſh and blood are, and indeede I doe marrie that I may repent.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Thy marriage ſooner then thy wickedneſſe.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I am out a friends Madam, and I hope to haue friends for my wiues ſake.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Such friends are thine enemies knaue.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Y' are ſhallow Madam in great friends, for the knaues come to doe that for me which I am a wearie of: he that eres my Land, ſpares my teame, and giues mee leaue to Inne the crop: if I be his cuckold hee's my drudge; he that comforts my wife, is the cheriſher of my fleſh and blood; hee that cheriſhes my fleſh and blood, loues my fleſh and blood; he that loues my fleſh and blood is my friend: ergo, he that kiſſes my wife is my friend: if men could be contented to be what they are, there were no feare in marriage, for yong Charbon the Puritan, and old Poyſam the Papiſt, how ſomere their hearts are ſeuer'd in Religion, their heads are both one, they may ioule horns together like any Deare i' th Herd.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Wilt thou euer be a foule mouth'd and calumnious knaue?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: A Prophet I Madam, and I ſpeake the truth the next waie, for I the Ballad will repeate, which men full true ſhall finde, your marriage comes by deſtinie, your Cuckow ſings by kinde.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Get you gone ſir, Ile talke with you more anon.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: May it pleaſe you Madam, that hee bid Hellen come to you, of her I am to ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Sirra tell my gentlewoman I would ſpeake with her, Hellen I meane.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Was this faire face the cauſe, quoth ſhe,
Why the Grecians ſacked Troy,
Fond done, done, fond was this King Priams ioy,
With that ſhe ſighed as ſhe ſtood, bis
sp.p: And gaue this ſentence then, among nine bad if one be good, among nine bad if one be good, there's yet one good in ten.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: What, one good in tenne? you corrupt the ſong ſirra.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: One good woman in ten Madam, which is a purifying ath' ſong: would God would ſerue the world ſo all the yeere, weed finde no fault with the tithe woman if I were the Parſon, one in ten quoth a? and wee might haue a good woman borne but ore euerie blazing ſtarre, or at an earthquake, 'twould mend the Lotterie well, a man may draw his heart out ere a plucke one.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Youle begone ſir knaue▪ and doe as I command you?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: That man ſhould be at womans command, and yet no hurt done, though honeſtie be no Puritan, yet it will doe no hurt, it will weare the Surplis of humilitie ouer the blacke-Gowne of a bigge heart: I am going forſooth, the buſineſſe is for Helen to come hither.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Well now.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: I know Madam you loue your Gentlewoman intirely.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Faith I doe: her Father bequeath'd her to mee, and ſhe her ſelfe without other aduantage, may lawfullie make title to as much loue as ſhee findes, there is more owing her then is paid, and more ſhall be paid her then ſheele demand.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Madam, I was verie late more neere her then I thinke ſhee wiſht mee, alone ſhee was, and did communicate to her ſelfe her owne words to her owne eares, ſhee thought, I dare vowe for her, they toucht not anie ſtranger ſence, her matter was, ſhee loued your Sonne; Fortune ſhee ſaid was no goddeſſe, that had put ſuch difference betwixt their two eſtates: Loue no god, that would not extend his might onelie, where qualities were leuell, Queene of Virgins, that would ſuffer her poore Knight ſurpris'd without reſcue in the firſt aſſault or ranſome afterward: This ſhee deliuer'd in the moſt bitter touch of ſorrow that ere I heard Virgin exclaime in, which I held my dutie ſpeedily to acquaint you withall, ſithence in the loſſe that may happen, it concernes you ſomething to know it.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: You haue diſcharg'd this honeſtlie, keepe it to your ſelfe, manie likelihoods inform'd mee of this before, which hung ſo tottring in the ballance, that I could neither beleeue nor miſdoubt: praie you leaue mee, ſtall this in your boſome, and I thanke you for your honeſt care: I will ſpeake with you further anon.

sp.speaker: Old. Cou.
sp.l: Euen ſo it vvas vvith me when I was yong:
If euer vve are natures, theſe are ours, this thorne
Doth to our Roſe of youth righlie belong
Our bloud to vs, this to our blood is borne,
It is the ſhow, and ſeale of natures truth,
Where loues ſtrong paſſion is impreſt in youth,
By our remembrances of daies forgon,
Such were our faults, or then we thought them none,
Her eie is ſicke on't, I obſerue her now.

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.p: What is your pleaſure Madam?

sp.speaker: Ol. Cou.
sp.p: You know Hellen I am a mother to you.

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.p: Mine honorable Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Ol. Cou.
sp.l: Nay a mother, why not a mother? when I ſed a mother
Me thought you ſaw a ſerpent, what's in mother,
That you ſtart at it? I ſay I am your mother,
And put you in the Catalogue of thoſe
That were enwombed mine, 'tis often ſeene
Adoption ſtriues vvith nature, and choiſe breedes
A natiue ſlip to vs from forraine ſeedes:
You nere oppreſt me with a mothers groane,
Yet I expreſſe to you a mothers care,
(Gods mercie maiden) dos it curd thy blood
To ſay I am thy mother? vvhat's the matter,
That this diſtempered meſſenger of wet?
The manie colour'd Iris rounds thine eye?
—Why, that you are my daughter?

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.p: That I am not.

sp.speaker: Old. Cou.
sp.p: I ſay I am your Mother.

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.l: Pardon Madam.
The Count Roſillion cannot be my brother:
I am from humble, he from honored name:
No note vpon my Parents, his all noble,
My Maſter, my deere Lord he is, and I
His ſeruant liue, and will his vaſſall die:
He muſt not be my brother.

sp.speaker: Ol. Cou.
sp.p: Nor I your Mother.

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.l: You are my mother Madam, would you were
So that my Lord your ſonne were not my brother,
Indeede my mother, or were you both our mothers,
I care no more for, then I doe for heauen,
So I were not his ſiſter, cant no other,
But I your daughter, he muſt be my brother.

sp.speaker: Old. Cou.
sp.l: Yes Hellen, you might be my daughter in law,
God ſhield you meane it not, daughter and mother
So ſtriue vpon your pulſe; vvhat pale agen?
My feare hath catcht your fondneſſe! now I ſee
The miſtrie of your louelineſſe, and finde
Your ſalt teares head, now to all ſence 'tis groſſe:
You loue my ſonne, inuention is aſham'd
Againſt the proclamation of thy paſſion
To ſay thou dooſt not: therefore tell me true,
But tell me then 'tis ſo, for looke, thy cheekes
Confeſſe it 'ton tooth to th' other, and thine eies
See it ſo groſely ſhowne in thy behauiours,
That in their kinde they ſpeake it, onely ſinne
And helliſh obſtinacie tye thy tongue
That truth ſhould be ſuſpected, ſpeake, iſt ſo?
If it be ſo, you haue wound a goodly clewe:
If it be not, forſweare't how ere I charge thee,
As heauen ſhall worke in me for thine auaile
To tell me truelie.

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.p: Good Madam pardon me.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Do you loue my Sonne?

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.p: Your pardon noble Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Loue you my Sonne?

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.p: Doe not you loue him Madam?

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.l: Goe not about; my loue hath in't a bond
Whereof the world takes note: Come, come, diſcloſe:
The ſtate of your affection, for your paſſions
Haue to the full appeach'd.

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.l: Then I confeſſe
Here on my knee, before high heauen and you,
That before you, and next vnto high heauen, I loue your Sonne:
My friends were poore but honeſt, ſo's my loue:
Be not offended, for it hurts not him
That he is lou'd of me; I follow him not
By any token of preſumptuous ſuite,
Nor would I haue him, till I doe deſerue him,
Yet neuer know how that deſert ſhould be:
I know I loue in vaine, ſtriue againſt hope:
Yet in this captious, and intemible Siue.
I ſtill poure in the waters of my loue
And lacke not to looſe ſtill; thus Indian like
Religious in mine error, I adore
The Sunne that lookes vpon his worſhipper,
But knowes of him no more. My deereſt Madam,
Let not your hate incounter with my loue,
For louing where you doe; but if your ſelfe,
Whoſe aged honor cites a vertuous youth,
Did euer, in ſo true a flame of liking,
Wiſh chaſtly, and loue dearely, that your Dian
Was both her ſelfe and loue, O then giue pittie
To her whoſe ſtate is ſuch, that cannot chooſe
But lend and giue where ſhe is ſure to looſe;
That ſeekes not to finde that, her ſearch implies,
But riddle like, liues ſweetely where ſhe dies.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.l: Had you not lately an intent, ſpeake truely,
To goe to Paris?

sp.speaker: Hell
sp.p: Madam I had.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Wherefore? tell true.

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.l: I will tell truth▪ by grace it ſelfe I ſweare:
You know my Father left me ſome preſcriptions
Of rare and prou'd effects, ſuch as his reading
And manifeſt experience, had collected
For generall ſoueraigntie: and that he wil'd me
In heedefull'ſt reſeruation to beſtow them,
As notes, whoſe faculties incluſiue were,
More then they were in note: Amongſt the reſt,
There is a remedie, approu'd, ſet downe,
To cure the deſperate languiſhings whereof
The King is render'd loſt.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: This was your motiue for Paris, was it, ſpeake?

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.l: My Lord, your ſonne, made me to think of this;
Elſe Paris, and the medicine, and the King,
Had from the conuerſation of my thoughts,
Happily beene abſent then.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.l: But thinke you Hellen,
If you ſhould tender your ſuppoſed aide,
He would receiue it? He and his Phiſitions
Are of a minde, he, that they cannot helpe him:
They, that they cannot helpe, how ſhall they credit
A poore vnlearned Virgin, when the Schooles
Embowel'd of their doctrine, haue left off
The danger to it ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.l: There's ſomething in't
More then my Fathers skill, which was the great'ſt
Of his profeſſion, that his good receipt,
Shall for my legacie be ſanctified
By th' luckieſt ſtars in heauen, and would your honor
But giue me leaue to trie ſucceſſe, I'de venture
The well loſt life of mine, on his Graces cure,
By ſuch a day, an houre.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.p: Doo'ſt thou beleeue't?

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.p: I Madam knowingly.

sp.speaker: Cou.
sp.l: Why Hellen thou ſhalt haue my leaue and loue,
Meanes and attendants, and my louing greetings
To thoſe of mine in Court, Ile ſtaie at home
And praie Gods bleſſing into thy attempt:
Begon to morrow, and be ſure of this,
What I can helpe thee to, thou ſhalt not miſſe.

div.head: Actus Secundus.
div.stage: Enter the King with diuers yong Lords, taking leaue for the Florentine warre: Count, Roſſe, and Parrolles, Floriſh Cornets.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Farewell yong Lords, theſe warlike principles
Doe not throw from you, and you my Lords farewell:
Share the aduice betwixt you, if both gaine, all
The guift doth ſtretch it ſelfe as 'tis receiu'd,
And is enough for both.

sp.speaker: Lord. G.
sp.l: 'Tis our hope ſir,
After well entred ſouldiers, to returne
And finde your grace in health.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: No, no, it cannot be; and yet my heart
Will not confeſſe he owes the mallady
That doth my life beſiege: farwell yong Lords,
Whether I liue or die, be you the ſonnes
Of worthy French men: let higher Italy
(Thoſe bated that inherit but the fall
Of the laſt Monarchy) ſee that you come
Not to wooe honour, but to wed it, when
The braueſt queſtant ſhrinkes: finde what you ſeeke,
That fame may cry you loud: I ſay farewell.

sp.speaker: L.G.
sp.p: Health at your bidding ſerue your Maieſty.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Thoſe girles of Italy, take heed of them,
They ſay our French, lacke language to deny
If they demand: beware of being Captiues
Before you ſerue.

sp.speaker: Bo.
sp.p: Our hearts receiue your warnings.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Farewell, come hether to me.

sp.speaker: 1. Lo. G.
sp.p: Oh my ſweet Lord yt you wil ſtay behind vs.

sp.speaker: Parr.
sp.p: 'Tis not his fault the ſpark.

sp.speaker: 2. Lo. E.
sp.p: Oh 'tis braue warres.

sp.speaker: Parr.
sp.p: Moſt admirable, I haue ſeene thoſe warres.

sp.speaker: Roſſill.
sp.l: I am commanded here, and kept a coyle with,
Too young, and the next yeere, and 'tis too early.

sp.speaker: Parr.
sp.l: And thy minde ſtand too't boy,
Steale away brauely.

sp.speaker: Roſſill.
sp.l: I ſhal ſtay here the for-horſe to a ſmocke,
Creeking my ſhooes on the plaine Maſonry,
Till honour be bought vp, and no ſword worne
But one to dance with: by heauen, Ile ſteale away.

sp.speaker: 1. Lo. G.
sp.p: There's honour in the theft.

sp.speaker: Parr.
sp.p: Commit it Count.

sp.speaker: 2. Lo. E.
sp.p: I am your acceſſary, and ſo farewell.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: I grow to you, & our parting is a tortur'd body.

sp.speaker: 1. Lo. G.
sp.p: Farewll Captaine.

sp.speaker: 2. Lo. E.
sp.p: Sweet Mounſier Parolles.

sp.speaker: Parr.
sp.p: Noble Heroes; my ſword and yours are kinne, good ſparkes and luſtrous, a word good mettals. You ſhall finde in the Regiment of the Spinij, one Captaine Spurio his ſicatrice, with an Embleme of warre heere on his ſiniſter cheeke; it was this very ſword entrench'd it: ſay to him I liue, and obſerue his reports for me.

sp.speaker: Lo. G.
sp.p: We ſhall noble Captaine.

sp.speaker: Parr.
sp.p: Mars doate on you for his nouices, what will ye doe?

sp.speaker: Roſſ.
sp.p: Stay the King.

sp.speaker: Parr.
sp.p: Vſe a more ſpacious ceremonie to the Noble Lords, you haue reſtrain'd your ſelfe within the Liſt of too cold an adieu: be more expreſſiue to them; for they weare themſelues in the cap of the time, there do muſter true gate; eat, ſpeake, and moue vnder the influence of the moſt receiu'd ſtarre, and though the deuill leade the meaſure, ſuch are to be followed: after them, and take a more dilated farewell.

sp.speaker: Roſſ.
sp.p: And I will doe ſo.

sp.speaker: Parr.
sp.p: Worthy fellowes, and like to prooue moſt ſinewie ſword-men.

sp.speaker: L. Laf.
sp.p: Pardon my Lord for mee and for my tidings.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Ile ſee thee to ſtand vp.

sp.speaker: L. Laf.
sp.l: Then heres a man ſtands that has brought his pardon,
I would you had kneel'd my Lord to aske me mercy,
And that at my bidding you could ſo ſtand vp.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I would I had, ſo I had broke thy pate
And askt thee mercy for't.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.l: Good faith a-croſſe, but my good Lord 'tis thus,
Will you be cur'd of your infirmitie?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.l: O will you eat no grapes my royall foxe?
Yes but you will, my noble grapes, and if
My royall foxe could reach them: I haue ſeen a medicine
That's able to breath life into a ſtone,
Quicken a rocke, and make you dance Canari
With ſprightly fire and motion, whoſe ſimple touch
Is powerfull to arayſe King Pippen, nay
To giue great Charlemaine a pen in's hand
And write to her a loue-line.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: What her is this?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.l: Why doctor ſhe: my Lord, there's one arriu'd,
If you will ſee her: now by my faith and honour,
If ſeriouſly I may conuay my thoughts
In this my light deliuerance, I haue ſpoke
With one, that in her ſexe, her yeeres, profeſſion,
Wiſedome and conſtancy, hath amaz'd mee more
Then I dare blame my weakeneſſe: will you ſee her?
For that is her demand, and know her buſineſſe?
That done, laugh well at me.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Now good Lafew,
Bring in the admiration, that we with thee
May ſpend our wonder too, or take off thine
By wondring how thou tookſt it.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.l: Nay, Ile fit you,
And not be all day neither.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Thus he his ſpeciall nothing euer prologues.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Nay, come your waies.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: This haſte hath wings indeed.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.l: Nay, come your waies,
This is his Maieſtie, ſay your minde to him,
A Traitor you doe looke like, but ſuch traitors
His Maieſty ſeldome feares, I am Creſſeds Vncle,
That dare leaue two together, far you well.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Now faire one, do's your buſines follow vs?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: I my good Lord,
Gerard de Narbon was my father,
In what he did profeſſe, well found.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: I knew him.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: The rather will I ſpare my praiſes towards him,
Knowing him is enough on's bed of death,
Many receits he gaue me, chieflie one,
Which as the deareſt iſſue of his practice
And of his olde experience, th' onlie darling,
He bad me ſtore vp, as a triple eye,
Safer then mine owne two: more deare I haue ſo,
And hearing your high Maieſtie is toucht
With that malignant cauſe, wherein the honour
Of my deare fathers gift, ſtands cheefe in power,
I come to tender it, and my appliance,
With all bound humbleneſſe.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: We thanke you maiden,
But may not be ſo credulous of cure,
When our moſt learned Doctors leaue vs, and
The congregated Colledge haue concluded,
That labouring Art can neuer ranſome nature
From her inaydible eſtate: I ſay we muſt not
So ſtaine our iudgement, or corrupt our hope,
To proſtitute our paſt-cure malladie
To empericks, or to diſſeuer ſo
Our great ſelfe and our credit, to eſteeme
A ſenceleſſe helpe, when helpe paſt ſence we deeme.

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.l: My dutie then ſhall pay me for my paines:
I will no more enforce mine office on you,
Humbly intreating from your royall thoughts,
A modeſt one to beare me backe againe.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I cannot giue thee leſſe to be cal'd gratefull:
Thou thoughtſt to helpe me, and ſuch thankes I giue,
As one neere death to thoſe that wiſh him liue:
But what at full I know, thou knowſt no part,
I knowing all my perill, thou no Art.

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.l: What I can doe, can doe no hurt to try,
Since you ſet vp your reſt 'gainſt remedie:
He that of greateſt workes is finiſher,
Oft does them by the weakeſt miniſter:
So holy Writ, in babes hath iudgement ſhowne,
When Iudges haue bin babes; great flouds haue flowne
From ſimple ſources: and great Seas haue dried
When Miracles haue by the great'ſt beene denied.
Oft expectation failes, and moſt oft there
Where moſt it promiſes: and oft it hits,
Where hope is coldeſt, and deſpaire moſt ſhifts.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I muſt not heare thee, fare thee wel kind maide,
Thy paines not vs'd, muſt by thy ſelfe be paid,
Proffers not tooke, reape thanks for their reward.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Inſpired Merit ſo by breath is bard,
It is not ſo with him that all things knowes
As 'tis with vs, that ſquare our gueſſe by ſhowes:
But moſt it is preſumption in vs, when
The help of heauen we count the act of men.
Deare ſir, to my endeauors giue conſent,
Of heauen, not me, make an experiment.
I am not an Impoſtrue, that proclaime
My ſelfe againſt the leuill of mine aime,
But know I thinke, and thinke I know moſt ſure,
My Art is not paſt power, nor you paſt cure.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Art thou ſo confident? Within what ſpace
Hop'ſt thou my cure?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: The greateſt grace lending grace,
Ere twice the horſes of the ſunne ſhall bring
Their fiery torcher his diurnall ring,
Ere twice in murke and occidentall dampe
Moiſt Heſperus, hath quench'd her ſleepy Lampe:
Or foure and twenty times the Pylots glaſſe
Hath told the theeuiſh minutes, how they paſſe:
What is infirme, from your ſound parts ſhall flie,
Health ſhall liue free, and ſickeneſſe freely dye.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Vpon thy certainty and confidence,
What dar'ſt thou venter?

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.l: Taxe of impudence,
A ſtrumpets boldneſſe, a divulged ſhame
Traduc'd by odious ballads: my maidens name
Seard otherwiſe, ne worſe of worſt extended
With vildeſt torture, let my life be ended.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Methinks in thee ſome bleſſed ſpirit doth ſpeak
His powerfull ſound, within an organ weake:
And what impoſſibility would ſlay
In common ſence, ſence ſaues another way:
Thy life is deere, for all that life can rate
Worth name of life, in thee hath eſtimate:
Youth, beauty, wiſedome, courage, all
That happines and prime, can happy call:
Thou this to hazard, needs muſt intimate
Skill infinite, or monſtrous deſperate,
Sweet practiſer, thy Phyſicke I will try,
That miniſters thine owne death if I die.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: If I breake time, or flinch in property
Of what I ſpoke, vnpittied let me die,
And well deſeru'd: not helping, death's my ſee,
But if I helpe, what doe you promiſe me.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Make thy demand.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: But will you make it euen?

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: I by my Scepter, and my hopes of helpe.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Then ſhalt thou giue me with thy kingly hand
What husband in thy power I will command:
Exempted be from me the arrogance
To chooſe from forth the royall bloud of France,
My low and humble name to propagate
With any branch or image of thy ſtate:
But ſuch a one thy vaſſall, whom I know
Is free for me to aske, thee to beſtow.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Heere is my hand, the premiſes obſeru'd,
Thy will by my performance ſhall be ſeru'd:
So make the choice of thy owne time, for I
Thy reſolv'd Patient, on thee ſtill relye:
More ſhould I queſtion thee, and more I muſt,
Though more to know, could not be more to truſt:
From whence thou can'ſt, how tended on, but reſt
Vnqueſtion'd welcome, and vndoubted bleſt.
Giue me ſome helpe heere hoa, if thou proceed,
As high as word, my deed ſhall match thy deed.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Come on ſir, I ſhall now put you to the height of your breeding.

sp.speaker: Clown.
sp.p: I will ſhew my ſelfe highly fed, and lowly taught, I know my buſineſſe is but to the Court.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: To the Court, why what place make you ſpeciall, when you put off that with ſuch contempt, but to the Court?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Truly Madam, if God haue lent a man any manners, hee may eaſilie put it off at Court: hee that cannot make a legge, put off's cap, kiſſe his hand, and ſay nothing, has neither legge, hands, lippe, nor cap; and indeed ſuch a fellow, to ſay preciſely, were not for the Court, But for me, I haue an anſwere will ſerue all men.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Marry that's a bountifull anſwere that fits all queſtions.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: It is like a Barbers chaire that fits all buttockes, the pin buttocke, the quatch-buttocke, the brawn buttocke, or any buttocke.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Will your anſwere ſerue fit to all queſtions?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: As fit as ten groats is for the hand of an Atturney, as your French Crowne for your taffety punke, as Tibs ruſh for Toms fore-finger, as a pancake for Shroue-tueſday, a Morris for May-day, as the naile to his hole, the Cuckold to his horne, as a ſcolding queane to a wrangling knaue, as the Nuns lip to the Friers mouth, nay as the pudding to his skin.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: Haue you, I ſay, an anſwere of ſuch fitneſſe for all queſtions?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: From below your Duke, to beneath your Conſtable, it will fit any queſtion.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: It muſt be an anſwere of moſt monſtrous ſize, that muſt fit all demands.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: But a triflle neither in good faith, if the learned ſhould ſpeake truth of it: heere it is, and all that belongs to't. Aske mee if I am a Courtier, it ſhall doe you no harme to learne.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: To be young againe if we could: I will bee a foole in queſtion, hoping to bee the wiſer by your anſwer.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: I pray you ſir, are you a Courtier?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O Lord ſir theres a ſimple putting off: more, more, a hundred of them.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Sir I am a poore freind of yours, that loues you.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O Lord ſir, thicke, thicke, ſpare not me.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: I thinke ſir, you can eate none of this homely meate.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O Lord ſir; nay put me too't, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: You were lately whipt ſir as I thinke.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O Lord ſir, ſpare not me.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Doe you crie O Lord ſir at your whipping, and ſpare not me? Indeed your O Lord ſir, is very ſequent to your whipping: you would anſwere very well to a whipping if you were but bound too't.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I nere had worſe lucke in my life in my O Lord ſir: I ſee things may ſerue long, but not ſerue euer.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: I play the noble huſwife with the time, to entertaine it ſo merrily with a foole.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O Lord ſir, why there't ſerues well agen.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: And end ſir to your buſineſſe: giue Hellen this,
And vrge her to a preſent anſwer backe,
Commend me to my kinſmen, and my ſonne,
This is not much.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Not much commendation to them.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Not much imployement for you, you vnderſtand me.

sp.speaker: Clo
sp.p: Moſt fruitfully, I am there, before my legegs.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Haſt you agen.

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: They ſay miracles are paſt, and we haue our Philoſophicall perſons, to make moderne and familiar things ſupernaturall and cauſeleſſe. Hence is it, that we make trifles of terrours, enſconcing our ſelues into ſeeming knowledge, when we ſhould ſubmit our ſelues to an vnknowne feare.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why 'tis the rareſt argument of wonder, that hath ſhot out in our latter times.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: And ſo 'tis.

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: To be relinquiſht of the Artiſts.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: So I ſay both of Galen and Paracelſus.

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: Of all the learned and authenticke fellowes.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Right ſo I ſay.

sp.speaker: Ol Laf.
sp.p: That gaue him out incureable.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why there 'tis, ſo ſay I too.

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: Not to be help'd.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Right, as 'twere a man aſſur'd of a—

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: Vncertaine life, and ſure death.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Iuſt, you ſay well: ſo would I haue ſaid.

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: I may truly ſay, it is a noueltie to the world.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: It is indeede if you will haue it in ſhewing, you ſhall reade it in what do ye call there.

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: A ſhewing of a heauenly effect in an earthly Actor.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: That's it, I would haue ſaid, the verie ſame.

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.l: Why your Dolphin is not luſtier: fore mee
I ſpeake in reſpect—

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Nay 'tis ſtrange, 'tis very ſtraunge, that is the breefe and the tedious of it, and he's of a moſt facinerious ſpirit, that will not acknowledge it to be the—

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: Very hand of heauen.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I, ſo I ſay.

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: In a moſt weake—

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: And debile miniſter great power, grear trancendence, which ſhould indeede giue vs a further vſe to be made, then alone then recou'ry of the king, as to bee

sp.speaker: Old Laf.
sp.p: Generally thankfull.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I would haue ſaid it, you ſay well: heere comes the King.

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: Luſtique, as the Dutchman ſaies: Ile like a maide the Better whil'ſt I haue a tooth in my head: why he's able to leade her a Carranto.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Mor du vinager, is not this Helen?

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: Fore God I thinke ſo.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Goe call before mee all the Lords in Court,
Sit my preſeruer by thy patients ſide,
And with this healthfull hand whoſe baniſht ſence
Thou haſt repeal'd, a ſecond time receyue
The confirmation of my promis'd guift,
Which but attends thy naming.

div.l: Faire Maide ſend forth thine eye, this youthfull parcell
Of Noble Batchellors, ſtand at my beſtowing,
Ore whom both Soueraigne power, and fathers voice
I haue to vſe; thy franke election make,
Thou haſt power to chooſe, and they none to forſake.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: To each of you, one faire and vertuous Miſtris;
Fall when loue pleaſe, marry to each but one.

sp.speaker: Old Laf.
sp.l: I'de giue bay curtall, and his furniture
My mouth no more were broken then theſe boyes,
And writ as little beard.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Peruſe them well:
Not one of thoſe, but had a Noble father.

div.stage: She addreſſes her to a Lord.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Gentlemen, heauen hath through me, reſtor'd the king to health.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: We vnderſtand it, and thanke heauen for you.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: I am a ſimple Maide, and therein wealthieſt
That I proteſt, I ſimply am a Maide:
Pleaſe it your Maieſtie, I haue done already:
The bluſhes in my cheekes thus whiſper mee,
We bluſh that thou ſhouldſt chooſe, but be refuſed;
Let the white death ſit on thy cheeke for euer,
Wee'l nere come there againe.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Make choiſe and ſee,
Who ſhuns thy loue, ſhuns all his loue in mee.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Now Dian from thy Altar do I fly,
And to imperiall loue, that God moſt high
Do my ſighes ſtreame: Sir, wil you heare my ſuite?

sp.speaker: 1. Lo
sp.p: And grant it.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Thankes ſir, all the reſt is mute.

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: I had rather be in this choiſe, then throw Ameſ-ace for my life.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: The honor ſir that flames in your faire eyes,
Before I ſpeake too threatningly replies:
Loue make your fortunes twentie times aboue
Her that ſo vviſhes, and her humble loue.

sp.speaker: 2. Lo.
sp.p: No better if you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: My wiſh receiue,
Which great loue grant, and ſo I take my leaue.

sp.speaker: Ol. Laf.
sp.p: Do all they denie her? And they were ſons of mine, I'de haue them whip'd, or I would ſend them to 'th Turke to make Eunuches of.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Be not afraid that I your hand ſhould take,
Ile neuer do you wrong for your owne ſake:
Bleſſing vpon your vowes, and in your bed
Finde fairer fortune, if you euer wed.

sp.speaker: Old Laf.
sp.p:
Theſe boyes are boyes of Ice, they'le none
haue heere: ſure they are baſtards to the Engliſh, the French nere got em.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: You are too young, too happie, and too good
To make your ſelfe a ſonne out of my blood.

sp.speaker: 4. Lord.
sp.p: Faire one, I thinke not ſo.

sp.speaker: Ol. Lord
sp.p: There's one grape yet, I am ſure thy father drunke wine. But if thou beſt not an aſſe, I am a youth of fourteene: I haue knowne thee already.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: I dare not ſay I take you, but I giue
Me and my ſeruice, euer whilſt I liue
Into your guiding power: This is the man.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Why then young Bertram take her ſhee's thy wife.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: My wife my Leige? I ſhal beſeech your highnes
In ſuch a buſines, giue me leaue to vſe
The helpe of mine owne eies.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Know'ſt thou not Bertram what ſhee ha's done for mee?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Yes my good Lord, but neuer hope to know why I ſhould marrie her.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Thou know'ſt ſhee ha's rais'd me from my ſickly bed.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: But followes it my Lord, to bring me downe
Muſt anſwer for your raiſing? I knowe her well:
Shee had her breeding at my fathers charge:
A poore Phyſitians daughter my wife? Diſdaine
Rather corrupt me euer.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Tis onely title thou diſdainſt in her, the which
I can build vp: ſtrange is it that our bloods
Of colour, waight, and heat, pour'd all together,
Would quite confound diſtinction: yet ſtands off
In differences ſo mightie. If ſhe bee
All that is vertuous (ſaue what thou diſlik'ſt)
A poore Phiſitians daughter, thou diſlik'ſt
Of vertue for the name: but doe not ſo:
From loweſt place, whence vertuous things proceed,
The place is dignified by th' doers deede.
Where great additions ſwell's, and vertue none,
It is a dropſied honour. Good a lone,
Is good without a name? Vileneſſe is ſo:
The propertie by what is is, ſhould go,
Not by the title. Shee is young, wiſe, faire,
In theſe, to Nature ſhee's immediate heire:
And theſe breed honour: that is honours ſcorne,
Which challenges it ſelfe as honours borne,
And is not like the fire: Honours thriue,
When rather from our acts we them deriue
Then our fore-goers: the meere words, a ſlaue
Deboſh'd on euerie tombe, on euerie graue:
A lying Trophee, and as oft is dumbe,
Where duſt, and damn'd obliuion is the Tombe.
Of honour'd bones-indeed, what ſhould be ſaide?
If thou canſt like this creature, as a maide,
I can create the reſt: Vertue, and ſhee
Is her owne dower: Honour and wealth, from mee.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I cannot loue her, nor will ſtriue to doo't.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Thou wrong'ſt thy ſelfe, if thou ſhold'ſt ſtriue to chooſe.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: That you are well reſtor'd my Lord, I'me glad:
Let the reſt go.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: My Honor's at the ſtake, which to defeate
I muſt produce my power. Heere, take her hand,
Proud ſcornfull boy, vnworthie this good gift,
That doſt in vile miſpriſion ſhackle vp
My loue, and her deſert: that canſt not dreame,
We poizing vs in her defectiue ſcale,
Shall weigh thee to the beame: That wilt not know,
It is in Vs to plant thine Honour, where
We pleaſe to haue it grow. Cheeke thy contempt:
Obey Our will, which trauailes in thy good:
Beleeue not thy diſdaine, but preſentlie
Do thine owne fortunes that obedient right
Which both thy dutie owes, and Our power claimes,
Or I will throw thee from my care for euer
Into the ſtaggers, and the careleſſe lapſe
Of youth and ignorance: both my reuenge and hate
Looſing vpon thee, in the name of iuſtice,
Without all termes of pittie. Speake, thine anſwer.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Pardon my gracious Lord: for I ſubmit
My fancie to your eies, when I conſider
What great creation, and what dole of honour
Flies where you bid it: I finde that ſhe which late
Was in my Nobler thoughts, moſt baſe: is now
The praiſed of the King, who ſo ennobled,
Is as 'twere borne ſo.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Take her by the hand,
And tell her ſhe is thine: to whom I promiſe
A counterpoize: If not to thy eſtate,
A ballance more repleat.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I take her hand.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Good fortune, and the fauour of the King
Smile vpon this Contract: whoſe Ceremonie
Shall ſeeme expedient on the now borne briefe,
And be perform'd to night: the ſolemne Feaſt
Shall more attend vpon the coming ſpace,
Expecting abſent friends. As thou lou'ſt her,
Thy loue's to me Religious: elſe, do's erre.

div.stage: Parolles and Lafew ſtay behind, commenting of this wedding.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Do you heare Monſieur? A word with you.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Your pleaſure ſir.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Your Lord and Maſter did well to make his recantation.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Recantation? My Lord? my Maſter?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I: Is it not a Language I ſpeake?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: A moſt harſh one, and not to bee vnderſtoode without bloudie ſucceeding My Maſter▪

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Are you Companion to the Count Roſillion?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: To any Count, to all Counts: to what is man.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: To what is Counts man: Counts maiſter is of another ſtile.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: You are too old ſir: Let it ſatisfie you, you are too old.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I muſt tell thee ſirrah, I write Man: to which title age cannot bring thee.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: What I dare too well do, I dare not do.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I did thinke thee for two ordinaries: to bee a prettie wiſe fellow, thou didſt make tollerable vent of thy trauell, it might paſſe: yet the ſcarffes and the bannerets about thee, did manifoldlie diſſwade me from beleeuing thee a veſſell of too great a burthen. I haue now found thee, when I looſe thee againe, I care not: yet art thou good for nothing but taking vp, and that th' ourt ſcarce worth.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Hadſt thou not the priuiledge of Antiquity vpon thee.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Do not plundge thy ſelfe to farre in anger, leaſt thou haſten thy triall: which if, Lord haue mercie on thee for a hen, ſo my good window of Lettice fare thee well, thy caſement I neede not open, for I look through thee. Giue me thy hand.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: My Lord, you giue me moſt egregious indignity.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I with all my heart, and thou art worthy of it.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I haue not my Lord deſeru'd it.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Yes good faith, eu'ry dramme of it, and I will not b • te thee a ſcruple.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Well, I ſhall be wiſer.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Eu'n as ſoone as thou can'ſt, for thou haſt to pull at a ſmacke a' th contrarie. If euer thou bee'ſt bound in thy skarfe and beaten, thou ſhall finde what it is to be proud of thy bondage, I haue a deſire to holde my acquaintance with thee, or rather my knowledge, that I may ſay in the default, he is a man I know.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: My Lord you do me moſt inſupportable vexation.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I would it were hell paines for thy ſake, and my poore doing eternall: for doing I am paſt, as I will by thee, in what motion age will giue me leaue.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Well, thou haſt a ſonne ſhall take this diſgrace off me; ſcuruy, old, filthy, ſcuruy Lord: Well, I muſt be patient, there is no fettering of authority. Ile beate him (by my life) if I can meete him with any conuenience, and he were double and double a Lord. Ile haue no more pittie of his age then I would haue of—Ile beate him, and if I could but meet him agen.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Sirra, your Lord and maſters married, there's newes for you: you haue a new Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I moſt vnfainedly beſeech your Lordſhippe to make ſome reſeruation of your wrongs. He is my good Lord, whom I ſerue aboue is my maſter.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Who? God.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I ſir.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: The deuill it is, that's thy maſter. Why dooeſt thou garter vp thy armes a this faſhion? Doſt make hoſe of thy ſleeues? Do other ſeruants ſo? Thou wert beſt ſet thy lower part where thy noſe ſtands. By mine Honor, If I were but two houres yonger, I'de beate thee: meethink'ſt thou art a generall offence, and euery man ſhold beate thee: I thinke thou waſt created for men to breath themſelues vpon thee.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: This is hard and vndeſerued meaſure my Lord.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Go too ſir, you were beaten in Italy for picking a kernell out of a Pomgranat, you are a vagabond, and no true traueller: you are more ſawcie with Lordes and honourable perſonages, then the Commiſsion of your birth and vertue giues you Heraldry. You are not worth another word, elſe I'de call you knaue. I leaue you.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Good, very good, it is ſo then: good, very good, let it be conceal'd awhile.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: Vndone, and forfeited to cares for euer.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: What's the matter ſweet-heart?

sp.speaker: Roſsill.
sp.p: Although before the ſolemne Prieſt I haue ſworne, I will not bed her.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: What? what ſweet heart?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: O my Parrolles, they haue married me:
Ile to the Tuſcan warres, and neuer bed her.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: France is a dog-hole, and it no more merits,
The tread of a mans foot: too 'th warres.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: There's letters from my mother: What th' import is, I know not yet.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I that would be knowne: too 'th warrs my boy, too 'th warres:
He weares his honor in a boxe vnſeene,
That hugges his kickie wickie heare at home,
Spending his manlie marrow in her armes
Which ſhould ſuſtaine the bound and high curuet
Of Marſes fierie ſteed: to other Regions,
France is a ſtable, wee that dwell in't Iades,
Therefore too 'th warre.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: It ſhall be ſo, Ile ſend her to my houſe,
Acquaint my mother with my hate to her,
And wherefore I am fled: Write to the King
That which I durſt not ſpeake. His preſent gift
Shall furniſh me to thoſe Italian fields
Where noble fellowes ſtrike: Warres is no ſtrife
To the darke houſe, and the detected wife.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Will this Caprichio hold in thee, art ſure?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: Go with me to my chamber, and aduice me.
Ile ſend her ſtraight away: To morrow,
Ile to the warres, ſhe to her ſingle ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Why theſe bals bound, ther's noiſe in it. Tis hard
A yong man maried, is a man that's mard:
Therefore away, and leaue her brauely: go,
The King ha's done you wrong: but huſh 'tis ſo.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: My mother greets me kindly, is ſhe well?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: She is not well, but yet ſhe has her health, ſhe's very merrie, but yet ſhe is not well: but thankes be giuen ſhe's very well, and wants nothing i' th world: but yet ſhe is not well.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: If ſhe be verie wel, what do's ſhe ayle, that ſhe's not verie well?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Truly ſhe's very well indeed, but for two things

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: What two things?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: One, that ſhe's not in heauen, whether God ſend her quickly: the other, that ſhe's in earth, from whence God ſend her quickly.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Bleſſe you my fortunate Ladie.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I hope ſir I haue your good will to haue mine owne good fortune.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: You had my prayers to leade them on, and to keepe them on, haue them ſtill. O my knaue, how do's my old Ladie?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: So that you had her wrinkles, and I her money,
I would ſhe did as you ſay.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why I ſay nothing.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Marry you are the wiſer man: for many a mans tongue ſhakes out his maſters vndoing: to ſay nothing, to do nothing, to know nothing, and to haue nothing, is to be a great part of your title, which is within a verie little of nothing.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Away, th' art a knaue.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: You ſhould haue ſaid ſir before a knaue, th' art a knaue, that's before me th' art a knaue: this had beene truth ſir.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Go too, thou art a wittie foole, I haue found thee.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Did you finde me in your ſelfe ſir, or were you taught to finde me?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: The ſearch ſir was profitable, and much Foole may you find in you, euen to the worlds pleaſure, and the encreaſe of laughter.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: A good knaue ifaith, and well fed.
Madam, my Lord will go awaie to night,
A verie ſerrious buſineſſe call's on him:
The great prerogatiue and rite of loue,
Which as your due time claimes, he do's acknowledge,
But puts it off to a compell'd reſtraint:
Whoſe want, and whoſe delay▪ is ſtrew'd with ſweets
Which they diſtill now in the curbed time,
To make the comming houre oreflow with ioy,
And pleaſure drowne the brim.

sp.speaker: Hel▪
sp.p: What's his will elſe?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: That you will take your inſtant leaue a' th king,
And make this haſt as your owne good proceeding,
Strengthned with what Apologie you thinke
May make it probable neede.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: What more commands hee?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: That hauing this obtain'd, you preſentlie
Attend his further pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: In euery thing I waite vpon his will.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I ſhall report it ſo,

sp.speaker: Hell.
sp.p: I pray you come ſirrah.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: But I hope your Lordſhippe thinkes not him a ſouldier.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Yes my Lord and of verie valiant approofe.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: You haue it from his owne deliuerance.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: And by other warranted teſtimonie.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Then my Diall goes not true, I tooke this Larke for a bunting.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I do aſſure you my Lord he is very great in knowledge, and accordinglie valiant.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I haue then ſinn'd againſt his experience, and tranſgreſt againſt his valour, and my ſtate that way is dangerous, ſince I cannot yet find in my heart to repent: Heere he comes, I pray you make vs freinds, I will purſue the amitie.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Theſe things ſhall be done ſir.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Pray you ſir whoſe his Tailor?

sp.speaker: Par
sp.p: Sir?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: O I know him well, I ſir, hee ſirs a good workeman, a verie good Tailor.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Is ſhee gone to the king?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Shee is.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Will ſhee away to night?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: As you'le haue her.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: I haue writ my letters, casketted my treaſure,
Giuen order for our horſes, and to night,
When I ſhould take poſſeſſion of the Bride,
And ere I doe begin.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: A good Trauailer is ſomething at the latter end of a dinner, but on that lies three thirds, and vſes a known truth to paſſe a thouſand nothings with, ſhould bee once hard, and thrice beaten. God ſaue you Captaine.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Is there any vnkindnes betweene my Lord and you Monſieur?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I know not how I haue deſerued to run into my Lords diſpleaſure.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: You haue made ſhift to run into't, bootes and ſpurres and all: like him that leapt into the Cuſtard, and out of it you'le runne againe, rather then ſuffer queſtion for your reſidence.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: It may bee you haue miſtaken him my Lord.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: And ſhall doe ſo euer, though I tooke him at's prayers. Fare you well my Lord, and beleeue this of me, there can be no kernell in this light Nut: the ſoule of this man is his cloathes: Truſt him not in matter of heauie conſequence: I haue kept of them tame, & know their natures. Farewell Monſieur, I haue ſpoken better of you, then you haue or will to deſerue at my hand, but we muſt do good againſt euill.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: An idle Lord, I ſweare.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I thinke ſo.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why do you not know him?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Yes, I do know him well, and common ſpeech
Giues him a worthy paſſe. Heere comes my clog.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: I haue ſir as I was commanded from you
Spoke with the King, and haue procur'd his leaue
For preſent parting, onely he deſires
Some priuate ſpeech with you.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: I ſhall obey his will.
You muſt not meruaile Helen at my courſe,
Which holds not colour with the time, nor does
The miniſtration, and required office
On my particular. Prepar'd I was not
For ſuch a buſineſſe, therefore am I found
So much vnſetled: This driues me to intreate you,
That preſently you take your way for home,
And rather muſe then aske why I intreate you,
For my reſpects are better then they ſeeme,
And my appointments haue in them a neede
Greater then ſhewes it ſelfe at the firſt view,
To you that know them not. This to my mother,
'Twill be two daies ere I ſhall ſee you, ſo
I leaue you to your wiſedome.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Sir, I can nothing ſay,
But that I am your moſt obedient ſeruant.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Come, come, no more of that.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: And euer ſhall
With true obſeruance ſeeke to eeke out that
Wherein toward me my homely ſtarres haue faild
To equall my great fortune.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Let that goe: my haſt is verie great. Farwell:
Hie home.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Pray ſir your pardon.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Well, what would you ſay?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: I am not worthie of the wealth I owe,
Nor dare I ſay 'tis mine: and yet it is,
But like a timorous theefe, moſt faine would ſteale
What law does vouch mine owne.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: What would you haue?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Something, and ſcarſe ſo much: nothing indeed,
I would not tell you what I would my Lord: Faith yes,
Strangers and foes do ſunder, and not kiſſe.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I pray you ſtay not, but in haſt to horſe.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: I ſhall not breake your bidding, good my Lord:
Where are my other men? Monſieur, farwell.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Go thou toward home, where I wil neuer come,
Whilſt I can ſhake my ſword, or heare the drumme:
Away, and for our flight.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Brauely, Coragio.

div.head: Actus Tertius.
div.stage: Enter the Duke of Florence, the two Frenchmen, with a troope of Souldiers.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: So that from point to point, now haue you heard
The fundamentall reaſons of this warre,
Whoſe great deciſion hath much blood let forth
And more thirſts after.

sp.speaker: 1. Lord.
sp.l: Holy ſeemes the quarrell
Vpon your Graces part: blacke and fearefull
On the oppoſer.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Therefore we meruaile much our Coſin France
Would in ſo iuſt a buſineſſe, ſhut his boſome
Againſt our borrowing prayers.

sp.speaker: French E.
sp.l: Good my Lord,
The reaſons of our ſtare I cannot yeelde,
But like a common and an outward man,
That the great figure of a Counſaile frames,
By ſelfe vnable motion, therefore dare not
Say what I thinke of it, ſince I haue found
My ſelfe in my incertaine grounds to faile
As often as I gueſt.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Be it his pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Fren. G.
sp.l: But I am ſure the yonger of our nature,
That ſurfet on their eaſe, will day by day
Come heere for Phyſicke.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Welcome ſhall they bee:
And all the honors that can flye from vs,
Shall on them ſettle: you know your places well,
When better fall, for your auailes they fell,
To morrow to 'th the field.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: It hath happen'd all, as I would haue had it, ſaue that he comes not along with her.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: By my troth I take my young Lord to be a verie melancholly man.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: By what obſeruance I pray you.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Why he will looke vppon his boote, and ſing: mend the Ruffe and ſing, aske queſtions and ſing, picke his teeth, and ſing: I know a man that had this tricke of melancholy hold a goodly Mannor for a ſong.

sp.speaker: Lad.
sp.p: Let me ſee what he writes, and when he meanes to come.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I haue no minde to Isbell ſince I was at Court. Our old Lings, and our Isbels a' th Country, are nothing like your old Ling and your Isbels a' th Court: the brains of my Cupid's knock'd out, and I beginne to loue, as an old man loues money, with no ſtomacke.

sp.speaker: Lad.
sp.p: What haue we heere?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: In that you haue there.

p.hi: I haue ſent you a daughter-in-Law, ſhee hath recouered the King, and vndone me: I haue wedded her, not bedded her, and ſworne to make the not eternall. You ſhall heare I am runne away, know it before the report come. If there bee bredth enough in the world, I will hold a long diſtance. My duty to you.

sp.l: This is not well raſh and vnbridled boy,
To flye the fauours of ſo good a King,
To plucke his indignation on thy head,
By the miſpriſing of a Maide too vertuous
For the contempt of Empire.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: O Madam, yonder is heauie newes within betweene two ſouldiers, and my yong Ladie.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: What is the matter.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Nay there is ſome comfort in the newes, ſome comfort, your ſonne will not be kild ſo ſoone as I thoght he would.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Why ſhould he be kill'd?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: So ſay I Madame, if he runne away, as I heare he does, the danger is in ſtanding too't, that's the loſſe of men, though it be the getting of children. Heere they come will tell you more. For my part I onely heare your ſonne was run away.

sp.speaker: French E.
sp.p: Saue you good Madam.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Madam, my Lord is gone, for euer gone.

sp.speaker: French G.
sp.p: Do not ſay ſo.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Thinke vpon patience, pray you Gentlemen,
I haue felt ſo many quirkes of ioy and greefe,
That the firſt face of neither on the ſtart
Can woman me vntoo't. Where is my ſonne I pray you?

sp.speaker: Fren. G.
sp.l: Madam he's gone to ſerue the Duke of Florence,
We met him thitherward, for thence we came:
And after ſome diſpatch in hand at Court,
Thither we bend againe.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Looke on his Letter Madam, here's my Paſport.
sp.q: When thou canſt get the Ring vpon my finger, which neuer ſhall come off, and ſhew mee a childe begotten of thy bodie, that I am father too, then call me husband: but in ſuch a (then) I write a Neuer.
sp.l: This is a dreadfull ſentence.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Brought you this Letter Gentlemen?

sp.speaker: 1. G.
sp.p: I Madam, and for the Contents ſake are ſorrie for our paines.

sp.speaker: Old La.
sp.l: I prethee Ladie haue a better cheere,
If thou engroſſeſt, all the greefes are thine,
Thou robſt me of a moity: He was my ſonne,
But I do waſh his name out of my blood,
And thou art all my childe. Towards Florence is he?

sp.speaker: Fren. G.
sp.p: I Madam.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: And to be a ſouldier.

sp.speaker: Fren. G.
sp.l: Such is his noble purpoſe, and beleeu't
The Duke will lay vpon him all the honor
That good conuenience claimes.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Returne you thither.

sp.speaker: Fren. E.
sp.p: I Madam, with the ſwifteſt wing of ſpeed.

sp.speaker: Hel.

l.hi: Till I haue no wife, I haue nothing in France,

sp.l: 'Tis bitter.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Finde you that there?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I Madame.

sp.speaker: Fren. E.
sp.p: 'Tis but the boldneſſe of his hand haply, which his heart was not conſenting too.

sp.speaker: Lad.
sp.l: Nothing in France, vntill he haue no wife:
There's nothing heere that is too good for him
But onely ſhe, and ſhe deſerues a Lord
That twenty ſuch rude boyes might tend vpon,
And call her hourely Miſtris. Who was with him?

sp.speaker: Fren. E.
sp.p: A ſeruant onely, and a Gentleman: whlch I haue ſometime knowne.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Parolles was it not?

sp.speaker: Fren. E.
sp.p: I my good Ladie, hee.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: A verie tainted fellow, and full of wickedneſſe,
My ſonne corrupts a well deriued nature
With his inducement.

sp.speaker: Fren. E.
sp.p: Indeed good Ladie the fellow has a deale of that, too much, which holds him much to haue.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p:
Y' are welcome Gentlemen, I will intreate you when you ſee my ſonne, to tell him that his ſword can neuer winne the honor that he looſes: more Ile intreate
you written to beare along.

sp.speaker: Fren. G.
sp.p: We ſerue you Madam in that and all your worthieſt affaires.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Not ſo, but as we change our courteſies,
Will you draw neere?

sp.speaker: Hel.

l.hi: Till I haue no wife I haue nothing in France.

sp.l: Nothing in France vntill he has no wife:
Thou ſhalt haue none Roſſillion, none in France,
Then haſt thou all againe: poore Lord, is't I
That chaſe thee from thy Countrie, and expoſe
Thoſe tender limbes of thine, to the euent
Of the none-ſparing warre? And is it I,
That driue thee from the ſportiue Court, where thou
Was't ſhot at with faire eyes, to be the marke
Of ſmoakie Musk • ts? O you leaden meſſengers,
That ride vpon the violent ſpeede of fire,
Fly with falſe ayme, moue the ſtill-peering aire
That ſings with piercing, do not touch my Lord:
Who euer ſhoots at him, I ſet him there.
Who euer charges on his forward breſt
I am the Caitiffe that do hold him too't,
And though I kill him not, I am the cauſe
His death was ſo effected: Better 'twere
I met the rauine Lyon when he roar'd
With ſharpe conſtraint of hunger: better 'twere,
That all the miſeries which nature owes
Were mine at once. No come thou home Roſſillion,
Whence honor but of danger winnes a ſcarre,
As oft it looſes all. I will be gone:
My being heere it is, that holds thee hence,
Shall I ſtay heere to doo't? No, no, although
The ayre of Paradiſe did fan the houſe,
And Angles offic'd all: I will be gone,
That pittifull rumour may report my flight
To conſolate thine eare. Come night, end day,
For with the darke (poore theefe) Ile ſteale away.

div.stage: Flouriſh. Enter the Duke of Florence, Roſſillion, drum and trumpets, ſoldiers, Parrolles.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: The Generall of our horſe thou art, and we
Great in our hope, lay our beſt loue and credence
Vpon thy promiſing fortune▪

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Sir it is
A charge too heauy for my ſtrength, but yet
Wee'l ſtriue to beare it for your worthy ſake,
To th' extreme edge of hazard.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: Then go thou for • h,
And fortune play vpon thy proſperous helme
As thy auſpicious miſtris.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: This very day
Great Mars I put my ſelfe into thy file,
Make me but like my thoughts, and I ſhall proue
A louer of thy drumme, hater of loue.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: Alas! and would you take the letter of her:
Might you not know ſhe would do, as ſhe has done,
By ſending me a Letter. Reade it agen.

body.head: Letter.
body.l: I am S. Iaques Pilgrim, thither gone:
Ambitious loue hath ſo in me offended,
That bare-foot plod I the cold ground vpon
With ſainted vow my faults to haue amended.
Write, write, that from the bloodie courſe of warre,
My deereſt Maſter your deare ſonne, may hie,
Bleſſe him at home in peace. Whilst I from farre,
His name with zealous feruour ſanctifie:
His taken labours bid him me forgiue:
I his deſpightfull Iuno ſent him forth,
From Courtly friends, with Camping foes to liue,
Where death and danger dogges the heeles of worth.
He is too good and faire for death, and mee,
Whom I my ſelfe embrace, to ſet him free.

sp.l: Ah what ſharpe ſtings are in her mildeſt words?
Rynaldo, you did neuer lacke aduice ſo much,
As letting her paſſe ſo: had I ſpoke with her,
I could haue well diuerted her intents,
Which thus ſhe hath preuented.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: Pardon me Madam,
If I had giuen you this at ouer-night,
She might haue beene ore-tane: and yet ſhe writes
Purſuite would be but vaine.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.l: What Angell ſhall
Bleſſe this vnworthy husband, he cannot thriue,
Vnleſſe her prayers, whom heauen delights to beare
And loues to grant, repreeue him from the wrath
Of greateſt Iuſtice. Write, write Rynaldo,
To this vnworthy husband of his wife,
Let euerie word waigh heauie of her worth,
That he does waigh too light: my greateſt greefe,
Though little he do feele it, ſet downe ſharpely.
Diſpatch the moſt conuenient meſſenger,
When haply he ſhall heare that ſhe is gone,
He will returne, and hope I may that ſhee
Hearing ſo much, will ſpeede her foote againe,
Led hither by pure loue: which of them both
Is deereſt to me, I haue no skill in ſence
To make diſtinction: prouide this Meſſenger:
My heart is heauie, and mine age is weake,
Greefe would haue teares, and ſorrow bids me ſpeake.

div.stage: Enter old Widdow of Florence, her daughter, Violenta and Mariana, with other Citizens.

sp.speaker: Widdow.
sp.l: Nay come,
For if they do approach the Citty,
We ſhall looſe all the ſight.

sp.speaker: Diana.
sp.l: They ſay, the French Count has done
Moſt honourable ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: It is reported,
That he has taken their great'ſt Commander,
And that with his owne hand he ſlew
The Dukes brother: we haue loſt our labour,
They are gone a contrarie way • harke,
you may know by their Trumpets.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.l: Come lets returne againe,
And ſuffice our ſelues with the report of it.
Well Diana, take heed of this French Earle,
The honor of a Maide is her name,
And no Legacie is ſo rich
As honeſtie.

sp.speaker: Widdow.
sp.l: I haue told my neighbour
How you haue beene ſolicited by a Gentleman
His Companion.

sp.speaker: Maria.
sp.p: I know that knaue, hang him, one Parolles, a filthy Officer he is in thoſe ſuggeſtions for the young Earle, beware of them Diana; their promiſes, entiſements, oathes, tokens, and all theſe engines of luſt, are not the things they go vnder: many a maide hath beene ſeduced by them, and the miſerie is example, that ſo terrible ſhewes in the wracke of maiden-hood, cannot for all that diſſwade ſucceſſion, but that they are limed with the twigges that threatens them. I hope I neede not to aduiſe you further, but I hope your owne grace will keepe you where you are, though there were no further danger knowne, but the modeſtie which is ſo loſt.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: You ſhall not neede to feare me.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I hope ſo: looke here comes a pilgrim, I know ſhe will lye at my houſe, thither they ſend one another, Ile queſtion her. God ſaue you pilgrim, whether are bound?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: To S. Iaques la grand.
Where do the Palmers lodge, I do beſeech you?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: At the S. Francis heere beſide the Port.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Is this the way?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: I marrie iſt. Harke you, they come this way:
If you will tarrie holy Pilgrime
