But till the troopes come by,
I will conduct you where you ſhall be lodg'd,
The rather for I thinke I know your hoſteſſe
As ample as my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Is it your ſelfe?

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: If you ſhall pleaſe ſo Pilgrime.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I thanke you, and will ſtay vpon your leiſure.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: you came I thinke from France?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I did ſo.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: Heere you ſhall ſee a Countriman of yours
That has done worthy ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: His name I pray you?

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: The Count Roſſillion: know you ſuch a one?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: But by the eare that heares moſt nobly of him:
His face I know not.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: What ſomere he is
He's brauely taken heere. He ſtole from France
As 'tis reported: for the King had married him
Againſt his liking. Thinke you it is ſo?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I ſurely meere the truth, I know his Lady.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: There is a Gentleman that ſerues the Count,
Reports but courſely of her.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: What's his name?

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: Monſieur Parrolles.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Oh I beleeue with him,
In argument of praiſe, or to the worth
Of the great Count himſelfe, ſhe is too meane
To haue her name repeated, all her deſeruing
Is a reſerued honeſtie, and that
I haue not heard examin'd.

sp.speaker: Dian.
sp.l: Alas poore Ladie,
'Tis a hard bondage to become the wife
Of a deteſting Lord.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: I write good creature, whereſoere ſhe is,
Her hart waighes ſadly: this yong maid might do her
A ſhrewd turne if ſhe pleas'd.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: How do you meane?
May be the amorous Count ſolicites her
In the vnlawfull purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: He does indeede,
And brokes with all that can in ſuch a ſuite
Corrupt the tender honour of a Maide:
But ſhe is arm'd for him, and keepes her guard
In honeſteſt defence.

div.stage: Enter Count Roſſillion, Parrolles, and the whole Armie.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: The goddes forbid elſe.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: So, now they come:
That is Anthonio the Dukes eldeſt ſonne,
That Eſcalus.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Which is the Frenchman?

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: Hee,
That with the plume, 'tis a moſt gallant fellow,
I would he lou'd his wife: if he were honeſter
He were much goodlier. Is't not a handſom Gentleman

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I like him well.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: 'Tis pitty he is not honeſt: yonds that ſame knaue
That leades him to theſe places: were I his Ladie,
I would poiſon that vile Raſcall.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Which is he?

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: That Iacke an-apes with ſcarfes. Why is hee melancholly?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Perchance he • s hurt i' th battaile.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Looſe our drum? Well.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: He's ſhrewdly vext at ſomething. Looke he has ſpyed vs.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Marrie hang you.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: And your curteſie, for a ring-carrier.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: The troope is paſt: Come pilgrim, I wil bring you, Where you ſhall hoſt: Of inioyn'd penitents
There's foure or fiue, to great S. Iaques bound,
Alreadie at my houſe.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: I humbly thanke you:
Pleaſe it this Matron, and this gentle Maide
To eate with vs to night, the charge and thanking
Shall be for me▪ and to requite you further,
I will beſtow ſome precepts of this Virgin,
Worthy the note.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: Wee'l take your offer kindly.

div.stage: Enter Count Roſſillion and the Frenchmen, as at firſt.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: Nay good my Lord put him too't: let him haue his way.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: If your Lordſhippe finde him not a Hilding, hold me no more in your reſpect.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: On my life my Lord▪ a bubble.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Do you thinke I am ſo farre
Deceiued in him.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: Beleeue it my Lord, in mine owne direct knowledge, without any malice, but to ſpeake of him as my kinſman, hee's a moſt notable Coward, an infinite and endleſſe Lyar, an hourely promiſe-breaker, the owner of no one good qualitie, worthy your Lordſhips entertainment.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: It were fit you knew him, leaſt▪ repoſing too farre in his vertue which he hath not, he might at ſome great and truſtie buſineſſe, in a maine daunger, fayle you.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I would I knew in what particular action to try him.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: None better then to let him fetch off his drumme, which you heare him ſo confidently vndertake to do.

sp.speaker: C.E.
sp.p:
I with a troop of Florentines wil ſodainly ſurprize
him; ſuch I will haue whom I am ſure he knowes not from the enemie: wee will binde and hoodwinke him ſo, that he ſhall ſuppoſe no other but that he is carried into the Leager of the aduerſaries, when we bring him to our owne tents: be but your Lordſhip preſent at his examination, if he do not for the promiſe of his life, and in the higheſt compulſion of baſe feare, offer to betray you, and deliuer all the intelligence in his power againſt you, and that with the diuine forfeite of his ſoule vpon oath, neuer truſt my iudgement in anie thing.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: O for the loue of laughter, let him fetch his drumme, he ſayes he has a ſtratagem for't: when your Lordſhip ſees the bottome of this ſucceſſe in't, and to what mettle this counterfeyt lump of ours will be melted if you giue him not Iohn drummes entertainement, your inclining cannot be remoued. Heere he comes.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: O for the loue of laughter hinder not the honor of his deſigne, let him fetch off his drumme in any hand.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: How now Monſieur? This drumme ſticks ſorely in your diſpoſition.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: A pox on't, let it go, 'tis but a drumme.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: But a drumme: Iſt but a drumme? A drum ſo loſt. There was excellent command, to charge in with our horſe vpon our owne wings, and to rend our owne ſouldiers.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: That was not to be blam'd in the command of the ſeruice: it was a diſaſter of warre that Caeſar him ſelfe could not haue preuented, if he had beene there to command.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Well, wee cannot greatly condemne our ſucceſſe: ſome diſhonor wee had in the loſſe of that drum, but it is not to be recouered.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: It might haue beene recouered.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: It might, but it is not now.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: It is to be recouered, but that the merit of ſeruice is ſildome attributed to the true and exact performer, I would haue that drumme or another, or hic iacet.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Why if you haue a ſtomacke, too't Monſieur: if you thinke your myſterie in ſtratagem, can bring this inſtrument of honour againe into his natiue quarter, be magnanimious in the enterprize and go on, I wil grace the attempt for a worthy exploit: if you ſpeede well in it, the Duke ſhall both ſpeake of it, and extend to you what further becomes his greatneſſe, euen to the vtmoſt ſyllable of your worthineſſe.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: By the hand of a ſouldier I will vndertake it.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: But you muſt not now ſlumber in it.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Ile about it this euening, and I will preſently pen downe my dilemma's, encourage my ſelfe in my certaintie, put my ſelfe into my mortall preparation: and by midnight looke to heare further from me.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: May I bee bold to acquaint his grace you are gone about it.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I know not what the ſucceſſe wil be my Lord, but the attempt I vow.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: I know th' art valiant,
And to the poſsibility of thy ſouldierſhip,
Will ſubſcribe for thee: Farewell.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I loue not many words.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: No more then a fiſh loues water. Is not this a ſtrange fellow my Lord, that ſo confidently ſeemes to vndertake this buſineſſe, which he knowes is not to be done, damnes himſelfe to do, & dares better be damnd then to doo't.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: You do not know him my Lord as we doe, certaine it is that he will ſteale himſelfe into a mans fauour, and for a weeke eſcape a great deale of diſcoueries, but when you finde him out, you haue him euer after.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Why do you thinke he will make no deede at all of this that ſo ſeriouſlie hee dooes addreſſe himſelfe vnto?

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: None in the world, but returne with an inuention, and clap vpon you two or three probable lies: but we haue almoſt imboſt him, you ſhall ſee his fall to night; for indeede he is not for your Lordſhippes reſpect.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: Weele make you ſome ſport with the Foxe ere we caſe him. He was firſt ſmoak'd by the old Lord Lafew, when his diſguiſe and he is parted, tell me what a ſprat you ſhall finde him, which you ſhall ſee this verie night.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.l: I muſt go looke my twigges,
He ſhall be caught.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Your brother he ſhall go along with me.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: As't pleaſe your Lordſhip, Ile leaue you.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Now wil I lead you to the houſe, and ſhew you
The Laſſe I ſpoke of.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: But you ſay ſhe's honeſt.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: That's all the fault: I ſpoke with hir but once,
And found her wondrous cold, but I ſent to her
By this ſame Coxcombe that we haue i' th winde
Tokens and Letters, which ſhe did reſend,
And this is all I haue done: She's a faire creature,
Will you go ſee her?

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: With all my heart my Lord.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: If you miſdoubt me that I am not ſhee,
I know not how I ſhall aſſure you further,
But I ſhall looſe the grounds I worke vpon.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: Though my eſtate be falne, I was well borne,
Nothing acquainted with theſe buſineſſes,
And would not put my reputation now
In any ſtaining act.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Nor would I wiſh you.
Firſt giue me truſt, the Count he is my husband,
And what to your ſworne counſaile I haue ſpoken,
Is ſo from word to word: and then you cannot
By the good ayde that I of you ſhall borrow,
Erre in beſtowing it.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: I ſhould beleeue you,
For you haue ſhew'd me that which well approues
Y' are great in fortune.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Take this purſe of Gold,
And let me buy your friendly helpe thus farre,
Which I will ouer-pay, and pay againe
When I haue found it. The Count he woes your daughter,
Layes downe his wanton ſiedge before her beautie,
Reſolue to carrie her: let her in fine conſent
As wee'l direct her how 'tis beſt to beare it:
Now his important blood will naught denie,
That ſhee'l demand: a ring the Countie weares,
That downward hath ſucceeded in his houſe
From ſonne to ſonne, ſome foure or fiue diſcents,
Since the firſt father wore it. This Ring he holds
In moſt rich choice: yet in his idle fire,
To buy his will, it would not ſeeme too deere,
How ere repented after.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Now I ſee the bottome of your purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: You ſee it lawfull then, it is no more,
But that your daughter ere ſhe ſeemes as wonne,
Deſires this Ring; appoints him an encounter;
In fine, deliuers me to fill the time,
Her ſelfe moſt chaſtly abſent: after
To marry her, Ile adde three thouſand Crownes
To what is paſt already.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: I haue yeelded:
Inſtruct my daughter how ſhe ſhall perſeuer,
That time and place with this deceite ſo lawfull
May proue coherent. Euery night he comes
With Muſickes of all ſorts, and ſongs compos'd
To her vnworthineſſe: It nothing ſteeds vs
To chide him from our eeues, for he perſiſts
As if his life lay on't.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Why then to night
Let vs aſſay our plot, which if it ſpeed,
Is wicked meaning in a lawfull deede;
And lawfull meaning in a lawfull act,
Where both not ſinne, and yet a ſinfull fact.
But let's about it.

div.head: Actus Quartus.
div.stage: Enter one of the Frenchmen, with fiue or ſixe other ſouldiers in ambuſh.

sp.speaker: 1. Lord. E.
sp.p: He can come no other way but by this hedge corner: when you ſallie vpon him, ſpeake what terrible Language you will: though you vnderſtand it not your ſelues, no matter: for we muſt not ſeeme to vnderſtand him, vnleſſe ſome one among vs, whom wee muſt produce for an Interpreter.

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.p: Good Captaine, let me be th' Interpreter.

sp.speaker: Lor. E.
sp.p: Art not acquainted with him? knowes he not thy voice?

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.p: No ſir I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Lo. E.
sp.p: But what linſie wolſy haſt thou to ſpeake to vs againe.

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.p: E'n ſuch as you ſpeake to me.

sp.speaker: Lo. E.
sp.p: He muſt thinke vs ſome band of ſtrangers, i' th aduerſaries entertainment. Now he hath a ſmacke of all neighbouring Languages: therefore we muſt euery one be a man of his owne fancie, not to know what we ſpeak one to another: ſo we ſeeme to know, is to know ſtraight our purpoſe: Choughs language, gabble enough, and good enough. As for you interpreter, you muſt ſeeme very politicke. But couch hoa, heere hee comes, to beguile two houres in a ſleepe, and then to returne & ſwear the lies he forges.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Ten a clocke: Within theſe three houres 'twill be time enough to goe home. What ſhall I ſay I haue done? It muſt bee a very plauſiue inuention that carries it. They beginne to ſmoake mee, and diſgraces haue of late, knock'd too often at my doore: I finde my tongue is too foole-hardie, but my heart hath the feare of Ma • s before it, and of his creatures, not daring the reports of my tongue.

sp.speaker: Lo. E.
sp.p: This is the firſt truth that ere thine own tongue was guiltie of.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: What the diuell ſhould moue mee to vndertake the recouerie of this drumme, being not ignorant of the impoſſibility, and knowing I had no ſuch purpoſe? I muſt giue my ſelfe ſome hurts, and ſay I got them in exploit: yet ſlight ones will not carrie it. They will ſay, came you off with ſo little? And great ones I dare not giue, wherefore what's the inſtance. Tongue, I muſt put you into a Butter-womans mouth, and buy my ſelfe another of Baiazeths Mule, if you prattle mee into theſe perilles.

sp.speaker: Lo. E.
sp.p: Is it poſſible he ſhould know what hee is, and be that he is.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I would the cutting of my garments wold ſerue the turne, or the breaking of my Spaniſh ſword.

sp.speaker: Lo. E.
sp.p: We cannot affoord you ſo.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Or the baring of my beard, and to ſay it was in ſtratagem.

sp.speaker: Lo. E.
sp.p: 'Twould not do.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Or to drowne my cloathes, and ſay I was ſtript.

sp.speaker: Lo. E.
sp.p: Hardly ſerue.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Though I ſwore I leapt from the window of the Citadell.

sp.speaker: Lo. E.
sp.p: How deepe?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Thirty fadome.

sp.speaker: Lo. E.
sp.p: Three great oathes would ſcarſe make that be beleeued.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I would I had any drumme of the enemies, I would ſweare I recouer'd it.

sp.speaker: Lo. E.
sp.p: You ſhall heare one anon.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: A drumme now of the enemies.

p.hi: Cargo, cargo, cargo, villianda par corbo, cargo.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: O ranſome, ranſome,
Do not hide mine eyes.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I know you are the Mu • kos Regiment,
And I ſhall looſe my life for want of language.
If there be heere German or Dane, Low Dutch,
Italian, or French, let him ſpeake to me,
Ile diſcouer that, which ſhal vndo the Florentine.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Boskos vauvado, I vnderſtand thee, & can ſpeake thy tongue: Kerelybonto ſir, betake thee to thy faith, for ſeuenteene ponyards are at thy boſome.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Inter.
sp.l: Oh pray, pray, pray,

l.hi: Manka re • ania dulche.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.l: The Generall is content to ſpare thee yet,
And hoodwinkt as thou art, will leade thee on
To gather from thee. Haply thou mayſt informe
Something to ſaue thy life.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: O let me liue,
And all the ſecrets of our campe Ile ſhew,
Their force, their purpoſes: Nay, Ile ſpeake that,
Which you will wonder at.

sp.speaker: Inter.
sp.p: But wilt thou faithfully?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: If I do not, damne me.

sp.speaker: Inter.

l.hi: Acordo linta.

sp.l: Come on, thou are granted ſpace.

sp.speaker: L.E.
sp.l: Go tell the Count Roſſillion and my brother,
We haue caught the woodcocke, and will keepe him mufled
Till we do heare from them.

sp.speaker: Sol.
sp.p: Captaine I will.

sp.speaker: L.E.
sp.l: A will betray vs all vnto our ſelues,
Informe on that.

sp.speaker: Sol.
sp.p: So I will ſir.

sp.speaker: L.E.
sp.p: Till then Ile keepe him darke and ſafely lockt.

div.stage: Enter Bertram, and the Maide called Diana.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: They told me that your name was Fontybell.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: No my good Lord, Diana.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Titled Goddeſſe,
And worth it with addition: but faire ſoule,
In your fine frame hath loue no qualitie?
If the quicke fire of youth light not your minde,
You are no Maiden but a monument
When you are dead you ſhould be ſuch a one
As you are now: for you are cold and ſterne,
And now you ſhould be as your mother was

When your ſweet ſelf •
▪ was got.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: She then was honeſt.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: So ſhould you be.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: No:
My mother did but dutie, ſuch (my Lord)
As you owe to your wife.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: No more a' that:
I prethee do not ſtriue againſt my vowes:
I was compell'd to her, but I loue thee
By loues owne ſweet conſtraint, and will for euer
Do thee all rights of ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: I ſo you ſerue vs
Till we ſerue you: But when you haue our Roſes,
You barely leaue our thornes to pricke our ſelues,
And mocke vs with our bareneſſe.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: How haue I ſworne.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: Tis not the many oathes that makes the truth,
But the plaine ſingle vow, that is vow'd true:
What is not holie, that we ſweare not by,
But take the high'ſt to witneſſe: then pray you tell me.
If I ſhould ſweare by Ioues great attributes,
I lou'd you deerely, would you beleeue my oathes,
When I did loue you ill? This ha's no holding
To ſweare by him whom I proteſt to loue
That I will worke againſt him. Therefore your oathes
Are words and poore conditions, but vnſeal'd
At leſt in my opinion.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Change it, change it:
Be not ſo holy cruell: Loue is holie,
And my integritie ne're knew the crafts
That you do charge men with: Stand no more off,
But giue thy ſelfe vnto my ſicke deſires,
Who then recouers. Say thou art mine, and euer
My loue as it beginnes, ſhall ſo perſeuer.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: I ſee that men make rope's in ſuch a ſcarre,
That wee'l forſake our ſelues. Giue me that Ring.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Ile lend it thee my deere; but haue no power
To giue it from me.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: Will you not my Lord?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: It is an honour longing to our houſe,
Bequeathed downe from manie Anceſtors,
Which were the greateſt obloquie i' th world,
In me to looſe.

sp.speaker: Dian.
sp.l: Mine Honors ſuch a Ring,
My chaſtities the Iewell of our houſe,
Bequeathed downe from many Anceſtors,
Which were the greateſt obloquie i' th world,
In mee to looſe. Thus your owne proper wiſedome
Brings in the Champion honor on my part,
Againſt your vaine aſſault.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Heere, take my Ring,
My houſe, mine honor, yea my life be thine,
And Ile be bid by thee.

sp.speaker: Dia▪
sp.l: When midnight comes, knocke at my chamber window:
Ile order take, my mother ſhall not heare.
Now will I charge you in the band of truth,
When you haue conquer'd my yet maiden-bed,
Remaine there but an houre, nor ſpeake to mee:
My reaſons are moſt ſtrong, and you ſhall know them,
When backe againe this Ring ſhall be deliuer'd:
And on your finger in the night, Ile put
Another Ring, that what in time proceeds,
May token to the future, our paſt deeds.
Adieu till then, then faile not: you haue wonne
A wife of me, though there my hope be done.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: A heauen on earth I haue won by wooing thee.

sp.speaker: Di.
sp.l: For which, liue long to thank both heauen & me,
You may ſo in the end.
My mother told me iuſt how he would woo,
As if ſhe ſate in's heart. She ſayes, all men
Haue the like oathes: He had ſworne to marrie me
When his wife's dead: therfore Ile lye with him
When I am buried. Since Frenchmen are ſo braide,
Marry that will, I liue and die a Maid:
Onely in this diſguiſe, I think't no ſinne,
To coſen him that would vniuſtly winne.

div.stage: Enter the two French Captaines, and ſome two or three Souldiours.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: You haue not giuen him his mothers letter.

sp.speaker: Cap E.
sp.p: I haue deliu'red it an houre ſince, there is ſom thing in't that ſtings his nature: for on the reading it, he chang'd almoſt into another man.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: He has much worthy blame laid vpon him, for ſhaking off ſo good a wife, and ſo ſweet a Lady.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: Eſpecially, hee hath incurred the euerlaſting diſpleaſure of the King, who had euen tun'd his bounty to ſing happineſſe to him. I will tell you a thing, but you ſhall let it dwell darkly with you.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: When you haue ſpoken it 'tis dead, and I am the graue of it.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: Hee hath peruerted a young Gentlewoman heere in Florence, of a moſt chaſte renown, & this night he fleſhes his will in the ſpoyle of her honour: hee hath giuen her his monumentall Ring, and thinkes himſelfe made in the vnchaſte compoſition.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: Now God delay our rebellion as we are our ſelues, what things are we.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: Meerely our owne traitours. And as in the common courſe of all treaſons, we ſtill ſee them reueale themſelues, till they attaine to their abhorr'd ends: ſo he that in this action contriues againſt his owne Nobility in his proper ſtreame, ore-flowes himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: Is it not meant damnable in vs, to be Trumpeters of our vnlawfull intents? We ſhall not then haue his company to night?

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: Not till after midnight: for hee is dieted to his houre.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p:
That approaches apace: I would gladly haue him ſee his company anathomiz'd, that hee might take
a meaſure of his owne iudgements, wherein ſo curiouſly he had ſet this counterfeit.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: We will not meddle with him till he come; for his preſence muſt be the whip of the other.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: In the meane time, what heare you of theſe Warres?

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: I heare there is an ouerture of peace.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: Nay, I aſſure you a peace concluded.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: What will Count Roſſillion do then? Will he trauaile higher, or returne againe into France?

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: I perceiue by this demand, you are not altogether of his councell.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: Let it be forbid ſir, ſo ſhould I bee a great deale of his act.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: Sir, his wife ſome two months ſince fledde from his houſe, her pretence is a pilgrimage to Saint Iaques le grand; which holy vndertaking, with moſt auſtere ſanctimonie ſhe accompliſht: and there reſiding, the tenderneſſe of her Nature, became as a prey to her greefe: in fine, made a groane of her laſt breath, & now ſhe ſings in heauen.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: How is this iuſtified?

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: The ſtronger part of it by her owne Letters, which makes her ſtorie true, euen to the poynt of her death: her death it ſelfe, which could not be her office to ſay, is come: was faithfully confirm'd by the Rector of the place.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: Hath the Count all this intelligence?

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: I, and the particular confirmations, point from point, to the full arming of the veritie.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: I am heartily ſorrie that hee'l bee gladde of this.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: How mightily ſometimes, we make vs comforts of our loſſes.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: And how mightily ſome other times, wee drowne our gaine in teares, the great dignitie that his valour hath here acquir'd for him, ſhall at home be encountred with a ſhame as ample.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: The webbe of our life, is of a mingled yarne, good and ill together: our vertues would bee proud, if our faults whipt them not, and our crimes would diſpaire if they were not cheriſh'd by our vertues.
How now? Where's your maſter?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: He met the Duke in the ſtreet ſir, of whom hee hath taken a ſolemne leaue: his Lordſhippe will next morning for France. The Duke hath offered him Letters of commendations to the King.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: They ſhall bee no more then needfull there, if they were more then they can commend.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: They cannot be too ſweete for the Kings tartneſſe, heere's his Lordſhip now. How now my Lord, i'ſt not after midnight?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I haue to night diſpatch'd ſixteene buſineſſes, a moneths length a peece, by an abſtract of ſucceſſe: I haue congied with the Duke, done my adieu with his neereſt; buried a wife, mourn'd for her▪ writ to my Ladie mother, I am returning, entertain'd my Conuoy, & betweene theſe maine parcels of diſpatch, affected many nicer needs: the laſt was the greateſt, but that I haue not ended yet.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: If the buſineſſe bee of any difficulty, and this morning your departure hence, it requires haſt of your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I meane the buſineſſe is not ended, as fearing to heare of it hereafter: but ſhall we haue this dialogue betweene the Foole and the Soldiour. Come, bring forth this counterfet module, ha • s deceiu'd mee, like a double-meaning Propheſier.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: Bring him forth, ha's ſate i' th ſtockes all night poore gallant knaue.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: No matter, his heeles haue deſeru'd it, in vſurping his ſpurres ſo long. How does he carry himſelfe?

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: I haue told your Lordſhip alreadie: The ſtockes carrie him. But to anſwer you as you would be vnderſtood, hee weepes like a wench that had ſhed her milke, he hath confeſt himſelfe to Morgan, whom hee ſuppoſes to be a Friar, frō the time of his remembrance to this very inſtant diſaſter of his ſetting i' th ſtockes: and what thinke you he hath confeſt?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Nothing of me, ha's a?

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: His confeſſion is taken, and it ſhall bee read to his face, if your Lordſhippe be in't, as I beleeue you are, you muſt haue the patience to heare it.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: A plague vpon him, muffeld; he can ſay nothing of me: huſh, huſh.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: Hoodman comes: Portotartaroſſa.

sp.speaker: Inter.
sp.p: He calles for the tortures, what will you ſay without em.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: I will confeſſe what I know without conſtraint,
If ye pinch me like a Paſty, I can ſay no more.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: You are a mercifull Generall: Our Generall bids you anſwer to what I ſhall aske you out of a Note.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: And truly, as I hope to liue.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Firſt demand of him, how many horſe the Duke is ſtrong. What ſay you to that?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Fiue or ſixe thouſand, but very weake and vnſeruiceable: the troopes are all ſcattered, and the Commanders verie poore rogues, vpon my reputation and credit, and as I hope to liue.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Shall I ſet downe your anſwer ſo?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Do, Ile take the Sacrament on't, how & which way you will: all's one to him.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: What a paſt-ſauing ſlaue is this?

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: Y'are deceiu'd my Lord, this is Mounſieur Parrolles the gallant militariſt, that was his owne phraſe that had the whole theoricke of warre in the knot of his ſcarfe, and the practiſe in the chape of his dagger.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: I will neuer truſt a man againe, for keeping his ſword cleane, nor beleeue he can haue euerie thing in him, by wearing his apparrell neatly.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Well, that's ſet downe.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Fiue or ſix thouſand horſe I ſed, I will ſay true, or thereabouts ſet downe, for Ile ſpeake truth.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: He's very neere the truth in this.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: But I con him no thankes for't in the nature he deliuers it.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Poore rogues, I pray you ſay.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Well, that's ſet downe.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I humbly thanke you ſir, a truth's a truth, the Rogues are maruailous poore.

sp.speaker: Interp.
sp.p: Demaund of him of what ſtrength they are a foot. What ſay you to that?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p:
By my troth ſir, if I were to liue this preſent houre, I will tell true. Let me ſee, Spurio a hundred &
fiftie, Sebaſtian ſo many, Corambus ſo many, Iaques ſo many: Guiltian, Coſmo, Lodowicke, and Gratij, two hundred fiftie each: Mine owne Company, Chitopher, Ʋaumond, Bentij, two hundred fiftie each: ſo that the muſter file, rotten and ſound, vppon my life amounts not to fifteene thouſand pole, halfe of the which, dare not ſhake the ſnow from off their Caſſockes, leaſt they ſhake themſelues to peeces.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: What ſhall be done to him?

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: Nothing, but let him haue thankes. Demand of him my condition: and what credite I haue with the Duke.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Well that's ſet downe: you ſhall demaund of him, whether one Captaine Dumaine bee i' th Campe, a Frenchman: what his reputation is with the Duke, what his valour, honeſtie, and expertneſſe in warres: or whether he thinkes it were not poſſible with well-waighing ſummes of gold to corrupt him to a reuolt. What ſay you to this? What do you know of it?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I beſeech you let me anſwer to the particular of the intergatories. Demand them ſingly.

sp.speaker: Int,
sp.p: Do you know this Captaine Dumaine?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I know him, a was a Botchers Prentize in Paris, from whence he was whipt for getting the Shrieues fool with childe, a dumbe innocent that could not ſay him nay.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Nay, by your leaue hold your hands, though I know his braines are forfeite to the next tile that fals.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Well, is this Captaine in the Duke of Florences campe?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Vpon my knowledge he is, and lowſie.

sp.speaker: Cay. G.
sp.p: Nay looke not ſo vpon me: we ſhall heare of your Lord anon.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: What is his reputation with the Duke?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: The Duke knowes him for no other, but a poore Officer of mine, and writ to mee this other day, to turne him out a' th band. I thinke I haue his Letter in my pocket.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Marry we'll ſearch.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: In good ſadneſſe I do not know, either it is there, or it is vpon a file with the Dukes other Letters, in my Tent.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Heere 'tis, heere's a paper, ſhall I reade it to you?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I do not know if it be it or no.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Our Interpreter do's it well.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: Excellently.

p.hi: Dian, the Counts a foole, and full of gold.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: That is not the Dukes letter ſir: that is an aduertiſement to a proper maide in Florence, one Diana, to take heede of the allurement of one Count Roſſillion, a fooliſh idle boy: but for all that very ruttiſh. I pray you ſir put it vp againe.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Nay, Ile reade it firſt by your fauour.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: My meaning in't I proteſt was very honeſt in the behalfe of the maid: for I knew the young Count to be a dangerous and laſciuious boy, who is a whale to Virginity and deuours vp all the fry it finds.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Damnable both-ſides rogue.

sp.speaker: Int Let.

l.hi: When he ſweares oathes, hid him drop gold, and take it:
After he ſcores, he neuer payes the ſcore:
Halfe won is match well made, match and well make it,
He nere payes after debts, take it before,
And ſay a ſouldier (Dian) told thee this:
Men are to mell with, boyes are not to kis.
For count of this, the Counts a Fool • I know it,
Who payes before, but not when he does owe it.

sp.l: Thine as he vow'd to thee in thine eare,

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: He ſhall be whipt through the Armie with this rime in's forehead.

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: This is your deuoted friend ſir, the manifold Linguiſt, and the army-potent ſouldier.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I could endure any thing before but a Cat, and now he's a Cat to me.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: I perceiue ſir by your Generals lookes, wee ſhall be faine to hang you.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: My life ſir in any caſe: Not that I am afraide to dye, but that my offences beeing many, I would repent out the remainder of Nature. Let me liue ſir in a dungeon, i' th ſtockes, or any where, ſo I may liue.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Wee'le ſee what may bee done, ſo you confeſſe freely: therefore once more to this Captaine Dumaine: you haue anſwer'd to his reputation with the Duke, and to his valour. What is his honeſtie?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: He will ſteale ſir an Egge out of a Cloiſter: for rapes and rauiſhments he paralels Neſſus. Hee profeſſes not keeping of oaths, in breaking em he is ſtronger then Hercules. He will lye ſir, with ſuch volubilitie, that you would thinke truth were a foole: drunkenneſſe is his beſt vertue, for he will be ſwine-drunke, and in his ſleepe he does little harme, ſaue to his bed-cloathes about him: but they know his conditions, and lay him in ſtraw. I haue but little more to ſay ſir of his honeſty, he ha's euerie thing that an honeſt man ſhould not haue; what an honeſt man ſhould haue, he has nothing.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: I begin to loue him for this.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: For this deſcription of thine honeſtie? A pox vpon him for me, he's more and more a Cat.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: What ſay you to his expertneſſe in warre?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Faith ſir, ha's led the drumme before the Engliſh Tragedians: to belye him I will not, and more of his ſouldierſhip I know not, except in that Country, he had the honour to be the Officer at a place there called Mile-end, to inſtruct for the doubling of files. I would doe the man what honour I can, but of this I am not certaine.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: He hath out-villain'd villanie ſo farre, that the raritie redeemes him.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: A pox on him, he's a Cat ſtill.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: His qualities being at this poore price. I neede not to aske you, if Gold will corrupt him to reuolt.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Sir, for a Cardceue he will ſell the fee-ſimple of his ſaluation, the inheritance of it, and cut th' intaile from all remainders, and a perpetuall ſucceſsion for it perpetually.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: What's his Brother, the other Captain Dumain?

sp.speaker: Cap. E.
sp.p: Why do's he aske him of me?

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: What's he?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: E'ne a Crow a' th ſame neſt: not altogether ſo great as the firſt in goodneſſe, but greater a great deale in euill. He excels his Brother for a coward, yet his Brother is reputed one of the beſt that is. In a retreate hee outrunnes any Lackey; marrie in comming on, hee ha's the Crampe.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: If your life be ſaued, will you vndertake to betray the Florentine.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I, and the Captaine of his horſe, Count Roſſillion.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: Ile whiſper with the Generall, and knowe his pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p:
Ile no more drumming, a plague of all drummes, onely to ſeeme to deſerue well, and to beguile the ſuppoſition
o' that laſciuious yong boy the Count, haue I run into this danger: yet who would haue ſuſpected an ambuſh where I was taken?

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: There is no remedy ſir, but you muſt dye: the Generall ſayes, you that haue ſo traitorouſly diſcouerd the ſecrets of your army, and made ſuch peſtifferous reports of men very nobly held, can ſerue the world for no honeſt vſe: therefore you muſt dye. Come headeſman, off with his head.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: O Lord ſir let me liue, or let me ſee my death.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.l: That ſhall you, and take your leaue of all your friends:
So, looke about you, know you any heere?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Good morrow noble Captaine.

sp.speaker: Lo. E.
sp.p: God bleſſe you Captaine Parolles.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: God ſaue you noble Captaine.

sp.speaker: Lo. E.
sp.p: Captain, what greeting will you to my Lord Lafew? I am for France.

sp.speaker: Cap. G.
sp.p: Good Captaine will you giue me a Copy of the ſonnet you writ to Diana in behalfe of the Count Roſſillion, and I were not a verie Coward, I'de compell it of you, but far you well.

sp.speaker: Int.
sp.p: You are vndone Captaine all but your ſcarfe, that has a knot on't yet.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Who cannot be cruſh'd with a plot?

sp.speaker: Inter.
sp.p: If you could finde out a Countrie where but women were that had receiued ſo much ſhame, you might begin an impudent Nation. Fare yee well ſir, I am for France too, we ſhall ſpeake of you there.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.l: Yet am I thankfull: if my heart were great
'Twould burſt at this: Captaine Ile be no more,
But I will eate, and drinke, and ſleepe as ſoft
As Captaine ſhall. Simply the thing I am
Shall make me liue: who knowes himſelfe a braggart
Let him feare this; for it will come to paſſe,
That euery braggart ſhall be found an Aſſe.
Ruſt ſword, coole bluſhes, and Parrolles liue
Safeſt in ſhame: being fool'd, by fool'rie thriue;
There's place and meanes for euery man aliue.
Ile after them.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: That you may well perceiue I haue not wrong'd you,
One of the greateſt in the Chriſtian world
Shall be my ſuretie: for whoſe throne 'tis needfull
Ere I can perfect mine intents, to kneele.
Time was, I did him a deſired office
Deere almoſt as his life, which gratitude
Through flintie Tartars boſome would peepe forth,
And anſwer thankes. I duly am inform'd,
His grace is at Marcellae, to which place
We haue conuenient conuoy: you muſt know
I am ſuppoſed dead, the Army breaking,
My husband hies him home, where heauen ayding,
And by the leaue of my good Lord the King,
Wee'l be before our welcome.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: Gentle Madam,
You neuer had a ſeruant to whoſe truſt
Your buſines was more welcome.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Nor your Miſtris
Euer a friend, whoſe thoughts more truly labour
To recompence your loue: Doubt not but heauen
Hath brought me vp to be your daughters dower,
As it hath fated her to be my motiue
And helper to a husband. But O ſtrange men,
That can ſuch ſweet vſe make of what they hate,
When ſawcie truſting of the coſin'd thoughts
Defiles the pitchy night, ſo luſt doth play
With what it loathes, for that which is away,
But more of this heereafter: you Diana,
Vnder my poore inſtructions yet muſt ſuffer
Something in my behalfe.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: Let death and honeſtie
Go with your impoſitions, I am yours
Vpon your will to ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Yet I pray you:
But with the word the time will bring on ſummer,
When Briars ſhall haue leaues as well as thornes,
And be as ſweet as ſharpe: we muſt away,
Our Wagon is prepar'd, and time reuiues vs,
All's well that ends well, ſtill the fines the Crowne;
What ere the courſe, the end is the renowne.

div.stage: Enter Clowne, old Lady, and Lafew.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: No, no, no, your ſonne was miſled with a ſnipt taffata fellow there, whoſe villanous ſaffron wold haue made all the vnbak'd and dowy youth of a nation in his colour: your daughter-in-law had beene aliue at this houre, and your ſonne heere at home, more aduanc • d by the King, then by that red-tail'd humble Bee I ſpeak of.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: I would I had not knowne him, it was the death of the moſt vertuous gentlewoman, that euer Nature had praiſe for creating. If ſhe had pertaken of my fleſh and coſt mee the deereſt groanes of a mother, I could not haue owed her a more rooted loue.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Twas a good Lady, 'twas a good Lady. Wee may picke a thouſand ſallets ere wee light on ſuch another hearbe.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Indeed ſir ſhe was the ſweete Margerom of the ſallet, or rather the hearbe of grace.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: They are not hearbes you knaue, they are noſe-hearbes.

sp.speaker: Clowne.
sp.p: I am no great Nabuchadnezar ſir, I haue not much skill in grace.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Whether doeſt thou profeſſe thy ſelfe, a knaue or a foole?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: A foole ſir at a womans ſeruice, and a knaue at a mans.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Your diſtinction.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I would couſen the man of his wife, and do his ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: So you were a knaue at his ſeruice indeed.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: And I would giue his wife my bauble ſir to doe her ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I will ſubſcribe for thee, thou art both knaue and foole.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: At your ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: No, no, no.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Why ſir, if I cannot ſerue you, I can ſerue as great a prince as you are.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Whoſe that, a Frenchman?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Faith ſir a has an Engliſh maine, but his fiſnomie is more hotter in France then there.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: What prince is that?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: The blacke prince ſir, alias the prince of darkeneſſe, alias the diuell.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Hold thee there's my purſe, I giue thee not this to ſuggeſt thee from thy maſter thou talk'ſt off, ſerue him ſtill.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I am a woodland fellow ſir, that alwaies loued a great fire, and the maſter I ſpeak of euer keeps a good fire, but ſure he is the Prince of the world, let his Nobilitie remaine in's Court. I am for the houſe with the narrow gate, which I take to be too little for pompe to enter: ſome that humble themſelues may, but the manie will be too chill and tender, and theyle bee for the flowrie way that leads to the broad gate, and the great fire.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Go thy waies, I begin to bee a wearie of thee, and I tell thee ſo before, becauſe I would not fall out with thee. Go thy wayes, let my horſes be wel look'd too, without any trickes.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: If I put any trickes vpon em ſir, they ſhall bee Iades trickes, which are their owne right by the law of Nature.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: A ſhrewd knaue and an vnhappie.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: So a is. My Lord that's gone made himſelfe much ſport out of him, by his authoritie hee remaines heere, which he thinkes is a pattent for his ſawcineſſe, and indeede he has no pace, but runnes where he will.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I like him well, 'tis not amiſſe: and I was about to tell you, ſince I heard of the good Ladies death, and that my Lord your ſonne was vpon his returne home. I moued the King my maſter to ſpeake in the behalfe of my daughter, which in the minoritie of them both, his Maieſtie out of a ſelfe gracious remembrance did firſt propoſe, his Highneſſe hath promis'd me to doe it, and to ſtoppe vp the diſpleaſure he hath conceiued againſt your ſonne, there is no fitter matter. How do's your Ladyſhip like it?

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: With verie much content my Lord, and I wiſh it happily effected.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: His Highneſſe comes poſt from Marcellus, of as able bodie as when he number'd thirty, a will be heere to morrow, or I am deceiu'd by him that in ſuch intelligence hath ſeldome fail'd.

sp.speaker: La.
sp.p: Ir reioyces me, that I hope I ſhall ſee him ere I die. I haue letters that my ſonne will be heere to night: I ſhall beſeech your Lordſhip to remaine with mee, till they meete together.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Madam, I was thinking with what manners I might ſafely be admitted.

sp.speaker: Lad.
sp.p: You neede but pleade your honourable priuiledge.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Ladie, of that I haue made a bold charter, but I thanke my God, it holds yet.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O Madam, yonders my Lord your ſonne with a patch of veluet on's face, whether there bee a ſcar vnder't or no, the Veluet knowes, but 'tis a goodly patch of Veluet, his left cheeke is a cheeke of two pile and a halfe, but his right cheeke is worne bare.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.l: A ſcarre nobly got,
Or a noble ſcarre, is a good liu'rie of honor,
So belike is that.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: But it is your carbinado'd face.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.l: Let vs go ſee
your ſonne I pray you, I long to talke
With the yong noble ſouldier.

sp.speaker: Clowne.
sp.p: Faith there's a dozen of em, with delicate fine hats, and moſt courteous feathers, which bow the head, and nod at euerie man.

div.head: Actus Quintus.
div.stage: Enter Hellen, Widdow, and Diana, with two Attendants.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: But this exceeding poſting day and night,
Muſt wear your ſpirits low, we cannot helpe it:
But ſince you haue made the daies and nights as one,
To weare your gentle limbes in my affayres,
Be bold you do ſo grow in my requitall,
As nothing can vnroote you. In happie time,
This man may helpe me to his Maieſties eare,
If he would ſpend his power. God ſaue you ſir.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: And you.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Sir, I haue ſeene you in the Court of France.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: I haue beene ſometimes there.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: I do preſume ſir, that you are not falne
From the report that goes vpon your goodneſſe,
And therefore goaded with moſt ſharpe occaſions,
Which lay nice manners by, I put you to
The vſe of your owne vertues, for the which
I ſhall continue thankefull.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: What's your will?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: That it will pleaſe you
To giue this poore petition to the King,
And ayde me with that ſtore of power you haue
To come into his preſence.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.p: The Kings not heere.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Not heere ſir?

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Not indeed,
He hence remou'd laſt night, and with more haſt
Then is his vſe.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Lord how we looſe our paines.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: All's well that ends well yet,
Though time ſeeme ſo aduerſe, and meanes vnfit:
I do beſeech you, whither is he gone?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.l: Marrie as I take it to Roſſillion,
Whither I am going.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: I do beſeech you ſir,
Since you are like to ſee the King before me,
Commend the paper to his gracious hand,
Which I preſume ſhall render you no blame,
But rather make you thanke your paines for it,
I will come after you with what good ſpeede
Our meanes will make vs meanes.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: This Ile do for you.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: And you ſhall finde your ſelfe to be well thankt what e're falles more. We muſt to horſe againe, Go, go, prouide.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Good Mr Lauatch giue my Lord Lafew this letter, I haue ere now ſir beene better knowne to you, when I haue held familiaritie with freſher cloathes: but I am now ſir muddied in fortunes mood, and ſmell ſomewhat ſtrong of her ſtrong diſpleaſure.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Truely, Fortunes diſpleaſure is but ſluttiſh if it ſmell ſo ſtrongly as thou ſpeak'ſt of: I will hencefoorth eate no Fiſh of Fortunes butt'ring. Pre thee alow the winde.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Nay you neede not to ſtop your noſe ſir: I ſpake but by a Metaphor.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Indeed ſir, if your Metaphor ſtinke, I will ſtop my noſe, or againſt any mans Metaphor. Prethe get thee further.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Pray you ſir deliuer me this paper.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Foh, prethee ſtand away: a paper from fortunes cloſe-ſtoole, to giue to a Nobleman. Looke heere he comes himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Heere is a purre of Fortunes ſir, or of Fortunes Cat, but not a Muſcat, that ha's falne into the vncleane fiſh-pond of her diſpleaſure, and as he ſayes is muddied withall. Pray you ſir, vſe the Carpe as you may, for he lookes like a poore decayed, ingenious, fooliſh, raſcally knaue. I doe pittie his diſtreſſe in my ſmiles of comfort, and leaue him to your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: My Lord I am a man whom fortune hath cruelly ſcratch'd.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: And what would you haue me to doe? 'Tis too late to paire her nailes now. Wherein haue you played the knaue with fortune that ſhe ſhould ſcratch you, who of her ſelfe is a good Lady, and would not haue knaues thriue long vnder? There's a Cardecue for you: Let the Iuſtices make you and fortune friends; I am for other buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I beſeech your honour to heare mee one ſingle word▪

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: you begge a ſingle peny more: Come you ſhall ha • t, ſaue your word.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: My name my good Lord is Parrolles.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: You begge more then word then. Cox my paſſion, giue me your hand: How does your drumme?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: O my good Lord, you were the firſt that found mee.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Was I inſooth? And I was the firſt that loſt thee.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: It lies in you my Lord to bring me in ſome grace for you did bring me out.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Out vpon thee knaue, doeſt thou put vpon mee at once both the offiee of God and the diuel: one brings thee in grace, and the other brings thee out. The Kings comming I know by his Trumpets. Sirrah, inquire further after me, I had talke of you laſt night, though you are a foole and a knaue, you ſhall eate, go too, follow.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I praiſe God for you.

div.stage: Enter King, old Lady, Lafew, the two French Lords, with attendants.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: We loſt a Iewell of her, and our eſteeme
Was made much poorer by it: but your ſonne,
As mad in folly, lack'd the ſence to know
Her eſtimation home.

sp.speaker: Old La.
sp.l: 'Tis paſt my Liege,
And I beſeech your Maieſtie to make it
Naturall rebellion, done i' th blade of youth,
When oyle and fire, too ſtrong for reaſons force,
Ore-beares it, and burnes on.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: My honour'd Lady,
I haue forgiuen and forgotten all,
Though my reuenges were high bent vpon him,
And watch'd the time to ſhoote.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.l: This I muſt ſay,
But firſt I begge my pardon: the yong Lord
Did to his Maieſty, his Mother, and his Ladie,
Offence of mighty note; but to himſelfe
The greateſt wrong of all. He loſt a wife,
Whoſe beauty did aſtoniſh the ſuruey
Of richeſt eies: whoſe words all eares tooke captiue,
Whoſe deere perfection, hearts that ſcorn'd to ſerue,
Humbly call'd Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Praiſing what is loſt,
Makes the remembrance deere. Well, call him hither,
We are reconcil'd, and the firſt view ſhall kill
All repetition: Let him not aske our pardon,
The nature of his great offence is dead,
And deeper then obliuion, we do burie
Th' incenſing reliques of it. Let him approach
A ſtranger, no offender; and informe him
So 'tis our will he ſhould▪

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: I ſhall my Liege.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: What ſayes he to your daughter,
Haue you ſpoke?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: All that he is, hath reference to your Highnes.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Then ſhall we haue a match. I haue letters ſent me, that ſets him high in fame.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: He lookes well on't.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: I am not a day of ſeaſon,
For thou maiſt ſee a ſun-ſhine, and a haile
In me at once: But to the brighteſt beames
Diſtracted clouds giue way, ſo ſtand thou forth,
The time is faire againe.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: My high repented blames
Deere Soueraigne pardon to me.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: All is whole,
Not one word more of the conſumed time,
Let's take the inſtant by the forward top:
For we are old, and on our quick'ſt decrees
Th' inaudible, and noiſeleſſe foot of time
Steales, ere we can effect them. You remember
The daughter of this Lord?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: Admiringly my Liege, at firſt
I ſtucke my choice vpon her, ere my heart
Durſt make too bold a herauld of my tongue:
Where the impreſſion of mine eye enfixing,
Contempt his ſcornfull Perſpectiue did lend me,
Which warpt the line, of euerie other fauour,
Scorn'd a faire colour, or expreſt it ſtolne,
Extended or contracted all proportions
To a moſt hideous obiect. Thence it came,
That ſhe whom all men prais'd, and whom my ſelfe,
Since I haue loſt, haue lou'd; was in mine eye
The duſt that did offend it.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Well excus'd:
That thou didſt loue her, ſtrikes ſome ſcores away
From the great compt: but loue that comes too late,
Like a remorſefull pardon ſlowly carried
To the great ſender, turnes a ſowre offence,
Crying, that's good that's gone: Our raſh faults,
Make triuiall price of ſerious things we haue,
Not knowing them, vntill we know their graue,
Oft our diſpleaſures to our ſelues vniuſt,
Deſtroy our friends, and after weepe their duſt:
Our owne loue waking, cries to ſee what's don,e
While ſhamefull hate ſleepes out the afternoone.
Be this ſweet Helens knell, and now forget her.
Send forth your amorous token for faire Maudlin,
The maine conſents are had, and heere wee'l ſtay
To ſee our widdowers ſecond marriage day:
Which better then the firſt, O deere heauen bleſſe,
Or, ere they meete in me, O Nature ceſſe.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.l: Come on my ſonne, in whom my houſes name
Muſt be digeſted: giue a fauour from you
To ſparkle in the ſpirits of my daughter,
That ſhe may quickly come. By my old beard,
And eu'rie haire that's on't, Helen that's dead
Was a ſweet creature: ſuch a ring as this,
The laſt that ere I tooke her leaue at Court,
I ſaw vpon her finger.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Hers it was not.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Now pray you let me ſee it. For mine eye,
While I was ſpeaking, oft was faſten'd too't:
This Ring was mine, and when I gaue it Hellen,
I bad her if her fortunes euer ſtoode
Neceſſitied to helpe, that by this token
I would releeue her. Had you that craft to reaue her
Of what ſhould ſtead her moſt?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: My gracious Soueraigne,
How ere it pleaſes you to take it ſo,
The ring was neuer hers.

sp.speaker: Old La.
sp.l: Sonne, on my life
I haue ſeene her weare it, and ſhe reckon'd it
At her liues rate.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I am ſure I ſaw her weare it.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: You are deceiu'd my Lord, ſhe neuer ſaw it:
In Florence was it from a caſement throwne mee,
Wrap'd in a paper, which contain'd the name
Of her that threw it: Noble ſhe was, and thought
I ſtood ingag'd▪ but when I had ſubſcrib'd
To mine owne fortune, and inform'd her fully,
I could not anſwer in that courſe of Honour
As ſhe had made the ouerture, ſhe ceaſt
In heauie ſatisfaction, and would neuer
Receiue the Ring againe.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Platus himſelfe,
That knowes the tinct and multiplying med'cine,
Hath not in natures myſterie more ſcience,
Then I haue in this Ring. 'Twas mine, 'twas Helens,
Who euer gaue it you: then if you know
That you are well acquainted with your ſelfe,
Confeſſe 'twas hers, and by what rough enforcement
You got it from her. She call'd the Saints to ſuretie,
That ſhe would neuer put it from her finger,
Vnleſſe ſhe gaue it to your ſelfe in bed,
Where you haue neuer come: or ſent it vs
Vpon her great diſaſter.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: She neuer ſaw it.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Thou ſpeak'ſt it falſely: as I loue mine Honor,
And mak'ſt connecturall feares to come into me,
Which I would faine ſhut out, if it ſhould proue
That thou art ſo inhumane, 'twill not proue ſo:
And yet I know not, thou didſt hate her deadly,
And ſhe is dead, which nothing but to cloſe
Her eyes my ſelfe, could win me to beleeue,
More then to ſee this Ring. Take him away,
My fore-paſt proofes, how ere the matter fall
Shall taze my feares of little vanitie,
Hauing vainly fear'd too little. Away with him,
Wee'l ſift this matter further.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: If you ſhall proue
This Ring was euer hers, you ſhall as eaſie
Proue that I husbanded her bed in Florence,
Where yet ſhe neuer was.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: I am wrap • d in diſmall thinkings.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.l: Gracious Soueraigne.
Whether I haue beene too blame or no, I know not,
Here's a petition from a Florentine,
Who hath for foure or fiue remoues come ſhort,
To tender it her ſelfe. I vndertooke it,
Vanquiſh'd thereto by the faire grace and ſpeech
Of the poore ſuppliant, who by this I know
Is heere attending: her buſineſſe lookes in her
With an importing viſage, and ſhe told me
In a ſweet verball breefe, it did concerne
Your Highneſſe with her ſelfe.

p.hi: Ʋpon his many proteſtations to marrie mee when his wife was dead, I bluſh to ſay it, he wonne me. Now is the Count Roſſillion a Widdower, his vowes are forfeited to mee, and my honors payed to him. Hee ſtole from Florence, taking no leaue, and I follow him to his Countrey for Iuſtice: Grant it me, O King, in you it beſt lies, otherwiſe a ſeducer flouriſhes, and a poore Maid is vndone.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I will buy me a ſonne in Law in a faire, and toule for this. Ile none of him.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: The heauens haue thought well on thee Lafew,
To bring forth this diſcou'rie, ſeeke theſe ſutors:
Go ſpeedily, and bring againe the Count.
I am a-feard the life of Hellen (Ladie)
Was fowly ſnatcht.

sp.speaker: Old La.
sp.p: Now iuſtice on the doers.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I wonder ſir, ſir, wiues are monſters to you,
And that you flye them as you ſweare them Lordſhip,
Yet you deſire to marry. What woman's that?

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: I am my Lord a wretched Florentine,
Deriued from the ancient Capilet,
My ſuite as I do vnderſtand you know,
And therefore know how farre I may be pittied.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.l: I am her Mother ſir, whoſe age and honour
Both ſuffer vnder this complaint we bring,
And both ſhall ceaſe, without your remedie.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Come hether Count, do you know theſe Women?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: My Lord, I neither can nor will denie,
But that I know them, do they charge me further?

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: Why do you looke ſo ſtrange vpon your wife?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: She's none of mine my Lord.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: If you ſhall marrie
You giue away this hand, and that is mine,
You giue away heauens vowes, and thoſe are mine:
You giue away my ſelfe, which is knowne mine:
For I by vow am ſo embodied yours,
That ſhe which marries you, muſt marrie me,
Either both or none.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: your reputation comes too ſhort for my daughter, you are no husband for her.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: My Lord, this is a fond and deſperate creature,
Whom ſometime I haue laugh'd with: Let your highnes
Lay a more noble thought vpon mine honour,
Then for to thinke that I would ſinke it heere.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Sir for my thoughts, you haue them il to friend,
Till your deeds gaine them fairer: proue your honor,
Then in my thought it lies.

sp.speaker: Dian.
sp.l: Good my Lord,
Aske him vpon his oath, if hee do's thinke
He had not my virginity.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: What ſaiſt thou to her?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.l: She's impudent my Lord,
And was a common gameſter to the Campe.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: He do's me wrong my Lord: If I were ſo,
He might haue bought me at a common price.
Do not beleeue him. O behold this Ring,
Whoſe high reſpect and rich validitie
Did lacke a Paralell: yet for all that
He gaue it to a Commoner a' th Campe
If I be one.

sp.speaker: Coun.
sp.l: He bluſhes, and 'tis hit:
Of ſixe preceding Anceſtors, that Iemme
Confer'd by teſtament to 'th ſequent iſſue
Hath it beene owed and worne. This is his wife,
That Ring's a thouſand proofes.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Me thought you ſaide
You ſaw one heere in Court could witneſſe it.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: I did my Lord, but loath am to produce
So bad an inſtrument, his names Parrolles.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I ſaw the man to day, if man he bee.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Finde him, and bring him hether.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: What of him:
He's quoted for a moſt pe fidious ſlaue
With all the ſpots a' th world, taxt and deboſh'd,
Whoſe nature ſickens: but to ſpeake a truth,
Am I, or that or this for what he'l vtter,
That will ſpeake any thing.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: She hath that Ring of yours.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: I thinke ſhe has; certaine it is I lyk'd her,
And boorded her i' th wanton way of youth:
She knew her diſtance, and did angle for mee,
Madding my eagerneſſe with her reſtraint,
As all impediments in fancies courſe
Are motiues of more fancie, and in fine,
Her inſuite comming with her moderne grace,
Subdu'd me to her rate, ſhe got the Ring,
And I had that which any inferiour might
At Market price haue bought.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: I muſt be patient:
You that haue turn'd off a firſt ſo noble wife,
May iuſtly dyet me. I pray you yet,
(Since you lacke vertue, I will looſe a husband)
Send for your Ring, I will returne it home,
And giue me mine againe.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: I haue it not.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: What Ring was yours I pray you?

sp.speaker: Dian.
sp.p: Sir much like the ſame vpon your finger.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Know you this Ring, this Ring was his of late.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: And this was it I gaue him being a bed.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: The ſtory then goes falſe, you threw it him
Out of a Caſement.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: I haue ſpoke the truth.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: My Lord, I do confeſſe the ring was hers.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: You boggle ſhrewdly, euery feather ſtarts you:
Is this the man you ſpeake of?

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: I, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Tell me ſirrah, but tell me true I charge you,
Not fearing the diſpleaſure of your maſter:
Which on your iuſt proceeding, Ile keepe off,
By him and by this woman heere, what know you?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: So pleaſe your Maieſty, my maſter hath bin an honourable Gentleman. Trickes hee hath had in him, which Gentlemen haue.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Come, come, to' th' purpoſe: Did hee loue this woman?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Faith ſir he did loue her, but how.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: How I pray you?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: He did loue her ſir, as a Gent. loues a Woman.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: How is that?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: He lou'd her ſir, and lou'd her not.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: As thou art a knaue and no knaue, what an equiuocall Companion is this?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I am a poore man, and at your Maieſties command.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Hee's a good drumme my Lord, but a naughtie Orator.

sp.speaker: Dian.
sp.p: Do you know he promiſt me marriage?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Faith I know more then Ile ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: But wilt thou not ſpeake all thou know'ſt?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Yes ſo pleaſe your Maieſty: I did goe betweene them as I ſaid, but more then that he loued her, for indeede he was madde for her, and talkt of Sathan, and of Limbo, and of Furies, and I know not what: yet I was in that credit with them at that time, that I knewe of their going to bed, and of other motions, as promiſing her marriage, and things which would deriue mee ill will to ſpeake of, therefore I will not ſpeake what I know.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Thou haſt ſpoken all alreadie, vnleſſe thou canſt ſay they are maried, but thou art too fine in thy euidence, therefore ſtand aſide. This Ring you ſay was yours.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: I my good Lord.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Where did you buy it? Or who gaue it you?

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: It was not giuen me, nor I did not buy it.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Who lent it you?

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: It was not lent me neither.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Where did you finde it then?

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: I found it not.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: If it were yours by none of all theſe wayes,
How could you giue it him?

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: I neuer gaue it him.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: This womans an eaſie gloue my Lord, ſhe goes off and on at pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: This Ring was mine, I gaue it his firſt wife.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: It might be yours or hers for ought I know.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Take her away, I do not like her now,
To priſon with her: and away with him,
Vnleſſe thou telſt me where thou hadſt this Ring,
Thou dieſt within this houre.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: Ile neuer tell you.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Take her away.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: Ile put in baile my liedge.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: I thinke thee now ſome common Cuſtomer.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: By Ioue if euer I knew man 'twas you.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Wherefore haſt thou accuſde him al this while.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: Becauſe he's guiltie, and he is not guilty:
He knowes I am no Maid, and hee'l ſweare too't:
Ile ſweare I am a Maid, and he knowes not.
Great King I am no ſtrumpet, by my life,
I am either Maid, or elſe this old mans wife.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: She does abuſe our eares, to priſon with her.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.l: Good mother fetch my bayle. Stay Royall ſir,
The Ieweller that owes the Ring is ſent for,
And he ſhall ſurety me. But for this Lord,
Who hath abus'd me as he knowes himſelfe,
Though yet he neuer harm'd me, heere I quit him.
He knowes himſelfe my bed he hath defil'd,
And at that time he got his wife with childe:
Dead though ſhe be, ſhe feeles her yong one kicke:
So there's my riddle, one that's dead is quicke,
And now behold the meaning.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: Is there no exorciſt
Beguiles the truer Office of mine eyes?
Is't reall that I ſee?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: No my good Lord,
'Tis but the ſhadow of a wife you ſee,
The name, and not the thing.

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.p: Both, both, O pardon.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: Oh my good Lord, when I was like this Maid,
I found you wondrous kinde, there is your Ring,
And looke you, heeres your letter: this it ſayes,
When from my finger you can get this Ring,
And is by me with childe, &c. This is done,
Will you be mine now you are doubly wonne?

sp.speaker: Roſ.
sp.l: If ſhe my Liege can make me know this clearly,
Ile loue her dearely, euer, euer dearly.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.l: If it appeare not plaine, and proue vntrue,
Deadly diuorce ſtep betweene me and you.
O my deere mother do I ſee you liuing?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.l: Mine eyes ſmell Onions, I ſhall weepe anon:
Good Tom Drumme lend me a handkercher.
So I thanke thee, waite on me home, Ile make ſport with thee: Let thy curtſies alone, they are ſcuruy ones.

sp.speaker: King
sp.l: Let vs from point to point this ſtorie know,
To make the euen truth in pleaſure flow:
If thou beeſt yet a freſh vncropped flower,
Chooſe thou thy husband, and Ile pay thy dower.
For I can gueſſe, that by thy honeſt ayde,
Thou keptſt a wife her ſelfe, thy ſelfe a Maide▪
Of that and all the progreſſe more and leſſe,
Reſolduedly more leaſure ſhall expreſſe:
All yet ſeemes well, and if it end ſo meete,
The bitter paſt, more welcome is the ſweet.

lg.head: Flouriſh.
lg.l: THe Kings a Begger, now the Play is done,
All is well ended, if this ſuite be wonne,
That you expreſſe Content: which we will pay,
With ſtrift to pleaſe you, day exceeding day:
Ours be your patience then, and yours our parts,
Your gentle hands lends vs, and take our hearts.

div.head: Twelfe Night, Or what you will.
Scaena Prima.
div.stage: Enter Orſino Duke of Illyria, Curio, and other Lords.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.l: IF Muſicke be the food of Loue, play on,
Giue me exceſſe of it: that ſurfetting,
The appetite may ſicken, and ſo dye.
That ſtraine agen, it had a dying fall:
O, it came ore my eare, like the ſweet ſound
That breathes vpon a banke of Violets;
Stealing, and giuing Odour. Enough, no more,
'Tis not ſo ſweet now, as it was before.
O ſpirit of Loue, how quicke and freſh art thou,
That notwithſtanding thy capacitie,
Receiueth as the Sea. Nought enters there,
Of what validity, and pitch ſo ere,
But falles into abatement, and low price
Euen in a minute; ſo full of ſhapes is fancie,
That it alone, is high fantaſticall.

sp.speaker: Cu.
sp.p: Will you go hunt my Lord?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: What Curio?

sp.speaker: Cu.
sp.p: The Hart.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Why ſo I do, the Nobleſt that I haue:
O when mine eyes did ſee Oliuia firſt,
Me thought ſhe purg'd the ayre of peſtilence;
That inſtant was I turn'd into a Hart,
And my deſires like fell and cruell hounds,
Ere ſince purſue me. How now what newes from her?

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: So pleaſe my Lord, I might not be admitted,
But from her handmaid do returne this anſwer:
The Element it ſelfe, till ſeuen yeares heate,
Shall not behold her face at ample view:
But like a Cloyſtreſſe ſhe will vailed walke,
And water once a day her Chamber round
With eye-offending brine: all this to ſeaſon
A brothers dead loue, which ſhe would keepe freſh
And laſting, in her ſad remembrance.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: O ſhe that hath a heart of that fine frame
To pay this debt of loue but to a brother,
How will ſhe loue, when the rich golden ſhaft
Hath kill'd the flocke of all affections elſe
That liue in her. When Liuer, Braine, and Heart,
Theſe ſoueraigne thrones, are all ſupply'd and fill'd
Her ſweete perfections with one ſelfe king:
Away before me, to ſweet beds of Flowres,
Loue-thoughts lye rich, when canopy'd with bowres.

div.head: Scena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Viola, a Captaine, and Saylors.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: What Country (Friends) is this?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: This is Illyria Ladie.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: And what ſhould I do in Illyria?
My brother he is in Elizium,
Perchance he is not drown'd: What thinke you ſaylors?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: It is perchance that you your ſelfe were ſaued.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: O my poore brother, and ſo perchance may he be.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: True Madam, and to comfort you with chance,
Aſſure your ſelfe, after our ſhip did ſplit,
When you, and thoſe poore number ſaued with you,
Hung on our driuing boate: I ſaw your brother
Moſt prouident in perill, binde himſelfe,
(Courage and hope both teaching him the practiſe)
To a ſtrong Maſte, that liu'd vpon the ſea:
Where like Orion on the Dolphines backe,
I ſaw him hold acquaintance with the waues,
So long as I could ſee.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.l: For ſaying ſo, there's Gold:
Mine owne eſcape vnfoldeth to my hope,
Whereto thy ſpeech ſerues for authoritie
The like of him. Know'ſt thou this Countrey?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: I Madam well, for I was bred and borne
Not three houres trauaile from this very place:

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Who gouernes heere?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.p: A noble Duke in nature, as in name.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: What is his name?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Orſino: I haue heard my father name him.
He was a Batchellor then.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: And ſo is now, or was ſo very late:
For but a month ago I went from hence,
And then 'twas freſh in murmure (as you know
What great ones do, the leſſe will prattle of,)
That he did ſeeke the loue of faire Oliuia.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: What's ſhee?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: A vertuous maid, the daughter of a Count
That dide ſome tweluemonth ſince, then leauing her
In the protection of his ſonne, her brother,
Who ſhortly alſo dide: for whoſe deere loue
(They ſay) ſhe hath abiur'd the ſight
And company of men.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: O that I ſeru'd that Lady,
And might not be deliuered to the world
Till I had made mine owne occaſion mellow
What my eſtate is.

sp.speaker: Cap
sp.l: That were hard to compaſſe,
Becauſe ſhe will admit no kinde of ſuite,
No not the Dukes.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: There is a faire behauiour in thee Captaine,
And though that nature, with a beauteous wall
Doth oft cloſe in pollution: yet of thee
I will beleeue thou haſt a minde that ſuites
With this thy faire and outward charracter.
I prethee (and Ile pay thee bounteouſly)
Conceale me what I am, and be my ayde,
For ſuch diſguiſe as haply ſhall become
The forme of my intent. Ile ſerue this Duke,
Thou ſhalt preſent me as an Eunuch to him,
It may be worth thy paines: for I can ſing,
And ſpeake to him in many ſorts of Muſicke,
That will allow me very worth his ſeruice.
What elſe may hap, to time I will commit,
Onely ſhape thou thy ſilence to my wit.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Be you his Eunuch, and your Mute Ile bee,
When my tongue blabs, then let mine eyes not ſee.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.p: I thanke thee: Lead me on.

sp.speaker: Sir To.
sp.p: What a plague meanes my Neece to take the death of her brother thus? I am ſure care's an enemie to life.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: By my troth ſir Toby, you muſt come in earlyer a nights▪ your Coſin, my Lady, takes great exceptions to your ill houres.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Why let her except, before excepted.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: I, but you muſt confine your ſelfe within the modeſt limits of order.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Confine? Ile confine my ſelfe no finer then I am: theſe cloathes are good enough to drinke in, and ſo bee theſe boots too: and they be not, let them hang themſelues in their owne ſtraps.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: That quaffing and drinking will vndoe you: I heard my Lady talke of it yeſterday: and of a fooliſh knight that you brought in one night here, to be hir woer

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Who, Sir Andrew Ague-cheeke?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: I he.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: He's as tall a man as any's in Illyria.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: What's that to th' purpoſe?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Why he ha's three thouſand ducates a yeare.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: I, but hee'l haue but a yeare in all theſe ducates: He's a very foole, and a prodigall.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Fie, that you'l ſay ſo: he playes o' th Viol-de-ga • -boys, and ſpeaks three or four languages word for word without booke, & hath all the good gifts of nature.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: He hath indeed, almoſt naturall: for beſides that he's a foole, he's a great quarreller: and but that hee hath the gift of a Coward, to allay the guſt he hath in quarrelling, 'tis thought among the prudent, he would quickely haue the gift of a graue.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.p: By this hand they are ſcoundrels and ſubſtractor▪ that ſay ſo of him. Who are they?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: They that adde moreour, hee's drunke nightly in your company.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: With drinking healths to my Neece: Ile drinke to her as long as there is a paſſage in my throat, & drinke in Illyria: he's a Coward and a Coyſtrill that will not drinke to my Neece▪ till his braines turne o' th toe, like a pariſh top. What wench? Caſtiliano vulgo: for here coms Sir Andrew Agueface.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Sir Toby Belch. How now ſir Toby Belch?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Sweet ſir Andrew.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Bleſſe you faire Shrew.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: And you too ſir.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.p: Accoſt Sir Andrew, accoſt.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: My Neeces Chamber-maid.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Good Miſtris accoſt, I deſire better acquaintance

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: My name is Mary ſir.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Good miſtris Mary, accoſt.

sp.speaker: To,
sp.p: You miſtake knight: Accoſt, is front her, boord her, woe her, aſſayle her.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: By my troth I would not vndertake her in this company. Is that the meaning of Accoſt?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Far you well Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: And thou let part ſo Sir Andrew, would thou mightſt neuer draw ſword agen.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And you part ſo miſtris, I would I might neuer draw ſword agen: Faire Lady, doe you thinke you haue fooles in hand?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Sir, I haue not you by 'th hand.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Marry but you ſhall haue, and heeres my hand.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Now ſir▪ thought is free: I pray you bring your hand to 'th Buttry barre, and let it drinke.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Wherefore (ſweet-heart?) What's your Metaphor?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: It's dry ſir.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Why I thinke ſo: I am not ſuch an aſſe, but I can keepe my hand dry. But what's your ieſt?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: A dry ieſt Sir.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Are you full of them?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: I Sir, I haue them at my fingers ends: marry now I let go your hand, I am barren.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: O knight, thou lack'ſt a cup of Canarie: when did I ſee thee ſo put downe?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Neuer in your life I thinke, vnleſſe you ſee Canarie put me downe: mee thinkes ſometimes I haue no more wit then a Chriſtian, or an ordinary man ha's: but I am a great eater of beefe, and I beleeue that does harme to my wit.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: No queſtion.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: And I thought that, I'de forſweare it. Ile ride home to morrow ſir Toby.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Pur-quoy my deere knight?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: What is purquoy? Do, or not do? I would I had beſtowed that time in the tongues, that I haue in fencing dancing, and beare-bayting; O had I but followed the Arts.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Then hadſt thou had an excellent head of haire.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Why, would that haue mended my haire?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Paſt queſtion, for thou ſeeſt it will not coole my nature

sp.speaker: An
sp.p: But it becoms we wel enough, doſt not?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Excellent, it hangs like flax on a diſtaffe: & I hope to ſee a huſwife take thee between her legs, & ſpin it off.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Faith Ile home to morrow ſir Toby, your niece wil not be ſeene, or if ſhe be it's four to one, ſhe'l none of me: the Count himſelfe here hard by, wooes her,

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Shee'l none o' th Count, ſhe'l not match aboue hir degree, neither in eſtate, yeares, nor wit: I haue heard her ſwear't. Tut there's life in't man.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Ile ſtay a moneth longer. I am a fellow o' th ſtrangeſt minde i' th world: I delight in Maskes and Reuels ſometimes altogether.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Art thou good at theſe kicke-chawſes Knight?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: As any man in Illyria, whatſoeuer he be, vnder the degree of my betters, & yet I will not compare with an old man.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: What is thy excellence in a galliard, knight?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Faith, I can cut a caper.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: And I can cut the Mutton too't.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And I thinke I haue the backe-tricke, ſimply as ſtrong as any man in Illyria.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Wherefore are theſe things hid? Wherefore haue theſe gifts a Curtaine before 'em? Are they like to take duſt, like miſtris Mals picture? Why doſt thou not goe to Church in a Galliard, and come home in a Carranto? My verie walke ſhould be a Iigge: I would not ſo much as make water but in a Sinke-a-pace: What dooeſt thou meane? Is it a world to hide vertues in? I did thinke by the excellent conſtitution of thy legge, it was form'd vnder the ſtarre of a Galliard.

sp.speaker: And,
sp.p: I, 'tis ſtrong, and it does indifferent well in a dam'd colour'd ſtocke. Shall we ſit about ſome Reuels?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: What ſhall we do elſe: were we not borne vnder Taurus?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Taurus? That ſides and heart.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: No ſir, it is leggs and thighes: let me ſee thee caper. Ha, higher: ha, ha, excellent.

div.head: Scena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Valentine, and Viola in mans attire.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: If the Duke continue theſe fauours towards you Ceſario, you are like to be much aduanc'd, he hath known you but three dayes, and already you are no ſtranger.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: You either feare his humour, or my negligence, that you call in queſtion the continuance of his loue. Is he inconſtant ſir, in his fauours.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: No beleeue me.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I thanke you: heere comes the Count.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Who ſaw Ceſario hoa?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: On your attendance my Lord heere.

sp.speaker: Du
sp.l: Stand you a-while aloofe. Ceſario,
Thou knowſt no leſſe, but all: I haue vnclaſp'd
To thee the booke euen of my ſecret ſoule.
Therefore good youth, addreſſe thy gate vnto her,
Be not deni'de acceſſe, ſtand at her doores,
And tell them, there thy fixed foot ſhall grow
Till thou haue audience.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.l: Sure my Noble Lord,
If ſhe be ſo abandon'd to her ſorrow
As it is ſpoke, ſhe neuer will admit me.

sp.speaker: Du,
sp.l: Be clamorous, and leape all ciuill bounds,
Rather then make vnprofited returne,

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Say I do ſpeake with her (my Lord) what then?
