sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: O then, vnfold the paſsion of my loue,
Surprize her with diſcourſe of my deere faith;
It ſhall become thee well to act my woes:
She will attend it better in thy youth,
Then in a Nuntio's of more graue aſpect.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I thinke not ſo, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Deere Lad, beleeue it;
For they ſhall yet belye thy happy yeeres,
That ſay thou art a man: Dianas lip
Is not more ſmooth, and rubious: thy ſmall pipe
Is as the maidens organ, ſhrill, and ſound,
And all is ſemblatiue a womans part.
I know thy conſtellation is right apt
For this affayre: ſome foure or fiue attend him,
All if you will: for I my ſelfe am beſt
When leaſt in companie: proſper well in this,
And thou ſhalt liue as freely as thy Lord,
To call his fortunes thine.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.l: Ile do my beſt
To woe your Lady: yet a barrefull ſtrife,
Who ere I woe, my ſelfe would be his wife.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Nay, either tell me where thou haſt bin, or I will not open my lippes ſo wide as a briſsle may enter, in way of thy excuſe: my Lady will hang thee for thy abſence.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Let her hang me: hee that is well hang'de in this world, needs to feare no colours.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Make that good.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: He ſhall ſee none to feare.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: A good lenton anſwer: I can tell thee where yt ſaying was borne, of I feare no colours.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Where good miſtris Mary?

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: In the warrs, & that may you be bolde to ſay in your foolerie.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Well, God giue them wiſedome that haue it: & thoſe that are fooles, let them vſe their talents.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Yet you will be hang'd for being ſo long abſent, or to be turn'd away: is not that as good as a hanging to you?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Many a good hanging, preuents a bad marriage: and for turning away, let ſummer beare it out.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: You are reſolute then?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Not ſo neyther, but I am reſolu'd on two points

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: That if one breake, the other will hold: or if both breake, your gaskins fall.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Apt in good faith, very apt: well go thy way, if ſir Toby would leaue drinking, thou wert as witty a piece of Eues fleſh, as any in Illyria.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Peace you rogue, no more o' that: here comes my Lady: make your excuſe wiſely, you were beſt.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Wit, and't be thy will, put me into good fooling: thoſe wits that thinke they haue thee, doe very oft proue fooles: and I that am ſure I Iacke thee, may paſſe for a wiſe man. For what ſaies Quinapalus, Better a witty foole, then a fooliſh wit. God bleſſe thee Lady.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Take the foole away.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Do you not heare fellowes, take away the Ladie.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Go too, y' are a dry foole: Ile no more of you: beſides you grow diſ-honeſt.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p:
Two faults Madona, that drinke & good counſell wil amend: for giue the dry foole drink, then is the foole not dry: bid the diſhoneſt man mend himſelf, if he mend, he is no longer diſhoneſt; if hee cannot, let the Botcher mend him: any thing that's mended, is but patch'd: vertu that tranſgreſſes, is but patcht with ſinne, and ſin that amends, is but patcht with vertue. If that this ſimple Sillogiſme will ſerue, ſo: if it will not, vvhat remedy?
As there is no true Cuckold but calamity, ſo beauties a flower; The Lady bad take away the foole, therefore I ſay againe, take her away.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Sir, I bad them take away you.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Miſpriſion in the higheſt degree. Lady, Cucullus non facit monachum: that's as much to ſay, as I weare not motley in my braine: good Madona, giue mee leaue to proue you a foole.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Can you do it?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Dexteriouſly, good Madona.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Make your proofe.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I muſt catechize you for it Madona, Good my Mouſe of vertue anſwer mee.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Well ſir, for want of other idleneſſe, Ile bide your proofe.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Good Madona, why mournſt thou?

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Good foole, for my brothers death.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I thinke his ſoule is in hell, Madona.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: I know his ſoule is in heauen, foole.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: The more foole (Madona) to mourne for your Brothers ſoule, being in heauen. Take away the Foole, Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: What thinke you of this foole Maluolio, doth he not mend?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Yes, and ſhall do, till the pangs of death ſhake him: Infirmity that decaies the wiſe, doth euer make the better foole.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: God ſend you ſir, a ſpeedie Infirmity, for the better increaſing your folly: Sir Toby will be ſworn that I am no Fox, but he wil not paſſe his word for two pence that you are no Foole.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: How ſay you to that Maluolio?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: I maruell your Ladyſhip takes delight in ſuch a barren raſcall: I ſaw him put down the other day, with an ordinary foole, that has no more braine then a ſtone. Looke you now, he's out of his gard already: vnles you laugh and miniſter occaſion to him, he is gag'd. I proteſt I take theſe Wiſemen, that crow ſo at theſe ſet kinde of fooles, no better then the fooles Zanies.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: O you are ficke of ſelfe-loue Maluolio, and taſte with a diſtemper'd appetite. To be generous, guitleſſe, and of free diſpoſition, is to take thoſe things for Bird-bolts, that you deeme Cannon bullets: There is no ſlander in an allow'd foole, though he do nothing but rayle; nor no rayling, in a knowne diſcreet man, though hee do nothing but reproue.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Now Mercury indue thee with leaſing, for thou ſpeak'ſt well of fooles.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Madam, there is at the gate, a young Gentleman, much deſires to ſpeake with you.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: From the Count Orſino, is it?

sp.speaker: Ma
sp.p: I know not (Madam) 'tis a faire young man, and well attended.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Who of my people hold him in delay▪

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Sir Toby Madam, your kinſman.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Fetch him off I pray you, he ſpeakes nothing but madman: Fie on him. Go you Maluolio; If it be a • ſuit from the Count, I am ſicke, or not at home. What you will, to diſmiſſe it.
Now you ſee ſir, how your fooling growes old, & people diſlike it.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Thou haſt ſpoke for vs (Madona) as if thy eldeſt ſonne ſhould be a foole: whoſe ſcull, Ioue cramme with braines, for heere he comes.
One of thy kin has a moſt weake Pia-mater.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: By mine honor halfe drunke. What is he at the gate Coſin?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: A Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: A Gentleman? What Gentleman?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: 'Tis a Gentleman heere. A plague o' theſe pickle herring: How now Sot.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Good Sir Toby.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Coſin, Coſin, how haue you come ſo earely by this Lethargie?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Letcherie, I defie Letchery: there's one at the gate.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: I marry, what is he?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Let him be the diuell and he will, I care not: giue me faith ſay I. Well, it's all one.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: What's a drunken man like, foole?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Like a drown'd man, a foole, and a madde man:
One draught aboue heate, makes him a foole, the ſecond maddes him, and a third drownes him.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Go thou and ſeeke the Crowner, and let him ſitte o' my Coz: for he's in the third degree of drinke: hee's drown'd: go looke after him.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: He is but mad yet Madona, and the foole ſhall looke to the madman.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Madam, yond young fellow ſweares hee will ſpeake with you. I told him you were ſicke, he takes on him to vnderſtand ſo much, and therefore comes to ſpeak with you. I told him you were aſleepe, he ſeems to haue a fore knowledge of that too, and therefore comes to ſpeake with you. What is to be ſaid to him Ladie, hee's fortified againſt any deniall.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Tell him, he ſhall not ſpeake with me.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Ha's beene told ſo: and hee ſayes hee'l ſtand at your doore like a Sheriffes poſt, and be the ſupporter to a bench, but hee'l ſpeake with you.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: What kinde o' man is he?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Why of mankinde.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: What manner of man?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Of verie ill manner: hee'l ſpeake with you, will you, or no.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Of what perſonage, and yeeres is he?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Not yet old enough for a man, nor yong enough for a boy: as a ſquaſh is before tis a peſcod, or a Codling when tis almoſt an Apple: Tis with him in ſtanding water, betweene boy and man. He is verie well-fauour'd, and he ſpeakes verie ſhrewiſhly: One would thinke his mothers milke were ſcarſe out of him.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Let him approach: Call in my Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Gentlewoman, my Lady calles.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Giue me my vaile: come throw it ore my face,
Wee'l once more heare Orſinos Embaſſie.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: The honorable Ladie of the houſe, which is ſhe?

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Speake to me, I ſhall anſwer for her: your will.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.p: Moſt radiant, exquiſite, and vnmatchable beautie. I pray you tell me if this bee the Lady of the houſe, for I neuer ſaw her. I would bee loath to caſt away my ſpeech: for beſides that it is excellently well pend, I haue taken great paines to con it. Good Beauties, let mee ſuſtaine no ſcorne; I am very comptible, euen to the leaſt ſiniſter vſage.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Whence came you ſir?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p:
I can ſay little more then I haue ſtudied, & that queſtion's out of my part. Good gentle one, giue mee modeſt aſſurance, if you be the Ladie of the houſe, that
may proceede in my ſpeech.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Are you a Comedian?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: No my profound heart: and yet (by the verie phangs of malice, I ſweare) I am not that I play. Are you the Ladie of the houſe?

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: If I do not vſurpe my ſelfe, I am.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.p: Moſt certaine, if you are ſhe, you do vſurp your ſelfe: for what is yours to beſtowe, is, not yours to reſerue. But this is from my Commiſſion: I will on with my ſpeech in your praiſe, and then ſhew you the heart of my meſſage.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Come to what is important in't: I forgiue you the praiſe.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Alas, I tooke great paines to ſtudie it, and 'tis Poeticall.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: It is the more like to be feigned, I pray you keep it in. I heard you were ſawcy at my gates, & allowd your approach rather to wonder at you, then to heare you. If you be not mad, be gone: if you haue reaſon, be breefe: 'tis not that time of Moone with me, to make one in ſo skipping a dialogue.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Will you hoyſt ſayle ſir, here lies your way.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: No good ſwabber, I am to hull here a little longer. Some mollification for your Giant, ſweete Ladie; tell me your minde, I am a meſſenger.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Sure you haue ſome hiddeous matter to deliuer, when the curteſie of it is ſo fearefull. Speake your office.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: It alone concernes your eare: I bring no ouerture of warre, no taxation of homage; I hold the Olyffe in my hand: my words are as full of peace, as matter.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Yet you began rudely. What are you? What would you?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: The rudeneſſe that hath appear'd in mee, haue I learn'd from my entertainment. What I am, and what I would, are as ſecret as maiden-head: to your eares, Diuinity; to any others, prophanation.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Giue vs the place alone,
We will heare this diuinitie. Now ſir, what is your text?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Moſt ſweet Ladie.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: A comfortable doctrine, and much may bee ſaide of it. Where lies your Text?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: In Orſinoes boſome.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: In his boſome? In what chapter of his boſome?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: To anſwer by the method in the firſt of his hart.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: O, I haue read it: it is hereſie. Haue you no more to ſay?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Good Madam, let me ſee your face.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Haue you any Commiſsion from your Lord, to negotiate with my face: you are now out of your Text: but we will draw the Curtain, and ſhew you the picture. Looke you ſir, ſuch a one I was this preſent: Iſt not well done?

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.p: Excellently done, if God did all.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: 'Tis in graine ſir, 'twill endure winde and weather.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Tis beauty truly blent, whoſe red and white,
Natures owne ſweet, and cunning hand laid on:
Lady, you are the cruell'ſt ſhee aliue,
If you will leade theſe graces to the graue,
And leaue the world no copie.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: O ſir, I will not be ſo hard-hearted: I will giue out diuers ſcedules of my beautie. It ſhalbe Inuentoried and euery particle and vtenſile labell'd to my will: As, Item two lippes indifferent redde, Item two grey eyes, with lids to them: Item, one necke, one chin, & ſo forth. Were you ſent hither to praiſe me?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I ſee you what you are, you are too proud:
But if you were the diuell, you are faire:
My Lord, and maſter loues you: O ſuch loue
Could be but recompenc'd, though you were crown'd
The non-pareil of beautie.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: How does he loue me?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: With adorations, fertill teares,
With groanes that thunder loue, with ſighes of fire.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Your Lord does know my mind, I cannot loue him
Yet I ſuppoſe him vertuous, know him noble,
Of great eſtate, of freſh and ſtainleſſe youth;
In voyces well divulg'd, free, learn'd, and valiant,
And in dimenſion, and the ſhape of nature,
A gracious perſon; But yet I cannot loue him:
He might haue tooke his anſwer long ago.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: If I did loue you in my maſters flame,
With ſuch a ſuffring, ſuch a deadly life:
In your deniall, I would finde no ſence,
I would not vnderſtand it.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Why, what would you?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Make me a willow Cabine at your gate,
And call vpon my ſoule within the houſe,
Write loyall Cantons of contemned loue,
And ſing them lowd euen in the dead of night:
Hallow your name to the reuerberate hilles,
And make the babling Goſsip of the aire,
Cry out Oliuia: O you ſhould not reſt
Betweene the elements of ayre, and earth,
But you ſhould pittie me.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: You might do much:
What is your Parentage?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Aboue my fortunes, yet my ſtate is well:
I am a Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Get you to your Lord:
I cannot loue him: let him ſend no more,
Vnleſſe (perchance) you come to me againe,
To tell me how he takes it: Fare you well:
I thanke you for your paines: ſpend this for mee.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I am no feede poaſt, Lady; keepe your purſe,
My Maſter, not my ſelfe, lackes recompence.
Loue make his heart of flint, that you ſhal loue,
And let your feruour like my maſters be,
Plac'd in contempt: Farwell fayre crueltie.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: What is your Parentage?
Aboue my fortunes, yet my ſtate is well;
I am a Gentleman. Ile be ſworne thou art,
Thy tongue, thy face, thy limbes, actions, and ſpirit.
Do giue thee fiue-fold blazon: not too faſt: ſoft, ſoft,
Vnleſſe the Maſter were the man. How now?
Euen ſo quickly may one catch the plague?
Me thinkes I feele this youths perfections
With an inuiſible, and ſubtle ſtealth
To creepe in at mine eyes. Well, let it be.
What hoa, Maluolio.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Heere Madam, at your ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Run after that ſame peeuiſh Meſſenger
The Countes man: he left this Ring behinde him
Would I, or not: tell him, Ile none of it.
Deſire him not to flatter with his Lord,
Nor hold him vp with hopes, I am not for him:
If that the youth will come this way to morrow,
Ile giue him reaſons for't: hie thee Maluolio.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Madam, I will.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: I do I know not what, and feare to finde
Mine eye too great a flatterer for my minde:
Fate, ſhew thy force, our ſelues we do not owe,
What is decreed, muſt be: and be this ſo.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Will you ſtay no longer: nor will you not that I go with you.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: By your patience, no: my ſtarres ſhine darkely ouer me; the malignancie of my fate, might perhaps diſtemper yours; therefore I ſhall craue of you your leaue, that I may beare my euils alone. It were a bad recompence for your loue, to lay any of them on you.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Let me yet know of you, whither you are bound.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: No ſooth ſir: my determinate voyage is meere extrauagancie. But I perceiue in you ſo excellent a touch of modeſtie, that you will not extort from me, what I am willing to keepe in: therefore it charges me in manners, the rather to expreſſe my ſelfe: you muſt know of mee then Antonio, my name is Sebaſtian (which I call'd Rodorigo) my father was that Sebaſtian of Meſſaline, whom I know you haue heard of. He left behinde him, my ſelfe, and a ſiſter, both borne in an houre: if the Heauens had beene pleas'd, would we had ſo ended. But you ſir, alter'd that, for ſome houre before you tooke me from the breach of the ſea, was my ſiſter drown'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Alas the day.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: A Lady ſir, though it was ſaid ſhee much reſembled me, was yet of many accounted beautiful: but • hogh I could not with ſuch eſtimable wonder ouer-farre beleeue that, yet thus farre I will boldly publiſh her, ſhee bore a minde that enuy could not but call faire: Shee is drown'd already ſir with ſalt water, though I ſeeme to drowne her remembrance againe with more.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Pardon me ſir, your bad entertainment.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: O good Antonio, forgiue me your trouble.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: If you will not murther me for my loue, let mee be your ſeruant.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: If you will not vndo what you haue done, that is kill him, whom you haue recouer'd, deſire it not. Fare ye well at once, my boſome is full of kindneſſe, and I am yet ſo neere the manners of my mother, that vpon the leaſt occaſion more, mine eyes will tell tales of me: I am bound to the Count Orſino's Court, farewell.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The gentleneſſe of all the gods go with thee:
I haue many enemies in Orſino's Court,
Elſe would I very ſhortly ſee thee there:
But come what may, I do adore thee ſo,
That danger ſhall ſeeme ſport, and I will go.

div.head: Scaena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Viola and Maluolio, at ſeuerall doores.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Were not you eu'n now, with the Counteſſe Oliuia?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Euen now ſir, on a moderate pace, I haue ſince ariu'd but hither.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: She returnes this Ring to you (ſir) you might haue ſaued mee my paines, to haue taken it away your ſelfe. She adds moreouer, that you ſhould put your Lord into a deſperate aſſurance, ſhe will none of him. And one thing more, that you be neuer ſo hardie: o come againe in his affaires, vnleſſe it bee to report your Lords taking of this: receiue it ſo.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: She tooke the Ring of me, Ile none of it.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Come ſir, you peeuiſhly threw it to her: and her will is, it ſhould be ſo return'd: If it bee worth ſtooping for, there it lies, in your eye: if not, bee it his that findes it.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I left no Ring with her: what meanes this Lady?
Fortune forbid my out-ſide haue not charm'd her:
She made good view of me, indeed ſo much,
That me thought her eyes had loſt her tongue,
For ſhe did ſpeake in ſtarts diſtractedly.
She loues me ſure, the cunning of her paſsion
Inuites me in this churliſh meſſenger:
None of my Lords Ring? Why he ſent her none;
I am the man, if it be ſo, as tis,
Poore Lady, ſhe were better loue a dreame:
Diſguiſe, I ſee thou art a wickedneſſe,
Wherein the pregnant enemie does much.
How eaſie is it, for the proper falſe
In womens waxen hearts to ſet their formes:
Alas, O frailtie is the cauſe, not wee,
For ſuch as we are made, if ſuch we bee:
How will this fadge? My maſter loues her deerely,
And I (poore monſter) fond aſmuch on him:
And ſhe (miſtaken) ſeemes to dote on me:
What will become of this? As I am man,
My ſtate is deſperate for my maiſters loue:
As I am woman (now alas the day)
What thriftleſſe ſighes ſhall poore Oliuia breath?
O time, thou muſt vntangle this, not I,
It is too hard a knot for me t'vnty.

div.head: Scoena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Sir Toby, and Sir Andrew.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Approach Sir Andrew: not to bee a bedde after midnight, is to be vp betimes, and Deliculo ſurgere, thou know'ſt.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Nay by my troth I know not: but I know, to be vp late, is to be vp late.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: A falſe concluſion: I hate it as an vnfill'd Canne. To be vp after midnight, and to go to bed then is early: ſo that to go to bed after midnight, is to goe to bed betimes. Does not our liues conſiſt of the foure Elements?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Faith ſo they ſay, but I thinke it rather conſiſts of eating and drinking.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Th' art a ſcholler; let vs therefore eate and drinke Marian I ſay, a ſtoope of wine.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Heere comes the foole yfaith.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: How now my harts: Did you neuer ſee the Picture of we three?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Welcome aſſe, now let's haue a catch.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p:
By my troth the foole has an excellent breaſt. I had rather then forty ſhillings I had ſuch a legge, and ſo ſweet a breath to ſing, as the foole has. Inſooth thou waſt in very gracious fooling laſt night, when thou ſpok'ſt of Pigrogromitus, of the Ʋapians paſsing the Equinoctial of Queubus: 'twas very good yfaith: I ſent thee ſixe pence
for thy Lemon, hadſt it?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I did impeticos thy gratillity: for Maluolios noſe is no Whip-ſtocke. My Lady has a white hand, and the Mermidons are no bottle-ale houſes.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Excellent: Why this is the beſt fooling, when all is done. Now a ſong.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Come on, there is ſixe pence for you. Let's haue a ſong.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: There's a teſtrill of me too: if one knight giue a

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Would you haue a loue-ſong, or a ſong of good life?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: A loue ſong, a loue ſong.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I, I. I care not for good life.

l.hi: O Miſtris mine where are you roming?
O ſtay and heare, your true loues coming,
That can ſing both high and low.
Trip no further prettie ſweeting.
Iourneys end in louers meeting,
Euery wiſe mans ſonne doth know.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Excellent good, ifaith.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Good, good.

l.hi: What is loue, tis not heereafter,
Preſent mirth, hath preſent laughter:
What's to come, is ſtill vnſure.
In delay there lies no plentie,
Then come kiſſe me ſweet and twentie:
Youths a ſtuffe will not endure.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: A mellifluous voyce, as I am true knight.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: A contagious breath.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Very ſweet, and contagious ifaith.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: To heare by the noſe, it is dulcet in contagion. But ſhall we make the Welkin dance indeed? Shall wee rowze the night-Owle in a Catch, that will drawe three ſoules out of one Weauer? Shall we do that?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And you loue me, let's doo't: I am dogge at a Catch.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Byrlady ſir, and ſome dogs will catch well.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Moſt certaine: Let our Catch be, Thou Knaue.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Hold thy peace, thou Knaue knight. I ſhall be conſtrain'd in't, to call thee knaue, Knight.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: 'Tis not the firſt time I haue conſtrained one to call me knaue. Begin foole: it begins, Hold thy peace.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I ſhall neuer begin if I hold my peace.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Good ifaith: Come begin.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: What a catterwalling doe you keepe heere? If my Ladie haue not call'd vp her Steward Maluolio, and bid him turne you out of doores, neuer truſt me.

sp.speaker: To,
sp.p: My Lady's a Catayan, we are politicians, Maluolios a Peg-a-ramſie, and Three merry men be wee. Am not I conſanguinious? Am I not of her blood: tilly vally. Ladie, There dwelt a man in Babylon, Lady, Lady.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Beſhrew me, the knights in admirable fooling.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I, he do's well enough if he be diſpos'd, and ſo do I too: he does it with a better grace, but I do it more naturall.

p.hi: O the twelfe day of December.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: For the loue o' God peace.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: My maſters are you mad? Or what are you? Haue you no wit, manners, nor honeſtie, but to gabble like Tinkers at this time of night? Do yee make an Alehouſe of my Ladies houſe, that ye ſqueak out your Coziers Catches without any mitigation or remorſe of voice? Is there no reſpect of place, perſons, nor time in you?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: We did keepe time ſir in our Catches. Snecke vp.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Sir Toby, I muſt be round with you. My Lady bad me tell you, that though ſhe harbors you as her kinſman, ſhe's nothing ally'd to your diſorders. If you can ſeparate your ſelfe and your miſdemeanors, you are welcome to the houſe: if not, and it would pleaſe you to take leaue of her, ſhe is very willing to bid you farewell.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Farewell deere heart, ſince I muſt needs be gone.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Nay good Sir Toby.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: His eyes do ſhew his dayes are almoſt done.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Is't euen ſo?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: But I will neuer dye.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Sir Toby there you lye.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: This is much credit to you.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: What and if you do?

p.hi: Shall I bid him go, and ſpare not?
O no, no, no, no, you dare not.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Out o' tune ſir, ye lye: Art any more then a Steward? Doſt thou thinke becauſe thou art vertuous, there ſhall be no more Cakes and Ale?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Yes by S. Anne, and Ginger ſhall bee hotte y' th mouth too.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Th' art i' th right. Goe ſir, rub your Chaine with crums. A ſtope of Wine Maria.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Miſtris Mary, if you priz'd my Ladies ſauour at any thing more then contempt, you would not giue meanes for this vnciuill rule; the ſhall know of it by this hand.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Go ſhake your eares.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: 'Twere as good a deede as to drink when a mans a hungrie, to challenge him the field, and then to breake promiſe with him, and make a foole of him.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Doo't knight, Ile write thee a Challenge: or Ile deliuer thy indignation to him by word of mouth.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Sweet Sir Toby be patient for to night: Since the youth of the Counts was to day with my Lady, ſhe is much out of quiet. For Monſieur Maluolio, let me alone with him: If I do not gull him into an ayword, and make him a common recreation, do not thinke I haue witte enough to lye ſtraight in my bed: I know I can do it.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Poſſeſſe vs, poſſeſſe vs, tell vs ſomething of him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Marrie ſir, ſometimes he is a kinde of Puritane.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: O, if I thought that, Ide beate him like a dogge.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: What for being a Puritan, thy exquiſite reaſon, deere knight.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I haue no exquiſite reaſon for't, but I haue reaſon good enough.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: The diu'll a Puritane that hee is, or any thing conſtantly but a time-pleaſer, an affection'd Aſſe, that cons State without booke, and vtters it by great ſwarths. The beſt perſwaded of himſelfe: ſo cram'd (as he thinkes) with excellencies, that it is his grounds of faith, that all that looke on him, loue him: and on that vice in him, will my reuenge finde notable cauſe to worke.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: What wilt thou do?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I will drop in his way ſome obſcure Epiſtles of loue, wherein by the colour of his beard, the ſhape of his legge, the manner of his gate, the expreſſure of his eye, forehead, and complection, he ſhall finde himſelfe moſt feelingly perſonated. I can write very like my Ladie your Neece, on a forgotten matter wee can hardly make diſtinction of our hands.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Excellent, I ſmell a deuice.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I hau't in my noſe too.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p:
He ſhall thinke by the Letters that thou wilt drop
that they come from my Neece, and that ſhee's in loue with him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: My purpoſe is indeed a horſe of that colour.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: And your horſe now would make him an Aſſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Aſſe, I doubt not.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: O twill be admirable.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Sport royall I warrant you: I know my Phyſicke will worke with him, I will plant you two, and let the Foole make a third, where he ſhall finde the Letter: obſerue his conſtruction of it: For this night to bed, and dreame on the euent: Farewell.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Good night Penthiſilea.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Before me ſhe's a good wench.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: She's a beagle true bred, and one that adores me: what o' that?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I was ador'd once too.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Let's to bed knight: Thou hadſt neede ſend for more money.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: If I cannot recouer your Neece, I am a foule way out.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Send for money knight, if thou haſt her not i' th end, call me Cut.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: If I do not, neuer truſt me, take it how you will.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Come, come, Ile go burne ſome Sacke, tis too late to go to bed now: Come knight, come knight.

div.head: Scena Quarta.
div.stage: Enter Duke, Viola, Curio, and others.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Giue me ſome Muſick; Now good morow frends.
Now good Ceſario, but that peece of ſong,
That old and Anticke ſong we heard laſt night;
Me thought it did releeue my paſſion much,
More then light ayres, and recollected termes
Of theſe moſt briske and giddy-paced times.
Come, but one verſe.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: He is not heere (ſo pleaſe your Lordſhippe) that ſhould ſing it?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: Who was it?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p:
Feſt •
the leſter my Lord, a foole that the Ladie Oliuiaes Father tooke much delight in. He is about the houſe.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: Seeke him out, and play the tune the while.
sp.l: Come hither Boy, if euer thou ſhalt loue
In the ſweet pangs of it, remember me:
For ſuch as I am, all true Louers are,
Vnſtaid and skittiſh in all motions elſe,
Saue in the conſtant image of the creature
That is belou'd. How doſt thou like this tune?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: It giues a verie eccho to the ſeate
Where loue is thron • d.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Thou doſt ſpeake maſterly,
My life vpon't, yong though thou art, thine eye
Hath ſtaid vpon ſome fauour that it loues:
Hath it not boy?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: A little, by your fauour.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: What kinde of woman iſt?

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.p: Of your complection.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: She is not worth thee then. What yeares ifaith?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: About your yeeres my Lord.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Too old by heauen: Let ſtill the woman take
An elder then her ſelfe, ſo weares ſhe to him;
So ſwayes ſhe leuell in her husbands heart:
For boy, howeuer we do praiſe our ſeiues,
Our fancies are more giddie and vnfirme,
More longing, wauering, ſooner loſt and worne,
Then womens are.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.p: I thinke it well my Lord.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Then let thy Loue be yonger then thy ſelfe,
Or thy affection cannot hold the bent:
For women are as Roſes, whoſe faire flowre
Being once diſplaid, doth fall that verie howre.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: And ſo they are: alas, that they are ſo:
To die, euen when they to perfection grow.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: O fellow come, the ſong we had laſt night:
Marke it Ceſario, it is old and plaine;
The Spinſters and the Knitters in the Sun,
And the free maides that weaue their thred with bones,
Do vſe to chaunt it: it is ſilly ſooth,
And dallies with the innocence of loue,
Like the old age.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Are you ready Sir?

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: I prethee ſing.

lg.l: Come away, come away death,
And in ſad cypreſſe let me be laide.
Fye away, fie away breath,
I am ſlaine by a faire cruell maide:
My ſhrowd of white, ſtuck all with Ew, O prepare it.
My part of death no one ſo true did ſhare it.
Not a flower, not a flower ſweete
On my blacke coffin, let there be ſtrewne:
Not a friend, not a friend greet
My poore corpes, where my bones ſhall be throwne:
A thouſand thouſand ſighes to ſaue, lay me ô where
Sad true louer neuer find my graue, to weepe there.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: There's for thy paines.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: No paines ſir, I take pleaſure in ſinging ſir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: Ile pay thy pleaſure then.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Truely ſir, and pleaſure will be paide one time, or another.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: Giue me now leaue, to leaue thee.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Now the melancholly God protect thee, and the Tailor make thy doublet of changeable Taffata, for thy minde is a very Opall. I would haue men of ſuch conſtancie put to Sea, that their buſineſſe might be euery thing, and their intent euerie where, for that's it, that alwayes makes a good voyage of nothing. Farewell.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: Let all the reſt giue place: Once more Ceſario,
Get thee to yond ſame ſoueraigne crueltie:
Tell her my loue, more noble then the world
Prizes not quantitie of dirtie lands,
The parts that fortune hath beſtow'd vpon her:
Tell her I hold as giddily as Fortune:
But 'tis that miracle, and Queene of Iems
That nature prankes her in, attracts my ſoule.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: But if ſhe cannot loue you ſir.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: It cannot be ſo anſwer'd.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Sooth but you muſt.
Say that ſome Lady, as perhappes there is,
Hath for your loue as great a pang of heart
As you haue for Oliuia: you cannot loue her:
You tel her ſo: Muſt ſhe not then be anſwer'd?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: There is no womans ſides
Can bide the beating of ſo ſtrong a paſſion,
As loue doth giue my heart: no womans heart
So bigge, to hold ſo much, they lacke retention.
Alas, their loue may be call'd appetite,
No motion of the Liuer, but the Pallat,
That ſuffer ſurfet, cloyment, and reuolt,
But mine is all as hungry as the Sea,
And can digeſt as much, make no compare
Betweene that loue a woman can beare me,
And that I owe Oliuia.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.p: I but I know.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: What doſt thou knowe?

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.l: Too well what loue women to men may owe:
In faith they are as true of heart, as we.
My Father had a daughter lou'd a man
As it might be perhaps, were I a woman
I ſhould your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.p: And what's her hiſtory?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: A blanke my Lord: ſhe neuer told her loue,
But let concealment like a worme i' th budde
Feede on her damaske cheeke: ſhe pin'd in thought,
And with a greene and yellow melancholly,
She ſate like Patience on a Monument,
Smiling at greefe. Was not this loue indeede?
We men may ſay more, ſweare more, but indeed
Our ſhewes are more then will: for ſtill we proue
Much in our vowes, but little in our loue.

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: But di'de thy ſiſter of her loue my Boy?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I am all the daughters of my Fathers houſe,
And all the brothers too: and yet I know not.
Sir, ſhall I to this Lady?

sp.speaker: Du.
sp.l: I that's the Theame,
To her in haſte: giue her this Iewell: ſay,
My loue can giue no place, bide no denay.

div.head: Scena Quinta.
div.stage: Enter Sir Toby, Sir Andrew, and Fabian.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Come thy wayes Signior Fabian.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: Nay Ile come: if I looſe a ſcruple of this ſport, let me be boyl'd to death with Melancholly.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Wouldſt thou not be glad to haue the niggardly Raſcally ſheepe-biter, come by ſome notable ſhame?

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: I would exult man: you know he brought me out o' fauour with my Lady, about a Beare-baiting heere.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: To anger him wee'l haue the Beare againe, and we will foole him blacke and blew, ſhall we not ſir Andrew?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: And we do not, it is pittie of our liues.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Heere comes the little villaine: How now my Mettle of India?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Get ye all three into the box tree: Maluolio's comming downe this walke, he has beene yonder i' the Sunne practiſing behauiour to his own ſhadow this halfe houre: obſerue him for the loue of Mockerie: for I know this Letter wil make a contemplatiue Ideot of him. Cloſe in the name of ieaſting, lye thou there: for heere comes the Trowt, that muſt be caught with tickling.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: 'Tis but Fortune, all is fortune. Maria once told me ſhe did affect me, and I haue heard her ſelf come thus neere, that ſhould ſhee fancie, it ſhould bee one of my complection. Beſides ſhe vſes me with a more exalted reſpect, then any one elſe that followes her. What ſhould I thinke on't?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Heere's an ouer-weening rogue.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: Oh peace: Contemplation makes a rare Turkey Cocke of him, how he iets vnder his aduanc'd plumes.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Slight I could ſo beate the Rogue.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Peace I ſay.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: To be Count Maluolio.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Ah Rogue.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Piſtoll him, piſtoll him.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Peace, peace.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: There is example for't: The Lady of the Strachy, married the yeoman of the wardrobe.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Fie on him Iezabel.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: O peace, now he's deepely in: looke how imagination blowes him.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Hauing beene three moneths married to her, ſitting in my ſtate.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: O for a ſtone-bow to hit him in the eye.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Calling my Officers about me, in my branch'd Veluet gowne: hauing come from a day bedde, where I haue left Oliuia ſleeping.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Fire and Brimſtone.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: O peace, peace.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: And then to haue the humor of ſtate: and after a demure trauaile of regard: telling them I knowe my place, as I would they ſhould doe theirs: to aske for my kinſman Toby.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Boltes and ſhackles.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: Oh peace, peace, peace, now, now.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Seauen of my people with an obedient ſtart, make out for him: I frowne the while, and perchance winde vp my watch, or play with my ſome rich Iewell: Toby approaches; curtſies there to me.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Shall this fellow liue?

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: Though our ſilence be drawne from vs with cars, yet peace.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: I extend my hand to him thus: quenching my familiar ſmile with an auſtere regard of controll.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: And do's not Toby take you a blow o' the lippes, then?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Saying, Coſine Toby, my Fortunes hauing caſt me on your Neece, giue me this prerogatiue of ſpeech.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: What, what?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: You muſt amend your drunkenneſſe.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Out ſcab.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: Nay patience, or we breake the ſinewes of our plot?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Beſides you waſte the treaſure of your time, with a fooliſh knight.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: That's mee I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: One ſir Andrew.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: I knew 'twas I, for many do call mee foole.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: What employment haue we heere?

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: Now is the Woodcocke neere the gin.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Oh peace, and the ſpirit of humors intimate reading aloud to him.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: By my life this is my Ladies hand: theſe bee her very C's▪ her Ʋ's, and her T's, and thus makes ſhee het great P's. It is in contempt of queſtion her hand.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Her C's, her Ʋ's, and her T's: why that?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: To the vnknowne belou'd, this, and my good Wiſhes: Her very Phra • es: By your leaue wax. Soft, and the impreſſure her Lucrece, with which ſhe vſes to ſeale: tis my Lady: To whom ſhould this be?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: This winnes him, Liuer and all.

sp.speaker: Mal.

l.hi: Ioue knowes I loue, but who,
Lips do not mooue, no man muſt know.

sp.l: No man muſt know. What followes?
The numbers alter • d: No man muſt know,
If this ſhould be thee Maluolio?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Marrie hang thee brocke.

l.hi: I may command where I adore, but ſilence like a Lucreſſe knife:
With bloodleſſe ſtroke my heart doth gore, M.O.A.I. doth ſway my life.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: A fuſtian riddle.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Excellent Wench, ſay I.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: M.O.A.I. doth ſway my life. Nay but firſt let me ſee, let me ſee, let me ſee.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: What diſh a poyſon has ſhe dreſt him?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: And with what wing the ſtallion checkes at it?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: I may command, where I adore: Why ſhee may command me: I ſerue her, ſhe is my Ladie. Why this is euident to any formall capacitie. There is no obſtruction in this, and the end: What ſhould that Alphabeticall poſition portend, if I could make that reſemble ſomething in me? Softly, M.O.A.I.

sp.speaker: To
sp.p: O I, make vp that, he is now at a cold ſent.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: Sowter will cry vpon't for all this, though it bee as ranke as a Fox.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: M. Maluolio, M. why that begins my name.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: Did not I ſay he would worke it out, the Curre is excellent at faults.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: M. But then there is no conſonancy in the ſequell that ſuffers vnder probation: A. ſhould follow, but O. does.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: And O ſhall end, I hope.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: I, or Ile cudgell him, and make him cry O.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: And then I. comes behind.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: I, and you had any eye behinde you, you • might ſee more detraction at your heeles, then Fortunes before you.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: M, O, A, I. This ſimulation is not as the former: and yet to cruſh this a little, it would bow to mee, for euery one of theſe Letters are in my name. Soft, here followes proſe: If this fall into thy hand, reuolue. In my ſtars I am aboue thee, but be not affraid of greatneſſe: Some are become great, ſome atcheeues greatneſſe, and ſome haue greatneſſe thruſt vppon em. Thy fates open theyr hands, let thy blood and ſpirit embrace them, and to invre thy ſelfe to what thou art like to be: caſt thy humble ſlough, and appeare freſh. Be oppoſite with a kinſman, ſurly with ſeruants: Let thy tongue tang arguments of ſtate; put thy ſelfe into the tricke of ſingularitie. Shee thus aduiſes thee, that ſighes for thee. Remember who commended thy yellow ſtockings, and wiſh'd to ſee thee euer croſſe garter'd: I ſay remember, goe too, thou art made if thou deſir'ſt to be ſo: If not, let me ſee thee a ſteward ſtill, the fellow of ſeruants, and not woorthie to touch Fortunes ſingers Farewell, Shee that would alter ſeruices with thee, tht fortunate vnhappy daylight and champian diſcouers not more: This is open, I will bee proud, I will reade pollticke Authours, I will baffle Sir Toby, I will waſh off groſſe acquaintance, I will be point deuiſe, the very man. I do not now foole my ſelfe, to let imagination iade mee; for euery reaſon excites to this, that my Lady loues me. She did commend my yellow ſtockings of late, ſhee did praiſe my legge being croſſe-garter'd, and in this ſhe manifeſts her ſelfe to my loue, & with a kinde of iniunction driues mee to theſe habites of her liking. I thanke my ſtarres, I am happy: I will bee ſtrange, ſtout, in yellow ſtockings, and croſſe Garter'd, euen with the ſwiftneſſe of putting on. Ioue, and my ſtarres be praiſed. Heere is yet a poſtſcript. Thou canſt not chooſe but know who I am. If thou entertainſt my loue, let it appeare in thy ſmiling, thy ſmiles become thee well. Therefore in my preſence ſtill ſmile, deero my ſweete, I prethee. Ioue I thanke thee, I will ſmile, I wil do euery thing that thou wilt haue me.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: I will not giue my part of this ſport for a penſion of thouſands to be paid from the Sophy.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: I could marry this wench for this deuice.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: So could I too.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: And aske no other dowry with her, but ſuch another ieſt.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Nor I neither.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: Heere comes my noble gull catcher.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Wilt thou ſet thy foote o' my necke.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Or o' mine either?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Shall I play my freedome at tray-trip, and becom thy bondſlaue?

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Ifaith, or I either?

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.p: Why, thou haſt put him in ſuch a dreame, that when the image of it leaues him, he muſt run mad.

sp.speaker: Ma.
sp.p: Nay but ſay true, do's it worke vpon him?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Like Aqua vite with a Midwife.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: If you will then ſee the fruites of the ſport, mark his firſt approach before my Lady: hee will come to her in yellow ſtockings, and 'tis a colour ſhe abhorres, and croſſe garter'd, a faſhion ſhee deteſts: and hee will ſmile vpon her, which will now be ſo vnſuteable to her diſpoſition, being addicted to a melancholly, as ſhee is, that it cannot but turn him into a notable contempt: if you wil ſee it follow me.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: To the gates of Tartar, thou moſt excellent diuell of wit.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Ile make one too.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Saue thee Friend and thy Muſick: doſt thou liue by thy Tabor?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: No ſir, I liue by the Church.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Art thou a Churchman?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: No ſuch matter ſir, I do liue by the Church: For, I do liue at my houſe, and my houſe dooth ſtand by the Church

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: So thou maiſt ſay the Kings lyes by a begger, if a begger dwell neer him: or the Church ſtands by thy Tabor, if thy Tabor ſtand by the Church.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: You haue ſaid ſir: To ſee this age: A ſentence is but a cheu'rill gloue to a good witte, how quickely the wrong ſide may be turn'd outward.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Nay that's certaine: they that dally nicely with words, may quickely make them wanton.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I would therefore my ſiſter had had no name Sir.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Why man?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Why ſir, her names a word, and to dallie with that word, might make my ſiſter wanton: But indeede, words are very Raſcals, ſince bonds diſgrac'd them.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Thy reaſon man?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Troth ſir, I can yeeld you none without wordes, and wordes are growne ſo falſe, I am loath to proue reaſon with them.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I warrant thou art a merry fellow, and car'ſt for nothing.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Not ſo ſir, I do care for ſomething: but in my conſcience ſir, I do not care for you: if that be to care for nothing ſir, I would it would make you inuiſible.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.p: Art not thou the Lady Oliuia's foole?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: No indeed ſir, the Lady Oliuia has no folly, ſhee will keepe no foole ſir, till ſhe be married, and fooles are as like husbands, as Pilchers are to Herrings, the Huſbands the bigger, I am indeede not her foole, but hir corrupter of words.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I ſaw thee late at the Count Orſino's.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Foolery ſir, does walke about the Orbe like the Sun, it ſhines euery where. I would be ſorry ſir, but the Foole ſhould be as oft with your Maſter, as with my Miſtris: I thinke I ſaw your wiſedome there.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Nay, and thou paſſe vpon me, Ile no more with thee. Hold there's expences for thee.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Now Ioue in his next commodity of hayre, ſend thee a beard.
By my troth Ile tell thee, I am almoſt ſicke for one, though I would not haue it grow on my chinne. Is thy Lady within?

sp.speaker: Clo
sp.p: Would not a paire of theſe haue bred ſir?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Yes being kept together, and put to vſe.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I would play Lord Pandarus of Phrygia ſir, to bring a Creſſida to this Troylus.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I vnderſtand you ſir, tis well begg'd.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: The matter I hope is not great ſir; begging, but a begger: Creſſida was a begger. My Lady is within ſir. I will conſter to them whence you come, who you are, and what you would are out of my welkin, I might ſay Element, but the word is ouer-worne.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: This fellow is wiſe enough to play the foole,
And to do that well, craues a kinde of wit:
He muſt obſerue their mood on whom he ieſts,
The quality of perſons, and the time:
And like the Haggard, checke at euery Feather
That comes before his eye. This is a practice,
As full of labour as a Wiſe-mans Art:
For folly that he wiſely ſhewes, is fit;
But wiſemens folly falne, quite taint their wit.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Saue you Gentleman.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.p: And you ſir.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I hope ſir, you are, and I am yours.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Will you incounter the houſe, my Neece is deſirous you ſhould enter, if your trade be to her.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I am bound to your Neece ſir, I meane ſhe is the liſt of my voyage.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Taſte your legges ſir, put them to motion.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: My legges do better vnderſtand me ſir, then I vnderſtand what you meane by bidding me taſte my legs.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: I meane to go ſir, to enter.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I will anſwer you with gate and entrance, but we are preuented.
Moſt excellent accompliſh'd Lady, the heauens raine Odours on you.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: That youth's a rare Courtier, raine odours, wel.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: My matter hath no voice Lady, but to your owne moſt pregnant and vouchſafed eare.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Odours, pregnant, and vouchſafed: Ile get 'em all three already.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Let the Garden doore be ſhut, and leaue mee to my hearing. Giue me your hand ſir.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.p: My dutie Madam, and moſt humble ſeruice •

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: What is your name?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Ceſario is your ſeruants name, faire Princeſſe.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: My ſeruant ſir? 'Twas neuer merry world, Since lowly feigning was call'd complement: y' are ſeruant to the Count Orſino youth.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: And he is yours, and his muſt needs be yours: your ſeruants ſeruant, is your ſeruant Madam.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: For him, I thinke not on him: for his thoughts,
Would they were blankes, rather then fill'd with me.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Madam, I come to whet your gentle thoughts
On his behalfe.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: O by your leaue I pray you.
I bad you neuer ſpeake againe of him;
But would you vndertake another ſuite
I had rather heare you, to ſolicit that,
Then Muſicke from the ſpheares.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Deere Lady.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Giue me leaue, beſeech you: I did ſend,
After the laſt enchantment you did heare,
A Ring in chace of you. So did I abuſe
My ſelfe, my ſeruant, and I feare me you:
Vnder your hard conſtruction muſt I ſit,
To force that on you in a ſhamefull cunning
Which you knew none of yours. What might you think?
Haue you not ſet mine Honor at the ſtake,
And baited it with all th' vnmuzled thoughts
That tyrannous heart can think? To one of your receiuing
Enough is ſhewne, a Cipreſſe, not a boſome,
Hides my heart: ſo let me heare you ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I pittie you.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: That's a degree to loue.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: No not a grize: for tis a vulgar proofe
That verie oft we pitty enemies.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Why then me thinkes 'tis time to ſmile agen:
O world, how apt the poore are to be proud?
If one ſhould be a prey, how much the better
To fall before the Lion, then the Wolfe?
The clocke vpbraides me with the waſte of time:
Be not affraid good youth, I will not haue you,
And yet when wit and youth is come to harueſt,
your wife is like to reape a proper man:
There lies your way, due Weſt.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Then Weſtward hoe:
Grace and good diſpoſition attend your Ladyſhip:
you'l nothing Madam to my Lord, by me:

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Stay: I prethee tell me what thou thinkſt of me?

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: That you do thinke you are not what you are.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: If I thinke ſo, I thinke the ſame of you.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.p: Then thinke you right: I am not what I am.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: I would you were, as I would haue you be.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Would it be better Madam, then I am?
I wiſh it might, for now I am your foole.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: O what a deale of ſcorne, lookes beautifull?
In the contempt and anger of his lip,
A murdrous guilt ſhewes not it ſelfe more ſoone,
Then loue that would ſeeme hid: Loues night, is noone.
Ceſario, by the Roſes of the Spring,
By maid-hood, honor, truth, and euery thing,
I loue thee ſo, that maugre all thy pride,
Nor wit, nor reaſon, can my paſſion hide:
Do not extort thy reaſons from this clauſe,
For that I woo, thou therefore haſt no cauſe:
But rather reaſon thus, with reaſon fetter;
Loue ſought, is good: but giuen vnſought, is better.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.l: By innocence I ſweare, and by my youth,
I haue one heart, one boſome, and one truth,
And that no woman has, nor neuer none
Shall miſtris be of it, ſaue I alone.
And ſo adieu good Madam, neuer more,
Will I my Maſters teares to you deplore.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Yet come againe: for thou perhaps mayſt moue
That heart which now abhorres, to like his loue.

div.head: Scoena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Sir Toby, Sir Andrew, and Fabian.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: No faith, Ile not ſtay a iot longer:

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Thy reaſon deere venom, giue thy reaſon.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: You muſt neede • yeelde your reaſon, Sir Andrew?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Marry I ſaw your Neece do more fauours to the Counts Seruing-man, then euer ſhe beſtow'd vpon mee: I ſaw't i' th Orchard.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Did ſhe ſee the while, old boy, tell me that.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: As plaine as I ſee you now.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: This was a great argument of loue in her toward you.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: S'light; will you make an Aſſe o'me.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: I will proue it legitimate ſir, vpon the Oathes of iudgement, and reaſon.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: And they haue beene grand Iurie men, ſince before Noah was a Saylor.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: Shee did ſhew fauour to the youth in your ſight, onely to exaſperate you, to awake your dormouſe valour, to put fire in your Heart, and brimſtone in your Liuer: you ſhould then haue accoſted her, and with ſome excellent ieſts, fire-new from the mint, you ſhould haue bangd the youth into dumbeneſſe: this was look'd for at your hand, and this was b • ulkt: the double gilt of this opportunitie you let time waſh off▪ and you are now ſayld into the North of my Ladies opinion, where you will hang like an yſickle on a Dutchmans beard, vnleſſe you do redeeme it, by ſome laudable attempt, either of valour or policie.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And't be any way, it muſt be with Valour, for policie I hate: I had as liefe be a Browniſt, as a Politician.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Why then build me thy fortunes vpon the baſis of valour. Challenge me the Counts youth to ſight with him hurt him in eleuen places, my Neece ſhall take note of it, and aſſure thy ſelfe, there is no loue-Broker in the world, can more preuaile in mans commendation with woman, then report of valour.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: There is no way but this ſir Andrew.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Will either of you beare me a challenge to him?

sp.speaker: To
sp.p: • o, write it in a martial hand, be curſt and briefe: it is no matter how wittie, ſo it bee eloquent, and full of inuention: taunt hi • with the licenſe of Inke: if thou thou'ſt him ſome thrice, it ſhall not be amiſſe, and as many Lyes, as will lye in thy ſheete of paper, although the ſheete were bigge enough for the bedde of Ware in England, ſet 'em downe, go about it. Let there bee gaulle enough in thy inke, though thou write with a Goo • e-pen, no matter: about it.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Where ſhall I finde you?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Wee'l call thee at the Cubiculo: Go.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: This is a deere Manakin to you Sir Toby.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: I haue beene deere to him lad, ſome two thouſand ſtrong, or ſo.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: We ſhall haue a rare Letter from him; but you'le not deliuer't.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Neuer truſt me then: and by all meanes ſtirre on the youth to an anſwer. I thinke Oxen and waine-ropes cannot hale them together. For Andrew, if he were open'd and you finde ſo much blood in his Liuer, as will clog the foote of a flea, Ile eate the reſt of th' anatomy.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: And his oppoſit the youth beares in his viſage no great preſage of cruelty.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Looke where the youngeſt Wren of mine comes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: If you deſire the ſpleene, and will laughe your ſelues into ſtitches, follow me; yond gull Maluolio is turned Heathen, a verie Renegatho; for there is no chriſtian that meanes to be ſaued by beleeuing rightly, can euer beleeue ſuch impoſſible paſſages of groſſeneſſe. Hee's in yellow ſtockings.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: And croſſe garter'd?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Moſt villanouſly: like a Pedant that keepes a Schoole i' th Church: I haue dogg'd him like his murtherer. He does obey euery point of the Letter that I dropt, to betray him: He does ſmile his face into more lynes, then is in the new Mappe, with the augmentation of the Indies: you haue not ſeene ſuch a thing as tis: I can hardly forbeare hu • ling things at him, I know my Ladie will ſtrike him: if ſhee doe, hee'l ſmile, and take't for a great fauour.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Come bring vs, bring vs where he is.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: I would not by my will have troubled you,
But ſince you make your pleaſure of your paines,
I will no further chide you.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I could not ſtay behinde you: my deſire
(More ſharpe then filed ſteele) did ſpurre me forth,
And not all loue to ſee you (though ſo much
As might haue drawne one to a longer voyage)
But iealouſie, what might befall your rrauell,
Being skilleſſe in theſe parts: which to a ſtranger,
Vnguided, and vnfriended, often proue
Rough, and vnhoſpitable. My willing loue,
The rather by theſe arguments of feare
Set forth in your purſuite.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: My kinde Anthonio,
I can no other anſwer make, but thankes,
And thankes: and euer oft good turnes,
Are ſhuffel'd off with ſuch vncurrant pay:
But were my worth, as is my conſcience firme,
You ſhould finde better dealing: what's to do?
Shall we go ſee the reliques of this Towne?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: To morrow ſir, beſt firſt go ſee your Lodging?

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: I am not weary, and 'tis long to night
I pray you let vs ſatisfie our eyes
With the memorials, and the things of fame
That do renowne this City.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Would youl'd pardon me:
I do not without danger walke theſe ſtreetes.
Once in a ſea-fight 'gainſt the Count his gallies,
I did ſome ſeruice, of ſuch note indeede,
That were I tane heere, it would ſcarſe be anſwer'd.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: Belike you ſlew great number of his people.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Th offence is not of ſuch a bloody nature,
Albeit the quality of the time, and quarrell
Might well haue giuen vs bloody argument:
It might haue ſince bene anſwer'd in repaying
What we tooke from them, which for Traffiques ſake
Moſt of our City did. Onely my ſelfe ſtood out,
For which if I be lapſed in this place
I ſhall pay deere.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: Do not then walke too open.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: It doth not fit me: hold ſir, here's my purſe,
In the South Suburbes at the Elephant
Is beſt to lodge: I will beſpeake our dyet,
Whiles you beguile the time, and feed your knowledge
With viewing of the Towne, there ſhall you haue me.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: Why I your purſe?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Haply your eye ſhall light vpon ſome toy
You haue deſire to purchaſe: and your ſtore
I thinke is not for idle Markets, ſir.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.l: Ile be your purſe-bearer, and leaue you
For an houre.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: To th' Elephant.

sp.speaker: Seb.
sp.p: I do remember.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: I haue ſent after him, he ſayes hee'l come:
How ſhall I feaſt him? What beſtow of him?
For youth is bought more oft, then begg'd, or borrow'd.
I ſpeake too loud: Where's Maluolio, he is ſad, and ciuill,
And ſuites well for a ſeruant with my fortunes,
Where is Maluolio?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: He's comming Madame:
But in very ſtrange manner. He is ſure poſſeſt Madam.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Why what's the matter, does he raue?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: No Madam, he does nothing but ſmile: your Ladyſhip were beſt to haue ſome guard about you, if hee come, for ſure the man is tainted in's wits.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Go call him hither.
I am as madde as hee,
If ſad and merry madneſſe equall bee.
How now Maluolio?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Sweet Lady, ho, ho.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Smil'ſt thou? I ſent for thee vpon a ſad occaſion.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Sad Lady, I could be ſad:
This does make ſome obſtruction in the blood:
This croſſe-gartering, but what of that?
If it pleaſe the eye of one, it is with me as the very true
Sonnet is: Pleaſe one, and pleaſe all.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: Why how doeſt thou man?
What is the matter with thee?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Not blacke in my minde, though yellow in my legges: It did come to his hands, and Commaunds ſhall be executed. I thinke we doe know the ſweet Romane hand.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Wilt thou go to bed Maluolio?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: To bed? I ſweet heart, and Ile come to thee.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: God comfort thee: Why doſt thou ſmile ſo, and kiſſe thy hand ſo oft?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: How do you Maluolio?

sp.speaker: Maluo.
sp.l: At your requeſt:
Yes Nightingales anſwere Dawes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Why appeare you with this ridiculous boldneſſe before my Lady.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Be not afraid of greatneſſe: 'twas well writ.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: What meanſt thou by that Maluolio?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Some are borne great.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Ha?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Some atcheeue greatneſſe.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: What ſayſt thou?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: And ſome haue greatneſſe thruſt vpon them.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Heauen reſtore thee.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Remember who commended thy yellow ſtockings.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Thy yellow ſtockings?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: And wiſh'd to ſee thee croſſe garter'd.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Croſſe garter'd?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Go too, thou art made, if thou deſir'ſt to be ſo.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Am I made?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: If not, let me ſee thee a ſeruant ſtill.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.p: Why this is verie Midſommer madneſſe.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Madame, the young Gentleman of the Count Orſino's is return'd, I could hardly entreate him backe: he attends your Ladyſhips pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Ile come to him.
sp.p: Good Maria, let this fellow be look • d too. Where's my Coſine Toby, let ſome of my people haue a ſpeciall care of him, I would not haue him miſcarrie for the halfe of my Dowry.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Oh ho, do you come neere me now: no worſe man then ſir Toby to looke to me. This concurres directly with the Letter, ſhe ſends him on purpoſe, that I may appeare ſtubborne to him: for ſhe incites me to that in the Letter. Caſt thy humble ſlough ſayes ſhe: be oppoſite with a Kinſman, ſurly with ſeruants, let thy tongue langer with arguments of ſtate, put thy ſelfe into the tricke of ſingularity: and conſequently ſetts downe the manner how: as a ſad face, a reuerend carriage, a ſlow tongue, in the habite of ſome Sir of note, and ſo foorth. I haue lymde her, but it is Ioues doing, and Ioue make me thankefull. And when ſhe went away now, let this Fellow be look'd too: Fellow? not Maluolio, nor after my degree, but Fellow. Why euery thing adheres togither, that no dramme of a ſcruple, no ſcruple of a ſcruple, no obſtacle, no incredulous or vnſafe circumſtance: What can be ſaide? Nothing that can be, can come betweene me, and the full proſpect of my hopes. Well Ioue, not I, is the doer of this, and he is to be thanked.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Which way is hee in the name of ſanctity. If all the diuels of hell be drawne in little, and Legion himſelfe poſſeſt him, yet Ile ſpeake to him.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.l: Heere he is, heere he is: how iſt with you ſir?
How iſt with you man?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Go off, I diſcard you: let me enioy my priuate: go off.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Lo, how hollow the ſ • end ſpeakes within him; did not I tell you? Sir Toby, my Lady prayes you to haue a care of him.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Ah ha, does ſhe ſo?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Go too, go too: peace, peace, wee muſt deale gently with him: Let me alone. How do you Maluolio? How iſt with you? What man, defie the diuell: conſider, he's an enemy to mankinde.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Do you know what you ſay?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: La you, and you ſpeake ill of the diuell, how he takes it at heart Pray God he be not bewitch'd.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: Carry his water to th' wiſe woman.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Marry and it ſhall be done to morrow morning if I liue. My Lady would not looſe him for more then ile ſay.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: How now miſtris?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Oh Lord.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Prethee hold thy peace, this is not the way: Doe you not ſee you moue him? Let me alone with him.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: No way but gentleneſſe, gently, gently: the Fiend is rough, and will not be roughly vs'd.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Why how now my bawcock? how doſt yu chuck?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Sir.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: I biddy, come with me. What man, tis not for grauity to play at cherrie pit with ſathan Hang him foul Col • i • r.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Get him to ſay his prayers, good ſir Toby gette him to pray.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: My prayers Minx.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: No I warrant you, he will not heare of godlyneſſe.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: Go hang your ſelues all: you are ydle ſhallowe things, I am not of your element, you ſhall knowe more heereafter.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Iſt poſsible?

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: If this were plaid vpon a ſtage now, I could condemne it as an improbable fiction.

sp.speaker: To
sp.p: His very genius hath taken the infection of the deuice man.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Nay purſue him now, leaſt the deuice take ayre, and taint.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: Why we ſhall make him mad indeede.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: The houſe will be the quieter.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Come, wee'l haue him in a darke room & bound. My Neece is already in the beleefe that he's mad: we may carry it thus for our pleaſure, and his pennance, til our very paſtime tyred out of breath, prompt vs to haue mercy on him: at which time, we wil bring the deuice to the bar and crowne thee for a finder of madmen: but ſee, but ſee.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: More matter for a May morning.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Heere's the Challenge, reade it: I warrant there's vinegar and pepper in't.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: Iſt ſo ſawcy?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: I, iſt? I warrant him: do but read.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: Giue me.

l.hi: Youth, whatſoeuer thou art, thou art but a ſcuruy fellow.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: Good, and valiant.

p.hi: Wonder not, nor admire not in thy minde why I doe call thee ſo, for I will ſhew thee no reaſon for't.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: A good note, that keepes you from the blow of ye Law

p.hi: Thou comſt to the Lady Oliuia, and in my ſight ſhe vſes thee kindly: but thou lyeſt in thy throat, that is not the matter I challenge thee for.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: Very breefe, and to exceeding good ſence-leſſe.

p.hi: I will way-lay thee going home, where if it be thy chance to kill me.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: Good.

p.hi: Thou kilſt me like a rogue and a villaine.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: Still you keepe o' th windie ſide of the Law: good.

sp.speaker: Tob.
sp.p: Fartheewell, and God haue mercie vpon one of our ſoules. He may haue mercie vpon mine, but my hope is better, and ſo looke to thy ſelfe. Thy friend as thou vſeſt him, & thy ſworne enemie, Andrew Ague-cheeke.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: If this Letter moue him not, his legges cannot:
Ile giu't him.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: You may haue verie ſit occaſion fot't: he is now in ſome commerce with my Ladie, and will by and by depart.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Go ſir Andrew: ſcout mee for him at the corner of the Orchard like a bum-Baylie: ſo ſoone as euer thou ſeeſt him, draw, and as thou draw'ſt, ſweare horrible: for • t comes to paſſe oft, that a terrible oath, with a ſwaggering accent ſharpely twang'd off, giues manhoode more approbation, then euer proofe it ſelfe would haue earn'd him. Away.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Nay let me alone for ſwearing.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Now will not I deliuer his Letter: for the behauiour of the yong Gentleman, giues him out to be of good capacity, and breeding: his employment betweene his Lord and my Neece, confirmes no leſſe. Therefore, this Letter being ſo excellently ignorant, will breed no terror in the youth: he will finde it comes from a Clodde-pole. But ſir, I will deliuer his Challenge by word of mouth; ſet vpon Ague-cheeke a notable report of valor, and driue the Gentleman (as I know his youth will aptly receiue it) into a moſt hideous opinion of his rage, skill, furie, and impetuoſitie. This will ſo fright them both, that they wil kill one another by the looke, like Cockatrices.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: Heere he comes with your Neece, giue them way till he take leaue, and preſently after him.

sp.speaker: To
sp.p: I wil meditate the while vpon ſome horrid meſſage for a Challenge.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: I haue ſaid too much vnto a hart of ſtone,
And laid mine honour too vnchary on't:
There's ſomething in me that reproues my fault:
But ſuch a head-ſtrong potent fault it is,
That it but mockes reproofe.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: With the ſame hauiour that your paſſion beares,
Goes on my Maſters greefes.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Heere, weare this Iewell for me, tis my picture:
Refuſe it not, it hath no tongue, to vex you:
And I beſeech you come againe to morrow.
What ſhall you aske of me that Ile deny,
That honour (ſau'd) may vpon asking giue.

sp.speaker: Ʋio.
sp.p: Nothing but this, your true loue for my maſter.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: How with mine honor may I giue him that,
Which I haue giuen to you.

sp.speaker: Vio
sp.p: I will acquit you.

sp.speaker: Ol.
sp.l: Well▪ come againe to morrow: far-thee-well,
A Fiend like thee might beare my ſoule to hell.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Gentleman, God ſaue thee.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: And you ſir.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: That defence thou haſt, betake the too't: of what nature the wrongs are thou haſt done him, I knowe not: but thy intercepter full of deſpight, bloody as the Hunter, attends thee at the Orchard end: diſmount thy tucke, be yare in thy preparation, for thy aſſaylant is quick, skilfull, and deadly.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: You miſtake ſir I am ſure, no man hath any quarrell to me: my remembrance is very free and cleere from any image of offence done to any man.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: You'l finde it otherwiſe I aſſure you: therefore, if you hold your life at any price, betake you to your gard: for your oppoſite hath in him what youth, ſtrength, skill, and wrath, can furniſh man withall.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I pray you ſir what is he?

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: He is knight dubb'd with vnhatch'd Rapier, and on carpet conſideration, but he is a diuell in priuate brall, ſoules and bodies hath he diuorc'd three, and his incenſement at this moment is ſo implacable, that ſatisfaction can be none, but by pangs of death and ſepulcher: Hob, nob, is his word: giu't or take't.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I will returne againe into the houſe, and deſire ſome conduct of the Lady. I am no fighter, I haue heard of ſome kinde of men, that put quarrells purpoſely on others, to taſte their valour: belike this is a man of that quirke.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Sir, no: his indignation deriues it ſelfe out of a very computent iniurie, therefore get you on, and giue him his deſire. Backe you ſhall not to the houſe, vnleſſe you vndertake that with me, which with as much ſafetie you might anſwer him: therefore on, or ſtrippe your ſword ſtarke naked: for meddle you muſt that's certain, or forſweare to weare iron about you.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: This is as vnciuill as ſtrange. I beſeech you doe me this courteous office, as to know of the Knight what my offence to him is: it is ſomething of my negligence, nothing of my purpoſe.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: I will doe ſo. Signiour Fabian, ſtay you by this Gentleman, till my returne.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Pray you ſir, do you know of this matter?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: I know the knight is incenſt againſt you, euen to a mortall arbitrement, but nothing of the circumſtance more.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I beſeech you what manner of man is he?

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: Nothing of that wonderfull promiſe to read him by his forme, as you are like to finde him in the proofe of his valour. He is indeede ſir, the moſt skilfull, bloudy, & fatall oppoſite that you could poſsibly haue found in anie part of Illyria: will you walke towards him, I will make your peace with him, if I can.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I ſhall bee much bound to you for't: I am one, that had rather go with ſir Prieſt, then ſir knight: I care not who knowes ſo much of my mettle.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Why man hee • s a verie diuell, I haue not ſeen ſuch a firago: I had a paſſe with him, rapier, ſcabberd, and all: and he giues me the ſtucke in with ſuch a mortall motion that it is ineuitable: and on the anſwer, he payes you as ſurely, as your feete hits the ground they ſtep on. They ſay, he has bin Fencer to the Sophy.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Pox on't, Ile not meddle with him.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.l: I but he will not now be pacified,
Fabian can ſcarſe hold him yonder.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: Plague on't, and I thought he had beene vallant, and ſo cunning in Fence, I'de haue ſeene him damn'd ere I'de haue challeng'd him. Let him let the matter ſlip, and Ile giue him my horſe, gray Capilet.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Ile make the motion: ſtand heere, make a good ſhew on't, this ſhall end without the perdition of ſoules, marry Ile ride your horſe as well as I ride you.
I haue his horſe to take vp the quarrell, I haue perſwaded him the youths a diuell.

sp.speaker: Fa.
sp.p: He is as horribly conceited of him: and pants, & lookes pale, as if a Beare were at his heeles.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: There's no remedie ſir, he will fight with you for's oath ſake: marrie hee hath better bethought him of his quarrell, and hee findes that now ſcarſe to bee worth talking of: therefore draw for the ſupportance of his vowe, he proteſts he will not hurt you.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Pray God defend me: a little thing would make me tell them how much I lacke of a man.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: Giue ground if you ſee him furious.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Come ſir Andrew, there's no remedie, the Gentleman will for his honors ſake haue one bowt with you: he cannot by the Duello auoide it: but hee has promiſed me, as he is a Gentleman and a Soldiour, he will not hurt you. Come on, too't.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Pray God he keepe his oath.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: I do aſſure you tis againſt my will.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Put vp your ſword: if this yong Gentleman
Haue done offence, I take the fault on me:
If you offend him, I for him defie you.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: You ſir? Why, what are you?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: One ſir, that for his loue dares yet do more
Then you haue heard him brag to you he will.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Nay, if you be an vndertaker, I am for you.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: O good ſir Toby hold: heere come the Officers.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Ile be with you anon.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.p: Pray ſir, put your ſword vp if you pleaſe.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Marry will I ſir: and for that I promis'd you Ile be as good as my word. Hee will beare you eaſily, and raines well.

sp.speaker: 1. Off.
sp.p: This is the man, do thy Office.

sp.speaker: 2 Off.
sp.p: Anthonio, I arreſt thee at the ſuit of Count Orſino

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: You do miſtake me ſir.

sp.speaker: 1. Off.
sp.l: No ſir, no iot: I know your fauour well:
Though now you haue no ſea-cap on your head:
Take him away, he knowes I know him well.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I muſt obey. This comes with ſeeking you:
But there's no remedie, I ſhall anſwer it:
What will you do: now my neceſſitie
Makes me to aske you for my purſe. It greeues mee
Much more, for what I cannot do for you,
Then what befals my ſelfe: you ſtand amaz'd,
But be of comfort.

sp.speaker: 2 Off.
sp.p: Come ſir away.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I muſt entreat of you ſome of that money.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: What money ſir?
For the fayre kindneſſe you haue ſhew'd me heere,
And part being prompted by your preſent trouble,
Out of my leane and low ability
Ile lend you ſome • hing: my hauing is not much,
Ile make diuiſion of my preſent with you:
Hold, there's halfe my Coffer.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Will you deny me now,
Iſt poſſible that my deſerts to you
Can lacke perſwaſion. Do not tempt my miſery,
Leaſt that it make me ſo vnſound a man
As to vpbraid you with thoſe kindneſſes
That I haue done for you.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: I know of none,
Nor know I you by voyce, or any feature:
I hate ingratitude more in a man,
Then lying, vainneſſe, babling drunkenneſſe,
Or any taint of vice, whoſe ſtrong corruption
Inhabites our fraile blood.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Oh heauens themſelues.

sp.speaker: 2. Off.
sp.p: Come ſir, I pray you go.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let me ſpeake a little. This youth that you ſee heere,
I ſnatch'd one halfe out of the iawes of death,
Releeu'd him with ſuch ſanctitie of Ioue;
And to his image, which me thought did promiſe
Moſt venerable worth, did I deuotion.

sp.speaker: 1. Off.
sp.p: What's that to vs, the time goes by: Away.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: But oh, how vilde an idoll proues this God:
Thou haſt Sebaſtian done good feature, ſhame.
In Nature, there's no blemiſh but the minde:
None can be call'd deform'd, but the vnkinde.
Vertue is beauty, but the beauteous euill
Are empty trunkes, ore-flouriſh'd by the deuill.

sp.speaker: 1. Off.
sp.l: The man growes mad, away with him:
Come, come ſir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Leade me on.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: Me thinkes his words do from ſuch paſsion flye
That he beleeues himſelfe, ſo do not I:
Proue true imagination, oh proue true,
That I deere brother, be now tane for you.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Come hither Knight, come hither Fabian: Weel whiſper ore a couplet or two of moſt ſage ſawes.

sp.speaker: Vio.
sp.l: He nam'd Sebaſtian: I my brother know
Yet liuing in my glaſſe: euen ſuch, and ſo
In fauour was my Brother, and he went
Still in this faſhion, colour, ornament,
For him I imitate: Oh if it proue,
Tempeſts are kinde, and ſalt waues freſh in loue.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: A very diſhoneſt paltry boy, and more a coward then a Hare, his diſhoneſty appeares, in leauing his frend heere in neceſſity, and denying him: and for his cowardſhip aske Fabian.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: A Coward, a moſt deuout Coward, religious in it.

sp.speaker: And,
sp.p: Slid Ile after him againe, and beate him.

sp.speaker: To.
sp.p: Do, cuffe him ſoundly, but neuer draw thy ſword

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: And I do not.

sp.speaker: Fab.
sp.p: Come, let's ſee the euent.

sp.speaker: To.
