sp.l: It is the purpoſe that makes ſtrong the vowe;
But vowes to euery purpoſe muſt not hold:
Vnatme ſweete Hector.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.l: Hold you ſtill I ſay;
Mine honour keepes the weather of my fate:
Life euery man holds deere, but the deere man
Holds honor farre more precious, deere, then life.
How now yong man? mean'ſt thou to fight to day?

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Caſſandra, call my father to perſwade.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.l: No faith yong Troylus; doffe thy harneſſe youth:
I am to day ith' vaine of Chiualrie:
Let grow thy Sinews till their knots be ſtrong;
And tempt nor yet the bruſhes of the warre.
Vnarme thee, goe; and doubt thou not braue boy,
Ile ſtand to day, for thee, and me, and Troy.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: Brother, you haue a vice of mercy in you;
Which better fits a Lyon, then a man.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.p: What vice is that? good Troylus chide me for it.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: When many times the captiue Grecian fals,
Euen in the fanne and winde of your faire Sword:
You bid them riſe, and liue.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.p: O 'tis faire play.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.p: Fooles play, by heauen Hector.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.p: How now? how now?

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: For th' loue of all the gods
Let's leaue the Hermit Pitty with our Mothers;
And when we haue our Armors buckled on,
The venom'd vengeance ride vpon our ſwords,
Spur them to ruthfull worke, reine them from ruth.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.p: Fie ſauage, fie.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.p: Hector, then 'tis warres.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.p: Troylus, I would not haue you fight to day.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: Who ſhould with-hold me?
Not fate, obedience, nor the hand of Mars,
Beckning with fierie trunchion my retire;
Not Priamus, and Hecuba on knees;
Their eyes ore-galled with recourſe of teares;
Nor you my brother, with your true ſword drawne
Oppoſ'd to hinder me, ſhould ſtop my way:
But by my ruine.

sp.speaker: Caſſ.
sp.l: Lay hold vpon him Priam, hold him faſt:
He is thy crutch; now if thou looſe thy ſtay,
Thou on him leaning, and all Troy on thee,
Fall all together.

sp.speaker: Priam.
sp.l: Come Hector, come, goe backe:
Thy wife hath dreampt: thy mother hath had viſions;
Caſſandra doth foreſee; and I my ſelfe,
Am like a Prophet ſuddenly en • apt, to tell thee that this day is ominous:
Therefore come backe.

sp.speaker: Hect
sp.l: Aeneas is a field,
And I do ſtand engag'd to many Greekes,
Euen in the faith of valour, to appeare
This morning to them.

sp.speaker: Priam.
sp.p: I, but thou ſhalt not goe,

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.l: I muſt not breake my faith:
You know me dutifull, therefore deare ſir,
Let me not ſhame reſpect; but giue me leaue
To take that courſe by your conſent and voice,
Which you doe here forbid me, Royall Priam.

sp.speaker: Caſſ.
sp.p: O Priam, yeelde not to him.

sp.speaker: And.
sp.p: Doe not deere father.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.l: Andromache I am offended with you:
Vpon the loue you beare me, get you in.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: This fooliſh, dreaming, ſuperſtitious girle,
Makes all theſe bodements.

sp.speaker: Caſſ.
sp.l: O farewell, deere Hector:
Looke how thou dieſt; looke how thy eye turnes pale:
Looke how thy wounds doth bleede at many vents:
Harke how Troy roares; how Hecuba cries out;
How poore Andromache ſhrils her dolour forth;
Behold diſtraction, frenzie, and amazement,
Like witleſſe Antickes one another meete,
And all cry Hector, Hectors dead: O Hector!

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.p: Away, away.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Farewell: yes, ſoft: Hector I take my leaue;
Thou do'ſt thy ſelfe, and all our Troy deceiue.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.l: You are amaz'd, my Liege, at her exclaime:
Goe in and cheere the Towne, weele forth and fight:
Doe deedes of praiſe, and tell you them at night.

sp.speaker: Priam.
sp.p: Farewell: the gods with ſafetie ſtand about thee.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: They are at it, harke: proud Diomed, beleeue
I come to looſe my arme, or winne my ſleeue.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: Doe you heare my Lord? do you heare?

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.p: What now?

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: Here's a Letter come from yond poore girle.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.p: Let me reade.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: A whorſon tiſicke, a whorſon raſcally tiſicke, ſo troubles me; and the fooliſh fortune of this girle, and what one thing, what another, that I ſhall leaue you one o' th's dayes: and I haue a rheume in mine eyes too; and ſuch an ache in my bones; that vnleſſe a man were curſt, I cannot tell what to thinke on't. What ſayes ſhee there?

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: Words, words, meere words, no matter from the heart;
Th' effect doth operate another way.
Goe winde to winde, there turne and change together:
My loue with words and errors ſtill ſhe feedes;
But edifies another with her deedes.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: Why, but heare you?

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: Hence brother lackie; ignomie and ſhame
Purſue thy life, and liue aye with thy name.

sp.speaker: Ther.
sp.p: Now they are clapper-clawing one another, Ile goe looke on: that diſſembling abhominable varlet Diomede, has got that ſame ſcuruie, doting, fooliſh yong knaues Sleeue of Troy, there in his Helme: I would faine ſee them meet; that, that ſame yong Troian aſſe, that loues the whore there, might ſend that Greekiſh whore-maiſterly villaine, with the Sleeue, backe to the diſſembling luxurious drabbe, of a ſleeueleſſe errant. O' th' tother ſide, the pollicie of thoſe craftie ſwearing raſcals; that ſtole old Mouſe-eaten dry cheeſe, Neſtor: and that ſame dog-foxe Vliſſes is not prou'd worth a Black-berry. They ſet me vp in pollicy, that mungrill curre Aiax, againſt that dogge of as bad a kinde, Achilles. And now is the curre Aiax prouder then the curre Achilles, and will not arme to day. Whereupon, the Grecians began to proclaime barbariſme; and pollicie growes into an ill opinion.
Soft, here comes Sleeue, and th' other.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: Flye not: for ſhould'ſt thou take the Riuer Stix,
I would ſwim after.

sp.speaker: Diom.
sp.l: Thou do'ſt miſcall retire:
I doe not flye; but aduantagious care
Withdrew me from the oddes of multitude:
Haue at thee?

sp.speaker: Ther.
sp.p: Hold thy whore Grecian: now for thy whore Troian: Now the Sleeue, now the Sleeue.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.l: What art thou Greek? art thou for Hectors match?
Art thou of bloud, and honour?

sp.speaker: Ther.
sp.p: No, no: I am a raſcall: a ſcuruie railing knaue: a very filthy roague.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.p: I doe beleeue thee, liue.

sp.speaker: Ther.
sp.p: God a mercy, that thou wilt beleeue me; but a plague breake thy necke—for frighting me: what's become of the wenching rogues? I thinke they haue ſwallowed one another. I would laugh at that miracle—yet in a ſort, lecherie eares it ſelfe: Ile ſeeke them.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.l: Goe, goe, my ſeruant, take thou Troylus Horſe;
Preſent the faire Steede to my Lady Creſſid:
Fellow, commend my ſeruice to her beauty;
Tell her, I haue chaſtiſ'd the amorous Troyan.
And am her Knight by proofe.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: I goe my Lord.

sp.speaker: Aga.
sp.l: Renew, renew, the fierce Polidamus
Hath beate downe Menon: baſtard Margarelon
Hath Doreus priſoner.
And ſtands Caloſſus-wiſe wauing his beame,
Vpon the paſhed courſes of the Kings:
Epiſtropus and Cedus, Polixines is ſlaine;
Amphimacus, and Thous deadly hurt;
Patroclus tane or ſlaine, and Palamedes
Sore hurt and bruiſed; the dreadfull Sagittary
Appauls our numbers, haſte we Diomed
To re-enforcement, or we periſh all.

sp.speaker: Neſt.
sp.l: Coe beare Patroclus body to Achilles,
And bid the ſnaile-pac'd Aiax arme for ſhame;
There is a thouſand Hectors in the field:
Now here he fights on Galathe his Horſe,
And there lacks worke: ano • he's there a foote,
And there they flye or dye, like ſcaled ſculs,
Before the belching Whale; then is he yonder,
And there the ſtraying Greekes, ripe for his edge,
Fall downe before him, like the mowers ſwath;
Here, there, and euery where, he leaues and takes;
Dexteritie ſo obaying appetite,
That what he will, he does, and does ſo much,
That proofe is call'd impoſſibility.

sp.speaker: Ʋliſ.
sp.l: Oh, courage, courage Princes: great Achilles
Is arming, weeping, curſing, vowing vengeance;
Patroclus wounds haue rouz'd his drowzie bloud,
Together with his mangled Myrmidons,
That noſeleſſe, handleſſe, hackt and chipt, come to him;
Crying on Hector. Aiax hath loſt a friend,
And foames at mouth, and he is arm'd, and at it:
Roaring for Troylus; who hath done to day.
Mad and fantaſticke execution;
Engaging and redeeming of himſelfe,
With ſuch a careleſſe force, and forceleſſe care,
As if that luck in very ſpight of cunning, bad him win all.

sp.speaker: Aia.
sp.p: Troylus, thou coward Troylus.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.p: I, there, there.

sp.speaker: Neſt.
sp.p: So, ſo, we draw together.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Where is this Hector?
Come, come, thou boy-queller, ſhew thy face:
Know what it is to meete Achilles angry.
Hector, wher's Hector? I will none but Hector.

sp.speaker: Aia.
sp.p: Troylus, thou coward Troylus, ſhew thy head.

sp.speaker: Diom.
sp.p: Troylus, I ſay, wher's Troylus?

sp.speaker: Aia.
sp.p: What would'ſt thou?

sp.speaker: Diom.
sp.p: I would correct him.

sp.speaker: Aia.
sp.l: Were I the Generall,
Thou ſhould'ſt haue my office,
Ere that correction: Troylus I ſay, what Troylus?

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: Oh traitour Diomed!
Turne thy falſe face thou traytor,
And pay thy life thou oweſt me for my horſe.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.p: Ha, art thou there?

sp.speaker: Aia.
sp.p: Ile fight with him alone, ſtand Diomed.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.p: He is my prize, I will not looke vpon.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.p: Come both you coging Greekes, haue at you both.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.p: Yea Troylus? O well fought my yongeſt Brother.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.p: Now doe I ſee thee; haue at thee Hector.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.p: Pauſe if thou wilt.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: I doe diſdaine thy curteſie, proud Troian;
Be happy that my armes are out of vſe:
My reſt and negligence befriends thee now,
But thou anon ſhalt heare of me againe:
Till when, goe ſeeke thy fortune.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.l: Fare thee well:
I would haue beene much more a freſher man,
Had I expected thee: how now my Brother?

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: Aiax hath tane Aeneas; ſhall it be?
No, by the flame of yonder glorious heauen,
He ſhall not carry him: Ile be tane too,
Or bring him off: Fate heare me what I ſay;
I wreake nor, though thou end my life to day.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.l: Stand, ſtand, thou Greeke,
Thou art a goodly marke:
No? wilt thou not? I like thy armour well,
Ile fruſh it, and vnlocke the riuets all,
But Ile be maiſter of it: wilt thou not beaſt abide?
Why then flye on, Ile hunt thee for thy hide.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Come here about me you my Myrmidons:
Marke what I ſay; attend me where I wheele:
Strike not a ſtroake, but keepe your ſelues in breath;
And when I haue the bloudy Hector found,
Empale him with your weapons round about:
In felleſt manner execute your arme.
Follow me ſirs, and my proceedings eye;
It is decreed, Hector the great muſt dye.

sp.speaker: Ther.
sp.p: The Cuckold and the Cuckold maker are at it: now bull, now dogge, lowe; Paris lowe; now my double hen'd ſparrow; lowe Paris, lowe; the bull has the game: ware hornes ho?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Turne ſlaue and fight.

sp.speaker: Ther.
sp.p: What art thou?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: A Baſtard Sonne of Priams.

sp.speaker: Ther.
sp.p: I am a Baſtard too, I loue Baſtards, I am a Baſtard begot, Baſtard inſtructed, Baſtard in minde, Baſtard in valour, in euery thing illegitimate: one Beare will not bite another, and wherefore ſhould one Baſtard? take heede, the quarrel's moſt ominous to vs: if the Sonne of a whore fight for a whore, he tempts iudgement: farewell Baſtard.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: The diuell take thee coward.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.l: Moſt putrified core ſo faire without:
Thy goodly armour thus hath coſt thy life.
Now is my daies worke done; Ile take good breath:
Reſt Sword, thou haſt thy fill of bloud and death.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Looke Hector how the Sunne begins to ſet;
How vgly night comes breathing at his heeles,
Euen with the vaile and darking of the Sunne.
To cloſe the day vp, Hectors life is done.

sp.speaker: Hect.
sp.p: I am vnarm'd, forgoe this vantage Greeke.

sp.speaker: Achil.
sp.l: Strike fellowes, ſtrike, this is the man I ſeeke.
So Illion fall thou: now Troy ſinke downe;
Here lyes thy heart, thy ſinewes, and thy bone.
On Myrmidons, cry you all a maine,
Achilles hath the mighty Hector ſlaine.
Harke, a retreat vpon our Grecian part.

sp.speaker: Gree.
sp.p: The Troian Trumpets ſounds the like my Lord.

sp.speaker: Achi.
sp.l: The dragon wing of night ore-ſpreds the earth
And ſtickler-like the Armies ſeperates
My halfe ſupt Sword, that frankly would haue fed,
Pleas'd with this dainty bed; thus goes to bed.
Come, tye his body to my horſes tayle;
Along the field, I will the Troian traile.

div.stage: Enter Agamemnon, Aiax, Menelaus, Neſtor, Diomed, and the reſt marching.

sp.speaker: Aga.
sp.p: Harke, harke, what ſhout is that?

sp.speaker: Neſt.
sp.p: Peace Drums.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.p: Achilles, Achilles, Hector's ſlaine, Achilles.

sp.speaker: Dio.
sp.p: The bruite is, Hector's ſlaine, and by Achilles.

sp.speaker: Aia.
sp.l: If it be ſo, yet bragleſſe let it be:
Great Hector was a man as good as he.

sp.speaker: Agam.
sp.l: March patiently along; let one be ſent
To pray Achilles ſee vs at our Tent.
If in his death the gods haue vs befrended,
Great Troy is ours, and our ſharpe wars are ended.

div.stage: Enter Aeneas, Paris, Anthenor and Deiphoebus.

sp.speaker: Aene.
sp.l: Stand hoe, yet are we maiſters of the field,
Neuer goe home; here ſtarue we out the night.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.p: Hector is ſlaine.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Hector? the gods forbid.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: Hee's dead: and at the murtherers Horſes taile,
In beaſtly ſort, drag'd through the ſhamefull Field▪
Frowne on you heauens, effect your rage with ſpeede:
Sit gods vpon your throanes, and ſmile at Troy.
I ſay at once, let your briefe plagues be mercy,
And linger not our ſure deſtructions on.

sp.speaker: Aene.
sp.p: My Lord, you doe diſcomfort all the Hoſte.

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: You vnderſtand me not, that tell me ſo:
I doe not ſpeake of flight, of feare, of death,
But dare all imminence that gods and men,
Addreſſe their dangers in. Hector is gone:
Who ſhall tell Priam ſo? or Hecuba?
Let him that will a ſcreechoule aye be call'd,
Goe in to Troy, and ſay there, Hector's dead:
There is a word will Priam turne to ſtone;
Make wels, and Niobes of the maides and wiues;
Coole ſtatues of the youth: and in a word,
Scarre Troy out of it ſelfe. But march away,
Hector is dead: there is no more to ſay.
Stay yet: you vile abhominable Tents,
Thus proudly pight vpon our Phrygian plaines:
Let Titan riſe as early as he dare,
Ile through, and through you; & thou great ſiz'd coward:
No ſpace of Earth ſhall ſunder our two hates,
Ile haunt thee, like a wicked conſcience ſtill,
That mouldeth goblins ſwift as frenſies thoughts.
Strike a free march to Troy, with comfort goe:
Hope of reuenge, ſhall hide our inward woe.

sp.speaker: Pand.
sp.p: But heare you? heare you?

sp.speaker: Troy.
sp.l: Hence broker, lackie, • gnomy, and ſhame
Purſue thy life, and liue aye with thy name.

sp.speaker: Pan.
sp.p: A goodly medcine for mine aking bones: oh world, world, world! thus is the poore agent diſp • ſde: Oh traitours and bawdes; how earneſtly are you ſet aworke, and how ill requited? why ſhould our indeuour be ſo deſir'd, and the performance ſo loath'd? What Verſe for it? what inſtance for it? let me ſee.
sp.l: Full merrily the humble Bee-doth ſing,
Till he hath loſt his hony, and his ſting.
And being once ſubdu'd in armed taile,
Sweete hony, and ſweete notes together faile.
Good traders in the fleſh, ſet this in your painted cloathes;
As many as be here of Panders hall,
Your eyes halfe out, weepe out at Pandar's fall:
Or if you cannot weepe, yet giue ſome grones;
Though not for me yet for your aking bones:
Brethren and ſiſters of the hold-dore trade,
Some two months hence, my will ſhall here be made:
It ſhould be now, but that my feare is this:
Some galled Gooſe of Wincheſter would hiſſe:
Till then, Ile ſweate, and ſeeke about for eaſes;
And at that time be queath you my diſeaſes.

div.head: Scoena Prima.
div.stage: Enter a Company of Mutinous Citizens, with Staues, Clubs, and other weapons.

sp.speaker: 1. Citizen.
sp.p: BEfore we proceed any further, heare me ſpeake.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Speake, ſpeake.

sp.speaker: 1. Cit.
sp.p: You are all reſolu'd rather to dy then to famiſh?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Reſolu'd, reſolu'd.

sp.speaker: 1. Cit.
sp.p: Firſt you know, Caius Martius is chiefe enemy to the people.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: We know't, we know't.

sp.speaker: 1. Cit.
sp.p: Let vs kill him, and wee'l haue Corne at our own price. Is't a Verdict?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: No more talking on't; Let it be done, away, away

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.p: One word, good Citizens.

sp.speaker: 1. Cit.
sp.p: We are accounted poore Citizens, the Patricians good: what Authority ſurfets one, would releeue vs. If they would yeelde vs but the ſuperfluitie while it were wholſome, wee might gueſſe they releeued vs humanely: But they thinke we are too deere, the leanneſſe that afflicts vs, the obiect of our miſery, is as an inuentory to particularize their abundance, our ſufferance is a gaine to them. Let vs reuenge this with our Pikes, ere we become Rakes. For the Gods know, I ſpeake this in hunger for Bread, not in thirſt for Reuenge.

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.p: Would you proceede eſpecially againſt Caius Martius.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Againſt him firſt: He's a very dog to the Commonalty.

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.p: Conſider you what Seruices he ha's done for his Country?

sp.speaker: 1. Cit.
sp.p: Very well, and could bee content to giue him good report for't, but that hee payes himſelfe with beeing proud.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Nay, but ſpeak not maliciouſly.

sp.speaker: 1. Cit.
sp.p: I ſay vnto you, what he hath done Famouſlie, he did it to that end: though ſoft conſcienc'd men can be content to ſay it was for his Countrey, he did it to pleaſe his Mother and to be partly proud, which he is, euen to the altitude of his vertue.

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.p: What he cannot helpe in his Nature, you account a Vice in him: You muſt in no way ſay he is couetous.

sp.speaker: 1. Cit.
sp.p: If I muſt not, I neede not be barren of Accuſations he hath faults (with ſurplus) to tyre in repetition.
What ſhowts are theſe? The other ſide a' th City is riſen: why ſtay we prating heere? To th' Capitoll.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Come, come.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: Soft, who comes heere?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: Worthy Menenius Agrippa, one that hath alwayes lou'd the people.

sp.speaker: 1 Cit.
sp.p: He's one honeſt enough, wold al the reſt wer ſo.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: What work's my Countrimen in hand?
Where go you with Bats and Clubs? The matter
Speake I pray you.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: Our buſines is not vnknowne to th' Senat, they haue had inkling this fortnight what we intend to do, wt now wee'l ſhew em in deeds: they ſay poore Suters haue ſtrong breaths, they ſhal know we haue ſtrong arms too.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: Why Maſters, my good Friends, mine honeſt Neighbours, will you vndo your ſelues?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: We cannot Sir, we are vndone already.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I tell you Friends, moſt charitable care
Haue the Patricians of you for your wants.
Your ſuffering in this dearth, you may as well
Strike at the Heauen with your ſtaues, as lift them
Againſt the Roman State, whoſe courſe will on
The way it takes: cracking ten thouſand Curbes
Of more ſtrong linke aſſunder, then can euer
Appeare in your impediment. For the Dearth,
The Gods, not the Patricians make it, and
Your knees to them (not armes) muſt helpe. Alacke,
You are tranſported by Calamity
Thether, where more attends you, and you ſlander
The Helmes o' th State; who care for you like Fathers,
When you curſe them, as Enemies.

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.p: Care for vs? True indeed, they nere car'd for vs yet. Suffer vs to famiſh, and their Store-houſes cramm'd with Graine: Make Edicts for Vſurie, to ſupport Vſurers; repeale daily any wholſome Act eſtabliſhed againſt the rich, and prouide more piercing Statutes daily, to chaine vp and reſtraine the poore. If the Warres eate vs not vppe, they will; and there's all the loue they beare vs.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.l: Either you muſt
Confeſſe your ſelues wondrous Malicious,
Or be accus'd of Folly. I ſhall tell you
A pretty Tale, it may be you haue heard it,
But ſince it ſerues my purpoſe, I will venture
To ſcale't a little more.

sp.speaker: 2 Citizen.
sp.l: Well,
Ile heare it Sir: yet you muſt not thinke
To fobbe off our diſgrace with a tale:
But and't pleaſe you deliuer.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: There was a time, when all the bodies members
Rebell'd againſt the Belly; thus accus'd it:
That onely like a Gulfe it did remaine
I' th midd'ſt a th' body, idle and vnactiue,
Still cubbording the Viand, neuer bearing
Like labour with the reſt, where th' other Inſtruments
Did ſee, and heare, deuiſe, inſtruct, walke, feele,
And mutually participate, did miniſter
Vnto the appetite; and affection common
Of the whole body, the Belly anſwer'd.

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.p: Well ſir, what anſwer made the Belly.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Sir, I ſhall tell you with a kinde of Smile,
Which ne're came from the Lungs, but euen thus:
For looke you I may make the belly Smile,
As well as ſpeake, it taintingly replyed
To' th' diſcontented Members, the mutinous parts
That enuied his receite: euen ſo moſt fitly,
As you maligne our Senators, for that
They are not ſuch as you.

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.l: Your Bellies anſwer: What
The Kingly crown'd head, the vigilant eye,
The Counſailor Heart, the Arme our Souldier,
Our Steed the Legge, the Tongue our Trumpeter,
With other Muniments and petty helpes
In this our Fabricke, if that they—

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: What then? Foreme, this Fellow ſpeakes.
What then? What then?

sp.speaker: 2 Cit.
sp.l: Should by the Cormorant belly be reſtrain'd,
Who is the ſinke a th' body.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Well, what then?

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.l: The former Agents, if they did complaine,
What could the Belly anſwer?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: I will tell you,
If you'l beſtow a ſmall (of what you haue little)
Patience awhile; you'ſt heare the Bellies anſwer.

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.p: Y' are long about it.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Note me this good Friend;
Your moſt graue Belly was deliberate,
Not raſh like his Accuſers, and thus anſwered.
True is it my Incorporate Friends (quoth he)
That I receiue the generall Food at firſt
Which you do liue vpon: and fit it is,
Becauſe I am the Store-houſe, and the Shop
Of the whole Body. But, if you do remember,
I ſend it through the Riuers of your blood
Euen to the Court, the Heart, to th' ſeate o' th' Braine,
And through the Crankes and Offices of man,
The ſtrongeſt Nerues, and ſmall inferiour Veines
From me receiue that naturall competencie
Whereby they liue. And though that all at once
(You my good Friends, this ſayes the Belly) marke me.

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.p: I ſir, well, well.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Though all at once, cannot
See what I do deliuer out to each,
Yet I can make my Awdit vp, that all
From me do backe receiue the Flowre of all,
And leaue me but the Bran. What ſay you too't?

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.p: It was an anſwer, how apply you this?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: The Senators of Rome, are this good Belly,
And you the mutinous Members: For examine
Their Counſailes, and their Cares; diſgeſt things rightly,
Touching the Weale a' th Common, you ſhall finde
No publique benefit which you receiue
But it proceeds, or comes from them to you,
And no way from your ſelues. What do you thinke?
You, the great Toe of this Aſſembly?

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.p: I the great Toe? Why the great Toe?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: For that being one o' th loweſt, baſeſt, pooreſt
Of this moſt wiſe Rebellion, thou goeſt formoſt:
Thou Raſcall, that art worſt in blood to run,
Lead'ſt firſt to win ſome vantage.
But make you ready your ſtiffe bats and clubs,
Rome, and her Rats, are at the point of battell,
The one ſide muſt haue baile.
Hayle, Noble Martius.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Thanks. What's the matter you diſſentious rogues
That rubbing the poore Itch of your Opinion,
Make your ſelues Scabs.

sp.speaker: 2. Cit.
sp.p: We haue euer your good word.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: He that will giue good words to thee, wil flatter
Beneath abhorring. What would you haue, you Curres,
That like nor Peace, nor Warre? The one affrights you,
The other makes you proud. He that truſts to you,
Where he ſhould finde you Lyons, findes you Hares:
Where Foxes, Geeſe you are: No ſurer, no,
Then is the coale of fire vpon the Ice,
Or Hailſtone in the Sun. Your Vertue is,
To make him worthy, whoſe offence ſubdues him,
And curſe that Iuſtice did it. Who deſerues Greatnes,
Deſerues your Hate: and your Affections are
A ſickmans Appetite; who deſires moſt that
Which would encreaſe his euill. He that depends
Vpon your fauours, ſwimmes with finnes of Leade,
And hewes downe Oakes, with ruſhes. Hang ye: truſt ye?
With euery Minute you do change a Minde,
And call him Noble, that was now your Hate:
Him vilde, that was your Garland. What's the matter,
That in theſe ſeuerall places of the Citie,
You cry againſt the Noble Senate, who
(Vnder the Gods) keepe you in awe, which elſe
Would feede on one another? What's their ſeeking?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: For Corne at their owne rates, wherof they ſay
The Citie is well ſtor'd.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Hang 'em: They ſay?
They'l ſit by th' fire, and preſume to know
What's done i' th Capitoll: Who's like to riſe,
Who thriues, & who declines: Side factions, & giue out
Coniecturall Marriages, making parties ſtrong▪
And feebling ſuch as ſtand not in their liking,
Below their cobled Shooes. They ſay ther's grain enough?
Would the Nobility lay aſide their ruth,
And let me vſe my Sword, I'de make a Quarrie
With thouſands of theſe quarter'd ſlaues, as high
As I could picke my Lance.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.l: Nay theſe are almoſt thoroughly perſwaded:
For though abundantly they lacke diſcretion
Yet are they paſsing Cowardly. But I beſeech you,
What ſayes the other Troope?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: They are diſſolu'd: Hang em;
They ſaid they were an hungry, ſigh'd forth Prouerbes
That Hunger-broke ſtone wals: that dogges muſt eate
That meate was made for mouths. That the gods ſent not
Corne for the Richmen onely: With theſe ſhreds
They vented their Complainings, which being anſwer'd
And a petition granted them, a ſtrange one,
To breake the heart of generoſity,
And make bold power looke pale, they threw their caps
As they would hang them on the hornes a' th Moone,
Shooting their Emulation.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: What is graunted them?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Fiue Tribunes to defend their vulgar wiſdom •
Of their owne choice. One's Iunius Brutus,
Sicinius Velutus, and I know not. Sdeath,
The rabble ſhould haue firſt vnroo'ft the City
Ere ſo preuayl'd with me; it will in time
Win vpon power, and throw forth greater Theames
For Inſurrections arguing.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: This is ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Go get you home you Fragments.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: Where's Caius Martius?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Heere: what's the matter?

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: The newes is ſir, the Volcies are in Armes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I am glad on't, then we ſhall ha meanes to vent
Our muſtie ſuperfluity. See our beſt Elders.

div.stage: Enter Sicinius Velutus, Annius Brutus Cominius, Titus Lartius, with other Senatours.

sp.speaker: 1. Sen.
sp.l: Martius 'tis true, that you haue lately told vs,
The Volces are in Armes.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: They haue a Leader,
Tullus Auffidius that will put you too't:
I ſinne in enuying his Nobility:
And were I any thing but what I am,
I would wiſh me onely he.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.p: You haue fought together?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Were halfe to halfe the world by th' eares, & he vpon my partie, I'de reuolt to make
Onely my warres with him. He is a Lion
That I am proud to hunt.

sp.speaker: 1. Sen.
sp.l: Then worthy Martius,
Attend vpon Cominius to theſe Warres.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.p: It is your former promiſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir it is,
And I am conſtant: Titus Lucius, thou
Shalt ſee me once more ſtrike at Tullus face.
What art thou ſtiffe? Stand'ſt out?

sp.speaker: Tit.
sp.l: No Caius Martius,
Ile leane vpon one Crutch, and fight with tother,
Ere ſtay behinde this Buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Oh true-bred.

sp.speaker: Sen.
sp.l: Your Company to' th' Capitoll, where I know
Our greateſt Friends attend vs.

sp.speaker: Tit.
sp.p: Lead you on: Follow Cominius, we muſt followe you, right worthy you Priority.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.p: Noble Martius.

sp.speaker: Sen.
sp.p: Hence to your homes, be gone.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Nay let them follow,
The Volces haue much Corne: take theſe Rats thither,
To gnaw their Garners. Worſhipfull Mutiners,
Your valour puts well forth: Pray follow.

div.stage: Citizens ſteale away. Manet Sicin. & Brutus.

sp.speaker: Sicin.
sp.p: Was euer man ſo proud as is this Martius?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: He has no equall.

sp.speaker: Sicin.
sp.p: When we were choſen Tribunes for the people.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Mark'd you his lip and eyes.

sp.speaker: Sicin.
sp.p: Nay, but his taunts.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Being mou'd, he will not ſpare to gird the Gods.

sp.speaker: Sicin.
sp.p: Bemocke the modeſt Moone.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: The preſent Warres deuoure him, he is growne
Too proud to be ſo valiant.

sp.speaker: Sicin.
sp.p: Such a Nature, tickled with good ſucceſſe, diſdaines the ſhadow which he treads on at noone, but I do wonder, his inſolence can brooke to be commanded vnder Cominius?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Fame, at the which he aymes,
In whom already he's well grac'd, cannot
Better be held, nor more attain'd then by
A place below the firſt: for what miſcarries
Shall be the Generals fault, though he performe
To th' vtmoſt of a man, and giddy cenſure
Will then cry out of Martius: Oh, if he
Had borne the buſineſſe.

sp.speaker: Sicin.
sp.l: Beſides, if things go well,
Opinion that ſo ſtickes on Martius, ſhall
Of his demerits rob Cominius.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Come: halfe all Cominius Honors are to Martius
Though Martius earn'd them not: and all his faults
To Martius ſhall be Honors, though indeed
In ought he merit not.

sp.speaker: Sicin.
sp.l: Let's hence, and heare
How the diſpatch is made, and in what faſhion
More then his ſingularity, he goes
Vpon this preſent Action.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Let's along.

div.stage: Enter Tullus Auffidius with Senators of Coriolus.

sp.speaker: 1. Sen.
sp.l: So, your opinion is Auffidius,
That they of Rome are entred in our Counſailes,
And know how we proceede,

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: Is it not yours?
What euer haue bin thought one in this State
That could be brought to bodily act, ere Rome
Had circumuention: 'tis not foure dayes gone
Since I heard thence, theſe are the words, I thinke
I haue the Letter heere: yes, heere it is;
They haue preſt a Power, but it is not knowne
Whether for Eaſt or Weſt: the Dearth is great,
The people Mutinous: And it is • umour'd,
Cominius, Martius your old Enemy
(Who is of Rome worſe hated then of you)
And Titus Lartius, a moſt valiant Roman,
Theſe three leade on this Preparation
Whether 'tis bent: moſt likely, 'tis for you:
Conſider of it.

sp.speaker: 1. Sen.
sp.l: Our Armie's in the Field:
We neuer yet made doubt but Rome was ready
To anſwer vs.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: Nor did you thinke it folly,
To keepe your great pretences vayl'd, till when
They needs muſt ſhew themſelues, which in the hatching
It ſeem'd appear'd to Rome. By the diſcouery,
We ſhalbe ſhortned in our ayme, which was
To take in many Townes, ere (almoſt) Rome
Should know we were a-foot.

sp.speaker: 2. Sen.
sp.l: Noble Auffidius,
Take your Commiſſion, hye you to your Bands,
Let vs alone to guard Corioles
If they ſet downe before's: for the remoue
Bring vp your Army: but (I thinke) you'l finde
Th' haue not prepar'd for vs.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: O doubt not that,
I ſpeake from Certainties. Nay more,
Some parcels of their Power are forth already,
And onely hitherward. I leaue your Honors.
If we, and Caius Martius chance to meete,
'Tis ſworne betweene vs, we ſhall euer ſtrike
Till one can do no more.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: The Gods aſsiſt you.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.p: And keepe your Honors ſafe.

sp.speaker: 1. Sen.
sp.p: Farewell.

sp.speaker: 2. Sen.
sp.p: Farewell.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Farewell.

stage.hi: Enter Volumnia and Ʋirgilia, mother and wife to Martius: They ſet them downe on two lowe ſtooles and ſowe.

sp.speaker: Ʋolum.
sp.p: I pray you daughter ſing, or expreſſe your ſelfe in a more comfortable ſort: If my Sonne were my Huſband, I ſhould freelier reioyce in that abſence wherein he wonne Honor, then in the embracements of his Bed, where he would ſhew moſt loue. When yet hee was but tender-bodied, and the onely Sonne of my womb; when youth with comelineſſe pluck'd all gaze his way; when for a day of Kings entreaties, a Mother ſhould not ſel him an houre from her beholding; I conſidering how Honour would become ſuch a perſon, that it was no better then Picture-like to hang by th' wall, if renowne made it not ſtirre, was pleas'd to let him ſeeke danger, where he was like to finde fame: To a cruell Warre I ſent him, from whence he return'd, his browes bound with Oake. I tell thee Daughter, I ſprang not more in ioy at firſt hearing he was a Man-child, then now in firſt ſeeing he had proued himſelfe a man.

sp.speaker: Virg.
sp.p: But had he died in the Buſineſſe Madame, how then?

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.p: Then his good report ſhould haue beene my Sonne, I therein would haue found iſſue. Heare me profeſſe ſincerely, had I a dozen ſons each in my loue alike, and none leſſe deere then thine, and my good Martius, I had rather had eleuen dye Nobly for their Countrey, then one voluptuouſly ſurfet out of Action.

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: Madam, the Lady Valeria is come to viſit you.

sp.speaker: Virg.
sp.p: Beſeech you giue me leaue to retire my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.l: Indeed you ſhall not:
Me thinkes, I heare hither your Husbands Drumme:
See him plucke Auffidius downe by th' haire:
(As children from a Beare) the Volces ſhunning him:
Me thinkes I ſee him ſtampe thus, and call thus,
Come on you Cowards, you were got in feare
Though you were borne in Rome; his bloody brow
With his mail'd hand, then wiping, forth he goes
Like to a Harueſt man, that task'd to mowe
Or all, or looſe his hyre.

sp.speaker: Virg.
sp.p: His bloody Brow? Oh Iupiter, no blood.

sp.speaker: Ʋolum.
sp.l: Away you Foole; it more becomes a man
Then gilt his Trophe. The breſts of Hecuba
When ſhe did ſuckle Hector, look'd not louelier
Then Hectors forhead, when it ſpit forth blood
At Grecian ſword. Contenning, tell Valeria
We are fit to bid her welcome.

sp.speaker: Ʋir.
sp.p: Heauens bleſſe my Lord from fell Auffidius.

sp.speaker: Ʋol,
sp.l: Hee'l beat Auffidius head below his knee,
And treade vpon his necke.

div.stage: Enter Valeria with an Vſher, and a Gentlewoman.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: My Ladies both good day to you.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.p: Sweet Madam.

sp.speaker: Ʋir.
sp.p: I am glad to ſee your Ladyſhip.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: How do you both? You are manifeſt houſe-keepers. What are you ſowing heere? A fine ſpotte in good faith. How does your little Sonne?

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.p: I thanke your Lady-ſhip: Well good Madam.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.p: He had rather ſee the ſwords, and heare a Drum, then looke vpon his Schoolmaſter.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: A my word the Fathers Sonne: Ile ſweare 'tis a very pretty boy. A my troth, I look'd vpon him a Wenſday halfe an houre together: ha's ſuch a confirm'd countenance. I ſaw him run after a gilded Butterfly, & when he caught it, he let it go againe, and after it againe, and ouer and ouer he comes, and vp againe: catcht it again: or whether his fall enrag'd him, or how 'twas, hee did ſo ſet his teeth, and teare it. Oh, I warrant how he mammockt it.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.p: One on's Fathers moods.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Indeed la, tis a Noble childe.

sp.speaker: Virg.
sp.p: A Cracke Madam.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Come, lay aſide your ſtitchery, I muſt haue you play the idle Huſwife with me this afternoone.

sp.speaker: Virg.
sp.l: No (good Madam)
I will not out of doores.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Not out of doores?

sp.speaker: Ʋolum.
sp.p: She ſhall, ſhe ſhall.

sp.speaker: Virg.
sp.p: Indeed no, by your patience; Ile not ouer the threſhold, till my Lord returne from the Warres.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.l: Fye, you confine your ſelfe moſt vnreaſonably:
Come, you muſt go viſit the good Lady that lies in.

sp.speaker: Virg.
sp.p: I will wiſh her ſpeedy ſtrength, and viſite her with my prayers: but I cannot go thither.

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.p: Why I pray you.

sp.speaker: Vlug.
sp.p: 'Tis not to ſaue labour, nor that I want loue.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: You would be another Penelope: yet they ſay, all the yearne ſhe ſpun in Vliſſes abſence, did but fill Athica full of Mothes. Come, I would your Cambrick were ſenſible as your finger, that you might leaue pricking it for pitie. Come you ſhall go with vs.

sp.speaker: Vir.
sp.p: No good Madam, pardon me, indeed I will not foorth.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: In truth la go with me, and Ile tell you excellent newes of your Husband.

sp.speaker: Virg.
sp.p: Oh good Madam, there can be none yet.

sp.speaker: Ʋal.
sp.p: Verily I do not ieſt with you: there came newes from him laſt night.

sp.speaker: Ʋir.
sp.p: Indeed Madam.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: In earneſt it's true; I heard a Senatour ſpeake it. Thus it is: the Volcies haue an Army forth, againſt whō Cominius the Generall is gone, with one part of our Romane power. Your Lord, and Titus Lartius, are ſet down before their Citie Carioles, they nothing doubt preuailing, and to make it breefe Warres. This is true on mine Honor, and ſo I pray go with vs.

sp.speaker: Virg.
sp.p: Giue me excuſe good Madame, I will obey you in euery thing heereafter.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.l: Let her alone Ladie, as ſhe is now:
She will but diſeaſe our better mirth.

sp.speaker: Valeria.
sp.l: In troth I thinke ſhe would:
Fare you well then. Come good ſweet Ladie.
Prythee Virgilia turne thy ſolemneſſe out a doore,
And go along with vs.

sp.speaker: Virgil.
sp.l: No
At a word Madam; Indeed I muſt not,
I wiſh you much mirth.

sp.speaker: Val.
sp.p: Well, then farewell.

div.stage: Enter Martius, Titus Lartius, with Drumme and Colours, with Captaines and Souldiers, as before the City Corialus: to them a Meſſenger.

sp.speaker: Martius.
sp.l: Yonder comes Newes:
A Wager they haue met.

sp.speaker: Lar.
sp.p: My horſe to yours, no.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Tis done.

sp.speaker: Lart.
sp.p: Agreed.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Say, ha's our Generall met the Enemy?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: They lye in view, but haue not ſpoke as yet.

sp.speaker: Lart.
sp.p: So, the good Horſe is mine.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.p: Ile buy him of you.

sp.speaker: Lart.
sp.l: No, Ile nor ſel, nor giue him: Lend you him I will
For halfe a hundred yeares: Summon the Towne.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: How farre off lie theſe Armies?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: Within this mile and halfe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Then ſhall we heare their Larum, & they Ours.
Now Mars, I prythee make vs quicke in worke,
That we with ſmoaking ſwords may march from hence
To helpe our fielded Friends. Come, blow thy blaſt.
sp.stage: They Sound a Parley: Enter two Senators with others on the Walles of Corialus.
sp.l: Tullus Auffidious, is he within your Walles?

sp.speaker: 1. Senat.
sp.l: No, nor a man that feares you leſſe then he,
That's leſſer then a little:
Hearke, our Drummes
Are bringing forth our youth: Wee'l breake our Walles
Rather then they ſhall pound vs vp our Gates,
Which yet ſeeme ſhut, we haue but pin'd with Ruſhes,
They'le open of themſelues. Harke you, farre off
There is Auffidious. Liſt what worke he makes
Among'ſt your clouen Army.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.p: Oh they are at it.

sp.speaker: Lart.
sp.p: Their noiſe be our inſtruction. Ladders hoa.

div.stage: Enter the Army of the Ʋolces.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: They feare vs not, but iſſue forth their Citie.
Now put your Shields before your hearts, and fight
With hearts more proofe then Shields.
Aduance braue Titus,
They do diſdaine vs much beyond our Thoughts,
which makes me ſweat with wrath. Come on my fellows
He that retires, Ile take him for a Volce,
And he ſhall feele mine edge.

div.stage: Alarum, the Romans are beat back to their Trenches Enter Martius Curſing.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: All the contagion of the South, light on you,
You Shames of Rome: you Heard of Byles and Plagues
Plaiſter you o're, that you may be abhorr'd
Farther then ſeene, and one infect another
Againſt the Winde a mile: you ſoules of Geeſe,
That beare the ſhapes of men, how haue you run
From Slaues, that Apes would beate; Pluto and Hell,
All hurt behinde, backes red, and faces pale
With flight and agued feare, mend and charge home,
Or by the fires of heauen, Ile leaue the Foe,
And make my Warres on you: Looke too't: Come on,
If you'l ſtand faſt, wee'l beate them to their Wiues,
As they vs to our Trenches followes.
sp.stage: Another Alarum, and Martius followes them to gates, and is ſhut in.
sp.l: So, now the gates are ope: now proue good Seconds,
'Tis for the followers Fortune, widens them,
Not for the flyers: Marke me, and do the like.

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.p: Foole-hardineſſe, not I.

sp.speaker: 2. Sol.
sp.p: Nor I.

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.p: See they haue ſhut him in.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: To th' pot I warrant him.

sp.speaker: Tit.
sp.p: What is become of Martius?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Slaine (Sir) doubtleſſe.

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.l: Following the Flyers at the very heeles,
With them he enters: who vpon the ſodaine
Clapt to their Gates, he is himſelfe alone,
To anſwer all the City.

sp.speaker: Lar.
sp.l: Oh Noble Fellow!
Who ſenſibly out-dares his ſenceleſſe Sword,
And when it bowes, ſtand'ſt vp: Thou art left Martius,
A Carbuncle intire: as big as thou art
Weare not ſo rich a Iewell. Thou was't a Souldier
Euen to Calues wiſh, not fierce and terrible
Onely in ſtrokes, but with thy grim lookes, and
The Thunder-like percuſſion of thy ſounds
Thou mad'ſt thine enemies ſhake, as if the World
Were Feauorous, and did tremble.

div.stage: Enter Martius bleeding, aſſaulted by the Enemy.

sp.speaker: 1. Sol.
sp.p: Looke Sir.

sp.speaker: Lar.
sp.l: O 'tis Martius.
Let's fetch him off, or make remaine alike.

div.stage: They fight, and all enter the City.

sp.speaker: 1. Rom.
sp.p: This will I carry to Rome.

sp.speaker: 2. Rom.
sp.p: And I this.

sp.speaker: 3. Rom.
sp.p: A Murrain on't, I tooke this for Siluer.

div.stage: Enter Martius, and Titus with a Trumpet.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: See heere theſe mouers, that do prize their hours
At a crack'd Drachme: Cuſhions, Leaden Spoones,
Irons of a Doit, Dublets that Hangmen would
Bury with thoſe that wore them. Theſe baſe ſlaues,
Ere yet the fight be done, packe vp, downe with them.
And harke, what noyſe the Generall makes: To him
There is the man of my ſoules hate, Auffidious,
Piercing our Romanes: Then Valiant Titus take
Conuenient Numbers to make good the City,
Whil'ſt I with thoſe that haue the ſpirit, wil haſte
To helpe Cominius.

sp.speaker: Lar.
sp.l: Worthy Sir, thou bleed'ſt,
Thy exerciſe hath bin too violent,
For a ſecond courſe of Fight.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Sir, praiſe me not:
My worke hath yet not warm'd me. Fare you well:
The blood I drop, is rather Phyſicall
Then dangerous to me: To Auffidious thus, I will appear and fight.

sp.speaker: Lar.
sp.l: Now the faire Goddeſſe Fortune,
Fall deepe in loue with thee, and her great charmes
Miſguide thy Oppoſers ſwords, Bold Gentleman:
Proſperity be thy Page.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Thy Friend no leſſe,
Then thoſe ſhe placeth higheſt: So farewell.

sp.speaker: Lar.
sp.l: Thou worthieſt Martius,
Go ſound thy Trumpet in the Market place,
Call thither all the Officers a' th' Towne,
Where they ſhall know our minde. Away.

div.stage: Enter Cominius as it were in retire, with ſoldiers.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Breath you my friends, wel fought, we are come off,
Like Romans, neither fooliſh in our ſtands,
Nor Cowardly in retyre: Beleeue me Sirs,
We ſhall be charg'd againe. Whiles we haue ſtrooke
By Interims and conueying guſts, we haue heard
The Charges of our Friends. The Roman Gods,
Leade their ſucceſſes, as we wiſh our owne,
That both our powers, with ſmiling Fronts encountring,
May giue you thankfull Sacrifice. Thy Newes?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: The Cittizens of Corioles haue yſſued,
And giuen to Lartius and to Martius Battaile:
I ſaw our party to their Trenches driuen,
And then I came away.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Though thou ſpeakeſt truth,
Me thinkes thou ſpeak'ſt not well. How long is't ſince?

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Aboue an houre, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: 'Tis not a mile: briefely we heard their drummes.
How could'ſt thou in a mile confound an houre,
And bring thy Newes ſo late?

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: Spies of the Ʋolces
Held me in chace, that I was forc'd to wheele
Three or foure miles about, elſe had I ſir
Halfe an houre ſince brought my report.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Whoſe yonder,
That doe's appeare as he were Flead? O Gods,
He has the ſtampe of Martius, and I haue
Before time ſeene him thus.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Come I too late?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: The Shepherd knowes not Thunder frō a Taber,
More then I know the ſound of Martius Tongue
From euery meaner man.

sp.speaker: Martius.
sp.p: Come I too late?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: I, if you come not in the blood of others,
But mantled in your owne.

sp.speaker: Mart.
sp.l: Oh! let me clip ye
In Armes as ſound, as when I woo'd in heart;
As merry, as when our Nuptiall day was done,
And Tapers burnt to Bedward.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.p: Flower of Warriors, how is't with Titus Lartius?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: As with a man buſied about Decrees:
Condemning ſome to death, and ſome to exile,
Ranſoming him, or pittying, threatning th' other;
Holding Corioles in the name of Rome,
Euen like a fawning Grey-hound in the Leaſh,
To let him ſlip at will.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Where is that Slaue
Which told me they had beate you to your Trenches?
Where is he? Call him hither.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Let him alone,
He did informe the truth: but for our Gentlemen,
The common file, (a plague-Tribunes for them)
The Mouſe ne're ſhunn'd the Cat, as they did budge
From Raſcals worſe then they.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.p: But how preuail'd you?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Will the time ſerue to tell, I do not thinke:
Where is the enemy? Are you Lords a' th Field?
If not, why ceaſe you till you are ſo?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Martius, we haue at diſaduantage fought,
And did retyre to win our purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: How lies their Battell? Know you on wc ſide
They haue plac'd their men of truſt?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: As I gueſſe Martius,
Their Bands i' th Vaward are the Antients
Of their beſt truſt: O're them Auffidious,
Their very heart of Hope.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: I do beſeech you,
By all the Battailes wherein we haue fought,
By th' Blood we haue ſhed together,
By th' Vowes we haue made
To endure Friends, that you directly ſet me
Againſt Affidious, and his Antiats,
And that you not delay the preſent (but
Filling the aire with Swords aduanc'd) and Darts,
We proue this very houre.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Though I could wiſh,
You were conducted to a gentle Bath,
And Balmes applyed to you, yet dare I neuer
Deny your asking, take your choice of thoſe
That beſt can ayde your action.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Thoſe are they
That moſt are willing; if any ſuch be heere,
(As it were ſinne to doubt) that loue this painting
Wherein you ſee me ſmear'd, if any feare
Leſſen his perſon, then an ill report:
If any thinke, braue death out-weighes bad life,
And that his Countries deerer then himſelfe,
Let him alone: Or ſo many ſo minded,
Waue thus to expreſſe his diſpoſition,
And follow Martius.
sp.stage: They all ſhout and waue their ſwords, take him vp in their Armes, and caſt vp their Caps.
sp.l: Oh me alone, make you a ſword of me:
If theſe ſhewes be not outward, which of you
But is foure Volces? None of you, but is
Able to beare againſt the great Auffidious
A Shield, as hard as his. A certaine number
(Though thankes to all) muſt I ſelect from all:
The reſt ſhall beare the buſineſſe in ſome other fight
(As cauſe will be obey'd:) pleaſe you to March,
And foure ſhall quickly draw out my Command,
Which men are beſt inclin'd.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: March on my Fellowes:
Make good this oſtentation, and you ſhall
Diuide in all, with vs.

div.stage: Titus Lartius, hauing ſet a guard vpon Carioles, going with Drum and Trumpet toward Cominius, and Caius Martius, Enters with a Lieutenant, other Souldiours, and a Scout.

sp.speaker: Lar.
sp.l: So, let the Ports be guarded; keepe your Duties
As I haue ſet them downe. If I do ſend, diſpatch
Thoſe Centuries to our ayd, the reſt will ſerue
For a ſhort holding, if we looſe the Field,
We cannot keepe the Towne.

sp.speaker: Lieu.
sp.p: Feare not our care Sir.

sp.speaker: Lart.
sp.l: Hence; and ſhut your gates vpon's:
Our Guider come, to th' Roman Gampe conduct vs.

div.stage: Enter Martius and Auffidius at ſeueral doores.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Ile fight with none but thee, for I do hate thee
Worſe then a Promiſe-breaker.

sp.speaker: Auffid.
sp.l: We hate alike:
Not Affricke ownes a Serpent I abhorre
More then thy Fame and Enuy: Fix thy foot.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Let the firſt Budger dye the others Slaue,
And the Gods doome him after.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.p: If I flye Martius, hollow me like a Hare.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Within theſe three houres Tullus
Alone I fought in your Corioles walles,
And made what worke I pleas'd: 'Tis not my blood,
Wherein thou ſeeſt me maskt, for thy Reuenge
Wrench vp thy power to th' higheſt.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: Wer't thou the Hector,
That was the whip of your bragg'd Progeny,
Thou ſhould'ſt not ſcape me heere.
sp.stage: Heere they fight, and certaine Volces come in the ayde of Auffi. Martius fights til they be driuen in breathles.
sp.l: Officious and not valiant, you haue ſham'd me
In your condemned Seconds.

stage.hi: Flouriſh. Alarum. A Retreat is ſounded. Enter at one Doore Cominius, with the Romanes: At another Doore Martius, with his Arms in a Scarfe.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: If I ſhould tell thee o're this thy dayes Worke,
Thou't not beleeue thy deeds: but Ile report it,
Where Senators ſhall mingle teares with ſmiles,
Where great Patricians ſhall attend, and ſhrug,
I' th' end admire: where Ladies ſhall be frighted,
And gladly quak'd, heare more: where the dull Tribunes,
That with the fuſtie Plebeans, hate thine Honors,
Shall ſay againſt their hearts, We thanke the Gods
Our Rome hath ſuch a Souldier.
Yet cam'ſt thou to a Morſell of this Feaſt,
Hauing fully din'd before.

div.stage: Enter Titus with his Power, from the Purſuit.

sp.speaker: Titus Lartius.
sp.l: Oh Generall:
Here is the Steed, wee the Capariſon:
Hadſt thou beheld—

sp.speaker: Martius.
sp.l: Pray now, no more:
My Mother, who ha's a Charter to extoll her Bloud,
When ſhe do's prayſe me, grieues me:
I haue done as you haue done, that's what I can,
Induc'd as you haue beene, that's for my Countrey:
He that ha's but effected his good will,
Hath ouerta'ne mine Act.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: You ſhall not be the Graue of your deſeruing,
Rome muſt know the value of her owne:
'Twere a Concealement worſe then a Theft,
No leſſe then a Traducement,
To hide your doings, and to ſilence that,
Which to the ſpire, and top of prayſes vouch'd,
Would ſeeme but modeſt: therefore I beſeech you,
In ſigne of what you are, not to reward
What you haue done, before our Armie heare me.

sp.speaker: Martius.
sp.l: I haue ſome Wounds vpon me, and they ſmart
To heare themſelues remembred.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Should they not:
Well might they feſter 'gainſt Ingratitude,
And tent themſelues with death: of all the Horſes,
Whereof we haue ta'ne good, and good ſtore of all,
The Treaſure in this field atchieued, and Citie,
We render you the Tenth, to be ta'ne forth,
Before the common diſtribution,
At your onely choyſe.

sp.speaker: Martius.
sp.l: I thanke you Generall:
But cannot make my heart conſent to take
A Bribe, to pay my Sword: I doe refuſe it,
And ſtand vpon my common part with thoſe,
That haue beheld the doing.

div.stage: A long flouriſh. They all cry▪ Martius, Martius, caſt vp their Caps and Launces: Cominius and Lartius ſtand bare.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: May theſe ſame Inſtruments, which you prophane,
Neuer ſound more: when Drums and Trumpets ſhall
I' th' field proue flatterers, let Courts and Cities be
Made all of falſe-fac'd ſoothing:
When Steele growes ſoft, as the Phraſites Silke,
Let him be made an Ouerture for th' Warres:
No more I ſay, for that I haue not waſh'd
My Noſe that bled, or foyl'd ſome debile Wretch,
Which without note, here's many elſe haue done,
You ſhoot me forth in acclamations hyperbolicall,
As if I lou'd my little ſhould be dieted
In prayſes, ſawc'ſt with Lyes.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Too modeſt are you:
More cruell to your good report, then gratefull
To vs, that giue you truly: by your patience,
If 'gainſt your ſelfe you be incens'd, wee'le put you
(Like one that meanes his proper harme) in Manacles,
Then reaſon ſafely with you: Therefore be it knowne,
As to vs, to all the World, That Caius Martius
Weares this Warres Garland: in token of the which,
My Noble Steed, knowne to the Campe, I giue him,
With all his trim belonging; and from this time,
For what he did before Corioles, call him,
With all th' applauſe and Clamor of the Hoaſt,

sp.speaker: Marcus Caius Coriolanus.
sp.p: Beare th' addition Nobly euer?

div.stage: Flouriſh. Trumpets ſound, and Drums. Omnes. Marcus Caius Coriolanus.

sp.speaker: Martius.
sp.l: I will goe waſh:
And when my Face is faire, you ſhall perceiue
Whether I bluſh, or no: howbeit, I thanke you,
I meane to ſtride your Steed, and at all times
To vnder-creſt your good Addition,
To th' faireneſſe of my power.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: So, to our Tent:
Where ere we doe repoſe vs, we will write
To Rome of our ſucceſſe: you Titus Lartius
Muſt to Corioles backe, ſend vs to Rome
The beſt, with whom we may articulate,
For their owne good, and ours.

sp.speaker: Lartius.
sp.p: I ſhall, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Martius.
sp.l: The Gods begin to mocke me:
I that now refus'd moſt Princely gifts,
Am bound to begge of my Lord Generall.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.p: Tak't, 'tis yours: what is't?

sp.speaker: Martius.
sp.l: I ſometime lay here in Corioles,
At a poore mans houſe: he vs'd me kindly,
He cry'd to me: I ſaw him Priſoner:
But then Auffidius was within my view,
And Wrath o're-whelm'd my pittie: I requeſt you
To giue my poore Hoſt freedome.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Oh well begg'd:
Were he the Butcher of my Sonne, he ſhould
Be free, as is the Winde: deliuer him, Titus.

sp.speaker: Lartius.
sp.p: Martius, his Name.

sp.speaker: Martius.
sp.l: By Iupiter forgot:
I am wearie, yea my memorie is tyr'd:
Haue we no Wine here?

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Goe we to our Tent:
The bloud vpon your Viſage dryes, 'tis time
It ſhould be lookt too: come.

stage.hi: A flouriſh. Cornets. Enter Tullus Auffidius blondi • , with two or three Souldiors.

sp.speaker: Auffi.
sp.p: The Towne is ta'ne.

sp.speaker: Sould.
sp.p: 'Twill be deliuer'd backe on good Condition.

sp.speaker: Auffid.
sp.l: Condition?
I would I were a Roman, for I cannot.
Being a Ʋolce, be that I am. Condition?
What good Condition can a Treatie finde
I' th' part that is at mercy? fiue times, Martius,
I haue fought with thee; ſo often haſt thou beat me:
And would'ſt doe ſo, I thinke, ſhould we encounter
As often as we eate. By th' Elements,
If ere againe I meet him beard to beard,
He's mine, or I am his: Mine Emulation
Hath not that Honor in't it had: For where
I thought to cruſh him in an equall Force,
True Sword to Sword: Ile potche at him ſome way,
Or Wrath, or Craft may get him.

sp.speaker: Sol.
sp.p: He's the diuell.

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: Bolder, though not ſo ſubtle: my valors poiſon'd,
With onely ſuff'ring ſtaine by him: for him
Shall flye out of it ſelfe, nor ſleepe, nor ſanctuary,
Being naked, ſicke; nor Phane, nor Capitoll,
The Prayers of Prieſts, nor times of Sacrifice:
Embarquements all of Fury, ſhall lift vp
Their rotten Priuiledge, and Cuſtome 'gainſt
My hate to Martius. Where I finde him, were it
At home, vpon my Brothers Guard, euen there
Againſt the hoſpitable Canon, would I
Waſh my fierce hand in's heart. Go you to th' Citie,
Learne how 'tis held, and what they are that muſt
Be Hoſtages for Rome.

sp.speaker: Soul.
sp.p: Will not you go?

sp.speaker: Auf.
sp.l: I am attended at the Cyprus groue▪ I pray you
('Tis South the City Mils) bring me word thither
How the world goes: that to the pace of it
I may ſpurre on my iourney.

sp.speaker: Soul.
sp.p: I ſhall ſir.

div.head: Actus Secundus.
div.stage: Enter Menenius with the two Tribunes of the people, Sicinius & Brutus.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: The Agurer tels me, wee ſhall haue Newes to night.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Good or bad?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Not according to the prayer of the people, for they loue not Martius.

sp.speaker: Sicin.
sp.p: Nature teaches Beaſts to know their Friends.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Pray you, who does the Wolfe loue?

sp.speaker: Sicin.
sp.p: The Lambe.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: I, to deuour him, as the hungry Plebeians would the Noble Martius.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: He's a Lambe indeed, that baes like a Beare.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.l: Hee's a Beare indeede, that liues like a Lambe.
You two are old men, tell me one thing that I ſhall aske you.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: Well ſir.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: In what enormity is Martius poore in, that you two haue not in abundance?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: He's poore in no one fault, but ſtor'd withall.

sp.speaker: Sicin.
sp.p: Eſpecially in Pride.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: And topping all others in boaſting.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: This is ſtrange now: Do you two know, how you are cenſured heere in the City, I mean of vs a' th' right hand File, do you?

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: Why? ho ware we cenſur'd?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Becauſe you talke of Pride now, will you not be angry.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: Well, well ſir, well.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Why 'tis no great matter: for a very little theefe of Occaſion, will rob you of a great deale of Patience: Giue your diſpoſitions the reines, and bee angry at your pleaſures (at the leaſt) if you take it as a pleaſure to you, in being ſo: you blame Martius for being proud.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.p: We do it not alone, ſir.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: I know you can doe very little alone, for your helpes are many, or elſe your actions would growe wondrous ſingle: your abilities are to Infant-like, for dooing much alone. You talke of Pride: Oh, that you could turn your eyes toward the Napes of your neckes, and make but an Interiour ſuruey of your good ſelues. Oh that you could.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: What then ſir?

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Why then you ſhould diſcouer a brace of vnmeriting, proud, violent, teſtie Magiſtrates (alias Fooles) as any in Rome.

sp.speaker: Sicin.
sp.p: Menenius, you are knowne well enough too.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: I am knowne to be a humorous Patritian, and one that loues a cup of hot Wine, with not a drop of alaying Tiber in't: Said, to be ſomething imperfect in fauouring the firſt complaint, haſty and Tinder-like vppon, to triuiall motion: One, that conuerſes more with the Buttocke of the night, then with the forhead of the morning. What I think, I vtter, and ſpend my malice in my breath. Meeting two ſuch Weales men as you are (I cannot call you Licurguſſes,) if the drinke you giue me, touch my Palat aduerſly, I make a crooked face at it, I can ſay, your Worſhippes haue deliuer'd the matter well, when I finde the Aſſe in compound, with the Maior part of your ſyllables. And though I muſt be content to beare with thoſe, that ſay you are reuerend graue men, yet they lye deadly, that tell you haue good faces, if you ſee this in the Map of my Microcoſme, followes it that I am knowne well enough too? What harme can your beeſome Conſpectuities gleane out of this Charracter, if I be knowne well enough too.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Come ſir come, we know you well enough.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: You know neither mee, your ſelues, nor any thing: you are ambitious, for poore knaues cappes and legges: you weare out a good wholeſome Forenoone, in hearing a cauſe betweene an Orendge wife, and a Forſetſeller, and then reiourne the Controuerſie of three-pence to a ſecond day of Audience. When you are hearing a matter betweene party and party, if you chaunce to bee pinch'd with the Collicke, you make faces like Mummers, ſet vp the bloodie Flagge againſt all Patience, and in roaring for a Chamber-pot, diſmiſſe the Controuerſie bleeding, the more intangled by your hearing: All the peace you make in their Cauſe, is calling both the parties Knaues. You are a payre of ſtrange ones.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Come, come, you are well vnderſtood to bee a perfecter gyber for the Table, then a neceſſary Bencher in the Capitoll.

sp.speaker: Men.
sp.p: Our very Prieſts muſt become Mockers, if they ſhall encounter ſuch ridiculous Subiects as you are, when you ſpeake beſt vnto the purpoſe. It is not woorth the wagging of your Beards, and your Beards deſerue not ſo honourable a graue, as to ſtuffe a Botchers Cuſhion, or to be intomb'd in an Aſſes Packe-ſaddle; yet you muſt bee ſaying, Martius is proud: who in a cheape eſtimation, is worth all your predeceſſors, ſince Deucalion, though peraduenture ſome of the beſt of 'em were hereditarie hangmen. Godden to your Worſhips, more of your conuerſation would infect my Braine, being the Heardſmen of the Beaſtly Plebeans. I will be bold to take my leaue of you.
How now (my as faire as Noble) Ladyes, and the Moone were ſhee Earthly, no Nobler; whither doe you follow your Eyes ſo faſt?

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.p: Honorable Menenius, my Boy Martius approches: for the loue of Iuno let's goe.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: Ha? Martius comming home?

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.p: I, worthy Menenius▪ and with moſt proſperous approbation.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: Take my Cappe Iupiter, and I thanke thee: hoo, Martius comming home?

sp.speaker: 2. Ladies.
sp.p: Nay, 'tis true.

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.p: Looke, here's a Letter from him, the State hath another, his Wife another, and (I thinke) there's one at home for you.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.l: I will make my very houſe reele to night:
A Letter for me?

sp.speaker: Virgil.
sp.p: Yes certaine, there's a Letter for you, I ſaw't.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: A Letter for me? it giues me an Eſtate of ſeuen yeeres health; in which time, I will make a Lippe at the Phyſician: The moſt ſoueraigne Preſcription in Galen, is but Emperick qutique; and to this Preſeruatiue, of no better report then a Horſe-drench. Is he not wounded? he was wont to come home wounded?

sp.speaker: Virgil.
sp.p: Oh no, no, no.

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.p: Oh, he is wounded, I thanke the Gods for't.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: So doe I too, if it be not too much: brings a Victorie in his Pocket? the wounds become him.

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.p: On's Browes: Menenius, hee comes the third time home with the Oaken Garland.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: Ha's he diſciplin'd Auffidius ſoundly?

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.p: Titus Lartius writes, they fought together, but Auffidius got off.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: And 'twas time for him too, Ile warrant him that: and he had ſtay'd by him, I would not haue been ſo fiddious'd, for all the Cheſts in Carioles, and the Gold that's in them. Is the Senate poſſeſt of this?

sp.speaker: Ʋolum.
sp.p: Good Ladies let's goe. Yes, yes, yes: The Senate ha's Letters from the Generall, wherein hee giues my Sonne the whole Name of the Warre: he hath in this action out-done his former deeds doubly.

sp.speaker: Valer.
sp.p: In troth, there's wondrous things ſpoke of him.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: Wondrous: I, I warrant you, and not without his true purchaſing.

sp.speaker: Virgil.
sp.p: The Gods graunt them true.

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.p: True? pow waw.

sp.speaker: Mene.
sp.p: True? Ile be ſworne they are true: where is hee wounded, God ſaue your good Worſhips? Martius is comming home: hee ha's more cauſe to be prowd: where is he wounded?

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.p: Ith' Shoulder, and ith' left Arme: there will be large Cicatrices to ſhew the People, when hee ſhall ſtand for his place: he receiued in the repulſe of Tarquin ſeuen hurts ith' Body.

sp.speaker: Mene.
sp.p: One ith' Neck, and two ith' Thigh, there's nine that I know.

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.p: Hee had, before this laſt Expedition, twentie fiue Wounds vpon him.

sp.speaker: Mene.
sp.p: Now it's twentie ſeuen; euery gaſh was an Enemies Graue. Hearke, the Trumpets.

sp.speaker: Ʋolum.
sp.l: Theſe are the Vſhers of Martius:
Before him, hee carryes Noyſe;
And behinde him, hee leaues Teares:
Death, that darke Spirit, in's neruie Arme doth lye,
Which being aduanc'd, declines, and then men dye.

div.stage: Enter Cominius the Generall, and Titus Latius: betweene them Coriolanus, crown'd with an Oaken Garland, with Captaines and Souldiers, and a Herauld.

sp.speaker: Herauld.
sp.l: Know Rome, that all alone Martius did fight
Within Corioles Gates: where he hath wonne,
With Fame, a Name to Martius Caius:
Theſe in honor followes Martius Caius Coriolanus.
Welcome to Rome, renowned Coriolanus.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Welcome to Rome, renowned Coriolanus.

sp.speaker: Coriol.
sp.p: No more of this, it does offend my heart: pray now no more.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.p: Looke, Sir, your Mother.

sp.speaker: Coriol.
sp.p: Oh! you haue, I know, petition'd all the Gods for my proſperitie.

sp.speaker: Ʋolum.
sp.l: Nay, my good Souldier, vp:
My gentle Martius, worthy Caius,
And by deed-atchieuing Honor newly nam'd,
What is it (Coriolanus) muſt I call thee?
But oh, thy Wife.

sp.speaker: Corio.
sp.l: My gracious ſilence, hayle:
Would'ſt thou haue laugh'd, had I come Coffin'd home,
That weep'ſt to ſee me triumph? Ah my deare,
Such eyes the Widowes in Carioles were,
And Mothers that lacke Sonnes.

sp.speaker: Mene.
sp.p: Now the Gods Crowne thee.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.p: And liue you yet? Oh my ſweet Lady, pardon.

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.l: I know not where to turne.
Oh welcome home: and welcome Generall,
And y' are welcome all.

sp.speaker: Mene.
sp.l: A hundred thouſand Welcomes:
I could weepe, and I could laugh,
I am light, and heauie; welcome:
A Curſe begin at very root on's heart,
That is not glad to ſee thee.
You are three, that Rome ſhould dote on:
Yet by the faith of men, we haue
Some old Crab-trees here at home,
That will not be grafted to your Ralliſh.
Yet welcome Warriors:
Wee call a Nettle, but a Nettle;
And the faults of fooles, but folly.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.p: Euer right.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Menenius, euer, euer.

sp.speaker: Herauld.
sp.p: Giue way there, and goe on.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Your Hand, and yours?
Ere in our owne houſe I doe ſhade my Head,
The good Patricians muſt be viſited,
From whom I haue receiu'd not onely greetings,
But with them, change of Honors.

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.l: I haue liued,
To ſee inherited my very Wiſhes,
And the Buildings of my Fancie:
Onely there's one thing wanting,
Which (I doubt not) but our Rome
Will caſt vpon thee.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Know, good Mother,
I had rather be their ſeruant in my way,
Then ſway with them in theirs.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.p: On, to the Capitall.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: All tongues ſpeake of him, and the bleared ſights
Are ſpectacled to ſee him. Your pratling Nurſe
Into a rapture lets her Baby crie,
While ſhe chats him: the Kitchin Malkin pinnes
Her richeſt Lockram 'bout her reechie necke,
Clambring the Walls to eye him:
Stalls, Bulkes, Windowes, are ſmother'd vp,
Leades fill'd, and Ridges hors'd
With variable Complexions; all agreeing
In earneſtneſſe to ſee him: ſeld-ſhowne Flamins
Doe preſſe among the popular Throngs, and puffe
To winne a vulgar ſtation: our veyl'd Dames
Commit the Warre of White and Damaske
In their nicely gawded Cheekes, toth' wanton ſpoyle
Of Phoebus burning Kiſſes: ſuch a poother,
As if that whatſoeuer God, who leades him,
Were ſlyly crept into his humane powers,
And gaue him gracefull poſture.

sp.speaker: Scicin.
sp.p: On the ſuddaine, I warrant him Conſull.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.p: Then our Office may, during his power, goe ſleepe.

sp.speaker: Scicin.
sp.l: He cannot temp'rately tranſport his Honors,
From where he ſhould begin, and end, but will
Loſe thoſe he hath wonne.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.p: In that there's comfort.

sp.speaker: Scici.
sp.l: Doubt not,
The Commoners, for whom we ſtand, but they
Vpon their ancient mallice, will forget
With the leaſt cauſe, theſe his new Honors,
Which that he will giue them, make I as little queſtion,
As he is prowd to doo't.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.l: I heard him ſweare,
Were he to ſtand for Conſull, neuer would he
Appeare i' th' Market place, nor on him put
The Naples Veſture of Humilitie,
Nor ſhewing (as the manner is) his Wounds
Toth' People, begge their ſtinking Breaths.

sp.speaker: Scicin.
sp.p: 'Tis right.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.l: It was his word:
Oh he would miſſe it, rather then carry it,
But by the ſuite of the Gentry to him,
And the deſire of the Nobles.

sp.speaker: Scicin.
sp.p: I wiſh no better, then haue him hold that purpoſe, and to put it in execution.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.p: 'Tis moſt like he will.

sp.speaker: Scicin.
sp.p: It ſhall be to him then, as our good wills; a ſure deſtruction.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.l: So it muſt fall out
To him, or our Authorities, for an end.
We muſt ſuggeſt the People, in what hatred
He ſtill hath held them: that to's power he would
Haue made them Mules, ſilenc'd their Pleaders,
And diſpropertied their Freedomes; holding them,
In humane Action, and Capacitie,
Of no more Soule, nor fitneſſe for the World,
Then Cammels in their Warre, who haue their Prouand
Onely for bearing Burthens, and ſore blowes
For ſinking vnder them.

sp.speaker: Scicin.
sp.l: This (as you ſay) ſuggeſted,
At ſome time, when his ſoaring Inſolence
Shall teach the People, which time ſhall not want,
If he be put vpon't, and that's as eaſie,
As to ſet Dogges on Sheepe, will be his fire
To kindle their dry Stubble: and their Blaze
Shall darken him for euer.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.p: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: You are ſent for to the Capitoll:
'Tis thought, that Martius ſhall be Conſull:
I haue ſeene the dumbe men throng to ſee him,
And the blind to heare him ſpeak: Matrons flong Gloues,
Ladies and Maids their Scarffes, and Handkerchers,
Vpon him as he paſs'd: the Nobles bended
As to Ioues Statue, and the Commons made
A Shower, and Thunder, with their Caps, and Showts:
I neuer ſaw the like.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.l: Let's to the Capitoll,
And carry with vs Eares and Eyes for th' time,
But Hearts for the euent.

sp.speaker: Scicin.
sp.p: Haue with you.

div.stage: Enter two Officers, to lay Cuſhions, as it were, in the Capitoll.

sp.speaker: 1. Off.
sp.p: Come, come, they are almoſt here: how many ſtand for Conſulſhips?

sp.speaker: 2. Off.
sp.p: Three, they ſay: but 'tis thought of euery one, Coriolanus will carry it.

sp.speaker: 1. Off.
sp.p: That's a braue fellow: but hee's vengeance prowd, and loues not the common people.

sp.speaker: 2. Off.
sp.p: 'Faith, there hath beene many great men that haue flatter'd the people, who ne're loued them; and there be many that they haue loued, they know not wherefore: ſo that if they loue they know not why, they hate vpon no better a ground. Therefore, for Coriolanus neyther to care whether they loue, or hate him, manifeſts the true knowledge he ha's in their diſpoſition, and out of his Noble careleſneſſe lets them plainely ſee't.

sp.speaker: 1. Off.
sp.p: If he did not care whether he had their loue, or no, hee waued indifferently, 'twixt doing them neyther good, nor harme: but hee ſeekes their hate with greater deuotion, then they can render it him; and leaues nothing vndone, that may fully diſcouer him their oppoſite. Now to ſeeme to affect the mallice and diſpleaſure of the People, is as bad, as that which he diſlikes, to flatter them for their loue.

sp.speaker: 2. Off.
sp.p: Hee hath deſerued worthily of his Countrey, and his aſſent is not by ſuch eaſie degrees as thoſe, who hauing beene ſupple and courteous to the People, Bonnetted, without any further deed, to haue them at all into their eſtimation, and report: but hee hath ſo planted his Honors in their Eyes, and his actions in their Hearts, that for their Tongues to be ſilent, and not confeſſe ſo much, were a kinde of ingratefull Iniurie: to report otherwiſe, were a Mallice, that giuing it ſelfe the Lye, would plucke reproofe and rebuke from euery Eare that heard it.

sp.speaker: 1. Off.
sp.p: No more of him, hee's a worthy man: make way, they are comming.
sp.stage: A Sennet. Enter the Patricians, and the Tribunes of the People, Lictors before them: Coriolanus, Menenius, Cominius the Conſul: Scicinius and Brutus take their places by themſelues: Coriolanus ſtands.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.l: Hauing determin'd of the Volces,
And to ſend for Titus Lartius: it remaines,
As the maine Point of this our after-meeting,
To gratifie his Noble ſeruice, that hath
Thus ſtood for his Countrey. Therefore pleaſe you,
Moſt reuerend and graue Elders, to deſire
The preſent Conſull, and laſt Generall,
In our well-found Succeſſes, to report
A little of that worthy Worke, perform'd
By Martius Caius Coriolanus: whom
We met here, both to thanke, and to remember,
With Honors like himſelfe.

sp.speaker: 1. Sen.
sp.l: Speake, good Cominius:
Leaue nothing out for length, and make vs thinke
Rather our ſtates defectiue for requitall,
Then we to ſtretch it out. Maſters a' th' People,
We doe requeſt your kindeſt eares: and after
Your louing motion toward the common Body,
To yeeld what paſſes here.

sp.speaker: Scicin.
sp.p: We are conuented vpon a pleaſing Treatie, and haue hearts inclinable to honor and aduance the Theame of our Aſſembly.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.p: Which the rather wee ſhall be bleſt to doe, if he remember a kinder value of the People, then he hath hereto priz'd them at.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: That's off, that's off: I would you rather had been ſilent: Pleaſe you to heare Cominius ſpeake?

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.p: Moſt willingly: but yet my Caution was more pertinent then the rebuke you giue it.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: He loues your People, but tye him not to be their Bed-fellow: Worthie Cominius ſpeake.
sp.stage: Coriolanus riſes, and offers to goe away.
sp.l: Nay, keepe your place.

sp.speaker: Senat.
sp.l: Sit Coriolanus: neuer ſhame to heare
What you haue Nobly done.

sp.speaker: Coriol.
sp.l: Your Honors pardon:
I had rather haue my Wounds to heale againe,
Then heare ſay how I got them.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.p: Sir, I hope my words dis-bench'd you not?

sp.speaker: Coriol.
sp.l: No Sir: yet oft,
When blowes haue made me ſtay, I fled from words.
You ſooth'd not, therefore hurt not: but your People,
I loue them as they weigh—

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: Pray now ſit downe.

sp.speaker: Corio.
sp.l: I had rather haue one ſcratch my Head i' th' Sun,
When the Alarum were ſtrucke, then idly ſit
To heare my Nothings monſter'd.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.l: Maſters of the People,
Your multiplying Spawne, how can he flatter?
That's thouſand to one good one, when you now ſee
He had rather venture all his Limbes for Honor,
Then on ones Eares to heare it. Proceed Cominius.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: I ſhall lacke voyce: the deeds of Coriolanus
Should not be vtter'd feebly: it is held,
That Valour is the chiefeſt Vertue,
And moſt dignifies the hauer: if it be,
The man I ſpeake of, cannot in the World
Be ſingly counter-poys'd. At ſixteene yeeres,
When Tarquin made a Head for Rome, he fought
Beyond the marke of others: our then Dictator,
Whom with all prayſe I point at, ſaw him fight,
When with his Amazonian Shinne he droue
The brizled Lippes before him: he beſtrid
An o're-preſt Roman, and i' th' Conſuls view
Slew three Oppoſers: Tarquins ſelfe he met,
And ſtrucke him on his Knee: in that dayes feates,
When he might act the Woman in the Scene,
He prou'd beſt man i' th' field, and for his meed
Was Brow-bound with the Oake. His Pupill age
Man-entred thus, he waxed like a Sea,
And in the brunt of ſeuenteene Battailes ſince,
He lurcht all Swords of the Garland: for this laſt,
Before, and in Corioles, let me ſay
I cannot ſpeake him home: he ſtopt the flyers,
And by his rare example made the Coward
Turne terror into ſport: as Weeds before
A Veſſell vnder ſayle, ſo men obey'd,
And fell below his Stem: his Sword, Deaths ſtampe,
Where it did marke, it tooke from face to foot:
He was a thing of Blood, whoſe euery motion
Was tim'd with dying Cryes: alone he entred
The mortall Gate of th' Citie, which he painted
With ſhunleſſe deſtinie: aydeleſſe came off,
And with a ſudden re-inforcement ſtrucke
Carioles like a Planet: now all's his,
When by and by the dinne of Warre gan pierce
His readie ſence: then ſtraight his doubled ſpirit
Requickned what in fleſh was fatigate,
And to the Battaile came he, where he did
Runne reeking o're the liues of men, as if 'twere
A perpetuall ſpoyle: and till we call'd
Both Field and Citie ours, he neuer ſtood
To eaſe his Breſt with panting.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: Worthy man.

sp.speaker: Senat.
sp.p: He cannot but with meaſure fit the Honors which we deuiſe him.

sp.speaker: Com.
sp.l: Our ſpoyles he kickt at,
And look'd vpon things precious, as they were
The common Muck of the World: he couets leſſe
Then Miſerie it ſelfe would giue, rewards his deeds
With doing them, and is content
To ſpend the time▪ to end it.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: Hee's right Noble, let him be call'd for.

sp.speaker: Senat.
sp.p: Call Coriolanus.

sp.speaker: Off.
sp.p: He doth appeare.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: The Senate, Coriolanus, are well pleas'd to make thee Conſull.

sp.speaker: Corio.
sp.p: I doe owe them ſtill my Life, and Seruices.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.p: It then remaines, that you doe ſpeake to the People.

sp.speaker: Corio.
sp.l: I doe beſeech you,
Let me o're-leape that cuſtome: for I cannot
Put on the Gowne, ſtand naked, and entreat them
For my Wounds ſake, to giue their ſufferage:
Pleaſe you that I may paſſe this doing.

sp.speaker: Scicin.
sp.l: Sir, the People muſt haue their Voyces,
Neyther will they bate one iot of Ceremonie.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.l: Put them not too't:
Pray you goe fit you to the Cuſtome,
And take to you, as your Predeceſſors haue,
Your Honor with your forme.

sp.speaker: Corio.
sp.l: It is a part that I ſhall bluſh in acting,
And might well be taken from the People.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.p: Marke you that.

sp.speaker: Corio.
sp.l: To brag vnto them, thus I did, and thus
Shew them th' vnaking Skarres, which I ſhould hide,
As if I had receiu'd them for the hyre
Of their breath onely.

sp.speaker: Menen.
sp.l: Doe not ſtand vpon't:
We recommend to you Tribunes of the People
Our purpoſe to them, and to our Noble Conſull
Wiſh we all Ioy, and Honor.

sp.speaker: Senat.
sp.p: To Coriolanus come all ioy and Honor.

div.stage: Then Exeunt. Manet Sicinius and Brutus.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: You ſee how he intends to vſe the people.

sp.speaker: Scicin.
