Thus did Mark Antony bid me fall downe,
And being proſtrate, thus he bad me ſay:
Brutus is Noble, Wiſe, Valiant, and Honeſt;
Caeſar was Mighty, Bold, Royall, and Louing:
Say, I loue Brutus, and I honour him;
Say, I fear'd Caeſar, honour'd him, and lou'd him.
If Brutus will vouchſafe, that Antony
May ſafely come to him, and be reſolu'd
How Caeſar hath deſeru'd to lye in death,
Mark Antony, ſhall not loue Caeſar dead
So well as Brutus liuing; but will follow
The Fortunes and Affayres of Noble Brutus,
Thorough the hazards of this vntrod State,
With all true Faith. So ſayes my Maſter Antony.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Thy Maſter is a Wiſe and Valiant Romane,
I neuer thought him worſe:
Tell him, ſo pleaſe him come vnto this place
He ſhall be ſatisfied: and by my Honor
Depart vntouch'd.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Ile fetch him preſently.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: I know that we ſhall haue him well to Friend.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: I wiſh we may: But yet haue I a minde
That feares him much: and my miſgiuing ſtill
Falles ſhrewdly to the purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: But heere comes Antony:
Welcome Mark Antony.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: O mighty Caeſar! Doſt thou lye ſo lowe?
Are all thy Conqueſts, Glories, Triumphes, Spoiles,
Shrunke to this little Meaſure? Fare thee well.
I know not Gentlemen what you intend,
Who elſe muſt be let blood, who elſe is ranke:
If I my ſelfe, there is no houre ſo fit
As Caeſars deaths houre; nor no Inſtrument
Of halfe that worth, as thoſe your Swords; made rich
With the moſt Noble blood of all this World.
I do beſeech yee, if you beare me hard,
Now, whil'ſt your purpled hands do reeke and ſmoake,
Fulfill your pleaſure. Liue a thouſand yeeres,
I ſhall not finde my ſelfe ſo apt to dye.
No place will pleaſe me ſo, no meane of death,
As heere by Caeſar, and by you cut off,
The Choice and Maſter Spirits of this Age.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: O Antony! Begge not your death of vs:
Though now we muſt appeare bloody and cruell,
As by our hands, and this our preſent Acte
You ſee we do: Yet ſee you but our hands,
And this, the bleeding buſineſſe they haue do • e:
Our hearts you ſee not, they are pittifull:
And pitty to the generall wrong of Rome,
As fire driues out fire, ſo pitty; pitty
Hath done this deed on Caeſar. For your part,
To you, our Swords haue leaden points Marke Antony:
Our Armes in ſtrength of malice, and our Hearts
Of Brothers temper, do receiue you in,
With all kinde loue, good thoughts, and reuerence.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Your voyce ſhall be as ſtrong as any mans,
In the diſpoſing of new Dignities.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Onely be patient, till we haue appeas'd
The Multitude, beſide themſelues with feare,
And then, we will deliuer you the cauſe,
Why I, that did loue Caeſar when I ſtrooke him,
Haue thus proceeded.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I doubt not of your Wiſedome:
Let each man render me his bloody hand.
Next Caius Caſſius do I take your hand;
Now Decius Brutus yours; now yours Metellus;
Yours Cinna; and my valiant Caska, yours;
Though laſt, not leaſt in loue, yours good Trebonius
Gentlemen all: Alas, what ſhall I ſay,
My credit now ſtands on ſuch ſlippery ground,
That one of two bad wayes you muſt conceit me,
Either a Coward, or a Flatterer.
That I did loue thee Caeſar, O 'tis true:
If then thy Spirit looke vpon vs now,
Shall it not greeue thee deerer then thy death,
To ſee thy Antony making his peace,
Shaking the bloody fingers of thy Foes?
Moſt Noble, in the preſence of thy Coarſe,
Had I as many eyes, as thou haſt wounds,
Weeping as faſt as they ſtreame forth thy blood,
It would become me better, then to cloſe
In tearmes of Friendſhip with thine enemies.
Pardon me Iulius, heere was't thou bay'd braue Hart,
Heere did'ſt thou fall, and heere thy Hunters ſtand
Sign'd in thy Spoyle, and Crimſon'd in thy Lethee.
O World! thou waſt the Forreſt to this Hart,
And this indeed, O World, the Hart of thee.
How like a Deere, ſtroken by many Princes,
Doſt thou heere lye?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Pardon me Caius Caſſius:
The Enemies of Caeſar, ſhall ſay this:
Then, in a Friend, it is cold Modeſtie.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: I blame you not for praiſing Caeſar ſo,
But what compact meane you to haue with vs?
Will you be prick'd in number of our Friends,
Or ſhall we on, and not depend on you?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Therefore I tooke your hands, but was indeed
Sway'd from the point, by looking downe on Caeſar.
Friends am I with you all, and loue you all,
Vpon this hope, that you ſhall giue me Reaſons,
Why, and wherein, Caeſar was dangerous.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Or elſe were this a ſauage Spectacle:
Our Reaſons are ſo full of good regard,
That were you Antony, the Sonne of Caeſar,
You ſhould be ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: That's all I ſeeke,
And am moreouer ſutor, that I may
Produce his body to the Market-place,
And in the Pulpit as becomes a Friend,
Speake in the Order of his Funerall.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: You ſhall Marke Antony.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Brutus, a word with you:
You know not what you do; Do not conſent
That Antony ſpeake in his Funerall:
Know you how much the people may be mou'd
By that which he will vtter.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: By your pardon:
I will my ſelfe into the Pulpit firſt,
And ſhew the reaſon of our Caeſars death.
What Antony ſhall ſpeake, I will proteſt
He ſpeakes by leaue, and by permiſsion:
And that we are contented Caeſar ſhall
Haue all true Rites, and lawfull Ceremonies,
It ſhall aduantage more, then do vs wrong.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: I know not what may fall, I like it not.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Mark Antony, heere take you Caeſars body:
You ſhall not in your Funerall ſpeech blame vs,
But ſpeake all good you can deuiſe of Caeſar,
And ſay you doo't by our permiſsion:
Elſe ſhall you not haue any hand at all
About his Funerall. And you ſhall ſpeake
In the ſame Pulpit whereto I am going,
After my ſpeech is ended.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Be it ſo:
I do deſire no more.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Prepare the body then, and follow vs.
O pardon me, thou bleeding peece of Earth:
That I am meeke and gentle with theſe Butchers.
Thou art the Ruines of the Nobleſt man
That euer liued in the Tide of Times.
Woe to the hand that ſhed this coſtly Blood.
Ouer thy wounds, now do I Propheſie,
(Which like dumbe mouthes do ope their Ruby lips,
To begge the voyce and vtterance of my Tongue)
A Curſe ſhall light vpon the limbes of men;
Domeſticke Fury, and fierce Ciuill ſtrife,
Shall cumber all the parts of Italy:
Blood and deſtruction ſhall be ſo in vſe,
And dreadfull Obiects ſo familiar,
That Mothers ſhall but ſmile, when they behold
Their Infants quartered with the hands of Warre:
All pitty choak'd with cuſtome of fell deeds,
And Caeſars Spirit ranging for Reuenge,
With Ate by his ſide, come hot from Hell,
Shall in theſe Confines, with a Monarkes voyce,
Cry hauocke, and let ſlip the Dogges of Warre,
That this foule deede, ſhall ſmell aboue the earth
With Carrion men, groaning for Buriall.
You ſerue Octauius Caeſar, do you not?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: I do Marke Antony.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Caeſar did write for him to come to Rome.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: He did receiue his Letters, and is comming,
And bid me ſay to you by word of mouth—
O Caeſar!

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Thy heart is bigge: get thee a-part and weepe:
Paſsion I ſee is catching from mine eyes,
Seeing thoſe Beads of ſorrow ſtand in thine,
Began to water. Is thy Maſter comming?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: He lies to night within ſeuen Leagues of Rome.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Poſt backe with ſpeede,
And tell him what hath chanc'd:
Heere is a mourning Rome, a dangerous Rome,
No Rome of ſafety for Octauius yet,
Hie hence, and tell him ſo. Yet ſtay a-while,
Thou ſhalt not backe, till I haue borne this courſe
Into the Market place: There ſhall I try
In my Oration, how the People take
The cruell iſſue of theſe bloody men,
According to the which, thou ſhalt diſcourſe
To yong Octauius, of the ſtate of things.
Lend me your hand.

div.stage: Enter Brutus and goes into the Pulpit, and Caſſius, with the Plebeians.

sp.speaker: Ple.
sp.p: We will be ſatisfied: let vs be ſatisfied▪

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Then follow me, and giue me Audience friends.
Caſſius go you into the other ſtreete,
And part the Numbers:
Thoſe that will heare me ſpeake, let 'em ſtay heere;
Thoſe that will follow Caſſius, go with him,
And publike Reaſons ſhall be rendred
Of Caeſars death.

sp.speaker: 1. Ple.
sp.p: I will heare Brutus ſpeake.

sp.l: I will heare Caſſius, and compare their Reaſons,
When ſeuerally we heare them rendred.

sp.p: The Noble Brutus is aſcended: Silence.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Be patient till the laſt. Romans, Countrey-men, and Louers, heare mee for my cauſe, and be ſilent, that you may heare. Beleeue me for mine Honor, and haue reſpect to mine Honor, that you may beleeue. Cenſure me in your Wiſedom, and awake your Senſes, that you may the better Iudge. If there bee any in this Aſſembly, any deere Friend of Caeſars, to him I ſay, that Brutus loue to Caeſar, was no leſſe then his. If then, that Friend demand, why Brutus roſe againſt Caeſar, this is my anſwer: Not that I lou'd Caeſar leſſe, but that I lou'd Rome more. Had you rather Caeſar were liuing, and dye all Slaues; then that Caeſar were dead, to liue all Free-men? As Caeſar lou'd mee, I weepe for him; as he was Fortunate, I reioyce at it; as he was Valiant, I honour him: But, as he was Ambitious, I ſlew him. There is Teares, for his Loue: Ioy, for his Fortune: Honor, for his Valour: and Death, for his Ambition. Who is heere ſo baſe, that would be a Bondman? If any, ſpeak, for him haue I offended. Who is heere ſo rude, that would not be a Roman? If any, ſpeak, for him haue I offended. Who is heere ſo vile, that will not loue his Countrey? If any, ſpeake, for him haue I offended. I pauſe for a Reply.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: None Brutus, none.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.p: Then none haue I offended. I haue done no more to Caeſar, then you ſhall do to Brutus. The Queſtion of his death, is inroll'd in the Capitoll: his Glory not extenuated, wherein he was worthy; nor his offences enforc'd, for which he ſuffered death.
sp.stage: Enter Mark Antony, with Caeſars body.
sp.p: Heere comes his Body, mourn'd by Marke Antony, who though he had no hand in his death, ſhall receiue the benefit of his dying, a place in the Cōmonwealth, as which of you ſhall not. With this I depart, that as I ſlewe my beſt Louer for the good of Rome, I haue the ſame Dagger for my ſelfe, when it ſhall pleaſe my Country to need my death.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Liue Brutus, liue, liue.
Bring him with Triumph home vnto his houſe.
Giue him a Statue with his Anceſtors.
Let him be Caeſar.

sp.l: Caeſars better parts,
Shall be Crown'd in Brutus.
Wee'l bring him to his Houſe,
With Showts and Clamors.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: My Country-men.
Peace, ſilence, Brutus ſpeakes.
Peace ho.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Good Countrymen, let me depart alone,
And (for my ſake) ſtay heere with Antony:
Do grace to Caeſars Corpes, and grace his Speech
Tending to Caeſars Glories, which Marke Antony
(By our permiſſion) is allow'd to make.
I do intreat you, not a man depart,
Saue I alone, till Antony haue ſpoke.

sp.p: Stay ho, and let vs heare Mark Antony.

sp.l: Let him go vp into the publike Chaire,
Wee'l heare him: Noble Antony go vp.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: For Brutus ſake, I am beholding to you.
What does he ſay of Brutus?

sp.l: He ſayes, for Brutus ſake
He findes himſelfe beholding to vs all.

sp.p: 'Twere beſt he ſpeake no harme of Brutus heere?
This Caeſar was a Tyrant.

sp.l: Nay that's certaine:
We are bleſt that Rome is rid of him.

sp.p: Peace, let vs heare what Antony can ſay.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: You gentle Romans.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Peace hoe, let vs heare him.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: Friends, Romans, Countrymen, lend me your ears:
I come to bury Caeſar, not to praiſe him:
The euill that men do, liues after them,
The good is oft enterred with their bones,
So let it be with Caeſar. The Noble Brutus,
Hath told you Caeſar was Ambitious:
If it were ſo, it was a greeuous Fault,
And greeuouſly hath Caeſar anſwer'd it.
Heere, vnder leaue of Brutus, and the reſt
(For Brutus is an Honourable man,
So are they all; all Honourable m • n)
Come I to ſpeake in Caeſars Funerall.
He was my Friend, faithfull, and iuſt to me;
But Brutus ſayes; he was Ambitious,
And Brutus is an Honourable man.
He hath brought many Captiues home to Rome▪
Whoſe Ranſomes, did the generall Coffers fill:
Did this in Caeſar ſeeme Ambitious?
When that the poore haue cry'de, Caeſar hath wept:
Ambition ſhould be made of ſterner ſtuffe,
Yet Brutus ſayes, he was Ambitious:
And Brutus is an Honourable man.
You all did ſee, that on the Lupercall,
I thrice preſented him a Kingly Crowne,
Which he did thrice refuſe. Was this Ambition?
Yet Brutus ſayes, he was Ambitious:
And ſure he is an Honourable man.
I ſpeake not to diſprooue what Brutus ſpoke,
But heere I am, to ſpeake what I do know;
You all did loue him once, not without cauſe,
What cauſe with-holds you then, to mourne for him?
O Iudgement! thou are fled to brutiſh Beaſts,
And Men haue loſt their Reaſon. Beare with me,
My heart is in the Coffin there with Caeſar,
And I muſt pawſe, till it come backe to me.

sp.p: Me thinkes there is much reaſon in his ſayings.

sp.l: If thou conſider rightly of the matter,
Caeſar ha's had great wrong.

sp.p: Ha's hee Maſters? I feare there will a worſe come in his place.

sp.l: Mark'd ye his words? he would not take ye Crown,
Therefore 'tis certaine, he was not Ambitious.

sp.p: If it be found ſo, ſome will deere abide it.
Poore ſoule, his eyes are red as fire with weeping.
There's not a Nobler man in Rome then Antony.
Now marke him, he begins againe to ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: But yeſterday, the word of Caeſar might
Haue ſtood againſt the World: Now lies he there,
And none ſo poore to do him reuerence.
O Maiſters! If I were diſpos'd to ſtirre
Your hearts and mindes to Mutiny and Rage,
I ſhould do Brutus wrong, and Caſſius wrong:
Who (you all know) are Honourable men.
I will not do them wrong: I rather chooſe
To wrong the dead, to wrong my ſelfe and you,
Then I will wrong ſuch Honourable men,
But heere's a Parchment, with the Seale of Caeſar,
I found it in his Cloſſet, 'tis his Will:
Let but the Commons heare this Teſtament:
(Which pardon me) I do not meane to reade,
And they would go and kiſſe dead Caeſars wounds.
And dip their Napkins in his Sacred Blood;
Yea, begge a haire of him for Memory,
And dying, mention it within their Willes,
Bequeathing it as a rich Legacie
Vnto their iſſue.

sp.p: Wee'l heare the Will, reade it Marke Antony.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: The Will, the Will; we will heare Caeſars Will.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Haue patience gentle Friends, I muſt not read it.
It is not meete you know how Caeſar lou'd you:
You are not Wood, you are not Stones▪ but men:
And being men, hearing the Will of Caeſar,
It will inflame you, it will make you mad:
'Tis good you know not that you are his Heires,
For if you ſhould, O what would come of it?
Read the Will, wee'l heare it Antony:
You ſhall reade vs the Will, Caeſars Will.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Will you be Patient? Will you ſtay a-while?
I haue o're-ſhot my ſelfe to tell you of it,
I feare I wrong the Honourable men,
Whoſe Daggers haue ſtabb'd Caeſar: I do feare it.

sp.p: They were Traitors: Honourable men?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: The Will, the Teſtament.
They were Villaines, Murderers: the Will, read the Will.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You will compell me then to read the Will:
Then make a Ring about the Corpes of Caeſar,
And let me ſhew you him that made the Will:
Shall I deſcend? And will you giue me leaue?

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Come downe.
Deſcend.
You ſhall haue leaue.
A Ring, ſtand round.
Stand from the Hearſe, ſtand from the Body.
Roome for Antony, moſt Noble Antony.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Nay preſſe not ſo vpon me, ſtand farre off.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Stand backe: roome, beare backe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: If you haue teares, prepare to ſhed them now.
You all do know this Mantle, I remember
The firſt time euer Caeſar put it on,
'Twas on a Summers Euening in his Tent,
That day he ouercame the Neruij.
Looke, in this place ran Caſſius Dagger through:
See what a rent the enuious Caska made:
Through this, the wel-beloued Brutus ſtabb'd,
And as he pluck'd his curſed Steele away:
Marke how the blood of Caeſar followed it,
As ruſhing out of doores, to be reſolu'd
If Brutus ſo vnkindely knock'd, or no:
For Brutus, as you know, was Caeſars Angel.
Iudge, O you Gods, how deerely Caeſar lou'd him:
This was the moſt vnkindeſt cut of all.
For when the Noble Caeſar ſaw him ſtab,
Ingratitude, more ſtrong then Traitors armes,
Quite vanquiſh'd him: then burſt his Mighty heart,
And in his Mantle, muffling vp his face,
Euen at the Baſe of Pompeyes Statue
(Which all the while ran blood) great Caeſar fell.
O what a fall was there, my Countrymen?
Then I, and you, and all of vs fell downe,
Whil'ſt bloody Treaſon flouriſh'd ouer vs.
O now you weepe, and I perceiue you feele
The dint of pitty: Theſe are gracious droppes.
Kinde Soules, what weepe you, when you but behold
Our Caeſars Veſture wounded? Looke you heere,
Heere is Himſelfe, marr'd as you ſee with Traitors.

sp.p: O pitteous ſpectacle!
O Noble Caeſar!
O wofull day!
O Traitors, Villaines!
O moſt bloody ſight!

sp.l: We will be reueng'd: Reuenge
About, ſeeke, burne, fire, kill, ſlay,
Let not a Traitor liue.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Stay Country-men.
Peace there, heare the Noble Antony.
Wee'l heare him, wee'l follow him, wee'l dy with him.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Good Friends, ſweet Friends, let me not ſtirre you vp
To ſuch a ſodaine Flood of Mutiny:
They that haue done this Deede, are honourable.
What priuate greefes they haue, alas I know not,
That made them do it: They are Wiſe and Honourable,
And will no doubt with Reaſons anſwer you.
I come not (Friends) to ſteale away your hearts,
I am no Orator, as Brutus is;
But (as you know me all) a plaine blunt man
That loue my Friend, and that they know full well,
That gaue me publike leaue to ſpeake of him:
For I haue neyther writ nor words, nor worth,
Action, nor Vtterance, nor the power of Speech,
To ſtirre mens Blood. I onely ſpeake right on:
I tell you that, which you your ſelues do know,
Shew you ſweet Caeſars wounds, poor poor dum mouths
And bid them ſpeake for me: But were I Brutus,
And Brutus Antony, there were an Antony
Would ruffle vp your Spirits, and put a Tongue
In euery Wound of Caeſar, that ſhould moue
The ſtones of Rome, to riſe and Mutiny.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Wee'l Mutiny.
Wee'l burne the houſe of Brutus.
Away then, come, ſeeke the Conſpirators.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Yet heare me Countrymen, yet heare me ſpeake

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Peace hoe, heare Antony, moſt Noble Antony.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Why Friends, you go to do you know not what:
Wherein hath Caeſar thus deſeru'd your loues?
Alas you know not, I muſt tell you then:
You haue forgot the Will I told you of.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Moſt true, the Will, let's ſtay and heare the Wil.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Heere is the Will, and vnder Caeſars Seale:
To euery Roman Citizen he giues,
To euery ſeuerall man, ſeuenty fiue Drachmaes.

sp.speaker: 2 Ple.
sp.p: Moſt Noble Caeſar, wee'l reuenge his death.

sp.speaker: 3 Ple.
sp.p: O Royall Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Heare me with patience.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Peace hoe

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Moreouer, he hath left you all his Walkes,
His priuate Arbors, and new-planted Orchards,
On this ſide Tyber, he hath left them you,
And to your heyres for euer: common pleaſures
To walke abroad, and recreate your ſelues.
Heere was a Caeſar: when comes ſuch another?

sp.speaker: 1. Ple.
sp.l: Neuer, neuer: come, away, away:
Wee'l burne his body in the holy place,
And with the Brands fire the Traitors houſes.
Take vp the body.

sp.speaker: 2. Ple.
sp.p: Go fetch fire.

sp.speaker: 3. Ple.
sp.p: Plucke downe Benches.

sp.speaker: 4. Ple.
sp.p: Plucke downe Formes, Windowes, any thing.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Now let it worke: Miſcheefe thou art a-foot,
Take thou what courſe thou wilt.
How now Fellow?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: Sir, Octauius is already come to Rome.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Where is hee?

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.p: He and Lepidus are at Caeſars houſe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: And thither will I ſtraight, to viſit him:
He comes vpon a wiſh. Fortune is merry,
And in this mood will giue vs any thing.

sp.speaker: Ser.
sp.l: I heard him ſay, Brutus and Caſſius
Are rid like Madmen through the Gates of Rome.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Belike they had ſome notice of the people
How I had moued them. Bring me to Octauius.

div.stage: Enter Cinna the Poet, and after him the Plebeians.

sp.speaker: Cinna.
sp.l: I dreamt to night, that I did feaſt with Caeſar,
And things vnluckily charge my Fantaſie:
I haue no will to wander foorth of doores,
Yet ſomething leads me foorth.

sp.p: What is your name?
Whether are you going?
Where do you dwell?
Are you a married man, or a Batchellor?
Anſwer euery man directly.
I, and breefely.
I, and wiſely.
I, and truly, you were beſt.

sp.speaker: Cin.
sp.p: What is my name? Whether am I going? Where do I dwell? Am I a married man, or a Batchellour? Then to anſwer euery man, directly and breefely, wiſely and truly: wiſely I ſay, I am a Batchellor.
That's as much as to ſay, they are fooles that marrie: you'l beare me a bang for that I feare: proceede directly.

sp.speaker: Cinna.
sp.p: Directly I am going to Caeſars Funerall.
As a Friend, or an Enemy?

sp.speaker: Cinna.
sp.p: As a friend.
That matter is anſwered directly.
For your dwelling: breefely.

sp.speaker: Cinna.
sp.p: Breefely, I dwell by the Capitoll.
Your name ſir, truly.

sp.speaker: Cinna.
sp.p: Truly, my name is Cinna.
Teare him to peeces, hee's a Conſpirator.

sp.speaker: Cinna,
sp.p: I am Cinna the Poet I am Cinna the Poet.
Teare him for his bad verſes, teare him for his bad Verſes.

sp.speaker: Cin.
sp.p: I am not Cinna the Conſpirator.
It is no matter, his name's Cinna, plucke but his name out of his heart, and turne him going.
Teare him, tear him; Come Brands hoe, Firebrands: to Brutus, to Caſſius, burne all. Some to Decius Houſe, and ſome to Caska's; ſome to Ligarius: Away, go.

div.head: Actus Quartus.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Theſe many then ſhall die, their names are prickt

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.p: Your Brother too muſt dye: conſent you Lepidus?

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: I do conſent.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.p: Pricke him downe Antony.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.l: Vpon condition Publius ſhall not liue,
Who is your Siſters ſonne, Marke Antony.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: He ſhall not liue; looke, with a ſpot I dam him.
But Lepidus, go you to Caeſars houſe:
Fetch the Will hither, and we ſhall determine
How to cut off ſome charge in Legacies.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: What? ſhall I finde you heere?

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.p: Or heere, or at the Capitoll.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This is a ſlight vnmeritable man,
Meet to be ſent on Errands: is it fit
The three-fold World diuided, he ſhould ſtand
One of the three to ſhare it?

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: So you thought him,
And tooke his voyce who ſhould be prickt to dye
In our blacke Sentence and Proſcription.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Octauius, I haue ſeene more dayes then you,
And though we lay theſe Honours on this man,
To eaſe our ſelues of diuers ſland'rous loads,
He ſhall but beare them, as the Aſſe beares Gold,
To groane and ſwet vnder the Buſineſſe,
Either led or driuen, as we point the way:
And hauing brought our Treaſure, where we will,
Then take we downe his Load, and turne him off
(Like to the empty Aſſe) to ſhake his eares,
And graze in Commons.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: You may do your will:
But hee's a tried, and valiant Souldier.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: So is my Horſe Octauius, and for that
I do appoint him ſtore of Prouender.
It is a Creature that I teach to fight,
To winde, to ſtop, to run directly on:
His corporall Motion, gouern'd by my Spirit,
And in ſome taſte, is Lepidus but ſo:
He muſt be taught, and train'd, and bid go forth:
A barren ſpirited Fellow; one that feeds
On Obiects, Arts, and Imitations.
Which out of vſe, and ſtal'de by other men
Begin his faſhion. Do not talke of him,
But as a property: and now Octauius,
Liſten great things. Brutus and Caſſius
Are leuying Powers; We muſt ſtraight make head:
Therefore let our Alliance be combin'd.
Our beſt Friends made, our meanes ſtretcht,
And let vs preſently go ſit in Councell,
How couert matters may be beſt diſclos'd,
And open Perils ſureſt anſwered.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: Let vs do ſo: for we are at the ſtake,
And bayed about with many Enemies,
And ſome that ſmile haue in their hearts I feare
Millions of Miſcheefes.

div.stage: Drum. Enter Brutus, Lucillius, and the Army. Titinius and Pindarus meete them.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Stand ho.

sp.speaker: Lucil.
sp.p: Giue the word ho, and Stand.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: What now Lucillius, is Caſſius neere?

sp.speaker: Lucil.
sp.l: He is at hand, and Pindarus is come
To do you ſalutation from his Maſter.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: He greets me well. Your Maſter Pindarus
In his owne change, or by ill Officers,
Hath giuen me ſome worthy cauſe to wiſh
Things done, vndone: But if he be at hand
I ſhall be ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: I do not doubt
But that my Noble Maſter will appeare
Such as he is, full of regard, and Honour.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: He is not doubted. A word Lucillius
How he receiu'd you: let me be reſolu'd.

sp.speaker: Lucil.
sp.l: With courteſie, and with reſpect enough,
But not with ſuch familiar inſtances,
Nor with ſuch free and friendly Conference
As he hath vs'd of old.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Thou haſt deſcrib'd
A hot Friend, cooling: Euer note Lucillius,
When Loue begins to ſicken and decay
It vſeth an enforced Ceremony.
There are no trickes, in plaine and ſimple Faith:
But hollow men, like Horſes hot at hand,
Make gallant ſhew, and promiſe of their Mettle:
But when they ſhould endure the bloody Spurre,
They fall their Creſts, and like deceitfull Iades
Sinke in the Triall. Comes his Army on?

sp.speaker: Lucil.
sp.l: They meane this night in Sardis to be quarter'd:
The greater part, the Horſe in generall
Are come with Caſſius.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Hearke, he is arriu'd:
March gently on to meete him.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: Stand ho.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Stand ho, ſpeake the word along.
Stand.
Stand.
Stand.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: Moſt Noble Brother, you haue done me wrong.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Iudge me you Gods; wrong I mine Enemies?
And if not ſo, how ſhould I wrong a Brother.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Brutus, this ſober forme of yours, hides wrongs,
And when you do them—

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.l: Caſſius, be content,
Speake your greefes ſoftly, I do know you well.
Before the eyes of both our Armies heere
(Which ſhould perceiue nothing but Loue from vs)
Let vs not wrangle. Bid them moue away:
Then in my Tent Caſſius enlarge your Greefes,
And I will giue you Audience.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.

l.hi: Pindarus,

sp.l: Bid our Commanders leade their Charges off
A little from this ground.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Lucillius, do you the like, and let no man
Come to our Tent, till we haue done our Conference.
Let Lucius and Titinius guard our doore.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: That you haue wrong'd me, doth appear in this▪
You haue condemn'd, and noted Lucius Pella
For taking Bribes heere of the Sardians;
Wherein my Letters, praying on his ſide,
Becauſe I knew the man was ſlighted off.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: You wrong'd your ſelfe to write in ſuch a caſe.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: In ſuch a time as this, it is not meet
That euery nice offence ſhould beare his Comment.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Let me tell you Caſſius, you your ſelfe
Are much condemn'd to haue an itching Palme,
To ſell, and Mart your Offices for Gold
To Vndeſeruers.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: I, an itching Palme?
You know that you are Brutus that ſpeakes this,
Or by the Gods, this ſpeech were elſe your laſt.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: The name of Caſſius Honors this corruption,
And Chaſticement doth therefore hide his head.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: Chaſticement?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Remember March, the Ides of March remēber:
Did not great Iulius bleede for Iuſtice ſake?
What Villaine touch'd his body, that did ſtab,
And not for Iuſtice? What? Shall one of Vs,
That ſtrucke the Formoſt man of all this World,
But for ſupporting Robbers: ſhall we now,
Contaminate our fingers, with baſe Bribes?
And ſell the mighty ſpace of our large Honors
For ſo much traſh, as may be graſped thus?
I had rather be a Dogge, and bay the Moone,
Then ſuch a Roman.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Brutus, baite not me,
Ile not indure it: you forget your ſelfe
To hedge me in. I am a Souldier, I,
Older in practice, Abler then your ſelfe
To make Conditions.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Go too: you are not Caſſius.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: I am.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: I ſay, you are not.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Vrge me no more, I ſhall forget my ſelfe:
Haue minde vpon your health: Tempt me no farther.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Away ſlight man.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: Is't poſſible?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Heare me, for I will ſpeake.
Muſt I giue way, and roome to your raſh Choller?
Shall I be frighted, when a Madman ſtares?

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: O ye Gods, ye Gods, Muſt I endure all this?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: All this? I more: Fret till your proud hart break.
Go ſhew your Slaues how Chollericke you are,
And make your Bondmen tremble. Muſt I bouge?
Muſt I obſerue you? Muſt I ſtand and crouch
Vnder your Teſtie Humour? By the Gods,
You ſhall digeſt the Venom of your Spleene
Though it do Split you. For, from this day forth,
Ile vſe you for my Mirth, yea for my Laughter
When you are Waſpiſh.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: Is it come to this?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: You ſay, you are a better Souldier:
Let it appeare ſo; make your vaunting true,
And it ſhall pleaſe me well. For mine owne part,
I ſhall be glad to learne of Noble men.

sp.speaker: Caſſ.
sp.l: You wrong me euery way:
You wrong me Brutus:
I ſaide, an Elder Souldier, not a Better.
Did I ſay Better?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: If you did, I care not.

sp.speaker: Caſſ.
sp.p: When Caeſar liu'd, he durſt not thus haue mou'd me.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.p: Peace, peace, you durſt not ſo haue tempted him.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: I durſt not.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: What? durſt not tempt him?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: For your life you durſt not.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Do not preſume too much vpon my Loue,
I may do that I ſhall be ſorry for.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: You haue done that you ſhould be ſorry for.
There is no terror Caſſius in your threats:
For I am Arm'd ſo ſtrong in Honeſty,
That they paſſe by me, as the idle winde,
Which I reſpect not. I did ſend to you
For certaine ſummes of Gold, which you deny'd me,
For I can raiſe no money by vile meanes:
By Heauen, I had rather Coine my Heart,
And drop my blood for Drachmaes, then to wring
From the hard hands of Peazants, their vile traſh
By any indirection. I did ſend
To you for Gold to pay my Legions,
Which you deny'd me: was that done like Caſſius?
Should I haue anſwer'd Caius Caſſius ſo?
When Marcus Brutus growes ſo Couetous,
To locke ſuch Raſcall Counters from his Friends,
Be ready Gods with all your Thunder-bolts,
Daſh him to peeces.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: I deny'd you not.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: You did.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: I did not. He was but a Foole
That brought my anſwer back. Brutus hath riu'd my hart:
A Friend ſhould beare his Friends infirmities;
But Brutus makes mine greater then they are.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: I do not, till you practice them on me.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: You loue me not.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: I do not like your faults.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: A friendly eye could neuer ſee ſuch faults.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: A Flatterers would not, though they do appeare
As huge as high Olympus.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Come Antony, and yong Octauius come,
Reuenge your ſelues alone on Caſſius,
For Caſſius is a-weary of the World:
Hated by one he loues, brau'd by his Brother,
Check'd like a bondman, all his faults obſeru'd,
Set in a Note-booke, learn'd, and con'd by roate
To caſt into my Teeth. O I could weepe
My Spirit from mine eyes. There is my Dagger,
And heere my naked Breaſt: Within, a Heart
Deerer then Pluto's Mine, Richer then Gold:
If that thou bee'ſt a Roman, take it foorth.
I that deny'd thee Gold, will giue my Heart:
Strike as thou did'ſt at Caeſar: For I know,
When thou did'ſt hate him worſt, yu loued'ſt him better
Then euer thou loued'ſt Caſſius.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Sheath your Dagger:
Be angry when you will, it ſhall haue ſcope:
Do what you will, Diſhonor, ſhall be Humour.
O Caſſius, you are yoaked with a Lambe
That carries Anger, as the Flint beares fire,
Who much inforced, ſhewes a haſtie Sparke,
And ſtraite is cold agen.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Hath Caſſius liu'd
To be but Mirth and Laughter to his Brutus.
When greefe and blood ill temper'd, vexeth him?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: When I ſpoke that, I was ill temper'd too.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: Do you confeſſe ſo much? Giue me your hand.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: And my heart too.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: O Brutus!

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Haue not you loue enough to beare with me,
When that raſh humour which my Mother gaue me
Makes me forgetfull.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Yes Caſsius, and from henceforth
When you are ouer-earneſt with your Brutus,
Hee'l thinke your Mother chides, and leaue you ſo.

sp.speaker: Poet.
sp.l: Let me go in to ſee the Generals,
There is ſome grudge betweene 'em, 'tis not meete
They be alone.

sp.speaker: Lucil.
sp.p: You ſhall not come to them.

sp.speaker: Poet.
sp.p: Nothing but death ſhall ſtay me.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: How now? What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Poet.
sp.l: For ſhame you Generals; what do you meane?
Loue, and be Friends, as two ſuch men ſhould bee,
For I haue ſeene more yeeres I'me ſure then yee.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Ha, ha, how vildely doth this Cynicke rime?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Get you hence ſirra: Sawcy Fellow, hence.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Beare with him Brutus, 'tis his faſhion.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.l: Ile know his humor, when he knowes his time:
What ſhould the Warres do with theſe ligging Fooles?
Companion, hence.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Away, away be gone.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Lucillius and Titinius bid the Commanders
Prepare to lodge their Companies to night.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: And come your ſelues, & bring Meſſala with you Immediately to vs.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Lucius, a bowle of Wine.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: I did not thinke you could haue bin ſo angry.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: O Caſſius, I am ſicke of many greefes.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Of your Philoſophy you make no vſe,
If you giue place to accidentall euils.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: No man beares ſorrow better. Portia is dead.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Ha? Portia?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: She is dead.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: How ſcap'd I killing, when I croft you ſo?
O inſupportable, and touching loſſe!
Vpon what ſickneſſe?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Impatient of my abſence▪
And greefe, that yong Octauius with Mark Antony
Haue made themſelues ſo ſtrong: For with her death
That tydings came. With this ſhe fell diſtract,
And (her Attendants abſent) ſwallow'd fire.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: And dy'd ſo?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Euen ſo.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: O ye immortall Gods!

div.stage: Enter Boy with Wine, and Tapers.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Speak no more of her: Giue me a bowl of wine,
In this I bury all vnkindneſſe Caſsius.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: My heart is thirſty for that Noble pledge.
Fill Lucius, till the Wine ore-ſwell the Cup:
I cannot drinke too much of Brutus loue.

sp.speaker: Brutus.
sp.l: Come in Titinius:
Welcome good Meſſala:
Now ſit we cloſe about this Taper heere,
And call in queſtion our neceſſities.

sp.speaker: Caſſ.
sp.p: Portia, art thou gone?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: No more I pray you
Meſſala, I haue heere receiued Letters,
That yong Octauius, and Mark Antony
Come downe vpon vs with a mighty power,
Bending their Expedition toward Philippi.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: My ſelfe haue Letters of the ſelfe-ſame Tenure.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: With what Addition.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: That by proſcription, and billes of Outlarie,
Octauius, Antony, and Lepidus,
Haue put to death, an hundred Senators.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Therein our Letters do not well agree:
Mine ſpeake of ſeuenty Senators, that dy'de
By their proſcriptions, Cicero being one.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: Cicero one?

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.l: Cicero is dead, and by that order of proſcription
Had you your Letters from your wife, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: No Meſſala.

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.p: Nor nothing in your Letters writ of her?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Nothing Meſſala.

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.p: That me thinkes is ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Why aske you?
Heare you ought of her, in yours?

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.p: No my Lord.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Now as you are a Roman tell me true.

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.l: Then like a Roman, beare the truth I tell,
For certaine ſhe is dead, and by ſtrange manner.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Why farewell Portia: We muſt die Meſſala:
With meditating that ſhe muſt dye once,
I haue the patience to endure it now.

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.p: Euen ſo great men, great loſſes ſhold indure.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: I haue as much of this in Art as you,
But yet my Nature could not beare it ſo.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Well, to our worke aliue. What do you thinke
Of marching to Philippi preſently.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: I do not thinke it good.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Your reaſon?

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: This it is:
'Tis better that the Enemie ſeeke vs,
So ſhall he waſte his meanes, weary his Souldiers,
Doing himſelfe offence, whil'ſt we lying ſtill,
Are full of reſt, defence, and nimbleneſſe.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Good reaſons muſt of force giue place to better:
The people 'twixt Philippi, and this ground
Do ſtand but in a forc'd affection:
For they haue grug'd vs Contribution.
The Enemy, marching along by them,
By them ſhall make a fuller number vp,
Come on refreſht, new added, and encourag'd:
From which aduantage ſhall we cut him off.
If at Philippi we do face him there,
Theſe people at our backe.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: Heare me good Brother.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Vnder your pardon. You muſt note beſide,
That we haue tride the vtmoſt of our Friends:
O • Legions are brim full, our cauſe is ripe,
The Enemy encreaſeth euery day,
We at the height, are readie to decline.
There is a Tide in the affayres of men,
Which taken at the Flood, leades on to Fortune:
Omitted, all the voyage of their life,
Is bound in Shallowes, and in Miſeries.
On ſuch a full Sea are we now a-float,
And we muſt take the current when it ſerues,
Or looſe our Ventures.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Then with your will go on: wee'l along
Our ſelues, and meet them at Philippi.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: The deepe of night is crept vpon our talke,
And Nature muſt obey Neceſſitie,
Which we will niggard with a little reſt:
There is no more to ſay.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: No more, good night,
Early to morrow will we riſe, and hence.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Lucius my Gowne: farewell good Meſſala,
Good night Titinius: Noble, Noble Caſſius,
Good night, and good repoſe.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: O my deere Brother:
This was an ill beginning of the night:
Neuer come ſuch diuiſion 'tweene our ſoules:
Let it not Brutus.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Euery thing is well.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: Good night my Lord.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Good night good Brother.

sp.speaker: Tit. Meſſa.
sp.p: Good night Lord Brutus.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Farwell euery one.
Giue me the Gowne. Where is thy Inſtrument?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Heere in the Tent.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: What, thou ſpeak'ſt drowſily?
Poore knaue I blame thee not, thou art ore-watch'd.
Call Claudio, and ſome other of my men,
Ile haue them ſleepe on Cuſhions in my Tent.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Varrus, and Claudio.

sp.speaker: Var.
sp.p: Cals my Lord?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: I pray you ſirs, lye in my Tent and ſleepe,
It may be I ſhall raiſe you by and by
On buſineſſe to my Brother Caſſius.

sp.speaker: Var.
sp.l: So pleaſe you, we will ſtand,
And watch your pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: I will it not haue it ſo: Lye downe good ſirs,
It may be I ſhall otherwiſe bethinke me.
Looke Lucius, heere's the booke I ſought for ſo:
I put it in the pocket of my Gowne.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I was ſure your Lordſhip did not giue it me.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Beare with me good Boy, I am much forgetfull.
Canſt thou hold vp thy heauie eyes a-while,
And touch thy Inſtrument a ſtraine or two.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I my Lord, an't pleaſe you.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: It does my Boy:
I trouble thee too much, but thou art willing.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: It is my duty Sir.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.l: I ſhould not vrge thy duty paſt thy might,
I know yong bloods looke for a time of reſt.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: I haue ſlept my Lord already.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: It was well done, and thou ſhalt ſleepe againe:
I will not hold thee long. If I do liue,
I will be good to thee.
This is a ſleepy Tune: O Murd'rous ſlumbler!
Layeſt thou thy Leaden Mace vpon my Boy,
That playes thee Muſicke? Gentle knaue good night:
I will not do thee ſo much wrong to wake thee:
If thou do'ſt nod, thou break'ſt thy Inſtrument,
Ile take it from thee, and (good Boy) good night.
Let me ſee, let me ſee; is not the Leafe turn'd downe
Where I left reading? Heere it is I thinke.
How ill this Taper burnes. Ha! Who comes heere?
I thinke it is the weakeneſſe of mine eyes
That ſhapes this monſtrous Apparition.
It comes vpon me: Art thou any thing?
Art thou ſome God, ſome Angell, or ſome Diuell,
That mak'ſt my blood cold, and my haire to ſtare?
Speake to me, what thou art.

sp.speaker: Ghoſt.
sp.p: Thy euill Spirit Brutus?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Why com'ſt thou?

sp.speaker: Ghoſt.
sp.p: To tell thee thou ſhalt ſee me at Philippi.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.p: Well: then I ſhall ſee thee againe?

sp.speaker: Ghoſt.
sp.p: I, at Philippi.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.l: Why I will ſee thee at Philippi then:
Now I haue taken heart, thou vaniſheſt.
Ill Spirit, I would hold more talke with thee.
Boy, Lucius, Varrus, Claudio, Sirs: Awake:

l.hi: Claudio.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: The ſtrings my Lord, are falſe.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: He thinkes he ſtill is at his Inſtrument▪
Lucius, awake.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Did'ſt thou dreame Lucus, that thou ſo cryedſt out?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: My Lord, I do not know that I did cry.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Yes that thou did'ſt: Did'ſt thou ſee any thing?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: Nothing my Lord.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Sleepe againe Lucius: Sirra Claudio, Fellow,
Thou: Awake.

sp.speaker: Var.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Claeu.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Why did you ſo cry out ſirs, in your ſleepe?

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: Did we my Lord?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: I: ſaw you any thing?

sp.speaker: Var.
sp.p: No my Lord, I ſaw nothing.

sp.speaker: Clau.
sp.p: Nor I my Lord.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Go, and commend me to my Brother Caſſius:
Bid him ſet on his Powres betimes before,
And we will follow.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: It ſhall be done my Lord.

div.head: Actus Quintus.
div.stage: Enter Octauius, Antony, and their Army.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: Now Antony, our hopes are anſwered,
You ſaid the Enemy would not come downe,
But keepe the Hilles and vpper Regions:
It proues not ſo: their battailes are at hand,
They meane to warne vs at Philippi heere:
Anſwering before we do demand of them.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Tut I am in their boſomes, and I know
Wherefore they do it: They could be content
To viſit other places, and come downe
With fearefull brauery: thinking by this face
To faſten in our thoughts that they haue Courage;
But 'tis not ſo.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: Prepare you Generals,
The Enemy comes on in gallant ſhew:
Their bloody ſigne of Battell is hung out,
And ſomething to be done immediately.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Octauius, leade your Battaile ſoftly on
Vpon the left hand of the euen Field.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.p: Vpon the right hand I, keepe thou the left.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Why do you croſſe me in this exigent.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.p: I do not croſſe you: but I will do ſo.

div.stage: Drum. Enter Brutus, Caſſius, & their Army.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: They ſtand, and would haue parley.

sp.speaker: Caſſi▪
sp.p: 〈◊〉 faſt Titinius, we muſt out and talke.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.p: Mark Antony, ſhall we giue ſigne of Battaile?

sp.l: No Caeſar, we will anſwer on their Charge.
Make forth, the Generals would haue ſome words.

sp.speaker: Oct.
sp.p: Stirre not vntill the Signall.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Words before blowes: is it ſo Countrymen?

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.p: Not that we loue words better, as you do.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Good words are better then bad ſtrokes Octauius.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.l: In your bad ſtrokes Brutus, you giue good words
Witneſſe the hole you made in Caeſars heart,
Crying long liue, Haile Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.

l.hi: Antony,

sp.l: The poſture of your blowes are yet vnknowne;
But for your words, they rob the Hibla Bees,
And leaue them Hony-leſſe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Not ſtingleſſe too.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: O yes, and ſoundleſſe too:
For you haue ſtolne their buzzing Antony,
And very wiſely threat before you ſting.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Villains: you did not ſo, when your vile daggers
Hackt one another in the ſides of Caeſar:
You ſhew'd your teethes like Apes,
And fawn'd like Hounds,
And bow'd like Bondmen, kiſſing Caeſars feete;
Whil'ſt damned Caska, like a Curre, behinde
Strooke Caeſar on the necke. O you Flatterers.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Flatterers? Now Brutus thanke your ſelfe,
This tongue had not offended ſo to day,
If Caſſius might haue rul'd.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: Come, come, the cauſe. If arguing make vs ſwet,
The proofe of it will turne to redder drops:
Looke, I draw a Sword againſt Conſpirators,
When thinke you that the Sword goes vp againe?
Neuer till Caeſars three and thirtie wounds
Be well aueng'd; or till another Caeſar
Haue added ſlaughter to the Sword of Traitors.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.l: Caeſar, thou canſt not dye by Traitors hands,
Vnleſſe thou bring'ſt them with thee.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: So I hope:
I was not borne to dye on Brutus Sword.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: O if thou wer't the Nobleſt of thy Straine,
Yong-man, thou could'ſt not dye more honourable.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: A peeuiſh School-boy, worthles of ſuch Honor
Ioyn'd with a Masker, and a Reueller.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Old Caſſius ſtill.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: Come Antony: away:
Defiance Traitors, hurle we in your teeth.
If you dare fight to day, come to the Field;
If not, when you haue ſtomackes.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Why now blow winde, ſwell Billow,
And ſwimme Barke:
The Storme is vp, and all is on the hazard.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Ho Lucillius, hearke, a word with you.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.p: What ſayes my Generall?

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Meſſala, this is my Birth-day: as this very day
Was Caſſius borne. Giue me thy hand Meſſala:
Be thou my witneſſe, that againſt my will
(As Pompey was) am I compell'd to ſet
Vpon one Battell all our Liberties.
You know, that I held Epicurus ſtrong,
And his Opinion: Now I change my minde,
And partly credit things that do preſage.
Comming from Sardis, on our former Enſigne
Two mighty Eagles fell, and there they pearch'd,
Gorging and feeding from our Soldiers hands,
Who to Philippi heere conſorted vs:
This Morning are they fled away, and gone,
And in their ſteeds, do Rauens, Crowes, and Kites
Fly ore our heads, and downward looke on vs
As we were ſickely prey; their ſhadowes ſeeme
A Canopy moſt fatall, vnder which
Our Army lies, ready to giue vp the Ghoſt.

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.p: Beleeue not ſo.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: I but beleeue it partly,
For I am freſh of ſpirit, and reſolu'd
To meete all perils, very conſtantly.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Euen ſo Lucillius.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Now moſt Noble Brutus,
The Gods to day ſtand friendly, that we may
Louers in peace, leade on our dayes to age.
But ſince the affayres of men reſts ſtill incertaine,
Let's reaſon with the worſt that may befall.
If we do loſe this Battaile, then is this
The very laſt time we ſhall ſpeake together:
What are you then determined to do?

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Euen by the rule of that Philoſophy,
By which I did blame Cato, for the death
Which he did giue himſelfe, I know not how:
But I do finde it Cowardly, and vile,
For feare of what might fall, ſo to preuent
The time of life, arming my ſelfe with patience,
To ſtay the prouidence of ſome high Powers,
That gouerne vs below.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Then, if we looſe this Battaile,
You are contented to be led in Triumph
Thorow the ſtreets of Rome.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: No Caſſius, no:
Thinke not thou Noble Romane,
That euer Brutus will go bound to Rome,
He beares too great a minde. But this ſame day
Muſt end that worke, the Ides of March begun.
And whether we ſhall meete againe, I know not:
Therefore our euerlaſting farewell take:
For euer, and for euer, farewell Caſſius,
If we do meete againe, why we ſhall ſmile;
If not, why then this parting was well made.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: For euer, and for euer, farewell Brutus:
If we do meete againe, wee'l ſmile indeede;
If not, 'tis true, this parting was well made.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Why then leade on. O that a man might know
The end of this dayes buſineſſe, ere it come:
But it ſufficeth, that the day will end,
And then the end is knowne. Come ho, away.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Ride, ride Meſſala, ride and giue theſe Billes
Vnto the Legions, on the other ſide.
Let them ſet on at once: for I perceiue
But cold demeanor in Octauio's wing:
And ſodaine puſh giues them the ouerthrow:
Ride, ride Meſſala, let them all come downe.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: O looke Titinius, looke, the Villaines flye:
My ſelfe haue to mine owne turn'd Enemy:
This Enſigne heere of mine was turning backe,
I ſlew the Coward, and did take it from him.

sp.speaker: Titin.
sp.l: O Caſſius, Brutus gaue the word too early,
Who hauing ſome aduantage on Octauius,
Tooke it too eagerly: his Soldiers fell to ſpoyle,
Whil'ſt we by Antony are all inclos'd.

sp.speaker: Pind.
sp.l: Fly further off my Lord: flye further off,
Mark Antony is in your Tents my Lord:
Flye therefore Noble Caſſius, flye farre off.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: This Hill is farre enough. Looke, look Titinius
Are thoſe my Tents where I perceiue the fire?

sp.speaker: Tit.
sp.p: They are, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Titinius, if thou loueſt me,
Mount thou my horſe, and hide thy ſpurres in him,
Till he haue brought thee vp to yonder Troopes
And heere againe, that I may reſt aſſur'd
Whether yond Troopes, are Friend or Enemy.

sp.speaker: Tit.
sp.p: I will be heere againe, euen with a thought.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Go Pindarus, get higher on that hill,
My ſight was euer thicke: regard Titinius,
And tell me what thou not'ſt about the Field.
This day I breathed firſt, Time is come round,
And where I did begin, there ſhall I end,
My life is run his compaſſe. Sirra, what newes?

sp.speaker: Pind.
sp.p: Aboue. O my Lord.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.p: What newes?

sp.speaker: Pind.
sp.l: Titinius is encloſed round about
With Horſemen, that make to him on the Spurre,
Yet he ſpurres on. Now they are almoſt on him:
Now Titinius. Now ſome light: O he lights too.
Hee's tane.
And hearke, they ſhout for ioy.

sp.speaker: Caſſi.
sp.l: Come downe, behold no more:
O Coward that I am, to liue ſo long,
To ſee my beſt Friend tane before my face.
Come hither ſirrah: In Parthia did I take thee Priſoner,
And then I ſwore thee, ſauing of thy life,
That whatſoeuer I did bid thee do,
Thou ſhould'ſt attempt it. Come now, keepe thine oath,
Now be a Free-man, and with this good Sword
That ran through Caeſars bowels, ſearch this boſome.
Stand not to anſwer: Heere, take thou the Hilts,
And when my face is couer'd, as 'tis now,
Guide thou the Sword — Caeſar, thou art reueng'd,
Euen with the Sword that kill'd thee.

sp.speaker: Pin.
sp.l: So, I am free,
Yet would not ſo haue beene
Durſt I haue done my will. O Caſſius,
Farre from this Country Pindarus ſhall run,
Where neuer Roman ſhall take note of him.

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.l: It is but change, Titinius: for Octauius
Is ouerthrowne by Noble Brutus power,
As Caſſius Legions are by Antony.

sp.speaker: Titin.
sp.p: Theſe tydings will well comfort Caſſius.

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.l: Where did you leaue him.

sp.speaker: Titin.
sp.l: All diſconſolate,
With Pindarus his Bondman, on this Hill.

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.p: Is not that he that lyes vpon the ground?

sp.speaker: Titin.
sp.p: He lies not like the Liuing. O my heart!

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.p: Is not that hee?

sp.speaker: Titin.
sp.l: No, this was he Meſſala,
But Caſſius is no more. O ſetting Sunne:
As in thy red Rayes thou doeſt ſinke to night;
So in his red blood Caſsius day is ſet.
The Sunne of Rome is ſet. Our day is gone,
Clowds, Dewes, and Dangers come; our deeds are done:
Miſtruſt of my ſucceſſe hath done this deed.

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.l: Miſtruſt of good ſucceſſe hath done this deed.
O hatefull Error, Melancholies Childe:
Why do'ſt thou ſhew to the apt thoughts of men▪
The things that are not? O Error ſoone conceyu'd,
Thou neuer com'ſt vnto a happy byrth,
But kil'ſt the Mother that engendred thee.

sp.speaker: Tit.
sp.p: What Pindarus? Where art thou Pindarus?

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.l: Seeke him Titinius, whilſt I go to meet
The Noble Brutus, thruſting this report
Into his eares; I may ſay thruſting it:
For piercing Steele, and Darts inuenomed,
Shall be as welcome to the eares of Brutus,
As tydings of this ſight.

sp.speaker: Tit.
sp.l: Hye you Meſſala,
And I will ſeeke for Pindarus the while:
Why did'ſt thou ſend me forth braue Caſsius?
Did I not meet thy Friends, and did not they
Put on my Browes this wreath of Victorie,
And bid me giue it thee? Did'ſt thou not heare their ſhowts?
Alas, thou haſt miſconſtrued euery thing.
But hold thee, take this Garland on thy Brow,
Thy Brutus bid me giue it thee, and I
Will do his bidding. Brutus, come apace,
And ſee how I regarded Caius Caſsius:
By your leaue Gods: This is a Romans part,
Come Caſsius Sword, and finde Titinius hart.

div.stage: Alarum. Enter Brutus, Meſſala, yong Cato, Strato, Volumnius, and Lucillius.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Where, where Meſſala, doth his body lye?

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.p: Loe yonder, and Titinius mourning it.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Titinius face is vpward.

sp.speaker: Cato.
sp.p: He is ſlaine.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: O Iulius Caeſar, thou art mighty yet,
Thy Spirit walkes abroad, and turnes our Swords
In our owne proper Entrailes.

sp.speaker: Cato.
sp.l: Braue Titinius,
Looke where he haue not crown'd dead Caſsius.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Are yet two Romans liuing ſuch as theſe?
The laſt of all the Romans, far thee well:
It is impoſſible, that euer Rome
Should breed thy fellow. Friends I owe mo teares
To this dead man, then you ſhall ſee me pay.
I ſhall finde time, Caſsius: I ſhall finde time.
Come therefore, and to Tharſus ſend his body,
His Funerals ſhall not be in our Campe,
Leaſt it diſcomfort vs. Lucillius come,
And come yong Cato, let vs to the Field,
Labio and Flauio ſet our Battailes on:
'Tis three a clocke, and Romans yet ere night,
We ſhall try Fortune in a ſecond fight.

div.stage: Alarum. Enter Brutus, Meſſala, Cato, Lucillius, and Flauius.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.p: Yet Country-men: O yet, hold vp your heads.

sp.speaker: Cato.
sp.l: What Baſtard doth not? Who will go with me?
I will proclaime my name about the Field.
I am the Sonne of Marcus Cato, hoe.
A Foe to Tyrants, and my Countries Friend.
I am the Sonne of Marcus Cato, hoe.
And I am Brutus, Marcus Brutus, I,
Brutus my Countries Friend: Know me for Brutus.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: O yong and Noble Cato, art thou downe?
Why now thou dyeſt, as brauely as Titinius,
And may'ſt be honour'd, being Cato's Sonne.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.p: Yeeld, or thou dyeſt.

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Onely I yeeld to dye:
There is ſo much, that thou wilt kill me ſtraight:
Kill Brutus, and be honour'd in his death.

sp.speaker: Sold.
sp.p: We muſt not: a Noble Priſoner.

sp.speaker: 2. Sold.
sp.p: Roome hoe: tell Antony, Brutus is tane.

sp.speaker: 1. Sold.
sp.l: Ile tell thee newes. Heere comes the Generall,
Brutus is tane, Brutus is tane my Lord.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Where is hee?

sp.speaker: Luc.
sp.l: Safe Antony, Brutus is ſafe enough:
I dare aſſure thee, that no Enemy
Shall euer take aliue the Noble Brutus:
The Gods defend him from ſo great a ſhame,
When you do finde him, or aliue, or dead,
He will be found like Brutus, like himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This is not Brutus friend, but I aſſure you,
A prize no leſſe in worth; keepe this man ſafe,
Giue him all kindneſſe. I had rather haue
Such men my Friends, then Enemies. Go on,
And ſee where Brutus be aliue or dead,
And bring vs word, vnto Octauius Tent:
How euery thing is chanc'd.

div.stage: Enter Brutus, Dardanius, Clitus, Strato, and Ʋolumnius.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.p: Come poore remaines of friends, reſt on this Rocke.

sp.speaker: Clit.
sp.l: Statillius ſhew'd the Torch-light, but my Lord
He came not backe: he is or tane, or ſlaine.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.l: Sit thee downe, Clitus: ſlaying is the word,
It is a deed in faſhion. Hearke thee, Clitus.

sp.speaker: Clit.
sp.p: What I, my Lord? No, not for all the World.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.p: Peace then, no words.

sp.speaker: Clit.
sp.p: Ile rather kill my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.p: Hearke thee, Dardanius.

sp.speaker: Dard.
sp.p: Shall I doe ſuch a deed?

sp.speaker: Clit.
sp.p: O Dardanius.

sp.speaker: Dard.
sp.p: O Clitus.

sp.speaker: Clit.
sp.p: What ill requeſt did Brutus make to thee?

sp.speaker: Dard.
sp.p: To kill him, Clitus: looke he meditates.

sp.speaker: Clit.
sp.l: Now is that Noble Veſſell full of griefe,
That it runnes ouer euen at his eyes.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.p: Come hither, good Ʋolumnius, liſt a word.

sp.speaker: Ʋolum.
sp.p: What ſayes my Lord?

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.l: Why this, Volumnius:
The Ghoſt of Caeſar hath appear'd to me
Two ſeuerall times by Night: at Sardis, once;
And this laſt Night, here in Philippi fields:
I know my houre is come.

sp.speaker: Volum.
sp.p: Not ſo, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Brut.
sp.l: Nay, I am ſure it is, Volumnius.
Thou ſeeſt the World, Volumnius, how it goes,
Our Enemies haue beat vs to the Pit:
It is more worthy, to leape in our ſelues,
Then tarry till they puſh vs. Good Volumnius,
Thou know'ſt, that we two went to Schoole together:
Euen for that our loue of old, I prethee
Hold thou my Sword Hilts, whileſt I runne on it.

sp.speaker: Vol.
sp.p: That's not an Office for a friend, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Cly.
sp.p: Fly, flye my Lord, there is no tarrying heere.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Farewell to you, and you, and you Volumnius.
Strato, thou haſt bin all this while aſleepe:
Farewell to thee, to Strato, Countrymen:
My heart doth ioy, that yet in all my life,
I found no man, but he was true to me.
I ſhall haue glory by this looſing day
More then Octauius, and Marke Antony,
By this vile Conqueſt ſhall attaine vnto.
So fare you well at once, for Brutus tongue
Hath almoſt ended his liues Hiſtory:
Night hangs vpon mine eyes, my Bones would reſt,
That haue but labour'd, to attaine this houre.

sp.speaker: Cly.
sp.p: Fly my Lord, flye.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Hence: I will follow:
I prythee Strato, ſtay thou by thy Lord,
Thou art a Fellow of a good reſpect:
Thy life hath had ſome ſmatch of Honor in it,
Hold then my Sword, and turne away thy face,
While I do run vpon it. Wilt thou Strato?

sp.speaker: Stra.
sp.p: Giue me your hand firſt. Fare you wel my Lord.

sp.speaker: Bru.
sp.l: Farewell good Strato. —Caeſar, now be ſtill,
I kill'd not thee with halfe ſo good a will.

div.stage: Enter Antony, Octauius, Meſſala, Lucillius, and the Army.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.p: What man is that?

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.p: My Maſters man. Strato, where is thy Maſter?

sp.speaker: Stra.
sp.l: Free from the Bondage you are in Meſſala,
The Conquerors can but make a fire of him:
For Brutus onely ouercame himſelfe,
And no man elſe hath Honor by his death.

sp.speaker: Lucil.
sp.l: So Brutus ſhould be found. I thank thee Brutus
That thou haſt prou'd Lucillius ſaying true,

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: All that ſeru'd Brutus, I will entertaine them.
Fellow, wilt thou beſtow thy time with me?

sp.speaker: Stra.
sp.p: I, if Meſſala will preferre me to you.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.p: Do ſo, good Meſſala.

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.p: How dyed my Maſter Strato?

sp.speaker: Stra.
sp.p: I held the Sword, and he did run on it.

sp.speaker: Meſſa.
sp.l: Octauius, then take him to follow thee,
That did the lateſt ſeruice to my Maſter.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: This was the Nobleſt Roman of them all:
All the Conſpirators ſaue onely hee,
Did that they did, in enuy of great Caeſar:
He, onely in a generall honeſt thought,
And common good to all, made one of them.
His life was gentle, and the Elements
So mixt in him, that Nature might ſtand vp,
And ſay to all the world; This was a man.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.l: According to his Vertue, let vs vſe him
Withall Reſpect, and Rites of Buriall.
Within my Tent his bones to night ſhall ly▪
Moſt like a Souldier ordered Honourably:
So call the Field to reſt, and let's away,
To part the glories of this happy day.

div.head: Scoena Prima.
div.stage: Thunder and Lightning. Enter three Witches.

sp.l: WHen ſhall we three meet againe?
In Thunder, Lightning, or in Raine?
When the Hurley-burley's done,
When the Battaile's loſt, and wonne.

sp.p: That will be ere the ſet of Sunne.
Where the place?
Vpon the Heath.
There to meet with Macbeth.
I come, Gray-Malkin.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: Padock calls anon: faire is foule, and foule is faire,
Houer through the fogge and filthie ayre.

div.head: Scena Secunda.
div.stage: Alarum within. Enter King Malcome, Donalbaine, Lenox, with attendants, meeting a bleeding Captaine.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What bloody man is that? he can report,
As ſeemeth by his plight, of the Reuolt
The neweſt ſtate.

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: This is the Serieant,
Who like a good and hardie Souldier fought
'Gainſt my Captiuitie: Haile braue friend;
Say to the King, the knowledge of the Broyle,
As thou didſt leaue it.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Doubtfull it ſtood,
As two ſpent Swimmers, that doe cling together,
And choake their Art: The mercileſſe Macdonwald
(Worthie to be a Rebell, for to that
The multiplying Villanies of Nature
Doe ſwarme vpon him) from the Weſterne Iſles
Of Kernes and Gallowgroſſes is ſupply'd,
And Fortune on his damned Quarry ſmiling,
Shew'd like a Rebells Whore: but all's too weake:
For braue Macbeth (well hee deſerues that Name)
Diſdayning Fortune, with his brandiſht Steele,
Which ſmoak'd with bloody execution
(Like Valours Minion) caru'd out his paſſage,
Till hee fac'd the Slaue:
Which neu'r ſhooke hands, nor bad farwell to him,
Till he vnſeam'd him from the Naue toth' Chops,
And fix'd his Head vpon our Battlements.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: O valiant Couſin, worthy Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: As whence the Sunne gins his reflection,
Shipwracking Stormes, and direfull Thunders:
So from that Spring, whence comfort ſeem'd to come,
Diſcomfort ſwells: Marke King of Scotland, marke,
No ſooner Iuſtice had, with Valour arm'd,
Compell'd theſe skipping Kernes to truſt their heeles,
But the Norweyan Lord, ſurueying vantage,
With furbuſht Armes, and new ſupplyes of men,
Began a freſh aſſault.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Diſmay'd not this our Captaines, Macbeth and Banquoh?

sp.speaker: Cap.
sp.l: Yes, as Sparrowes, Eagles;
Or the Hare, the Lyon:
If I ſay ſooth, I muſt report they were
As Cannons ouer-charg'd with double Cracks,
So they doubly redoubled ſtroakes vpon the Foe:
Except they meant to bathe in reeking Wounds,
Or memorize another Golgotha,
I cannot tell: but I am faint,
My Gaſhes cry for helpe.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: So well thy words become thee, as thy wounds,
They ſmack of Honor both: Goe get him Surgeons.
Who comes here?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.p: The worthy Thane of Roſſe.

sp.speaker: Lenox.
sp.l: What a haſte lookes through his eyes?
So ſhould he looke, that ſeemes to ſpeake things ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Roſſe.
sp.p: God ſaue the King.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Whence cam'ſt thou, worthy Thane?

sp.speaker: Roſſe.
sp.l: From Fiffe, great King,
Where the Norweyan Banners flowt the Skie,
And fanne our people cold.
Norway himſelfe, with terrible numbers,
Aſſiſted by that moſt diſloyall Traytor,
The Thane of Cawdor, began a diſmall Conflict,
Till that Bellona's Bridegroome, lapt in proofe,
Confronted him with ſelfe-compariſons,
Point againſt Point, rebellious Arme 'gainſt Arme,
Curbing his lauiſh ſpirit: and to conclude,
The Victorie fell on vs.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Great happineſſe.

sp.speaker: Roſſe.
sp.l: That now Sweno, the Norwayes King,
Craues compoſition:
Nor would we deigne him buriall of his men,
Till he disburſed, at Saint Colmes ynch,
Ten thouſand Dollars, to our generall vſe.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: No more that Thane of Cawdor ſhall deceiue
Our Boſome intereſt: Goe pronounce his preſent death,
And with his former Title greet Macbeth.

sp.speaker: Roſſe.
sp.p: Ile ſee it done.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: What he hath loſt, Noble Macbeth hath wonne.
Where haſt thou beene, Siſter?
Killing Swine.
Siſter, where thou?

sp.l: A Saylors Wife had Cheſtnuts in her Lappe,
And mouncht, & mouncht, and mouncht:
Giue me, quoth I.
Aroynt thee, Witch, the rumpe-fed Ronyon cryes.
Her Husband's to Aleppo gone, Maſter o' th' Tiger:
But in a Syue Ile thither ſayle,
And like a Rat without a tayle,
Ile doe, Ile doe, and Ile doe.

sp.p: Ile giue thee a Winde.
Th' art kinde.
And I another.

sp.l: I my ſelfe haue all the other,
And the very Ports they blow,
All the Quarters that they know,
I' th' Ship-mans Card.
Ile dreyne him drie as Hay:
Sleepe ſhall neyther Night nor Day
Hang vpon his Pent-houſe Lid:
He ſhall liue a man forbid:
Wearie Seu'nights, nine times nine,
Shall he dwindle, peake, and pine:
Though his Barke cannot be loſt,
Yet it ſhall be Tempeſt-toſt▪
Looke what I haue.

sp.p: Shew me, ſhew me.

sp.l: Here I haue a Pilots Thumbe,
Wrackt, as homeward he did come.
A Drumme, a Drumme:
Macbeth doth come.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.l: The weyward Siſters, hand in hand,
Poſters of the Sea and Land,
Thus doe goe, about, about,
Thrice to thine, and thrice to mine,
And thrice againe, to make vp nine.
Peace, the Charme's wound vp.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.p: So foule and faire a day I haue not ſeene.

sp.speaker: Banquo.
sp.l: How farre is't call'd to Soris? What are theſe,
So wither'd, and ſo wilde in their attyre,
That looke not like th' Inhabitants o' th' Earth,
And yet are on't? Liue you, or are you aught
That man may queſtion? you ſeeme to vnderſtand me,
By each at once her choppie finger laying
Vpon her skinnie Lips: you ſhould be Women,
And yet your Beards forbid me to interprete
That you are ſo.

sp.speaker: Mac.
sp.p: Speake if you can: what are you?
All haile Macbeth, haile to thee Thane of Glamis.
All haile Macbeth, haile to thee Thane of Cawdor.
All haile Macbeth, that ſhalt be King hereafter.

sp.speaker: Banq.
sp.l: Good Sir, why doe you ſtart, and ſeeme to feare
Things that doe ſound ſo faire? i' th' name of truth
Are ye fantaſticall, or that indeed
Which outwardly ye ſhew? My Noble Partner
You greet with preſent Grace, and great prediction
Of Noble hauing, and of Royall hope,
That he ſeemes wrapt withall: to me you ſpeake not.
If you can looke into the Seedes of Time,
And ſay, which Graine will grow, and which will not,
Speake then to me, who neyther begge, nor feare
Your fauors, nor your hate.

sp.p: Hayle.
Hayle.
Hayle.
Leſſer then Macbeth, and greater.
Not ſo happy, yet much happyer.

sp.l: Thou ſhalt get Kings, though thou be none:
So all haile Macbeth, and Banquo.

sp.p: Banquo, and Macbeth, all haile.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: Stay you imperfect Speakers, tell me more:
By Sinells death, I know I am Thane of Glamis,
But how, of Cawdor? the Thane of Cawdor liues
A proſperous Gentleman: And to be King,
Stands not within the proſpect of beleefe,
No more then to be Cawdor. Say from whence
You owe this ſtrange Intelligence, or why
Vpon this blaſted Heath you ſtop our way
With ſuch Prophetique greeting?
Speake, I charge you.

sp.speaker: Banq.
sp.l: The Earth hath bubbles, as the Water ha's,
And theſe are of them: whither are they vaniſh'd?

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: Into the Ayre: and what ſeem'd corporall,
Melted, as breath into the Winde.
Would they had ſtay'd.

sp.speaker: Banq.
sp.l: Were ſuch things here, as we doe ſpeake about?
Or haue we eaten on the inſane Root,
That takes the Reaſon Priſoner?

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.p: Your Children ſhall be Kings.

sp.speaker: Banq.
sp.p: You ſhall be King.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.p: And Thane of Cawdor too: went it not ſo?

sp.speaker: Banq.
sp.p: Toth' ſelfe-ſame tune▪ and words: who's here?

sp.speaker: Roſſe.
sp.l: The King hath happily receiu'd, Macbeth▪
The newes of thy ſucceſſe: and when he reades
Thy perſonall Venture in the Rebels fight,
His Wonders and his Prayſes doe contend,
Which ſhould be thine, or his: ſilenc'd with that,
In viewing o're the reſt o' th' ſelfe-ſame day,
He findes thee in the ſtout Norweyan Rankes▪
Nothing afeard of what thy ſelfe didſt make
Strange Images of death, as thick as Tale
Can poſt with poſt, and euery one did beare
Thy prayſes in his Kingdomes great defence,
And powr'd them downe before him.

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Wee are ſent,
To giue thee from our Royall Maſter thanks,
Onely to harrold thee into his ſight,
Not pay thee▪

sp.speaker: Roſſe.
sp.l: And for an earneſt of a greater Honor,
He bad me, from him, call thee Thane of Cawdor:
In which addition, haile moſt worthy Thane,
For it is thine.

sp.speaker: Banq.
sp.p: What, can the Deuill ſpeake true?

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: The Thane of Cawdor liues:
Why doe you dreſſe me in borrowed Robes?

sp.speaker: Ang.
sp.l: Who was the Thane, liues yet,
But vnder heauie Iudgement beares that Life,
Which he deſerues to looſe.
Whether he was combin'd with thoſe of Norway,
Or did lyne the Rebell with hidden helpe,
And vantage; or that with both he labour'd
In his Countreyes wracke, I know not:
But Treaſons Capitall, confeſs'd, and prou'd,
Haue ouerthrowne him.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: Glamys, and Thane of Cawdor:
The greateſt is behinde. Thankes for your paines.
Doe you not hope your Children ſhall be Kings,
When thoſe that gaue the Thane of Cawdor to me,
Promis'd no leſſe to them.

sp.speaker: Banq.
sp.l: That truſted home,
Might yet enkindle you vnto the Crowne,
Beſides the Thane of Cawdor. But 'tis ſtrange:
And oftentimes, to winne vs to our harme,
The Inſtruments of Darkneſſe tell vs Truths,
Winne vs with honeſt Trifles, to betray's
In deepeſt conſequence.
Couſins, a word, I pray you.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: Two Truths are told,
As happy Prologues to the ſwelling Act
Of the Imperiall Theame. I thanke you Gentlemen:
This ſupernaturall ſolliciting
Cannot be ill; cannot be good.
If ill? why hath it giuen me earneſt of ſucceſſe,
Commencing in a Truth? I am Thane of Cawdor.
If good? why doe I yeeld to that ſuggeſtion,
Whoſe horrid Image doth vnfixe my Heire,
And make my ſeated Heart knock at my Ribbes,
Againſt the vſe of Nature? Preſent Feares
Are leſſe then horrible Imaginings:
My Thought, whoſe Murther yet is but fantaſticall,
Shakes ſo my ſingle ſtate of Man,
That Function is ſmother'd in ſurmiſe,
And nothing is, but what is not.

sp.speaker: Banq.
sp.p: Looke how our Partner's rapt.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: If Chance will haue me King,
Why Chance may Crowne me,
Without my ſtirre.

sp.speaker: Banq.
sp.l: Now Honors come vpon him
Like our ſtrange Garments, cleaue not to their mould,
But with the aid of vſe.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: Come what come may,
Time, and the Houre, runs through the rougheſt Day.

sp.speaker: Banq.
sp.p: Worthy Macbeth, wee ſtay vpon your leyſure.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: Giue me your fauour:
My dull Braine was wrought with things forgotten.
Kinde Gentlemen, your paines are regiſtred,
Where euery day I turne the Leaſe,
To reade them.
Let vs toward the King: thinke vpon
What hath chanc'd: and at more time,
The Interim hauing weigh'd it▪ let vs ſpeake
Our free Hearts each to other.

sp.speaker: Banq.
sp.p: Very gladly.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: Till then enough:
Come friends.

div.head: Scena Quarta.
div.stage: Flouriſh. Enter King, Lenox, Malcolme, Donalbaine, and Attendants.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Is execution done on Cawdor?
Or not thoſe in Commiſſion yet return'd?

sp.speaker: Mal.
sp.l: My Liege, they are not yet come back.
But I haue ſpoke with one that ſaw him die:
Who did report, that very frankly hee
Confeſs'd his Treaſons, implor'd your Highneſſe Pardon,
And ſet forth a deepe Repentance:
Nothing in his Life became him,
Like the leauing it. Hee dy'de,
As one that had beene ſtudied in his death,
To throw away the deareſt thing he ow'd,
As 'twere a careleſſe Trifle.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: There's no Art,
To finde the Mindes conſtruction in the Face:
He was a Gentleman, on whom I built
An abſolute Truſt.
sp.stage: Enter Macbeth, Banquo, Roſſe, and Angus.
sp.l: O worthyeſt Couſin,
The ſinne of my Ingratitude euen now
Was heauie on me. Thou art ſo farre before,
That ſwifteſt Wing of Recompence is ſlow,
To ouertake thee. Would thou hadſt leſſe deſeru'd,
That the proportion both of thanks, and payment,
Might haue beene mine: onely I haue left to ſay,
More is thy due, then more then all can pay.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: The ſeruice, and the loyaltie I owe,
In doing it, payes it ſelfe.
Your Highneſſe part, is to receiue our Duties:
And our Duties are to your Throne, and State,
Children, and Seruants; which doe but what they ſhould,
By doing euery thing ſafe toward your Loue
And Honor.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Welcome hither:
I haue begun to plant thee, and will labour
To make thee full of growing. Noble Banquo,
That haſt no leſſe deſeru'd, nor muſt be knowne
No leſſe to haue done ſo: Let me enfold thee,
And hold thee to my Heart.

sp.speaker: Banq.
sp.l: There if I grow,
The Harueſt is your owne.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: My plenteous Ioyes,
Wanton in fulneſſe, ſeeke to hide themſelues
In drops of ſorrow. Sonnes, Kinſmen, Thanes,
And you whoſe places are the neareſt, know,
We will eſtabliſh our Eſtate vpon
Our eldeſt, Malcolme, whom we name hereafter,
The Prince of Cumberland: which Honor muſt
Not vnaccompanied, inueſt him onely,
But ſignes of Nobleneſſe, like Starres, ſhall ſhine
On all deſeruers▪ From hence to Envernes,
And binde vs further to you.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: The Reſt is Labor, which is not vs'd for you:
Ile be my ſelfe the Herbenger, and make ioyfull
The hearing of my Wife, with your approach:
So humbly take my leaue.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: My worthy Cawdor.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: The Prince of Cumberland: that is a ſtep,
On which I muſt fall downe, or elſe o're-leape,
For in my way it lyes. Starres hide your fires,
Let not Light ſee my black and deepe deſires:
The Eye winke at the Hand; yet let that bee,
Which the Eye feares, when it is done to ſee.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: True, worthy Banquo: he is full ſo valiant,
And in his commendations, I am fed:
It is a Banquet to me. Let's after him,
Whoſe care is gone before, to bid vs welcome:
It is a peereleſſe Kinſman.

div.head: Scena Quinta.
div.stage: Enter Macbeths Wife alone with a Letter.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: They met me in the day of ſucceſſe: and I haue learn'd by the perfect'ſt report, they haue more in them, then mortall knowledge. When I burnt in deſire to queſtion them further▪ they made themſelues Ayre, into which they vaniſh'd. Whiles I ſtood rapt in the wonder of it, came Miſſiues from the King, who all-hail'd me Thane of Cawdor, by which Title before, theſe weyward Siſters ſaluted me, and referr • d me to the comming on of time, with haile King that ſhalt be. This haue I thought good to deliuer thee (my deareſt Partner of Greatneſſe) that thou might'st not looſe the dues of reioycing by being ignorant of what Greatneſſe is promis'd thee. Lay it to thy heart, and farewell.
sp.l: Glamys thou art, and Cawdor, and ſhalt be
What thou art promis'd: yet doe I feare thy Nature,
It is too full o' th' Milke of humane kindneſſe,
To catch the neereſt way. Thou would'ſt be great,
Art not without Ambition, but without
The illneſſe ſhould attend it. What thou would'ſt highly,
That would'ſt thou holily: would'ſt not play falſe,
And yet would'ſt wrongly winne.
Thould'ſt haue, great Glamys that which cryes,
Thus thou muſt doe, if thou haue it;
And that which rather thou do'ſt feare to doe,
Then wiſheſt ſhould be vndone. High thee hither,
That I may powre my Spirits in thine Eare,
And chaſtiſe with the valour of my Tongue
All that impeides thee from the Golden Round,
Which Fate and Metaphyſicall ayde doth ſeeme
To haue thee crown'd withall.
What is your tidings?

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: The King comes here to Night.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Thou'rt mad to ſay it.
Is not thy Maſter with him? who, wer't ſo,
Would haue inform'd for preparation.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.l: So pleaſe you, it is true: our Thane is comming:
One of my fellowes had the ſpeed of him;
Who almoſt dead for breath, had ſcarcely more
Then would make vp his Meſſage.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Giue him tending,
He brings great newes.
The Rauen himſelfe is hoarſe,
That croakes the fatall entrance of Duncan
Vnder my Battlements. Come you Spirits,
That tend on mortall thoughts, vnſex me here,
And fill me from the Crowne to the Toe, top-full
Of direſt Crueltie: make thick my blood,
Stop vp th' acceſſe, and paſſage to Remorſe,
That no compunctious viſitings of Nature
Shake my fell purpoſe, nor keepe peace betweene
Th' effect, and hit. Come to my Womans Breſts,
And take my Milke for Gall, you murth'ring Miniſters,
Where-euer, in your ſightleſſe ſubſtances,
You wait on Natures Miſchiefe. Come thick Night,
And pall thee in the dunneſt ſmoake of Hell,
That my keene Knife ſee not the Wound it makes,
Nor Heauen peepe through the Blanket of the darke,
To cry, hold, hold.
Great Glamys, worthy Cawdor,
Greater then both, by the all-ha • le hereafter,
Thy Letters haue tranſported me beyond
This ignorant preſent, and I feele now
The future in the inſtant.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.l: My deareſt Loue,
Duncan comes here to Night.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.p: And when goes hence?

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.p: To morrow, as he purpoſes.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: O neuer,
Shall Sunne that Morrow ſee.
Your Face, my Thane, is as a Booke, where men
May reade ſtrange matters, to beguile the time.
Looke like the time, beare welcome in your Eye,
Your Hand, your Tongue: looke like th' innocent flower,
But be the Serpent vnder't. He that's comming,
Muſt be prouided for: and you ſhall put
This Nights great Buſineſſe into my diſpatch,
Which ſhall to all our Nights, and Dayes to come,
Giue ſolely ſoueraigne ſway, and Maſterdome.

sp.speaker: Macb.
sp.p: We will ſpeake further.

sp.speaker: Lady.
sp.l: Onely looke vp cleare:
To alter fauor, euer is to feare:
Leaue all the reſt to me.

div.head: Scena Sexta.
div.stage: Hoboyes, and Torches. Enter King, Malcolme, Donalbaine, Banquo, Lenox, Macduff, Roſſe, Angus, and Attendants.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: This Caſtle hath a pleaſant ſeat,
The ayre nimbly and ſweetly recommends it ſelfe
