sp.p: There's another: why might not that bee the Scull of of a Lawyer? where be his Quiddits now? his Quillets? his Caſes? his Tenures, and his Tricks? why doe's he ſuffer this rude knaue now to knocke him about the Sconce with a dirty Shouell, and will not tell him of his Action of Battery? hum. This fellow might be in's time a great buyer of Land, with his Statutes, his Recognizances, his Fines, his double Vouchers, his Recoueries: Is this the fine of his Fines, and the recouery of his Recoueries, to haue his fine Pate full of fine Dirt? will his Vouchers vouch him no more of his Purchaſes, and double ones too, then the length and breadth of a paire of Indentures? the very Conueyances of his Lands will hardly lye in this Boxe; and muſt the Inheritor himſelfe haue no more? ha?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Not a iot more, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Is not Parchment made of Sheep-skinnes?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: I my Lord, and of Calue-skinnes too.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: They are Sheepe and Calues that ſeek out aſſurance in that. I will ſpeake to this fellow: whoſe Graue's this Sir?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: Mine Sir:

l.hi: O a Pit of Clay for to be made,
for ſuch a Gueſt is meete.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: I thinke it be thine indeed: for thou lieſt in't.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: You lye out on't Sir, and therefore it is not yours: for my part, I doe not lye in't; and yet it is mine.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Thou doſt lye in't, to be in't and ſay 'tis thine: 'tis for the dead, not for the quicke, therefore thou lyeſt.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: 'Tis a quicke lye Sir, 'twill a way againe from me to you.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: What man doſt thou digge it for?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: For no man Sir.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: What woman then?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: For none neither.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Who is to be buried in't?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: One that was a woman Sir; but reſt her Soule, ſhee's dead.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: How abſolute the knaue is? wee muſt ſpeake by the Carde, or equiuocation will vndoe vs: by the Lord Horatio, theſe three yeares I haue taken note of it, the Age is growne ſo picked, that the toe of the Peſant comes ſo neere the heeles of our Courtier, hee galls his Kibe. How long haſt thou been a Graue-maker?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Of all the dayes i' th' yeare, I came too't that day that our laſt King Hamlet o're came Fortinbras.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: How long is that ſince?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Cannot you tell that? euery foole can tell that: It was the very day, that young Hamlet was borne, hee that was mad, and ſent into England.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: I marry, why was he ſent into England?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Why, becauſe he was mad; hee ſhall recouer his wits there; or if he do not, it's no great matter there.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: 'Twill not be ſeene in him, there the men are as mad as he.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: How came he mad?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Very ſtrangely they ſay.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: How ſtrangely?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Faith e'ene with looſing his wits.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Vpon what ground?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Why heere in Denmarke: I haue bin ſixeteene heere, man and Boy thirty yeares.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: How long will a man lie 'i th' earth ere he rot?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I faith, if he be not rotten before he die (as we haue many pocky Coarſes now adaies, that will ſcarce hold the laying in) he will laſt you ſome eight yeare, or nine yeare. A Tanner will laſt you nine yeare.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Why he, more then another?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Why ſir, his hide is ſo tan'd with his Trade, that he will keepe out water a great while. And your water, is a ſore Decayer of your horſon dead body. Heres a Scull now: this Scul, has laine in the earth three & twenty years.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Whoſe was it?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: A whoreſon mad Fellowes it was;
Whoſe doe you thinke it was?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Nay, I know not.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: A peſtlence on him for a mad Rogue, a pou'rd a Flaggon of Reniſh on my head once. This ſame Scull Sir, this ſame Scull ſir, was Yoricks Scull, the Kings Ieſter.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: This?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: E'ene that.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Let me ſee. Alas poore Yorick, I knew him Horatio, a fellow of infinite Ieſt; of moſt excellent fancy, he hath borne me on his backe a thouſand times: And how abhorred my Imagination is, my gorge riſes at it. Heere hung thoſe lipps, that I haue kiſt I know not how oft. VVhere be your libes now? Your Gambals? Your Songs? Your flaſhes of Merriment that were wont to ſet the Table on a Rore? No one now to mock your own Ieering? Quite chopfalne? Now get you to my Ladies Chamber, and tell her, let her paint an inch thicke, to this fauour ſhe muſt come. Make her laugh at that: prythee Horatio tell me one thing.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: What's that my Lord?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Doſt thou thinke Alexander lookt o' this faſhion i' th' earth?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: E'ene ſo.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: And ſmelt ſo? Puh.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: E'ene ſo, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: To what baſe vſes we may returne Horatio. Why may not Imagination trace the Noble duſt of Alexander, till he find it ſtopping a bunghole.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: 'Twere to conſider: to curiouſly to conſider ſo.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: No faith, not a iot. But to follow him thether with modeſtie enough, & likeliehood to lead it; as thus. Alexander died: Alexander was buried: Alexander returneth into duſt; the duſt is earth; of earth we make Lome, and why of that Lome (whereto he was conuerted) might they not ſtopp a Beere-barrell?
sp.l: Imperiall Caeſar, dead and turn'd to clay,
Might ſtop a hole to keepe the winde away.
Oh, that that earth, which kept the world in awe,
Should patch a Wall, t' expell the winters flaw.
But ſoft, but ſoft, aſide; heere comes the King.
sp.stage: Enter King, Queene, Laertes, and a Coffin, with Lords attendant.
sp.l: The Queene, the Courtiers. Who is that they follow,
And with ſuch maimed rites? This doth betoken,
The Coarſe they follow, did with diſperate hand,
Fore do it owne life; 'twas ſome Eſtate.
Couch we a while, and mark.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: What Cerimony elſe?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: That is Laertes, a very Noble youth: Marke.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: What Cerimony elſe?

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: Her Obſequies haue bin as farre inlarg'd.
As we haue warrantis, her death was doubtfull,
And but that great Command, o're-ſwaies the order,
She ſhould in ground vnſanctified haue lodg'd,
Till the laſt Trumpet. For charitable praier,
Shardes, Flints, and Peebles, ſhould be throwne on her:
Yet heere ſhe is allowed her Virgin Rites,
Her Maiden ſtrewments, and the bringing home
Of Bell and Buriall.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: Muſt there no more be done?

sp.speaker: Prieſt.
sp.l: No more be done:
We ſhould prophane the ſeruice of the dead,
To ſing ſage Requiem, and ſuch reſt to her
As to peace-parted Soules.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.l: Lay her i' th' earth,
And from her faire and vnpolluted fleſh,
May Violets ſpring. I tell thee (churliſh Prieſt)
A Miniſtring Angell ſhall my Siſter be,
When thou lieſt howling?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: What, the faire Ophelia?

sp.speaker: Queene.
sp.l: Sweets, to the ſweet farewell.
I hop'd thou ſhould'ſt haue bin my Hamlets wife:
I thought thy Bride-bed to haue deckt (ſweet Maid)
And not t' haue ſtrew'd thy Graue.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.l: Oh terrible woer,
Fall ten times trebble, on that curſed head
Whoſe wicked deed▪ thy moſt Ingenious ſence
Depriu'd thee of. Hold off the earth a while,
Till I haue caught her once more in mine armes:
Now pile your duſt, vpon the quicke, and dead,
Till of this flat a Mountaine you haue made,
To o're top old Pelion, or the skyiſh head
Of blew Olympus.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: What is he, whoſe griefes
Beares ſuch an Emphaſis? whoſe phraſe of Sorrow
Coniure the wandring Starres, and makes them ſtand
Like wonder-wounded hearers? This is I,
Hamlet the Dane.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: The deuill take thy ſoule.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Thou prai'ſt not well,
I prythee take thy fingers from my throat;
Sir though I am not Spleenatiue, and raſh,
Yet haue I ſomething in me dangerous,
Which let thy wiſeneſſe feare. Away thy hand.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Pluck them aſunder.

sp.speaker: Gen.
sp.p: Good my Lord be quiet.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Why I will fight with him vppon this Theme.
Vntill my eielids will no longer wag.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Oh my Sonne, what Theame?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: I lou'd Ophelia; fortie thouſand Brothers
Could not (with all there quantitie of Loue)
Make vp my ſumme. What wilt thou do for her?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Oh he is mad Laertes,

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: For loue of God forbeare him.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Come ſhow me what thou'lt doe.
Woo't weepe? Woo't fight? Woo't teare thy ſelfe?
Woo't drinke vp Eſile, eate a Crocodile?
Ile doo't. Doſt thou come heere to whine;
To outface me with leaping in her Graue?
Be buried quicke with her, and ſo will I.
And if thou prate of Mountaines; let them throw
Millions of Akers on vs; till our ground
Sindging his pate againſt the burning Zone,
Make Oſſa like a wart. Nay, and thoul't mouth,
Ile rant as well as thou.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: This is meere Madneſſe:
And thus awhile the fit will worke on him:
Anon as patient as the female Doue,
When that her golden Cuplet are diſclos'd;
His ſilence will ſit drooping.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Heare you Sir:
What is the reaſon that you vſe me thus?
I loud you euer; but it is no matter:
Let Hercules himſelfe doe what he may,
The Cat will Mew, and Dogge will haue his day.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.l: I pray you good Horatio wait vpon him,
Strengthen you patience in our laſt nights ſpeech,
Wee'l put the matter to the preſent puſh:
Good Gertrude ſet ſome watch ouer your Sonne,
This Graue ſhall haue a liuing Monument:
An houre of quiet ſhortly ſhall we ſee;
Till then, in patience our proceeding be.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: So much for this Sir; now let me ſee the other,
You doe remember all the Circumſtance.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Remember it my Lord?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Sir, in my heart there was a kinde of fighting,
That would not let me ſleepe; me thought I lay
Worſe then the mutines in the Bilboes, raſhly,
(And praiſe be raſhneſſe for it) let vs know,
Our indiſcretion ſometimes ſerues vs well,
When our deare plots do paule, and that ſhould teach vs,
There's a Diuinity that ſhapes our ends,
Rough-hew them how we will.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: That is moſt certaine.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Vp from my Cabin
My ſea-gowne ſcarft about me in the darke,
Grop'd I to finde out them; had my deſire,
Finger'd their Packet, and in fine, withdrew
To mine owne roome againe, making ſo bold,
(My feares forgetting manners) to vnſeale
Their grand Commiſſion, where I found Horatio,
Oh royall knauery: An exact command,
Larded with many ſeuerall ſorts of reaſon;
Importing Denmarks health, and Englands too,
With hoo, ſuch Bugges and Goblins in my life,
That on the ſuperuize no leaſure bated,
No not to ſtay the grinding of the Axe,
My head ſhoud be ſtruck off.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Iſt poſſible?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Here's the Commiſſion, read it at more leyſure:
But wilt thou heare me how I did proceed?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: I beſeech you.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Being thus benetted round with Villaines,
Ere I could make a Prologue to my braines,
They had begun the Play. I ſate me downe,
Deuis'd a new Commiſſion, wrote it faire,
I once did hold it as our Statiſts doe,
A baſeneſſe to write faire; and laboured much
How to forget that learning: but Sir now,
It did me Yeomans ſeruice: wilt thou know
The effects of what I wrote?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: I, good my Lord.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: An earneſt Coniuration from the King,
As England was his faithfull Tributary,
As loue betweene them, as the Palme ſhould flouriſh,
As Peace ſhould ſtill her wheaten Garland weare,
And ſtand a Comma 'tweene their amities,
And many ſuch like Aſſis of great charge,
That on the view and know of theſe Contents,
Without debatement further, more or leſſe,
He ſhould the bearers put to ſodaine death,
Not ſhriuing time allowed.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: How was this ſeal'd?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Why, euen in that was Heauen ordinate;
I had my fathers Signet in my Purſe,
Which was the Modell of that Daniſh Seale:
Folded the Writ vp in forme of the other,
Subſcrib'd it, gau't th' impreſſion, plac't it ſafely,
The changeling neuer knowne: Now, the next day
Was our Sea Fight, and what to this was ſement,
Thou know'ſt already.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: So Guildenſterne and Roſincrance, go too't.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Why man, they did make loue to this imployment
They are not neere my Conſcience; their debate
Doth by their owne inſinuation grow:
'Tis dangerous, when the baſer nature comes
Betweene the paſſe, and fell incenſed points
Of mighty oppoſites.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Why, what a King is this?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Does it not, thinkſt thee, ſtand me now vpon
He that hath kil'd my King, and whor'd my Mother,
Popt in betweene th' election and my hopes,
Throwne out his Angle for my proper life,
And with ſuch coozenage; is't not perfect conſcience,
To quit him with this arme? And is't not to be damn'd
To let this Canker of our nature come
In further euill.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: It muſt be ſhortly knowne to him from England
What is the iſſue of the buſineſſe there.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: It will be ſhort,
The interim's mine, and a mans life's no more
Then to ſay one: but I am very ſorry good Horatio,
That to Laertes I forgot my ſelfe;
For by the image of my Cauſe, I ſee
The Portraiture of his; Ile count his fauours:
But ſure the brauery of his griefe did put me
Into a Towring paſſion.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Peace, who comes heere?

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: Your Lordſhip is right welcome back to Denmarke.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: I humbly thank you Sir, doſt know this waterflie?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: No my good Lord.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Thy ſtate is the more gracious; for 'tis a vice to know him: he hath much Land, and fertile; let a Beaſt be Lord of Beaſts, and his Crib ſhall ſtand at the Kings Meſſe; 'tis a Chowgh; but as I ſaw ſpacious in the poſſeſſion of dirt.

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.l: Sweet Lord, if your friendſhip were at leyſure,
I ſhould impart a thing to you from his Maieſty.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: I will receiue it with all diligence of ſpirit; put your Bonet to his right vſe, 'tis for the head.

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: I thanke your Lordſhip, 'tis very hot.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: No, beleeue mee 'tis very cold, the winde is Northerly.

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: It is indifferent cold my Lord indeed.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Mee thinkes it is very ſoultry, and hot for my Complexion.

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: Exceedingly, my Lord, it is very ſoultry, as 'twere I cannot tell how: but my Lord, his Maieſty bad me ſignifie to you, that he ha's laid a great wager on your head: Sir, this is the matter.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: I beſeech you remember.

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: Nay, in good faith, for mine eaſe in good faith: Sir, you are not ignorant of what excellence Laertes is at his weapon.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: What's his weapon?

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: Rapier and dagger.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: That's two of his weapons; but well.

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: The ſir King ha's wag'd with him ſix Barbary Horſes, againſt the which he impon'd as I take it, ſixe French Rapiers and Poniards, with their aſſignes, as Girdle, Hangers or ſo: three of the Carriages infaith are very deare to fancy, very reſponſiue to the hilts, moſt delicate carriages, and of very liberall conceit.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: What call you the Carriages?

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: The Carriages Sir, are the hangers.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: The phraſe would bee more Germaine to the matter: If we could carry Cannon by our ſides; I would it might be Hangers till then; but on ſixe Barbary Horſes againſt ſixe French Swords: their Aſſignes, and three liberall conceited Carriages, that's the French but againſt the Daniſh; why is this impon'd as you call it?

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: The King Sir, hath laid that in a dozen paſſes betweene you and him, hee ſhall not exceed you three hits; He hath one twelue for mine, and that would come to imediate tryall, if your Lordſhip would vouchſafe the Anſwere.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: How if I anſwere no?

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: I meane my Lord, the oppoſition of your perſon in tryall.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Sir, I will walke heere in the Hall; if it pleaſe his Maieſtie, 'tis the breathing time of day with me; let the Foyles bee brought, the Gentleman willing, and the King hold his purpoſe; I will win for him if I can: if not, Ile gaine nothing but my ſhame, and the odde hits.

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: Shall I redeliuer you ee'n ſo?

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: To this effect Sir, after what flouriſh your nature will.

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: I commend my duty to your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Yours, yours; hee does well to commend it himſelfe, there are no tongues elſe for's tongue.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: This Lapwing runs away with the ſhell on his head.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: He did Complie with his Dugge before hee ſuck't it: thus had he and mine more of the ſame Beauy that I know the droſſie age dotes on; only got the tune of the time, and outward habite of encounter, a kinde of yeſty collection, which carries them through & through the moſt fond and winnowed opinions; and doe but blow them to their tryalls: the Bubbles are out.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: You will loſe this wager, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: I doe not thinke ſo, ſince he went into France, I haue beene in continuall practice; I ſhall winne at the oddes: but thou wouldeſt not thinke how all heere about my heart: but it is no matter.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: Nay, good my Lord.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: It is but foolery; but it is ſuch a kinde of gain-giuing as would perhaps trouble a woman.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.p: If your minde diſlike any thing, obey. I will foreſtall their repaire hither, and ſay you are not fit.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Not a whit, we defie Augury; there's a ſpeciall Prouidence in the fall of a ſparrow. If it be now, 'tis not to come: if it bee not to come, it will bee now: if it be not now; yet it will come; the readineſſe is all, ſince no man ha's ought of what he leaues. What is't to leaue betimes?

div.stage: Enter King, Queene, Laertes and Lords, with other Attendants with Foyles, and Gauntlets, a Table and Flagons of Wine on it.

sp.speaker: Kin.
sp.p: Come Hamlet, come, and take this hand from me.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Giue me your pardon Sir, I'ue done you wrong,
But pardon't as you are a Gentleman.
This preſence knowes,
And you muſt needs haue heard how I am puniſht
With ſore diſtraction? What I haue done
That might your nature honour, and exception
Roughly awake, I heere proclaime was madneſſe:
Was • t Hamlet wrong'd Laertes? Neuer Hamlet.
If Hamlet from himſelfe be tane away:
And when he's not himſelfe, do's wrong Laertes,
Then Hamlet does it not, Hamlet denies it:
Who does it then? His Madneſſe? If't be ſo,
Hamlet is of the Faction that is wrong'd,
His madneſſe is poore Hamlets Enemy.
Sir, in this Audience,
Let my diſclaiming from a purpos'd euill,
Free me ſo farre in your moſt generous thoughts,
That I haue ſhot mine Arrow o're the houſe,
And hurt my Mother.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.l: I am ſatisfied in Nature,
Whoſe motiue in this caſe ſhould ſtirre me moſt
To my Reuenge. But in my termes of Honor
I ſtand aloofe, and will no reconcilement,
Till by ſome elder Maſters of knowne Honor,
I haue a voyce, and preſident of peace
To keepe my name vngorg'd. But till that time,
I do receiue your offer'd loue like loue,
And wil not wrong it.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: I do embrace it freely,
And will this Brothers wager frankely play.
Giue vs the Foyles: Come on.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: Come one for me.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Ile be your foile Laertes, in mine ignorance,
Your Skill ſhall like a Starre i' th' darkeſt night,
Sticke fiery off indeede.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: You mocke me Sir.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: No by this hand.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Giue them the Foyles yong Oſricke,
Couſen Hamlet, you know the wagot.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Verie well my Lord,
Your Grace hath laide the oddes a' th' weaker ſide.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I do not feare it,
I haue ſeene you both:
But ſince he is better'd, we haue therefore oddes.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.l: This is too heauy,
Let me ſee another.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: This likes me well,
Theſe Foyles haue all a length.

sp.speaker: Oſricke.
sp.p: I my good Lord.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Set me the Stopes of wine vpon that Table:
If Hamlet giue the firſt, or ſecond hit,
Or quit in anſwer of the third exchange,
Let all the Battlements their Ordinance fire,
The King ſhal drinke to Hamlets better breath,
And in the Cup an vnion ſhal he throw
Richer then that, which foure ſucceſſiue Kings
In Denmarkes Crowne haue worne.
Giue me the Cups,
And let the Kettle to the Trumpets ſpeake,
The Trumpet to the Cannoneer without,
The Cannons to the Heauens, the Heauen to Earth,
Now the King drinkes to Hamlet. Come, begin,
And you the Iudges beare a wary eye.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Come on ſir.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: Come on ſir.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: One.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Iudgement.

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: A hit, a very palpable hit.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: Well: againe.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Stay, giue me drinke.
Hamlet, this Pearle is thine,
Here's to thy health. Giue him the cup,

div.stage: Trumpets ſound, and ſhot goes off.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Ile play this bout firſt, ſet by a-while.
Come: Another hit; what ſay you?

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: A touch, a touch, I do confeſſe.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Our Sonne ſhall win.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: He's fat, and ſcant of breath.
Heere's a Napkin, rub thy browes,
The Queene Carowſes to thy fortune, Hamlet.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Good Madam.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Gertrude, do not drinke.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: I will my Lord;
I pray you pardon me.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: It is the poyſon'd Cup, it is too late.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: I dare not drinke yet Madam,
By and by.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.p: Come, let me wipe thy face.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: My Lord, Ile hit him now.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: I do not thinke't.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: And yet 'tis almoſt 'gainſt my conſcience.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Come for the third.
Laertes, you but daily,
I pray you paſſe with your beſt violence,
I am affear'd you make a wanton of me.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: Say you ſo? Come on.

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: Nothing neither way.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.p: Haue at you now.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Part them, they are incens'd.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: Nay come, againe.

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: Looke to the Queene there hoa.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: They bleed on both ſides. How is't my Lord?

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.p: How is't Laertes?

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.l: Why as a Woodcocke
To mine Sprindge, Oſricke,
I am iuſtly kill'd with mine owne Treacherie.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.p: How does the Queene?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: She ſounds to ſee them bleede.

sp.speaker: Qu.
sp.l: No, no, the drinke, the drinke.
Oh my deere Hamlet, the drinke, the drinke,
I am poyſon'd.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Oh Villany! How? Let the doore be lock'd.
Treacherie, ſeeke it out.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.l: It is heere Hamlet.
Hamlet, thou art ſlaine,
No Medicine in the world can do thee good.
In thee, there is not halfe an houre of life;
The Treacherous Inſtrument is in thy hand.
Vnbated and envenom'd: the foule practiſe
Hath turn'd it ſelfe on me. Loe, heere I lye,
Neuer to riſe againe: Thy Mothers poyſon'd:
I can no more, the King, the King's too blame.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: The point envenom'd too,
Then venome to thy worke.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Treaſon, Treaſon.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: O yet defend me Friends, I am but hurt.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Heere thou inceſtuous, murdrous,
Damned Dane,
Drinke off this Potion: Is thy Vnion heere?
Follow my Mother.

sp.speaker: Laer.
sp.l: He is • uſtly ſeru'd.
It is a poyſon temp'red by himſelfe:
Exchange forgiueneſſe with me, Noble Hamlet;
Mine and my Fathers death come not vpon thee,
Nor thine on me.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: Heauen make thee free of it, I follow thee.
I am dead Horatio, wretched Queene adiew,
You that looke pale, and tremble at this chance,
That are but Mutes or audience to this acte:
Had I but time (as this fell Sergeant death
Is ſtrick'd in his Arreſt) oh I could tell you.
But let it be: Horatio, I am dead,
Thou liu'ſt, report me and my cauſes right.
To the vnſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: Neuer beleeue it.
I am more an Antike Roman then a Dane:
Heere's yet ſome Liquor left.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: As th' art a man, giue me the Cup.
Let go, by Heauen Ile haue't.
Oh good Horatio, what a wounded name,
(Things ſtanding thus vnknowne) ſhall liue behind me.
If thou did'ſt euer hold me in thy heart,
Abſent thee from felicitie awhile,
And in this harſh world draw thy breath in paine,
To tell my Storie.
sp.stage: March afarre off, and ſhout within.
sp.l: What warlike noyſe is this?

sp.speaker: Oſr.
sp.l: Yong Fortinbras, with conqueſt come frō Poland
To th' Ambaſſadors of England giues this warlike volly.

sp.speaker: Ham.
sp.l: O I dye Horatio:
The potent poyſon quite ore-crowes my ſpirit,
I cannot liue to heare the Newes from England,
But I do propheſie th' election lights
On Fortinbras, he ha's my dying voyce,
So tell him with the occurrents more and leſſe,
Which haue ſolicited. The reſt is ſilence.

sp.speaker: Hora.
sp.l: Now cracke a Noble heart:
Goodnight ſweet Prince,
And flights of Angels ſing thee to thy reſt,
Why do's the Drumme come hither?

div.stage: Enter Fortinbras and Engliſh Ambaſſador, with Drumme, Colours, and Attendants.

sp.speaker: Fortin.
sp.p: Where is this ſight?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: What is it ye would ſee;
If ought of woe, or wonder, ceaſe your ſearch.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l: His quarry cries on hauocke. Oh proud death,
What feaſt is toward in thine eternall Cell.
That thou ſo many Princes, at a ſhoote,
So bloodily haſt ſtrooke.

sp.speaker: Amb.
sp.l: The ſight is diſmall,
And our affaires from England come too late,
The eares are ſenſeleſſe that ſhould giue vs hearing,
To tell him his command'ment is fulfill'd,
That Roſincrance and Guildenſterne are dead:
Where ſhould we haue our thankes?

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: Not from his mouth,
Had it th' abilitie of life to thanke you:
He neuer gaue command'ment for their death.
But ſince ſo iumpe vpon this bloodie queſtion,
You from the Polake warres, and you from England
Are heere arriued. Giue order that theſe bodies
High on a ſtage be placed to the view,
And let me ſpeake to th' yet vnknowing world,
How theſe things came about. So ſhall you heare
Of carnall, bloudie, and vnnaturall acts,
Of accidentall iudgements, caſuall ſlaughters
Of death's put on by cunning, and forc'd cauſe,
And in this vpſhot, purpoſes miſtooke,
Falne on the Inuentors heads. All this can I
Truly deliuer.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l: Let vs haſt to heare it,
And call the Nobleſt to the Audience.
For me, with ſorrow, I embrace my Fortune,
I haue ſome Rites of memory in this Kingdome,
Which are ro claime, my vantage doth
Inuite me,

sp.speaker: Hor.
sp.l: Of that I ſhall haue alwayes cauſe to ſpeake,
And from his mouth
Whoſe voyce will draw on more:
But let this ſame be preſently perform'd,
Euen whiles mens mindes are wilde,
Leſt more miſchance
On plots, and errors happen.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l: Let foure Captaines
Beare Hamlet like a Soldier to the Stage,
For he was likely, had he beene put on
To haue prou'd moſt royally:
And for his paſſage,
The Souldiours Muſicke, and the rites of Warre
Speake lowdly for him.
Take vp the body; Such a ſight as this
Becomes the Field, but heere ſhewes much amis.
Go, bid the Souldiers ſhoote.

div.stage: Exeunt Marching: after the which, a Peale of Ordenance are ſhot off.

div.head: Scoena Prima.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I Thought the King had more affected the Duke of Albany, then Cornwall.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: It did alwayes ſeeme ſo to vs: But now in the diuiſion of the Kingdome, it appeares not which of the Dukes hee valewes moſt, for qualities are ſo weigh'd, that curioſity in neither, can make choiſe of eithers moity.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Is not this your Son, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: His breeding Sir, hath bin at my charge. I haue ſo often bluſh'd to acknowledge him, that now I am braz'd too't.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I cannot conceiue you.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Sir, this yong Fellowes mother could; wherevpon ſhe grew round womb'd, and had indeede (Sir) a Sonne for her Cradle, ere ſhe had a husband for her bed. Do you ſmell a fault?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I cannot wiſh the fault vndone, the iſſue of it, being ſo proper.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: But I haue a Sonne, Sir, by order of Law, ſome yeere elder then this; who, yet is no deerer in my account, though this Knaue came ſomthing ſawcily to the world before he was ſent for: yet was his Mother fayre, there was good ſport at his making, and the horſon muſt be acknowledged. Doe you know this Noble Gentleman, Edmond?

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.p: No, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.l: My Lord of Kent:
Remember him heereafter, as my Honourable Friend.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.p: My ſeruices to your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I muſt loue you, and ſue to know you better.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.p: Sir, I ſhall ſtudy deſeruing.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: He hath bin out nine yeares, and away he ſhall againe. The King is comming.

div.stage: Sennet. Enter King Lear, Cornwall, Albany, Gonerill, Regan, Cordelia, and attendants.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Attend the Lords of France & Burgundy, Gloſter.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: I ſhall, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Meane time we ſhal expreſſe our darker purpoſe.
Giue me the Map there. Know, that we haue diuided
In three our Kingdome: and 'tis our faſt intent,
To ſhake all Cares and Buſineſſe from our Age,
Conferring them on yonger ſtrengths, while we
Vnburthen'd crawle toward death. Our ſon of Cornwal,
And you our no leſſe louing Sonne of Albany,
We haue this houre a conſtant will to publiſh
Our daughters ſeuerall Dowers, that future ſtrife
May be preuented now. The Princes, France & Burgundy,
Great Riuals in our yongeſt daughters loue,
Long in our Court, haue made their amorous ſoiourne,
And heere are to be anſwer'd. Tell me my daughters
(Since now we will diueſt vs both of Rule,
Intereſt of Territory, Cares of State)
Which of you ſhall we ſay doth loue vs moſt,
That we, our largeſt bountie may extend
Where Nature doth with merit challenge.
Our eldeſt borne, ſpeake firſt.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Sir, I loue you more then word can weild ye matter,
Deerer then eye-ſight, ſpace, and libertie,
Beyond what can be valewed, rich or rare,
No leſſe then life, with grace, health, beauty, honor:
As much as Childe ere lou'd, or Father found.
A loue that makes breath poore, and ſpeech vnable,
Beyond all manner of ſo much I loue you.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: What ſhall Cordelia ſpeake? Loue, and be ſilent.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Of all theſe bounds euen from this Line, to this,
With ſhadowie Forreſts, and with Champains rich'd
With plenteous Riuers, and wide-skirted Meades
We make thee Lady. To thine and Albanies iſſues
Be this perpetuall. What ſayes our ſecond Daughter?
Our deereſt Regan, wife of Cornwall?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: I am made of that ſelfe-mettle as my Siſter,
And prize me at her worth. In my true heart,
I finde ſhe names my very deede of loue:
Onely ſhe comes too ſhort, that I profeſſe
My ſelfe an enemy to all other ioyes,
Which the moſt precious ſquare of ſenſe profeſſes,
And finde I am alone felicitate
In your deere Highneſſe loue.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Then poore Cordelia,
And yet not ſo, ſince I am ſure my loue's
More ponderous then my tongue.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: To thee, and thine hereditarie euer,
Remaine this ample third of our faire Kingdome,
No leſſe in ſpace, validitie, and pleaſure
Then that confeir'd on Gonerill. Now our Ioy,
Although our laſt and leaſt; to whoſe yong loue▪
The Vines of France, and Milke of Burgundie,
Striue to be intereſt. What can you ſay, to draw
A third, more opilent then your Siſters? ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Nothing my Lord.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Nothing?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Nothing will come of nothing, ſpeake againe.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Vnhappie that I am, I cannot heaue
My heart into my mouth: I loue your Maieſty
According to my bond, no more nor leſſe.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: How, how Cordelia? Mend your ſpeech a little,
Leaſt you may marre your Fortunes.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Good my Lord,
You haue begot me, bred me, lou'd me.
I returne thoſe duties backe as are right fit,
Obey you, Loue you, and moſt Honour you.
Why haue my Siſters Husbands, if they ſay
They loue you all? Happily when I ſhall wed,
That Lord, whoſe hand muſt take my plight, ſhall carry
Halfe my loue with him, halfe my Care, and Dutie,
Sure I ſhall neuer marry like my Siſters.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: But goes thy heart with this?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: I my good Lord.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: So young, and ſo vntender?

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: So young my Lord, and true.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Let it be ſo, thy truth then be thy dowre:
For by the ſacred radience of the Sunne,
The miſeries of Heccat and the night:
By all the operation of the Orbes,
From whom we do exiſt, and ceaſe to be,
Heere I diſclaime all my Paternall care,
Propinquity and property of blood,
And as a ſtranger to my heart and me,
Hold thee from this for euer. The barbarous Scythian,
Or he that makes his generation meſſes
To gorge his appetite, ſhall to my boſome
Be as well neighbour'd, pittied, and releeu'd,
As thou my ſometime Daughter.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Good my Liege.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Peace Kent,
Come not betweene the Dragon and his wrath,
I lou'd her moſt, and thought to ſet my reſt
On her kind nurſery. Hence and avoid my ſight:
So be my graue my peace, as here I giue
Her Fathers heart from her; call France, who ſtirres?
Call Burgundy, Cornwall, and Albanie,
With my two Daughters Dowres, digeſt the third,
Let pride, which ſhe cals plainneſſe, marry her:
I doe inueſt you ioyntly with my power,
Preheminence, and all the large effects
That troope with Maieſty. Our ſelfe by Monthly courſe,
With reſeruation of an hundred Knights.
By you to be ſuſtain'd, ſhall our abode
Make with you by due turne, onely we ſhall retaine
The name, and all th' addition to a King: the Sway,
Reuennew Execution of the reſt,
Beloued Sonnes be yours, which to confirme,
This Coronet part betweene you.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Royall Lear,
Whom I haue euer honor'd as my King▪
Lou'd as my Father, as my Maſter follow'd,
As my great Patron thought on in my praiers.

sp.speaker: Le.
sp.p: The bow is bent & drawne, make from the ſhaft.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Let it fall rather, though the forke inuade
The region of my heart, be Kent vnmannerly,
When Lear is mad, what wouldeſt thou do old man?
Think'ſt thou that dutie ſhall haue dread to ſpeake,
When power to flattery bowes?
To plainneſſe honour's bound,
When Maieſty falls to folly, reſerue thy ſtate,
And in thy beſt conſideration checke
This hideous raſhneſſe, anſwere my life, my iudgement:
Thy yongeſt Daughter do's not loue thee leaſt,
Nor are thoſe empty hearted, whoſe low founds
Reuerbe no hollowneſſe.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Kent, on thy life no more.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: My life I neuer held but as pawne
To wage againſt thine enemies, nere feare to looſe it,
Thy ſafety being motiue.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Out of my ſight.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: See better Lear, and let me ſtill remaine
The true blanke of thine eie.

sp.speaker: Kear.
sp.p: Now by Apollo,

sp.speaker: Lent.
sp.l: Now by Apollo, King
Thou ſwear▪ſt thy Gods in vaine.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: O Vaſſall! Miſcreant.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.p: Cor. Deare Sir forbeare.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Kill thy Phyſition, and thy ſee beſtow
Vpon the foule diſeaſe, reuoke thy guift,
Or whil'ſt I can vent clamour from my throate,
Ile tell thee thou doſt euill.

sp.speaker: Lea.
sp.l: Heare me recreant, on thine allegeance heare me;
That thou haſt ſought to make vs breake our vowes,
Which we durſt neuer yet; and with ſtrain'd pride,
To come betwixt our ſentences, and our power.
Which, nor our nature, nor our place can beare;
Our potencie made good, take thy reward.
Fiue dayes we do allot thee for prouiſion,
To ſhield thee from diſaſters of the world,
And on the ſixt to turne thy hated backe
Vpon our kingdome; if on the tenth day following,
Thy baniſht trunke be found in our Dominions,
The moment is thy death, away. By Iupiter,
This ſhall not be reuok'd,

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: Fare thee well King, ſith thus thou wilt appeare,
Freedome liues hence, and baniſhment is here;
The Gods to their deere ſhelter take thee Maid,
That iuſtly think'ſt, and haſt moſt rightly ſaid:
And your large ſpeeches, may your deeds approue,
That good effects may ſpring from words of loue:
Thus Kent, O Princes, bids you all adew,
Hee'l ſhape his old courſe, in a Country new.

div.stage: Flouriſh. Enter Gloſter with France, and Burgundy Attendants.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Heere's France and Burgundy, my Noble Lord.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: My Lord of Bugundie,
We firſt addreſſe toward you, who with this King
Hath riuald for our Daughter; what in the leaſt
Will you require in preſent Dower with her,
Or ceaſe your queſt of Loue?

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Moſt Royall Maieſty,
I craue no more then hath your Highneſſe offer'd,
Nor will you tender leſſe?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Right Noble Burgundy,
When ſhe was deare to vs, we did hold her ſo,
But now her price is fallen: Sir, there ſhe ſtands,
If ought within that little ſeeming ſubſtance,
Or all of it with our diſpleaſure piec'd,
And nothing more may fitly like your Grace,
Shee's there, and ſhe is yours.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.p: I know no anſwer.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Will you with thoſe infirmities ſhe owes,
Vnfriended, new adopted to our hate,
Dow'rd with our curſe, and ſtranger'd with our oath,
Take her or, leaue her.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Pardon me Royall Sir,
Election makes not vp in ſuch conditions.

sp.speaker: Le.
sp.l: Then leaue her ſir, for by the powre that made me,
I tell you all her wealth. For you great King,
I would not from your loue make ſuch a ſtray,
To match you where I hate, therefore beſeech you
T' auert your liking a more worthier way,
Then on a wretch whom Nature is aſham'd
Almoſt t' acknowledge hers.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: This is moſt ſtrange,
That ſhe whom euen but now, was your obiect.
The argument of your praiſe▪ balme of your age,
The beſt, the deereſt, ſhould in this trice of time
Commit a thing ſo monſtrous, to diſmantle
So many folds of fauour: ſure her offence
Muſt be of ſuch vnnaturall degree,
That monſters it: Or your fore-voucht affection
Fall into taint, which to beleeue of her
Muſt be a faith that reaſon without miracle
Should neuer plant in me.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: I yet beſeech your Maieſty.
If for I want that glib and oylie Art,
To ſpeake and purpoſe not, ſince what I will intend,
Ile do't before I ſpeake, that you make knowne
It is no vicious blot, murther, or fouleneſſe,
No vnchaſte action or diſhonoured ſtep
That hath depriu'd me of your Grace and fauour,
But euen for want of that, for which I am richer,
A ſtill ſoliciting eye, and ſuch a tongue,
That I am glad I haue not, though not to haue it,
Hath loft me in your liking.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Better thou had'ſt▪
Not beene borne, then not t haue pleas'd me better.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Is it but this? A tardineſſe in nature,
Which often leaues the hiſtory vnſpoke
That it intends to do: my Lord of Burgundy,
What ſay you to the Lady? Loue's not loue
When it is mingled with regards, that ſtands
Aloofe from th' intire point, will you haue her?
She is herſelfe a Dowrie.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: Royall King,
Giue but that portion which your ſelfe propos'd,
And here I take Cordelia by the hand,
Dutcheſſe of Burgundie.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Nothing, I haue ſworne, I am firme.

sp.speaker: Bur.
sp.l: I am ſorry then you haue ſo loſt a Father,
That you muſt looſe a husband.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Peace be with Burgundie,
Since that reſpect and Fortunes are his loue,
I ſhall not be his wife.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.l: Faireſt Cordelia, that art moſt rich being poore,
Moſt choiſe forſaken, and moſt lou'd deſpis'd,
Thee and thy vertues here I ſeize vpon,
Be it lawfull I take vp what's caſt away.
Gods, Gods! 'Tis ſtrange, that from their cold'ſt neglect
My Loue ſhould kindle to enflam'd reſpect.
Thy dowreleſſe Daughter King, throwne to my chance,
Is Queene of vs, of ours, and our faire France:
Not all the Dukes of watriſh Burgundy,
Can buy this vnpriz'd precious Maid of me.
Bid them farewell Cordelia, though vnkinde,
Thou looſeſt here a better where to finde.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Thou haſt her France, let her be thine, for we
Haue no ſuch Daughter, nor ſhall euer ſee
That face of hers againe, therfore be gone,
Without our Grace, our Loue, our Benizon:
Come Noble Burgundie.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Bid farwell to your Siſters.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: The Iewels of our Father, with waſh'd eies
Cordelia leaues you, I know you what you are,
And like a Siſter am moſt loth to call
Your faults as they are named. Loue well our Father:
To your profeſſed boſomes I commit him,
But yet alas, ſtood I within his Grace,
I would prefer him to a better place,
So farewell to you both.

sp.speaker: Regn.
sp.p: Preſcribe not vs our dutie.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Let your ſtudy
Be to content your Lord, who hath receiu'd you
At Fortunes almes, you haue obedience ſcanted,
And well are worth the want that you haue wanted▪

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Time ſhall vnfold what plighted cunning hides,
Who couers faults, at laſt with ſhame derides:
Well may you proſper.

sp.speaker: Fra.
sp.p: Come my faire Cordelia.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Siſter, it is not little I haue to ſay,
Of what moſt neerely appertaines to vs both,
I thinke our Father will hence to night.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: That's moſt certaine, and with you: next moneth with vs.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: You ſee how full of changes his age is, the obſeruation we haue made of it hath beene little: he alwaies lou'd our Siſter moſt, and with what poore iudgement he hath now caſt her off, appeares too groſſely.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: 'Tis the infirmity of his age, yet he hath euer but ſlenderly knowne himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: The beſt and ſoundeſt of his time hath bin but raſh, then muſt we looke from his age, to receiue not alone the imperfections of long ingrafted condition, but therewithall the vnruly way wardneſſe, that infirme and cholericke yeares bring with them.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: Such vnconſtant ſtarts are we like to haue from him, as this of Kents baniſhment.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: There is further complement of leaue-taking betweene France and him, pray you let vs ſit together, it our Father carry authority with ſuch diſpoſition as he beares, this laſt ſurrender of his will but offend vs.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.p: We ſhall further thinke of it.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: We muſt do ſomething, and i' th' heate.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.l: Thou Nature art my Goddeſſe, to thy Law
My ſeruices are bound, wherefore ſhould I
Stand in the plague of cuſtome, and permit
The curioſity of Nations, to depriue me?
For that I am ſome twelue, or fourteene Moonſhines
Lag of a Brother? Why Baſtard? Wherefore baſe?
When my Dimenſions are as well compact,
My minde as generous, and my ſhape as true
As honeſt Madams iſſue? Why brand they vs
With Baſe? With baſenes Barſtadie? Baſe, Baſe?
Who in the luſtie ſtealth of Nature, take
More compoſition, and fierce qualitie,
Then doth within a dull ſtale tyred bed
Goe to th' creating a whole tribe of Fops
Got 'tweene a ſleepe, and wake? Well then,
Legitimate Edgar, I muſt haue your land,
Our Fathers loue, is to the Baſtard Edmond,
As to th' legitimate: fine word: Legitimate.
Well, my Legittimate, if this Letter ſpeed,
And my inuention thriue, Edmond the baſe
Shall to' th' Legitimate: I grow, I proſper:
Now Gods, ſtand vp for Baſtards.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.l: Kent baniſh'd thus? and France in choller parted?
And the King gone to night? Preſcrib'd his powre,
Confin'd to exhibition? All this done
Vpon the gad? Edmond, how now? What newes?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: So pleaſe your Lordſhip, none.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Why ſo earneſtly ſeeke you to put vp yt Letter?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: I know no newes, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: What Paper were you reading?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Nothing my Lord.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: No? what needed then that terrible diſpatch of it into your Pocket? The quality of nothing, hath not ſuch neede to hide it ſelfe. Let's ſee: come, if it bee nothing, I ſhall not neede Spectacles.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: I beſeech you Sir, pardon mee; it is a Letter from my Brother, that I haue not all ore-read; and for ſo much as I haue perus'd, I finde it not fit for your ore-looking.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Giue me the Letter, Sir.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.l: I ſhall offend, either to detaine, or giue it:
The Contents, as in part I vnderſtand them.
Are too blame.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Let's ſee, let's ſee.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: I hope for my Brothers iuſtification, hee wrote this but as an eſſay, or taſte of my Vertue.

p.hi: This policie, and reuerence of Age, makes the world bitter to the beſt of our times: keepes our Fortunes from vs, till our oldneſſe cannot relliſh them. I begin to finde an idle and fond bondage, in the oppreſſion of aged tyranny, who ſwayes not as it hath power, but as it is ſuffer'd. Come to me, that of this I may ſpeake more. If our Father would ſleepe till I wak'd him, you ſhould enioy halfe his Reuennew for euer, and liue the beloued of your Brother.

sp.p: Hum? Conſpiracy? Sleepe till I wake him, you ſhould enioy halfe his Reuennew: my Sonne Edgar, had hee a hand to write this? A heart and braine to breede it in? When came you to this? Who brought it?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: It was not brought mee, my Lord; there's the cunning of it. I found it throwne in at the Caſement of my Cloſſet.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: You know the character to be your Brothers?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: If the matter were good my Lord, I durſt ſwear it were his: but in reſpect of that, I would faine thinke it were not.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: It is his.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: It is his hand, my Lord: but I hope his heart is not in the Contents.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p: Has he neuer before ſounded you in this buſines?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Neuer my Lord. But I haue heard him oft maintaine it to be fit, that Sonnes at perfect age, and Fathers declin'd, the Father ſhould bee as Ward to the Son, and the Sonne manage his Reuennew.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: O Villain, villain: his very opinion in the Letter. Abhorred Villaine, vnnaturall, deteſted, brutiſh Villaine; worſe then brutiſh: Go ſirrah, ſeeke him: Ile apprehend him. Abhominable Villaine, where is he?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: I do not well know my L. If it ſhall pleaſe you to ſuſpend your indignation againſt my Brother, til you can deriue from him better teſtimony of his intent, you ſhold run a certaine courſe: where, if you violently proceed againſt him, miſtaking his purpoſe, it would make a great gap in your owne Honor, and ſhake in peeces, the heart of his obedience. I dare pawne downe my life for him, that he hath writ this to feele my affection to your Honor, & to no other pretence of danger.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Thinke you ſo?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: If your Honor iudge it meere, I will place you where you ſhall heare vs conferre of this, and by an Auricular aſſurance haue your ſatisfaction, and that without any further delay, then this very Euening.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: He cannot bee ſuch a Monſter. Edmond ſeeke him out: winde me into him, I pray you: frame the Buſineſſe after your owne wiſedome. I would vnſtate my ſelfe, to be in a due reſolution.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: I will ſeeke him Sir, preſently: conuey the buſineſſe as I ſhall find meanes, and acquaint you withall.

sp.speaker: Glou.
sp.p: Theſe late Eclipſes in the Sun and Moone portend no good to vs: though the wiſedome of Nature can reaſon it thus, and thus, yet Nature finds it ſelfe ſcourg'd by the ſequent effects. Loue cooles, friendſhip falls off, Brothers diuide. In Cities, mutinies; in Countries, diſcord; in Pallaces, Treaſon; and the Bond crack'd, 'twixt Sonne and Father. This villaine of mine comes vnder the prediction; there's Son againſt Father, the King fals from by as of Nature, there's Father againſt Childe. We haue ſeene the beſt of our time. Machinations, hollowneſſe, treacherie, and all ruinous diſorders follow vs diſquietly to our Graues. Find out this Villain▪ Edmond, it ſhall loſe thee nothing, do it carefully: and the Noble & true-harted Kent baniſh'd; his offence, honeſty. 'Tis ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: This is the excellent foppery of the world, that when we are ſicke in fortune, often the ſurfers of our own behauiour, we make guilty of our diſaſters, the Sun, the Moone, and Starres, as if we were villaines on neceſſitie, Fooles by heauenly compulſion, Knaues, Theeues, and Treachers by Sphericall predominance. Drunkards, Lyars, and Adulterers by an inforc'd obedience of Planatary influence; and all that we are euill in, by a diuine thruſt • ng on. An admirable euaſion of Whore-maſter-man, to lay his Goatiſh diſpoſition on the charge of a Starre, My father compounded with my mother vnder the Dragons taile, and my Natiuity was vnder Vrſa Maior, ſo that it followes, I am rough and Leacherous. I ſhould haue bin that I am, had the maidenleſt Starre in the Firmament twinkled on my baſtardizing.
Pat: he comes like the Cataſtrophe of the old Comedie: my Cue is villanous Melancholly, with a ſighe like Tom o' Bedlam. — O theſe Eclipſes do portend theſe diuiſions. Fa, Sol, La, Me.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: How now Brother Edmond, what ſerious contemplation are you in?

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: I am thinking Brother of a prediction I read this other day, what ſhould follow theſe Eclipſes.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Do you buſie your ſelfe with that?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.l: I promiſe you, the effects he writes of, ſucceede vnhappily.
When ſaw you my Father laſt?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: The night gone by.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Spake you with him?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: I, two houres together.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Parted you in good termes? Found you no diſpleaſure in him, by word, nor countenance?

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: None at all,

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p:
Bethink your ſelfe wherein you may haue offended him: and at my entreaty forbeare his preſence, vntill ſome little time hath qualified the heat of his diſpleaſure, which at this inſtant ſo rageth in him, that with the miſchiefe
of your perſon, it would ſcarſely alay.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Some Villaine hath done me wrong.

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.p: That's my feare, I pray you haue a continent forbearance till the ſpeed of his rage goes ſlower: and as I ſay, retire with me to my lodging, from whence I will fitly bring you to heare my Lord ſpeake: pray ye goe, there's my key: if you do ſtirre abroad, goe arm'd.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Arm'd, Brother?

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.p: Brother, I aduiſe you to the beſt, I am no honeſt man, if ther be any good meaning toward you: I haue told you what I haue ſeene, and heard: But faintly, Nothing like the image, and horror of it, pray you away.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: Shall I heare from you anon?

sp.speaker: Edm.
sp.l: I do ſerue you in this buſineſſe:
A Credulous Father, and a Brother Noble,
Whoſe nature is ſo farre from doing harmes,
That he ſuſpects none: on whoſe fooliſh honeſtie
My practiſes ride eaſie: I ſee the buſineſſe.
Let me, if not by birth, haue lands by wit,
All with me's meete, that I can faſhion fit.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: Did my Father ſtrike my Gentleman for chiding of his Foole?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: I Madam.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: By day and night, he wrongs me, euery howre
He flaſhes into one groſſe crime, or other,
That ſets vs all at ods: Ile not endure it;
His Knights grow riotous, and himſelfe vpbraides vs
On euery trifle. When he returnes from hunting,
I will not ſpeake with him, ſay I am ſicke,
If you come ſlacke of former ſeruices,
You ſhall do well, the fault of it Ile anſwer.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: He's comming Madam, I heare him.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Put on what weary negligence you pleaſe,
You and your Fellowes: I'de haue it come to queſtion;
If he diſtaſte it, let him to my Siſter,
Whoſe mind and mine I know in that are one,
Remember what I haue ſaid.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Well Madam.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: And let his Knights haue colder lookes among you: what growes of it no matter, aduiſe your fellowes ſo, Ile write ſtraight to my Siſter to hold my courſe; prepare for dinner.

div.head: Scena Quarta.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.l: If but as will I other accents borrow,
That can my ſpeech defuſe, my good intent
May carry through it ſelfe to that full iſſue
For which I raiz'd my likeneſſe. Now baniſht Kent,
If thou canſt ſerue where thou doſt ſtand condemn'd,
So may it come, thy Maſter whom thou Iou'ſt,
Shall find thee full of labours.

div.stage: Hornes within. Enter Lear and Attendants.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Let me not ſtay a iot for dinner, go get it ready: how now, what art thou?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: A man Sir.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What doſt thou profeſſe? What would'ſt thou with vs?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I do profeſſe to be no leſſe then I ſeeme; to ſerue him truely that will put me in truſt, to loue him that is honeſt, to conuerſe with him that is wiſe and ſaies little, to feare iudgement, to fight when I cannot chooſe, and to eate no fiſh.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What art thou?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: A very honeſt hearted Fellow, and as poore as the King.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: If thou be'ſt as poore for a ſubiect, as hee's for a King, thou art poore enough. What wouldſt thou?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Seruice.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Who wouldſt thou ſerue?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: You.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Do'ſt thou know me fellow?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: No Sir, but you haue that in your countenance, which I would faine call Maſter.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What's that?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Authority.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What ſeruices canſt thou do?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I can keepe honeſt counſaile, ride, run, marre a curious tale in telling it, and deliuer a plaine meſſage bluntly: that which ordinary men are fit for, I am quallified in, and the beſt of me, is Dilligence.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: How old art thou?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Not ſo young Sir to loue a woman for ſinging, nor ſo old to dote on her for any thing. I haue yeares on my backe forty eight.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Follow me, thou ſhalt ſerue me, if I like thee no worſe after dinner, I will not part from thee yet. Dinner ho, dinner, where's my knaue? my Foole? Go you and call my Foole hither. You you Sirrah, where's my Daughter?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: So pleaſe you —

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What ſaies the Fellow there? Call the Clot-pole backe: wher's my Foole? Ho, I thinke the world's aſleepe, how now? Where's that Mungrell?

sp.speaker: Knigh.
sp.p: He ſaies my Lord, your Daughters is not well.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Why came not the ſlaue backe to me when I call'd him?

sp.speaker: Knigh.
sp.p: Sir, he anſwered me in the roundeſt manner, he would not.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: He would not?

sp.speaker: Knight.
sp.p: My Lord, I know not what the matter is, but to my iudgement your Highneſſe is not entertain'd with that Ceremonious affection as you were wont, theres a great abatement of kindneſſe appeares as well in the generall dependants, as in the Duke himſelfe alſo, and your Daughter.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Ha? Saiſt thou ſo?

sp.speaker: Knigh.
sp.p: I beſeech you pardon me my Lord, if I bee miſtaken, for my duty cannot be ſilent, when I thinke your Highneſſe wrong'd.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Thou but remembreſt me of mine owne Conception, I haue perceiued a moſt faint neglect of late, which I haue rather blamed as mine owne iealous curioſitie, then as a very pretence and purpoſe of vnkindneſſe; I will looke further intoo't • : but where's my Foole? I haue not ſeene him this two daies.

sp.speaker: Knight.
sp.l: Since my young Ladies going into France
Sir, the Foole hath much pined away.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: No more of that, I haue noted it well, goe you and tell my Daughter, I would ſpeake with her. Goe you call hither my Foole; Oh you Sir, you, come you hither Sir, who am I Sir?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: My Ladies Father.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: My Ladies Father? my Lords knaue, you whorſon dog, you ſlaue, you curre.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.l: I am none of theſe my Lord,
I beſeech your pardon.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Do you bandy lookes with me, you Raſcall?

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Ile not be ſtrucken my Lord.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Nor tript neither, you baſe Foot-ball plaier.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: I thanke thee fellow.
Thou ſeru'ſt me, and Ile loue thee.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Come ſir, ariſe, away, Ile teach you differences: away, away, if you will meaſure your lubbers length againe, tarry, but away, goe too, haue you wiſedome, ſo.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Now my friendly knaue I thanke thee, there's earneſt of thy ſeruice.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Let me hire him too, here's my Coxcombe.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: How now my pretty knaue, how doſt thou?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Sirrah, you were beſt take my Coxcombe.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Why my Boy?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Why? for taking ones part that's out of fauour, nay, & thou canſt not ſmile as the wind ſits, thou'lt catch colde ſhortly, there take my Coxcombes why this fellow ha's baniſh'd two on's Daughters, and did the third a bleſſing againſt his will, if thou follow him, thou muſt needs weare my Coxcombe. How now Nunckle? would I had two Coxcombes and two Daughters.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Why my Boy?

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p: If I gaue them all my liuing, I'ld keepe my Coxcombes my ſelfe, there's mine, beg another of thy Daughters.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Take heed Sirrah, the whip.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Truth's a dog muſt to kennell, hee muſt bee whipt out, when the Lady Brach may ſtand by' th' fire and ſtinke.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: A peſtilent gall to me.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Sirha, Ile teach thee a ſpeech.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Do.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: Marke it Nuncle;
Haue more then thou ſhoweſt,
Speake leſſe then thou knoweſt,
Lend leſſe then thou oweſt,
Ride more then thou goeſt,
Learne more then thou troweſt,
Set leſſe then thou throweſt;
Leaue thy drinke and thy whore,
And keepe in a dore,
And thou ſhalt haue more,
Then two tens to a ſcore.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: This is nothing Foole.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Then 'tis like the breath of an vnfeed Lawyer, you gaue me nothing for't, can you make no vſe of nothing Nuncle?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Why no Boy,
Nothing can be made out of nothing.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Prythee tell him, ſo much the rent of his land comes to, he will not beleeue a Foole.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: A bitter Foole.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Do'ſt thou know the difference my Boy, betweene a bitter Foole, and a ſweet one.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: No Lad, teach me.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Nunckle, giue me an egge, and Ile giue thee two Crownes.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What two Crownes ſhall they be?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Why after I haue cut the egge i' th' middle and eate vp the meate, the two Crownes of the egge: when thou cloueſt thy Crownes i' th' middle, and gau'ſt away both parts, thou boar'ſt thine Aſſe on thy backe o're the durt, thou had'ſt little wit in thy bald crowne, when thou gau'ſt thy golden one away; if I ſpeake like my ſelfe in this, let him be whipt that firſt findes it ſo.
sp.l: Fooles had nere leſſe grace in a yeere,
For wiſemen are growne foppiſh,
And know not how their wits to weare,
Their manners are ſo apiſh.

sp.speaker: Le.
sp.p: When were you wont to be ſo full of Songs ſirrah?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: I haue vſed it Nunckle, ere ſince thou mad'ſt thy Daughters thy Mothers, for when thou gau'ſt them the rod, and put'ſt downe thine owne breeches, then they
sp.l: For ſodaine ioy did weepe,
And I for ſorrow ſung,
That ſuch a King ſhould play bo-peepe,
And goe the Foole among.
Pry' thy Nunckle keepe a Schoolemaſter that can teach
thy Foole to lie, I would faine learne to lie.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: And you lie ſirrah, wee'l haue you whipt.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: I maruell what kin thou and thy daughters are, they'l haue me whipt for ſpeaking true: thou'lt haue me whipt for lying; and ſometimes I am whipt for holding my peace. I had rather be any kind o' thing then a foole, and yet I would not be thee Nunckle, thou haſt pared thy wit o' both ſides, and left nothing i' th' middle; heere comes one o' the parings.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: How now Daughter? what makes that Frontlet on? You are too much of late i' th' frowne.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Thou waſt a pretty fellow when thou hadſt no need to care for her frowning, now thou art an O without a figure, I am better then thou art now, I am a Foole, thou art nothing. Yes forſooth I will hold my tongue, ſo your face bids me, though you ſay nothing.
sp.l: Mum, mum, he that keepes nor cruſt, not crum,
Weary of all, ſhall want ſome. That's a ſheal'd Peſcod.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Not only Sir this, your all-lycenc'd Foole,
But other of your inſolent retinue
Do hourely Carpe and Quarrell, breaking forth
In ranke, and (not to be endur'd) riots Sir.
I had thought by making this well knowne vnto you,
To haue found a ſafe redreſſe, but now grow fearefull
By what your ſelfe too late haue ſpoke and done,
That you protect this courſe, and put it on
By your allowance, which if you ſhould, the fault
Would not ſcape cenſure, nor the redreſſes ſleepe,
Which in the tender of a wholeſome weale,
Might in their working do you that offence,
Which elſe were ſhame, that then neceſſitie
Will call diſcreet proceeding.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: For you know Nunckle, the Hedge-Sparrow fed the Cuckoo ſo long, that it's had it head bit off by it young, ſo out went the Candle, and we were left darkling.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Are you our Daughter?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: I would you would make vſe of your good wiſedome
(Whereof I know you are fraught) and put away
Theſe diſpoſitions, which of late tranſport you
From what you rightly are.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: May not an Aſſe know, when the Cart drawes the Horſe?
Whoop Iugge I loue thee.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Do's any heere know me?
This is not Lear:
Do's Lear walke thus? Speake thus? Where are his eies?
Either his Notion weakens, his Diſcernings
Are Lethargied. Ha! Waking? 'Tis not ſo?
Who is it that can tell me who I am?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Lears ſhadow.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Your name, faire Gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: This admiration Sir, is much o' th' ſauour
Of other your new prankes. I do beſeech you
To vnderſtand my purpoſes aright:
As you are Old, and Reuerend, ſhould be Wiſe.
Heere do you keepe a hundred Knights and Squires,
Men ſo diſorder'd, ſo deboſh'd, and bold,
That this our Court infected with their manners,
Shewes like a riotous Inne; Epicuriſme and Luſt
Makes it more like a Tauerne, or a Brothell,
Then a grac'd Pallace. The ſhame it ſelfe doth ſpeake
For inſtant remedy. Be then deſir'd
By her, that elſe will take the thing ſhe begges,
A little to diſquantity your Traine,
And the remainders that ſhall ſtill depend,
To be ſuch men as may beſort your Age,
Which know themſelues, and you.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Darkneſſe, and Diuels.
Saddle my horſes: call my Traine together.
Degenerate Baſtard, Ile not trouble thee;
Yet haue I left a daughter.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: You ſtrike my people, and your diſorder'd rable, make Seruants of their Betters.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Woe, that too late repents:
Is it your will, ſpeake Sir? Prepare my Horſes.
Ingratitude! thou Marble-hearted Fiend,
More hideous when thou ſhew'ſt thee in a Child,
Then the Sea-monſter.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.p: Pray Sir be patient.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Deteſted Kite, thou lyeſt.
My Traine are men of choice, and rareſt parts,
That all particulars of dutie know,
And in the moſt exact regard, ſupport
The worſhips of their name. O moſt ſmall fault,
How vgly did'ſt thou in Cordelia ſhew?
Which like an Engine, wrencht my frame of Nature
From the fixt place: drew from my heart all loue,
And added to the gall. O Lear, Lear, Lear!
Beate at this gate that let thy Folly in,
And thy deere Iudgement out. Go, go, my people.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: My Lord, I am guiltleſſe, as I am ignorant
Of what hath moued you.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: It may be ſo, my Lord.
Heare Nature, heare deere Goddeſſe, heare:
Suſpend thy purpoſe, if thou did'ſt intend
To make this Creature fruitfull:
Into her Wombe conuey ſtirrility,
Drie vp in her the Organs of increaſe,
And from her derogate body, neuer ſpring
A Babe to honor her. If ſhe muſt teeme,
Create her childe of Spleene, that it may liue
And be a thwart diſnatur'd torment to her.
Let it ſtampe wrinkles in her brow of youth,
With cadent Teares fret Channels in her cheekes,
Turne all her Mothers paines, and benefits
To laughter, and contempt: That ſhe may feele,
How ſharper then a Serpents tooth it is,
To haue a thankleſſe Childe. Away, away.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: Now Gods that we adore,
Whereof comes this?

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Neuer afflict your ſelfe to know more of it:
But let his diſpoſition haue that ſcope
As dotage giues it.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: What fiftie of my Followers at a clap?
Within a fortnight?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.p: What's the matter, Sir?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.l: Ile tell thee:
Life and death, I am aſham'd
That thou haſt power to ſhake my manhood thus,
That theſe hot teares, which breake from me perforce
Should make thee worth them.
Blaſtes and Fogges vpon thee:
Th' vntented woundings of a Fathers curſe
Pierce euerie ſenſe about thee. Old fond eyes,
Beweepe this cauſe againe, Ile plucke ye out,
And caſt you with the waters that you looſe
To temper Clay. Ha? Let it be ſo.
I haue another daughter,
Who I am ſure is kinde and comfortable:
When ſhe ſhall heare this of thee, with her nailes
Shee'l flea thy Woluiſh viſage. Thou ſhalt finde,
That Ile reſume the ſhape which thou doſt thinke
I haue caſt off for euer.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.p: Do you marke that?

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: I cannot be ſo partiall Gonerill,
To the great loue I beare you.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Pray you content. What Oſwald, hoa?
You Sir, more Knaue then Foole, after your Maſter.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.l: Nunkle Lear, Nunkle Lear,
Tarry, take the Foole with thee:
A Fox, when one has caught her.
And ſuch a Daughter,
Should ſure to the Slaughter,
If my Cap would buy a Halter,
So the Foole followes after.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: This man hath had good Counſell,
A hundred Knights?
'Tis politike, and ſafe to let him keepe
At point a hundred Knights: yes, that on euerie dreame,
Each buz, each fancie, each complaint, diſlike,
He may enguard his dotage with their powres,
And hold our liues in mercy. Oſwald, I ſay.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.p: Well, you may feare too farre.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Safer then truſt too farre;
Let me ſtill take away the harmes I feare,
Not feare ſtill to be taken. I know his heart,
What he hath vtter'd I haue writ my Siſter:
If ſhe ſuſtaine him, and his hundred Knights
When I haue ſhew'd th' vnfitneſſe.
How now Oſwald?
What haue you writ that Letter to my Siſter?

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: I Madam.

sp.speaker: Gon.
sp.l: Take you ſome company, and away to horſe,
Informe her full of my particular feare,
And thereto adde ſuch reaſons of your owne,
As may compact it more. Get you gone,
And haſten your returne; no, no, my Lord,
This milky gentleneſſe, and courſe of yours
Though I condemne not, yet vnder pardon
Your are much more at task for want of wiſedome,
Then prai'sd for harmefull mildneſſe.

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.l: How farre your eies may pierce I cannot tell;
Striuing to better, oft we marre what's well.

sp.speaker: Con.
sp.p: Nay then —

sp.speaker: Alb.
sp.p: Well, well, the'uent.

div.head: Scena Quinta.
div.stage: Enter Lear, Kent, Gentleman, and Foole.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Go you before to Gloſter with theſe Letters; acquaint my Daughter no further with any thing you know, then comes from her demand out of the Letter, if your Dilligence be not ſpeedy, I ſhall be there afore you.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I will not ſleepe my Lord, till I haue deliuered your Letter.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: If a mans braines were in's heeles, wert not in danger of kybes?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: I Boy.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Then I prythee be merry, thy wit ſhall not go ſlip-ſhod.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.p: Shalt ſee thy other Daughter will vſe thee kindly, for though ſhe's as like this, as a Crabbe's like an Apple, yet I can tell what I can tell.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: What can'ſt tell Boy?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: She will taſte as like this as, a Crabbe do's to a Crab: thou canſt tell why ones noſe ſtands i' th' middle on's face?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Why to keepe ones eyes of either ſide's noſe, that what a man cannot ſmell out, he may ſpy into.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: I did her wrong.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Can'ſt tell how an Oyſter makes his ſhell?

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Nor I neither; but I can tell why a Snaile ha's a houſe.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Why to put's head in, not to giue it away to his daughters, and leaue his hornes without a caſe.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: I will forget my Nature, ſo kind a Father? Be my Horſſes ready?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Thy Aſſes are gone about 'em; the reaſon why the ſeuen Starres are no mo then ſeuen, is a pretty reaſon.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Becauſe they are not eight.

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Yes indeed, thou would'ſt make a good Foole.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: To tak't againe perforce; Monſter Ingratitude!

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: If thou wert my Foole Nunckle, Il'd haue thee beaten for being old before thy time.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: How's that?

sp.speaker: Foole.
sp.p: Thou ſhouldſt not haue bin old, till thou hadſt bin wiſe.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: O let me not be mad, not mad ſweet Heauen▪ keepe me in temper, I would not be mad. How now are the Horſes ready?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: Ready my Lord.

sp.speaker: Lear.
sp.p: Come Boy.

sp.speaker: Fool.
sp.l: She that's a Maid now, & laughs at my departure,
Shall not be a Maid long, vnleſſe things be cut ſhorter.

div.head: Scena Prima.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Saue thee Curan.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: And your Sir, I haue bin
With your Father, and giuen him notice
That the Duke of Cornwall, and Regan his Ducheſſe
Will be here with him this night.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: How comes that?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.p: Nay I know not, you haue heard of the newes abroad, I meane the whiſper'd ones, for they are yet but ear • -kiſſing arguments.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Not I: pray you what are they?

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: Haue you heard of no likely Warres toward,
'Twixt the Dukes of Cornwall, and Albany?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Not a word.

sp.speaker: Cur.
sp.l: You may do then in time,
Fare you well Sir.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.l: The Duke be here to night? The better beſt,
This weaues it ſelfe perforce into my buſineſſe,
My Father hath ſet guard to take my Brother,
And I haue one thing of a queazie queſtion
Which I muſt act, Briefeneſſe, and Fortune worke.
Brother, a word, diſcend; Brother I ſay,
My Father watches: O Sir, fly this place,
Intelligence is giuen where you are hid;
You haue now the good aduantage of the night,
Haue you not ſpoken 'gainſt the Duke of Cornewall?
Hee's comming hither, now i' th' night, i' th' haſte,
And Regan with him, haue you nothing ſaid
Vpon his partie 'gainſt the Duke of Albany?
Aduiſe your ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Edg.
sp.p: I am ſure on't, not a word.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.l: I heare my Father comming, pardon me:
In cunning, I muſt draw my Sword vpon you:
Draw, ſeeme to defend your ſelfe,
Now quit you well.
Yeeld, come before my Father, light hoa, here,
Fly Brother, Torches, Torches, ſo farewell.
Some blood drawne on me, would beget opinion
Of my more fierce endeauour. I haue ſeene drunkards
Do more then this in ſport▪ Father, Father,
Stop, ſtop, no helpe?

div.stage: Enter Gloſter and Seruants with Torches.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p: Now Edmund, where's the villaine?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.l: Here ſtood he in the dark, his ſharpe Sword out,
Mumbling of wicked charmes, coniuring the Moone
To ſtand auſpicious Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p: But where is he?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Looke Sir, I bleed.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p: Where is the villaine, Edmund?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Fled this way Sir, when by no meanes he could.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p: Purſue him, ho: go after. By no meanes, what?

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.l: Perſwade me to the murther of your Lordſhip,
But that I told him the reuenging Gods,
'Gainſt Paricides did all the thunder bend,
Spoke with how manifold, and ſtrong a Bond
The Child was bound to' th' Father; Sir in fine,
Seeing how lothly oppoſite I ſtood
To his vnnaturall purpoſe, in fell motion
With his prepared Sword, he charges home
My vnprouided body, latch'd mine arme;
And when he ſaw my beſt alarum'd ſpirits
Bold in the quarrels right, rouz'd to th' encounter,
Or whether gaſted by the noyſe I made,
Full ſodainely he fled.

sp.speaker: Gloſt.
sp.l: Let him fly farre:
Not in this Land ſhall he remaine vncaught
And found; diſpatch, the Noble Duke my Maſter,
My worthy Arch and Patron comes to night,
By his authoritie I will proclaime it,
That he which finds him ſhall deſerue our thankes,
Bringing the murderous Coward to the ſtake:
He that conceales him death.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.l: When I diſſwaded him from his intent,
And found him pight to doe it, with curſt ſpeech
I threaten'd to diſcouer him; he replied,
Thou vnpoſſeſſing Baſtard, doſt thou thinke,
If I would ſtand againſt thee, would the repoſall
Of any truſt, vertue, or worth in thee
Make thy words faith'd? No, what ſhould I denie,
(As this I would, though thou didſt produce
My very Character) I'ld turne it all
To thy ſuggeſtion, plot, and damned practiſe:
And thou muſt make a dullard of the world,
If they not thought the profits of my death
Were very pregnant and potentiall ſpirits
To make thee ſeeke it.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.l: O ſtrange and faſtned Villaine,
Would he deny his Letter, ſaid he?
Harke, the Dukes Trumpets, I know not wher he comes;
All Ports Ile barre, the villaine ſhall not ſcape,
The Duke muſt grant me that: beſides, his picture
I will ſend farre and neere, that all the kingdome
May haue due note of him, and of my land,
(Loyall and naturall Boy) Ile worke the meanes
To make thee capable.

sp.speaker: Corn.
sp.l: How now my Noble friend, ſince I came hither
(Which I can call but now,) I haue heard ſtrangeneſſe.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: If it be true; all vengeance comes too ſhort
Which can purſue th' offender; how doſt my Lord?

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p: O Madam, my old heart is crack'd, it's crack'd.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: What, did my Fathers Godſonne ſeeke your life?
He whom my Father nam'd, your Edgar?

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p: O Lady, Lady, ſhame would haue it hid.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Was he not companion with the riotous Knights
That tended vpon my Father?

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p: I know not Madam, 'tis too bad, too bad.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: Yes Madam, he was of that conſort.

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: No maruaile then, though he were ill affected,
'Tis they haue put him on the old mans death,
To haue th' expence and waſt of his Reuenues:
I haue this preſent euening from my Siſter
Beene well inform'd of them, and with ſuch cautions,
That if they come to ſoiourne at my houſe,
Ile not be there.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: Nor I, aſſure thee Regan;
Edmund, I heare that you haue ſhewne your Father
A Child-like Office.

sp.speaker: Bast.
sp.p: It was my duty Sir.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.l: He did bewray his practiſe, and receiu'd
This hurt you ſee, ſtriuing to apprehend him.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: Is he purſued?

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p: I my good Lord.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.l: If he be taken, he ſhall neuer more
Be fear'd of doing harme, make your owne purpoſe,
How in my ſtrength you pleaſe: for you Edmund,
Whoſe vertue and obedience doth this inſtant
So much commend it ſelfe, you ſhall be ours,
Nature's of ſuch deepe truſt, we ſhall much need:
You we firſt ſeize on.

sp.speaker: Baſt.
sp.p: I ſhall ſerue you Sir truely, how euer elſe.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.p: For him I thanke your Grace.

sp.speaker: Cor.
sp.p: You know not why we came to viſit you?

sp.speaker: Reg.
sp.l: Thus out of ſeaſon, thredding darke ey'd night,
Occaſions Noble Gloſter of ſome prize,
Wherein we muſt haue vſe of your aduiſe.
Our Father he hath writ, ſo hath our Siſter,
Of differences, which I beſt though it fit
To anſwere from our home: the ſeuerall Meſſengers
From hence attend diſpatch, our good old Friend,
Lay comforts to your boſome, and beſtow
Your needfull counſaile to our buſineſſes,
Which craues the inſtant vſe.

sp.speaker: Glo.
sp.l: I ſerue you Madam,
Your Graces are right welcome.

div.head: Scena Secunda.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Good dawning to thee Friend, art of this houſe?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Where may we ſet our horſes?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I' th' myre.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Prythee, if thou lou'ſt me, tell me.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: I loue thee not.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Why then I care not for thee.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: If I had thee in Lipsbury Pinfold, I would make thee care for me.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: Why do'ſt thou vſe me thus? I know thee not.

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: Fellow I know thee.

sp.speaker: Ste.
sp.p: What do'ſt thou know me for?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p: A Knaue, a Raſcall, an eater of broken meates, a baſe, proud, ſhallow, beggerly, three-ſuited-hundred pound, filthy wooſted-ſtocking knaue, a Lilly-liuered, action-taking, whoreſon glaſſe-gazing ſuper-ſeruiceable finicall Rogue, one Trunke-inheriting ſlaue, one that would'ſt be a Baud in way of good ſeruice, and art nothing but the compoſition of a Knaue, Begger, Coward, Pandar, and the Sonne and Heire of a Mungrill Bitch, one whom I will beate into clamours whining, if thou deny'ſt the leaſt ſillable of thy addition.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Why, what a monſtrous Fellow art thou, thus to raile on one, that is neither knowne of thee, nor knowes thee?

sp.speaker: Kent.
sp.p:
What a brazen-fac'd Varlet art thou, to deny thou knoweſt me? Is it two dayes ſince I tript vp thy heeles, and beate thee before the King? Draw you rogue,
for though it be night, yet the Moone ſhines, Ile make a ſop oth' Moonſhine of you, you whoreſon Cullyenly Barber-monger, draw.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Away, I haue nothing to do with thee.

sp.speaker: Kent.
