How this foule Rout began: Who ſet it on,
And he that is approu'd in this offence,
Though he had twinn'd with me, both at a birth,
Shall looſe me. What in a Towne of warre,
Yet wilde, the peoples hearts brim-full of feare,
To Manage priuate, and domeſticke Quarrell?
In night, and on the Court and Guard of ſafetie?
'Tis monſtrous: Iago, who began't?

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: If partially Affin'd, or league in office,
Thou doſt deliuer more, or leſſe then Truth.
Thou art no Souldier.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Touch me not ſo neere,
I had rather haue this tongue cut from my mouth,
Then it ſhould do offence to Michaell Caſſio.
Yet I perſwade my ſelfe, to ſpeake the truth
Shall nothing wrong him. This it is Generall:
Montano and my ſelfe being in ſpeech,
There comes a Fellow crying out for helpe,
And Caſſio following him with determin'd Sword
To execute vpon him. Sir, this Gentleman,
Steppes in to Caſſio, and entreats his pauſe:
My ſelfe, the crying Fellow did purſue,
Leaſt by his clamour (as it ſo fell out)
The Towne might fall in fright. He, (ſwift of foote)
Out-ran my purpoſe: and I return'd then rather
For that I heard the clinke▪ and fall of Swords,
And Caſſio high in oath: Which till to night
I nere might ſay before. When I came backe
(For this was briefe) I found them cloſe together
At blow, and thruſt, euen as againe they were
When you your ſelfe did part them.
More of this matter cannot I report.
But Men are Men: The beſt ſometimes forget,
Though Caſſio did ſome little wrong to him,
As men in rage ſtrike thoſe that wiſh them beſt,
Yet ſurely Caſſio. I beleeue receiu'd
From him that fled, ſome ſtrange Indignitie,
Which patience could not paſſe.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: I know Iago
Thy honeſtie, and loue doth mince this matter,
Making it light to Caſſio: Caſſio, I loue thee,
But neuer more be Officer of mine.
Looke if my gentle Loue be not rais'd vp:
Ile make thee an example.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: What is the matter (Deere?)

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: All's well, Sweeting:
Come away to bed. Sir for your hurts,
My ſelfe will be your Surgeon. Lead him off:
Iago, looke with care about the Towne,
And ſilence thoſe whom this vil'd brawle diſtracted.
Come Deſdemona, 'tis the Soldiers life,
To haue their Balmy ſlumbers wak'd with ſtrife.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: What are you hurt Lieutenant?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: I, paſt all Surgery.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Marry Heauen forbid.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Reputation, Reputation, Reputation: Oh I haue loſt my Reputation. I haue loſt the immortall part of myſelfe, and what remaines is beſtiall. My Reputation, Iago, my Reputation.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: As I am an honeſt man I had thought you had receiued ſome bodily wound; there is more ſence in that then in Reputation. Reputation is an idle, and moſt falſe impoſition; oft got without merit, and loſt without deſeruing. You haue loſt no Reputation at all, vnleſſe you repute your ſelfe ſuch a looſer. What man, there are more wayes to recouer the Generall againe. You are but now caſt in his moode, (a puniſhment more in policie, then in malice) euen ſo as one would beate his offenceleſſe dogge, ro affright an Imperious Lyon. Sue to him againe, and he's yours.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: I will rather ſue to be deſpis'd, then to deceiue ſo good a Commander, with ſo ſlight, ſo drunken, and ſo indiſcreet an Officer. Drunke? And ſpeake Parrat? And ſquabble? Swagger? Sweare? And diſcourſe Fuſtian with ones owne ſhadow? Oh thou inviſible ſpirit of Wine, if thou haſt no name to be knowne by, let vs call thee Diuell.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: What was he that you follow'd with your Sword? What had he done to you?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: I know not.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Is't poſſible?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: I remember a maſſe of things, but nothing diſtinctly: a Quarrell, but nothing wherefore. Oh, that men ſhould put an Enemie in their mouthes, to ſteale away their Braines? that we ſhould with ioy, pleaſance, reuell and applauſe, transforme our ſelues into Beaſts.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Why? But you are now well enough: how came you thus recouered?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: It hath pleas'd the diuell drunkenneſſe, to giue place to the diuell wrath, one vnpe • fectneſſe, ſhewes me another to make me frankly deſpiſe my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Come, you are too ſeuere • a Moraller. As the Time, the Place, & the Condition of this Country ſtands I could hartily wiſh this had not befalne: but ſince it is, as it is, mend it for your owne good.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: I will aske him for my Place againe, he ſhall tell me, I am a drunkard: had I as many mouthes as Hydra, ſuch an anſwer would ſtop them all. To be now a ſenſible man, by and by a Foole, an • preſently a Beaſt. Oh ſtrange! Euery inordinate cup is vnbleſs'd, and the Ingredient is a diuell.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Come, come: good wine, is a good famillar Creature, if it be well vs'd: exclaime no more againſt it. And good Lieutenant, I thinke, you thinke I loue you.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: I haue well approued it, Sir. I drunke?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: You, or any man liuing, may be drunke at a time man. I tell you what you ſhall do: Our General's Wife, is now the Generall. I may ſay ſo, in this reſpect, for that he hath deuoted, and giuen vp himſelfe to the Contemplation, marke: and deuotement of her parts and Graces. Confeſſe your ſelfe freely to her: Importune her helpe to put you in your place againe. She is of ſo free, ſo kinde, ſo apt, ſo bleſſed a diſpoſition, ſhe holds it a vice in her goodneſſe, not to do more then ſhe is requeſted. This broken ioynt betweene you, and her husband, entreat her to ſplinter. And my Fortunes againſt any lay worth naming, this cracke of your Loue, ſhall grow ſtronger, then it was before.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: You aduiſe me well.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I proteſt in the ſinceritie of Loue, and honeſt kindneſſe.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: I thinke it freely: and betimes in the morning, I will beſeech the vertuous Deſdemona to vndertake for me: I am deſperate of my Fortunes if they check me.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: You are in the right: good night Lieutenant, I muſt to the Watch.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: Good night, honeſt Iago.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: And what's he then,
That ſaies I play the Villaine?
When this aduiſe is free I giue, and honeſt,
Proball to thinking, and indeed the courſe
To win the Moore againe.
For 'tis moſt eaſie
Th' inclyning Deſdemona to ſubdue
In any honeſt Suite. She's fram'd as fruitefull
As the free Elements. And then for her
To win the Moore, were to renownce his Baptiſme,
All Seales, and Simbols of redeemed ſin:
His Soule is ſo enfetter'd to her Loue,
That ſhe may make, vnmake, do what ſhe liſt,
Euen as her Appetite ſhall play the God,
With his weake Function. How am I then a Villaine,
To Counſell Caſſio to this paralell courſe,
Directly to his good? Diuinitie of hell,
When diuels will the blackeſt ſinnes put on,
They do ſuggeſt at firſt with heauenly ſhewes,
As I do now. For whiles this honeſt Foole
Plies Deſdemona, to repaire his Fortune,
And ſhe for him, pleades ſtrongly to the Moore,
Ile powre this peſtilence into his eare:
That ſhe repeales him, for her bodies Luſt.
And by how much ſhe ſtriues to do him good,
She ſhall vndo her Credite with the Moore.
So will I turne her vertue into pitch,
And out of her owne goodneſſe make the Net,
That ſhall en-maſh them all.
How now Rodorigo?

sp.speaker: Rodorigo.
sp.p:
I do follow heere in the Chace, not like a Hound that hunts, but one that filles vp the Crie. My Money is almoſt ſpent; I haue bin to night exceedingly well Cudgell'd: And I thinke the iſſue
will bee, I ſhall haue ſo much experience for my paines; And ſo, with no money at all, and a little more Wit, returne againe to Venice.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: How poore are they that haue not Patience?
What wound did euer heale but by degrees?
Thou know'ſt we worke by Wit, and not by Witchcraft
And Wit depends on dilatory time:
Dos't not go well? Caſſio hath beaten thee,
And thou by that ſmall hurt hath caſheer'd Caſſio:
Though other things grow faire againſt the Sun,
Yet Fruites that bloſſome firſt, will firſt be ripe:
Content thy ſelfe, a-while. Introth 'tis Morning;
Pleaſure, and Action, make the houres ſeeme ſhort.
Retire thee, go where thou art Billited:
A way, I ſay, thou ſhalt know more heereafter:
Nay get thee gone.
Two things are to be done:
My Wife muſt moue for Caſſio to her Miſtris:
Ile ſet her on my ſelfe, a while, to draw the Moor apart,
And bring him iumpe, when he may Caſſio finde
Soliciting his wife: I, that's the way:
Dull not Deuice, by coldneſſe, and delay.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: Maſters, play heere, I wil content your paines,
Something that's briefe: and bid, goodmorrow General.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Why Maſters, haue your Inſtruments bin in Naples, that they ſpeake i' th' Noſe thus?

sp.speaker: Muſ.
sp.p: How Sir? how?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Are theſe I pray you, winde Inſtruments?

sp.speaker: Muſ.
sp.p: I marry are they ſir.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Oh, thereby hangs a tale.

sp.speaker: Muſ.
sp.p: Whereby hangs a tale, ſir?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Marry ſir, by many a winde Inſtrument that I know. But Maſters, heere's money for you: and the Generall ſo likes your Muſick, that he deſires you for loues ſake to make no more noiſe with it.

sp.speaker: Muſ.
sp.p: Well Sir, we will not.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: If you haue any Muſicke that may not be heard, too't againe. But (as they ſay) to heare Muſicke, the Generall do's not greatly care.

sp.speaker: Muſ.
sp.p: We haue none ſuch, ſir.

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: Then put vp your Pipes in your bagge, for Ile away. Go, vaniſh into ayre, away.

sp.speaker: Caſſio
sp.p: Doſt thou heare me, mine honeſt Friend?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.l: No, I heare not your honeſt Friend:
I heare you.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: Prythee keepe vp thy Quillets, ther's a poore peece of Gold for thee: if the Gentlewoman that attends the Generall be ſtirring, tell her, there's one Caſſio entreats her a little fauour of Speech. Wilt thou do this?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: She is ſtirring ſir: if ſhe will ſtirre hither, I ſhall ſeeme to notifie vnto her.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: You haue not bin a-bed then?

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: Why no: the day had broke before we parted.
I haue made bold (Iago) to ſend in to your wife:
My ſuite to her is, that ſhe will to vertuous Deſdemona
Procure me ſome acceſſe.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Ile ſend her to you preſently:
And Ile deuiſe a meane to draw the Moore
Out of the way, that your conuerſe and buſineſſe
May be more free.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: I humbly thanke you for't. I neuer knew
A Flo • ntine more kinde, and honeſt.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Goodmorrow (good Lieutenant) I am ſorrie
For your diſpleaſure: but all will ſure be well.
The Generall and his wife are talking of it,
And ſhe ſpeakes for you ſtoutly. The Moore replies,
That he you hurt is of great Fame in Cyprus,
And great Affinitie: and that in wholſome Wiſedome
He might not but refuſe you. But he proteſts he loues you
And needs no other Suitor, but his likings
To bring you in againe.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: Yet I beſeech you,
If you thinke fit, or that it may be done,
Giue me aduantage of ſome breefe Diſcourſe
With Deſdemon alone.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Pray you come in:
I will beſtow you where you ſhall haue time
To ſpeake your boſome freely.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: I am much bound to you.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: Theſe Letters giue (Iago) to the Pylot,
And by him do my duties to the Senate:
That done, I will be walking on the Workes,
Repaire there to mee.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Well, my good Lord, Ile doo't.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: This Fortification (Gentlemen) ſhall we ſee't?

sp.speaker: Gent.
sp.p: Well waite vpon your Lordſhip.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Be thou aſſur'd (good Caſſio) I will do
All my abilities in thy behalfe.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Good Madam do:
I warrant it greeues my Husband,
As if the cauſe were his.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Oh that's an honeſt Fellow, Do not doubt Caſſio
But I will haue my Lord, and you againe
As friendly as you were.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: Bounteous Madam,
What euer ſhall become of Michael Caſſio,
He's neuer any thing but your true Seruant.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: I know't: I thanke you: you do loue my Lord:
You haue knowne him long, and be you well aſſur'd
He ſhall in ſtrangeneſſe ſtand no farther off,
Then in a politique diſtance.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: I, but Lady,
That policie may either laſt ſo long,
Or feede vpon ſuch nice and wateriſh diet,
Or breede it ſelfe ſo out of Circumſtances,
That I being abſent, and my place ſupply'd,
My Generall will forget my Loue, and Seruice.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Do not doubt • hat: before Aemilia here,
I giue thee warrant of thy place. Aſſure thee,
If I do vow a friendſhip, Ile performe it
To the laſt Article. My Lord ſhall neuer reſt,
Ile watch him tame, and talke him out of patience;
His Bed ſhall ſeeme a Schoole, his Boord a Shrift,
Ile intermingle euery thing he do's
With Caſſio's ſuite: Therefore be merry Caſſio,
For thy Solicitor ſhall rather dye,
Then giue thy cauſe away.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Madam, heere comes my Lord.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: Madam, Ile take my leaue.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Why ſtay, and heare me ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: Madam, not now: I am very ill at eaſe,
Vnfit for mine owne purpoſes.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Well, do your diſcretion.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Hah? I like not that,

sp.speaker: Othel.
sp.p: What doſt thou ſay?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Nothing my Lord; or if—I know not what.

sp.speaker: Othel.
sp.p: Was not that Caſſio parted from my wife?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Caſſio my Lord? No ſure, I cannot thinke it
That he would ſteale away ſo guilty-like,
Seeing your comming.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I do beleeue 'twas he.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: How now my Lord?
I haue bin talking with a Suitor heere,
A man that languiſhes in your diſpleaſure.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Who is't you meane?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Why your Lieutenant Caſſio: Good my Lord,
If I haue any grace, or power to moue you,
His preſent reconciliation take.
For if he be not one, that truly loues you,
That erres in Ignorance, and not in Cunning,
I haue no iudgement in an honeſt face.
I prythee call him backe.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Went he hence now?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: I ſooth; ſo humbled,
That he hath left part of his greefe with mee
To ſuffer with him. Good Loue, call him backe.

sp.speaker: Othel.
sp.p: Not now (ſweet Deſdemon) ſome other time.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: But ſhall't be ſhortly?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: The ſooner (Sweet) for you.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Shall't be to night, at Supper?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: No, not to night.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: To morrow Dinner then?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I ſhall not dine at home:
I meete the Captaines at the Cittadell.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Why then to morrow night, on Tueſday morne,
On Tueſday noone, or night; on Wenſday Morne.
I prythee name the time, but let it not
Exceed three dayes. Infaith hee's penitent:
And yet his Treſpaſſe, in our common reaſon
(Saue that they ſay the warres muſt make example)
Out of her beſt, is not almoſt a fault
T' encurre a priuate checke. When ſhall he come?
Tell me Othello. I wonder in my Soule
What you would aske me, that I ſhould deny.
Or ſtand ſo mam'ring on? What? Michael Caſſio,
That came a woing wirh you? and ſo many a time
(When I haue ſpoke of you diſpraiſingly)
Hath tane your part, to haue ſo much to do
To bring him in? Truſt me, I could do much.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Prythee no more: Let him come when he will:
I will deny thee nothing.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Why, this is not a Boone:
'Tis as I ſhould entreate you weare your Gloues,
Or feede on nouriſhing diſhes, or keepe you warme,
Or ſue to you, to do a peculiar profit
To your owne perſon. Nay, when I haue a ſuite
Wherein I meane to touch your Loue indeed,
It ſhall be full of poize, and difficult waight,
And fearefull to be granted.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I will deny thee nothing.
Whereon, I do beſeech thee, grant me this,
To leaue me but a little to my ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Shall I deny you? No: farewell my Lord.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Farewell my Deſdemona, Ile come to thee ſtrait.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Aemilia come; be as your Fancies teach you:
What ere you be, I am obedient.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Excellent wretch: Perdition catch my Soule
But I do loue thee: and when I loue thee not,
Chaos is come againe.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: My Noble Lord.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: What doſt thou ſay, Iago?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Did Michael Caſſio
When he woo'd my Lady, know of your loue?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: He did, from firſt to laſt:
Why doſt thou aske?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: But for a ſatisfaction of my Thought,
No further harme.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Why of thy thought, Iago?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I did not thinke he had bin acquainted with hir.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: O yes, and went betweene vs very oft.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Indeed?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Indeed? I indeed. Diſcern'ſt thou ought in that?
Is he not honeſt?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Honeſt, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Honeſt? I, Honeſt.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: My Lord, for ought I know.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: What do'ſt thou thinke?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Thinke, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Thinke, my Lord? Alas, thou ecchos't me;
As if there were ſome Monſter in thy thought
Too hideous to be ſhewne. Thou doſt mean ſomthing:
I heard thee ſay euen now, thou lik'ſt not that,
When Caſsio left my wife. What didd'ſt not like?
And when I told thee, he was of my Counſaile,
Of my whole courſe of wooing; thou cried'ſt, Indeede?
And didd'ſt contract, and purſe thy brow together,
As if thou then hadd'ſt ſhut vp in thy Braine
Some horrible Conceite. If thou do'ſt loue me,
Shew me thy thought.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: My Lord, you know I loue you.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I thinke thou do'ſt:
And for I know thou'rt full of Loue, and Honeſtie,
And weigh'ſt thy words before thou giu'ſt them breath,
Therefore theſe ſtops of thine, fright me the more:
For ſuch things in a falſe diſloyall Knaue
Are trickes of Cuſtome: but in a man that's iuſt,
They're cloſe dilations, working from the heart,
That Paſſion cannot rule.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: For Michael Caſsio,
I dare be ſworne, I thinke that he is honeſt.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I thinke ſo too.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Men ſhould be what they ſeeme,
Or thoſe that be not, would they might ſeeme none.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Certaine, men ſhould be what they ſeeme.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Why then I thinke Caſsio's an honeſt man.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Nay, yet there's more in this?
I prythee ſpeake to me, as to thy thinkings,
As thou doſt ruminate, and giue thy worſt of thoughts
The worſt of words.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Good my Lord pardon me,
Though I am bound to euery Acte of dutie,
I am not bound to that: All Slaues are free:
Vtter my Thoughts? Why ſay, they are vild, and falce?
As where's that Palace, whereinto foule things
Sometimes intrude not? Who ha's that breaſt ſo pure,
Wherein vncleanly Apprehenſions
Keepe Leetes, and Law-dayes, and in Seſſions ſit
With meditations lawfull?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Thou do'ſt conſpire againſt thy Friend (Iago)
If thou but think'ſt him wrong'd, and mak'ſt his eare
A ſtranger to thy Thoughts.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: I do beſeech you,
Though I perchance am vicious in my gueſſe
(As I confeſſe it is my Natures plague
To ſpy into Abuſes, and of my iealouſie
Shapes faults that are not) that your wiſedome
From one, that ſo imperfectly conceits,
Would take no notice, nor build your ſelfe a trouble
Out of his ſcattering, and vnſure obſeruance:
It were not for your quiet, nor your good,
Nor for my Manhood, Honeſty, and Wiſedome,
To let you know my thoughts.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: What doſt thou meane?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Good name in Man, & woman (deere my Lord)
Is the immediate Iewell of their Soules;
Who ſteales my purſe, ſteales traſh:
'Tis ſomething, nothing;
'Twas mine, 'tis his, and has bin ſlaue to thouſands:
But he that filches from me my good Name,
Robs me of that, which not enriches him,
And makes me poore indeed.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Ile know thy Thoughts.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: You cannot, if my heart were in your hand,
Nor ſhall not, whil'ſt 'tis in my cuſtodie.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Ha?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Oh, beware my Lord, of iealouſie,
It is the greene-ey'd Monſter, which doth mocke
The meate it feeds on. That Cuckold liues in bliſſe,
Who certaine of his Fate, loues not his wronger:
But oh, what damned minutes • els he ore,
Who dotes, yet doubts: Suſpects, yet ſoundly loues?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: O miſerie.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Poore, and Content, is rich, and rich enough,
But Riches fineleſſe, is as poore as Winter,
To him that euer feares he ſhall be poore:
Good Heauen, the Soules of all my Tribe defend
From Iealouſie.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Why? why is this?
Think'ſt thou, I'ld make a Life of Iealouſie;
To follow ſtill the changes of the Moone
With freſh ſuſpitions? No: to be once in doubt,
Is to be reſolu'd: Exchange me for a Goat,
When I ſhall turne the buſineſſe of my Soule
To ſuch exufflicate, and blow'd Surmiſes,
Matching thy inference. Tis not to make me Iealious,
To ſay my wife is faire, feeds well, loues company,
Is free of Speech, Sings, Playes, and Dances:
Where Vertue is, theſe are more vertuous.
Nor from mine owne weake merites, will I draw
The ſmalleſt feare, or doubt of her reuolt,
For ſhe had eyes, and choſe me. No Iago,
Ile ſee before I doubt; when I doubt, proue;
And on the proofe, there is no more but this,
Away at once with Loue, or Iealouſie.

sp.speaker: Ia.
sp.l: I am glad of this: For now I ſhall haue reaſon
To ſhew the Loue and Duty that I beare you
With franker ſpirit. Therefore (as I am bound)
Receiue it from me. I ſpeake not yet of proofe:
Looke to your wife, obſerue her well with Caſsio,
Weare your eyes, thus: not Iealious, nor Secure:
I would not haue your free, and Noble Nature,
Out of ſelfe-Bounty, be abus'd: Looke too't:
I know our Country diſpoſition well:
In Venice, they do let Heauen ſee the prankes
They dare not ſhew their Husbands.
Their beſt Conſcience,
Is not to leaue't vndone, but kept vnknowne.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Doſt thou ſay ſo?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: She did deceiue her Father, marrying you,
And when ſhe ſeem'd to ſhake, and feare your lookes,
She lou'd them moſt.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: And ſo ſhe did.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Why go too then:
Shee that ſo young could giue out ſuch a Seeming
To ſeele her Fathers eyes vp, cloſe as Oake,
He thought 'twas Witchcraft.
But I am much too blame:
I humbly do beſeech you of your pardon
For too much louing you.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I am bound to thee for euer.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I ſee this hath a little daſh'd your Spirits:

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Not a iot, not a iot.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Truſt me, I feare it has:
I hope you will conſider what is ſpoke
Comes from your Loue.
But I do ſee y'are moou'd:
I am to pray you, not to ſtraine my ſpeech
To groſſer iſſues, nor to larger reach,
Then to Suſpition.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I will not.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Should you do ſo (my Lord)
My ſpeech ſhould fall into ſuch vilde ſucceſſe,
Which my Thoughts aym'd not.
Caſſio's my worthy Friend:
My Lord, I ſee y'are mou'd.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: No, not much mou'd:
I do not thinke but Deſdemona's honeſt.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Long liue ſhe ſo;
And long liue you to thinke ſo.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: And yet how Nature erring from it ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: I, there's the point:
As (to be bold with you)
Not to affect many propoſed Matches
Of her owne Clime, Complexion, and Degree,
Whereto we ſee in all things, Nature tends:
Foh, one may ſmel in ſuch, a will moſt ranke,
Foule diſproportions, Thoughts vnnaturall.
But (pardon me) I do not in poſition
Diſtinctly ſpeake of her, though I may feare
Her will, recoyling to her better iudgement,
May fal to match you with her Country formes,
And happily repent.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Farewell, farewell:
If more thou doſt perceiue, let me know more:
Set on thy wife to obſerue.
Leaue me Iago.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: My Lord, I take my leaue.

sp.speaker: Othel.
sp.l: Why did I marry?
This honeſt Creature (doubtleſſe)
Sees, and knowes more, much more then he vnfolds.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: My Lord, I would I might intreat your Honor
To ſcan this thing no farther: Leaue it to time,
Although 'tis fit that Caſſio haue his Place;
For ſure he filles it vp with great Ability;
Yet if you pleaſe, to him off a-while:
You ſhall by that perceiue him, and his meanes:
Note if your Lady ſtraine his Entertainment
With any ſtrong, or vehement importunitie,
Much will be ſeene in that: In the meane time,
Let me be thought too buſie in my feares,
(As worthy cauſe I haue to feare I am)
And hold her free, I do beſeech your Honor.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Feare not my gouernment.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I once more take my leaue.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: This Fellow's of exceeding honeſty,
And knowes all Quantities with a learn'd Spirit
Of humane dealings. If I do proue her Haggard,
Though that her leſſes were my deere heart-ſtrings,
I'ld whiſtle her off, and let her downe the winde
To prey at Fortune. Haply, for I am blacke,
And haue not thoſe ſoft parts of Conuerſation
That Chamberers haue: Or for I am declin'd
Into the vale of yeares (yet that's not much)
Shee's gone. I am abus'd, and my releefe
Muſt be to loath her. Oh Curſe of Marriage!
That we can call theſe delicate Creatures ours,
And not their Appetites? I had rather be a Toad,
And liue vpon the vapour of a Dungeon,
Then keepe a corner in the thing I loue
For others vſes. Yet 'tis the plague to Great-ones,
Prerogatiu'd are they leſſe then the Baſe,
'Tis deſtiny vnſhunnable, like death:
Euen then, this forked plague is Fated to vs,
When we do quicken. Looke where ſhe comes:
If ſhe be falſe, Heauen mock'd it ſelfe:
Ile not beleeue't.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: How now, my deere Othello?
Your dinner, and the generous Iſlanders
By you inuited, do attend your preſence.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I am too blame.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Why do you ſpeake ſo faintly?
Are you not well?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I haue a paine vpon my Forehead, heere.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Why that's with watching, 'twill away againe.
Let me but binde it hard, within this houre
It will be well.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Your Napkin is too little:
Let it alone: Come, Ile go in with you.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I am very ſorry that you are not well.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: I am glad I haue found this Napkin:
This was her firſt remembrance from the Moore,
My wayward Husband hath a hundred times
Woo'd me to ſteale it. But ſhe ſo loues the Token,
(For he coniur'd her, ſhe ſhould euer keepe it)
That ſhe reſerues it euermore about her,
To kiſſe, and talke too. Ile haue the worke tane out,
And giu't Iago: what he will do with it
Heauen knowes, not I:
I nothing, but to pleaſe his Fantaſie.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: How now? What do you heere alone?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Do not you chide: I haue a thing for you.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: You haue a thing for me?
It is a common thing —

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Hah?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: To haue a fooliſh wife.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Oh, is that all? What will you giue me now
For that ſame Handkerchiefe.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: What Handkerchiefe?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: What Handkerchiefe?
Why that the Moore firſt gaue to Deſdemona,
That which ſo often you did bid me ſteale.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Haſt ſtolne it from her?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: No: but ſhe let it drop by negligence,
And to th' aduantage, I being heere, took't vp:
Looke, heere 'tis.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: A good wench, giue it me.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: What will you do with't, that you haue bene ſo earneſt to haue me filch it?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Why, what is that to you?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: If it be not for ſome purpoſe of import,
Giu't me againe. Poore Lady, ſhee'l run mad
When ſhe ſhall lacke it.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Be not acknowne on't:
I haue vſe for it. Go, leaue me.
I will in Caſſio's Lodging looſe this Napkin,
And let him finde it. Trifles light as ayre,
Are to the iealious, confirmations ſtrong,
As proofes of holy Writ. This may do ſomething.
The Moore already changes with my poyſon:
Dangerous conceites, are in their Natures poyſons,
Which at the firſt are ſcarſe found to diſtaſte:
But with a little acte vpon the blood,
Burne like the Mines of Sulphure. I did ſay ſo.
Looke where he comes: Not Poppy, nor Mandragora,
Nor all the drowſie Syrrups of the world
Shall euer medicine thee to that ſweete ſleepe
Which thou owd'ſt yeſterday.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Ha, Ha, falſe to mee?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Why how now Generall? No more of that.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Auant, be gone: Thou haſt ſet me on the Racke:
I ſweare 'tis better to be much abus'd,
Then but to know't a little.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: How now, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: What ſenſe had I, in her ſtolne houres of Luſt?
I ſaw't not, thought it not: it harm'd not me:
I ſlept the next night well, fed well, was free, and merrie.
I found not Caſſio's kiſſes on her Lippes:
He that is robb'd, not wanting what is ſtolne,
Let him not know't, and he's not robb'd at all.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I am ſorry to heare this?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I had beene happy, if the generall Campe,
Pyoners and all, had taſted her ſweet Body,
So I had nothing knowne. Oh now, for euer
Farewell the Tranquill minde; farewell Content;
Farewell the plumed Troopes, and the bigge Warres,
That makes Ambition, Vertue! Oh farewell;
Farewell the neighing Steed, and the ſhrill Trumpe,
The Spirit-ſtirring Drum, th' Eare-piercing Fife,
The Royall Banner, and all Qualitie,
Pride, Pompe, and Circumſtance of glorious Warre:
And O you mortall Engines, whoſe rude throates
Th' immortall Ioues dread Clamours, counterfet,
Farewell: Othello's Occupation's gone.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Is't poſſible my Lord?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Villaine, be ſure thou proue my Loue a Whore;
Be ſure of it: Giue me the Occular proofe,
Or by the worth of mine eternall Soule,
Thou had'ſt bin better haue bin borne a Dog
Then anſwer my wak'd wrath.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Is't come to this?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Make me to ſee't: or (at the leaſt) ſo proue it,
That the probation beare no Hindge, nor Loope,
To hang a doubt on: Or woe vpon thy life.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: My Noble Lord.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: If thou doſt ſlander her, and torture me,
Neuer pray more: Abandon all remorſe
On Horrors head, Horrors accumulate:
Do deeds to make Heauen weepe, all Earth amaz'd;
For nothing canſt thou to damnation adde,
Greater then that.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: O Grace! O Heauen forgiue me!
Are you a Man? Haue you a Soule? or Senſe?
God buy you: take mine Office. Oh wretched Foole,
That lou'ſt to make thine Honeſty, a Vice!
Oh monſtrous world! Take note, take note (O World)
To be direct and honeſt, is not ſafe.
I thanke you for this profit, and from hence
Ile loue no Friend, ſith Loue breeds ſuch offence.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Nay ſtay: thou ſhould'ſt be honeſt.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: I ſhould be wiſe; for Honeſtie's a Foole,
And looſes that it workes for.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: By the World,
I thinke my Wife be honeſt, and thinke ſhe is not:
I thinke that thou art iuſt, and thinke thou art not:
Ile haue ſome proofe. My name that was as freſh
As Dians Viſage, is now begrim'd and blacke
As mine owne face. If there be Cords, or Kniues,
Poyſon, or Fire, or ſuffocating ſtreames,
Ile not indure it. Would I were ſatisfied.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: I ſee you are eaten vp with Paſſion:
I do repent me, that I put it to you.
You would be ſatisfied?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Would? Nay, and I will.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: And may: but how? How ſatisfied, my Lord?
Would you the ſuper-viſion groſſely gape on?
Behold her top'd?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Death, and damnation. Oh!

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: It were a tedious difficulty, I thinke,
To bring them to that Proſpect: Damne them then,
If euer mortall eyes do ſee them boulſter
More then their owne. What then? How then?
What ſhall I ſay? Where's Satisfaction?
It is impoſſible you ſhould ſee this,
Were they as prime as Goates, as hot as Monkeyes,
As ſalt as Wolues in pride, and Fooles as groſſe
As Ignorance, made drunke. But yet, I ſay,
If imputation, and ſtrong circumſtances,
Which leade directly to the doore of Truth,
Will giue you ſatisfaction, you might haue't.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Giue me a liuing reaſon ſhe's diſloyall.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: I do not like the Office.
But ſith I am entred in this cauſe ſo farre
(Prick'd too't by fooliſh Honeſty, and Loue)
I will go on. I lay with Caſſio lately,
And being troubled with a raging tooth,
I could not ſleepe. There are a kinde of men,
So looſe of Soule, that in their ſleepes will mutter
Their Affayres: one of this kinde is Caſſio:
In ſleepe I heard him ſay, ſweet Deſdemona,
Let vs be wary, let vs hide our Loues,
And then (Sir) would he gripe, and wring my hand:
Cry, oh ſweet Creature: then kiſſe me hard,
As if he pluckt vp kiſſes by the rootes,
That grew vpon my lippes, laid his Leg ore my Thigh,
And ſigh, and kiſſe, and then cry curſed Fate,
That gaue thee to the Moore.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: O monſtrous! monſtrous!

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Nay, this was but his Dreame.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: But this denoted a fore-gone concluſion,
'Tis a ſhrew'd doubt, though it be but a Dreame.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: And this may helpe to thicken other proofes,
That do demonſtrate thinly.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Ile teare her all to peeces.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Nay yet be wiſe; yet we ſee nothing done,
She may be honeſt yet: Tell me but this,
Haue you not ſometimes ſeene a Handkerchiefe
Spotted with Strawberries, in your wiues hand?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I gaue her ſuch a one: 'twas my firſt gift.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: I know not that: but ſuch a Handkerchiefe
(I am ſure it was your wiues) did I to day
See Caſſio wipe his Beard with.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: If it be that.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: If it be that, or any, it was hers.
It ſpeakes againſt her with the other proofes.

sp.speaker: Othel.
sp.l: O that the Slaue had forty thouſand liues:
One is too poore, too weake for my reuenge.
Now do I ſee 'tis true. Looke heere Iago,
All my fond loue thus do I blow to Heauen. 'Tis gone,
Ariſe blacke vengeance, from the hollow hell,
Yeeld vp (O Loue) thy Crowne, and hearted Throne
To tyrannous Hate. Swell boſome with thy fraught,
For 'tis of Aſpickes tongues.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Yet be content.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Oh blood, blood, blood.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Patience I ſay: your minde may change.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Neuer Iago. Like to the Ponticke Sea,
Whoſe Icie Current, and compulſiue courſe,
Neu'r keepes retyring ebbe, but keepes due on
To the Proponticke, and the Helleſpont:
Euen ſo my bloody thoughts, with violent pace
Shall neu'r looke backe, neu'r ebbe to humble Loue,
Till that a capeable, and wide Reuenge
Swallow them vp. Now by yond Marble Heauen,
In the due reuerence of a Sacred vow,
I heere engage my words.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Do not riſe yet:
Witneſſe you euer-burning Lights aboue,
You Elements, that clip vs round about,
Witneſſe that heere Iago doth giue vp
The execution of his wit, hands, heart,
To wrong'd Othello's Seruice. Let him command,
And to obey ſhall be in me remorſe,
What bloody buſineſſe euer.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I greet thy loue,
Not with vaine thanks, but with acceptance bounteous,
And will vpon the inſtant put thee too't.
Within theſe three dayes let me heare thee ſay,
That Caſſio's not aliue.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: My Friend is dead:
'Tis done at your Requeſt.
But let her liue.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Damne her lewde Minx:
O damne her, damne her.
Come go with me a-part, I will withdraw
To furniſh me with ſome ſwift meanes of death
For the faire Diuell.
Now art thou my Lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I am your owne for euer.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Do you know Sirrah, where Lieutenant Caſſio lyes?

sp.speaker: Clow.
sp.p: I dare not ſay he lies any where.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Why man?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: He's a Soldier, and for me to ſay a Souldier lyes, 'tis ſtabbing.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Go too: where lodges he?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: To tell you where he lodges, is to tel you where I lye.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Can any thing be made of this?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I know not where he lodges, and for mee to deuiſe a lodging, and ſay he lies heere, or he lies there, were to lye in mine owne throat.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Can you enquire him out? and be edified by report?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I will Catechize the world for him, that is, make Queſtions, and by them anſwer.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Seeke him, bidde him come hither: tell him, I haue moou'd my Lord on his behalfe, and hope all will be well.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: To do this, is within the compaſſe of mans Wit, and therefore I will attempt the doing it.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Where ſhould I looſe the Handkerchiefe, Aemilia?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: I know not Madam.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Beleeue me, I had rather haue loſt my purſe
Full of Cruzadoes. And but my Noble Moore
Is true of minde, and made of no ſuch baſeneſſe,
As iealious Creatures are, it were enough
To put him to ill-thinking.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Is he not iealious?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Who, he? I thinke the Sun where he was borne,
Drew all ſuch humors from him.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Looke where he comes.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: I will not leaue him now, till Caſſio be
Call'd to him. How is't with you, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Well my good Lady. Oh hardnes to diſſemble!
How do you, Deſdemona?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Well, my good Lord.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Giue me your hand.
This hand is moiſt my Lady.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: It hath felt no age, nor knowne no ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: This argues fruitfulneſſe, and liberall heart:
Hot, hot, and moyſt. This hand of yours requires
A ſequeſter from Liberty: Faſting, and Prayer,
Much Caſtigation, Exerciſe deuout,
For heere's a yong, and ſweating Diuell heere
That commonly rebels: 'Tis a good hand,
A franke one.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: You may (indeed) ſay ſo:
For 'twas that hand that gaue away my heart.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: A liberall hand. The hearts of old, gaue hands:
But our new Heraldry is hands, not hearts.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: I cannot ſpeake of this:
Come, now your promiſe.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: What promiſe, Chucke?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I haue ſent to bid Caſſio come ſpeake with you.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I haue a ſalt and ſorry Rhewme offends me:
Lend me thy Handkerchiefe.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Heere my Lord.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: That which I gaue you.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I haue it not about me.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Not?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: No indeed, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: That's a fault: That Handkerchiefe
Did an Aegyptian to my Mother giue:
She was a Charmer, and could almoſt read
The thoughts of people. She told her, while ſhe kept it,
'T would make her Amiable, and ſubdue my Father
Intirely to her loue: But if ſhe loſt it,
Or made a Guift of it, my Fathers eye
Should hold her loathed, and his Spirits ſhould hunt
After new Fancies. She dying, gaue it me,
And bid me (when my Fate would haue me W • u'd)
To giue it her. I did to; and take heede on't,
Make it a Darling, like your precious eye:
To looſe't, or giue't away, were ſuch perdition,
As nothing elſe could match.

sp.speaker: Deſ,
sp.p: Is't poſſible?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: 'Tis true: There's Magicke in the web of it:
A Sybill that had numbred in the world
The Sun to courſe, two hundred compaſſes,
In her Prophetticke furie ſow'd the Worke:
The Wormes were hallowed, that did breede the Silke,
And it was dyde in Mummey, which the Skilfull
Conſeru'd of Maidens hearts.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Indeed? Is't true?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Moſt veritable, therefore looke too't well.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Then would to Heauen, that I had neuer ſeene't?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Ha? wherefore?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Why do you ſpeake ſo ſtartingly and raſh?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Is't loſt? Is't gon? Speak, is't out o' th' way?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Bleſſe vs.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Say you?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: It is not loſt: but what and if it were?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: How?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I ſay it is not loſt.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Fetcht, let me ſee't.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Why ſo I can: but I will not now:
This is a tricke to put me from my ſuite,
Pray you let Caſſio be receiu'd againe.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Fetch me the Handkerchiefe,
My minde miſ-giues.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Come, come: you'l neuer meete a more ſufficient man.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: The Handkerchiefe.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: A man that all his time
Hath founded his good Fortunes on your loue;
Shar'd dangers with you.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: The Handkerchiefe.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Inſooth, you are too blame.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Away.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Is not this man iealious?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: I neu'r ſaw this before.
Sure, there's ſome wonder in this Handkerchikfe,
I am moſt vnhappy in the loſſe of it.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: 'Tis not a yeare or two ſhewes vs a man:
They are all but Stomackes, and we all but Food,
They eate vs hungerly, and when they are full
They belch vs.
Looke you, Caſſio and my Husband.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: There is no other way: 'tis ſhe muſt doo't:
And loe the happineſſe: go, and importune her.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: How now (good Caſſio) what's the newes with you?

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: Madam, my former ſuite. I do beſeech you,
That by your vertuous meanes, I may againe
Exiſt, and be a member of his loue,
Whom I, with all the Office of my heart
Intirely honour, I would not be delayd.
If my offence, be of ſuch mortall kinde,
That nor my Seruice paſt, nor preſent Sorrowes,
Nor purpos'd merit in futurity,
Can ranſome me into his loue againe,
But to know ſo, muſt be my benefit:
So ſhall I cloath me in a forc'd content,
And ſhut my ſelfe vp in ſome other courſe
To Fortunes Almes.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Alas (thrice-gentle Caſſio)
My Aduocation is not now in Tune;
My Lord, is not my Lord; nor ſhould I know him,
Were he in Fauour, as in Humour alter'd.
So helpe me euery ſpirit ſanctified,
As I haue ſpoken for you all my beſt,
And ſtood within the blanke of his diſpleaſure
For my free ſpeech. You muſt awhile be patient:
What I can do, I will: and more I will
Then for my ſelfe, I dare. Let that ſuffice you.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Is my Lord angry?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: He went hence but now:
And certainly in ſtrange vnquietneſſe.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Can he be angry? I haue ſeene the Cannon
When it hath blowne his Rankes into the Ayre,
And like the Diuell from his very Arme
Puff't his owne Brother: And is he angry?
Something of moment then: I will go meet him,
There's matter in't indeed, if he be angry.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: I prythee do ſo. Something ſure of State,
Either from Venice, or ſome vnhatch'd practiſe
Made demonſtrable heere in Cyprus, to him,
Hath pudled his cleare Spirit: and in ſuch caſes,
Mens Natures wrangle with inferiour things,
Though great ones are their obiect. 'Tis euen ſo.
For let our finger ake, and it endues
Our other healthfull members, euen to a ſenſe
Of paine. Nay, we muſt thinke men are not Gods,
Nor of them looke for ſuch obſeruancie
As fits the Bridall. Beſhrew me much, Aemilia,
I was (vnhandſome Warrior, as I am)
Arraigning his vnkindneſſe with my ſoule:
But now I finde, I had ſuborn'd the Witneſſe,
And he's Indited falſely.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Pray heauen it bee
State matters, as you thinke, and no Conception,
Nor no Iealious Toy, concerning you.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Alas the day, I neuer gaue him cauſe.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: But Iealious ſoules will not be anſwer'd ſo;
They are not euer iealious for the cauſe,
But iealious, for they're iealious. It is a Monſter
Begot vpon it ſelfe, borne on it ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Heauen keepe the Monſter from Othello's mind.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Lady, Amen.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: I will go ſeeke him. Caſſio, walke heere about:
If I doe finde him fit, Ile moue your ſuite,
And ſeeke to effect it to my vttermoſt.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: I humbly thanke your Ladyſhip.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: 'Saue you (Friend Caſſio.)

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: What make you from home?
How is't with you, my moſt faire Bianca?
Indeed (ſweet Loue) I was comming to your houſe.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: And I was going to your Lodging, Caſſio.
What? keepe a weeke away? Seuen dayes, and Nights?
Eight ſcore eight houres? And Louers abſent howres
More tedious then the Diall, eight ſcore times?
Oh weary reck'ning.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: Pardon me, Bianca:
I haue this while with leaden thoughts beene preſt,
But I ſhall in a more continuate time
Strike off this ſcore of abſence. Sweet Bianca
Take me this worke out.

sp.speaker: Bianca.
sp.l: Oh Caſſio, whence came this?
This is ſome Token from a newer Friend,
To the felt-Abſence: now I feele a Cauſe:
Is't come to this? Well, well.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: Go too, woman:
Throw your vilde geſſes in the Diuels teeth,
From whence you haue them. You are iealious now,
That this is from ſome Miſtris, ſome remembrance;
No, in good troth Bianca.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Why, who's is it?

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: I know not neither:
I found it in my Chamber,
I like the worke well; Ere it be demanded
(As like enough it will) I would haue it coppied:
Take it, and doo't, and leaue me for this time.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Leaue you? Wherefore?

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: I do attend heere on the Generall,
And thinke it no addition nor my wiſh
To haue him ſee me woman'd.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Why, I ptay you?

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: Not that I loue you not.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: But that you do not loue me.
I pray you bring me on the way a little,
And ſay, if I ſhall ſee you ſoone at night?

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: 'Tis but a little way that I can bring you,
For I attend heere: But Ile ſee you ſoone.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: 'Tis very good: I muſt be circumſtanc'd.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Will you thinke ſo?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Thinke ſo, Iago?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: What, to kiſſe in priuate?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: An vnauthoriz'd kiſſe?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Or to be naked with her Friend in bed,
An houre, or more, not meaning any harme?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Naked in bed (Iago) and not meane harme?
It is hypocriſie againſt the Diuell:
They that meane vertuouſly, and yet do ſo,
The Diuell their vertue tempts, and they tempt Heauen.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: If they do nothing, 'tis a Veniall ſlip:
But if I giue my wife a Handkerchiefe.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: What then?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Why then 'tis hers (my Lord) and being hers,
She may (I thinke) beſtow't on any man.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: She is Protectreſſe of her honor too:
May ſhe giue that?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Her honor is an Eſſence that's not ſeene,
They haue it very oft, that haue it not.
But for the Handkerchiefe.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: By heauen, I would moſt gladly haue forgot it:
Thou ſaidſt (oh, it comes ore my memorie,
As doth the Rauen o're the infectious houſe:
Boading to all) he had my Handkerchiefe.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I: what of that?

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: That's not ſo good now.

sp.speaker: Iag.
sp.l: What if I had ſaid, I had ſeene him do you wrong?
Or heard him ſay (as Knaues be ſuch abroad,
Who hauing by their owne importunate ſuit,
Or voluntary dotage of ſome Miſtris,
Conuinced or ſupply'd them cannot chuſe
But they muſt blab.)

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Hath he ſaid any thing?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: He hath (my Lord) but be you well aſſur'd,
No more then he'le vn-ſweare.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: What hath he ſaid?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Why, that he did: I know not what he did.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: What? What?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Lye.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: With her?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: With her? On her: what you will.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Lye with her? lye on her? We ſay lye on her, when they be-lye-her. Lye with her: that's fullſome: Handkerchiefe: Confeſſions: Handkerchiefe. To confeſſe, and be hang'd for his labour. Firſt, to be hang'd, and then to confeſſe: I tremble at it. Nature would not inueſt her ſelfe in ſuch ſhadowing paſſion, without ſome Inſtruction. It is not words that ſhakes me thus, (piſh) Noſes, Eares, and Lippes: is't poſſible. Confeſſe? Handkerchiefe? O diuell.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Worke on,
My Medicine workes. Thus credulous Fooles are caught,
And many worthy, and chaſt Dames euen thus,
(All guiltleſſe) meete reproach: what hoa? My Lord?
My Lord, I ſay: Othello.
How now Caſſio?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: My Lord is falne into an Epilepſie,
This is his ſecond Fit: he had one yeſterday.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Rub him about the Temples.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: The Lethargie muſt haue his quyet courſe:
If not, he foames at mouth: and by and by
Breakes out to ſauage madneſſe. Looke, he ſtirres:
Do you withdraw your ſelfe a little while,
He will recouer ſtraight: when he is gone,
I would on great occaſion, ſpeake with you.
How is it Generall? Haue you not hurt your head?

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Doſt thou mocke me?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: I mocke you not, by Heauen:
Would you would beare your Fortune like a Man.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: A Horned man's a Monſter, and a Beaſt.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Ther's many a Beaſt then in a populous Citty,
And many a ciuill Monſter.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Did he confeſſe it?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Good Sir, be a man:
Thinke euery bearded fellow that's but yoak'd
May draw with you. There's Millions now aliue,
That nightly lye in thoſe vnproper beds,
Which they dare ſweare peculiar. Your caſe is better.
Oh, 'tis the ſpight of hell, the Fiends Arch-mock,
To lip a wanton in a ſecure Cowch;
And to ſuppoſe her chaſt. No, let me know,
And knowing what I am, I know what ſhe ſhall be.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Oh, thou art wiſe: 'tis certaine.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Stand you a while apart,
Confine your ſelfe but in a patient Liſ • ,
Whil'ſt you were heere, o're-whelmed with your griefe
(A paſſion moſt reſulting ſuch a man)
Caſſio came hither. I ſhifted him away,
And layd good ſcuſes vpon your Extaſie,
Bad him anon returne: and heere ſpeake with me,
The which he promis'd. Do but encaue your ſelfe,
And marke the Fleeres, the Gybes, and notable Scornes
That dwell in euery Region of his face.
For I will make him tell the Tale anew;
Where, how, how oft, how long ago, and when
He hath, and is againe to cope your wife.
I ſay, but marke his geſture: marry Patience,
Or I ſhall ſay y' are all in all in Spleene,
And nothing of a man.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: Do'ſt thou heare, Iago,
I will be found moſt cunning in my Patience:
But (do'ſt thou heare) moſt bloody.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: That's not amiſſe,
But yet keepe time in all: will you withdraw?
Now will I queſtion Caſſio of Bianca,
A Huſwife, that by ſelling her deſires
Buyes her ſelfe Bread, and Cloath. It is a Creature
That dotes on Caſſio, (as 'tis the Strumpets plague
To be-guile many, and be be-guil'd by one)
He, when he heares of her, cannot reſtraine
From the exceſſe of Laughter. Heere he comes.
As he ſhall ſmile, Othells ſhall go mad:
And his vnbookiſh Ielouſie muſt conſerue
Poore Caſſio's ſmiles, geſtures, and light behauiours
Quite in the wrong. How do you Lieutenant?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: The worſer, that you giue me the addition,
Whoſe want euen killes me.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Ply Deſdemona well, and you are ſure on't:
Now, if this Suit lay in Bianca's dowre,
How quickely ſhould you ſpeed?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Alas poore Caitiffe.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Looke how he laughes already.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I neuer knew woman loue man ſo.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Alas poore Rogue, I thinke indeed ſhe loues me.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Now he denies it faintly: and laughes it out.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Do you heare Caſſio?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Now he importunes him
To tell it o're: go too, well ſaid, well ſaid.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: She giues it out, that you ſhall marry her.
Do you intend it?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Do ye triumph, Romaine? do you triumph?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I marry. What? A cuſtomer; prythee beare
Some Charitie to my wit, do not thinke it
So vnwholeſome. Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: So, ſo, ſo, ſo: they laugh, that winnes.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Why the cry goes, that you marry her.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Prythee ſay true.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I am a very Villaine elſe.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Haue you ſcoar'd me? Well.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: This is the Monkeys owne giuing out:
She is perſwaded I will marry her
Out of her owne loue & flattery, not out of my promiſe.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Iago becomes me: now he begins the ſtory.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: She was heere euen now: ſhe haunts me in euery place. I was the other day talking on the Sea-banke with certaine Venetians, and thither comes the Bauble, and falls me thus about my neck.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Crying oh deere Caſſio, as it were: his ieſture imports it.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: So hangs, and lolls, and weepes vpon me:
So ſhakes, and pulls me. Ha, ha, ha.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Now he tells how ſhe pluckt him to my Chamber: oh, I ſee that noſe of yours, but not that dogge, I ſhall throw it to.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: Well, I muſt leaue her companie.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Before me: looke where ſhe comes.

sp.speaker: Caſ
sp.l: 'Tis ſuch another Fitchew: marry a perfum'd one?
What do you meane by this haunting of me?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Let the diuell, and his dam haunt you: what did you meane by that ſame Handkerchiefe, you gaue me euen now? I was a fine Foole to take it: I muſt take out the worke? A likely piece of worke, that you ſhould finde it in your Chamber, and know not who left it there. This is ſome Minxes token, & I muſt take out the work • ? There, giue it your Hobbey-horſe, whereſoeuer you had it, Ile take out no worke on't.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: How now, my ſweete Bianca?
How now? How now?

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: By Heauen, that ſhould be my Handkerchiefe.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: If you'le come to ſupper to night you may, if you will not, come when you are next prepar'd for.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: After her: after her.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: I muſt, ſhee'l rayle in the ſtreets elſe.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Will you ſup there?

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: Yes, I intend ſo.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Well, I may chance to ſee you: for I would very fame ſpeake with you.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Prythee come: will you?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Go too: ſay no more.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: How ſhall I murther him, Iago.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Did you perceiue how he laugh'd at his vice?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Oh, Iago.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: And did you ſee the Handkerchiefe?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Was that mine?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Yours by this hand: and to ſee how he prizes the fooliſh woman your wife: ſhe gaue it him, and he hath giu'n it his whore.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I would haue him nine yeeres a killing:
A fine woman, a faire woman, a ſweete woman?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Nay, you muſt forget that.

sp.speaker: Othello.
sp.p: I, let her • ot and periſh, and be damn'd to night, for ſhe ſhall not liue. No, my heart is turn'd to ſtone: I ſtrike it, and it hurts my hand. Oh, the world hath not a ſweeter Creature: ſhe might lye by an Emperours ſide, and command him Taskes.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Nay, that's not your way.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Hang her, I do but ſay what ſhe is: ſo delicate with her Needle: an admirable Muſitian. Oh ſhe will ſing the Sauageneſſe out of a Beare: of ſo high and plenteous wit, and inuention?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: She's the worſe for all this.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: Oh, a thouſand, a thouſand times:
And the • of ſo gentle a condition?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I too gentle.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: Nay that's certaine:
But yet the pitty of it, Iago: oh Iago, the pitty of it Iago.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: If you are ſo fond ouer her iniquitie: giue her pattent to offend, for if it touch not you, it comes neere no body.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I will chop her into Meſſes: Cuckold me?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Oh, 'tis foule in her.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: With mine Officer?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: That's fouler.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Get me ſome poyſon, Iago, this night. Ile not expoſtulate with her: leaſt her body and beautie vnprouide my mind againe: this night Iago.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Do it not with poyſon, ſtrangle her in her bed,
Euen the bed ſhe hath contaminated.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Good, good:
The Iuſtice of it pleaſes: very good.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: And for Caſſio, let me be his vndertaker:
You ſhall heare more by midnight.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Excellent good: What Trumpet is that ſame?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: I warrant ſomething from Venice,
'Tis Lodouico, this, comes from the Duke.
See, your wife's with him.

sp.speaker: Lodo.
sp.p: Saue you worthy Generall.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: With all my heart Sir.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: The Duke, and the Senators of Venice greet you.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: I kiſſe the Inſtrument of their pleaſures.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: And what's the newes, good cozen Lodouico?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: I am very glad to ſee you Signior:
Welcome to Cyprus.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: I thanke you: how do's Lieutenant Caſſio?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Liues Sir,

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Cozen, there's falne betweene him, & my Lord,
An vnkind breach: but you ſhall make all well.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Are you ſure of that?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: My Lord?

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: This faile you not to do, as you will —

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: He did not call: he's buſie in the paper,
Is there deuiſion 'twixt my Lord, and Caſſio?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: A moſt vnhappy one: I would do much
T' attone them, for the loue I beare to Caſſio.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Fire, and brimeſtone.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Are you wiſe?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: What is he angrie?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: May be th Letter mou'd him.
For as I thinke, they do command him home,
Deputing Caſsio in his Gouernment.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Truſt me, I am glad on't.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Indeed?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: My Lord?

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: I am glad to ſee you mad.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Why, ſweete Othello?

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Diuell.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I haue not deſeru'd this.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: My Lord, this would not be beleeu'd in Venice,
Though I ſhould ſweare I ſaw't. 'Tis very much,
Make her amends: ſhe weepes.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: Oh diuell, diuell:
If that the Earth could teeme with womans teares,
Each drop ſhe falls, would proue a Crocodile:
Out of my ſight.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I will not ſtay to offend you.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Truely obedient Lady:
I do beſeech your Lordſhip call her backe.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: What would you with her, Sir?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: Who I, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: I, you did wiſh, that I would make her turne:
Sir, ſhe can turne, and turne: and yet go on
And turne againe. And ſhe can weepe, Sir, weepe.
And ſhe's obedient: as you ſay obedient.
Very obedient: proceed you in your teares.
Concerning this Sir, (oh well-painted paſſion)
I am commanded home: get you away:
Ile ſend for you anon. Sir I obey the Mandate,
And will returne to Venice. Hence, auaunt:
Caſſio ſhall haue my Place. And Sir, to night
I do entreat, that we may ſup together.
You are welcome Sir to Cyprus.
Goates, and Monkeys.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Is this the Noble Moore, whom our full Senate
Call all in all ſufficient? Is this the Nature
Whom Paſſion could not ſhake? Whoſe ſolid vertue
The ſhot of Accident, nor dart of Chance
Could neither graze, nor pierce?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: He is much chang'd.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: Are his wits ſafe? Is he not light of Braine?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: He's that he is: I may not breath my cenſure.
What he might be: if what he might, he is not,
I would to heauen he were.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: What? Strike his wife?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: 'Faith that was not ſo well: yet would I knew
That ſtroke would proue the worſt.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Is it his vſe?
Or did the Letters, worke vpon his blood,
And new create his fault?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Alas, alas:
It is not honeſtie in me to ſpeake
What I haue ſeene, and knowne. You ſhall obſerue him,
And his owne courſes will deonte him ſo,
That I may ſaue my ſpeech: do but go after
And marke how he continues.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: I am ſorry that I am deceiu'd in him.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: You haue ſeene nothing then?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Nor euer heard: nor euer did ſuſpect.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Yes; you haue ſeene Caſſio, and ſhe together.

sp.speaker: Aemi.
sp.l: But then I ſaw no harme: and then I heard,
Each ſyllable that breath made vp betweene them.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: What? Did they neuer whiſper?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Neuer my Lord.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Nor ſend you out o' th' way?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Neuer.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: To fetch her Fan, her Gloues, her Mask, nor nothing?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Neuer my Lord.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: That's ſtrange.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: I durſt (my Lord) to wager, ſhe is honeſt:
Lay downe my Soule at ſtake: If you thinke other,
Remoue your thought. It doth abuſe your boſome:
If any wretch haue put this in your head,
Let Heauen requit it with the Serpents curſe,
For if ſhe be not honeſt, chaſte, and true,
There's no man happy. The pureſt of their Wiues
Is foule as Slander.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: Bid her come hither: go.
She ſaies enough: yet ſhe's a ſimple Baud
That cannot ſay as much. This is a ſubtile Whore:
A Cloſſet Locke and Key of Villanous Secrets,
And yet ſhe'le kneele, and pray: I haue ſeene her do't.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: My Lord, what is your will?

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Pray you Chucke come hither.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: What is your pleaſure?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Let me ſee your eyes: looke in my face.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: What horrible Fancie's this?

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: Some of your Function Miſtris:
Leaue Procreants alone, and ſhut the doore:
Cough, or cry hem; if any body come:
Your Myſtery, your Myſtery: May diſpatch.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Vpon my knee, what doth your ſpeech import▪
I vnderſtand a Fury in your words.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Why? What art thou?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Your wife my Lord: your true and loyall wife.

sp.speaker: Othello.
sp.p: Come ſweare it: damne thy ſelfe, leaſt being like one of Heauen, the diuells themſelues ſhould feare to ceaze thee. Therefore be double damn'd: ſweare thou art honeſt.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Heauen doth truely know it.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Heauen truely knowes, that thou art falſe as hell.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: To whom my Lord?
With whom? How am I falſe?

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Ah Deſdemon, away, away, away.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Alas the heauy day: why do you weepe?
Am I the motiue of theſe teares my Lord?
If happely you my Father do ſuſpect,
An Inſtrument of this your calling backe,
Lay not your blame on me: if you haue loſt him,
I haue loſt him too.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: Had • t pleas'd Heauen,
To try me with Affliction, had they rain'd
All kind of Sores, and Shames on my bare-head:
Steep'd me in pouertie to the very lippes,
Giuen to Captiuitie, me, and my vtmoſt hopes,
I ſhould haue found in ſome place of my Soule
A drop of patience. But alas, to make me
The fixed Figure for the time of Scorne,
To point his ſlow, and mouing finger at.
Yet could I beare that too, well, very well:
But there where I haue garnerd vp my heart,
Where either I muſt liue, or beare no life,
The Fountaine from the which my currant runnes,
Or elſe dries vp: to be diſcarded thence,
Or keepe it as a Ceſterne, for foule Toades
To knot and gender in. Turne thy complexion there:
Patience, thou young and Roſe-lip'd Cherubin,
I heere looke grim as hell.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I hope my Noble Lord eſteemes me honeſt.

sp.l: Oh I, as Sommer Flyes are in the Shambles,
That quicken euen with blowing. Oh thou weed:
Who art ſo louely faire, and ſmell'ſt ſo ſweete,
That the Senſe akes at thee,
Would thou had'ſt neuer bin borne.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Alas, what ignorant ſin haue I committed?

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: Was this faire Paper? This moſt goodly Booke
Made to write Whore vpon? What commited,
Committed? Oh, thou publicke Commoner,
I ſhould make very Forges of my cheekes,
That would to Cynders burne vp Modeſtie,
Did I but ſpeake thy deedes. What commited?
Heauen ſtoppes the Noſe at it, and the Moone winks:
The baudy winde that kiſſes all it meetes,
Is huſh'd within the hollow Myne of Earth
And will not hear't. What commited?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: By Heauen you do me wrong.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Are not you a Strumpet?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: No, as I am a Chriſtian.
If to preſerue this veſſell for my Lord,
From any other foule vnlawfull touch
Be not to be a Strumpet, I am none.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: What, not a Whore?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: No, as I ſhall be ſau'd.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.p: Is't poſſible?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Oh Heauen forgiue vs.

sp.speaker: Othe.
sp.l: I cry you mercy then.
I tooke you for that cunning Whore of Venice,
That married with Othello. You Miſtris,
That haue the office oppoſite to Saint Peter,
And keepes the gate of hell. You, you: I you.
We haue done our courſe: there's money for your paines:
I pray you turne the key, and keepe our counſaile.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Alas, what do' • this Gentleman conceiue?
How do you Madam? how do you my good Lady?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Faith, halfe a ſleepe.

sp.speaker: Aemi.
sp.l: Good Madam,
What's the matter with my Lord?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: With who?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Why, with my Lord, Madam?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Who is thy Lord?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: He that is yours, ſweet Lady.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: I haue none: do not talke to me, Aemilia,
I cannot weepe: nor anſweres haue I none,
But what ſhould go by water. Prythee to night,
Lay on my bed my wedding ſheetes, remember,
And call thy husband hither.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Heere's a change indeed.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: 'Tis meete I ſhould be vs'd ſo: very meete.
How haue I bin behau'd, that he might ſticke
The ſmall'ſt opinion on my leaſt miſvſe?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: What is your pleaſure Madam?
How is't with you?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: I cannot tell: thoſe that do teach yong Babes
Do it with gentle meanes, and eaſie taskes.
He might haue chid me ſo: for in good faith
I am a Child to chiding.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: What is the matter Lady?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Alas (Iago) my Lord hath ſo bewhor'd her,
Throwne ſuch diſpight, and heauy termes vpon her
That true hear • s cannot beare it.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Am I that name, Iago?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: What name (faire Lady?)

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Such as ſhe ſaid my Lord did ſay I was.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: He call'd her whore: a Begger in his drinke:
Could not haue laid ſuch termes vpon his Callet.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Why did he ſo?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I do not know: I am ſure I am none ſuch.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Do not weepe, do not weepe: alas the day.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Hath ſhe forſooke ſo many Noble Matches?
Her Father? And her Country? And her Friends?
To be call'd Whore? Would it not make one weepe?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: It is my wretched Fortune.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Beſhrew him for't:
How comes this Tricke vpon him?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Nay, Heauen doth know.

sp.speaker: Aemi.
sp.l: I will be hang'd, if ſome eternall Villaine,
Some buſie and inſinuating Rogue,
Some cogging, cozening Slaue, to get ſome Office,
Haue not deuis'd this Slander: I will be hang'd elſe.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Fie, there is no ſuch man: it is impoſſible.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: If any ſuch there be, Heauen pardon him.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: A halter pardon him:
And hell gnaw his bones.
Why ſhould he call her Whore?
Who keepes her companie?
What Place? What Time?
What Forme? What liklyhood?
The Moore's abus'd by ſome moſt villanous Knaue,
Some baſe notorious Knaue, ſome ſcuruy Fellow.
Oh Heauens, that ſuch companions thou'd'ſt vnfold,
And put in euery honeſt hand a whip
To laſh the Raſcalls naked through the world,
Euen from the Eaſt to th' Weſt.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Speake within doore.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Oh fie vpon them: ſome ſuch Squire he was
That turn'd your wit, the ſeamy-ſide without,
And made you to ſuſpect me with the Moore.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: You are a Foole: go too.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Alas Iago,
What ſhall I do to win my Lord againe?
Good Friend, go to him: for by this light of Heauen,
I know not how I loſt him. Heere I kneele:
If ere my will did treſpaſſe 'gainſt his Loue,
Either in diſcourſe of thought, or actuall deed,
Or that mine Eyes, mine Eares, or any Sence
Delighted them: or any other Forme.
Or that I do not yet, and euer did,
And euer will, (though he do ſhake me off
To beggerly diuorcement) Loue him deerely,
Comfort forſweare me. Vnkindneſſe may do much,
And his vnkindneſſe may defeat my life,
But neuer taynt my Loue. I cannot ſay Whore,
It do's abhorre me now I ſpeake the word,
To do the Act, that might the addition earne,
Not the worlds Maſſe of vanitie could make me.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: I pray you be content: 'tis but his humour:
The buſineſſe of the State do's him offence.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: If 'twere no other.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: It is but ſo, I warrant,
Hearke how theſe Inſtruments ſummon to ſupper:
The Meſſengers of Venice ſtaies the meate,
Go in, and weepe not: all things ſhall be well.
How now Rodorigo?

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I do not finde
That thou deal'ſt iuſtly with me.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: What in the contrarie?

sp.speaker: Rodori.
sp.p: Euery day thou dafts me with ſome deuiſe Iago, and rather, as it ſeemes to me now, keep'ſt from me all conueniencie, then ſupplieſt me with the leaſt aduantage of hope: I will indeed no longer endure it. Nor am I yet perſwaded to put vp in peace, what already I haue fooliſhly ſuffred.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Will you heare me Rodorigo?

sp.speaker: Rodori.
sp.p: I haue heard too much: and your words and Performances are no kin together.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: You charge me moſt vniuſtly.

sp.speaker: Rodo.
sp.p: With naught but truth: I haue waſted my ſelfe out of my meanes. The Iewels you haue had from me to deliuer Deſdemona, would halfe haue corrupted a Votariſt. You haue told me ſhe hath receiu'd them, and return'd me expectations and comforts of ſodaine reſpect, and acquaintance, but I finde none.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Well, go too: very well.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: Very well▪ go too: I cannot go too, (man) nor tis not very well. Nay I think it is ſcuruy: and begin to finde my ſelfe fopt in it.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: Rodor.
sp.p: I tell you, 'tis not very well: I will make my ſelfe knowne to Deſdemona. If ſhe will returne me my Iewels, I will giue ouer my Suit, and repent my vnlawfull ſolicitation. If not, aſſure your ſelfe, I will ſeeke ſatisfaction of you.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: You haue ſaid now.

sp.speaker: Rodo.
sp.p: I: and ſaid nothing but what I proteſt intendment of doing.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Why, now I ſee there's mettle in thee: and euen from this inſtant do build on thee a better opinion then euer before: giue me thy • and Rodorigo. Thou haſt taken againſt me a moſt iuſt exception: but yet I proteſt I haue dealt moſt directly in thy Affaire.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: It hath not appeer'd.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I grant indeed it hath not appeer'd: and your ſuſpition is not without wit and iudgement. But Rodorigo, if thou haſt that in thee indeed, which I haue greater reaſon to▪ beleeue now then euer (I meane purpoſe, Courage, and Valour) this night ſhew it. If thou the next night following enioy not Deſdemona, take me from this world with Treacherie, and deuiſe Engines for my life.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: Well: what is it? Is it within, reaſon and compaſſe?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Sir, there is eſpeciall Commiſſion come from Venice to depute Caſſio in Othello's place.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: Is that true? Why then Othello and Deſdemona returne againe to Venice.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Oh no: he goes into Mauritania and taketh away with him the faire Deſdemona, vnleſſe his abode be lingred heere by ſome accident. Wherein none can be ſo determinate, as the remouing of Caſſio.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: How do you meane remouing him?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Why, by making him vncapable of Othello's place: knocking out his braines.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: And that you would haue me to do.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I: if you dare do your ſelfe a profit, and a right. He ſups to night with a Harlotry: and thither will I go to him. He knowes not yet of his Honourable Fortune, if you will watch his going thence (which I will faſhion to fall out betweene twelue and one) you may take him at your pleaſure. I will be neere to ſecond your Attempt, and he ſhall fall betweene vs. Come, ſtand not amaz'd at it, but go along with me: I will ſhew you ſuch a neceſſitie in his death, that you ſhall thinke your ſelfe bound to put it on him. It is now high ſupper time: and the night growes to waſt. About it.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: I will heare further reaſon for this.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: And you ſhalbe ſatisfi'd.

div.head: Scena Tertia.
div.stage: Enter Othello, Lodouico, Deſdemona Aemilia, and Atendants.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: I do beſeech you Sir, trouble your ſelfe no further.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Oh pardon me: 'twill do me good to walke.

sp.speaker: Lodoui.
sp.p: Madam, good night: I humbly thanke your Ladyſhip.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Your Honour is moſt welcome.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Will you walke Sir? Oh Deſdemona.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: My Lord.

sp.speaker: Othello.
sp.p: Get you to bed on th' inſtant, I will be return'd forth with: diſmiſſe your Attendant there: look't be done.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I will my Lord.

sp.speaker: Aem.
sp.p: How goes it now? He lookes gentler then he did.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: He ſaies he will returne incontinent,
And hath commanded me to go to bed,
And bid me to diſmiſſe you.

sp.speaker: Aemi.
sp.p: Diſmiſſe me?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: It was his bidding: therefore good Aemilia,
Giue me my nightly wearing▪ and adieu.
We muſt not now diſpleaſe him.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: I, would you had neuer ſeene him.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: So would not I: my loue doth ſo approue him,
That euen his ſtubborneſſe, his checks, his frownes,
(Prythee vn-pin me) haue grace and fauour.

sp.speaker: Aemi.
sp.p: I haue laid thoſe Sheetes you bad me on the bed.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: All's one: good Father, how fooliſh are our minds?
If I do die before, prythee ſhrow'd me
In one of theſe ſame Sheetes.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Come, come: you talke.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: My Mother had a Maid call'd Barbarie,
She was in loue: and he ſhe lou'd prou'd mad,
And did forſake her. She had a Song of Willough,
An old thing 'twas: but it expreſs'd her Fortune,
And ſhe dy'd ſinging it. That Song to night,
Will not go from my mind: I haue much to do,
But to go hang my head all at one ſide
And ſing it like poore Brabarie: prythee diſpatch.

sp.speaker: Aemi.
sp.p: Shall I go fetch your Night-gowne?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: No▪ va-pin me here,
This Lodouico is a proper man.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: A very handſome man.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: He ſpeakes well.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: I know a Lady in Venice would haue walk'd barefoot to Paleſtine for a touch of his nether lip.

sp.speaker: Deſ.

l.hi: The poore Soule ſat ſinging, by a Sicamour tree.

sp.l: Sing all a greene Willough:

l.hi: Her hand on her boſome her head on her knee,
Sing Willough, Willough, Willough.
The freſh Streames ran by her, and murmur'd her moanes
Sing Willough, &c.
Her ſalt teares fell from her, and ſoftned the ſtones,

sp.l: Sing Willough, &c. (Lay by theſe)
Willough, Willough. (Prythee high thee: he'le come anon)

l.hi: Sing all a greene Willough muſt be my Garland.
Let no body blame him, his ſcorne I approue.

sp.l: (Nay that's not next. Harke, who is't that knocks?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: It's the wind.

sp.speaker: Deſ.

l.hi: I call'd my Loue falſe Loue: but what ſaid he then?
Sing Willough, &c.
If I court mo women, you'le couch with mo men.

sp.l: So get thee gone, good night: mine eyes do itch:
Doth that boade weeping?

sp.speaker: Aemil,
sp.p: 'Tis neyther heere, nor there.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: I haue heard it ſaid ſo. O theſe Men, theſe men!
Do'ſt thou in conſcience thinke (tell me Aemilia)
That there be women do abuſe their husbands
In ſuch groſſe kinde?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: There be ſome ſuch, no queſtion.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Would'ſt thou do ſuch a deed for all the world?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Why, would not you?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: No, by this Heauenly light.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Nor I neither, by this Heauenly light:
I might doo't as well i' th' darke.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Would'ſt thou do ſuch a deed for al the world?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: The world's a huge thing:
It is a great price, for a ſmall vice.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Introth, I thinke thou would'ſt not.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Introth I thinke I ſhould, and vndoo't when I had done. Marry, I would not doe ſuch a thing for a ioynt Ring, nor for meaſures of Lawne, nor for Gownes, Petticoats, nor Caps, nor any petty exhibition. But for all the whole world: why, who would not make her husband a Cuckold, to make him a Monarch? I ſhould venture Purgatory for't.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Beſhrew me, if I would do ſuch a wrong
For the whole world.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Why, the wrong is but a wrong i' th' world; and hauing the world for your labour, 'tis a wrong in your owne world, and you might quickly make it right.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I do not thinke there is any ſuch woman.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Yes, a dozen: and as many to' th' vantage, as would ſtore the world they plaid for.
But I do thinke it is their Husbands faults
If Wiues do fall: (Say, that they ſlacke their duties,
And powre our Treaſures into forraigne laps;
Or elſe breake out in peeuiſh Iealouſies,
Throwing reſtraint vpon vs: Or ſay they ſtrike vs,
Or ſcant our former hauing in deſpight)
Why we haue galles: and though we haue ſome Grace,
Yet haue we ſome Reuenge. Let Husbands know,
Their wiues haue ſenſe like them: They ſee, and ſmell,
And haue their Palats both for ſweet, and ſowre,
As Husbands haue. What is it that they do,
When they change vs for others? Is it Sport?
I thinke it is: and doth Affection breed it?
I thinke it doth. Is't Frailty that thus erres?
It is ſo too. And haue not we Affections?
Deſires for Sport? and Frailty, as men haue?
