Then let them vſe vs well: elſe let them know,
The illes we do, their illes inſtruct vs ſo.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Good night, good night:
Heauen me ſuch vſes ſend,
Not to picke bad, from bad; but by bad, mend.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Heere, ſtand behinde this Barke,
Straight will he come:
Weare thy good Rapier bare, and put it home:
Quicke, quicke, feare nothing; Ile be at thy Elbow,
It makes vs, or it marres vs, thinke on that,
And fixe moſt firme thy Reſolution.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: Be neere at hand, I may miſcarry in't.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Heere, at thy hand: Be bold, & take thy ſtand.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.l: I haue no great deuotion to the deed,
And yet he hath giuen me ſatisfying Reaſons:
'Tis but a man gone. Forth my Sword: he dies.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: I haue rub'd this yong Q • at almoſt to the ſenſe,
And he growes angry. Now, whether he kill Caſſio,
Or Caſſio him, or each do kill the other,
Euery way makes my gaine. Liue Rodorigo,
He calles me to a reſtitution large
Of Gold, and Iewels, that I bob'd from him,
As Guifts to Deſdemona.
It muſt not be: If Caſſio do remaine,
He hath a dayly beauty in his life,
That makes me vgly: and beſides, the Moore
May vnfold me to him: there ſtand I in much perill:
No, he muſt dye. But ſo, I heard him comming.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: I know his gate, 'tis he: Villaine thou dyeſt.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: That thruſt had beene mine enemy indeed,
But that my Coate is better then thou know'ſt:
I will make proofe of thine.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: Oh, I am ſlaine.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: I am maym'd for euer:
Helpe hoa: Murther, murther.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: The voyce of Caſſio▪ Iago keepes his word.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: O Villaine that I am.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: It is euen ſo.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Oh helpe hoa: Light, a Surgeon.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: 'Tis he: O braue Iago, honeſt, and iuſt,
That haſt ſuch Noble ſenſe of thy Friends wrong,
Thou teacheſt me. Minion, your deere lyes dead,
And your vnbleſt Fate highes: Strumpet I come:
For of my heart, thoſe Charmes thine Eyes, are blotted.
Thy Bed luſt-ſtain'd, ſhall with Luſts blood bee ſpotted.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: What hoa? no Watch? No paſſage?
Murther, Murther.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: 'Tis ſome miſchance, the voyce is very direfull.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Oh helpe.

sp.speaker: Lodo.
sp.p: Hearke.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: Oh wretched Villaine.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Two or three groane. 'Tis heauy night;
Theſe may be counterfeits: Let's think't vnſafe
To come into the cry, without more helpe.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: Nobody come: then ſhall I bleed to death.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: Hearke.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: Here's one comes in his ſhirt, with Light, and Weapons.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Who's there?
Who's noyſe is this that cries on murther?

sp.speaker: Lodo.
sp.p: We do not know.

sp.speaker: Iago▪
sp.p: Do not you heare a cry?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Heere, heere: for heauen ſake helpe me.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: This is Othello's Ancient, as I take it.

sp.speaker: Lodo.
sp.p: The ſame indeede, a very valiant Fellow.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: What are you heere, that cry ſo greeuouſly?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: Iago? Oh I am ſpoyl'd, vndone by Villaines:
Giue me ſome helpe.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: O mee, Lieutenant!
What Villaines haue done this?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: I thinke that one of them is heereabout▪
And cannot make away.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Oh treacherous Villaines:
What are you there? Come in, and giue ſome helpe.

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: O helpe me there.

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: That's one of them.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Oh murd'rous Slaue! O Villaine!

sp.speaker: Rod.
sp.p: O damn'd Iago! O inhumane Dogge▪

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Kill men i' th' darke?
Where be theſe bloody Theeues?
How ſilent is this Towne? Hoa, murther, murther.
What may you be? Are you of good, or euill?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: As you ſhall proue vs, praiſe vs.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Signior Lodouico?

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: He Sir.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I cry you mercy: here's Caſſio hurt by Villaines.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: Caſſio?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: How is't Brother?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: My Legge is cut in two.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Marry heauen forbid:
Light Gentlemen, Ile binde it with my ſhirt.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: What is the matter hoa? Who is't that cry'd?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Who is't that cry'd?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: Oh my deere Caſſio,
My ſweet Caſſio: Oh Caſſio, Caſſio, Caſſio.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: O notable Strumpet. Caſſio, may you ſuſpect
Who they ſhould be, that haue thus mangled you?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.l: I am ſorry to finde you thus;
I haue beene to ſeeke you.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Lend me a Garter. So:—Oh for a Chaire
To beare him eaſily hence.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: Alas he faints. Oh Caſſio, Caſſio, Caſſio.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Gentlemen all, I do ſuſpect this Traſh
To be a party in this Iniurie.
Patience a while, good Caſſio. Come, come;
Lend me a Light: know we this face, or no?
Alas my Friend, and my deere Countryman
Rodorigo? No: Yes ſure: Yes, 'tis Rodorigo.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: What, of Venice?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Euen he Sir: Did you know him?

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: Know him? I.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Signior Gratiano? I cry your gentle pardon:
Theſe bloody accidents muſt excuſe my Manners,
That ſo neglected you.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: I am glad to ſee you.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: How do you Caſſio? Oh▪ a Chaire, a Chaire.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: Rodorigo?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: He, he, 'tis he:
Oh that's well ſaid, the Chaire.
Some good man beare him carefully from hence,
Ile fetch the Generall's Surgeon. For you Miſtris,
Saue you your labour. He that lies ſlaine heere (Caſſio)
Was my deere friend. What malice was between you?

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: None in the world: nor do I know the man?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: What? looke you pale? Oh beare him o' th' Ayre.
Stay you good Gentlemen. Looke you pale, Miſtris?
Do you perceiue the gaſtneſſe of her eye?
Nay, if you ſtare, we ſhall heare more anon.
Behold her well: I pray you looke vpon her:
Do you ſee Gentlemen? Nay, guiltineſſe will ſpeake
Though tongues were out of vſe.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Alas, what is the matter?
What is the matter, Husband?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Caſſio hath heere bin ſet on in the darke
By Rodorigo, and Fellowes that are ſcap'd:
He's almoſt ſlaine, and Rodorigo quite dead.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Alas good Gentleman: alas good Caſsio.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: This is the fruits of whoring. Prythe Aemilia,
Go know of Caſſio where he ſupt to night.
What, do you ſhake at that?

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.p: He ſupt at my houſe, but I therefore ſhake not.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: O did he ſo? I charge you go with me.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Oh fie vpon thee Strumpet.

sp.speaker: Bian.
sp.l: I am no Strumpet, but of life as honeſt,
As you that thus abuſe me.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: As I? Fie vpon thee.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: Kinde Gentlemen:
Let's go ſee poore Caſſio dreſt.
Come Miſtris, you muſt tel's another Tale.
Aemilia, run you to the Cittadell,
And tell my Lord and Lady, what hath happ'd:
Will you go on afore? This is the night
That either makes me, or foredoes me quight.

div.head: Scoena Secunda.
div.stage: Enter Othello, and Deſdemona in her bed.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: It is the Cauſe, it is the Cauſe (my Soule)
Let me not name it to you, you chaſte Starres,
It is the Cauſe. Yet Ile not ſhed her blood,
Nor ſcarre that whiter skin of hers, then Snow▪
And ſmooth as Monumentall Alablaſter:
Yet ſhe muſt dye, elſe ſhee'l betray more men:
Put out the Light, and then put out the Light:
If I quench thee, thou flaming Miniſter,
I can againe thy former light reſtore,
Should I repent me. But once put out thy Light,
Thou cunning'ſt Patterne of excelling Nature,

I know not where is that Promethae •
heate
That can thy Light re-Lume.
When I haue pluck'd thy Roſe,
I cannot giue it vitall growth againe,
It needs muſt wither. Ile ſmell thee on the Tree.
Oh Balmy breath, that doſt almoſt perſwade
Iuſtice to breake her Sword. One more, one more:
Be thus when thou art dead, and I will kill thee,
And loue thee after. One more, and that's the laſt.
So ſweet, was ne're ſo fatall. I muſt weepe,
But they are cruell Teares: This ſorrow's heauenly,
It ſtrikes, where it doth loue. She wakes.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Who's there? Othello?

sp.speaker: Othel.
sp.p: I Deſdemona.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Will you come to bed, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Haue you pray'd to night, Deſdemon?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I my Lord.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: If you bethinke your ſelfe of any Crime
Vnreconcil'd as yet to Heauen, and Grace,
Solicite for it ſtraight.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: Alacke, my Lord,
What may you meane by that?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Well, do it, and be breefe, I will walke by:
I would not kill thy vnprepared Spirit,
No, Heauens fore-fend) I would not kill thy Soule.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Talke you of killing?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I, I do.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Then Heauen haue mercy on mee.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Amen, with all my heart.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: If you ſay, I hope you will not kill me.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Humh.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: And yet I feare you: for you're fatall then
When your eyes rowle ſo.
Why I ſhould feare, I know not,
Since guiltineſſe I know not: But yet I feele I feare.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Thinke on thy ſinnes.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: They are Loue • I beare to you.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I, and for that thou dy'ſt.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: That death's vnnaturall, that kils for louing.
Alas, why gnaw you ſo your nether-lip?
Some bloody paſſion ſhakes your very Frame:
Theſe are portent • : but yet I hope, I hope,
They do not point on me.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Peace, and be ſtill.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I will ſo: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: That Handkerchiefe
Which I ſo lou'd, and gaue thee, thou gau'ſt to Caſſio.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: No by my Life, and Soule: ſend for the man,
And aske him.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Sweet Soule, take heed, take heed of Periury,
Thou art on thy death-bed.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: I, but not yet to dye.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Preſently.
Therefore confeſſe thee freely of thy ſinne:
For to deny each Article with Oath,
Cannot remoue, nor choake the ſtrong Conception
That I do grone withall. Thou art to dye.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: O Heauen haue mercy on me.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I ſay, Amen.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: And haue you mercy too. I neuer did
Offend you in my life: neuer lou'd Caſſio,
But with ſuch generall warrantie of Heauen,
As I might loue. I neuer gaue him Token.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: By Heauen I ſaw my Handkerchiefe in's hand.
O periur'd woman, thou do'ſt ſtone my heart,
And makes me call, what I intend to do,
A Murther, which I thought a Sacrifice.
I ſaw the Handkerchiefe.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: He found it then:
I neuer gaue it him: Send, for him hither:
Let him confeſſe a truth.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: He hath confeſt.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: What, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: That he hath vs'd thee.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: How? vnlawfully?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: He will not ſay ſo.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: No: his mouth is ſtopp'd:
Honeſt Iago hath 'tane order for't.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Oh, my feare interprets. What is he dead?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Had all his haires bin liues, my great Reuenge
Had ſtomacke for them all.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Alas, he is betray'd, and I vndone.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Out Strumpet: weep'ſt thou for him to my face?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: O baniſh me, my Lord, but kill me not.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Downe Strumpet.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: Kill me to morrow, let me liue to night.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Nay, if you ſtriue.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: But halfe an houre.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Being done, there is no pawſe.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: But while I ſay one prayer.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: It is too late.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: My Lord, my Lord? What hoa?
My Lord, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: What noiſe is this? Not dead? not yet quite dead?
I that am cruell, am yet mercifull,
I would not haue thee linger in thy paine?
So, ſo.

sp.speaker: Aemil. within.
sp.p: What hoa? my Lord, my Lord?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Who's there?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Oh good my Lord, I would ſpeake a word with you.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Yes: 'Tis Aemilia: by and by. Shee's dead.
'Tis like ſhe comes to ſpeake of Caſſio's death:
The noiſe was high. Hah, no more moouing?
Still as the Graue. Shall • he come in? Wer't good?
I thinke ſhe ſtirres againe. No, what's beſt to do?
If ſhe come in, ſhee'l ſure ſpeake to my wife:
My wife, my wife: what wife? I haue no wife.
Oh inſupportable! Oh heauy houre!
Me thinkes, it ſhould be now a huge Eclipſe
Of Sunne, and Moone; and that th' affrighted Globe
Did yawne at Alteration.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: I do beſeech you
That I may ſpeake with you. Oh good my Lord.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I had forgot thee: oh come in Aemilia.
Soft, by and by, let me the Curtaines draw.
Where art thou? What's the matter with thee now?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Oh my good Lord, yonders foule Murthers done.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: What? now?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: But now, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: It is the very error of the Moone,
She comes more neerer Earth then ſhe was wont,
And makes men mad.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Caſſio, my Lord, hath kill'd
A young Venetian, call'd Rodorigo.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Rodorigo kill'd? and Caſſio kill'd?

sp.speaker: Aemil
sp.p: No▪ Caſſio is not kill'd.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Not Caſſio kill'd? Then Murther's out of tune,
And ſweet Reuenge growes harſh.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: O falſely, falſely murder'd.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Alas! what cry is that?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: That? What?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Out, and alas, that was my Ladies voice.
Helpe, helpe hoa, helpe. Oh Ladie ſpeake againe,
Sweet Deſdemona, oh ſweet Miſtris, ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.p: A guiltleſſe death, I dye.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Oh who hath done this deed?

sp.speaker: Deſ.
sp.l: No body: I my ſelfe, farewell:
Commend me to my kinde Lord: oh farewell.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Why, how ſhould ſhe be murdred?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Alas: who knowes?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: You heare her ſay her ſelfe, it was not I.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: She ſaid ſo: I muſt needs report the truth.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: She's like a Liar gone to burning hell,
'Twas I that kill'd her.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Oh the more Angell ſhe, and you the blacker Diuell.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: She turn'd to folly: and ſhe was a whore.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: Thou do'ſt bely her, and thou art a diuell.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: She wa • falſe as water.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Thou a • t raſh as fire, to ſay
That ſhe was falſe. Oh ſhe was heauenly true.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Caſſio did top her: Ask thy husband elſe.
O, I were damn'd beneath all depth in hell:
But that I did proceed vpon iuſt grounds
To this extremity. Thy Husband knew it all.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: My Husband?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Thy Husband.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: That ſhe was falſe to Wedlocke?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I, with Caſſio: had ſhe bin true,
If Heauen would make me ſuch another world,
Of one entyre and perfect Chryſolite,
I'ld not haue ſold her for it.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: My Husband?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I, 'twas he that told me on her firſt,
An honeſt man he is, and hates the ſlime
That ſtickes on filthy deeds.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.p: My Husband?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: What needs this itterance, Woman?
I ſay, thy Husband.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Oh Miſtris,
Villany hath made mockes with loue:
My Husband ſay ſhe was falſe?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: He, Woman;
I ſay thy Husband: Do'ſt vnderſtand the word?
My Friend, thy Husband; honeſt, honeſt Iago.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: If he ſay ſo, may his pernicious Soule
Rot halfe a graine a day: he lyes to' th' heart,
She was too fond of her moſt filthy Bargaine.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Hah?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Do thy worſt:
This deede of thine is no more worthy Heauen,
Then thou was't worthy her.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Peace, you were beſt.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Thou haſt not halfe that powre to do me harm,
As I haue to be hurt. Oh Gull, oh dolt,
As ignorant as durt: thou haſt done a deed
(I care not for thy Sword) Ile make thee known,
Though I loſt twenty liues. Helpe, helpe, hoa, helpe:
The Moore hath kill'd my Miſtris. Murther, murther.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.p: What is the matter? How now Generall?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Oh, are you come, Iago: you haue done well,
That men muſt lay their Murthers on your necke.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: What is the matter?

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: Diſproue this Villaine, if thou bee'ſt a man:
He ſayes, thou told'ſt him that his wife was falſe:
I know thou did'ſt not: thou'rt not ſuch a Villain.
Speake, for my heart is full.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: I told him what I thought,
And told no more
Then what he found himſelfe was apt, and true.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: But did you euer tell him,
She was falſe?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I did.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: You • old a Lye an odious damned Lye:
Vpon my Soule, a Lye; a wicked Lye.
Shee falſe with Caſſio?
Did you ſay with Caſſio?

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: With Caſſio, Miſtris?
Go too, charme your tongue.

sp.speaker: Emil.
sp.l: I will not charme my Tongue;
I am bound to ſpeake,
My Miſtris heere lyes murthered in her bed.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Oh Heauens, foreſend.

sp.speaker: Emil.
sp.p: And your reports haue ſet the Murder on.

sp.speaker: Othello.
sp.l: Nay ſtare not Maſters,
It is true indeede.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: 'Tis a ſtrange Truth.

sp.speaker: Mont.
sp.p: O monſtrous Acte.

sp.speaker: Emil.
sp.l: Villany, villany, villany:
I thinke vpon't, I thinke: I ſmel't: O Villany:
I thought ſo then: Ile kill my ſelfe for greefe.
O villany! villany!

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.l: What, are you mad?
I charge you get you home.

sp.speaker: Emil.
sp.l: Good Gentlemen, let me haue leaue to ſpeake:
'Tis proper I obey him; but not now:
Perchance Iago, I will ne're go home.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Oh, oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Emil.
sp.l: Nay, lay thee downe, and roare:
For thou haſt kill'd the ſweeteſt innocent,
That ere did lift vp eye.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Oh ſhe was fowle!
I ſcarſe did know you Vnkle, there lies your Neece,
Whoſe breath (indeed) theſe hands haue newly ſtopp'd:
I know this acte ſhewes horrible and grim.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.l: Poore Deſdemon:
I am glad thy Father's dead,
Thy Match was mortall to him: and pure greefe
Shore his old thred in twaine. Did he liue now,
This ſight would make him do a deſperate turne:
Yea, curſe his better Angell from his ſide,
And fall to Reprobance.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: 'Tis pittifull: but yet Iago knowes
That ſhe with Caſſio, hath the Act of ſhame▪
A thouſand times committed. Caſſio confeſt it,
And ſhe did gratifie his amorous workes
With that Recognizance and pledge of Loue
Which I firſt gaue her: I ſaw it in his hand:
It was a Handkerchiefe, an Antique Token
My Father gaue my Mother.

sp.speaker: Emil.
sp.p: Oh Heauen! oh heauenly Powres!

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Come, hold your peace.

sp.speaker: Emil.
sp.l: 'Twill out, 'twill out▪ I peace?
No, I will ſpeake as liberall as the North;
Let Heauen, and Men, and Diuels, let them all,
All, all, crie ſhame againſt me, yet Ile ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Be wiſe, and get you home.

sp.speaker: Emil.
sp.p: I will not.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: Fye, your Sword vpon a Woman.

sp.speaker: Emil.
sp.l: Oh thou dull Moore,
That Handkerchiefe thou ſpeak'ſt of
I found by Fortune, and did giue my Husband:
For often, with a ſolemne earneſtneſſe,
(More then indeed belong'd to ſuch a Trifle)
He begg'd of me, to ſteale't.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Villanous Whore.

sp.speaker: Emil.
sp.l: She giue it Caſſio? No, alas I found it,
And I did giu't my Husband.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: Filth, thou lyeſt.

sp.speaker: Emil.
sp.l: By Heauen I do not, I do not Gentlemen:
Oh murd'rous Coxcombe, what ſhould ſuch a Foole
Do with ſo good a wife?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Are there no ſtones in Heauen,
But what ſerues for the Thunder?
Precious Villaine.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.l: The woman falles:
Sure he hath kill'd his Wife.

sp.speaker: Emil.
sp.p: I, I: oh lay me by my Miſtris ſide.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: Hee's gone, but his wife's kill'd.

sp.speaker: Mon.
sp.l: 'Tis a notorious Villain: take you this weapon
Which I haue recouer'd from the Moore:
Come guard the doore without, let him not paſſe,
But kill him rather. Ile after that ſame villaine,
For 'tis a damned Slaue.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I am not valiant neither:
But euery Punie whipſter gets my Sword.
But why ſhould Honor out-liue Honeſty?
Let it go all.

sp.speaker: Aemil.
sp.l: What did thy Song boad Lady?
Hearke, canſt thou heare me? I will play the Swan,
And dye in Muſicke: Willough, Willough, Willough.
Moore, ſhe was chaſte: She lou'd thee, cruell Moore,
So come my Soule to bliſſe, as I ſpeake true:
So ſpeaking as I thinke, alas, I dye.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I haue another weapon in this Chamber,
It was a Sword of Spaine, the Ice brookes temper:
Oh heere it is: Vnkle I muſt come forth.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.l: If thou attempt it, it will coſt thee deere;
Thou haſt no weapon, and perforce muſt ſuffer.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Looke in vpon me then, and ſpeake with me,
Or naked as I am I will aſſault thee.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: What is the matter?

sp.speaker: Othel.
sp.l: Behold, I haue a weapon:
A better neuer did it ſelfe ſuſtaine
Vpon a Soldiers Thigh. I haue ſeene the day,
That with this little Arme, and this good Sword,
I haue made my way through more impediments
Then twenty times your ſtop. But (oh vaine boaſt)
Who can controll his Fate? 'Tis not ſo now.
Be not affraid, though you do ſee me weapon'd:
Heere is my iournies end, heere is my butt
And verie Sea-marke of my vtmoſt Saile.
Do you go backe diſmaid? 'Tis a loſt feare:
Man but a Ruſh againſt Othello's breſt,
And he retires. Where ſhould Othello go?
Now: how doſt thou looke now? Oh ill-Starr'd wench,
Pale as thy Smocke: when we ſhall meete at compt,
This looke of thine will hurle my Soule from Heauen,
And Fiends will ſnatch at it. Cold, cold, my Girle?
Euen like thy Chaſtity. O curſed, curſed Slaue!
Whip me ye Diuels,
From the poſſeſſion of this Heauenly ſight:
Blow me about in windes, roaſt me in Sulphure,
Waſh me in ſteepe-downe gulfes of Liquid fire.
Oh Deſdemon! dead Deſdemon: dead. Oh, oh!

div.stage: Enter Lodouico, Caſſio, Montano, and Iago, with Officers.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: Where is this raſh, and moſt vnfortunate man?

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: That's he that was Othello: heere I am.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Where is that Viper?
Bring the Villaine forth.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I look down towards his feet; but that's a Fable,
If that thou bee'ſt a Diuell, I cannot kill thee.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: Wrench his Sword from him.

sp.speaker: Iago.
sp.p: I bleed Sir, but not kill'd.

sp.speaker: Othel.
sp.l: I am not ſorry neither, Il'd haue thee liue:
For in my ſenſe, 'tis happineſſe to die.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Oh thou Othello, that was once ſo good,
Falne in the practiſe of a curſed Slaue,
What ſhall be ſaide to thee.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Why any thing:
An honourable Murderer, if you will:
For nought I did in hate, but all in Honour.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: This wretch hath part confeſt his Villany:
Did you and he conſent in Caſſio's death.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: I.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.p: Deere Generall, I neuer gaue you cauſe.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I do beleeue it, and I aske your pardon:
Will you, I pray, demand that demy-Diuell,
Why he hath thus enſnar'd my Soule and Body.

sp.speaker: Iag.
sp.l: Demand me nothing: what you know, you know:
From this time forth, I neuer will ſpeake word.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: What? not to pray?

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: Torments will ope your lips.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: Well, thou doſt beſt.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Sir,
You ſhall vnderſtand what hath befalne,
(Which, as I thinke, you know not) heere is a Letter
Found in the pocket of the ſlaine Rodorigo,
And heere another, the one of them imports
The death of Caſſio, to be vndertooke
By Rodorigo.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.p: O Villaine!

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.p: Moſt Heatheniſh, and moſt groſſe.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Now, heere's another diſcontented paper
Found in his pocket too: and this it ſeemes
Rodorigo meant t' haue ſent this damned villaine:
But that (belike) Iago in the interim
Came in, and ſatisfi'd him.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Oh thou pernitious Caitiffe;
How came you (Caſſio) by that Handkerchiefe
That was my wiues?

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: I found it in my Chamber:
And he himſelfe confeſt it but euen now,
That there he dropt it for a ſpeciall purpoſe,
Which wrought to his deſire.

sp.speaker: Othel.
sp.p: O Foole, foole, foole!

sp.speaker: Caſſio.
sp.l: There is beſides, in Rodorigo's Letter,
How he vpbraides Iago, that he made him
Braue me vpon the Watch: whereon it came
That I was caſt: and euen but now he ſpake
(After long ſeeming dead) Iago hurt him,
Iago ſet him on.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: You muſt forſake this roome, and go with vs:
Your Power, and your Command is taken off,
And Caſſio rules in Cyprus. For this Slaue,
If there be any cunning Crueltie,
That can torment him much, and hold him long,
It ſhall be his. You ſhall cloſe Priſoner reſt,
Till that the Nature of your fault be knowne
To the Venetian State. Come, bring away.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: Soft you; a word or two before you goe:
I haue done the State ſome ſeruice, and they know't:
No more of that. I pray you in your Letters,
When you ſhall theſe vnluckie deeds relate,
Speake of me, as I am. Nothing extenuate,
Nor ſet downe ought in malice.
Then muſt you ſpeake,
Of one that lou'd not wiſely, but too well:
Of one, not eaſily Iealious, but being wrought,
Perplexed in the extreame: Of one, whoſe hand
(Like the baſe Iudean) threw a Pearle away
Richer then all his Tribe: Of one, whoſe ſubdu'd Eyes,
Albeit vn-vſed to the melting moode,
Drops teares as faſt as the Arabian Trees
Their Medicinable gumme. Set you downe this:
And ſay beſides, that in Aleppo once,
Where a malignant, and a Turbond-Turke
Beate a Venetian, and traduc'd the State,
I tooke by th' throat the circumciſed Dogge,
And ſmoate him, thus.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.p: Oh bloody period.

sp.speaker: Gra.
sp.p: All that is ſpoke, is marr'd.

sp.speaker: Oth.
sp.l: I kiſt thee, ere I kill'd thee: No way but this,
Killing my ſelfe, to dye vpon a kiſſe.

sp.speaker: Caſ.
sp.l: This did I feare, but thought he had no weapon:
For he was great of heart.

sp.speaker: Lod.
sp.l: Oh Sparton Dogge:
More fell then Anguiſh, Hunger, or the Sea:
Looke on the Tragicke Loading of this bed:
This is thy worke:
The Obiect poyſons Sight,
Let it be hid. Gratiano, keepe the houſe,
And ſeize vpon the Fortunes of the Moore,
For they ſucceede on you. To you, Lord Gouernor,
Remaines the Cenſure of this helliſh villaine:
The Time, the Place, the Torture, oh inforce it:
My ſelfe will ſtraight aboord, and to the State,
This heauie Act, with heauie heart relate.

list.item: Lodouico and Gratiano, two Noble Venetians.

div.head: THE TRAGEDIE OF Anthonie, and Cleopatra.
Scoena Prima.

sp.speaker: Philo.
sp.l: NAy, but this dotage of our Generals
Ore-flowes the meaſure: thoſe his goodly eyes
That o're the Files and Muſters of the Warre,
Haue glow'd like plated Mars:
Now bend, now turne
The Office and Deuotion of their view
Vpon a Tawny Front. His Captaines heart,
Which in the ſcuffles of great Fights hath burſt
The Buckles on his breſt, reneages all temper,
And is become the Bellowes and the Fan
To coole a Gypſies Luſt.
sp.stage: Enter Anthony, Cleopatra her Ladies, the Traine, with Eunuchs fanning her.
sp.l: Looke where they come:
Take but good note, and you ſhall ſee in him
(The triple Pillar of the world) transform'd
Into a Strumpets Foole. Behold and ſee.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: If it be Loue indeed, tell me how much.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: There's beggery in the loue that can be reckon'd

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Ile ſet a bourne how farre to be belou'd.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Then muſt thou needes finde our new Heauen, new Earth.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Newes (my good Lord) from Rome.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Grates me, the ſumme.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Nay heare them Anthony.
Fuluia perchance is angry: Or who knowes,
If the ſcarſe-bearded Caeſar haue not ſent
His powrefull Mandate to you. Do this, or this;
Take in that Kingdome, and Infranchiſe that:
Perform't, or elſe we damne thee.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: How, my Loue?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Perchance? Nay, and moſt like:
You muſt not ſtay heere longer, your diſmiſſion
Is come from Caeſar, therefore heare it Anthony.
Where's Fuluias Proceſſe? (Caeſars I would ſay) both?
Call in the Meſſengers: As I am Egypts Queene,
Thou bluſheſt Anthony, and that blood of thine
Is Caeſars homager: elſe ſo thy cheeke payes ſhame,
When ſhrill-tongu'd Fuluia ſcolds. The Meſſengers.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let Rome in Tyber melt, and the wide Arch
Of the raing'd Empire fall: Heere is my ſpace,
Kingdomes are clay: Our dungie earth alike
Feeds Beaſt as Man; the Nobleneſſe of life
Is to do thus: when ſuch a mutuall paire,
And ſuch a twaine can doo't in which I binde
One paine of puniſhment, the world to weete
We ſtand vp Peereleſſe.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Excellent falſhood:
Why did he marry Fuluia, and not loue her?
Ile ſeeme the Foole I am not. Anthony will be himſelfe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: But ſtirr'd by Cleopatra.
Now for the loue of Loue, and her ſoft houres,
Let's not confound the time with Conference harſh;
There's not a minute of our liues ſhould ſtretch
Without ſome pleaſure now. What ſport to night?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Heare the Ambaſſadors.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Fye wrangling Queene:
Whom euery thing becomes, to chide, to laugh,
To weepe: who euery paſſion fully ſtriues
To make it ſelfe (in Thee) faire, and admir'd.
No Meſſenger but thine, and all alone, to night
Wee'l wander through the ſtreets, and note
The qualities of people. Come my Queene,
Laſt night you did deſire it. Speake not to vs.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.p: Is Caeſar with Anthonius priz'd ſo ſlight?

sp.speaker: Philo.
sp.l: Sir ſometimes when he is not Anthony,
He comes too ſhort of that great Property
Which ſtill ſhould go with Anthony.

sp.speaker: Dem.
sp.p: I am full ſorry, that hee approues the common Lyar, who thus ſpeakes of him at Rome; but I will hope of better deeds to morrow. Reſt you happy.

div.stage: Enter Enobarbus, Lamprius, a Southſayer, Rannius, Lucillius, Charmian, Iras, Mardian the Eunuch, and Alexas.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: L. Alexas, ſweet Alexas, moſt any thing Alexas, almoſt moſt abſolute Alexas, where's the Soothſayer that you prais'd ſo to' th' Queene? Oh that I knewe this Husband, which you ſay, muſt change his Hornes with Garlands.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Soothſayer.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: Your will?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Is this the Man? Is't you ſir that know things?

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: In Natures infinite booke of Secrecie, a little I can read.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Shew him your hand.

sp.speaker: Enob.
sp.l: Bring in the Banket quickly: Wine enough,
Cleopatra's health to drinke.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Good ſir, giue me good Fortune.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: I make not, but foreſee.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Pray then, foreſee me one.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: You ſhall be yet farre fairer then you are.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: He meanes in fleſh.

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: No, you ſhall paint when you are old.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Wrinkles forbid.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Vex not his preſcience, be attentiue.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Huſh.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: You ſhall be more belouing, then beloued.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I had rather heate my Liuer with drinking.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Nay, heare him.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Good now ſome excellent Fortune: Let mee be married to three Kings in a forenoone, and Widdow them all: Let me haue a Childe at fifty, to whom Herode of Iewry may do Homage. Finde me to marrie me with Octauius Caeſar, and companion me with my Miſtris.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: You ſhall out-liue the Lady whom you ſerue.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Oh excellent, I loue long life better then Figs.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: You haue ſeene and proued a fairer former fortune, then that which is to approach.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Then belike my Children ſhall haue no names:
Prythee how many Boyes and Wenches muſt I haue.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: If euery of your wiſhes had a wombe, & foretell euery wiſh, a Million.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Out Foole, I forgiue thee for a Witch.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: You thinke none but your ſheets are priuie to your wiſhes.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Nay come, tell Iras hers.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Wee'l know all our Fortunes.

sp.speaker: Enob.
sp.p: Mine, and moſt of our Fortunes to night, ſhall be drunke to bed.

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: There's a Palme preſages Chaſtity, if nothing els.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: E'ne as the o're-flowing Nylus preſageth Famine.

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: Go you wilde Bedfellow, you cannot Soothſay.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Nay, if an oyly Palme bee not a fruitfull Prognoſtication, I cannot ſcratch mine eare. Prythee tel her but a worky day Fortune.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: Your Fortunes are alike.

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: But how, but how, giue me particulars.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: I haue ſaid.

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: Am I not an inch of Fortune better then ſhe?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Well, if you were but an inch of fortune better then I: where would you chooſe it.

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: Not in my Husbands noſe.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Our worſer thoughts Heauens mend.

sp.speaker: Alexas.
sp.p: Come, his Fortune, his Fortune. Oh let him mary a woman that cannot go, ſweet Iſis, I beſeech thee, and let her dye too, and giue him a worſe, and let worſe follow worſe, till the worſt of all follow him laughing to his graue, fifty-fold a Cuckold. Good Iſis heare me this Prayer, though thou denie me a matter of more waight: good Iſis I beſeech thee.

sp.speaker: Iras.
sp.p: Amen, deere Goddeſſe, heare that prayer of the people. For, as it is a heart-breaking to ſee a handſome man looſe-Wiu'd, ſo it is a deadly ſorrow, to beholde a foule Knaue vncuckolded: Therefore deere Iſis keep decorum, and Fortune him accordingly.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Amen.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Lo now, if it lay in their hands to make mee a Cuckold, they would make themſelues Whores, but they'ld doo't.

sp.speaker: Enob.
sp.p: Huſh, heere comes Anthony.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Not he, the Queene.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Saue you, my Lord.

sp.speaker: Enob.
sp.p: No Lady.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Was he not heere?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: No Madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: He was diſpos'd to mirth, but on the ſodaine
A Romane thought hath ſtrooke him.
Enobarbus?

sp.speaker: Enob.
sp.p: Madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Seeke him, and bring him hither: wher's Alexias?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: Heere at your ſeruice.
My Lord approaches.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: We will not looke vpon him:
Go with vs.

sp.speaker: Meſſen.
sp.l: Fuluia thy Wife,
Firſt came into the Field.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Againſt my Brother Lucius?

sp.speaker: Meſſen.
sp.l: I: but ſoone that Warre had end,
And the times ſtate
Made friends of them, ioynting their force 'gainſt Caeſar,
Whoſe better iſſue in the warre from Italy,
Vpon the firſt encounter draue them.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Well, what worſt.

sp.speaker: Meſſ.
sp.p: The Nature of bad newes infects the Teller.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: When it concernes the Foole or Coward: On.
Things that are paſt, are done, with me. 'Tis thus,
Who tels me true, though in his Tale lye death,
I heare him as he flatter'd.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: Labienus (this is ſtiffe-newes)
Hath with his Parthian Force
Extended Aſia: from Euphrates his conquering
Banner ſhooke, from Syria to Lydia,
And to Ionia, whil'ſt —

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Anthony thou would'ſt ſay.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Oh my Lord.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Speake to me home,
Mince not the generall tongue, name
Cleopatra as ſhe is call'd in Rome:
Raile thou in Fuluia's phraſe, and taunt my faults
With ſuch full Licenſe, as both Truth and Malice
Haue power to vtter. Oh then we forth weeds,
When our quicke windes lye ſtill, and our illes told vs
Is as our earing: fare thee well awhlle.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: At your Noble pleaſure.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: From Scicion how the newes? Speake there.

sp.speaker: 1. Meſ.
sp.l: The man from Scicion,
Is there ſuch an one?

sp.speaker: 2. Meſ.
sp.p: He ſtayes vpon your will.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let him appeare:
Theſe ſtrong Egyptian Fetters I muſt breake,
Or looſe my ſelfe in dotage.
sp.stage: Enter another Meſſenger with a Letter.
sp.l: What are you?

sp.speaker: 3. Meſ.
sp.p: Fuluia thy wife is dead.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Where dyed ſhe.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: In Scicion, her length of ſickneſſe,
With what elſe more ſerious,
Importeth thee to know, this beares.

sp.speaker: Antho.
sp.l: Forbeare me
There's a great Spirit gone, thus did I deſire it:
What our contempts doth of ten hurle from vs,
We with it ours againe. The preſent pleaſure,
By reuolution lowring, does become
The oppoſite of it ſelfe: ſhe's good being gon,
The hand could plucke her backe, that ſhou'd her on.
I muſt from this enchanting Queene breake off,
Ten thouſand harmes, more then the illes I know
My idleneſſe doth hatch.
How now Enobarbus.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: What's your pleaſure, Sir?

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: I muſt with haſte from hence.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Why then we kill all our Women. We ſee how mortall an vnkindneſſe is to them, if they ſuffer our departure death's the word.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: I muſt be gone.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p:
Vnder a compelling an occaſion, let women die. It were pitty to caſt them away for nothing, though betweene them and a great cauſe, they ſhould be eſteemed nothing. Cleopatra catching but the leaſt noyſe of this, 〈◊〉 inſtantly: I haue ſeene her dye twenty times vppon fa •
• orer moment: I do think there is mettle in death, which • mits ſome louing acte vpon her, ſhe hath ſuch a celerity in dying.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: She is cunning paſt mans thought.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Alacke Sir no, her paſſions are made of nothing but the fineſt part of pure Loue. We cannot cal her winds and waters, ſighes and teares: They are greater ſtormes and Tempeſts then Almanackes can report. This cannot be cunning in her; if it be, ſhe makes a ſhowre of Raine as well as Ioue.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Would I had neuer ſeene her.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Oh ſir, you had then left vnſeene a wonderfull peece of worke, which not to haue beene bleſt withall, would haue diſcredited your Trauaile.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Fuluia is dead.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Sir.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Fuluia is dead.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Fuluia?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Dead.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Why ſir, giue the Gods a thankefull Sacrifice: when it pleaſeth their Deities to take the wife of a man from him, it ſhewes to man the Tailors of the earth: comforting therein, that when olde Robes are worne out, there are members to make new. If there were no more Women but Fuluia, then had you indeede a cut, and the caſe to be lamented: This greefe is crown'd with Conſolation, your old Smocke brings foorth a new Petticoate, and indeed the teares liue in an Onion, that ſhould water this ſorrow.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: The buſineſſe ſhe hath broached in the State,
Cannot endure my abſence.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: And the buſineſſe you haue broach'd heere cannot be without you, eſpecially that of Cleopatra's, which wholly depends on your abode.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: No more light Anſweres:
Let our Officers
Haue notice what we purpoſe. I ſhall breake
The cauſe of our Expedience to the Queene,
And get her loue to part. For not alone
The death of Fuluia, with more vrgent touches
Do ſtrongly ſpeake to vs: but the Letters too
Of many our contriuing Friends in Rome,
Petition vs at home. Sextus Pompeius
Haue giuen the dare to Caeſar, and commands
The Empire of the Sea. Our ſlippery people,
Whoſe Loue is neuer link'd to the deſeruer,
Till his deſerts are paſt, begin to throw
Pompey the great, and all his Dignities
Vpon his Sonne, who high in Name and Power,
Higher then both in Blood and Life, ſtands vp
For the maine Souldier. Whoſe quality going on,
The ſides o' th' world may danger. Much is breeding,
Which like the Courſers heire, hath yet but life,
And not a Serpents poyſon. Say our pleaſure,
To ſuch whoſe places vnder vs, require
Our quicke remoue from hence.

sp.speaker: Enob.
sp.p: I ſhall doo't.

div.stage: Enter Cleopatra, Charmian, Alexas, and Iras.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Where is he?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: I did not ſee him ſince.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: See where he is,
Whoſe with him, what he does:
I did not ſend you. If you finde him ſad,
Say I am dauncing: if in Myrth, report
That I am ſodaine ſicke. Quicke, and returne.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Madam, me thinkes if you did loue him deerly,
You do not hold the method, to enforce
The like from him.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: What ſhould I do, I do not?

sp.speaker: Ch.
sp.p: In each thing giue him way, croſſe him in nothing.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Thou teacheſt like a foole: the way to loſe him.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Tempt him not ſo too farre. I wiſh forbeare,
In time we hate that which we often feare.
But heere comes Anthony.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: I am ſicke, and ſullen.

sp.speaker: An.
sp.p: I am ſorry to giue breathing to my purpoſe.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Helpe me away deere Charmian, I ſhall fall,
It cannot be thus long, the ſides of Nature
Will not ſuſtaine it.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Now my deereſt Queene.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Pray you ſtand farther from mee.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: What's the matter?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: I know by that ſame eye ther's ſome good news.
What ſayes the married woman you may goe?
Would ſhe had neuer giuen you leaue to come.
Let her not ſay 'tis I that keepe you heere,
I haue no power vpon you: Hers you are.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: The Gods beſt know.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Oh neuer was there Queene
So mightily betrayed: yet at the firſt
I ſaw the Treaſons planted.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Why ſhould I thinke you can be mine, & true,
(Though you in ſwearing ſhake the Throaned Gods)
Who haue beene falſe to Fuluia?
Riotous madneſſe,
To be entangled with thoſe mouth-made vowes,
Which breake themſelues in ſwearing.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Moſt ſweet Queene.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Nay pray you ſeeke no colour for your going,
But bid farewell, and goe:
When you ſued ſtaying,
Then was the time for words: No going then,
Eternity was in our Lippes, and Eyes,
Bliſſe in our browes bent: none our parts ſo poore,
But was a race of Heauen. They are ſo still,
Or thou the greateſt Souldier of the world,
Art turn'd the greateſt Lyar.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: How now Lady?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: I would I had thy inches, thou ſhould'ſt know
There were a heart in Egypt.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Heare me Queene:
The ſtrong neceſſity of Time, commands
Our Seruicles a-while: but my full heart
Remaines in vſe with you. Our Italy,
Shines o're with ciuill Swords; Sextus Pompeius
Makes his approaches to the Port of Rome,
Equality of two Domeſticke powers,
Breed ſcrupulous faction: The hated growne to ſtrength
Are newly growne to Loue: The condemn'd Pompey,
Rich in his Fathers Honor, creepes apace
Into the hearts of ſuch, as haue not thriued
Vpon the preſent ſtate, whoſe Numbers threaten,
And quietneſſe growne ſicke of reſt, would purge
By any deſperate change: My more particular,
And that which moſt with you ſhould ſafe my going,
Is Fuluias death.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Though age from folly could not giue me freedom
It does from childiſhneſſe. Can Fuluia dye?

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: She's dead my Queene.
Looke heere, and at thy Soueraigne leyſure read
The Garboyles ſhe awak'd: at the laſt, beſt,
See when, and where ſhee died.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: O moſt falſe Loue!
Where be the Sacred Violles thou ſhould'ſt fill
With ſorrowfull water? Now I ſee, I ſee,
In Fuluias death, how mine receiu'd ſhall be.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Quarrell no more, but bee prepar'd to know
The purpoſes I beare: which are, or ceaſe,
As you ſhall giue th' aduice. By the fire
That quickens Nylus ſlime, I go from hence
Thy Souldier, Seruant, making Peace or Warre,
As thou affects.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Cut my Lace, Charmian come,
But let it be, I am quickly ill, and well,
So Anthony loues.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: My precious Queene forbeare,
And giue true euidence to his Loue, which ſtands
An honourable Triall.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: So Fuluia told me.
I prythee turne aſide, and weepe for her,
Then bid adiew to me, and ſay the teares
Belong to Egypt. Good now, play one Scene
Of excellent diſſembling, and let it looke
Like perfect Honor.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: You'l heat my blood no more?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: You can do better yet: but this is meetly.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Now by Sword.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: And Target. Still he mends.
But this is not the beſt. Looke prythee Charmian,
How this Herculean Roman do's become
The carriage of his chafe.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Ile leaue you Lady.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Courteous Lord, one word:
Sir, you and I muſt part, but that's not it:
Sir, you and I haue lou'd, but there's not it:
That you know well, ſomething it is I would:
Oh, my Obliuion is a very Anthony,
And I am all forgotten.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: But that your Royalty
Holds Idleneſſe your ſubiect, I ſhould take you
For Idleneſſe it ſelfe.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: 'Tis ſweating Labour,
To beare ſuch Idleneſſe ſo neere the heart
As Cleopatra this. But Sir, forgiue me,
Since my becommings kill me, when they do not
Eye well to you. Your Honor calles you hence,
Therefore be deafe to my vnpittied Folly,
And all the Gods go with you. Vpon your Sword
Sit Lawrell victory, and ſmooth ſucceſſe
Be ſtrew'd before your feete.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Let vs go.
Come: Our ſeparation ſo abides and flies,
That thou reciding heere, goes yet with mee;
And I hence fleeting, heere remaine with thee.
Away.

div.stage: Enter Octauius reading a Letter, Lepidus, and their Traine.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: You may ſee Lepidus, and henceforth know,
It is not Caeſars Naturall vice, to hate
One great Competitor. From Alexandria
This is the newes: He fiſhes, drinkes, and waſtes
The Lampes of night in reuell: Is not more manlike
Then Cleopatra: nor the Queene of Ptolomy
More Womanly then he. Hardly gaue audience
Or vouchſafe to thinke he had Partners. You
Shall finde there a man, who is th' abſtracts of all faults,
That all men follow.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.l: I muſt not thinke
There are, euils enow to darken all his goodneſſe:
His faults in him, ſeeme as the Spots of Heauen,
More fierie by nights Blackneſſe; Hereditarie,
Rather then purchaſte: what he cannot change,
Then what he chooſes.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: You are too indulgent. Let's graunt it is not
Amiſſe to tumble on the bed of Ptolomy,
To giue a Kingdome for a Mirth, to ſit
And keepe the turne of Tipling with a Slaue,
To reele the ſtreets at noone, and ſtand the Buffet
With knaues that ſmels of ſweate: Say this becom • him
(As his compoſure muſt be rare indeed,
Whom theſe things cannot blemiſh) yet muſt Anthony
No way excuſe his foyles, when we do beare
So great waight in his lightneſſe. If he fill'd
His vacancie with his Voluptuouſneſſe,
Full ſurfets, and the drineſſe of his bones,
Call on him for't. But to confound ſuch time,
That drummes him from his ſport, and ſpeakes as lowd
As his owne State, and ours, 'tis to be chid:
As we rate Boyes, who being mature in knowledge,
Pawne their experience to their preſent pleaſure,
And ſo rebell to iudgement.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Heere's more newes.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: Thy biddings haue beene done, & euerie houre
Moſt Noble Caeſar, ſhalt thou haue report
How 'tis abroad. Pompey is ſtrong at Sea,
And it appeares, he is belou'd of thoſe
That only haue feard Caeſar: to the Ports
The diſcontents repaire, and mens reports
Giue him much wrong'd.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: I ſhould haue knowne no leſſe,
It hath bin taught vs from the primall ſtate
That he which is was wiſht, vntill he were:
And the ebb'd man,
Ne're lou'd, till ne're worth loue,
Comes fear'd, by being lack'd. This common bodie,
Like to a Vagabond Flagge vpon the Streame,
Goes too, and backe, lacking the varrying tyde
To rot it ſelfe with motion.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: Caeſar I bring thee word,
Menacrates and Menas famous Pyrates
Makes the Sea ſerue them, which they eare and wound
With keeles of euery kinde. Many hot inrodes
They make in Italy, the Borders Maritime
Lacke blood to thinke on't, and fluſh youth reuolt,
No Veſſell can peepe forth: but 'tis as ſoone
Taken as ſeene: for Pompeyes name ſtrikes more
Then could his Warre reſiſted.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.

l.hi: Anthony,

sp.l: Leaue thy laſciuious Vaſſailes. When thou once
Was beaten from Medena, where thou ſlew'ſt
Hirſius, and Pauſa Conſuls, at thy heele
Did Famine follow, whom thou fought'ſt againſt,
(Though daintily brought vp) with patience more
Then Sauages could ſuffer. Thou did'ſt drinke
The ſtale of Horſes, and the gilded Puddle
Which Beaſts would cough at. Thy pallat thē did daine
The rougheſt Berry, on the rudeſt Hedge.
Yea, like the Stagge, when Snow the Paſture ſheets,
The barkes of Trees thou brows'd. On the Alpes,
It is reported thou did'ſt eate ſtrange fleſh,
Which ſome did dye to looke on: And all this
(It wounds thine Honor that I ſpeake it now)
Was borne ſo like a Soldiour, that thy cheeke
So much as lank'd not.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: 'Tis pitty of him.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: Let his ſhames quickely
Driue him to Rome, 'tis time we twaine
Did ſhew our ſelues i' th' Field, and to that end▪
Aſſemble me immediate counſell, Pompey
Thriues in our Idleneſſe.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.l: To morrow Caeſar,
I ſhall be furniſht to informe you rightly
Both what by Sea and Land I can be able
To front this preſent time.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: Til which encounter, it is my buſines too. Farwell.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.l: Farwell my Lord, what you ſhal know mean time
Of ſtirres abroad, I ſhall beſeech you Sir
To let me be partaker.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.p: Doubt not ſir, I knew it for my Bond.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Ha, ha, giue me to drinke Mandragora.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Why Madam?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: That I might ſleepe out this great gap of time:
My Anthony is away.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: You thinke of him too much.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: O 'tis Treaſon.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Madam, I truſt not ſo.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Thou, Eunuch Mardian?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: What's your Highneſſe pleaſure?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Not now to heare thee ſing. I take no pleaſure
In ought an Eunuch ha's: Tis well for thee,
That being vnſeminar'd, thy freer thoughts
May not flye forth of Egypt. Haſt thou Affections?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Yes gracious Madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Indeed?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Not in deed Madam, for I can do nothing
But what in deede is honeſt to be done:
Yet haue I fierce Affections, and thinke
What Venus did with Mars.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Oh Charmion:
Where think'ſt thou he is now? Stands he, or ſits he?
Or does he walke? Or is he on his Horſe?
Oh happy horſe to beare the weight of Anthony!
Do brauely Horſe, for wot'ſt thou whom thou moou'ſt,
The demy Atlas of this Earth, the Arme
And Burganet of men. Hee's ſpeaking now,
Or murmuring, where's my Serpent of old Nyle▪
(For ſo he cals me:) Now I feede my ſelfe
With moſt delicious poyſon. Thinke on me
That am with Phoebus amorous pinches blacke,
And wrinkled deepe in time. Broad-fronted Caeſar,
When thou was't heere aboue the ground, I was
A morſell for a Monarke: and great Pompey
Would ſtand and make his eyes grow in my brow,
There would he anchor his Aspect, and dye
With looking on his life.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.p: Soueraigne of Egypt, haile.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: How much vnlike art thou Marke Anthony?
Yet comming from him, that great Med'cine hath
With his Tinct gilded thee.
How goes it with my braue Marke Anthonie?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: Laſt thing he did (deere Qu • ene)
He kiſt the laſt of many doubled kiſſes
This Orient Pearle. His ſpeech ſtickes in my heart.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Mine eare muſt plucke it thence.

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: Good Friend, quoth he:
Say the firme Roman to great Egypt ſends
This treaſure of an Oyſter: at whoſe foote
To mend the petty preſent, I will peece
Her opulent Throne, with Kingdomes. All the Eaſt,
(Say thou) ſhall call her Miſtris. So he nodded,
And ſoberly did mount an Arme-gaunt Steede,
Who neigh'd ſo hye, that what I would haue ſpoke,
Was beaſtly dumbe by him.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: What was he ſad, or merry?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: Like to the time o' th' yeare, between ye extremes
Of hot and cold, he was nor ſad▪ nor merrie.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Oh well diuided diſpoſition: Note him,
Note him good Charmian, 'tis the man; but note him.
He was not ſad, for he would ſhine on thoſe
That make their lookes by his. He was not merrie,
Which ſeem'd to tell them, his remembrance lay
In Egypt with his ioy, but betweene both.
Oh heauenly mingle! Bee'ſt thou ſad, or merrie,
The violence of either thee becomes,
So do's it no mans elſe. Met'ſt thou my Poſts?

sp.speaker: Alex.
sp.l: I Madam, twenty ſeuerall Meſſengers.
Why do you ſend ſo thicke?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Who's borne that day, when I forget to ſend to Anthonie, ſhall dye a Begger. Inke and paper Charmian. Welcome my good Alexas. Did I Charmian, euer loue Caeſar ſo?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Oh that braue Caeſar!

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Be choak'd with ſuch another Emphaſis,
Say the braue Anthony.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: The valiant Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: By Iſis, I will giue thee bloody teeth,
If thou with Caeſar Parago nagaine:
My man of men.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: By your moſt gracious pardon,
I ſing but after you.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: My Sallad dayes,
When I was greene in iudgement, cold in blood,
To ſay, as I ſaide then. But come, away,
Get me Inke and Paper,
he ſhall haue euery day a ſeuerall greeting, or Ile vnpeople Egypt.

div.stage: Enter Pompey, Menecrates, and Menas, in warlike manner.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.l: If the great Gods be iuſt, they ſhall aſſiſt
The deeds of iuſteſt men.

sp.speaker: Mene.
sp.p: Know worthy Pompey, that what they do delay, they not deny.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Whiles we are ſutors to their Throne, decayes the thing we ſue for.

sp.speaker: Mene.
sp.l: We ignorant of our ſelues,
Begge often our owne harmes, which the wiſe Powres
Deny vs for our good: ſo finde we profit
By looſing of our Prayers.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.l: I ſhall do well:
The people loue me, and the Sea is mine;
My powers are Creſſent, and my Auguring hope
Sayes it will come to' th' full. Marke Anthony
In Egypt ſits at dinner, and will make
No warres without doores. Caeſar gets money where
He looſes hearts: Lepidus flatters both,
Of both is flatter'd: but he neither loues,
Nor either cares for him.

sp.speaker: Mene.
sp.l: Caeſar and Lepidus are in the field,
A mighty ſtrength they carry.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.p: Where haue you this? 'Tis falſe.

sp.speaker: Mene.
sp.p: From Siluius, Sir.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.l: He dreames: I know they are in Rome together
Looking for Anthony: but all the charmes of Loue,
Salt Cleopatra ſoften thy wand lip,
Let Witchcraft ioyne with Beauty, Luſt with both,
Tye vp the Libertine in a field of Feaſts,
Keepe his Braine fuming. Epicurean Cookes,
Sharpen with cloyleſſe ſawce his Appetite,
That ſleepe and feeding may prorogue his Honour,
Euen till a Lethied dulneſſe—
How now Varrius?

sp.speaker: Var.
sp.l: This is moſt certaine, that I ſhall deliuer:
Marke Anthony is euery houre in Rome
Expected. Since he went from Egypt, 'tis
A ſpace for farther Trauaile.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.l: I could haue giuen leſſe matter
A better eare. Menas, I did not thinke
This amorous Surfetter would haue donn'd his Helme
For ſuch a petty Warre: His Souldierſhip
Is twice the other twaine: But let vs reare
The higher our Opinion, that our ſtirring
Can from the lap of Egypts Widdow, plucke
The neere Luſt-wearied Anthony.

sp.speaker: Mene.
sp.l: I cannot hope,
Caeſar and Anthony ſhall well greet together;
His Wife that's dead, did treſpaſſes to Caeſar,
His Brother wan'd vpon him, although I thinke
Not mou'd by Anthony.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.l: I know not Menas,
How leſſer Enmities may giue way to greater,
Were't not that we ſtand vp againſt them all:
'Twer pregnant they ſhould ſquare between themſelues,
For they haue entertained cauſe enough
To draw their ſwords: but how the feare of vs
May Ciment their diuiſions, and binde vp
The petty difference, we yet not know:
Bee't as our Gods will haue't; it onely ſtands
Our liues vpon, to vſe our ſtrongeſt hands
Come Menas.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.l: Good Enobarbus, 'tis a worthy deed,
And ſhall become you well, to intreat your Captaine
To ſoft and gentle ſpeech.

sp.speaker: Enob.
sp.l: I ſhall intreat him
To anſwer like himſelfe: if Caeſar moue him,
Let Anthony looke ouer Caeſars head,
And ſpeake as lowd as Mars. By Iupiter,
Were I the wearer of Anthonio's Beard,
I would not ſhaue't to day.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: 'Tis not a time for priuate ſtomacking.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Euery time ſerues for the matter that is then borne in't.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: But ſmall to greater matters muſt giue way.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Not if the ſmall come firſt.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.l: Your ſpeech is paſſion: but pray you ſtirre
No Embers vp. Heere comes the Noble Anthony.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: And yonder Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: If we compoſe well heere, to Parthia:
Hearke Ventidius.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.p: I do not know Mecenas, aske Agrippa.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.l: Noble Friends:
That which combin'd vs was moſt great, and let not
A leaner action rend vs. What's amiſſe,
May it be gently heard. When we debate
Our triuiall difference loud, we do commit
Murther in healing wounds. Then Noble Partners,
The rather for I earneſtly beſeech,
Touch you the ſowreſt points with ſweeteſt tearmes,
Nor curſtne • e grow to' th' matter.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: 'Tis ſpoken well:
Were we before our Armies, and to fight,
I ſhould do thus.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.p: Welcome to Rome.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: Thanke you.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.p: Sit.

sp.speaker: Ant,
sp.p: Sit ſir.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.p: Nay then.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I learne, you take things ill, which are not ſo:
Or being, concerne you not.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: I muſt be laught at, if or for nothing, or a little, I
Should ſay my ſelfe offended, and with you
Chiefely i' th' world. More laught at, that I ſhould
Once name you derogately: when to ſound your name
It not concern'd me.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: My being in Egypt Caeſar, what was't to you?

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: No more then my reciding heere at Rome
Might be to you in Egypt: yet if you there
Did practiſe on my State, your being in Egypt
Might be my queſtion.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: How intend you, practis'd?

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.l: You may be pleas'd to catch at mine intent,
By what did heere befall me. Your Wife and Brother
Made warres vpon me, and their conteſtation
Was Theame for you, you were the word of warre.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: You do miſtake your buſines, my Brother neuer
Did vrge me in his Act: I did inquire it,
And haue my Learning from ſome true reports
That drew their ſwords with you, did he not rather
Diſcredit my authority with yours,
And make the warres alike againſt my ſtomacke,
Hauing alike your cauſe. Of this, my Letters
Before did ſatisfie you. If you'l patch a quarrell,
As matter whole you haue to make it with,
It muſt not be with this.

sp.speaker: Caeſ.
sp.p: You praiſe your ſelfe, by laying defects of iudgement to me: but you patcht vp your excuſes.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.l: Not ſo, not ſo:
I know you could not lacke, I am certaine on't,
Very neceſſity of this thought, that I
Your Partner in the cauſe 'gainſt which he fought,
Could not with gracefull eyes attend thoſe Warres
Which fronted mine owne peace. As for my wife,
I would you had her ſpirit, in ſuch another,
The third oth' world is yours▪ which with a Snaffle,
You may pace eaſie, but not ſuch a wife.

sp.speaker: Enobar.
sp.p: Would we had all ſuch wiues, that the men might go to Warres with the women.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.l: So much vncurbable, her Garboiles (Caeſar)
Made out of her impatience: which not wanted
Shrodeneſſe of policie to: I greeuing grant,
Did you too much diſquiet, for that you muſt,
But ſay I could not helpe it?

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: I wrote to you, when rioting in Alexandria you
Did pocket vp my Letters: and with taunts
Did gibe my Miſi • e out of audience.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: Sir, he fell vpon me, ere admitted, then:
Three Kings I had newly feaſted, and did want
Of what I was i' th' morning: but next day
I told him of my ſelfe, which was as much
As to haue askt him pardon. Let this Fellow
Be nothing of our ſtrife: if we contend
Out of our queſtion wipe him.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.p: You haue broken the Article of your oath, which you ſhall neuer haue tongue to charge me with.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Soft Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: No Lepidus, let him ſpeake,
The Honour is Sacred which he talks on now,
Suppoſing that I lackt it: but on Caeſar,
The Article of my oath.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.p: To lend me Armes, and aide when I requir'd them, the which you both denied.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.l: Neglected rather:
And then when poyſoned houres had bound me vp
From mine owne knowledge, as neerely as I may,
Ile play the penitent to you. But mine honeſty,
Shall not make poore my greatneſſe, nor my power
Worke without it. Truth is, that Fuluia,
To haue me out of Egypt, made Warres heere,
For which my ſelfe, the ignorant motiue, do
So farre a • ke pardon, as befits mine Honour
To ſtoope in ſuch a caſe.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: 'Tis Noble ſpoken.

sp.speaker: Mece.
sp.l: If it might pleaſe you, to enforce no further
The griefes betweene ye: to forget them quite,
Were to remember: that the preſent neede,
Speakes to attone you.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Worthily ſpoken Mecenas.

sp.speaker: Enobar.
sp.p: Or if you borrow one anothers Loue for the inſtant, you may when you heare no more words of Pompey returne it againe: you ſhall haue time to wrangle in, when you haue nothing elſe to do.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: Thou art a Souldier, onely ſpeake no more.

sp.speaker: Enob.
sp.p: That trueth ſhould be ſilent, I had almoſt forgot.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: You wrong this preſence, therefore ſpeake no more.

sp.speaker: Enob.
sp.p: Go too then: your Conſiderate ſtone.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: I do not much diſlike the matter, but
The manner of his ſpeech: for't cannot be,
We ſhall remaine in friendſhip, our conditions
So diffring in their acts. Yet if I knew,
What Hoope ſhould hold vs ſtaunch from edge to edge
A th' world: I would perſue it.

sp.speaker: Agri.
sp.p: Giue me leaue Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.p: Speake Agrippa.

sp.speaker: Agri.
sp.l: Thou haſt a Siſter by the Mothers ſide, admir'd
Octauia. Great Mark Anthony is now a widdower.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.p: Say not, ſay Agrippa; if Cleopater heard you, your proofe were well deſerued of raſhneſſe.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: I am not marryed Caeſar: let me heere Agrippa further ſpeake.

sp.speaker: Agri.
sp.l: To hold you in perpetuall amitie,
To make you Brothers, and to knit your hearts
With an vn-ſlipping knot, take Anthony,
Octauia to his wife: whoſe beauty claimes
No worſe a husband then the beſt of men: whoſe
Vertue, and whoſe generall graces, ſpeake
That which none elſe can vtter. By this marriage,
All little Ielouſies which now ſeeme great,
And all great feares, which now import their dangers,
Would then be nothing. Truth's would be tales,
Where now halfe tales be truth's: her loue to both,
Would each to other, and all loues to both
Draw after her. Pardon what I haue ſpoke,
For 'tis a ſtudied not a preſent thought,
By duty ruminated.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: Will Caeſar ſpeake?

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Not till he heares how Anthony is toucht,
With what is ſpoke already.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.l: What power is in Agrippa,
If I would ſay Agrippa, be it ſo,
To make this good?

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: The power of Caeſar,
And his power, vnto Octauia.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.l: May I neuer
(To this good purpoſe, that ſo fairely ſhewes)
Dreame of impediment: let me haue thy hand
Further this act of Grace: and from this houre,
The heart of Brothers gouerne in our Loues,
And ſway our great Deſignes.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: There's my hand:
A Siſter I bequeath you, whom no Brother
Did euer loue ſo deerely. Let her liue
To ioyne our kingdomes, and our hearts, and neuer
Flie off our Loues againe.

sp.speaker: Lepi.
sp.p: Happily, Amen.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.l: I did not think to draw my Sword 'gainſt Pompey,
For he hath laid ſtrange courteſies, and great
Of late vpon me. I muſt thanke him onely,
Leaſt my remembrance, ſuffer ill report:
At heele of that, defie him.

sp.speaker: Lepi.
sp.l: Time cals vpon's,
Of vs muſt Pompey preſently be ſought,
Or elſe he ſeekes out vs.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: Where lies he?

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.p: About the Mount-Meſena.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: What is his ſtrength by land?

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: Great, and encreaſing:
But by Sea he is an abſolute Maſter.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.l: So is the Fame,
Would we had ſpoke together. Haſt we for it,
Yet ere we put our ſelues in Armes, diſpatch we
The buſineſſe we haue talkt of.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.l: With moſt gladneſſe,
And do inuite you to my Siſters view,
Whether ſtraight Ile lead you.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: Let vs Lepidus not lacke your companie.

sp.speaker: Lep.
sp.p: Noble Anthony, not ſickeneſſe ſhould detaine me.

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: Welcome from Aegypt Sir.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Halfe the heart of Caeſar, worthy Mecenas. My honourable Friend Agrippa.

sp.speaker: Agri.
sp.p: Good Enobarbus.

sp.speaker: Mece.
sp.p: We haue cauſe to be glad, that matters are ſo well diſgeſted: you ſtaid will by't in Egypt.

sp.speaker: Enob.
sp.p: I Sir, we did ſleepe day out of countenaunce: and made the night light with drinking.

sp.speaker: Mece.
sp.p: Eight Wilde-Boares roſted whole at a breakfaſt: and but twelue perſons there. Is this true?

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: This was but as a Flye by an Eagle: we had much more monſtrous matter of Feaſt, which worthily deſerued noting.

sp.speaker: Mecenas.
sp.p: She's a moſt triumphant Lady, if report be ſquare to her.

sp.speaker: Enob.
sp.p: When ſhe firſt met Marke Anthony, ſhe purſt vp his heart vpon the Riuer of Sidnis.

sp.speaker: Agri.
sp.p: There ſhe appear'd indeed: or my reporter deuis'd well for her.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.l: I will tell you,
The Barge ſhe ſat in, like a burniſht Throne
Burnt on the water: the Poope was beaten Gold,
Purple the Sailes: and ſo perfumed that
The Windes were Loue-ſicke.
With them the Owers were Siluer,
Which to the tune of Flutes kept ſtroke, and made
The water which they beate, to follow faſter;
As amorous of their ſtrokes. For her owne perſon,
It beggerd all diſcription, ſhe did lye
In her Pauillion, cloth of Gold, of Tiſſue,
O're-picturing that Venns, where we ſee
The fancie out-worke Nature. On each ſide her,
Stood pretty Dimpled Boyes, like ſmiling Cupids,
With diuers coulour'd Fannes whoſe winde did ſeeme,
To gloue the delicate cheekes which they did coole,
And what they vndid did.

sp.speaker: Agrip.
sp.p: Oh rare for Anthony.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.l: Her Gentlewoman, like the Nereides,
So many Mer-maides tended her i' th' eyes,
And made their bends adornings. At the Helme.
A ſeeming Mer-maide ſteeres: The Silken Tackle,
Swell with the touches of thoſe Flower-ſoft hands,
That yarely frame the office. From the Barge
A ſtrange inuiſible perfume hits the ſenſe
Of the adiacent Wharfes. The Citty caſt
Her people out vpon her: and Anthony
Enthron'd i' th' Market-place, did ſit alone,
Whiſling to' th' ayre: which but for vacancie,
Had gone to gaze on Cleopater too,
And made a gap in Nature.

sp.speaker: Agri.
sp.p: Rare Egiptian.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.l: Vpon her landing, Anthony ſent to her,
Inuited her to Supper: ſhe replyed,
It ſhould be better, he became her gueſt:
Which ſhe entreated, our Courteous Anthony,
Whom nere the word of no woman hard ſpeake,
Being barber'd ten times o're, goes to the Feaſt;
And for his ordinary, paies his heart,
For what his eyes eate onely.

sp.speaker: Agri.
sp.l: Royall Wench:
She made great Caeſar lay his Sword to bed,
He ploughed her, and ſhe cropt.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.l: I ſaw her once
Hop forty Paces through the publicke ſtreete.
And hauing loſt her breath, ſhe ſpoke, and panted,
That ſhe did make defect, perfection▪
And breathleſſe powre breath forth.

sp.speaker: Mece.
sp.p: Now Anthony, muſt leaue her vtterly.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.l: Neuer he will not:
Age cannot wither her, nor cuſtome ſtale
Her infinite variety: other women cloy
The appetites they feede, but ſhe makes hungry,
Where moſt ſhe ſatisfies. For vildeſt things
Become themſelues in her, that the holy Prieſts
Bleſſe her, when ſhe is Riggiſh.

sp.speaker: Mece
sp.l: If Beauty, Wiſedome, Modeſty, can ſettle
The heart of Anthony: Octauia is
A bleſſed Lottery to him.

sp.speaker: Agrip.
sp.p: Let vs go. Good Enobarbus, make your ſelfe my gueſt, whilſt you abide heere.

sp.speaker: Eno.
sp.p: Humbly Sir I thanke you.

div.stage: Enter Anthony, Caeſar, Octauia betweene them.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.l: The world, and my great office, will
Sometimes deuide me from your boſome.

sp.speaker: Octa.
sp.p: All which time, before the Gods my knee ſhall bowe my ptayers to them for you.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.l: Goodnight Sir. My Octauia
Read not my blemiſhes in the worlds report:
I haue not kept my ſquare, but that to come
Shall all be done by th' Rule: good night deere Lady:
Good night Sir.

sp.speaker: Caeſar.
sp.p: Goodnight.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: Now ſirrah: you do wiſh your ſelfe in Egypt?

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.p: Would I had neuer come from thence, nor you thither.

sp.speaker: Ant.
sp.p: If you can, your reaſon?

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.l: I ſee it in my motion: haue it not in my tongue,
But yet hie you to Egypt againe.

sp.speaker: Antho.
sp.p: Say to me, whoſe Fortunes ſhall riſe higher Caeſars or mine?

sp.l: Caeſars, Therefore (oh Anthony) ſtay not by his ſide
Thy Daemon that thy ſpirit which keepes thee, is
Noble, Couragious, high vnmatchable,
Where Caeſars is not. But neere him, • hy Angell
Becomes a feare: as being o're-powr'd, therefore
Make ſpace enough betweene you.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.p: Speake this no more.

sp.speaker: Sooth.
sp.l: To none but thee no more but: when to thee,
If thou doſt play with him at any game,
Thou art ſure to looſe: And of that Naturall lucke▪
He beats thee 'gainſt the oddes. Thy Luſter thickens,
When he ſhines by: I ſay againe, thy ſpirit
Is all affraid to gouerne thee neere him:
But he alway 'tis Noble.

sp.speaker: Anth.
sp.l: Get thee gone:
Say to Ventigius I would ſpeake with him.
He ſhall to Parthia, be it Art or hap,
He hath ſpoken true. The very Dice obey him,
And in our ſports my better cunning faints,
Vnder his chance, if we draw lots he ſpeeds,
His Cocks do winne the Battaile, ſtill of mine,
When it is all to naught: and his Quailes euer
And though I make this marriage for my peace,
I' th' Eaſt my pleaſure lies. Oh come Ventigius.
You muſt to Parthia, your Commiſſions ready:
Follow me, and reciue't.

sp.speaker: Lepidus.
sp.p: Trouble your ſelues no further: pray you haſten your Generals after.

sp.speaker: Agr.
sp.p: Sir▪ Marke Anthony, will e'ne but kiſſe Octauia, and weele follow.

sp.speaker: Lepi.
sp.l: Till I ſhall ſee you in your Souldiers dreſſe,
Which will become you both: Farewell.

sp.speaker: Mece.
sp.p: We ſhall: as I conceiue the iourney, be at Mount before you Lepidus.

sp.speaker: Lepi.
sp.p: Your way is ſhorter, my purpoſes do draw me much about, you'le win two dayes vpon me.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: Sir good ſucceſſe.

sp.speaker: Lepi.
sp.p: Farewell.

div.stage: Enter Cleopater, Charmian, Iras, and Alexas.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Giue me ſome Muſicke: Muſicke, moody foode of vs that trade in Loue.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: The Muſicke, hoa.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Let it alone, let's to Billards: come Charmian.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: My arme is ſore, beſt play with Mardian.

sp.speaker: Cleopa.
sp.p: As well a woman with an Eunuch plaide, as with a woman. Come you'le play with me Sir?

sp.speaker: Mardi.
sp.p: As well as I can Madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: And when good will is ſhewed,
Though't come to ſhort
The Actor may pleade pardon. Ile none now,
Giue me mine Angle, weele to' th' Riuer there
My Muſicke playing farre off. I will betray
Tawny fine fiſhes, my bended hooke ſhall pierce
Their ſlimy iawes: and as I draw them vp,
Ile thinke them euery one an Anthony,
And ſay, ah ha; y' are caught.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: 'Twas merry when you wager'd on your Angling, when your diuer did hang a ſalt fiſh on his hooke which he with feruencie drew vp.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: That time? Oh times:
I laught him out of patience: and that night
I laught him into patience, and next morne,
Ere the ninth houre, I drunke him to his bed:
Then put my Tires and Mantles on him, whilſt
I wore his Sword Phillippan. Oh from Italie,
Ramme thou thy fruitefull tidings in mine eares,
That long time haue bin barren.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Madam, Madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Anthonyo's dead.
If thou ſay ſo Villaine, thou kil'ſt thy Miſtris:
But well and free, if thou ſo yeild him.
There is Gold, and heere
My bleweſt vaines to kiſſe: a hand that Kings
Haue lipt, and trembled kiſſing.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Firſt Madam, he is well.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Why there's more Gold.
But ſirrah marke, we vſe
To ſay, the dead are well: bring it to that,
The Gold I giue thee, will I melt and powr
Downe thy ill vttering throate.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Good Madam heare me.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Well, go too I will:
But there's no goodneſſe in thy face if Anthony
Be free and healthfull; ſo tart a fauour
To trumpet ſuch good tidings. If not well,
Thou ſhouldſt come like a Furie crown'd with Snakes,
Not like a formall man.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Wilt pleaſe you heare me?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: I haue a mind to ſtrike thee ere thou ſpeak'ſt:
Yet if thou ſay Anthony liues, 'tis well,
Or friends with Caeſar, or not Captiue to him,
Ile ſet thee in a ſhower of Gold, and haile
Rich Pearles vpon thee.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Madam, he's well.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Well ſaid.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: And Friends with Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Th' art an honeſt man.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Caeſar, and he, are greater Friends then euer.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Make thee a Fortune from me.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: But yet Madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: I do not like but yet, it does alay
The good precedence, fie vpon but yet,
Bur yet is as a Iaylor to bring foorth
Some monſtrous Malefactor. Prythee Friend,
Powre out the packe of matter to mine eare,
The good and bad together: he's friends with Caeſar,
In ſtate of health thou ſaiſt, and thou ſaiſt, free.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: Free Madam, no: I made no ſuch report,
He's bound vnto Octauia.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: For what good turne?

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: For the beſt turne i' th' bed.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: I am pale Charmian.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Madam, he's married to Octauia.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: The moſt infectious Peſtilence vpon thee.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Good Madam patience.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: What ſay you?

Hence horrible Villaine, o •
• le ſpurne thine eyes
Like balls before me: Ile vnhaire thy head,
sp.stage: She hales him vp and downe.
sp.l: Thou ſhalt be whipt with Wyer, and ſtew'd in brine,
Smarting in lingring pickle.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: Gratious Madam,
I that do bring the newes, made not the match.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Say 'tis not ſo, a Prouince I will giue thee,
And make thy Fortunes proud: the blow thou had'ſt
Shall make thy peace, for mouing me to rage,
And I will boot thee with what guift beſide
Thy modeſtie can begge.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: He's married Madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: Rogue, thou haſt liu'd too long.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: Nay then Ile runne:
What meane you Madam, I haue made no fault.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.l: Good Madam keepe your ſelfe within your ſelfe,
The man is innocent.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Some Innocents ſcape not the thunderbolt:
Melt Egypt into Nyle: and kindly creatures
Turne all to Serpents. Call the ſlaue againe,
Though I am mad, I will not byte him: Call?

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: He is afeard to come.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: I will not hurt him,
Theſe hands do lacke Nobility, that they ſtrike
A meaner then my ſelfe: ſince I my ſelfe
Haue giuen my ſelfe the cauſe. Come hither Sir.
Though it be honeſt, it is neuer good
To bring bad newes: giue to a gratious Meſſage
An hoſt of tongues, but let ill tydings tell
Themſelues, when they be felt.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: I haue done my duty.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Is he married?
I cannot hate thee worſer then I do,
If thou againe ſay yes.

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: He's married Madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: The Gods confound thee,
Doſt thou hold there ſtill?

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: Should I lye Madame?

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Oh, I would thou didſt:
So halfe my Egypt were ſubmerg'd and made
A Ceſterne for ſcal'd Snakes. Go get thee hence,
Had'ſt thou Narciſſus in thy face to me,
Thou would'ſt appeere moſt vgly: He is married?

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.p: I craue your Highneſſe pardon.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: He is married?

sp.speaker: Meſ.
sp.l: Take no offence, that I would not offend you,
To punniſh me for what you make me do
Seemes much vnequall, he's married to Octauia.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: Oh that his fault ſhould make a knaue of thee,
That art not what th' art ſure of. Get thee hence,
The Marchandize which thou haſt brought from Rome
Are all too deere for me:
Lye they vpon thy hand, and be vndone by em.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Good your Highneſſe patience.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.p: In prayſing Anthony, I haue diſprais'd Caeſar.

sp.speaker: Char.
sp.p: Many times Madam.

sp.speaker: Cleo.
sp.l: I am paid for't now: lead me from hence,
I faint, oh Iras, Charmian: 'tis no matter.
Go to the Fellow, good Alexas bid him
Report the feature of Octauia: her yeares,
Her inclination, let him not leaue out
The colour of her haire. Bring me word quickly,
Let him for euer go, let him not Charmian,
Though he be painted one way like a Gorgon,
The other wayes a Mars. Bid you Alexas
Bring me word, how tall ſhe is: pitty me Charmian,
But do not ſpeake to me. Lead me to my Chamber.

div.stage: Flouriſh. Enter Pompey, at one doore with Drum and Trumpet: at another Caeſar, Lepidus, Anthony, Enobarbus, Mecenas, Agrippa, Menas with Souldiers Marching.

sp.speaker: Pom.
sp.l: Your Hoſtages I haue, ſo haue you mine:
